The numerical answer 44 is supported by these per-assignment weights, rather than by assuming the successive subtractions remove disjoint groups. Try two counts Exercise 1. Compute D₄ using the intersection ledger, naming the count of assignments that fix each chosen k-person set. Hint for exercise 1 The intersection for a specified k-set has (4−k)! assignments; there are C(4,k) such sets. Full solution to exercise 1 The terms are k=0: 4!=24; k=1: −C(4,1)3!=−24; k=2: +C(4,2)2!=+12; k=3: −C(4,3)1!=−4; k=4: +C(4,4)0!=+1. Their sum is 9. Exercise 2. Explain why fixing two named people in a five-person exchange leaves 3! assignments, and why this does not yet count derangements. Hint for exercise 2 Once two matches are required, how many gifts and recipients remain? Can any of those remaining people still receive their own gift? Full solution to exercise 2 After the two specified people take their own gifts, three people and three gifts remain, giving 3!=6 unconstrained assignments. Some of those six contain additional fixed points. Thus six is an intersection size used within inclusion–exclusion, not a derangement count. The later signed terms correct these additional overlaps. What to carry forward Derangements count permutations avoiding all named self-matches. Inclusion–exclusion works because an assignment with t violations has signed weight (1−1)^t, zero unless it has no violation. The resulting finite sum is exact and includes small boundary cases. Before adapting it to another exchange rule, verify that each forbidden event and every intersection have the stated sizes. Continue with Counting overlaps only once when you want to compare this count with a neighboring model.

title: A recurrence remembers its past
summary: Derive Fibonacci recurrence from last-step cases.
text: A staircase can be climbed in one- or two-step moves. A stair has five risers. A climb can be 1+1+1+1+1, 2+2+1, 1+2+2, and several others. How many move sequences reach the top exactly? The order of moves matters: 1+2+2 and 2+1+2 describe different paths through intermediate positions. Rather than list all paths for every height, classify a path by its final move. The final move must be one step from the previous riser or two steps from the riser before that. Prerequisite capsule. A recurrence defines later values from earlier ones. It requires initial values: a rule such as aₙ=aₙ₋₁+aₙ₋₂ alone does not determine a sequence. An addition principle says that if a collection splits into disjoint cases, its size is the sum of their sizes. We will count paths up a staircase, where each move is exactly one or two steps. Count a concrete case Worked example. Let aₙ count allowed move sequences that climb exactly n risers. For n=0, the empty sequence does the job once, so a₀=1. For n=1, only the single one-step move works, so a₁=1. For n≥2, paths ending in 1 correspond uniquely to paths up n−1 risers: remove or append that final 1. Similarly, paths ending in 2 correspond uniquely to paths up n−2 risers. The two classes are disjoint because their last moves differ and exhaustive because no other move is allowed. Thus aₙ=aₙ₋₁+aₙ₋₂. The values are 1,1,2,3,5,8 for n=0 through 5, so there are eight ways up five risers. Listing the five-riser paths gives 11111, 1112, 1121, 1211, 2111, 122, 212, 221. The exact rule and its proof a 0 = 1 , a 1 = 1 , a n = a n − 1 + a n − 2 Staircase recurrence. Under the stated move rules, the displayed initial conditions and equation hold for every integer n≥2. The remove-last-move correspondence above is a bijective proof: each shorter path produces one distinct longer path in its case, and every longer path is recovered from exactly one shorter path. No experiment on the first five heights proves the recurrence; the last-move classification works for arbitrary n. These are Fibonacci numbers with a shifted index if the familiar convention sets F₀=0 and F₁=1: aₙ=Fₙ₊₁. The index shift matters, especially at n=0. The recurrence is a counting model of legal stair paths, not a literal population model of rabbits. Where the rule fails. If a climb may include a three-step move, aₙ₋₁+aₙ₋₂ misses all paths ending in 3. At n=3, the original rule gives three paths—111,12,21—while the expanded rule has a fourth path, 3. A recurrence is valid only when its cases exhaust the allowed objects. Likewise, setting a₀=0 because “no steps means no climb” deletes the empty sequence and breaks later counts: the single two-step climb needs a path of length zero before appending its move. Worked example: counting the paths that use two long moves Among climbs of five risers using moves 1 or 2, how many use exactly two moves of size 2? The two long moves contribute four risers, so one move of size 1 supplies the remaining riser. Thus there are three moves in total. Choosing which of their three positions holds the 1 gives 122, 212, and 221: three paths. The other five paths have either no 2, giving 11111, or one 2 together with three 1s. In the latter case there are four possible positions for the 2. The total is therefore 1 + 4 + 3 = 8, agreeing with the recurrence. This second classification sorts by number of long moves rather than final move. Both count the same legal sequences; their agreement helps check our interpretation of order and exact arrival at the top. Try two counts Exercise 1. Count paths up six risers and explain the split by final move rather than merely reading a sequence. Hint for exercise 1 Use the proved counts for heights five and four. What are their values? Full solution to exercise 1 The paths ending with a 1 are in bijection with the eight paths up five risers; those ending with a 2 are in bijection with the five paths up four risers. These disjoint groups total a₆=8+5=13. Exercise 2. Suppose moves of one or three risers are allowed instead. State initial values a₀,a₁,a₂,a₃ and the recurrence for n≥3. Hint for exercise 2 List short paths, including the empty path. For a general long path, remove its last 1 or its last 3. Full solution to exercise 2 There is one empty path, one way to climb one riser (1), one way to climb two (11), and two ways to climb three (111 or 3). Hence a₀=1,a₁=1,a₂=1,a₃=2. For n≥3, deleting the last allowed move gives aₙ=aₙ₋₁+aₙ₋₃. At n=3 this yields a₂+a₀=1+1=2, consistent with the list. What to carry forward A recurrence is a compressed count supported by a disjoint decomposition and sufficient initial values. The staircase model shows how to prove the rule with remove-and-append bijections. When rules change, redo the case split and inspect the empty case. The first computed terms are useful checks, but the arbitrary-height correspondence is the proof. Continue with A doorway into Pascal's triangle when you want to compare this count with a neighboring model.

title: A polynomial is a counting machine
summary: Read coefficients of a generating function as counts of choices.
text: A bag of coins can be encoded by multiplying short polynomials. Suppose a box holds one token marked 1, one marked 2 and one marked 3. You may take or leave each token. How many selections have total mark 3? The two selections are {3} and {1,2}. The polynomial (1+x)(1+x²)(1+x³) records every selection: choose 1 from a factor when its token is left, and choose its x-power when taken. The exponent of the resulting term is the selected total. Different selections can produce the same exponent, which makes the coefficient count them. Prerequisite capsule. For a polynomial P(x), the notation [xᵏ]P(x) means the coefficient multiplying xᵏ after like terms are collected. We treat x as a bookkeeping symbol, not a numerical amount of money. Multiplying polynomials uses the distributive rule: choose one term from each factor, multiply the chosen terms, then add contributions with equal powers. A finite product therefore encodes a finite collection of choices without any convergence questions. Count a concrete case Worked example. First multiply (1+x)(1+x²)=1+x+x²+x³. Multiplying by (1+x³) gives 1+x+x²+2x³+x⁴+x⁵+x⁶. The coefficient 2 at x³ is a ledger of two choices: x³ from the third factor with 1 from the others, or x·x² from the first two factors with 1 from the third. The coefficient at x⁴ is one, for {1,3}; at x⁰ it is one, for taking no tokens. The sum of all coefficients is 8, also found by evaluating the polynomial at x=1: each of three binary choices doubles the number of subsets. This is an audit of the encoding, not a new assumption. The exact rule and its proof number of subsets with weight k = [ x k ] ∏ i = 1 r ( 1 + x w i ) Finite subset generating function. For r individually distinguishable tokens with nonnegative integer weights w₁,…,wᵣ, the displayed coefficient counts subsets whose weights sum to k. Proof: expanding the product chooses one of two terms from each factor, so each choice sequence corresponds to exactly one subset. Multiplying selected terms adds exponents, producing x to the total weight. Polynomial addition then collects one contribution per subset of that total. This is a complete finite-product argument; no infinite power series or analytic convergence is required. If two distinct tokens have the same weight, keep both factors: (1+x)²=1+2x+x² counts two different one-token selections. If the tokens are indistinguishable, that interpretation changes and the coefficient two is inappropriate. Where the rule fails. A tempting error is to read the exponent as the number of selected tokens when weights differ. In (1+x)(1+x²)(1+x³), the term x³ can arise from one token or two; it records total weight, not subset size. If negative weights are admitted, ordinary polynomials in nonnegative powers no longer cover every product term, so the stated model needs adjustment. If unlimited copies of a token are permitted, a factor 1+xʷ captures only zero or one copy; the allowed multiplicities must appear explicitly, perhaps as a finite longer factor. Worked example: a zero-weight token still makes a choice Take three distinguishable tokens with weights 0, 1, and 2. Their polynomial is (1 + x⁰)(1 + x)(1 + x²) = 2(1 + x)(1 + x²). The coefficient of x² is 2. The two subsets of total weight 2 are the weight-2 token alone and that token together with the weight-0 token. Their numerical totals agree, but the subsets differ. Replacing the first factor by 1 would lose the choice to take the zero-weight token. Conversely, evaluating the complete product at x = 1 gives 8, the full count of subsets of three distinguishable tokens. The theorem allows nonnegative weights, including zero, because its expansion argument tracks selections rather than requiring every selected item to raise the total. It is the coefficient that records multiplicity when different choices share one weight. Try two counts Exercise 1. Expand (1+x²)(1+x³)(1+x⁴) only as far as needed to count subsets with weight 5. Name the contributing selections. Hint for exercise 1 Find pairs or singletons among weights 2,3,4 that sum to 5. Each token can be used once. Full solution to exercise 1 Only the pair {2,3} totals 5. In the product this is x²·x³·1=x⁵, and no other selection gives x⁵, so [x⁵] of the product is 1. A singleton has weight 2,3 or 4; the other pairs total 6 or 7, and all three total 9. Exercise 2. Two separately labeled red tokens each have weight 1. Write the polynomial and interpret its coefficient of x. Then say what changes if the tokens are truly indistinguishable. Hint for exercise 2 Use one factor per labeled token. Ask whether selecting the first token differs from selecting the second. Full solution to exercise 2 For labeled tokens, (1+x)(1+x)=1+2x+x², so two one-token subsets produce coefficient 2. If the tokens are indistinguishable, choosing one red token has just one visible outcome. The appropriate inventory polynomial is 1+x+x², with coefficient 1 at x. The distinction is about what counts as a distinct selection, not about algebra failing. What to carry forward A finite generating polynomial translates choices into exponents and counts into coefficients. Its proof is a term-by-term correspondence between subsets and product expansion terms. Specify whether tokens are distinct, how many copies are permitted, and what the exponent measures. Then coefficients provide an exact count, while a small explicit list checks the interpretation. Continue with A recurrence remembers its past when you want to compare this count with a neighboring model.

title: Distributing identical treats
summary: Derive weak compositions with bars and stars.
text: How many ways to split identical pastries among friends? Three friends split four identical biscuits. One may receive none. How many allocations exist? A list such as (2,0,2) gives the three shares, but listing every nonnegative triple is tedious. Encode the biscuits as four stars and separate the three friends' portions with two bars. For example, **||** means shares (2,0,2): two stars before the first bar, none between bars, and two after the second. Each allocation becomes a short string. Prerequisite capsule. A weak composition of n into k parts is an ordered list (x₁,…,xₖ) of nonnegative integers with sum n. Here the parts are named recipients, so (2,0,1) differs from (1,0,2). The n items being distributed are identical, meaning we care only how many each person gets. C(a,b) counts b-element subsets of an a-element set; for this lesson n≥0 and k≥1. Count a concrete case Worked example. Four stars and two identical bars occupy six positions. Choosing the two bar positions determines the entire pattern, so there are C(6,2)=15 allocations. Adjacent bars encode a zero share; a bar at the beginning or end also permits zero. The all-to-first allocation (4,0,0) is ****||, while the all-to-second allocation (0,4,0) is |****|. For a smaller audit, two identical biscuits and three recipients give C(4,2)=6 solutions: (2,0,0),(0,2,0),(0,0,2),(1,1,0),(1,0,1),(0,1,1). Six bar-and-star strings encode those six triples exactly once. The order of recipients is fixed by their names; only the biscuits are indistinguishable. The exact rule and its proof # { ( x 1 , … , x k ) : ∑ i x i = n , x i ∈ ℤ ≥ 0 } = ( n + k − 1 k − 1 ) Stars-and-bars theorem. For nonnegative n and positive k, the displayed count is exact. Map each allocation to a string of n stars and k−1 bars: write x₁ stars, a bar, x₂ stars, and continue, ending with xₖ stars. The reverse map reads the number of stars in each segment. These maps undo each other, so this is a bijection, not just a suggestive picture. There are n+k−1 total positions and choosing which k−1 positions hold bars uniquely determines a string. For n=0, all positions hold bars and there is exactly one all-zero allocation; the formula gives C(k−1,k−1)=1. For k=1, no bars are needed and the sole allocation gives all n items to the one recipient. The proof assumes unbounded shares; upper limits require extra work. Where the rule fails. If the four biscuits are individually decorated and their identities matter, 15 is wrong. Each biscuit then has three possible recipients, yielding 3⁴=81 assignments. Stars and bars forgets which biscuit is which. Likewise, if every friend must receive at least one biscuit, strings with adjacent or boundary bars must be excluded. Subtract one biscuit per friend first: for four biscuits and three friends, the remaining one biscuit has three possible destinations, so there are only three positive-share allocations. Worked example: reserving an unequal minimum Split eight identical biscuits among named friends A,B,C, requiring A to receive at least two and B at least one, with no minimum for C. Set A's share to 2 + u , B's to 1 + v , and C's to w . The conditions become u , v , w ≥ 0 and u + v + w = 5. Thus five stars and two bars give C(7,2) = 21 allocations. The substitution is reversible: add the reserved biscuits back to recover one admissible original allocation. For example, residual shares (0,2,3) produce (2,3,3). No two residual triples produce the same original triple, and every original triple can have the prescribed reserves removed. This verifies that the new count solves the original constrained question, rather than merely a similar-looking equation. An upper limit would need additional restrictions; subtracting minima handles lower bounds only. Try two counts Exercise 1. Find the number of nonnegative solutions to x+y+z=5. Show the string length and number of bars. Hint for exercise 1 There are five stars and two bars. Count the choices of bar positions among all positions. Full solution to exercise 1 The encoding uses five stars and two bars, hence seven positions. Selecting two bar positions gives C(7,2)=21 solutions. For instance, **|***| represents (2,3,0). The bijection ensures no solution is omitted or duplicated. Exercise 2. Count positive integer solutions to a+b+c=7, explaining why you may apply a nonnegative formula after a change of variables. Hint for exercise 2 Give one unit to each variable, then count the distribution of the remaining units. Full solution to exercise 2 Set a=1+a′, b=1+b′, c=1+c′ with a′,b′,c′≥0. The new sum is a′+b′+c′=4. Stars and bars counts C(4+3−1,3−1)=C(6,2)=15 solutions. The substitution is reversible, so all positive solutions are counted once. What to carry forward Stars and bars is a bijection between nonnegative named shares of identical items and strings of stars separated by bars. Its boundary cases explain why zero shares are allowed. Before using C(n+k−1,k−1), check that recipients are distinct, items are indistinguishable, and no share has a hidden upper bound. Those assumptions determine whether the encoding preserves the outcomes you actually want to count. Continue with Choosing without caring about order when you want to compare this count with a neighboring model.

title: What squaring does to a square grid
summary: Use Cartesian and polar forms to track the square map, its paired inputs and its exceptional point.
text: A square grid under a square Take every point of a drawn grid and replace its complex coordinate z by z². Straight grid lines curve, two points often land together, and one point behaves exceptionally. We can predict all three effects without trusting a picture. Background capsule. Write z=x+iy, with real x,y and i²=−1. Its modulus is |z|=√(x²+y²). For nonzero z, polar form is z=r(cos θ+i sin θ), where r=|z| and θ is an angle measured modulo 2π. Multiplying nonzero complex numbers multiplies lengths and adds angles. The origin has modulus zero and no angle. Track four points and one line Worked example. Square 1+i: (1+i)²=1+2i−1=2i. Square −1−i and obtain the same 2i. Squaring 1−i gives −2i; squaring 2+i gives 3+4i. The pairs ±z coincide because (−z)²=z². More precisely, if z²=w² then (z−w)(z+w)=0. Complex numbers have no zero divisors, so w=z or w=−z. Conversely, any nonzero output s(cos φ+i sin φ) has inputs √s at angles φ/2 and φ/2+π. Thus the map is exactly two-to-one onto the nonzero plane. For a vertical grid line x=c, set z=c+iy. Its image is (c²−y²)+2ci. If c≠0 and image coordinates are U,V, then y=V/(2c), giving U=c²−V²/(4c²), a left-opening parabola. If c=0, the whole imaginary axis maps to the nonpositive real axis, traversed twice. This degenerate line shows why the center deserves separate attention. Exact point pairs under squaring Input z Output z² Paired input 1+i 2i −1−i 1−i −2i −1+i 2+i 3+4i −2−i Compare two different notions of size. For a fixed multiplier w, distances between outputs scale by |w|. In squaring, however, the multiplier is the input itself. The points 1 and 2 are one unit apart, while their squares 1 and 4 are three units apart; the points −1 and 1 are two units apart but have identical squares. The local derivative at a chosen point describes small nearby differences, while these finite comparisons expose the map's changing scale and global folding. Neither a constant global stretch factor nor a global inverse follows from local angle preservation. Double the angle, square the radius Distributing (x+iy)² gives x²−y²+2xyi. The polar rule gives a second, equivalent statement for r>0: ( r e i θ ) 2 = r 2 e 2 i θ Here e iθ abbreviates cos θ+i sin θ; the formula follows from the angle-addition identities, so it does not require an unproved exponential theory. The radius r becomes r². A point at θ and one at θ+π both land at angle 2θ modulo 2π. Local angle claim. At a nonzero input z, a small displacement h changes the output by (z+h)²−z²=2zh+h². Divide by h: the complex derivative is 2z. Multiplication by nonzero 2z rotates and scales small displacements. The remaining term h² is of smaller order than h because |h²|/|h|=|h|→0. This proves the first-order shape claim at each z≠0; it does not say finite grid cells remain exact squares or that a globally chosen inverse exists. At z=0 the derivative is zero. Every first-order displacement collapses there, so the local angle argument cannot use a nonzero rotation. Curves passing through zero can meet differently after mapping. The map is still differentiable at zero, but “conformal” in the angle-preserving local sense requires a nonzero derivative. There is no contradiction between differentiability and failure of this stronger condition. Calculate and challenge the picture 1. Calculate. Find the two solutions of z²=−3+4i and verify both in Cartesian form. Hint for 1 Try a+bi with a²−b²=−3 and 2ab=4. Small integers work. Worked solution for 1 Take a=1 and b=2: a²−b²=1−4=−3 and 2ab=4. Thus (1+2i)²=−3+4i. The other solution is −1−2i. The factorization argument proves there are no further solutions. 2. Explain. A sketch seems to show squaring preserves angles everywhere because it maps rays to rays. Find the flaw at zero and state a correct version. Hint for 2 Test the two rays with angles 0 and π/2, then compare their images. Worked solution for 2 At zero the positive real ray and positive imaginary ray meet at a right angle; their images are respectively the positive and negative real rays, which meet at a straight angle. The correct local statement applies at a point z≠0: its derivative 2z is a nonzero rotation and scale. The special point zero cannot be included. What this map really promises Squaring doubles angle and squares radius, while pairing z with −z. It preserves infinitesimal angles away from zero but folds the entire plane. In particular, a global square-root choice requires a domain restriction; the logarithm has a related branch problem. A finite drawing can suggest these facts, while the algebra supplies the exhaustive two-to-one claim.

title: A derivative must agree from every direction
summary: Contrast an all-direction derivative proof for z² with the failed derivative of conjugation.
text: One quotient, every possible approach A derivative of a real function checks steps from two sides of a line. For a complex function, the step h can approach zero along any path in a plane. A proposed answer must survive all such approaches. This extra demand explains why familiar real operations, such as reflection across the real axis, can fail complex differentiability. Background capsule. For z=x+iy, conjugation is z̄=x−iy, and |z|=√(x²+y²). A limit L of a complex quantity Q(h) as h→0 means: for every ε>0 there is δ>0 such that 0<|h|<δ implies |Q(h)−L|<ε. This tests all complex h in the punctured δ-disk, not merely a selected list of directions. Function composition and algebra work as usual when quantities are defined. A polynomial succeeds; a mirror fails Worked example. For f(z)=z², expand before taking a limit: [(z+h)²−z²]/h=2z+h whenever h≠0. Its distance from 2z is |h|, so choosing δ=ε proves the limit for every approach. In particular f′(z)=2z even at z=0. The calculation is stronger than checking the real and imaginary axes separately. For g(z)=z̄, the corresponding quotient is h̄/h. If h=t is nonzero real, it equals 1. If h=it is nonzero pure imaginary, it equals −1. Both can tend to zero, so no common limit exists at any z. Conjugation has real partial derivatives and is smooth as a map of real coordinates (x,y)↦(x,−y); nevertheless it has no complex derivative. Quotients for conjugation Approach h h̄/h Candidate limit positive real t 1 1 positive imaginary it −1 −1 Translate the derivative into a local prediction. At z=1+i, the square map has derivative 2+2i. A small real step h=0.01 has predicted output change 0.02+0.02i, and exact change 0.0201+0.02i. A small imaginary step h=0.01i instead has predicted change −0.02+0.02i and exact change −0.0201+0.02i. Both errors have modulus 0.0001=|h|². One multiplication predicts both directions, with the same relative error bound. The exact definition and its boundaries At an interior point z of a function's domain, complex differentiability means the following limit exists as a finite complex number: f ′ ( z ) = lim h → 0 f ( z + h ) − f ( z ) h An interior point is required so the function is defined on a full small disk around it. If the derivative exists at every point of an open set, the function is called holomorphic there. A derivative at a single point alone does not make a function holomorphic on a neighborhood. Complex differentiability also has an approximation form: f(z+h)=f(z)+Ah+r(h), with |r(h)|/|h|→0 and A=f′(z). For the square map, r(h)=h². This form explains why the derivative is multiplication by one complex number: a local rotation and scale when A≠0. It follows directly by multiplying the quotient's error by h, and conversely dividing the approximation by h. Two different approach paths are enough to disprove a limit, because a true limit would agree on both. Agreement on any finite collection is not enough to prove it. For example, define q(h)=1 when h lies on either coordinate axis and q(h)=0 elsewhere, for h≠0. Its values along both axes agree, but along the diagonal h=t(1+i) they are zero. A full δ-bound, as in the square-map calculation, is the positive evidence needed. Test a derivative and a tempting shortcut 1. Calculate. Determine whether f(z)=z̄² has a complex derivative at z=0. Then test z=1. Hint for 1 At zero, bound |h̄²/h|. At one, expand (1+h̄)²−1 and compare real and imaginary h. Worked solution for 1 At zero the quotient is h̄²/h, with modulus |h|, so it tends to zero in every direction. Thus f′(0)=0. At one the quotient is 2h̄/h+h̄²/h. The last term has modulus |h|→0, while the first tends to 2 along real steps and −2 along imaginary steps. No derivative exists at one. Differentiability at zero does not imply holomorphy nearby. 2. Explain. Someone checks h=t and h=it for f(z)=z² and announces a proof. Is the answer correct? Is the reasoning sufficient? Hint for 2 Compare the two path checks with the exact quotient 2z+h and the ε–δ definition. Worked solution for 2 The announced derivative 2z is correct, but two path checks do not prove it. The exact identity makes the error equal to h for every nonzero complex h. Hence its modulus is below ε whenever |h|<ε. That universal estimate is the missing proof. A demanding but usable test Expand and simplify when possible, then bound the error for arbitrary complex h. A mismatch along two paths certifies failure. Real smoothness and even a derivative at one exceptional point do not supply holomorphy on an open set. The Cauchy–Riemann equations next translate directional agreement into coordinate conditions, with a necessary regularity qualification for the converse.

title: Two equations behind rigid behavior
summary: Derive the Cauchy–Riemann equations and separate necessity from their qualified converse.
text: Two coordinate equations for one complex derivative A complex derivative is a single multiplication that describes the local map from every direction. The real coordinate derivatives cannot vary independently if that is true. The Cauchy–Riemann equations expose the constraint, while a regularity condition tells us when the equations really suffice. Background capsule. Write f(x+iy)=u(x,y)+iv(x,y), where u and v are real-valued functions. The partial derivative u x changes u with x while y stays fixed; u y changes it with y while x stays fixed. “Continuous first partials near a point” means all four first partial derivatives exist throughout an open neighborhood and vary continuously there. A complex derivative is the limit of [f(z+h)−f(z)]/h over all nonzero complex h→0. Compare the two axis steps Worked example. For f(z)=z², u=x²−y² and v=2xy. Consequently u x =2x, v x =2y, u y =−2y, v y =2x. The two requested equalities hold everywhere. The complex derivative computed directly is 2z=2x+2iy, agreeing with u x +iv x . For f(z)=z̄, u=x and v=−y. Then u x =1 but v y =−1, so the first equality fails; likewise u y =0 and −v x =0. One passing equation is not enough. The real-coordinate mirror is differentiable as a plane map but cannot be represented locally by multiplication by a complex number. Partial-derivative check Function u x , v y u y , −v x z² 2x, 2x −2y, −2y z̄ 1, −1 0, 0 Read the derivative matrix. Under the sufficient hypotheses, put a=u x and b=v x . The real derivative matrix has rows (a,−b) and (b,a), precisely the coordinate rule for multiplying by a+bi. Its determinant is a²+b². When this is positive, the linear approximation preserves orientation and scales every length by √(a²+b²). When both numbers vanish, the derivative is zero and this nonzero rotation-and-scale interpretation ceases to apply. The equations still hold in that exceptional case. Necessity and the qualified converse Necessary condition. If f has a complex derivative at an interior point z, then all four indicated partial derivatives at that point exist and satisfy u x = v y u y = − v x To prove it, let h=t be real. The quotient tends to u x +iv x . Let h=it; division by i turns its limit into v y −iu y . Both must equal the same f′(z). Equating real and imaginary parts yields the equations. This proves necessity without assuming continuity of partial derivatives. Sufficient condition with hypotheses. If all four first partials exist and are continuous throughout a neighborhood of z and the two equations hold at z, then f is complex differentiable at z. Real total differentiability follows from the continuous-partials theorem: for h=s+it, the change of f is (u x +iv x )s+(u y +iv y )t+o(|h|). The equations turn the linear part into (u x +iv x )(s+it). Divide the remainder by h to get zero. The cited real total-differentiability theorem is the one ingredient used here without proof. Equalities at one point alone do not imply a complex derivative. Consider f(0)=0 and, for z=x+iy≠0, f(z)=xy/√(x²+y²), a real-valued function. Along either coordinate axis f vanishes, so all four coordinate partials at zero are zero; both equations hold. Along h=t(1+i), however, f(h)/h has a nonzero constant value depending on the sign of t, so no complex derivative exists. This function lacks the needed total differentiability at zero. It makes the regularity qualification substantive. Check equations and their scope 1. Calculate. For f(z)=x²−y²+i(2xy+3), verify the equations and determine f′(z). Hint for 1 The added constant affects neither partial derivatives nor the difference quotient. Worked solution for 1 Here u x =2x=v y and u y =−2y=−v x . These partials are continuous everywhere, so the qualified converse applies at every point. The derivative is u x +iv x =2x+2iy=2z. Directly, f(z)=z²+3i gives the same result. 2. Explain. Why do equalities at just z=0 fail to settle the example f(z)=xy/√(x²+y²) with f(0)=0? Compute a diagonal quotient. Hint for 2 Set h=t(1+i) for t>0, find x=y=t, then divide by t(1+i). Worked solution for 2 For t>0, f(t+it)=t²/(√2t)=t/√2. Thus f(h)/h=1/[√2(1+i)]=(1−i)/(2√2), while along the real axis the quotient is zero. The derivative therefore fails despite the equalities at zero. Continuous partials near zero, which would supply a uniform linear approximation, are absent. Use both the equations and their premise Complex differentiability forces u x =v y and u y =−v x . Continuous first partials in a neighborhood make the equations sufficient at a point; if they hold throughout that neighborhood, f is holomorphic there. Bare pointwise equalities need not give a derivative. This precision matters before using contour theorems, which require holomorphy on an open region.

title: Why the logarithm needs a cut
summary: Construct a principal logarithm on a slit plane and prove why no continuous choice covers the punctured plane.
text: An angle that cannot return unchanged A nonzero complex number has many angle names differing by full turns. A logarithm records one of those angles, so choosing a single continuous logarithm across the entire punctured plane runs into a loop: after one circuit around zero the angle has gained 2π. A cut makes a consistent local choice possible. Background capsule. A nonzero z has polar form z=r(cos θ+i sin θ), with r=|z|>0; θ is defined only modulo 2π. The real logarithm ln r reverses the positive real exponential. For the complex exponential, e a+ib =e a (cos b+i sin b). Thus e w =z means the real part of w is ln r and its imaginary part is one of θ+2πk, k an integer. Continuity means nearby inputs have nearby outputs in the complex modulus. Choose and test a principal branch Worked example. Remove the nonpositive real ray, including zero, and call the remaining domain D. Every point of D has a unique angle Arg z in (−π,π). Define Log z=ln|z|+i Arg z there. For example, Log i=iπ/2, Log(−i)=−iπ/2, and Log(1+i)=ln√2+iπ/4. Exponentiating any result recovers the input. Approach −1 from above. Its principal angle tends to π; from below it tends to −π. The real parts of Log approach zero in both cases, but the imaginary parts differ by 2π. This is the branch jump. It is a feature of this chosen cut, not a singularity of every local logarithm at −1: a different cut can pass elsewhere and give a local logarithm around −1. Values approaching the cut Input Principal angle Limit as ε→0+ −1+iε near π π −1−iε near −π −π Check a product that stays in the domain. Set z=w=e 3πi/4 . Both principal logarithms equal 3πi/4, but zw=−i has principal logarithm −πi/2. Thus Log z+Log w=3πi/2 differs from Log(zw) by 2πi, even though all three logarithms are defined. Exponentiation erases that difference. A branch choice is therefore part of an additive logarithm identity, not just a convention for printing the answer. A branch is a domain choice On D, the exact formula is Log ( z ) = ln | z | + i Arg ( z ) − π < Arg ( z ) < π This branch is holomorphic on D and has derivative 1/z. One local verification uses a small disk that avoids the cut: differences in angle are continuous there, and the exponential inverse theorem (or a direct local argument) gives the derivative. The broader inverse-function theorem is used here, not proved from first principles. The main topological obstruction below needs only continuity. No global continuous logarithm on ℂ\{0}. Suppose a continuous L there satisfies e L(z) =z. On the unit circle z=e it , 0≤t≤2π, the real part of L is zero. Its imaginary part b(t) obeys e ib(t) =e it , hence b(t)−t is an integer multiple of 2π. Because b(t)−t is continuous and its possible values form a discrete set, that integer is constant. Therefore b(2π)=b(0)+2π. But the endpoints represent the same point z=1, and a single-valued L must give equal values there. Contradiction. This argument does not say every loop obstructs a logarithm. A simply connected region avoiding zero can support a branch, and a small disk around any nonzero point can. It says the entire punctured plane cannot. Nor does Log(zw)=Log z+Log w always hold for the principal branch: the angles on the right may cross the selected interval and differ from the left by 2πi. Compute with the cut in view 1. Calculate. Find Log(−i) and Log(i·i) using the principal branch whenever the input lies in D. Explain any undefined term. Hint for 1 Locate each input relative to the removed nonpositive real ray. Worked solution for 1 −i lies in D, has modulus one and principal angle −π/2, so Log(−i)=−iπ/2. But i·i=−1 lies on the removed ray; Log(i·i) is undefined in this chosen branch. The multivalued complex logarithm of −1 has values i(π+2πk), but that is a different statement. 2. Explain. A reader argues that Arg is continuous on the entire unit circle because each point has some angle. Identify the quantifier error using the loop proof. Hint for 2 “Each point has an angle” differs from “one continuous choice assigns an angle to all points.” Worked solution for 2 Every point e it does have infinitely many angle representatives, but selecting one continuously around the whole circle would produce b(t)=t+2πk with fixed k. It would assign b(2π)=b(0)+2π to the same point 1, impossible for a single-valued choice. Pointwise existence supplies no global continuous selection. Keep the domain in the formula The principal Log is a coherent choice on a slit plane, and its boundary jump records the obstruction to continuing that choice around zero. The excluded ray is conventional; zero is the unavoidable obstacle. Before using a logarithm in an integral or identity, specify a branch and ensure every input stays in its domain.

title: A loop that counts turns
summary: Evaluate a circle integral directly and connect orientation to winding around zero.
text: A loop that remembers a missing point The integrand 1/z is smooth along a circle centered at zero, yet its integral around that closed circle is not zero. The singularity inside the loop matters. A direct parameter calculation gives the answer and makes orientation visible without invoking a contour theorem prematurely. Background capsule. A piecewise continuously differentiable path γ:[a,b]→ℂ has a contour integral ∫ γ f(z) dz=∫ a b f(γ(t))γ′(t)dt, with ordinary real-variable integration applied to real and imaginary parts. A counterclockwise circle of radius r>0 has γ(t)=re it , 0≤t≤2π, where e it =cos t+i sin t. Its derivative is ire it . The path must avoid points where the integrand is undefined. Do the entire integral on the parameter Worked example. For γ(t)=2e it , division gives γ′(t)/γ(t)=i for every t. Therefore ∮ |z|=2 dz/z=∫ 0 2π i dt=2πi. Radius 2 disappears from the quotient. Radius 1 or 7 gives exactly the same result. Running backward, γ(t)=2e −it , gives γ′/γ=−i and the integral −2πi. A circle centered at 3 with radius 1 does not surround zero. On it, 1/z has a logarithm branch on a neighborhood of the closed disk, so its integral is zero by the fundamental theorem for contour integrals. More elementarily, one can expand 1/(3+e it ) as a uniformly convergent geometric series and integrate terms; every resulting nonconstant e int term averages to zero. This comparison shows that the value is not simply a property of circular shape. Circles that avoid the singularity Circle, counterclockwise Relation to zero Integral of 1/z center 0, radius 2 zero inside 2πi center 3, radius 1 zero outside 0 center 1, radius 1 zero on path undefined Relate the calculation to a continuous angle. Along the centered circle we can track a real angle t from 0 to 2π without wrapping it back to zero. The quotient dz/z=i dt records its incremental turning. Integrating adds all those increments, giving 2πi. The point on the plane returns to its start, but the tracked angle has gained one full turn. A globally single-valued logarithm would have to return to its original value too; this calculation shows why its derivative 1/z cannot have such a primitive throughout the punctured plane. Orientation and winding For every r>0, the direct calculation proves the exact statement ∮ | z | = r d z z = 2 π i The orientation is counterclockwise. Reversing any parametrized contour changes the sign: substitute the reversed parameter into the defining real integral. Traversing the same centered circle twice counterclockwise gives 4πi, not 2πi, because the parameter interval covers two turns. For a general closed piecewise smooth curve γ avoiding zero, the integer (1/2πi)∫ γ dz/z is its winding number around zero. Informally, it counts net turns. The full theorem that this quantity is an integer for every such curve needs a continuous lifted angle or equivalent argument; we state that theorem here and prove only the circular cases by parameterization. A self-crossing curve can have winding 0, 1, −1, or larger; “inside” is not a reliable replacement for the integer on arbitrary curves. The tempting claim “a holomorphic-looking integrand integrates to zero around a closed path” fails here because 1/z is not holomorphic at the point zero enclosed by the centered circle. Cauchy's theorem requires holomorphy on an appropriate region containing the contour and its interior, or an equivalent deformability condition. It cannot be applied across this hole. A numerical quadrature can illustrate the answer but cannot repair that missing hypothesis. Use the parameter, then test the domain 1. Calculate. Let γ(t)=5e −2it for 0≤t≤2π. Evaluate ∫ γ dz/z. Hint for 1 Differentiate γ, divide by γ, and count both direction and number of turns. Worked solution for 1 γ′(t)=−10ie −2it , so γ′(t)/γ(t)=−2i. Integrating from 0 to 2π gives −4πi. The path makes two clockwise turns; radius 5 has no effect. 2. Explain. Why is ∮ dz/z on the circle |z−1|=1 not a valid ordinary contour integral? Would “half of 2πi” be justified? Hint for 2 Check whether z=0 lies on the parametrized path and whether 1/z has a finite value there. Worked solution for 2 The circle passes through zero. At that path parameter the integrand is undefined and its parameter integrand has a singularity. The ordinary contour integral therefore is not defined. A principal value or indentation prescription would be a separate construction with extra choices; simply assigning half the centered-circle value has no basis in this definition. Know where the function is defined Parameterization proves the circular result, including its sign and repeated traversals. The general winding-number statement broadens the idea, but it requires its own theorem. A pole on the path invalidates the ordinary integral, and a pole inside prevents a naive use of Cauchy's zero-integral theorem.

title: The boundary knows every interior value
summary: Apply the disk form of Cauchy's integral formula and audit the holomorphy assumption.
text: Boundary values recover an interior value A holomorphic function has a striking rigidity: values on a surrounding circle determine every value inside. Cauchy's integral formula gives the reconstruction exactly. This lesson states its domain assumptions, checks a polynomial example and explains the mechanism, while keeping the proof debt of the full Cauchy theorem visible. Background capsule. A function is holomorphic on an open set when its complex derivative exists at every point there. A counterclockwise circle C: z=c+Re it , 0≤t≤2π, has radius R>0 and bounds the closed disk |z−c|≤R. A contour integral uses ∫ C g(z)dz=∫g(z(t))z′(t)dt. The kernel 1/(z−a) is singular at a; it is still integrable along C when a lies strictly inside, because then a is off the path. Reconstruct a quadratic at its center Worked example. Let f(z)=z²+1, use the unit circle C centered at zero, and choose a=0. Then f(z)/z=z+1/z. Parameterize z=e it . The first term integrates to ∫ 0 2π ie 2it dt=0, while the second integrates to 2πi. Thus (1/2πi)∮ C f(z)/z dz=1=f(0). The zero term is not magic: e 2it completes two periods and its positive and negative contributions cancel. For a=1/2, the same formula predicts f(1/2)=5/4. One could compute by expanding around a: z²+1=(a²+1)+2a(z−a)+(z−a)². Divide by z−a. The first term contributes (a²+1)·2πi because the circle encloses a; the remaining polynomial terms have entire antiderivatives and integrate to zero. This is a special-case derivation that does not yet prove the formula for arbitrary holomorphic f. Keep the target strictly away from the rim. On the unit circle and at a=1/2, the reverse triangle inequality gives |z−a|≥1/2, so the kernel's modulus is at most 2. That finite bound makes this interior reconstruction harmless along the contour despite its singularity at a inside. If a approaches the rim, the bound worsens; if a lies on the rim, the displayed ordinary formula has a singular integrand on its path and no longer applies. Changing the target therefore requires rechecking its location, not only substituting a different number. State the theorem with its circle Cauchy's integral formula, disk case. Let f be holomorphic on an open neighborhood of the closed disk |z−c|≤R. Let C be its counterclockwise boundary, and let |a−c|<R. Then f ( a ) = 1 2 π i ∮ C f ( z ) z − a d z The neighborhood assumption is stronger than merely knowing f on the circle: it permits Cauchy theory in the disk and on a slight enlargement. The theorem is invoked here; a full proof of Cauchy's theorem for arbitrary holomorphic f, including the analytic estimates behind shrinking a puncture, is deferred. The algebra below shows why the answer has this form once that theorem is available. Write f(z)/(z−a)=f(a)/(z−a)+[f(z)−f(a)]/(z−a). The second quotient extends holomorphically across a, taking value f′(a); this extension uses differentiability, and holomorphy of it follows from standard Cauchy theory. Its integral around C is zero by Cauchy's theorem. The first quotient has integral 2πi because C winds once counterclockwise around a. Hence the formula. This is a theorem-dependent derivation, not an independent proof of Cauchy's theorem itself. A derivative version follows under the same hypotheses by differentiating the formula with respect to a on compact subsets of the disk: f′(a)=(1/2πi)∮ C f(z)/(z−a)² dz. Justifying differentiation under this contour integral uses a uniform lower bound on |z−a| away from C. It is a consequence, not an assumption needed for the worked quadratic. Use the kernel and audit the domain 1. Calculate. Evaluate ∮ |z|=2 (3z+2)/(z−i) dz, counterclockwise. Hint for 1 Set f(z)=3z+2 and a=i; check |i|<2. Worked solution for 1 The polynomial is entire, and a=i lies inside the radius-two circle. Cauchy's formula gives the integral 2πi f(i)=2πi(2+3i)=−6π+4πi. The numerator's constant and linear parts are both accounted for. 2. Explain. A proposed use of the formula sets f(z)=1/z on |z|=2 and a=1. Why does this fail even though f(a)=1 exists? Hint for 2 Inspect every point of the closed disk, not merely a and the boundary. Worked solution for 2 The disk contains zero, where 1/z is undefined. Thus f is not holomorphic on a neighborhood of the closed disk, so the formula's hypothesis fails. Indeed the integrand 1/[z(z−1)] has poles at both zero and one; treating only the pole at a misses a contribution. Knowing f(a) is insufficient. Boundary data with a domain guarantee Under holomorphy near a closed disk, the boundary integral recovers an interior value. Polynomial calculations verify the mechanism directly; the universal theorem rests on Cauchy's theorem, which this article states but does not prove independently. A singularity anywhere in the disk can break the reconstruction hypothesis even if the desired interior value happens to exist.

title: A real integral solved by a complex detour
summary: Use one upper-half-plane residue and a proved arc estimate to evaluate a real improper integral.
text: Take a detour above the real line The real integral ∫ −∞ ∞ dx/(1+x²) has a familiar arctangent answer. A complex contour offers a second explanation: an upper semicircle encloses one pole, and its curved part contributes less and less as the radius grows. The arc estimate is essential; without it, the contour answer would not imply the real integral. Background capsule. For a function with a simple pole at a, its residue is lim z→a (z−a)f(z), when that limit exists. A counterclockwise contour integral ∮f(z)dz is computed from a piecewise smooth parameter path. The ordinary improper integral over the real line means the sum of the separately convergent integrals from −∞ to 0 and from 0 to ∞. For 1/(1+x²), both tails converge by comparison with 1/x² when |x|≥1, so its symmetric limits give that ordinary integral. Find the enclosed pole Worked example. Factor 1+z²=(z−i)(z+i). For radius R>1, let C R run along the real interval −R to R and then counterclockwise on the upper semicircle back to −R. The pole i lies inside; −i lies below. At i, the residue of f(z)=1/(1+z²) is lim z→i 1/(z+i)=1/(2i). The residue theorem gives ∮ C R f(z)dz=2πi·1/(2i)=π. Split this into the straight and curved pieces. If the curved integral tends to zero, the straight integral tends to π. This is the precise point where a real improper integral emerges from the complex calculation. Contour parts for R>1 Part Exact or bound Limit whole contour π by one residue π upper arc at most πR/(R²−1) in modulus 0 real interval whole minus arc π Make the arc estimate quantitative. For R≥2, R²−1≥3R²/4, so the omitted upper-arc contribution has modulus at most 4π/(3R). Consequently the symmetric finite real integral differs from π by at most this quantity. This bound is sufficient rather than sharp: the real tail can be estimated directly by 2/R. Both estimates tend to zero and justify passage to an infinite real interval. The important feature is a bound that holds for every sufficiently large R, rather than a small value observed for one radius. Account for the arc Residue theorem, used here. Let C be a positively oriented simple closed piecewise smooth contour. If f is holomorphic on an open neighborhood of C and its bounded interior except for finitely many isolated poles a k strictly inside, then ∮ C f ( z ) d z = 2 π i ∑ k Res ( f , a k ) The general theorem is stated, not proved in this lesson. Its hypotheses exclude a pole on the contour, and the orientation fixes the sign. Our rational function is holomorphic away from ±i, so C R is admissible for R>1. On the upper arc |z|=R. The reverse triangle inequality gives |1+z²|≥||z²|−1|=R²−1. Hence |f(z)|≤1/(R²−1). The arc length is πR, so the contour length estimate gives | ∫ arc d z 1 + z 2 | ≤ π R R 2 − 1 → 0 The estimate proves the arc disappears. Therefore the straight integral tends to π. This does not license dropping arbitrary semicircle arcs: the bound depends on the decay of this particular integrand. For 1/z on an upper semicircle, the arc integral is iπ, independent of radius. The same contour shape can have very different limits. As an independent real check, ∫dx/(1+x²)=arctan x, and arctan R−arctan(−R)→π. This confirms the answer but does not replace the arc proof in the complex method. Check a residue and challenge an arc 1. Calculate. Evaluate ∫ −∞ ∞ dx/(x²+4) by the same upper semicircle method. State the pole and an arc bound. Hint for 1 The upper pole is 2i. On |z|=R>2, use |z²+4|≥R²−4. Worked solution for 1 The residue at 2i is 1/(4i), so the contour integral is 2πi/(4i)=π/2. The upper arc has modulus at most πR/(R²−4), which tends to zero for R→∞. Thus the real integral is π/2. The contour avoids both poles when R>2. 2. Explain. Why does the claim “a semicircle gets far away, so every arc integral vanishes” fail for f(z)=1/z? Hint for 2 Parameterize the upper arc z=Re it , 0≤t≤π. Worked solution for 2 On that arc dz/z=i dt, so its integral is iπ for every R>0. Length grows like R while |1/z| shrinks like 1/R, leaving a constant product. Distance alone does not establish a vanishing contour contribution. The detour earns its answer One residue fixes the whole contour at π, and an explicit O(1/R) arc bound connects that contour to the real integral. The residue theorem is the cited general tool; the pole calculation and arc limit are derived here. For a different integrand, repeat all three checks: admissible contour, enclosed singularities, and an actual estimate of the extra path.

title: Why the biggest value lives on the edge
summary: Use Cauchy's mean-value consequence to locate a maximum of modulus on a closed disk.
text: Why a holomorphic peak cannot hide inside For a nonconstant holomorphic function, the largest modulus on a closed disk occurs on its boundary. The word “modulus” matters: complex numbers have no usual greater-than order, but their lengths do. The disk and continuity assumptions matter too, because the maximum must exist before we can locate it. Background capsule. The modulus |a+bi|=√(a²+b²) is the distance to zero. A closed disk |z−c|≤R is compact: a continuous real-valued function on it attains a maximum. Cauchy's integral formula says that for f holomorphic on a neighborhood of a closed disk, f(a)=(1/2πi)∮f(z)/(z−a)dz at interior a. On a centered circle this becomes an average of boundary values. We use this theorem and a standard equality case for the triangle inequality; the latter says an average of vectors has full common magnitude only when their directions agree. Test a polynomial on the unit disk Worked example. Let f(z)=z+1 on |z|≤1. The triangle inequality gives |z+1|≤|z|+1≤2. At boundary point z=1 equality holds, so the maximum is exactly 2. At center z=0 the modulus is 1. The inequality proves the bound for every point, which a sampled contour picture could not do. For f(z)=z², |f(z)|=|z|²; its largest value on the disk is 1 and occurs at every boundary point. An interior value, including zero, is strictly smaller. For a constant function f(z)=3i, however, every interior point also has the maximum modulus 3. Thus a correct maximum principle must allow the constant case rather than claim the maximum occurs only at the edge. Three disk examples Function on |z|≤1 Maximum modulus Where attained z+1 2 z=1 z² 1 all boundary points 3i 3 every point From a mean to a maximum Disk maximum-modulus theorem. If f is continuous on |z−c|≤R and holomorphic on the open disk |z−c|<R, then max | z − c | ≤ R | f ( z ) | = max | z − c | = R | f ( z ) | To see the local engine, take a small circle |z−a|=ρ entirely inside the disk. Cauchy's formula, applied on this smaller circle, gives f(a)=(1/2π)∫ 0 2π f(a+ρe it )dt. Therefore |f(a)|≤(1/2π)∫|f(a+ρe it )|dt. This mean-value inequality is proved from the cited Cauchy formula and triangle inequality. Suppose |f| has a global maximum M at an interior point a. Every value on each sufficiently small circle has modulus at most M, while its average is f(a) of modulus M. Equality in the integral triangle inequality forces those values to have the same phase as f(a) almost everywhere; continuity makes the equality hold everywhere. Hence f is constant on each such circle and on a neighborhood of a. The identity theorem, a standard consequence of Cauchy theory, then makes f constant throughout the connected open disk. Equivalently, if f is nonconstant, no interior maximum is possible. This argument states explicitly where the identity theorem enters; it is not proved independently here. The boundary equality follows because compactness supplies a maximum on the closed disk, and a nonconstant function cannot attain it inside. If f is constant, boundary and interior values are equal anyway. The function 1/z on the unit disk is an instructive failure case: it is singular at zero and unbounded near it, so neither continuity on the disk nor holomorphy inside holds. Bound a function and audit a peak 1. Calculate. Find the maximum of |2z−1| on |z|≤2, and identify a point attaining it. Hint for 1 Use |2z−1|≤2|z|+1, then find a boundary point where the two terms point the same way. Worked solution for 1 For |z|≤2, |2z−1|≤2|z|+1≤5. At z=−2, the value is |−5|=5. Thus the maximum is 5. The polynomial is entire, so the disk theorem also predicts that a boundary point suffices, while the triangle inequality supplies its exact value. 2. Explain. Why is f(z)=1/(z−1/2) on |z|≤1 no counterexample to the theorem when its modulus becomes arbitrarily large near 1/2? Hint for 2 Check whether f is defined and holomorphic throughout the open disk. Worked solution for 2 The point 1/2 is inside the unit disk and is a pole of f. The function is not defined there, is not continuous on the closed disk, and is not holomorphic on the open disk. The maximum-modulus theorem therefore makes no claim about this example; the unbounded behavior is compatible with its hypotheses being false. Check the closed disk and the open one Continuity on the closed disk gives an attained maximum; holomorphy inside moves that maximum to the boundary unless the function is constant. Cauchy's local mean-value formula supplies the core inequality. This lesson uses the identity theorem for the final constancy step, so a complete proof of all underlying Cauchy theory lies beyond this page. The boundary rule cannot be applied across an interior pole.

title: A distant singularity limits a local series
summary: Prove geometric expansions, their truncation errors and exact radii for selected rational functions.
text: A singularity sets a limit on a local expansion The geometric series reconstructs 1/(1−z) perfectly near zero and fails beyond the unit circle. That boundary matches the pole at z=1, even though the function is perfectly finite at many other points outside. Convergence belongs to a particular series centered at a particular point, not just to the formula it happens to represent. Background capsule. A power series centered at a is ∑ n=0 ∞ c n (z−a) n . It converges on some disk |z−a|<R and diverges when |z−a|>R; behavior on the boundary needs separate checking. A geometric series has finite sum ∑ n=0 N w n =(1−w N+1 )/(1−w) for w≠1. The modulus satisfies |w n |=|w| n . Compute an error, not just a pattern Worked example. For |z|<1, z N+1 →0, so 1/(1−z)=∑ n≥0 z n . The exact truncation error after N+1 terms is z N+1 /(1−z), with modulus at most |z| N+1 /(1−|z|). At z=1/2 and N=3, the partial sum 1+1/2+1/4+1/8=15/8; the exact value is 2 and the error is 1/8. The bound also gives (1/2) 4 /(1−1/2)=1/8, exactly sharp here. At z=−1, the terms alternate 1,−1,1,−1,… and do not approach zero, so the series diverges even though 1/(1−z)=1/2 is defined. At z=2, terms grow. This distinction prevents the false statement that the analytic expression's domain is automatically the convergence domain of one chosen expansion. The series centered at zero z Function 1/(1−z) Series ∑z n 1/2 2 converges to 2 −1 1/2 diverges 2 −1 diverges 1 undefined pole diverges Locate the radius precisely The central identity is 1 1 − z = ∑ n = 0 ∞ z n for | z | < 1 The finite identity proves convergence inside |z|<1. Outside, terms z n do not approach zero, so the series cannot converge. On |z|=1 they also have modulus one, so again the necessary term-to-zero condition fails. Thus the radius is exactly 1. This proof is self-contained for this particular series. For a rational example with two complex poles, write 1/(1+z²)=1/[(1−iz)(1+iz)]. A simple expansion is 1/(1+z²)=∑ n≥0 (−1) n z 2n by setting w=−z² in the geometric identity. It converges exactly when |z|<1; the poles at i and −i both lie on the boundary. The absence of odd powers is algebraic, not a claim that the function is constant in odd directions. A useful general theorem says a holomorphic function's Taylor series at a converges at least up to every closed disk centered at a on which the function is holomorphic on a neighborhood; Cauchy's coefficient estimates prove this. A more sweeping slogan, “radius equals distance to nearest singularity,” needs qualification: one must refer to the singularities of the analytic continuation of the germ, including whether apparent singularities are removable. We do not prove general analytic continuation here. For our rational examples, the explicit geometric identities and actual poles settle the radius directly. Shift the center and check the edge 1. Calculate. Expand 1/(3−z) around zero and give its exact radius of convergence and an error bound after N+1 terms when |z|<3. Hint for 1 Factor out 3 and use w=z/3 in the geometric sum. Worked solution for 1 1/(3−z)=(1/3)∑ n≥0 (z/3) n =∑ n≥0 z n /3 n+1 for |z|<3. The pole at z=3 and the term test outside show radius 3. The tail has modulus at most (1/3)(|z|/3) N+1 /(1−|z|/3). The exact complex tail is (1/3)(z/3) N+1 /(1−z/3). 2. Explain. Why does the finite value 1/2 at z=−1 not make ∑ n≥0 (−1) n converge to it? Can another expansion still represent the function near −1? Hint for 2 Check the necessary term-to-zero condition; then recenter with w=z+1. Worked solution for 2 The terms (−1) n never tend to zero, so their series diverges. Recenter: 1/(1−z)=1/(2−(z+1))=(1/2)∑ n≥0 ((z+1)/2) n for |z+1|<2. This new series converges at z=−1 and equals 1/2. A function can admit several local series with different centers and disks. Radius belongs to a center and a series Finite geometric sums prove the expansions and exact errors here. The unit-circle boundary for 1/(1−z) is set by the pole at 1, yet many points outside still have finite function values and admit other expansions. For general holomorphic functions, Cauchy estimates and analytic continuation provide the broader theory; do not use the nearest-singularity slogan without specifying that setting.

title: The mathematics of a cooling cup
summary: Derive and check exponential approach to a fixed ambient temperature, including time scales and model limits.
text: How can one rate rule draw a whole curve? A cup at 80°C in a 20°C room cools quickly at first and slowly later. Newton's cooling model says that the rate of change of temperature is proportional to the temperature difference from a constant ambient temperature. Here a prime means differentiation with respect to time: T′(t) is measured in °C per minute, while the constant k has units per minute. The model assumes a well-mixed cup, a fixed room temperature, and an effective heat-transfer coefficient that does not change over the interval being studied. Local background. The derivative of e at is ae at . An initial condition such as T(0)=80 chooses one curve from a family of possible curves. A negative derivative means decreasing temperature; it does not mean that the temperature itself is negative. Calculate a prediction Worked example. Take T a =20°C, T(0)=80°C and k=0.1 per minute. Write the excess temperature U=T−20. Its starting value is 60°C, and the rule becomes U′=−0.1U. Guess U(t)=60e −0.1t . Differentiating gives U′=−6e −0.1t =−0.1U, so the guess satisfies the equation and the initial value. After ten minutes, T=20+60e −1 ≈42.1°C. This is a model prediction, not a measurement. The temperature gap after one time constant 1/k=10 minutes is 1/e of its original size. Its half-life is (ln 2)/k≈6.93 minutes: solving 60e −0.1t =30 gives t=10 ln 2. Neither time depends on the starting gap in this particular model. Model temperature with a constant 20°C room Time, min Gap, °C Temperature, °C 0 60 80 10 60/e≈22.1 42.1 20 60/e²≈8.1 28.1 Why this curve, and when is it unique? For constant ambient temperature T a and k>0, the initial-value problem and its solution are d T d t = − k ( T − T a ) , T ( 0 ) = T 0 ; T ( t ) = T a + ( T 0 − T a ) e − k t Differentiation verifies the displayed formula. To see why no other differentiable solution with the same initial value exists, multiply U′=−kU by e kt . The product rule gives (e kt U)′=0. Thus e kt U is constant on an interval, and its initial value fixes that constant as T 0 −T a . This is a direct uniqueness proof for this linear equation; it does not assert uniqueness for arbitrary rate rules. The gap keeps its original sign because an exponential is positive. A cup above room temperature stays above it in the model and approaches it without crossing. The equation can also describe warming from below: then U<0, U′>0, and T rises toward T a . The equilibrium T=T a is stable in the precise sense that a small initial temperature error remains no larger later: its magnitude is multiplied by e −kt ≤1 for t≥0. It is also attracting because that factor tends to zero. One can formally separate dU/U=−k dt only where U≠0. The product-rule derivation includes the equilibrium U=0 automatically and avoids dividing by zero. If room temperature changes, U′ also contains −T a ′(t); simply replacing T a in the displayed answer by a changing function does not solve the modified equation. Try two checks 1. Recover a rate from two readings Exercise 1. A cup is 50°C above a fixed ambient temperature at t=0 and 25°C above it 5 minutes later. Find k and predict its excess temperature at t=15 minutes. Hint for 1 Use U(5)/U(0)=e −5k =1/2. Worked solution for 1 Taking logarithms gives −5k=ln(1/2)=−ln 2, hence k=(ln 2)/5 per minute. At 15 minutes three five-minute half-lives have elapsed, so U(15)=50(1/2) 3 =6.25°C. The absolute temperature would require the ambient reading, which was not supplied. 2. Test a claim about crossing Exercise 2. Someone says that a modeled hot cup becomes cooler than the room after enough time because it keeps cooling. Decide whether the claim follows from this model. Hint for 2 Check the sign of T(t)−T a . Worked solution for 2 If T 0 >T a , then T(t)−T a =(T 0 −T a )e −kt >0 at every finite t. The difference tends to zero as t grows, but the predicted temperature never crosses below a constant ambient temperature. What this model earns A proportional rate rule yields an exponential approach and a measurable time scale. The calculation also shows a useful boundary: an explicit formula may prove existence and uniqueness for this one problem, while physical validity remains a separate question. Evaporation, a changing room, a thermometer with lag, or a freezing transition can spoil the constant-k rule. To read such a rule without first finding a formula, continue to direction fields .

title: Read a differential equation without solving it
summary: Use signs and exact checks to read a slope field while separating it from existence and numerical claims.
text: Can slopes tell a story before a formula does? The rule y′=1−y assigns a slope at every point (t,y). At height y=0 the slope is +1, at y=1 it is zero, and at y=2 it is −1. Short marks with those slopes make a direction field . A differentiable solution curve must be tangent to the marks it meets. Reading the signs already suggests that y=1 is a resting level and that nearby curves move toward it as time increases. Local background. The derivative y′ is the tangent slope dy/dt. A horizontal tangent has slope zero. An equilibrium is a constant solution y(t)=c; it exists when the rate rule gives zero at c. An initial value, such as y(0)=3, picks a particular trajectory. Walk through a field Worked example. Start at (0,3). The initial slope is 1−3=−2. An Euler step of width h=1/4 follows this slope for one short move: y 1 =3+(1/4)(−2)=2.5. The next slope is −1.5, so y 2 =2.5−0.375=2.125. These are approximations, not points on the exact curve. For comparison, the exact solution verified below gives y(1/4)=1+2e −1/4 ≈2.558 and y(1/2)=1+2e −1/2 ≈2.213. Slopes and one approximate walk Height y Assigned slope 1−y Meaning 0 +1 Rising 1 0 Equilibrium 2 −1 Falling An optional field experiment can vary the step width. The static computations above remain enough to check its meaning without running it. Read the independent variable as well. Because 1−y has no t in it, every point at the same height receives the same slope, however far left or right it appears in the field. A solution from (t₀,y₀) is therefore y(t)=1+(y₀−1)e −(t−t₀) . Shifting the starting time slides a trajectory horizontally without changing its vertical behavior. This time-shift property comes from the autonomous equation; a rate containing t would need a fresh check. Separate a sketch from a theorem Set z=y−1. Then z′=y′=−z. The product rule gives (e t z)′=e t (z+z′)=0. Therefore, on any interval where the solution is defined, e t z=C. With y(0)=y 0 , C=y 0 −1, so y ( t ) = 1 + ( y 0 − 1 ) e − t Direct differentiation verifies that this formula solves y′=1−y, and substitution at t=0 checks the initial condition. The product-rule argument proves uniqueness for this equation. For t≥0 the distance from equilibrium is |y(t)−1|=|y 0 −1|e −t . This gives both stability (a small displacement stays small) and attraction (the displacement tends to zero). The sign diagram is an efficient summary: below 1, 1−y>0; above 1, 1−y<0. These arrows alone do not prove that a solution exists, nor do they distinguish two different curves that might pass through the same initial point for another equation. The exact calculation does that work here. More generally, a rate function f(t,y) locally Lipschitz in y has a unique local solution through each initial point under the usual continuity assumptions; proving that theorem requires an argument beyond a field sketch. Euler's rule y n+1 =y n +h(1−y n ) becomes z n+1 =(1−h)z n . If 0<h<1 it approaches from one side. If 1<h<2 it alternates sides while shrinking. If h>2 it grows in magnitude, even though the exact solution always settles. This is a numerical failure, not instability in the differential equation. Test the picture 1. Begin below equilibrium Exercise 1. For y(0)=−1, find y(t), its initial slope and the time when it first reaches y=0. Hint for 1 In the displayed solution, y 0 −1=−2. Solve e −t =1/2. Worked solution for 1 y(t)=1−2e −t . Its initial slope is 1−(−1)=2. It reaches zero when 1−2e −t =0, hence t=ln 2. Since y′=2e −t >0, it crosses y=0 only once and approaches 1 from below. 2. Detect a misleading step Exercise 2. Use one Euler step of width h=3 from y(0)=2. Does the output show that the exact equilibrium repels nearby solutions? Hint for 2 Compute z 1 =(1−h)z 0 and compare with e −3 z 0 . Worked solution for 2 z 0 =1, so Euler gives z 1 =−2 and y 1 =−1: the error from equilibrium has doubled. The exact solution gives y(3)=1+e −3 ≈1.050. Euler's factor −2 produces the spurious growth; it does not refute exact attraction. What to trust A direction field records local slopes, and sign analysis can suggest equilibria and approach directions. A verified solution and a separate uniqueness argument turn that suggestion into a conclusion for this equation. A coarse numerical walk may contradict the real curve. The cooling model uses the same exponential mechanism; the nonuniqueness example shows why a slope picture cannot settle every starting-value question.

title: Growth that runs out of room
summary: Derive positive logistic solutions, classify equilibria, and locate the rising curve’s inflection.
text:
What changes when growth meets a limit? Exponential growth assumes a fixed growth rate per individual, no matter how large a population becomes. A logistic model makes that rate shrink linearly with population P: P′=rP(1−P/K), where r>0 has units per time and K>0 has population units. K is called a carrying capacity in the model. It is a fitted parameter under stable conditions, not a universal biological constant. Local background. P′ is the population's instantaneous rate of change. A zero of the right-hand side is an equilibrium. The sign of P′ says which way a solution moves. Separation of variables means rearranging a nonzero solution so one side involves P and the other t; any division by P or K−P must leave the omitted equilibria for separate checking. A population with room to grow Worked example. Take r=0.4 per year, K=1000 and P(0)=200. The formula derived below gives P(t)=1000/[1+4e −0.4t ]. Initially P′=0.4·200·0.8=64 individuals per year. At t=(ln 4)/0.4≈3.47 years, e −0.4t =1/4 and P=500. The population is then halfway to K, where this model predicts its largest growth rate, rK/4=100 individuals per year. Sign analysis for positive population Population P′ Direction 0K Negative Down toward K Compare equal fractions at different scales. At P=K/4 the per-individual growth rate is P′/P=3r/4, while at P=3K/4 it is r/4. The larger population has the smaller rate per individual. Its total growth is nevertheless the same in both cases, 3rK/16, because the larger number of individuals offsets their slower individual rate. Distinguishing total growth from per-individual growth prevents a misleading interpretation of the capacity factor. Derive the curve and its limits For P>0 with P≠K, rearrange the equation: K dP/[P(K−P)]=r dt. Since K/[P(K−P)]=1/P+1/(K−P), integration yields ln|P|−ln|K−P|=rt+C. Solving and applying P(0)=P 0 >0 gives, on the branch where its denominator remains nonzero, P ( t ) = K 1 + ( K P 0 − 1 ) e − r t Substitution verifies the formula and initial value. The excluded constant solutions P=0 and P=K also satisfy the original equation. For 0

K, the forward-time denominator stays positive and the curve falls to K; extending it backward may meet a zero denominator, so no global-in-time claim follows. Differentiate the rate rule along a solution: P″=r(1−2P/K)P′. On a rising solution with 00, so concavity switches from upward to downward exactly as P crosses K/2. This identifies the S-curve's inflection. A solution starting above K is already decreasing; the same verbal S-curve description is inappropriate there. The sign table proves forward attraction to K for positive starting populations when combined with the explicit formula. Near P=0, a small positive population grows away, so zero is unstable on the nonnegative state space. Near K, small positive or negative departures move back, and the formula shows convergence. This scalar conclusion is about the logistic differential equation, not the discrete logistic map, whose stepwise iteration can behave very differently. Local uniqueness also follows because f(P)=rP(1−P/K) is a polynomial and therefore locally Lipschitz. The separation calculation by itself would be incomplete if it silently discarded P=0 or K. In empirical use, changing resources, migration and random births can break the rule; fitting r and K from a short run does not prove long-run capacity. Use signs and formulas 1. Find the midpoint time Exercise 1. For K=600, r=0.3 per day and P(0)=150, find the first time P reaches 300 and its rate then. Hint for 1 The coefficient K/P 0 −1 is 3. At P=K/2 the denominator is 2. Worked solution for 1 P(t)=600/[1+3e −0.3t ]. Setting P=300 gives 3e −0.3t =1, so t=(ln 3)/0.3≈3.66 days. At P=300, P′=0.3·300·(1−1/2)=45 individuals per day. 2. Check a generalization Exercise 2. A student claims that every positive logistic solution is an increasing S-curve. Give a counterexample and explain its forward behavior. Hint for 2 Choose P 0 >K and inspect the sign of 1−P/K. Worked solution for 2 With P 0 =2K, P′(0)=r(2K)(1−2)=−2rK<0. The explicit solution is P(t)=K/[1−(1/2)e −rt ] for t≥0, so it decreases toward K from above. It is neither increasing nor the usual rising S-curve. What is learned The logistic rule gives two equilibria, a solvable positive trajectory and a clear maximum growth rate at K/2 for a rising population. Its value lies in a transparent assumption about density-dependent growth, not in a guarantee about every population. The fold model shows a different way equilibria can change as a parameter moves.

title: One starting point, several futures
summary: Verify delayed solutions and identify why continuity alone does not secure a unique trajectory.
text: Can a motion law allow waiting? Consider the initial-value problem y′=2√|y| with y(0)=0. At height zero the assigned slope is zero, so the constant curve y=0 works. Surprisingly, the rule also permits a solution to rest for any chosen delay and then rise. This is an exact mathematical example of nonuniqueness, not a physical prediction that a particle can choose a departure time. Local background. A solution must be differentiable and satisfy the equation at every time in its interval, including a join between pieces. A function f(y) is locally Lipschitz near zero if there are L and a neighborhood such that |f(u)−f(v)|≤L|u−v| for all u,v there. This condition is stronger than continuity and is a sufficient ingredient in the standard local uniqueness theorem. Verify two futures Worked example. For any a≥0 define y a (t)=0 when t≤a and y a (t)=(t−a)² when t≥a. Choose a=0: at t=1 the solution is 1. Choose a=2: at t=1 it is still 0. Both pass through (0,0), so uniqueness fails. On t<a, both sides of the equation are zero. On t>a, y′=2(t−a) and 2√|y|=2√((t−a)²)=2(t−a), because t−a>0. At the join t=a, the left derivative is zero and the right derivative is lim h→0+ h²/h=0. Thus y is differentiable there with y′(a)=0=2√|y(a)|. We have checked the delicate point rather than assuming that two correct formulas can always be glued. Different exact solutions from y(0)=0 Delay a y(1) y(3) 0 1 9 2 0 1 Always zero 0 0 Locate the missing hypothesis The right-hand side f(y)=2√|y| is continuous, including at zero. Continuity of a rate rule is associated with local existence in the standard Peano theorem, but does not alone guarantee uniqueness. Here existence is already shown directly by the constant and delayed formulas. To test Lipschitz behavior at zero, compare u>0 with v=0: | f ( u ) − f ( 0 ) | | u − 0 | = 2 u → ∞ as u ↓ 0 No finite local Lipschitz constant can bound these ratios. That explains why the familiar sufficient uniqueness theorem does not apply. Failure of a sufficient condition by itself does not prove nonuniqueness; the explicit pair of solutions proves it here. A useful comparison is z′=2z with z(0)=0. This right-hand side is globally Lipschitz, since |2u−2v|=2|u−v|. Multiplying z′−2z=0 by e −2t gives (e −2t z)′=0, and the initial value makes z identically zero. Another comparison, z′=3z 2/3 with z(0)=0, again permits delayed cubic departure. The exponent below one makes the slope as a function of state too sharp near zero for a simple Lipschitz bound. For a continuous f(t,y) that is locally Lipschitz in y near an initial point, the Picard–Lindelöf theorem gives a unique solution on some time interval around that point. It does not promise a solution for all future times. The full existence proof constructs iterates and uses completeness of a space of continuous functions; it is outside this article. Even a smooth rule such as y′=y² has the solution y=1/(1−t) from y(0)=1, which blows up at t=1. Smoothness gives local uniqueness, not global duration. A sketch of slope marks at y=0 would show horizontal segments; it would not reveal whether the curve must stay there. Every delayed curve initially follows the same horizontal trace. Exact verification is the decisive test. Check the join and the theorem 1. A delayed cubic Exercise 1. For y′=3|y| 2/3 , y(0)=0, test y(t)=0 for t≤4 and y(t)=(t−4)³ for t≥4. Hint for 1 For t≥4, |(t−4)³| 2/3 =(t−4)². Examine both one-sided derivatives at t=4. Worked solution for 1 Before 4, derivative and right-hand side are zero. After 4, y′=3(t−4)²=3|y| 2/3 . At 4 both one-sided derivatives are zero, so y′(4)=0 equals the right-hand side. Since 0≤4, y(0)=0. The constant zero solution also works, so the initial value has at least two solutions. 2. Test an inference Exercise 2. A rate rule fails a Lipschitz test at an initial state. Must it have two solutions there? Hint for 2 Distinguish a sufficient theorem from its converse. Try y′=1+√|y| with y(0)=0: its speed never vanishes. Worked solution for 2 No. Failing a sufficient condition at one place does not logically assert nonuniqueness. For f(y)=1+√|y|, the quotient |f(u)−f(0)|/|u|=1/√u diverges as u↓0, so f is not locally Lipschitz at the initial state zero. Yet define F(y)=∫ 0 y ds/[1+√|s|]. Its integrand is continuous and positive, so F is differentiable and strictly increasing near zero. Every differentiable solution obeys dF(y(t))/dt=F′(y)y′=1 and F(y(0))=0; hence F(y(t))=t. A strictly increasing F has only one local inverse, giving a unique local solution. Failure of a sufficient condition alone proves nothing either way. What this counterexample proves A continuous rate rule can allow several differentiable trajectories through one initial point.
