The delayed curves establish the failure constructively, and the divergent Lipschitz ratio identifies the hypothesis missing from a standard local theorem. Do not infer global existence from local existence or a plotted direction field. The linear direction field supplies a contrasting direct uniqueness proof.

title: Three ways a spring can settle
summary: Classify linear spring motion by characteristic roots and check damping with an energy identity.
text: Why does the same spring settle in different ways? A mass m>0 displaced by x from equilibrium feels an ideal restoring force −kx with k>0. A linear damper adds force −cx′ with c≥0. Newton's law then gives mx″+cx′+kx=0. The initial displacement and velocity determine a specific motion. The three damping regimes follow from one quadratic discriminant; the labels describe a linear model with constant coefficients. Local background. A trial function e λt has derivatives λe λt and λ²e λt . Substitution converts the differential equation into a quadratic in λ. Complex roots a±ib correspond to real combinations e at cos(bt) and e at sin(bt). Those formulas can be checked by differentiating. Three parameter choices Worked example. Let m=k=1 and x(0)=1, x′(0)=0. With c=0, x(t)=cos t: no decay. With c=1, roots are (−1±i√3)/2, and the solution is e −t/2 [cos(√3t/2)+(1/√3)sin(√3t/2)]. Its oscillation envelope decays. With c=2, the repeated root is −1, and x(t)=(1+t)e −t , which returns without crossing zero. With c=3, the two roots (−3±√5)/2 are negative and distinct; the response is a sum of two decays. Regimes for m,k>0 and c≥0 Discriminant D=c²−4mk Roots Typical motion when c>0 D<0 Complex pair, real part −c/(2m) Decaying oscillation D=0 Repeated negative root Critical damping D>0 Two negative real roots Sum of decays Use initial data to interpret the critical example. For x(t)=(1+t)e −t , differentiation gives x′(t)=−te −t . Hence for t>0 the displacement stays positive and decreases, while velocity is negative and eventually returns toward zero. The initial zero velocity does not mean the mass stays fixed: the equation gives x″(0)=−1. Its first acceleration starts the return. These direct checks explain “no crossing” for this particular initial state; a damping label alone does not settle the signs of every solution with different initial velocity. Derive the classification Substituting x=e λt gives e λt (mλ²+cλ+k)=0. Because the exponential is never zero, λ must satisfy λ ± = − c ± c 2 − 4 m k 2 m When D<0 and c>0, set α=c/(2m) and β=√(4mk−c²)/(2m). The real solution is e −αt (A cos βt+B sin βt), so it oscillates while its envelope shrinks. When D>0, both roots are negative: √D<c because mk>0, hence −c+√D<0. When D=0, a second independent solution is te −ct/(2m) ; substitution verifies it. Initial x and x′ determine A,B or the corresponding real-root coefficients by a nonsingular two-equation system. At c=0, D<0 but the real part is zero. Thus “underdamped” alone is not enough to claim decay if zero damping is included. Energy gives another boundary check. Define E=(m/2)(x′)²+(k/2)x². Differentiating along a solution yields E′=x′(mx″+kx)=−c(x′)²≤0. It decreases when c>0 except at instants of zero velocity; with c=0 it stays constant. This identity supports the qualitative distinction without proving every detailed long-time claim by itself. Critical damping is often said to be the fastest return without oscillation. That slogan needs a specified initial condition and a definition of “return”; for example a specially chosen overdamped initial velocity may cross equilibrium sooner. What the discriminant proves here is the form of the homogeneous solution and the presence or absence of sinusoidal factors. A real spring may have nonlinear stiffness, dry friction, or changing damping; those require a different equation. Classify and verify 1. A critical case Exercise 1. For x″+4x′+4x=0, x(0)=2 and x′(0)=0, find x(t). Hint for 1 The root is −2 twice, so use (A+Bt)e −2t . Worked solution for 1 x(0)=A=2. Differentiating gives x′=e −2t [B−2A−2Bt], so x′(0)=B−4=0 and B=4. Hence x(t)=(2+4t)e −2t . The discriminant 4²−4·1·4=0 confirms critical damping. 2. Correct a tempting claim Exercise 2. A system has m=k=1, c=0. Someone classifies D<0 and concludes its energy tends to zero. Find the error and the actual energy for x(0)=1, x′(0)=0. Hint for 2 Use E′=−c(x′)² and solve x″+x=0. Worked solution for 2 D=−4<0 gives imaginary roots, but c=0 means their real part is zero, so there is no decaying envelope. The solution is x=cos t, x′=−sin t. Its energy is E=(sin²t+cos²t)/2=1/2 at every time, not a quantity tending to zero. What the discriminant settles The quadratic roots classify homogeneous linear motion when m,k>0 and c≥0. The energy calculation checks whether damping actually removes energy. The case c=0 matters: it is oscillatory but not settling. Periodic forcing asks what changes when energy is supplied continuously.

title: When a small push keeps adding up
summary: Derive undamped resonant growth and distinguish it from finite damped steady response.
text: Can a modest repeated push make a large motion? For a mass scaled to one, consider x″+ω 0 ²x=F cos(ωt), where ω 0 >0 is the natural angular frequency and F is forcing per unit mass. The right-hand side feeds energy to an otherwise undamped oscillator. If the forcing frequency matches ω 0 , the usual bounded sinusoidal guess fails; a growing factor t appears. That is exact resonance in this ideal model. Local background. The derivative of cos(ωt) is −ω sin(ωt); differentiating twice multiplies it by −ω². A particular solution solves the forced equation, while any solution of the homogeneous equation may be added to satisfy initial conditions. The word amplitude here means the size of a sinusoidal component, not an assertion that every transient has that size. Find the resonant response Worked example. Set ω=ω 0 and try x p (t)=Ct sin(ω 0 t). Differentiation gives x p ″+ω 0 ²x p =2Cω 0 cos(ω 0 t). Thus C=F/(2ω 0 ). For ω 0 =2 and F=1, x p =(t/4)sin(2t). This particular solution starts with x(0)=x′(0)=0, so it is also the solution for a mass initially at rest. At peak phases its envelope grows like t/4, although it crosses zero repeatedly. Forcing regimes for x″+2γx′+ω₀²x=F cos(ωt) Case Selected steady or particular response Bound γ=0, ω≠ω₀ F cos(ωt)/(ω₀²−ω²) Bounded particular response γ=0, ω=ω₀ Ft sin(ω₀t)/(2ω₀) Growing envelope γ>0 Sinusoid at ω Finite steady amplitude Where energy enters, and where it leaves For undamped off-resonance forcing, substituting A cos(ωt) gives A=F/(ω 0 ²−ω²). That formula is invalid at ω=ω 0 because its denominator vanishes; it does not describe an “infinite amplitude” solution at a finite time. The correct resonant particular solution is x p ( t ) = F 2 ω 0 t sin ( ω 0 t ) Its magnitude is at most |F|t/(2ω 0 ), and reaches that envelope at an unbounded sequence of peak phases. For F≠0, the undamped ideal model therefore has an unbounded long-time response. A finite observation interval still has finite displacement. Add linear damping: x″+2γx′+ω 0 ²x=F cos(ωt), γ>0. Write a steady particular solution a cos(ωt)+b sin(ωt). Equating cosine and sine coefficients gives (ω 0 ²−ω²)a+2γωb=F and (ω 0 ²−ω²)b−2γωa=0. Solving yields an amplitude A(ω)=|F|/√[(ω 0 ²−ω²)²+(2γω)²]. For fixed γ>0 and ω>0 this is finite. At ω=ω 0 , A=|F|/(2γω 0 ). The homogeneous transient decays because its characteristic roots have negative real parts; the response approaches the finite periodic particular solution. This statement assumes constant positive damping, constant forcing amplitude, and the linear model. The energy E=((x′)²+ω 0 ²x²)/2 satisfies E′=F x′cos(ωt)−2γ(x′)². The first term is instantaneous input power and can change sign; the dissipation term is always nonpositive. Their sum need not have a fixed sign, so a plot of displacement alone is not a proof about monotone energy. At resonance without damping, the well-timed input can accumulate over many cycles. With damping, average input can balance loss in steady state. Actual oscillators can leave the linear regime at large displacement, and a driven spring can break. The unbounded ideal response is a warning about a model's assumptions, not a promise of physical infinity. Test two frequency claims 1. Nonresonant forcing Exercise 1. Find a particular solution of x″+9x=2 cos(2t). Then say what happens to the proposed form if the forcing frequency becomes 3. Hint for 1 Substitute A cos(2t); its second derivative is −4A cos(2t). Worked solution for 1 (9−4)A=2, so A=2/5 and x p =(2/5)cos(2t). At frequency 3 the coefficient would be 9−9=0, so no finite A of this form solves the equation. A resonant particular solution for F=2 and ω 0 =3 is (t/3)sin(3t). 2. Damping at resonance Exercise 2. For x″+0.4x′+4x=cos(2t), compute the steady amplitude. Does the resonant response grow without bound? Hint for 2 Here ω 0 =2 and 2γ=0.4, so γ=0.2. Worked solution for 2 At ω=2, A=1/(2γω 0 )=1/(2·0.2·2)=1.25. The homogeneous transient decays because damping is positive, leaving a bounded sinusoid of amplitude 1.25. The undamped t-growth formula does not apply. The precise resonance claim Matching frequencies produce a linearly growing envelope in an undamped linear oscillator. Positive linear damping yields a finite steady frequency response. The difference follows from substituting actual solutions and accounting for energy input and loss. Continue to homogeneous spring motion for the root classification behind the transient.

title: Eigenvalues draw a phase portrait
summary: Use exact eigenmodes to classify representative planar linear phase portraits.
text: How can a matrix draw motion? A planar linear system gives a velocity vector at each point: u′=Au, where u=(x,y) and A is a fixed 2×2 matrix. Its phase portrait shows the resulting paths in the plane, with arrows for increasing time. Eigenvectors are especially useful because a state on one of their lines remains on that line. The sign and type of eigenvalues then reveal approach, escape, or rotation in elementary examples. Local background. Av=λv defines an eigenvector v≠0 and eigenvalue λ. If u(0)=cv, then u(t)=ce λt v solves u′=Au, as direct differentiation shows. For two independent eigenvectors, every initial state is their linear combination, so linearity combines the two corresponding solutions. Read three concrete matrices Worked example. First take A=diag(−2,−1). Then x(t)=x 0 e −2t and y(t)=y 0 e −t . Both coordinates decay. Unless y 0 =0, a trajectory approaches the origin tangent to the slower y-axis direction, although its exact shape depends on the initial state. This is a stable node. For A=diag(1,−2), x(t)=x 0 e t and y(t)=y 0 e −2t . The y-axis approaches the origin, while any x 0 ≠0 eventually escapes. This is a saddle, and a few trajectories approaching on the y-axis do not make the equilibrium stable. For A=[[-1,−2],[2,−1]], write u as a complex number z=x+iy. The equation becomes z′=(−1+2i)z. Thus z(t)=e −t e 2it z 0 : it rotates counterclockwise while its radius shrinks. The origin is a stable spiral. Three exact planar systems Matrix Eigenvalues Forward behavior diag(−2,−1) −2, −1 Node, all paths approach diag(1,−2) 1, −2 Saddle, most paths escape [[-1,−2],[2,−1]] −1±2i Spiral inward Prove what the picture shows If A has two linearly independent real eigenvectors v 1 ,v 2 with eigenvalues λ 1 ,λ 2 , write u 0 =c 1 v 1 +c 2 v 2 . Then u ( t ) = c 1 e λ 1 t v 1 + c 2 e λ 2 t v 2 Differentiating and using Av i =λ i v i verifies the equation and initial condition. Every solution has this form because any two solutions with the same initial state have a difference w satisfying w′=Aw, w(0)=0. For a fixed matrix, a standard norm inequality or the matrix-exponential construction gives uniqueness; alternatively, the component equations for these diagonalizable coordinates each have direct scalar uniqueness. This argument covers diagonalizable real matrices. A defective matrix needs terms such as te λt ; this article does not infer its portrait solely from a missing second eigenvector. When both real eigenvalues are negative, each exponential tends to zero, proving attraction. Stability in the formal small-start/small-trajectory sense also follows: choose coefficients continuously from the initial vector, and the decaying factors never exceed one for t≥0. If one eigenvalue is positive, arbitrarily small starts along its eigenvector eventually leave any fixed neighborhood, proving instability. If eigenvalues are −α±iβ with α>0, a real two-dimensional change of coordinates reduces the system to decay times rotation; the displayed spiral matrix makes this explicit. Eigenvalues with zero real part require additional care. The matrix [[0,−1],[1,0]] rotates circles and is stable but not attracting. The matrix [[0,1],[0,0]] has both eigenvalues zero yet solution y(t)=y 0 , x(t)=x 0 +ty 0 , which is unstable. The same real part can hide different behavior when a Jordan block is present. This is a theorem about linear constant-coefficient systems. For a nonlinear system u′=F(u), the Jacobian near an equilibrium is only a local approximation. When eigenvalues avoid the imaginary axis, a separate linearization theorem supports local conclusions under smoothness assumptions; zero-real-part cases require nonlinear analysis. Classify with evidence 1. Solve a diagonal system Exercise 1. For x′=−3x, y′=2y and (x(0),y(0))=(1,0.01), find the solution and classify the origin. Hint for 1 Solve each coordinate separately, then ask whether every small initial vector stays small forever. Worked solution for 1 x=e −3t , y=0.01e 2t . The eigenvalues are −3 and 2, so the origin is a saddle. This particular path eventually leaves any bounded neighborhood because its y-coordinate grows, despite the small initial y-value. 2. Compare two zero-eigenvalue systems Exercise 2. Why is knowing that all eigenvalues have real part zero insufficient to call a planar linear equilibrium stable? Hint for 2 Compare a rotation matrix with an upper triangular nilpotent matrix. Worked solution for 2 For A=[[0,−1],[1,0]], solutions rotate with constant radius, so sufficiently small starts remain equally small: stable. For B=[[0,1],[0,0]], a start (0,ε) yields (εt,ε), which eventually leaves any fixed ball: unstable. Both matrices have eigenvalues with zero real part. Jordan structure and the actual solution matter. Use eigenvalues within their scope For the solved linear examples, exponential modes make phase portraits and stability claims exact. Negative real parts give attraction, a positive real part gives escape, and zero real parts are a warning to inspect more structure. The linearization boundary shows an even sharper warning for nonlinear systems.

title: Where a local approximation stops deciding
summary: Prove opposite stability conclusions for two cubic equations with the same zero linearization.
text: What if the tangent rate is zero? Near an equilibrium x=0, a common first move is to replace x′=f(x) by x′≈f′(0)x. For f(x)=−x³ and g(x)=+x³, both derivatives at zero are zero. Their linear approximations are the identical equation x′=0, but their actual motions run in opposite directions. This is where first-order linearization stops deciding stability. Local background. An equilibrium x * obeys f(x * )=0. Lyapunov stability means: for every allowed radius ε>0, some δ>0 ensures that any solution starting within δ of x * remains within ε for all later times for which it exists. Attraction additionally means nearby solutions tend to x * . “Asymptotically stable” combines the two. These are statements about all nearby starting values, not one trajectory. Two opposite phase lines Worked example. For x′=−x³, a positive x has negative velocity and a negative x has positive velocity. Both arrows point toward zero. For x′=+x³, both arrows point away. For x 0 ≠0, separation gives the exact formulas x(t)=x 0 /√(1+2x 0 ²t) in the negative-cubic case, and x(t)=x 0 /√(1−2x 0 ²t) in the positive-cubic case while the denominator is positive. The signs are retained by choosing the branch with x(0)=x 0 . Identical linearization, opposite dynamics Equation f′(0) Forward outcome near zero x′=−x³ 0 Approaches zero x′=+x³ 0 Escapes; finite-time blow-up Compare departures on a finite timescale. With x₀=0.1, the negative-cubic solution at t=50 is 0.1/√2, while the positive-cubic solution's denominator reaches zero at t=50. At much shorter times both may look nearly stationary because their initial velocities are only ±0.001. A short, coarse plot can therefore conceal their opposite eventual behavior. The exact denominator gives the timescale and the domain of each formula; visual agreement near the initial point cannot replace that information. Prove the two stability claims For the negative cubic, differentiating x −2 where x≠0 gives d(x −2 )/dt=−2x −3 (−x³)=2. That produces the first formula. It exists for all t≥0, satisfies |x(t)|≤|x 0 | and tends to zero. Given ε, choose δ=ε. Every start |x 0 |<δ then remains inside ε, and attraction follows from the formula. The zero start stays at zero. Thus zero is asymptotically stable. For the positive cubic, d(x −2 )/dt=−2. The denominator in the second formula vanishes at t=1/(2x 0 ²). To prove instability without relying on the word “blow-up,” fix any ε>0. Whatever δ>0 is proposed, choose 0<x 0 <min(δ,ε). The solution rises continuously to ε at time (1/x 0 ²−1/ε²)/2, which is positive and precedes blow-up. It therefore leaves the ε-neighborhood. That contradicts the stability condition. f − ′ ( 0 ) = f + ′ ( 0 ) = 0 , f ± ( x ) = ± x 3 For a continuously differentiable scalar rate f with f(x * )=0 and f′(x * )<0, the derivative's continuity makes the local arrows point toward x * and gives local asymptotic stability. If f′(x * )>0, the arrows point away and the equilibrium is unstable. The broader multidimensional hyperbolic linearization principle likewise requires no eigenvalue with zero real part and enough regularity; this lesson does not prove that general theorem. Here f′(0)=0, so neither sign test applies. The cubic term supplies the decision directly. The negative-cubic approach is slower than exponential: for large t, |x(t)| is proportional to t −1/2 . A zero eigenvalue does not mean “nothing happens.” It means the first-order term vanishes and higher-order terms may control the timescale and direction. Inspect the first nonzero term 1. An even power Exercise 1. For x′=−x², classify zero on the whole real line. Is an inward arrow on the positive side enough? Hint for 1 On both sides, −x²<0. For x 0 <0 solve by separation. Worked solution for 1 Positive starts move toward zero, but negative starts move farther left. The solution x(t)=x 0 /(1+x 0 t) blows down at t=−1/x 0 >0 for x 0 <0. Arbitrarily small negative starts eventually leave a fixed neighborhood, so zero is unstable on ℝ. Restricting the state space to x≥0 would change the claim. 2. A parameter perturbation Exercise 2. For x′=−a x³ with a>0, give the solution from x(0)=b and a δ choice proving stability of zero. Hint for 2 Repeat the derivative of x −2 ; compare |x(t)| with |b|. Worked solution for 2 For b≠0, x(t)=b/√(1+2ab²t); for b=0, x=0. Because the denominator is at least one for t≥0, |x(t)|≤|b|. Given ε>0, δ=ε ensures starts |b|<δ stay below ε. The formula also tends to zero, proving asymptotic stability. What zero linearization means Matching zero derivatives can conceal attraction and instability. Exact sign and solution arguments decide these scalar examples. Linearization is powerful when its hypotheses apply; when a zero eigenvalue appears, inspect the nonlinear term and the state space. The fold model has a related nonhyperbolic boundary at its collision point.

title: A tiny parameter change can erase equilibrium
summary: Track two equilibria through a fold collision and justify their stability from signs.
text: How can two resting states disappear? Consider x′=μ−x², where μ is a fixed real parameter during each run. An equilibrium is a constant state whose right-hand side is zero. When μ>0 there are two; at μ=0 they meet; when μ<0 there are none. This is the saddle-node or fold normal form, a local model for an equilibrium collision. It does not assert that every real system follows this exact quadratic over a large range. Local background. For a scalar autonomous equation x′=f(x), a phase line marks zeros of f and draws arrows right where f>0 and left where f<0. An equilibrium attracts nearby trajectories if arrows on both sides point toward it. Its derivative f′(x * ) gives a local sign test when nonzero; a zero derivative needs direct analysis. Track the parameter Worked example. With μ=4, the equilibria are x=−2 and x=+2. Between them, x′=4−x²>0, so states move right. Outside them, x′<0, so states move left. At −2, arrows point away on both sides: unstable. At +2, arrows point in: attracting. If μ=−1, x′=−1−x²<0 everywhere, so no resting state exists. At μ=0, x′=−x²: states to the right move toward zero, but states to the left move away. The single equilibrium is one-sided attracting and unstable on the whole real line. Equilibria of x′=μ−x² Parameter Equilibria Local behavior μ>0 −√μ, +√μ Negative branch repels; positive branch attracts μ=0 0 Attracts from right only μ<0 None Velocity always negative The table is the static phase-line equivalent of the optional parameter experiment. Derive the branches and the boundary Setting μ−x²=0 gives x²=μ. Real roots exist only for μ≥0, with two distinct roots when μ>0. The rate derivative is f′(x)=−2x. At x=+√μ it is negative, which matches arrows toward the equilibrium. At x=−√μ it is positive, matching arrows away. As μ decreases to zero, the equilibrium branches meet at x=0 and the derivative there becomes zero. x ± ( μ ) = ± μ for μ > 0 , f ′ ( x ± ) = ∓ 2 μ At μ=0, linearization says x′≈0 and cannot classify the equilibrium. The exact sign f(x)=−x²≤0 shows why the two sides differ. On the right, x′<0 and x decreases toward zero. On the left, x′<0 and x becomes more negative. Indeed x(t)=x 0 /(1+x 0 t). For x 0 >0 it approaches zero; for x 0 <0 it diverges to negative infinity at t=−1/x 0 . Thus zero is unstable as a two-sided equilibrium. For μ<0, write μ=−a² with a>0. Then x′=−(a²+x²)≤−a², so every trajectory moves left at a speed at least a² while it exists. This inequality alone does not quantify its entire lifetime. Separation gives arctan(x/a)=−at+C; the tangent representation reaches a pole in finite forward time for every finite start. A numerical solver should stop before overflow rather than report a trajectory after this singular time. For μ>0, starts below the unstable lower equilibrium also can run toward negative infinity in finite time; the phase-line classification is local around each equilibrium. Calling this a generic saddle-node bifurcation requires conditions on a wider family F(x,μ), such as a nonzero parameter derivative and nonzero second state derivative at the collision. This page proves the behavior of the stated normal form only. The name supplies context, not an unproved universality claim. Move the branches 1. Change the scale Exercise 1. For x′=9−x², find equilibria and classify each using signs or derivatives. Hint for 1 Set x²=9, then evaluate −2x at both roots. Worked solution for 1 The equilibria are −3 and +3. At −3, f′=6>0 and nearby arrows move away, so it is unstable. At +3, f′=−6<0 and arrows move toward it, so it is locally asymptotically stable. 2. Inspect the collision Exercise 2. At μ=0, a student says that zero is stable because solutions starting just to its right move toward it. Identify the missing starts and demonstrate failure. Hint for 2 Choose an arbitrarily small negative x 0 and use x(t)=x 0 /(1+x 0 t). Worked solution for 2 Stability on ℝ requires all sufficiently nearby starts, including those to the left. For x 0 =−δ/2, the solution is negative and its magnitude grows as the positive denominator 1−δt/2 shrinks. It reaches any fixed negative threshold before its blow-up time 2/δ. Therefore no δ works for the full two-sided stability definition. The model's precise transition The fold normal form has two equilibria for positive μ, one nonhyperbolic equilibrium at zero, and none for negative μ. Phase arrows, not the root count alone, determine stability. The collision illustrates why a zero derivative calls for direct analysis. Compare the cubic examples for another zero-derivative boundary.

title: Simple repetition, complicated futures
summary: Prove local fixed-point results for a discrete logistic map while delimiting numerical chaos evidence.
text: What changes when time advances in steps? The logistic map repeats x n+1 =r x n (1−x n ). Here n is an integer step, x n is a fraction in [0,1], and r is a fixed parameter. This is a discrete dynamical system, not the logistic differential equation P′=rP(1−P/K). Similar formulas do not imply similar long-term behavior. The map is a compact setting for fixed points, loss of stability and sensitivity to initial conditions. Local background. Iteration means applying the same function repeatedly: x 1 =f(x 0 ), x 2 =f(f(x 0 )). A fixed point x * satisfies f(x * )=x * . For a differentiable map, a small error e near a fixed point is approximately multiplied by f′(x * ) each step. A bound |f′|<1 in a whole neighborhood proves local attraction by the mean value theorem; the derivative at one point alone only supplies the nearby candidate test when it is strictly inside or outside the unit circle. Two parameter values, different futures Worked example. At r=2, the nonzero fixed point is x * =1−1/2=1/2. From x 0 =0.2, the first steps are 0.32, 0.4352 and about 0.4916. They approach one-half rapidly. At r=3.2, the same fixed-point formula gives 0.6875, but its derivative is 2−3.2=−1.2, so small displacements from it grow while alternating sides. A numerical sequence may instead approach a two-cycle; a finite list of decimals can suggest that but cannot prove its exact period or long-term behavior. Fixed-point multipliers Parameter Fixed point Derivative there Local verdict r=0.8 0 0.8 Attracting r=2 1/2 0 Attracting r=3.2 0.6875 −1.2 Repelling Prove the bounded fixed-point claims For 0≤r≤4 and x∈[0,1], x(1−x) lies in [0,1/4], so f r (x)=rx(1−x) lies in [0,1]. Thus the state interval is invariant. Solve rx(1−x)=x: either x=0, or x=1−1/r when r≠0. The nonzero fixed point lies in (0,1) exactly when r>1. Differentiating gives f′ r (x)=r(1−2x), hence f r ′ ( 0 ) = r , f r ′ ( 1 − 1 / r ) = 2 − r For 0<r<1, zero is locally attracting because |r|<1. In fact f r (x)≤rx for x∈[0,1], so x n ≤r n x 0 →0. For 1<r<3, |2−r|<1, so the positive fixed point is locally attracting. For 3<r≤4, |2−r|>1, and nearby displacements from that point expand initially; it is repelling. At r=1 and r=3 the multiplier has absolute value one, so this derivative criterion is inconclusive. Those boundary values need higher-order or second-iterate analysis. The local attraction argument is exact: if |f′(x * )|<1, continuity of f′ gives a small interval around x * on which |f′|≤q<1. The mean value theorem then gives |f(x)−x * |≤q|x−x * |, keeps nearby points in the interval, and yields geometric convergence. If |f′(x * )|>1, continuity gives local expansion away from the fixed point for nonzero nearby errors; that proves it cannot attract all nearby starts. At r=4 there is an exact identity: if x=sin²(πθ), then 4x(1−x)=sin²(2πθ). Thus angle doubling generates particular exact trajectories of the map. Nearby angles can separate quickly before folding back through the sine-square projection. This identity gives a rigorous mechanism for complicated motion, but it does not by itself prove every formal definition of chaos for every starting value. A finite cobweb plot or a table of iterates is evidence about sampled behavior, not a proof of a period-doubling cascade or universality. Computer arithmetic also rounds states. At r=4, x 0 =1/2 maps to 1 and then 0 forever; other rational or rounded starts can eventually fall onto short cycles. A long numerical trace must be interpreted alongside exact mathematics and precision checks. Calculate, then qualify 1. Stability from a multiplier Exercise 1. For r=5/2, find both fixed points, their multipliers, and the local conclusion for each. Hint for 1 The multipliers are r at zero and 2−r at the positive fixed point. Worked solution for 1 The fixed points are 0 and 1−2/5=3/5. At zero, f′=5/2>1, so it repels positive nearby starts. At 3/5, f′=2−5/2=−1/2; continuity of f′ gives a local contraction neighborhood, so 3/5 attracts nearby starts with alternating error signs. 2. A false transfer from continuous time Exercise 2. A student says that because logistic differential equations approach carrying capacity, x n+1 =4x n (1−x n ) must approach 3/4. Refute the claim with one exact orbit. Hint for 2 Start at x 0 =1/2. Worked solution for 2 At r=4, the positive fixed point is 1−1/4=3/4, but x 0 =1/2 gives x 1 =1, x 2 =0, and then x n =0 for all n≥2. This exact orbit does not approach 3/4. Also f′(3/4)=−2, so the fixed point repels nearby starts. Continuous and discrete models have different update rules. What is established Fixed-point calculations and derivative bounds rigorously classify selected local behavior of the logistic map. The r=4 angle identity hints at sensitive behavior, while a finite numerical picture alone cannot certify chaos or universal period doubling. This is a bounded introduction to discrete dynamics; compare continuous logistic growth to see how the time rule changes the conclusion.

title: A square as an algebra machine
summary: Eight square symmetries, composition order, and a complete group-axiom proof.
text: Eight moves, one operation Label a square's corners 1, 2, 3, 4 clockwise, starting at the top left. These are the same labels and fixed vertical mirror used in the short turn-and-flip discovery . A symmetry puts the square back on its outline while possibly moving its labels. Four turns and four reflections do that. Could combining two of them ever produce a ninth kind? Background capsule. A function assigns one output to each input. Here its input is a corner's original position and its output is that corner's destination. A bijection uses each destination exactly once, so it can be undone. Two moves count as the same symmetry when every original corner reaches the same destination. We study those final actions, rather than how long a physical motion takes. The fixed positions of the square Positions 1, 2, 3, 4 run clockwise from top left. A dashed vertical mirror passes through the centre, between positions 1 and 2 and between 4 and 3. 1 2 3 4 Position numbers stay fixed on the page; each move carries the corner labels to new positions. Read a product from the right Call the clockwise quarter-turn R , the fixed vertical reflection F , and doing nothing E . The product FR , also written F ∘ R , means apply R first, then F . A superscript counts repetitions: R 2 is two quarter-turns, R 3 is three, and R 0 means E . These are powers of a move, not powers of a corner number. Follow a corner, then collect the moves Worked example. A quarter-turn sends positions 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 1. The vertical flip exchanges 1 with 2 and 4 with 3. To calculate FR on original corner 1, turn first: 1 goes to 2. Then flip: 2 goes to 1. Reversing the order sends 1 to 2 by the flip and then to 3 by the turn. The two products disagree on this one corner, so they are different symmetries. F ∘ R ≠ R ∘ F The table records destinations of original corners . For example, the R row says original corner 1 moves to position 2. It is not a list of the labels you see clockwise after moving the square; those are a different way of describing the same action. Where each original corner goes, with positions numbered as in the diagram Move Destinations of 1, 2, 3, 4 Action E 1, 2, 3, 4 Do nothing R 2, 3, 4, 1 Quarter-turn R 2 3, 4, 1, 2 Half-turn R 3 4, 1, 2, 3 Three quarter-turns F 2, 1, 4, 3 Vertical reflection FR 1, 4, 3, 2 Turn, then reflect FR 2 4, 3, 2, 1 Half-turn, then reflect FR 3 3, 2, 1, 4 Three quarter-turns, then reflect Why exactly eight? Original corner 1 has four possible destinations. Its adjacent corner 2 must then go to one of that destination's two neighbours. The image of corner 3 must be opposite the image of 1, and corner 4 takes the remaining position. That gives at most 4 × 2 = 8 possible actions. All eight rows are distinct and are realised by actual turns or reflections, so the count is exactly eight. The last four rows are reflections in the vertical, top-left-to-bottom-right diagonal, horizontal, and other diagonal axes, respectively. Four reasons this collection is a group Exact statement. The eight symmetries of this square form a group under composition. “Group” names a collection with one operation satisfying the following four requirements. In this example, the operation is doing one move after another. Closure: a product stays in the collection. A rigid motion preserves distances. Doing two such motions still preserves distances, and if each puts the square onto itself, their combination does too. We already counted every possible final symmetry, so that combination must be one of our eight. Identity: one action changes nothing. The move E leaves every corner fixed. Doing it before or after any symmetry leaves that symmetry's action unchanged. Inverses: every action can be undone. A quarter-turn is undone by three quarter-turns; a half-turn by another half-turn; and E by itself. Each of the four reflections is its own inverse: it swaps pairs of corners or fixes them, so repeating it restores every corner. Thus all inverse actions belong to our collection. Associativity: grouping does not change a fixed order. Take any three moves f , g and h , and any original corner i . Both ( fg ) h and f ( gh ) send it to f ( g ( h ( i ))). Each applies h first, then g , then f . The parentheses group the work but do not swap the moves, so the final actions agree on every corner. R 4 = E , F 2 = E The two equations record four quarter-turns and two vertical flips returning to the identity. This eight-element group is often called D 4 , the dihedral group of the square. A group is abelian if every pair of its actions commutes, meaning the order can be swapped. Ours is nonabelian : FR and RF already supplied a counterexample. Associativity holds even though commutativity fails; they ask different questions. Try a product, then test a claim 1. Calculation. Read ( FR )( R 2 ) from the right. Simplify it and find its inverse. Which position receives original corner 1? Hint for question 1 First do two quarter-turns, then the quarter-turn and flip in the left factor. Combine the three turns and find that row in the table. Full solution for question 1 Associativity lets us write ( FR )( R 2 ) = F ( RR 2 ) = FR 3 . The table gives destinations 3, 2, 1, 4, so original corner 1 goes to position 3. This is a reflection, swapping 1 and 3 and fixing 2 and 4; repeating it restores all corners. Its inverse is itself. 2. Explanation. Someone says, “Since parentheses do not matter in this group, the order of the moves does not matter either.” Give one corner that defeats this claim, and name the two properties being confused. Hint for question 2 Compare FR and RF on original corner 1. Parentheses and swapping are separate changes. Full solution for question 2 FR sends 1 to 2 by the turn, then to 1 by the flip. RF sends 1 to 2 by the flip, then to 3 by the turn. Their final actions differ. Associativity permits regrouping a fixed sequence of moves; commutativity would permit swapping two moves. The first holds here, and the second fails. A square you can reason with You have collected every symmetry of the square and justified closure, identity, inverses and associativity. One corner also proves that the group is nonabelian. The argument depends on exact destinations, not how a physical animation looks. A table of all 64 products could record the answers; the reasons above explain why the operation has the required laws. For another sitting, try explaining the difference between regrouping three moves and swapping two. If you want an example where every pair commutes, continue to addition on a modular clock .

title: Clock arithmetic is a group
summary: Residue classes form an abelian group under well-defined addition.
text: When do different integers mean the same hour? A twelve-hour clock identifies 1, 13 and −11. The hand lands in the same place after adding any multiple of twelve. We can make that observation exact for every integer modulus n≥2, then ask whether the resulting addition obeys the group rules. A clock picture is helpful, but a proof must explain why choosing different integer names for the same position cannot change an answer. Background capsule. Write a≡b (mod n) when n divides a−b; equivalently a−b=kn for some integer k. The residue class [a] contains all a+kn with k an integer. There are exactly n classes, represented by 0 through n−1. The class is the object; its printed representative is only a convenient name. Integer addition is associative and commutative, and every integer a has an additive opposite −a. A calculation with two names Worked example. Work modulo 7. Since 10≡3 and −4≡3, [10]=[−4]=[3]. Add the class [5]: 10+5=15 leaves remainder 1, while −4+5=1 leaves remainder 1. Thus [10]+[5]=[1] and [−4]+[5]=[1]. The two calculations agree despite the different representatives. Likewise, [5]+[2]=[0], so [2] is the additive inverse of [5]; [−5]=[2] is another way to write that inverse. One row of addition modulo 7 Second class [0] [1] [2] [3] [4] [5] [6] [5] plus [5] [6] [0] [1] [2] [3] [4] As the second entry runs through all seven classes, the outputs also run through all seven classes. Addition by [5] merely permutes the positions. This is why the equation [5]+[x]=[1] has one solution, namely [x]=[3]. It is not an invitation to divide by 5; addition and multiplication are different operations. Undo addition without choosing a special representative Solve [−3]+[x]=[4] modulo 11. Add [3], the additive inverse of [−3], to both sides. Associativity and the identity law give [x]=[7]. Checking with the representative 7 gives −3+7=4. Checking with the different representative 18 gives −3+18=15, and 15 differs from 4 by 11, so it gives the same output class. Both integers name one solution in the quotient group. There are infinitely many integer representatives, precisely 7+11k for integers k, but only one solution class. To prove uniqueness, if [x] and [y] both satisfy the equation, add [3] to both equalities; each must equal [7], hence they are the same class. This cancellation argument uses additive inverses, which exist modulo every n≥2. It never divides by a residue. A composite modulus would give the same additive cancellation even when multiplicative division fails. From a clock to a group Define addition of classes by the central rule [ a ] + [ b ] = [ a + b ] Exact statement and proof. For every integer n≥2, the residue classes modulo n form an abelian group under this addition. First establish well-definedness : if a′=a+kn and b′=b+ln, then (a′+b′)−(a+b)=(k+l)n. Thus [a′+b′]=[a+b], so the output depends only on input classes. Closure follows because a+b is an integer and therefore has a class. Associativity follows from integer associativity: ([a]+[b])+[c]=[(a+b)+c]=[a+(b+c)]=[a]+([b]+[c]). The identity is [0], since [a]+[0]=[a]. The inverse of [a] is [−a], since [a]+[−a]=[0]. Finally, [a]+[b]=[b]+[a] because a+b=b+a. This last property makes the group abelian. The proof is a model for constructing operations on equivalence classes. You must check that changing a representative leaves the result unchanged before using familiar integer laws on the classes. Without that step, notation such as [a]+[b] might depend on arbitrary choices. Multiplication of classes is also well-defined, but its nonzero elements do not always have multiplicative inverses. For example [2]·[3]=[0] modulo 6, so division by [2] cannot behave like division by a nonzero real number. Use classes rather than labels 1. Calculation. Modulo 9, solve [7]+[x]=[2]. Check your answer with representatives 16 for [7] and −7 for [2]. Hint for question 1 Add the inverse [−7] to both sides, and remember that −5 and 4 give the same class modulo 9. Full solution for question 1 [x]=[2−7]=[−5]=[4]. Check: [7]+[4]=[11]=[2]. With the alternate names, 16+4=20 and 20−(−7)=27, a multiple of 9, so [16]+[4]=[−7] as required. 2. Explanation. Someone defines [a]⊙[b]=[a+b+1] modulo 5 and claims [0] is its identity. Test that claim and find the actual identity if one exists. Hint for question 2 Compute [a]⊙[0]. Solve [a]⊙[e]=[a] for a possible e. Full solution for question 2 [a]⊙[0]=[a+1], which differs from [a], so [0] is not an identity. The equation [a+e+1]=[a] requires [e+1]=[0], hence [e]=[−1]=[4]. Indeed [a]⊙[4]=[a+5]=[a], and commutativity gives [4]⊙[a]=[a]. A familiar-looking set does not fix the identity independently of its chosen operation. The clock's precise promise Modulo-n addition is a group operation for every n≥2 because its class rule is well-defined and inherits the required laws from integers. The additive inverse of [a] is always [−a]. The failure case is multiplication: modulo 6, nonzero [2] and [3] multiply to zero, so this lesson's group conclusion does not say every nonzero class can be divided out. Next, repeat addition by a fixed class and count how long it takes to return to [0]. That count is the order of the element and reveals a smaller cyclic group inside the clock.

title: How long until a symmetry returns?
summary: Repeated powers return to the identity and form a cyclic subgroup in a finite group.
text: How many repeats bring you home? A quarter-turn of a square must be applied four times to restore the original labelled position. A half-turn needs two applications. The word order turns this return time into a property of any group element. It is a positive integer in a finite group, even when the group operation is addition and the notation looks different. Background capsule. A group G has an associative operation, an identity and an inverse for each element. An inverse undoes an action. A subgroup is a subset that itself has the group laws using the same operation. We will first count repeats, then show that the powers of one element form such a subset. Read the repeat notation G names the group and g names one of its elements. Here E names the identity: the do-nothing element. Write g² for doing g twice and g k for k repeats when k is positive. By convention g⁰ = E. Write g −1 for the inverse; g −k means k repeats of that inverse. A negative power does not mean a negative number of forward moves. Under addition, repeats are written kg instead: add g to itself k times. In addition modulo 8, [3] is the class of integers with remainder 3, and 2[3] = [6]. The identity is [0]. We write ord(g) for the least positive repeat count returning to the identity. The symbol ⟨g⟩ names the set of all integer powers, including the identity and inverse powers; it is called the cyclic subgroup generated by g. Two return paths Worked example. Keep the square lesson's moves: R is a clockwise quarter-turn and F is the fixed vertical reflection, with corners 1–4 clockwise from the top left. R has powers E, R, R², R³, E, …, so ord(R) = 4. F has E, F, E, …, so ord(F) = 2. In the additive group modulo 8, compare adding [2] with adding [3]. Start at [0] and add the named class once per repeat, modulo 8 Repeats k Add [2]: k[2] Add [3]: k[3] 0 [0] [0] 1 [2] [3] 2 [4] [6] 3 [6] [1] 4 [0] — first return [4] 5 [2] [7] 6 [4] [2] 7 [6] [5] 8 [0] [0] — first return Row zero is the starting state, so it does not count as a positive return. The first return for [2] is at k = 4, giving order 4. For [3] it is at k = 8, giving order 8. At k = 4, that second path has reached [4], not the identity [0]. Order counts repeats until the identity first reappears, not the label reached or the number of rows you chose to display. Why powers form a subgroup The exact definition in a finite group is ord ( g ) = min { k ∈ Z >0 : g k = E } Read this as “the smallest positive integer k for which k repeats of g give E.” The symbol ℤ >0 means positive integers; the braces collect the ones meeting the condition after the colon, and min selects the smallest. We still need to prove that this collection is nonempty when G is finite. Statement. In a finite group, g has a least positive return m, and ⟨g⟩ is a subgroup with exactly m elements. Find some return. Suppose G has N elements. Write N + 1 powers: E, g, g², …, g N . There are more entries than possible group elements, so two entries coincide: g i = g j for indices 0 ≤ i < j ≤ N. This is the pigeonhole principle. Multiply both sides by g −i , cancelling i repeats, to get E = g j−i . Since j − i is positive, a positive return exists. Let m be the least one. Count the distinct powers before it. E, g, …, g m−1 are distinct. Otherwise two of them, at indices i < j < m, would cancel to give a positive return j − i smaller than m, contradicting its choice. Account for every integer power. Divide any integer exponent k by m: k = qm + t, where q is an integer and 0 ≤ t < m. Then g k = (g m ) q g t = E q g t = g t . This works for negative k too. Every power therefore belongs to the m-element list in step 2, so that list is exactly ⟨g⟩. Check the subgroup laws. The identity g⁰ is in the set. For any integers a and b, the product g a g b = g a+b is still an integer power, and the inverse of g a is g −a , also in the set. Associativity comes from the operation in G. These are precisely the required group laws on the subset. The subgroup argument in step 4 works even in an infinite group. Finiteness was needed for the return and finite count in steps 1–3. Powers of one fixed element commute because adding their exponents commutes; unrelated group elements may still fail to commute, as R and F do. There is a useful divisibility test when the order is m: g k = E exactly when m divides k, meaning k is an integer multiple of m. Use k = qm + t again. The power is g t ; among 0 ≤ t < m, only t = 0 gives E, by the distinctness in step 2. Conversely, if t = 0, then g k = (g m ) q = E. Lagrange's theorem later connects this element order to the size of a finite group. Find and justify return times 1. Calculation. Find the order and full generated subgroup of [4] under addition modulo 10. Hint for question 1 Start at [0] and repeatedly add [4] until [0] first reappears. Full solution for question 1 The successive sums are [0],[4],[8],[12]=[2],[16]=[6],[20]=[0]. No earlier positive sum was [0], so ord([4])=5 and ⟨[4]⟩={[0],[4],[8],[2],[6]}. This set is closed under addition modulo 10 and contains additive inverses, as the general proof predicts. 2. Explanation. A learner sees g 6 =E and declares ord(g)=6. Why is this not enough? Supply an explicit square-symmetry counterexample. Hint for question 2 Choose a move that returns after two repetitions; six is also a multiple of two. Full solution for question 2 For the reflection F, F² = E, so F⁶ = (F²)³ = E. Yet ord(F) = 2 because 2 is the least positive return exponent. The equation g⁶ = E only implies that the actual order divides 6, by division with remainder; possibilities include 1, 2, 3 and 6. A finite return is guaranteed In a finite group, repeated powers must cycle back to the identity. The first return m counts exactly the elements of the cyclic subgroup ⟨g⟩. The finite hypothesis matters: in the infinite additive group of integers, repeatedly adding 1 never returns to zero, so 1 has infinite order. A finite animation of early powers cannot certify a return that has not occurred. For a next step, compare the size of ⟨g⟩ with the size of the whole group. The coset argument in Lagrange's theorem proves that the former divides the latter.

title: Why subgroup sizes divide
summary: Equal-sized cosets partition finite groups and force subgroup orders to divide group order.
text: Could four fit inside six? A group with six elements cannot have a subgroup with four elements. The obstruction is more precise than a failed search through examples: every subgroup cuts a finite group into equal-sized pieces called cosets. Counting those pieces proves a divisibility theorem. Background capsule. A group G is a set with an associative operation, identity and inverses. A subgroup H uses the same operation and contains its own products and inverses; its identity is the identity of G. Write |S| for the number of elements of a finite set S. For a fixed g in G, the left coset gH is {gh:h∈H}. The map h↦gh is a bijection, because multiplying by g −1 reverses it. Thus every left coset has |H| members, even when G is not commutative. Partition a six-element clock Worked example. Take G=Z/6Z under addition and H={[0],[2],[4]}. It is a subgroup: adding two even classes remains even, [0] is present, and the inverse of each listed class is listed. Its translate [1]+H is {[1],[3],[5]}. These two cosets are disjoint and cover all six classes. There are two pieces of three, so 6=2·3. We could choose [3] as a representative of the second coset and obtain the same set; distinct representatives need not produce distinct cosets. Left cosets of H in Z/6Z Representative Coset Size [0] {[0],[2],[4]} 3 [1] {[1],[3],[5]} 3 [3] {[3],[5],[1]} = [1]+H 3 Trying H with four elements would demand either one full piece of four and two leftovers, or some other unequal pieces. Both options conflict with the theorem's equal-piece partition. The theorem does not tell us which allowed sizes actually occur in a particular group: it only rules out sizes that do not divide the total. The equal-coset proof | G | = [ G : H ] | H | Lagrange's theorem, with proof. If H is a subgroup of a finite group G, its order divides |G|. The symbol [G:H] is the number of distinct left cosets. Every g lies in gH because the identity e belongs to H. Thus the cosets cover G. If aH and bH overlap, write ah₁=bh₂. Then b=a h₁ h₂ −1 , where h₁h₂ −1 belongs to H. For any h∈H, bh=a(h₁h₂ −1 h) lies in aH, so bH⊆aH. Reversing a and b gives equality. Hence any two cosets are disjoint or equal. Finally, h↦ah bijects H with aH; its inverse on that coset is x↦a −1 x. Counting [G:H] disjoint cosets of size |H| proves the displayed formula. Applying this to the cyclic subgroup ⟨g⟩ shows ord(g) divides |G| for every g in a finite group. For example, a group of order 10 cannot contain an element of order 3. The argument also shows g |G| =e: since ord(g) divides |G|, a power by the full group order is a multiple of the first return. The converse “every divisor of |G| occurs as a subgroup order” is false. The alternating group A₄ has order 12 but no subgroup of order 6: such a subgroup would have index 2 and hence be normal; the normal subgroups of A₄ are {e}, the Klein four group, and A₄ itself. That fact takes extra work, so the present proof does not establish it. Here the reliable conclusion is divisibility in one direction only. Count with care 1. Calculation. A finite group has 15 elements. What are the possible orders of an individual element? Can it have order 6? Hint for question 1 Apply Lagrange to ⟨g⟩, then list positive divisors of 15. Full solution for question 1 The order of g equals |⟨g⟩| and must divide 15. Its only possible values are 1, 3, 5 and 15. Therefore order 6 is impossible. The theorem does not assert that every listed value occurs in every group of order 15. 2. Explanation. Why is “aH and bH have a common element” enough to conclude they are the same set? Hint for question 2 Write the common element in both ways and solve for b in terms of a and an element of H. Full solution for question 2 If ah₁=bh₂, then b=ah₁h₂ −1 =ak for k∈H. Every bh equals a(kh), so bH⊆aH. Also a=bk −1 , so every ah lies in bH. Therefore aH=bH. This step uses closure and inverses in H, not commutativity of G. A one-way size test Cosets partition a finite group into equally sized blocks. This fully proves |H| divides |G| and, by taking H=⟨g⟩, ord(g) divides |G|. A divisor is only a candidate size. For existence questions, another construction or theorem is needed; even a perfectly divisible number need not correspond to a subgroup in every group. The same cosets will later become elements of a quotient group, but that requires an additional normality condition before multiplying cosets can make sense.

title: A map that respects the operation
summary: Operation-preserving maps, kernels and images through integer reduction.
text: What survives a simplifying map? A group homomorphism is a function that respects operations. It can collapse many inputs to one output while preserving the pattern of multiplication or addition. Reducing an integer modulo n is the cleanest example: different integers share a residue, yet adding before or after reduction gives the same class. Background capsule. A group operation may be written multiplicatively, ab, or additively, a+b. A function φ:G→K assigns each element of G an element of K. Its image is the set of outputs it actually reaches. Its kernel is the set of inputs sent to the identity of K. For the integer group under addition, the identity is 0 and the inverse of a is −a. In Z/nZ under addition, the identity is [0]. Congruence a≡b (mod n) means n divides a−b. Reduction modulo five Worked example. Let φ:Z→Z/5Z send a to [a]. Then φ(7+9)=[16]=[1], while φ(7)+φ(9)=[2]+[4]=[6]=[1]. Both paths agree. The kernel is all multiples of five: [a]=[0] exactly when 5 divides a. The image is every residue class because each class has an integer representative. In particular φ is onto, but not one-to-one: 0 and 5 share an output. One operation-preserving square Path Integer step Result class Add, then reduce 7+9=16 [16]=[1] Reduce, then add [7]=[2], [9]=[4] [2]+[4]=[1] This single square illustrates the rule but does not prove it for all integers. For that, use the definition of class addition: [a+b]=[a]+[b] for arbitrary a and b. The map is useful precisely because a large infinite group casts a five-element shadow with the same additive relation. Separate injectivity from surjectivity Consider d:Z→Z given by d(a)=2a, with addition as the operation in both groups. For arbitrary integers a,b, d(a+b)=2(a+b)=2a+2b=d(a)+d(b), so this is a homomorphism. Its kernel contains only 0, because 2a=0 forces a=0. Its image is the even integers: every output is even, and every even integer 2k is the output of k. This map is one-to-one: equal outputs 2a=2b force a=b. It is not onto its stated codomain Z, because no integer input maps to 1. If the codomain were instead declared to be 2Z, the same formula would be onto and would have inverse 2k↦k. The formula alone therefore does not settle surjectivity; the declared target matters. Compare reduction modulo five, whose image is its whole finite target but whose kernel has many elements. Neither operation preservation nor a small kernel should be confused with both halves of bijectivity. The operation-preserving equation φ ( a b ) = φ ( a ) φ ( b ) Exact statement and proof. For groups written multiplicatively, a homomorphism satisfies this equation for every a,b∈G. Reduction φ:Z→Z/nZ, a↦[a], is a homomorphism for every n≥2, with kernel nZ={kn:k∈Z} and image all of Z/nZ. The proof is direct: φ(a+b)=[a+b]=[a]+[b]. Also φ(a)=[0] exactly when a=kn, and every [r] is φ(r). No isomorphism theorem is needed for these conclusions. For an arbitrary group homomorphism, φ(e G )=e K . Indeed φ(e)=φ(e)φ(e), and multiplying by φ(e) −1 gives the claim. Likewise e=φ(aa −1 )=φ(a)φ(a −1 ), so φ(a −1 )=φ(a) −1 . These facts show the kernel is a subgroup: it contains e, and if a,b lie in it then φ(ab −1 )=e. The image is also a subgroup because products and inverses of attained outputs are attained. A kernel carries more information than mere size. If φ(a)=φ(b), then φ(b −1 a)=e, so b −1 a lies in the kernel. Conversely, that kernel condition implies φ(a)=φ(b). Thus fibers are cosets of the kernel. The first isomorphism theorem identifies the quotient by the kernel with the image, but this article has proved only the elementary kernel, image and fiber facts; the general quotient construction comes next. Check the operation first 1. Calculation. Define ψ:Z→Z/6Z by ψ(a)=[2a]. Find its kernel and image, and verify preservation of addition. Hint for question 1 Ask when 6 divides 2a. List the outputs of a=0,1,2,… until they repeat. Full solution for question 1 ψ(a+b)=[2(a+b)]=[2a]+[2b]=ψ(a)+ψ(b). Its kernel consists of a with 6|2a, equivalently 3|a, so ker ψ=3Z. Its image is {[0],[2],[4]}, since these are the outputs for a=0,1,2 and then the cycle repeats. 2. Explanation. Is f:Z→Z given by f(a)=a+1 a homomorphism of additive groups? Give one decisive test. Hint for question 2 An additive homomorphism must send 0 to 0. Full solution for question 2 No. f(0)=1, but the target group's identity is 0. Equivalently f(0+0)=1 while f(0)+f(0)=2. The failure is not repaired by the fact that f is a bijection; an operation-preserving map has a stronger requirement than one-to-one correspondence. What the shadow records A homomorphism preserves products, identity and inverses. The kernel tells exactly which inputs become the identity; for integer reduction it is nZ. The image tells which outputs occur. This article proved those claims directly and did not require a general isomorphism theorem. A tempting failure is to treat any convenient function as a homomorphism. Test the operation equation on arbitrary inputs or find a counterexample such as f(0)≠0. To turn kernel fibers into a new group, the quotient lesson explains the additional structural condition.

title: Collapse a normal subgroup
summary: Normal subgroups make multiplication of cosets independent of representatives.
text: When can whole blocks be multiplied? Reducing integers modulo n replaces every integer by a block of numbers that differ by multiples of n. The blocks can be added without ambiguity. In a general group, cosets are similar blocks, but multiplying them needs a precise condition. A quotient group exists when that condition, normality, holds. Background capsule. For a subgroup N of G, a left coset aN is {an:n∈N}. Two cosets are equal exactly when a −1 b∈N. A rule on cosets is well-defined if replacing a or b by another representative from the same coset does not change the output coset. A subgroup N is normal when gNg −1 =N for every g∈G; equivalently gN=Ng. In an abelian group every subgroup is normal because elements commute. Choose representatives, then change them Worked example. In the additive group Z, choose N=4Z. The coset 1+N is also represented by 5, and 2+N by −2. Adding representatives gives 1+2=3 or 5+(−2)=3, so both produce 3+N. Other choices can change the integer result by a multiple of four, but never its coset. This is the quotient Z/4Z as a group of four blocks. Contrast S₃, the permutations of {1,2,3}, with H={e,(12)}. H is a subgroup but not normal. Let a=(13) and h=(12), using right-to-left composition. The same coset aH can be represented by a or ah. If one tried to multiply it by a −1 H on the right, using a gives eH, but using ah gives aha −1 H=(23)H. These cosets differ because (23)∉H. So the proposed output depends on the chosen name of the input block. Representative test in S₃ Name for first coset Product representative Output coset a aa −1 =e H ah aha −1 =(23) (23)H≠H Count the blocks in a finite example Let G=Z/12Z under addition and let N={[0],[4],[8]}. Adding any two listed classes stays in N, and their additive inverses are again listed, so N is a subgroup. Since G is abelian, N is normal. There are four cosets: N, [1]+N={[1],[5],[9]}, [2]+N={[2],[6],[10]}, and [3]+N={[3],[7],[11]}. Each block has three members, accounting for all twelve elements without overlap. Add the first nonidentity coset to the last: ([1]+N)+([3]+N)=[4]+N=N. Changing representatives to [5] and [11] gives [16]=[4] in G and again the output N. The quotient's identity is the whole block N, which contains three elements of G; it is one element of G/N. Repeating [1]+N four times first reaches N, so this quotient element has order four. By contrast [2]+N returns after two additions. The quotient records which block a sum reaches, while forgetting which of the three original members supplied its representative. The normality criterion ( a N ) ( b N ) = a b N Exact statement and proof. If N is normal in G, this formula gives a well-defined group operation on the left cosets G/N. Suppose aN=a′N and bN=b′N. Then a′=an₁ and b′=bn₂ for some n₁,n₂∈N. Their product is a′b′=an₁bn₂=ab(b −1 n₁b)n₂. Normality puts b −1 n₁b in N, so the last two factors belong to N. Therefore a′b′N=abN. The rule is independent of representatives. Associativity follows from associativity in G; eN is the identity; a −1 N is the inverse of aN. Closure is automatic because abN is a coset. Normality is also necessary for this particular multiplication rule to be well-defined. If it were well-defined, eN=nN for every n∈N. Multiplying these equal cosets on the right by bN would give bN=nbN; hence b −1 nb∈N for every b,n. Replacing b by b −1 gives the reverse inclusion, so b −1 Nb=N. This is normality. The S₃ computation supplies a concrete failure when it is absent. For integers, N=nZ is normal because addition commutes. Its cosets a+nZ are precisely residue classes [a]. The quotient construction therefore explains why class addition works, while the direct clock proof remains a useful separate check. Quotient groups collapse a normal subgroup to one identity coset; they do not erase the original group operation. Audit a quotient rule 1. Calculation. In the quotient Z/(5Z), viewed as cosets of 5Z, compute (−2+5Z)+(9+5Z), then recompute using representatives 3 and 4. Hint for question 1 Both pairs name the same two input cosets. Add each pair and compare modulo 5. Full solution for question 1 The first representatives add to 7, giving 7+5Z=2+5Z. The alternatives add to 3+4=7, giving the same coset. Indeed 3−(−2)=5 and 4−9=−5 are multiples of 5. This checks one instance of representative independence; normality proves all instances. 2. Explanation. In S₃, H={e,(12)}. Explain in one computation why H is not normal. Hint for question 2 Conjugate (12) by (13). Full solution for question 2 (13)(12)(13)=(23), which is not in H. Thus (13)H(13) −1 ≠H, so H is not normal. Multiplying its left cosets by the proposed representative formula is consequently ambiguous, exactly as the worked example exhibits. What makes collapsing lawful A quotient group replaces elements by left cosets and multiplies them through representatives. That operation is well-defined exactly when the subgroup is normal. The proof handles both directions, not just the convenient integer case. A partition into equal-size cosets by itself is insufficient: Lagrange works for any subgroup, while quotient multiplication needs normality. Further questions include relating a homomorphism's kernel to a quotient. Kernels are always normal, but identifying the resulting quotient with the image is a separate theorem not proved here.

title: Polynomials are numbers with a variable
summary: Formal coefficient arithmetic, ring distributivity and the finite-field evaluation caveat.
text: Are polynomials just functions in disguise? Polynomials can be added and multiplied much like numbers, but it is useful to treat them as formal coefficient lists. Over a finite field, different polynomials can even produce the same value at every available input. This lesson proves a central ring law from finite sums and shows exactly where “same function” fails to mean “same polynomial.” Background capsule. A commutative ring R has addition, multiplication, zero and one with the familiar associative and distributive laws; additive inverses exist, but multiplicative inverses need not. A polynomial f∈R[x] is a finite formal sum a₀+a₁x+⋯+a d x d . Two polynomials are equal when every coefficient agrees, including trailing zeros. Evaluation at r∈R substitutes r for x and adds in R. The field F₂ has coefficients 0 and 1 with arithmetic modulo 2. Multiply coefficients, then evaluate Worked example. Let f=1+x and g=1+x+x² in Z[x]. Multiplication distributes every term of f over every term of g: fg=1+2x+2x²+x³. At x=2, f(2)=3 and g(2)=7, so f(2)g(2)=21. The product polynomial gives 1+4+8+8=21 as well. The agreement is a general algebraic law, not an accident of the chosen input. Convolution of coefficient lists Power Contributing products Coefficient x⁰ 1·1 1 x¹ 1·1+1·1 2 x² 1·1+1·1 2 x³ 1·1 1 Now work over F₂. The polynomial h=x²−x is not the zero polynomial: its x² coefficient is 1, and its x coefficient −1 equals 1 in F₂. Yet h(0)=0 and h(1)=1−1=0. It represents the zero function on F₂, whose only inputs are 0 and 1. An evaluation table cannot always recover formal coefficients. Why R[x] inherits distributivity ( f g ) k = ∑ i + j = k i , j ≥ 0 a i b j The displayed coefficient formula says that the coefficient of x k in fg is the sum of a i b j over pairs i+j=k; only finitely many terms are nonzero. Exact statement and proof. If R is a commutative ring with 1, then R[x] is also a commutative ring with 1. Addition is coefficientwise, giving associativity, commutativity, zero and additive inverses from R. Multiplication uses the displayed finite sum. Associativity follows because the coefficient of x k in (fg)h and f(gh) is in both cases the finite sum of a i b j c l over i+j+l=k; reassociating terms is valid in R. Its unit is the constant polynomial 1. Commutativity follows by exchanging i and j. For distributivity, write g=∑b j x j and h=∑c j x j . The coefficient of x k in f(g+h) is ∑ i+j=k a i (b j +c j ). Distributivity in R turns this into the sum of the k-coefficients of fg and fh. Equal coefficients mean equal formal polynomials. This proves f(g+h)=fg+fh for every polynomial, rather than relying on values at selected points. Evaluation preserves both addition and multiplication because substitution distributes through finite sums and products. The converse is delicate. Over an infinite integral domain, a nonzero polynomial cannot vanish everywhere; over F₂ the explicit h above does. Thus the polynomial ring and the ring of polynomial functions on F₂ are different objects. Track coefficients and functions 1. Calculation. Multiply (1+x)(1−x+x²) in Z[x], then evaluate both factors and the product at x=2. Hint for question 1 Distribute once and combine like powers; then use ordinary integer arithmetic at x=2. Full solution for question 1 The product is (1−x+x²)+(x−x²+x³)=1+x³. At x=2 it gives 1+8=9. The factors give 1+2=3 and 1−2+4=3, whose product is also 9. 2. Explanation. Over F₂, are x² and x the same polynomial? Are they the same function F₂→F₂? Hint for question 2 Compare coefficients first, then test both possible inputs. Full solution for question 2 They are different formal polynomials because their coefficients of x² and x differ. As functions they agree: at 0 both return 0, and at 1 both return 1. Their difference x²−x is nonzero as a polynomial and zero at every element of F₂. A formal object with evaluation maps Polynomial addition and multiplication form a ring because finite coefficient sums inherit the ring laws. Evaluation sends a formal polynomial to a function, but the map can merge distinct polynomials over finite fields. This is the failure case to remember when a table of outputs seems to determine an expression. Ideals provide another way to identify expressions, by declaring selected polynomial or integer relations to count as zero. That is a different construction from merely testing finitely many inputs.

title: Remainders as quotient rings
summary: Every ideal of the integers is nZ, yielding a quotient ring of residues.
text: Which integers may count as zero? Modulo n arithmetic declares every multiple of n equivalent to zero. The multiples are not just a subgroup under addition: multiplying any of them by any integer still produces a multiple of n. That absorbing property is what makes an ideal fit a quotient ring, where both addition and multiplication must survive. Background capsule. A commutative ring has addition, multiplication and distributivity. In Z the usual integer operations make a ring. An ideal I⊆Z is an additive subgroup with the extra rule that ri∈I whenever r∈Z and i∈I. Write nZ={nk:k∈Z}; the notation (n) means the ideal generated by n and equals nZ. Cosets a+I collect numbers differing by an element of I. The well-ordering principle says every nonempty set of positive integers has a least member. Collapse the multiples of four Worked example. Let I=4Z. Then 7+I=3+I because 7−3=4 belongs to I. Adding cosets gives (7+I)+(2+I)=9+I=1+I. Multiplying gives (7+I)(2+I)=14+I=2+I. If 7 is replaced by 3, the product becomes 3·2=6, which is still 2+I. The difference 14−6=8 belongs to I because it is a multiple of four. Representative audit modulo four First representative Second representative Product Coset 7 2 14 2+4Z 3 2 6 2+4Z 7 6 42 2+4Z The sample table supports the rule in this example, but the general calculation is stronger. If a′=a+i and b′=b+j with i,j∈I, then a′b′−ab=aj+bi+ij. Each term lies in I by absorption, so changing representatives cannot change the product coset. Addition is even simpler: (a+i)+(b+j) differs from a+b by i+j∈I. Every integer ideal has one generator Z / n Z = Z / ( n ) Exact statement and proof. Every ideal I of Z equals nZ for a unique integer n≥0. If I={0}, take n=0; this separate case matters because it has no positive element. Otherwise some nonzero a belongs to I, and its opposite −a also belongs, so I contains a positive integer. Let n be the least positive element of I. Closure under multiplication by arbitrary integers gives nZ⊆I. For any a∈I, integer division gives a=qn+r with 0≤r<n. Since qn∈I and I is an additive subgroup, r=a−qn∈I. Minimality of n forces r=0. Thus a∈nZ and I⊆nZ. Equality follows. Uniqueness follows because a nonzero nZ has n as its least positive member; 0Z alone has no positive member. For n≥2, the quotient ring Z/(n) consists of n cosets and uses [a]+[b]=[a+b] and [a][b]=[ab]. The representative calculation above proves both are well-defined. The zero coset is (n), and the multiplicative identity is 1+(n). When n=0, the quotient Z/(0) is just a copy of Z; when n=1 it has one element, so 0=1. The latter is a valid zero ring under some conventions but not a field. Naming these boundary cases prevents a false claim that every quotient ring has n distinct residues without restricting n. We proved a special classification for Z using integer division and well-ordering. It does not transfer unchanged to every ring. For instance the ideal (x,y) in the polynomial ring R[x,y] cannot be generated by a single polynomial when R is a field: any common generator would divide both x and y, so would be a nonzero constant and produce the whole ring, yet every polynomial in (x,y) has zero constant term. The point is that ideals encode relations, not that every ideal has one generator. Find the generator and test absorption 1. Calculation. Let I be an ideal of Z containing 18 and 30. What must I contain? If I is generated by just these two integers, what is I? Hint for question 1 Subtract integer multiples: 30−18=12 and 18−12=6. Check that both original generators are multiples of 6. Full solution for question 1 Every ideal containing 18 and 30 contains 30−18=12 and 18−12=6, then all multiples of 6 by absorption. The ideal generated by 18 and 30 is all integer combinations 18u+30v. Every such combination is divisible by 6, while 6=2·18−30 belongs to it. Hence the generated ideal is exactly 6Z. A larger ideal containing those integers could also exist, such as 3Z. 2. Explanation. The even integers are an ideal of Z. Are the odd integers an ideal? Identify the first failed requirement. Hint for question 2 An additive subgroup must contain zero and be closed under addition. Full solution for question 2 The odd integers do not contain zero, and 1+1=2 is not odd. They are therefore not an additive subgroup, so they cannot be an ideal. They also fail absorption: 2·1=2 is even. An ideal is more than a selected residue class; it is the set of elements treated as zero in a quotient. Relations as an ideal Every ideal of Z is nZ, including the zero ideal. The ideal property makes multiplication on cosets independent of representatives, giving the quotient ring Z/(n). The classification proof rests on least positive elements and integer division, so it is specific to integers. A coset such as 1+2Z is not an ideal: it is one block of the quotient, and it does not contain zero. The next question is when a nonzero coset has a multiplicative inverse. Prime moduli make every nonzero coset invertible; composite moduli create a zero-divisor obstruction.

title: Why division sometimes fails modulo n
summary: Bézout’s identity characterizes units and prime moduli characterize fields.
text: Why does division work modulo seven? Modulo 7, [3] has inverse [5] because 3·5=15≡1. Modulo 6, [2] has no inverse: its products with [0] through [5] are [0],[2],[4],[0],[2],[4], never [1]. The difference is governed by the greatest common divisor and, for the whole quotient ring, by primality of the modulus. Background capsule. In Z/nZ, [a][b]=[ab]. A multiplicative inverse of [a] is a class [b] with [a][b]=[1]. A field is a commutative ring with 0≠1 in which every nonzero element has an inverse. The greatest common divisor gcd(a,n) is the greatest positive integer dividing both. Bézout's identity says there are integers u,v with ua+vn=gcd(a,n). One can obtain it by repeatedly dividing with remainder: the last nonzero remainder is the gcd, and substituting backward expresses it as an integer combination. We use that stated identity as a local number-theory input. Two tiny multiplication tables Worked example. Modulo 7, Euclid's algorithm for 3 and 7 gives 7=2·3+1, so 1=7−2·3. Thus −2 is an inverse of 3 modulo 7, and [−2]=[5]. Multiplication confirms [3][5]=[15]=[1]. Modulo 6, gcd(2,6)=2, so no integer combination 2u+6v can equal 1. There is no inverse for [2]. More visibly, [2][3]=[0] although neither factor is zero. Each nonzero factor in such a product is called a zero divisor. Inverse check for two residues Ring Class gcd Consequence Z/7Z [3] gcd(3,7)=1 [3][5]=[1] Z/6Z [2] gcd(2,6)=2 [2][3]=[0] This distinction concerns multiplication. Both rings still have additive inverses for every class: modulo 6, [2]+[4]=[0]. A failed attempt to divide by [2] does not mean that modular addition has stopped being a group operation. Units, primes and the exact criterion [ a ] is invertible mod n ⇔ gcd ( a , n ) = 1 Exact statement and proof. Let n≥2. If gcd(a,n)=1, Bézout gives ua+vn=1. Taking classes modulo n gives [u][a]=[1], so [u] is an inverse. Conversely, if [a][b]=[1], then ab−1=kn for some integer k. Thus ab−kn=1 is an integer combination of a and n. Every common divisor of a and n divides 1, so their gcd is 1. This proves the displayed equivalence for every class, including [0], whose gcd with n is n and which is not a unit. Field criterion, with proof. Z/nZ is a field exactly when n is prime, for n≥2. If n=p is prime, every nonzero class [a] has p∤a, hence gcd(a,p)=1. The inverse criterion supplies an inverse, and 0≠1 because p≥2. Conversely, if n is composite, write n=uv with 1<u,v<n. Both [u] and [v] are nonzero, yet [u][v]=[n]=[0]. A field cannot contain nonzero zero divisors: multiplying xy=0 by x −1 would give y=0. Therefore Z/nZ is not a field. The argument also identifies the concrete failure, rather than merely saying that a multiplication table looks incomplete. A nonzero residue can still be invertible for composite n. For example [5] is its own inverse modulo 6 because 25≡1, while [2] is not. The field criterion requires every nonzero residue to be invertible. The excluded n=1 case has only one class, with [0]=[1], and fails the standard field axiom 0≠1. Find an inverse or prove none exists 1. Calculation. Find the inverse of [5] modulo 12, or justify that none exists. Then do the same for [8]. Hint for question 1 Compute each gcd with 12. For 5, use a small product; for 8, explain why an equation 8b−12k=1 is impossible. Full solution for question 1 gcd(5,12)=1, and 5·5=25=2·12+1, so [5] −1 =[5]. But gcd(8,12)=4. Every integer combination 8b−12k is divisible by 4, so it cannot equal 1; [8] has no multiplicative inverse. Indeed [8][3]=[24]=[0] with both factors nonzero. 2. Explanation. Someone claims Z/9Z is a field because [2] has an inverse. Diagnose the inference and provide a counterexample class. Hint for question 2 A field needs inverses for every nonzero class. Look at [3]. Full solution for question 2 [2] is invertible, with [2][5]=[1], but that checks only one nonzero class. The nonzero class [3] is not invertible because gcd(3,9)=3. Also [3][3]=[0], so a field is impossible. Nine is composite, exactly as the field criterion predicts. Division has an exact boundary For n≥2, a residue [a] is invertible exactly when gcd(a,n)=1. Consequently every nonzero residue is invertible exactly for prime n. The proof uses Bézout's identity for existence and zero divisors for failure. A table with a few successful divisions is not enough to call a ring a field; one nonzero zero divisor settles the question in the other direction. The same prime-versus-composite split appears when working with polynomial coefficients: over a field many familiar division algorithms work, while over a general ring extra care is needed.

title: Why prime powers force subgroups
summary: A precisely scoped statement of first Sylow and a worked small-order consequence.
text: Can the size of a group force a subgroup? Lagrange's theorem says a subgroup's size divides the size of a finite group. That is a restriction, not a general existence rule. Sylow's first theorem supplies a striking existence claim when the proposed size is the largest power of a chosen prime dividing the group order. This lesson states and proves its existence claim using translations of finite subsets; the extra counting ideas are developed below. Background capsule. A prime p has only 1 and p as positive divisors. Every positive integer N can be factored as p n m, where n≥0 and p does not divide m; p n is the largest p-power dividing N. A finite group subgroup H has order |H|, and Lagrange proves |H| divides |G|. A subgroup of order p n in a group of order p n m is called a Sylow p-subgroup. When p does not divide |G|, n=0 and the trivial subgroup of order 1 is the uninteresting case. Read a group order as several questions Worked example. Suppose |G|=12=2²·3. For p=2, the largest power is 4; for p=3, it is 3. Sylow's first theorem guarantees at least one subgroup of order 4 and at least one of order 3. It does not say those subgroups are unique, normal, cyclic, or visible from the number 12 alone. The square symmetry group D₄ has order 8=2³, so its entire group is a Sylow 2-subgroup; this case illustrates the statement but offers no insight into its difficult general proof. Forced prime-power subgroup sizes Group order Prime Largest prime power First Sylow conclusion 12 2 4 Some subgroup has order 4 12 3 3 Some subgroup has order 3 18 3 9 Some subgroup has order 9 A numerical table is a guide to the claim, not a proof of it. Inferring subgroup existence from one familiar example, such as a cyclic group of order 12, would leave every noncyclic group of the same order untreated.
