The theorem and its boundary | G | = p n m , p ∤ m ⇒ ∃ H ≤ G : | H | = p n First Sylow theorem, proved below. Let G be a finite group, p a prime, and |G|=p n m with p∤m. Then G has a subgroup H of order p n . Neither the table nor the example proves it. The proof below supplies the group action and counting argument needed beyond Lagrange's equal-coset count. The larger Sylow package also discusses conjugacy and the number of such subgroups, but those claims are not established here. A worked consequence, proved conditional on Sylow. Every group of order 30 has a subgroup of order 5. Factor 30=5·6 and note 5∤6; first Sylow provides a subgroup of order 5. Lagrange is consistent with this because 5 divides 30, but Lagrange alone would not produce it. The same theorem also gives subgroups of order 2 and 3 because 30=2·15=3·10. This application establishes only the listed prime-power sizes. It does not establish which other subgroup orders occur; divisibility alone is not a general existence theorem. One must choose the maximal p-power. For a group of order 12, first Sylow specifically supplies order 4 for p=2, not merely order 2. Once an order-4 subgroup exists, a separate argument can produce an order-2 subgroup: every group of order 4 has either an element of order 2 or is generated by an element of order 4 whose square has order 2. That elementary deduction does not extend to a general converse to Lagrange. A complete existence proof by translating subsets Counting lemma. Put q=p n . The number of q-element subsets of a set of size qm is the binomial coefficient C(qm,q), and it is not divisible by p when p∤m. To prove this, calculate polynomial coefficients modulo p. For 0<j<p, p divides C(p,j): in p!/[j!(p−j)!] the numerator has a factor p and the denominator does not. Thus (1+t) p ≡1+t p modulo p. Repeating this identity n times gives (1+t) q ≡1+t q . Raise both sides to m and compare coefficients of t q : C(qm,q)≡m modulo p. This is nonzero by assumption. Let Ω be the set of q-element subsets of G. Each g∈G sends S∈Ω to gS={gs:s∈S}. This is an action: the identity leaves S fixed, and g(hS)=(gh)S. The orbit of S consists of all its translates. Orbits partition Ω, since translating can be undone. Because |Ω| is not divisible by p, at least one orbit has size not divisible by p; otherwise adding the orbit sizes would make |Ω| divisible by p. Choose S in such an orbit. Let H={g∈G:gS=S}, its stabilizer . It is a subgroup: the identity fixes S, products of fixing elements fix S, and gS=S implies g −1 S=S. Two translates gS and hS agree exactly when h −1 g∈H, or equivalently gH=hH. Hence the orbit is in bijection with the left cosets of H. Lagrange's coset count gives |G|=|H|·|orbit|. Since the orbit size is not divisible by p, the full factor p n =q dividing |G| must divide |H|. On the other hand H acts on S by left multiplication. For each s∈S the map h↦hs is injective, because hs=h′s implies h=h′ after cancellation. Its image is the H-orbit of s, so every such orbit has exactly |H| elements. Those orbits partition S, which has q elements. Thus |H| divides q. Together q divides |H| and |H| divides q, forcing |H|=q. This is the required Sylow p-subgroup. The same argument includes n=0, when q=1 and the resulting subgroup is trivial. This proof establishes existence only. It neither counts all Sylow subgroups nor proves their conjugacy. The extra ingredient beyond Lagrange was the action on subsets and the coefficient count; a divisibility statement about subgroup sizes by itself could not supply H. Separate theorem use from proof 1. Calculation. A finite group has order 72=2³·3². What subgroup sizes does first Sylow force for p=2 and p=3? What does it not say about uniqueness? Hint for question 1 Use the largest full prime power dividing 72 for each selected prime. Full solution for question 1 For p=2, 72=2³·9 and 2∤9, so a subgroup of order 8 exists. For p=3, 72=3²·8 and 3∤8, so a subgroup of order 9 exists. First Sylow alone does not say either subgroup is unique. The counts of Sylow subgroups require additional Sylow theorems and hypotheses. 2. Explanation. A learner writes, “Since 4 divides 12, Lagrange proves every group of order 12 has a subgroup of order 4.” Repair the justification. Hint for question 2 Name which theorem restricts existing subgroups and which theorem produces maximal prime-power subgroups. Full solution for question 2 Lagrange proves that any existing subgroup order divides 12; it does not prove existence. Since 12=2²·3 and 2∤3, first Sylow guarantees a subgroup of order 2²=4. This is a correct theorem application, but it is not a proof of first Sylow from Lagrange or from the factorization alone. Know what was established You can state the first Sylow theorem with its finite-group and maximal-prime-power hypotheses, and use it to infer a forced subgroup size. The subset-action argument proves existence, including the trivial n=0 case. The failure case for overreach is the false converse to Lagrange: divisibility alone does not provide an arbitrary subgroup. Nor does first Sylow assert uniqueness or normality. A satisfying stopping point is to identify, for a given group order, which sizes are forbidden by Lagrange and which maximal prime-power sizes are guaranteed by first Sylow. Keep the two logical directions separate.

title: Draw the solutions of a polynomial
summary: Verify and describe real polynomial zero sets with exact substitution, including an empty-locus example.
text: Can one equation draw a shape? A polynomial equation in two coordinates selects the points where its value is zero. For example, x² + y² − 1 = 0 draws the unit circle in the real plane. The equation is an algebraic rule; the circle is its real zero locus . We will make that distinction precise, verify points exactly, and learn why a plot is only a guide. Background capsule. A polynomial in x and y is a finite sum of terms such as 3x²y and −5. To evaluate it at (a,b), replace x by a and y by b. The ordered pair belongs to its zero locus when the result equals zero. Coordinates are real throughout this lesson unless a different number system is named. A square of a real number cannot be negative; that simple fact will let us prove one zero set is empty without trusting a screen. Test before tracing Worked example. Set f(x,y)=y−x². At x=−2, substituting gives y=4, so (−2,4) is on the locus. At x=1, the point (1,2) fails because f(1,2)=2−1=1. Repeating this calculation for each chosen x makes the parabola. A numerical plot approximates a continuous curve with samples; exact substitution certifies only the selected points, while the equation y=x² describes every real point on it. Three polynomial rules with exact checks Rule Verified point or argument Real locus y−x² (−2,4): 4−4=0 Parabola x²+y²−1 (0,1): 0+1−1=0 Unit circle x²+y²+1 Every value is at least 1 Empty Notice that the last expression has a perfectly valid equation, despite having no real solutions. Over complex coordinates it does have solutions: (i,0) works because i²=−1. Changing the field changes the set under discussion. Even for real coordinates, a pixel-level drawing cannot prove emptiness or identify every component; the inequality above does that for this particular polynomial. The definition does the work Exact statement. For a real polynomial f in two variables, its real zero locus is V ℝ ( f ) = { ( a , b ) ∈ ℝ 2 : f ( a , b ) = 0 } This is a membership test, not a formula for how many points there are. Two different polynomials can have the same locus. Over real numbers, x²+y²=0 forces x=0 and y=0 because two nonnegative squares add to zero only if each is zero. The polynomial x²+y² and its square (x²+y²)² therefore have the same real locus, although their formulas differ and their algebraic behavior near the origin differs. Likewise, multiplying y−x² by 7 changes values away from the parabola but leaves its zero locus unchanged. Verified derivation for this example. For f=y−x², the condition f(a,b)=0 rearranges to b=a². Thus every chosen real a gives one point (a,a²), and conversely every point on the locus has that form. This proves the whole description of this locus, not just the table entries. For g=x²+y²+1, the inequalities x²≥0 and y²≥0 imply g≥1, so its real locus is empty. Neither argument extends merely by looking at a finite grid of sampled values. A polynomial can vanish between samples or at an isolated point they miss. A useful operation is to impose two equations at once: V ℝ (f,g) means points satisfying both. Geometrically it is the intersection of the separate zero loci. For instance, y−x²=0 and x=1 select only (1,1). That conclusion uses substitution, which becomes the main tool in curve intersections . We have proved descriptions only for the displayed examples; classifying zero loci of arbitrary polynomials is a much larger subject. Check a point and challenge a claim 1. Calculation. Describe all real points on V ℝ (y−2x+3), and decide whether (−1,−5) and (2,1) belong. Hint for question 1 Solve the equation for y, then substitute each ordered pair into the original polynomial. Full solution for question 1 Rearranging y−2x+3=0 gives y=2x−3, so the locus is {(t,2t−3):t∈ℝ}, a line. At (−1,−5), −5−2(−1)+3=0, so it belongs. At (2,1), 1−4+3=0, so it also belongs. Both checks agree with the parameter description: t=−1 gives −5 and t=2 gives 1. 2. Explanation. Someone says that every polynomial equation in x and y must draw a visible real curve. Test the claim with x²+y²+4=0, then say what happens over complex coordinates. Hint for question 2 Bound the left side below for real numbers. For complex numbers try x=2i and y=0. Full solution for question 2 For real x and y, x²+y²+4≥4, so equality to zero is impossible. Its real locus is empty, disproving the claim. Over complex numbers, (2i,0) is a solution because (2i)²+0+4=−4+4=0. A change of allowed coordinates changes the locus. What the picture can and cannot certify A zero locus is defined by exact evaluation, and a graph suggests where to test. The same real set can come from distinct equations, while a valid equation may have no real points. Stop here once you can describe a simple locus in both directions: prove each proposed point satisfies the equation, and prove every solution has the proposed form. The next step is to impose two equations and solve their common points.

title: Two curves, how many meetings?
summary: Classify line–circle meetings by a quadratic discriminant, with real and complex cases.
text: How many times does a line meet a circle? A line may appear to cross a circle twice, touch once, or miss it. Exact algebra distinguishes these cases and reveals something a real picture can hide: the missed intersections can still have complex coordinates. We will solve one family completely, without invoking a general curve-counting theorem. Background capsule. A point lies on both curves only if it satisfies both equations. Substitution replaces one variable using the line equation. A real quadratic at²+bt+c=0 with a≠0 has discriminant Δ=b²−4ac: positive means two distinct real roots, zero one repeated real root, and negative no real roots. In the complex numbers, a square root of a negative real exists because i²=−1, so the same quadratic still has roots counted with repetition. Move a horizontal line Worked example. Intersect the unit circle x²+y²=1 with y=t, where t is real. Substitution gives x²=1−t². If t=0, the two points are (−1,0) and (1,0). If t=1, the equation becomes x²=0, so there is one geometric point (0,1), reached by two coinciding roots. If t=2, then x²=−3; there is no real meeting, but over complex coordinates x=±i√3 gives two solutions (±i√3,2). Exact outcomes for the horizontal family Height Equation for x Real points t=0 x²=1 (−1,0), (1,0) t=1 x²=0 (0,1), tangent t=2 x²=−3 None The table is an exact alternative to a slider. A picture could make the t=1 case look like a narrow crossing if its pixels are coarse; the repeated algebraic root settles the question. The parameter t has no unit restriction: all three cases occur within the same family of lines. Substitution and the discriminant Exact result for this family. For a real t, the points common to y=t and x²+y²=1 obey x 2 − ( 1 − t 2 ) = 0 , Δ = 4 ( 1 − t 2 ) Derivation: replace y with t in the circle equation, then move 1−t² to the left. Here a=1, b=0, c=t²−1, hence Δ=0²−4(1)(t²−1)=4(1−t²). If |t|<1, the roots ±√(1−t²) are distinct real numbers. If |t|=1, both collapse to zero. If |t|>1, 1−t² is negative, so neither root is real. This accounts for every real t and every intersection in the affine coordinate plane; substitution is reversible because each candidate also has y=t. For a nonhorizontal line y=mx+b, the same method yields (1+m²)x²+2mbx+(b²−1)=0. Its leading coefficient is positive for real m. The discriminant is 4(1+m²−b²), after cancellation of 4m²b². Thus there are two, one or zero real intersection points according as b² is less than, equal to or greater than 1+m². The line may be slanted, but its closest distance to the origin is |b|/√(1+m²), which tells the same story geometrically. The algebra proves the root count; the distance interpretation is a cross-check. Counting a double root as two is a special-case multiplicity convention justified here by the substituted quadratic. It suggests, but does not prove, the general intersection multiplicity used in Bézout's theorem. That theorem also requires projective coordinates and an algebraically closed field. We will state its full hypotheses in the counting lesson ; this elementary calculation cannot establish it. Find and classify meetings 1. Calculation. Intersect x²+y²=1 with y=x. Give every real point and explain why there are no others. Hint for question 1 Replace y by x; solve 2x²=1 and restore y. Full solution for question 1 Substitution gives 2x²=1, hence x=±1/√2. Since y=x, the points are (1/√2,1/√2) and (−1/√2,−1/√2). Conversely both satisfy y=x and their squared coordinates sum to 1. The quadratic has only these two roots, so there are no further affine intersections. 2. Explanation. For the line y=−1, how many distinct real points and how many roots counted with quadratic multiplicity? Why are the answers different? Hint for question 2 Substitute y=−1 and factor the resulting polynomial in x. Full solution for question 2 The circle equation becomes x²+1=1, or x²=0. Its only coordinate is x=0, giving one point (0,−1). The polynomial is x·x, so x=0 is a root of multiplicity two. The line is tangent there; two roots have merged into one geometric point. What we have counted Substitution gives an exact answer for line-circle intersections, and the discriminant sorts the real cases. A repeated root records tangency in this family, and complex roots can persist when no real point is visible. Stop once you can solve and check both equations. Do not use this example alone to claim that every pair of curves has a degree-product count; shared components and points at infinity require a broader framework.

title: Tangents from derivatives of equations
summary: Derive a tangent line at a smooth point from the gradient and recognize the zero-gradient boundary.
text: Can an equation reveal a tangent? A tangent is a line giving the first-order direction of a curve near a point. When a curve is described by F(x,y)=0, its derivatives often reveal that line without solving globally for y. We will derive the rule at a regular point and see exactly why it can fail at a singular one. Background capsule. The partial derivative F x differentiates while y is held fixed; F y holds x fixed. Their pair ∇F=(F x ,F y ) is the gradient. For a differentiable polynomial F, a small displacement (h,k) from p=(a,b) changes F by approximately F x (p)h+F y (p)k. More precisely, the omitted error divided by √(h²+k²) tends to zero. A point is smooth for this plane curve when F(p)=0 and ∇F(p)≠(0,0). Read the tangent from a circle Worked example. Let F=x²+y²−5 and p=(1,2). First check F(p)=1+4−5=0. The partial derivatives are F x =2x and F y =2y, so ∇F(p)=(2,4), which is nonzero. The candidate tangent is 2(x−1)+4(y−2)=0, equivalently x+2y=5. Its direction vector (2,−1) is perpendicular to (2,4), because their dot product is 4−4=0. We can check the line without relying on a drawing. Put x=1+2t and y=2−t. The line equation holds for every t, while F(1+2t,2−t)=5t². The residual begins at order t², not order t. Thus moving along this line changes the curve equation more slowly near t=0 than a generic direction does. The line is a first-order match, though its other points are generally not on the circle. This is what tangent means here. Point and gradient checks F and point Gradient Linear equation x²+y²−5 at (1,2) (2,4) x+2y=5 y−x² at (1,1) (−2,1) y−1=2(x−1) y²−x³ at (0,0) (0,0) Rule supplies no line Derive the rule and mark its boundary Exact first-order tangent statement. Let F be a real polynomial, p=(a,b) satisfy F(p)=0, and assume ∇F(p)≠0. The linearized tangent line is F x ( p ) ( x − a ) + F y ( p ) ( y − b ) = 0 To derive it, take a differentiable path γ(t)=(x(t),y(t)) on F=0 with γ(0)=p. The chain rule yields 0=dF(γ(t))/dt at t=0, hence F x (p)x′(0)+F y (p)y′(0)=0. Every actual velocity is therefore perpendicular to the gradient. Since the gradient is nonzero, this perpendicular set is a unique line through the origin in velocity space; translate it through p to obtain the displayed line. If F y (p)≠0, the implicit-function theorem additionally guarantees a local differentiable graph y(x) with slope −F x /F y . If F y =0 but F x ≠0, solve locally for x as a function of y instead. We use the theorem for local existence, not a proof of it. The path argument proves that any existing differentiable branch has the stated direction. The local graph theorem supplies existence and uniqueness of that smooth local branch under the nonzero-gradient hypothesis. When both derivatives vanish, the displayed equation becomes 0=0 and selects every point, so it gives no tangent. That does not prove there is no tangent: the cusp y²=x³ has a limiting x-axis direction despite its zero gradient. Its local branch analysis belongs in the singularity lesson . Compute and test the boundary 1. Calculation. Find the tangent to xy−1=0 at (2,1/2), and verify the point lies on the curve. Hint for question 1 F x =y and F y =x. Insert the coordinates before writing the tangent equation. Full solution for question 1 At (2,1/2), xy−1=2·(1/2)−1=0. The gradient is (1/2,2), so the tangent is (1/2)(x−2)+2(y−1/2)=0. Multiplying by two and simplifying gives x+4y=4. It passes through the stated point because 2+4(1/2)=4. 2. Explanation. For F=(y−x²)², the gradient vanishes at every point of the parabola. Does that mean the parabola has no tangent at (1,1)? Hint for question 2 Compare the zero set of F with that of y−x², then parameterize its points near x=1. Full solution for question 2 No. Squaring changes the defining polynomial but not its zero set: F=0 exactly when y=x². Parameterize near (1,1) by (1+t,(1+t)²)=(1+t,1+2t+t²). The first-order direction is (1,2), so the tangent is y−1=2(x−1). The gradient of the squared equation vanishes because it carries a repeated factor; this particular defining equation fails the nonzero-gradient test. A condition on the equation matters At a zero with nonzero gradient, the gradient is normal to the tangent and the linear equation is justified by the chain rule and local graph theorem. A zero gradient makes this test inconclusive; it does not by itself settle the geometry of the underlying set. Stop once you can check F(p)=0, compute ∇F(p), and say explicitly whether the smooth-point hypothesis holds.

title: When a curve has no single tangent
summary: Distinguish a cusp from a node using local branches and lowest-degree terms.
text: A cusp and a crossing share a warning sign At the origin, both y²=x³ and y²=x²(x+1) have zero gradient. Yet their nearby real shapes differ: one has two half-branches meeting in a cusp, while the other has branches crossing. We will distinguish them by solving their equations near zero and by looking at their lowest-degree terms. Background capsule. A singular point of a chosen reduced plane-curve equation F=0 is a zero where F x =F y =0. A branch is a local route of solutions toward the point. The tangent cone records directions selected by the lowest nonzero homogeneous-degree terms of F. A repeated direction in that cone can signal branches sharing a tangent; it does not alone classify every singularity. We work over real coordinates for the branch pictures, with x+1 positive near x=0. Compute the branches Worked example. For the cusp F=y²−x³, real solutions require x≥0 because y²≥0. For x>0, y=±x√x. Both signs approach the origin from the right. Their slopes relative to the origin are y/x=±√x, which tend to zero. Thus both half-branches have the x-axis as limiting tangent direction. A convenient parametrization is (x,y)=(t²,t³); positive and negative t describe the two halves. Its derivative vanishes at t=0, another sign that ordinary regular-curve parametrization needs care. For the node G=y²−x²(x+1), take |x| small enough that x+1>0. Then y=±x√(1+x), where using x rather than |x| simply swaps the two signs for negative x. The two parametrized branches pass through zero and have slopes y/x=±√(1+x)→±1. Their limiting tangents are y=x and y=−x. Each branch continues to both sides of the origin, unlike the cusp's two right-hand halves. Local calculations at the origin Equation Lowest-degree part Real tangent directions y²−x³ y² y=0, repeated y²−x²(x+1) y²−x² y=x and y=−x What the algebra establishes Singular-point check. For the cusp, F x =−3x² and F y =2y. For the node, G x =−2x−3x² and G y =2y. Both equations and both derivative pairs vanish at (0,0): F ( p ) = F x ( p ) = F y ( p ) = 0 This condition says the smooth tangent formula cannot be used at the point. It does not distinguish cusp from node. To obtain the first tangent directions, separate each polynomial by total degree: x³ is degree three, while y² is degree two, so the cusp's degree-two part is y². For the node, expanding x²(x+1)=x²+x³ gives degree-two part y²−x²=(y−x)(y+x). A direction (u,v) in the tangent cone satisfies that lowest-degree equation: v²=0 for the cusp, or (v−u)(v+u)=0 for the node. The repeated cusp line and two distinct node lines match the explicit branch limits calculated above. Proof boundary. The formulas y=±x√x and y=±x√(1+x) fully establish the real local branch and tangent claims for these two polynomials. We have not proved a general theorem that every factor of a tangent cone corresponds to a separate real branch. Indeed, y²+x² has degree-two tangent expression y²+x² but only the origin as a real zero; over complex numbers it factors into two lines. The field matters, and higher-degree terms can change local behavior. A complete singularity classification uses tools beyond this lesson. Also beware a repeated defining equation. The zero set of (y−x²)² is a smooth parabola even though its gradient vanishes all along it. Thus “gradient zero” is an algebraic test for the chosen equation, not an automatic proof that the visible set has a cusp. In algebraic geometry one often first removes repeated factors, or treats the repeated structure deliberately. The next algebraic viewpoint appears in coordinate rings . Distinguish local directions 1. Calculation. For H=y²−4x²−x³, check the origin and find the two limiting real tangent lines near it. Hint for question 1 Factor the equation as y²=x²(4+x), which has a positive square root near zero. Full solution for question 1 H(0,0)=0, H x =−8x−3x² and H y =2y, so both derivatives vanish at zero. For |x| small, y=±x√(4+x) parameterizes two branches. Dividing by x for x≠0 and taking x→0 gives slopes ±2. The tangent lines are y=2x and y=−2x; the lowest-degree part y²−4x² gives the same result. 2. Explanation. Does the zero gradient of K=(y−x)² at (0,0) prove that its real zero set crosses itself? Hint for question 2 Solve K=0 before interpreting its derivative. Full solution for question 2 No. K=0 is equivalent to y−x=0, so its real zero set is a single straight line. Its gradient is 2(y−x)(−1,1), hence zero on that line because the polynomial repeats the factor. There is no crossing; the algebraic equation has repeated structure. Read singularities locally The cusp and node both defeat the nonzero-gradient rule, but explicit branch equations reveal different limiting directions. For these examples, the lowest-degree part gives the tangent cone and the branch formulas justify the real picture. Stop once you can state which part is an exact local calculation and which broader classification remains unproved.

title: Where parallel lines meet
summary: Compute the projective point shared by two parallel affine lines using homogeneous coordinates.
text: What could “meeting at infinity” mean? In the ordinary plane, y=1 and y=2 are parallel and share no point. Projective coordinates add a line of points at infinity so that these two lines meet at a definite new point. This is an algebraic construction, not a claim that a distant visible location exists. We will calculate it and see why the scaling rule is essential. Background capsule. In this lesson coordinates are real, so the numerical divisions below are valid; the same constructions work over ℂ. A projective point [X:Y:Z] is an equivalence class of nonzero triples: (X,Y,Z) and (λX,λY,λZ) represent the same point whenever λ≠0. The all-zero triple is excluded. In the chart Z≠0, scale by 1/Z to write [x:y:1], which corresponds to the familiar affine point (x,y). Points with Z=0 lie outside that chart and form the projective line at infinity. A projective line has an equation aX+bY+cZ=0 with coefficients not all zero. Two horizontal lines Worked example. To extend y=1, replace y by Y/Z in the chart Z≠0 and multiply by Z: Y−Z=0. Likewise y=2 becomes Y−2Z=0. Solve both homogeneous equations: subtracting gives Z=0, then Y=0. A projective triple with Z=Y=0 must have X≠0, so scaling gives the unique point [1:0:0]. It belongs to both lines and is at infinity because Z=0. The same calculation works for y=mx+b and y=mx+c when b≠c. Their projective equations are Y−mX−bZ=0 and Y−mX−cZ=0. Subtracting gives (c−b)Z=0, hence Z=0. The remaining equation Y=mX gives the common point [1:m:0]. The point depends on slope m, not the intercept. This is why parallel lines in one direction acquire a shared projective point. Affine line and its added direction point Affine equation Projective equation Point with Z=0 y=1 Y−Z=0 [1:0:0] y=2 Y−2Z=0 [1:0:0] y=2x+3 Y−2X−3Z=0 [1:2:0] Homogeneous coordinates are classes Exact definition. The projective plane over k consists of nonzero triples modulo common nonzero scaling: [ X : Y : Z ] = [ λ X : λ Y : λ Z ] for λ ≠ 0 For example, [1:2:0]=[3:6:0], so they are one point, not two intersections. A homogeneous linear equation is well-defined on classes: if aX+bY+cZ=0, then a(λX)+b(λY)+c(λZ)=λ·0=0. That scaling compatibility is why we use homogeneous equations. A nonhomogeneous expression like X+1=0 would not define a projective locus: [−1:0:0] satisfies it, while the same point represented as [−2:0:0] does not. We can prove directly that two distinct projective lines over ℝ meet in exactly one projective point. Their two coefficient rows are linearly independent. Eliminating one unknown with the first equation and a second with the other leaves one free scalar, so the simultaneous homogeneous system has a one-dimensional solution space. Every nonzero solution is a scalar multiple of every other, giving one equivalence class. This elementary linear-algebra fact is the precise scope of “two lines meet.” It does not say two arbitrary curves meet in one point, nor does it count tangencies. For a polynomial curve of degree d, one can homogenize by introducing suitable powers of Z to make every term total degree d, then examine its points with Z=0. We only carried this out for lines. The projective plane over ℝ and the one over ℂ have different available coordinates; later intersection counting uses ℂ so polynomial equations have the needed roots. See Bézout's hypotheses for the careful degree-product statement. Calculate with classes 1. Calculation. Extend y=3x+1 and y=3x−4 to projective lines. Find their common point. Hint for question 1 Replace x,y by X/Z,Y/Z and clear Z. Subtract the two equations. Full solution for question 1 The equations are Y−3X−Z=0 and Y−3X+4Z=0. Subtracting yields 5Z=0, so Z=0. Then Y=3X. Since the triple is nonzero, X≠0; scale it to [1:3:0]. This point is the unique common projective point. 2. Explanation. Are [2:4:0] and [−1:−2:0] different points? Could [0:0:0] repair a failed line intersection? Hint for question 2 Find a nonzero scalar relating the triples, and recall the exclusion in the definition. Full solution for question 2 Multiplying (2,4,0) by −1/2 gives (−1,−2,0), so the triples represent the same point. The zero triple is excluded because scaling would never yield a chart coordinate and it lies on every homogeneous equation without representing a direction. It cannot serve as an additional intersection. Infinity is a coordinate boundary The chart Z≠0 recovers the affine plane; Z=0 records directions omitted by that chart. Parallel affine lines with equal slope meet at one projective point, calculated by homogeneous linear equations. Stop once you can solve an intersection using classes and can explain why [1:m:0] is an exact algebraic answer rather than a plotted faraway point.

title: Bézout for a line and a conic
summary: State plane Bézout with precise hypotheses and calculate a tangent line–conic example.
text: When does degree predict intersections? A line has degree one and a conic degree two, so the slogan “one times two” predicts two intersections. An ordinary real plot can show two, one, or none. The slogan becomes a theorem only after specifying the field, the projective setting, common components, and multiplicity. We will state that theorem accurately and prove the line–conic case by restricting a quadratic to the line. Background capsule. A projective plane curve is the zero set of a nonzero homogeneous polynomial F(X,Y,Z). Its degree is the common total degree of its terms. A point is a nonzero triple [X:Y:Z] modulo nonzero scaling. Working over ℂ ensures every nonconstant one-variable polynomial has roots there. An intersection multiplicity I p (C,D) is a positive integer measuring how the curves meet at p; transverse smooth crossings have multiplicity one, while a tangent meeting can have more. Its full local-algebra definition is beyond this article. A line touches a conic Worked example. Take the complex projective conic C: X²+Y²−Z²=0 and the line L: Y−Z=0. In the affine chart Z=1, L is y=1 and C is x²+y²=1. Substitution gives x²=0, so the sole affine point is (0,1), or [0:1:1]. At infinity Z=0, the line requires Y=0, then the conic requires X²=0, which would force the forbidden zero triple. Thus there is no extra point there. Along this line, use homogeneous line coordinates [S:T] by [X:Y:Z]=[S:T:T]. Restricting the conic equation yields S²+T²−T²=S². The only zero of this degree-two homogeneous polynomial is [S:T]=[0:1], with root order two. In this line-conic case, that order is the intersection multiplicity, so the single point contributes two. The count is 1·2=2, despite there being just one distinct geometric point. Same conic, three affine appearances Line Affine substitution Complex projective count y=0 x²−1=0 Two simple points y=1 x²=0 One point of multiplicity 2 y=2 x²+3=0 Two complex points, no real points State the theorem with its conditions Bézout's plane-curve theorem, stated rather than proved. Let C and D be projective plane curves over an algebraically closed field, defined by homogeneous polynomials of degrees m and n with no common irreducible component. Then their intersection is finite and ∑ p ∈ C ∩ D I p ( C , D ) = m n Here “no common component” rules out two equations sharing a whole curve; otherwise there are infinitely many common points and the finite sum is not the right expression. The field condition matters: over ℝ, y=2 and the unit circle have no real intersections, while over ℂ they meet at x=±i√3. The projective condition matters because affine curves can miss points at infinity. For example, the affine line y=0 and parabola y=x²+1 have no real intersection and have two complex affine intersections, while other polynomial pairs can send an intersection to Z=0. Each hypothesis repairs a different way that an apparent real affine count can fall short. The full special-case argument below extends the preceding calculation: when a line is not a component of a homogeneous degree-two conic, substituting a projective parametrization of the line gives a nonzero homogeneous quadratic in two variables; over ℂ it has two roots counted with order. The local parameter calculation below explains those root orders as intersection multiplicities in this special case. We have not developed the local intersection theory needed for arbitrary singular curves, and we do not claim a proof of general Bézout. The MIT algebraic-geometry notes linked in the references give the broader theorem and proof context. Prove the line–conic count for every allowed line Special-case theorem. Let F be a nonzero homogeneous quadratic over an algebraically closed field k, and let L be a projective line that is not a component of F=0. Then the restriction of F to L has exactly two zeros counted with their root orders. Choose independent vectors u,v spanning the two-dimensional solution space of L's linear equation. Every point of L has a unique parameter [S:T] with representative Su+Tv, up to common nonzero scaling. Restriction gives Q(S,T)=F(Su+Tv)=aS²+bST+cT². This restriction is not identically zero. Indeed, extend u,v to a basis of k³. In those coordinates L has third coordinate zero. If F vanished identically after setting that coordinate to zero, every monomial of F would contain that coordinate as a factor. The line equation would divide F, making L a component, contrary to the hypothesis. There are three cases. If a≠0, the polynomial Q(S,1) has degree two. Algebraic closure and the factor theorem give two linear factors counted with repetition. They supply exactly two finite parameter roots counted with order, and Q(1,0)=a excludes the parameter point at infinity. If a=0 but b≠0, then Q=T(bS+cT). There is one root [1:0] at infinity and one root [−c:b] with T≠0, each simple. If a=b=0, nonzero restriction forces c≠0 and Q=cT², so [1:0] is the sole root, of order two. These cases exhaust all coefficients, including fields where a discriminant calculation needs care. For this special case, the multiplicity can be read entirely on the line. Near a root choose an affine parameter t that is zero at that point. The restricted polynomial is t r U(t), where U(0)≠0. Locally U is invertible, so imposing the conic equation is equivalent to imposing t r =0. The quotient has basis 1,t,…,t r−1 and dimension r. This is the line–curve local intersection multiplicity: a simple root contributes one and a double root two. The parameterization does not merge distinct projective parameters, so summing the computed root orders proves the line–conic total 2. For example, the parabola YZ−X²=0 and its line at infinity Z=0 restrict to −X² on that line. Their only intersection is [0:1:0], counted twice. An affine drawing would omit it completely. The general degree-product theorem for two arbitrary curves still needs its broader local intersection theory. Audit the count 1. Calculation. Intersect the conic X²+Y²−Z²=0 with the projective line X−Z=0. Find the points and their count over ℂ. Hint for question 1 Set X=Z in the conic equation, then check whether Z=0 gives a valid projective point. Full solution for question 1 Substituting X=Z leaves Y²=0. If Z=0, then X=Y=0, which is forbidden, so scale Z=1. The only point is [1:0:1]. The restricted polynomial has a double root Y=0, so this tangent intersection contributes multiplicity two. The total is 2=1·2. 2. Explanation. Why may we not apply the finite degree-product count to the curves XY=0 and XZ=0 as written in projective space? Hint for question 2 Factor both homogeneous equations and inspect their common zero set when X=0. Full solution for question 2 Both polynomials contain X, so the entire projective line X=0 lies in both curves. They share a component and thus infinitely many intersection points. Although both equations have degree two, the no-common-component hypothesis fails; the finite sum 2·2 is not applicable to this pair. Count with the right objects Degree products count complex projective intersections with multiplicity when there is no shared component. A real affine sketch may show fewer points, and tangency can merge distinct roots into one point. Stop once you can list all four conditions before invoking Bézout and can compute the line-conic tangent example directly.

title: Turn geometry into a ring
summary: Prove that the parabola coordinate ring is isomorphic to a one-variable polynomial ring.
text: What algebra lives on a parabola? On the parabola y=x², the expressions y and x² give the same value at every point. A coordinate ring records exactly this relation by treating their difference as zero. We will construct the quotient ring and prove, explicitly, that its arithmetic is the same as ordinary one-variable polynomial arithmetic. Background capsule. R[x,y] is the ring of polynomials in x and y with real coefficients. An ideal such as (y−x²) consists of all polynomial multiples H(x,y)(y−x²). In the quotient R[x,y]/(y−x²), two polynomials represent the same class when their difference is in this ideal. Brackets [P] denote the class of P. Ring addition and multiplication are performed on representatives, then classes are taken. The equation y=x² explains why [y]=[x²]. Reduce expressions by substitution Worked example. Consider P(x,y)=y²+3xy−2. Along y=x², this becomes x⁴+3x³−2. In the quotient, [P]=[x⁴+3x³−2] because P−(x⁴+3x³−2)=(y−x²)(y+x²+3x). Thus the two expressions differ by an explicit multiple of the defining equation. At x=2 on the parabola, where y=4, both give 16+24−2=38. The single point check is reassuring, but the factorization proves equality of classes for every point and within the quotient algebra. Define φ:R[x,y]→R[x] by φ(P)=P(x,x²). It replaces every y by x². It preserves sums and products because substitution does: φ(P+Q)=φ(P)+φ(Q), and φ(PQ)=φ(P)φ(Q). It is onto, since every polynomial q(x) already lies in R[x,y] and φ(q)=q. The main issue is its kernel: precisely which polynomials become zero after substitution? Three classes and their reductions Expression Class on y=x² Reason y x² y−x² is the relation xy x³ Multiply the relation by x y² x⁴ y²−x⁴=(y−x²)(y+x²) Prove the isomorphism Exact result. Substitution induces a ring isomorphism ℝ [ x , y ] / ( y − x 2 ) ≅ ℝ [ x ] To prove the kernel claim, treat P as a polynomial in y whose coefficients are polynomials in x. The elementary identity y n −a n =(y−a)(y n−1 +y n−2 a+⋯+a n−1 ) shows, term by term with a=x², that P(x,y)−P(x,x²) is divisible by y−x². Therefore P(x,x²)=0 exactly when P itself is a multiple of y−x². Hence ker φ=(y−x²). If two classes [P] and [Q] map to the same one-variable polynomial, then φ(P−Q)=0, so P−Q lies in that ideal and [P]=[Q]; the induced map is injective. Surjectivity was already checked, so it is an isomorphism. This proves the displayed statement without using the general first isomorphism theorem as a black box. The coordinate ring is a device for retaining polynomial functions subject to relations. We worked over ℝ and used the principal ideal generated by y−x². For an arbitrary collection of equations, defining a quotient by their ideal is straightforward, but the relation between all polynomial functions and geometric points is subtler. For instance, quotienting by (x²) remembers a nonzero class [x] whose square is zero, even though x=0 and x²=0 define the same ordinary point set. Such an element is nilpotent . We will examine it in the affine scheme window . Our explicit isomorphism does not establish the full ideals–varieties correspondence. Calculate in a quotient 1. Calculation. Reduce x²y+y² in R[x,y]/(y−x²), and give its value at (−1,1). Hint for question 1 Use [y]=[x²] twice, then substitute x=−1. Full solution for question 1 [x²y+y²]=[x²·x²+(x²)²]=[2x⁴]. At x=−1 this gives 2. Directly at (−1,1), x²y+y²=1·1+1=2, agreeing with the quotient reduction. 2. Explanation. Does equality of values at the single point (0,0) imply [P]=[Q] in the parabola's coordinate ring? Test P=x and Q=0. Hint for question 2 Compare P and Q at another parabola point, and use the substitution map. Full solution for question 2 No. At (0,0), both x and 0 evaluate to zero. But at (1,1), x evaluates to 1 while 0 evaluates to 0. Also φ(x)=x is not the zero polynomial, so x is not in the kernel (y−x²), and [x]≠[0]. One matching evaluation is much weaker than equality of polynomial classes. A relation becomes arithmetic The quotient R[x,y]/(y−x²) makes y and x² interchangeable, and the substitution proof identifies it exactly with R[x]. Stop once you can reduce a class and explain why the kernel is the defining ideal. The broader geometric meaning of ideals needs field and radical hypotheses that this example alone does not supply.

title: The Nullstellensatz in one variable
summary: Use a one-variable example to separate ideals, radicals and point sets under the Nullstellensatz.
text: Can points recover equations? The equations x=0 and x²=0 have the same points over ℂ, yet the ideals (x) and (x²) differ. The Nullstellensatz says precisely what point data can recover: the radical of an ideal, under an algebraically closed field hypothesis. We will state that result, prove its one-variable case, and exhibit a failure over ℝ. Background capsule. In k[x 1 ,…,x n ], an ideal I is closed under addition and multiplication by any polynomial. Its zero set V k (I) consists of all k-coordinate tuples where every element of I vanishes. For a set S of points, I(S) consists of all polynomials vanishing on every point of S. The radical √I contains polynomials f for which some positive power f m belongs to I. A field is algebraically closed if every nonconstant one-variable polynomial has a root in it; ℂ is the standard example, while ℝ is not. A single point, two ideals Worked example. Work in ℂ[x]. Both I=(x) and J=(x²) vanish exactly at 0, because x²(a)=0 if and only if a=0 in a field. Yet x∉(x²), so I≠J. Their radicals agree: √(x²)=(x). To see this directly, if a polynomial f has f(0)=0, it is divisible by x, so f² is divisible by x² and f∈√(x²). Conversely, if f(0)≠0, then every power f m also has nonzero constant term and cannot be divisible by x². Thus the radical retains exactly the vanishing condition in this example. Now switch to ℝ[x]. The ideal K=(x²+1) has no real zero, because x²+1>0 for all real x. Therefore V ℝ (K)=∅, and every polynomial vanishes vacuously on all points of that empty set: I(∅)=ℝ[x]. But √K is a proper ideal; for example 1 has no power inside K, since K contains no nonzero constant multiple of 1. In fact √K=K: the quotient ℝ[x]/(x²+1) is the field ℂ, so K is prime and therefore radical. Hence I(V ℝ (K))≠√K. This is the promised failure of the algebraically closed-field formula over ℝ. What points remember Field and ideal Zero set Radical ℂ, (x) {0} (x) ℂ, (x²) {0} (x) ℝ, (x²+1) ∅ (x²+1), proper The theorem and the proof boundary Hilbert's Nullstellensatz, geometric form, stated. If k is algebraically closed and I is an ideal of k[x 1 ,…,x n ] for finite n, then I ( V k ( I ) ) = I The inclusion √I⊆I(V k (I)) is elementary over any field: if f m ∈I and a is a common zero of I, then f(a) m =0. A field has no nonzero nilpotents, so f(a)=0. The reverse inclusion is the deep direction. It says that if a polynomial vanishes at every common k-point, a power of it lies in I. We prove that direction for one variable below; the several-variable direction remains an invoked Nullstellensatz theorem. The Stacks Project gives the theorem as the intersection of maximal ideals containing a radical ideal. Over an algebraically closed field, maximal ideals in a polynomial ring correspond to k-points, giving the displayed geometric form. One should distinguish “same set of classical points” from “same ideal.” The theorem identifies radical ideals with algebraic zero sets through mutually reversing operations V and I. It does not claim that every ideal equals I(V(I)): (x²) is the smallest counterexample. An ideal can retain nilpotent or multiplicity information invisible to point sets. Conversely, the real-field example shows that even taking a radical may not recover an ideal from real points. Real algebraic geometry has a different, stronger radical notion; it is outside our scope. For a zero-set calculation, always say which field supplies the coordinates. The notation V without a subscript can obscure the issue; here V k makes it explicit. Continue to Spec to see how a ring retains the (x²) distinction beyond its visible point set. Prove the theorem in one variable Weak Nullstellensatz for k[x]. If k is algebraically closed, every proper ideal I of k[x] has a common zero in k. Here is a complete proof. If I=(0), every point is a common zero. Otherwise choose a nonzero g∈I of least degree and divide it by its leading coefficient to make it monic. For any f∈I, polynomial division gives f=qg+r with either r=0 or deg r<deg g. Since r=f−qg belongs to I, minimality forces r=0. Thus I=(g). Properness excludes a nonzero constant g, since such a constant is invertible and would put 1 in I. Algebraic closure gives a root a of the nonconstant g. Every f∈I is a multiple of g, so every such f vanishes at a. This proves the claim. The same calculation also proves the full radical formula in this one-variable setting. For a proper nonzero ideal, factor its monic generator as g=∏(x−a i ) eᵢ , with distinct a i and positive integers e i . Such a factorization follows by repeatedly removing a root using polynomial division; the degree decreases at each removal. The common zero set of I is exactly {a i }. Put q=∏(x−a i ), using each distinct factor once. A polynomial f vanishes at every a i exactly when q divides f. To see the product divisibility, remove one factor using the factor theorem. At any other root a j , the removed factor has nonzero value, so the remaining quotient must still vanish there. Continue through the distinct roots. Consequently I(V(I))=(q). If q divides f, choose M at least every e i . Then g divides f M , so f lies in √I. Conversely if f M ∈I, evaluating at each a i gives f(a i ) M =0, hence f vanishes there and q divides f. Therefore √I=(q)=I(V(I)). The boundary ideals also fit. For I=k[x], the zero set is empty and both sides are k[x]. For I=(0), the zero set is k and both sides are zero: an algebraically closed field is infinite, and a nonzero polynomial has at most its degree many roots by successive division. For completeness, a finite field could not be algebraically closed, since ∏ a∈k (x−a)−1 is nonconstant and has no root in that field. Thus no hidden finiteness exception is being used. This completes the one-variable radical formula; the several-variable hard direction remains a separate theorem. Test ideals against points 1. Calculation. In ℂ[x], find V ℂ ((x−2)³), its radical, and I of that zero set. Hint for question 1 A power vanishes exactly when its base vanishes. Divide polynomials by x−2 to detect vanishing at 2. Full solution for question 1 The only zero is 2, so V ℂ ((x−2)³)={2}. A polynomial vanishes at 2 exactly when x−2 divides it, giving I({2})=(x−2). The radical of ((x−2)³) is also (x−2): if f has that factor then f³ lies in ((x−2)³); if f(2)≠0 then no power is divisible by x−2. The three results agree with the theorem. 2. Explanation. Why does (x²+1) in ℝ[x] disprove the same geometric formula with k=ℝ? Hint for question 2 First find real roots, then compute I(∅) from its definition. Full solution for question 2 It has no real roots, so V ℝ ((x²+1))=∅ and I(∅)=ℝ[x]. Yet 1∉√(x²+1), because no power of 1 is a multiple of x²+1. Thus the right side is proper while the left side is the whole ring. ℝ lacks the algebraically closed hypothesis. Recover the radical, under a hypothesis Over an algebraically closed field, classical zero sets recover radical ideals, not arbitrary ideals. The easy containment follows from evaluating powers; the hard containment is proved here in one variable, while its several-variable form remains an invoked theorem. Stop once you can explain the (x) versus (x²) comparison and produce the real-field counterexample without relying on a picture.

title: Why a ring can describe more than visible points
summary: Compute Spec of a nilpotent quotient and explain what its one-point topology omits.
text: How can one point carry extra arithmetic? The rings k[x]/(x) and k[x]/(x²) both have one classical k-point when k is a field. In the second ring, however, the class of x is nonzero and squares to zero. The spectrum construction keeps this difference in its ring even though the underlying set of prime ideals has one point in either case. We will compute both spectra completely and state what this small example does not teach about general schemes. Background capsule. A prime ideal p of a commutative ring A is a proper ideal with the property that ab∈p implies a∈p or b∈p. Equivalently, A/p has no zero divisors. Spec(A) is the set of all prime ideals of A, equipped with a topology: V(I) consists of primes containing I, and basic opens D(f) consist of primes not containing f. A nilpotent element u has u m =0 for some positive m. Every prime ideal contains each nilpotent, because u m ∈p forces u∈p by repeated use of primality. Two quotients, one visible point each Worked example. Let A=k[x]/(x). Every polynomial class is determined by its constant term, so A≅k. A field has exactly one prime ideal, (0): it is proper and its quotient is the field itself. Thus Spec(A) is a single point. The class [x] in A is zero because x belongs to the defining ideal. Let B=k[x]/(x²), and write ε=[x]. Every class has a unique form a+bε with a,b∈k and ε²=0. Uniqueness follows because a+bx belongs to (x²) only when a=b=0. So ε is genuinely nonzero and nilpotent. The ideal (ε) consists of bε; quotienting B by it gives k, hence (ε) is maximal and prime. Every prime of B must contain ε because ε²=0; any ideal containing (ε) corresponds to an ideal of B/(ε)=k, and only (0) and k occur there. Properness leaves only (ε). Therefore Spec(B) also has one point. Same underlying set, different ring arithmetic Ring Only prime Image of x k[x]/(x) ≅ k (0) 0 k[x]/(x²) ≅ k[ε]/(ε²) (ε) ε≠0, ε²=0 What Spec records, and what the set forgets Definition and proved calculation. For any commutative unital ring A, Spec ( A ) = { 𝔭 ⊂ A : 𝔭 is a prime ideal } Our proof gives exactly one prime for each quotient above. Their underlying topological spaces are consequently both the one-point space: the only opens are empty and the whole set. Indeed, for B the only prime contains ε, so D(ε)=∅; D(1)=Spec(B). Yet the rings are not isomorphic. A field has no nonzero nilpotent, while B has ε≠0 with ε²=0. Any ring isomorphism would preserve that property, so none exists. An affine scheme is more than the bare set Spec(A): it includes a structure sheaf of rings on the open subsets. For this one-point example, the ring of global sections is A itself, so the two affine schemes retain different arithmetic even though their point sets and topologies look identical. We have not constructed the structure sheaf here or proved the general global-sections theorem. Those are named facts from scheme theory; the verified part of this article is the elementary ring and prime-ideal calculation. For k algebraically closed, the sole maximal prime in each example corresponds to the classical solution x=0. If k is not algebraically closed, the calculation of these particular rings still works, but a general affine spectrum may have prime ideals that are not k-valued coordinate points. Spec is not simply a way to draw all graph points. It also includes nonmaximal primes in larger rings, such as (0) in k[x], and records algebra through its sheaf. Compare the radical-ideal theorem to see why ordinary point sets discard the square in (x²). Find primes and nilpotents 1. Calculation. For C=k[t]/(t³), write every class in a normal form, identify a nonzero nilpotent, and find all prime ideals. Hint for question 1 Reduce powers t³ and above. Every prime contains [t] because [t]³=0, then quotient by ([t]). Full solution for question 1 Every class has a unique form a+bτ+cτ² with τ=[t] and a,b,c∈k. The class τ is nonzero but τ³=0. Any prime contains τ. The ideal (τ) is prime because C/(τ)≅k is a field. A proper ideal strictly containing (τ) would correspond to a proper nonzero ideal of k, which does not exist. Thus (τ) is the unique prime and Spec(C) has one point. 2. Explanation. Why is (0) not a prime ideal of B=k[ε]/(ε²), even though it is prime in k? Hint for question 2 Use the product ε·ε and the fact ε itself is nonzero. Full solution for question 2 In B, ε·ε=0 belongs to (0), yet ε does not belong to (0). This violates the defining property of a prime ideal. In the field k, a product can be zero only when a factor is zero, so (0) is prime there. The nilpotent distinguishes the two rings even though each spectrum has one point. A small window into schemes The two example spectra each have one prime, but their rings differ by a nonzero nilpotent. This proves that the underlying point set and topology alone do not retain all affine-scheme information. Stop once you can compute the sole prime of k[x]/(x²) and explain the precise role of ε; the structure sheaf and general scheme theory remain further study.

title: Relationships before ingredients
summary: Build a path category and prove its identity and associativity laws.
text: When do routes form a category? Consider four places A, B, C, D and one-way roads a:A→B, b:B→C, c:A→C and d:C→D. A route is a finite sequence of roads whose ends match. The empty route at A stays at A; there is one at every place. We can follow a route by another compatible route. This modest system already has the structure of a category. Background capsule. A directed graph has vertices and directed edges. A path records edges in order, so the route using a then b differs from the single road c even though both start at A and finish at C. Writing q∘p means first travel p, then q. Two arrows compose only when the destination of p equals the source of q. A category consists of objects, arrows with specified sources and targets, identity arrows, and associative composition. Here the objects are places, but categories can instead have sets, groups or other mathematical objects. List actual arrows Worked example. The graph has four edges, but its path category has additional arrows ab:A→C, bd:B→D, cd:A→D and abd:A→D, where letters are written in travel order. In conventional composition notation, ab means b∘a. The direct edge c and two-edge path ab are parallel arrows, not equal arrows. Both cd and abd go from A to D, yet they record different trips. Empty paths 1 A , 1 B , 1 C , 1 D are arrows too. Selected path compositions First Then Result a:A→B b:B→C ab:A→C ab:A→C d:C→D abd:A→D a:A→B bd:B→D abd:A→D 1 A :A→A c:A→C c:A→C This finite acyclic graph has only finitely many paths. In a graph with a directed cycle, the same construction still works but may have infinitely many paths: going around the cycle different numbers of times yields different arrows. Finite objects therefore do not automatically mean finite arrows. Why path concatenation obeys the laws Exact statement and full proof. For any directed graph, vertices as objects and finite directed paths as arrows form a category. Source and target of a path are its first and last vertices. Composition is concatenation of compatible edge lists. The identity at a vertex is the empty list based there. For paths p:A→B, q:B→C and r:C→D, concatenation gives r ∘ ( q ∘ p ) = ( r ∘ q ) ∘ p Indeed, both sides are the same ordered edge list: all edges of p, then q, then r. Neither bracketing changes an edge or its position. The source is A and target D on both sides. Concatenating an empty list before or after a path leaves that path unchanged, so 1 B ∘p=p and p∘1 A =p. The empty list must carry its base vertex: otherwise the empty path at A could be mistaken for the one at B, destroying the source and target information. These checks prove all category axioms, including identities and associativity, for the entire path construction. The category keeps routes distinct unless an explicit relation identifies them. In particular, our graph does not say b∘a=c. Drawing the two routes with the same endpoints does not make the corresponding diagram commute. One can later impose an equality between paths, but then one is constructing a different category and must check the relation behaves under composition. Test the construction 1. Calculation. In the graph above, list every arrow A→D and calculate d∘(b∘a) and (d∘b)∘a. Hint for question 1 From A, either take c to C or a to B; continue until D. Full solution for question 1 The A→D arrows are the edge lists cd and abd. The route through B has d∘(b∘a)=abd. Grouping the last two roads first gives (d∘b)∘a=abd too. The route cd is a distinct arrow, even though its endpoints agree. 2. Explanation. Someone calls a:A→B followed by c:A→C a composite c∘a. Is that legal? If not, give one legal composite involving c and an identity. Hint for question 2 Compare a's target with c's source. Full solution for question 2 No. After a one is at B, but c starts at A, so c∘a is undefined. The composite c∘1 A is legal and equals c; also 1 C ∘c=c. A category does not demand that every pair of arrows compose, only pairs with matching endpoints. What the language buys you A category records which arrows connect which objects, and what happens when compatible arrows are composed. In a path category, arrows are literal routes and associativity is just the fact that parentheses do not alter an edge list. This is a complete example, rather than an analogy for categories. A graph alone supplies no equality between distinct paths with common endpoints; to ask whether routes agree after processing, continue to commuting diagrams .

title: Two routes, one result
summary: Check a finite square by comparing every input through both routes.
text: Do two routes give the same answer? A diagram is useful only when its arrows have actual meanings. Let A={0,1,2}, B={u,v}, C={even,odd}, and D={0,1}. We will compare two ways to turn an element of A into an element of D. The question is equality of functions , so every possible input matters. Background capsule. A function f:A→B assigns exactly one output in B to each input in A. For f:A→B and g:B→D, the composite g∘f:A→D sends a to g(f(a)); the rightmost function acts first. Functions are equal when they have the same domain and codomain and give the same output for every input. If a codomain is changed, even an identical value table may describe an arrow of another type. A square with complete tables Worked example. Define f:A→B by f(0)=u, f(1)=v, f(2)=u. Define g:B→D by g(u)=0 and g(v)=1. Along the other route, define h:A→C by h(0)=even, h(1)=odd, h(2)=even, and k:C→D by k(even)=0, k(odd)=1. All four sides now have explicit domains and codomains. The square has A at its upper left, B upper right, C lower left and D lower right, with f and h leaving A, g from B to D, and k from C to D. Every input in the square a∈A f(a) g(f(a)) h(a) k(h(a)) 0 u 0 even 0 1 v 1 odd 1 2 u 0 even 0 The two output columns match in all three rows. Hence the square commutes. If we change only k(odd) to 0, the a=1 row becomes 1 versus 0. That single counterexample proves the modified square does not commute. Testing only a=0 would miss the failure. The table is the complete static check; the interactive checker, when available, lets you alter a finite function and locate a first mismatch. The equation behind the picture Exact statement and full finite verification. For functions f:A→B, g:B→D, h:A→C, k:C→D, the square commutes exactly when the two functions A→D agree: g ∘ f = k ∘ h For the given A, checking all elements suffices by the definition of function equality. At 0 both paths yield 0; at 1 both yield 1; at 2 both yield 0. There are no other elements, so this is a complete proof for this finite square. The same definition works when A is infinite, but a finite sample would then not prove equality. One would need a symbolic argument for an arbitrary a∈A. The notation carries a useful type check. Both composites must start at A and finish at D. The phrase “the two paths look aligned” is not mathematical evidence if the arrows have not been defined. Nor is equality of intermediate values required: one route passes through u or v, the other through even or odd, which live in different sets. Only final outputs in D are compared. Equality is about the whole action, not the names or shape of the middle objects. Commuting squares become especially powerful when the vertices stand for algebraic structures and the arrows preserve structure. For now, the finite function version makes the content visible and checkable. It will be the local test for a functor and for naturality later. Decide by values 1. Calculation. Keep f,g,h above and replace k by k′ with k′(even)=0 and k′(odd)=0. Give both composite tables and decide whether the square commutes. Hint for question 1 Only the row whose h-value is odd changes. Full solution for question 1 g∘f has values (0,1,0) on inputs (0,1,2). k′∘h has values (0,0,0). The values differ at input 1, so the functions A→D are unequal and the new square does not commute. 2. Explanation. A learner sees matching outputs at 0 and 2 and declares the original square commutative. Explain what is missing, then state why the table above completes the argument. Hint for question 2 Recall the quantifier in function equality. Full solution for question 2 Equality requires agreement for every a∈A. Checking 0 and 2 leaves a=1 untested; a mismatch there is possible. The displayed table explicitly includes 0, 1 and 2, which exhaust A, and both composites share type A→D. It therefore establishes equality of the functions, not merely agreement on a sample. A diagram is a claim to check To verify a finite square, write each arrow's domain, codomain and table, then compare the resulting composites on every source element. One mismatch refutes commutativity. The method does not extend from finitely many tests to an infinite domain without an argument for an arbitrary input. A functor will preserve these compositional equalities when it translates one category into another.

title: A structure-preserving translation
summary: Translate a path category into Set while preserving identities and composition.
text: What does a translation preserve? Suppose a little graph of routes describes stages of a process. We want to assign a set to each stage and a function to each road, so that a whole route acts by composing its road functions. That assignment is a concrete functor from a path category to the category Set of sets and functions. Background capsule. In a category, arrows have typed sources and targets, each object has an identity arrow, and composition is associative. In Set, objects are sets, arrows are functions, identities leave each element fixed, and composition is usual function composition. A functor F:C→D sends objects of C to objects of D and each arrow p:X→Y to an arrow F(p):F(X)→F(Y). The source and target must be respected before any composition law can even be written. Assign data to three stages Worked example. Take the path category of A→B→C, with edges a:A→B and b:B→C, its length-two path ba=b∘a, and three empty paths. Set F(A)={0,1}, F(B)={u,v}, F(C)={red,blue}. Define F(a)(0)=u, F(a)(1)=v; define F(b)(u)=red, F(b)(v)=blue. To translate the whole path, assign F(ba)(0)=red and F(ba)(1)=blue. Assign F(1 A ), F(1 B ) and F(1 C ) the respective identity functions. Image arrows in Set Source arrow Image type Output table a:A→B F(A)→F(B) 0↦u; 1↦v b:B→C F(B)→F(C) u↦red; v↦blue ba:A→C F(A)→F(C) 0↦red; 1↦blue At 0, F(b)(F(a)(0))=red=F(ba)(0). At 1, both sides give blue. The finite table establishes equality of the two functions F(A)→F(C). It also makes a tempting error visible: assigning F(ba)(1)=red would break the functor law, although every assigned arrow would still be an individually valid function. Both functor laws matter Exact statement and proof for this example. A covariant functor preserves identities and composition: F ( q ∘ p ) = F ( q ) ∘ F ( p ) , F ( 1 X ) = 1 F ( X ) For our category, the three identities map to identities by definition. The only composition of two nonempty generating edges is b∘a, checked on both inputs above. Compositions with empty paths reduce to the identity-function laws; for example F(a∘1 A )=F(a)=F(a)∘1 F(A) . There are no other nonempty composable pairs, since the graph stops at C. This exhausts every case and proves the specified assignment is a functor. More generally, defining images of generating edges in a free path category determines each path's image as the corresponding function composite; associativity ensures different parenthesizations agree. Functoriality is stronger than a collection of arrows with plausible labels. If the arrow ba had been given the table (red,red), then F(b∘a)(1)=red while (F(b)∘F(a))(1)=blue. The assignment would fail. Another failure is an arrow image with wrong type, such as F(a):F(B)→F(A): it cannot be the image of a:A→B under a covariant functor. A contravariant construction reverses arrows and has a different type declaration; it is not a license to ignore typing here. Audit a translation 1. Calculation. Keep the object and edge assignments above, but propose F(ba)(0)=blue, F(ba)(1)=red. Is the assignment a functor? Give a decisive input. Hint for question 1 Compare F(ba) with F(b)∘F(a) at 0. Full solution for question 1 No. At 0, the proposed F(ba) gives blue, whereas F(b)(F(a)(0))=F(b)(u)=red. Since these are functions with the same source and target and disagree at one input, the composition law fails. 2. Explanation. Could we keep every nonidentity table correct but send 1 B to the constant function u on {u,v}? Explain using a composition. Hint for question 2 Try a∘1 A or 1 B ∘a. Full solution for question 2 No. The identity law already demands F(1 B )=id F(B) , which must fix v. The proposed constant map sends v to u. Explicitly, F(1 B ∘a)(1)=F(a)(1)=v, but (F(1 B )∘F(a))(1)=u. Thus even composition with an identity exposes the failure. The useful test A functor assigns typed image arrows and respects doing one thing then another. In a free path category, assign functions to generating edges and define every path image by their composite; identities and associativity then make the functor laws hold. If path images are assigned independently, check every composable pair. A finite table can certify the chosen example, but not functoriality of an unspecified construction over all sets. Next, compare two such translations through natural transformations .

title: A translation between translations
summary: Verify a naturality square for two finite Set-valued functors.
text: Can two translations agree systematically? Two functors can send the same source category into Set while choosing different sets and functions. A natural transformation compares their outputs at every object , and requires those comparisons to respect every arrow . A single matching picture is not enough; we will verify a complete finite case. Background capsule. A functor preserves arrow source and target, identities and composition. In Set, an arrow is a function. Let the source be the path category on one edge a:A→B, with identities 1 A and 1 B . We use G(a)∘η A for “compare at A, then use G's arrow”; η B ∘F(a) means “use F's arrow, then compare at B.” Both must have type F(A)→G(B). Two choices of data Worked example. Define F(A)={0,1}, F(B)={u,v}, with F(a)(0)=u and F(a)(1)=v. Define G(A)={p,q}, G(B)={red,blue}, with G(a)(p)=red and G(a)(q)=blue. Each functor sends identities to identity functions; since the source has no longer nonidentity path, these data determine valid functors. Define η A (0)=p, η A (1)=q and η B (u)=red, η B (v)=blue. The naturality square on the only nonidentity generator x∈F(A) η A (x) G(a)(η A (x)) F(a)(x) η B (F(a)(x)) 0 p red u red 1 q blue v blue The last outputs match on the entire source set F(A), so this square commutes. The components η A and η B are ordinary functions, but the compatibility equation makes their pair a natural transformation. A natural comparison can collapse data Keep the same functors F and G, but define a new comparison μ by μ A (0)=μ A (1)=p and μ B (u)=μ B (v)=red. For either input x in {0,1}, the route through G first compares x to p and then sends p to red. The route through F first sends x to u or v and then compares either of those to red. Both composites are the constant function with value red, so the nonidentity naturality square commutes. The identity squares commute because the functors preserve identities, exactly as before. These three checks cover every source arrow. Hence μ is a natural transformation even though neither component is one-to-one or onto its two-element target. Naturality is compatibility, not reversible relabeling. If we instead make μ B constant blue while leaving μ A constant p, the first route still ends at red and the second ends at blue. The modified family fails naturality at both inputs. Calling both components “constant” is therefore insufficient: the chosen constants must themselves agree with the target functor's arrow. Why a generator check is enough here Exact statement and full finite proof. For each arrow f:X→Y in the source category, naturality requires G ( f ) ∘ η X = η Y ∘ F ( f ) The table proves this equation for a. For 1 A , both sides equal η A , because F and G send identities to identities; similarly both sides at 1 B equal η B . These are all arrows in our tiny source category, so the proof is complete. In a path category with more edges, checking every generating edge also handles paths: if the equation holds for f:X→Y and g:Y→Z, substitute their equations into G(g)∘G(f)∘η X , reassociate, and obtain η Z ∘F(g)∘F(f). Functoriality turns this into the equation for g∘f. That reasoning relies on every path being a composite of the checked edges. Naturality is not a demand that η components are invertible. For example, constant functions can form a natural transformation when both routes send each input to the same constant. Conversely, even bijective components may fail naturality if the square does not commute. If we alter only η B (v) to red, the row x=1 compares blue with red. That pair of functions is no longer natural, though each component still has the right domain and codomain. Componentwise definitions alone therefore cannot certify the global compatibility. Check the square 1. Calculation. Retain F and G but set η A (0)=q, η A (1)=p while leaving η B as above. Is the pair natural? Show one row. Hint for question 1 Start at 0 and compare the two ways to reach G(B). Full solution for question 1 At 0, G(a)(η A (0))=G(a)(q)=blue. But η B (F(a)(0))=η B (u)=red. The functions F(A)→G(B) disagree, so naturality fails. 2. Explanation. Why do we not need a separate two-row table for the identity arrow 1 B ? Hint for question 2 Substitute F(1 B ) and G(1 B ) in the equation. Full solution for question 2 Functoriality gives F(1 B )=id F(B) and G(1 B )=id G(B) . Thus G(1 B )∘η B =η B =η B ∘F(1 B ) as functions F(B)→G(B). This is an algebraic proof for all elements, so another table is unnecessary. The compatibility is the content A natural transformation is a family of typed comparison arrows whose square commutes for every source arrow. The present proof covers our finite path category completely and explains why generator checks extend to its paths. For a category with relations or arrows not generated by a listed set, one must check the actual category, not assume this shortcut applies. The same naturality equation will control the finite Yoneda example .

title: Pairing as a universal property
summary: Prove existence and uniqueness of the pairing map into a Set product.
text: What makes ordered pairs universal? Suppose two measurements of the same input are needed: f:Z→X and g:Z→Y. We can package them into one function Z→X×Y, sending z to (f(z),g(z)). The useful claim is stronger than “pairs exist”: this package is the only function whose two coordinate projections recover f and g. Background capsule. X×Y is the set of ordered pairs (x,y) with x∈X and y∈Y. The projections π 1 :X×Y→X and π 2 :X×Y→Y select the first and second coordinates. Equality of ordered pairs means equality of both coordinates. In the category Set, objects are sets and arrows are functions. A universal property characterizes an object and its arrows by how other arrows factor through it, including both existence and uniqueness of the factor. Pair two finite observations Worked example. Let Z={0,1,2}, X={even,odd}, Y={small,large}. Set f(0)=even, f(1)=odd, f(2)=even; set g(0)=small, g(1)=small, g(2)=large. The paired function m:Z→X×Y is m(0)=(even,small), m(1)=(odd,small), m(2)=(even,large). The mediator and projections z m(z) π 1 (m(z))=f(z) π 2 (m(z))=g(z) 0 (even,small) even small 1 (odd,small) odd small 2 (even,large) even large The table displays existence for this Z. It also makes uniqueness concrete. Any candidate m′ with the two required projection equations must have m′(1)'s first coordinate odd and second coordinate small, so m′(1)=(odd,small). The same reasoning fixes m′ at 0 and 2. Prove the universal property in Set Exact statement and full proof. For any sets X,Y,Z and functions f:Z→X, g:Z→Y, there exists exactly one function ⟨f,g⟩:Z→X×Y such that π 1 ∘ ⟨ f , g ⟩ = f , π 2 ∘ ⟨ f , g ⟩ = g For existence define ⟨f,g⟩(z)=(f(z),g(z)). The first projection returns f(z), and the second returns g(z), for every z∈Z, proving both function equations. For uniqueness, suppose h:Z→X×Y obeys them. Write h(z)=(x,y). Then x=π 1 (h(z))=f(z), and y=π 2 (h(z))=g(z). Ordered-pair equality gives h(z)=(f(z),g(z)) for every z; therefore h=⟨f,g⟩. This also works when one of the sets is empty: when f and g exist, the same pointwise argument applies, and a function from an empty Z is unique. Notice the roles: X×Y is the product object, π 1 and π 2 are fixed arrows out of it, and the mediator points into it from Z. Reversing that mediator would express a different problem. Another product object can have a different coordinate presentation yet satisfy the same property. This article proves the canonical ordered-pair construction in Set; product existence in every category is not claimed. For a change of presentation, let X=Y={0,1} and label the four pairs with α, β, γ, δ in the order (0,0), (0,1), (1,0), (1,1). Call the symbol set Q. Define q 1 (β)=0 and q 2 (β)=1, and similarly read both coordinates from the other labels. The relabeling e:X×Y→Q is a bijection. Given f and g, the unique mediator into Q is e∘⟨f,g⟩. The two projection equations follow by construction. This shows why the universal property recognizes a product without requiring its elements to be written as coordinate pairs. Use existence and uniqueness 1. Calculation. Let Z={a,b}, X={0,1}, Y={red,blue}. If f(a)=1, f(b)=0 and g(a)=g(b)=red, write ⟨f,g⟩ and both projection composites. Hint for question 1 The mediator sends each z to the pair of its two observed values. Full solution for question 1 ⟨f,g⟩(a)=(1,red) and ⟨f,g⟩(b)=(0,red). Applying π 1 gives 1 at a and 0 at b, exactly f. Applying π 2 gives red at both a and b, exactly g. 2. Explanation. A proposed h sends a to (1,blue) and b to (0,red). Which requirement fails, and why does the first coordinate alone not establish a product mediator? Hint for question 2 Apply both projections at a. Full solution for question 2 π 1 ∘h=f, since the first coordinates are 1 and 0. But π 2 (h(a))=blue whereas g(a)=red. Thus π 2 ∘h≠g. The mediator must satisfy both equations; the first projection leaves the second coordinate undetermined. The arrow pattern survives new contexts The product of two sets is characterized by a unique way to pair any two maps sharing a domain. The ordered-pair proof is complete for Set, while products in other categories may use different objects. If two inputs must additionally agree after mapping to a shared target, the appropriate construction is a pullback .

title: A pullback matches shared data
summary: Construct a Set pullback from matching pairs and prove its universal property.
text: Which pairs really match? Two collections may carry labels in a common set Z. We want pairs whose labels agree. This leads to a pullback : a subset of a product equipped with two projections and a universal matching property. The construction resembles a database join, but ordinary database duplicate rows and missing values have extra semantics outside this Set example. Background capsule. A product X×Y contains every pair (x,y). A function f:X→Z assigns each x a label in Z, and g:Y→Z does the same for y. A commuting square means two composites of the same type agree. For arrows u:T→X and v:T→Y, compatibility is f∘u=g∘v:T→Z. The pullback's mediator must go from T into the set of compatible pairs. Match finite keys exactly Worked example. Take X={a,b,c}, Y={r,s}, Z={0,1}; define f(a)=0, f(b)=1, f(c)=0 and g(r)=0, g(s)=1. The compatible pairs are (a,r), (b,s), (c,r), since their key values match. Call this three-element set P. Projection p X :P→X takes first coordinates, and p Y :P→Y takes second coordinates. Matching-pair construction Pair in P p X p Y Common key (a,r) a r 0 (b,s) b s 1 (c,r) c r 0 For example, let T={α,β}, u(α)=a, u(β)=b and v(α)=r, v(β)=s. The compatibility equation holds on both elements. The forced mediator m:T→P has m(α)=(a,r), m(β)=(b,s), and each projection recovers u or v. The third possible pair in P is unused, which is fine: a mediator need not be onto. The table gives a complete static model of the same matching rule. The universal matching proof Exact statement and full proof in Set. Given functions f:X→Z and g:Y→Z, define P={(x,y)∈X×Y : f(x)=g(y)}. With restricted coordinate projections, the defining equation is P = { ( x , y ) ∈ X × Y : f ( x ) = g ( y ) } First, f∘p X =g∘p Y :P→Z because every member of P satisfies the displayed condition. Now take any set T and arrows u:T→X, v:T→Y with f∘u=g∘v. Define m(t)=(u(t),v(t)). Compatibility ensures m(t)∈P, so m:T→P is well-defined; its projections are u and v. If n:T→P has these same projections, its two coordinates at each t equal u(t) and v(t). Thus n(t)=m(t) for every t, hence n=m. This proves existence and uniqueness, for finite or infinite sets. It also handles T empty without a special construction. The word limit describes the general pattern: a diagram has compatible cones, and a limiting cone receives a unique arrow from each compatible cone. We have proved the special pullback case in Set. We have not proved that arbitrary diagrams have limits in arbitrary categories. That broader theorem needs additional hypotheses on the category and size of the diagram; the finite matching proof does not supply them.
