If one tried to include (a,s), the proposed projection square would fail there: f(a)=0 while g(s)=1. This is why taking the whole product X×Y is generally wrong. The product solves two independent observations; the pullback solves two observations constrained by a common result. Build a matching set 1. Calculation. Let X={1,2,3}, Y={p,q}, Z={red,blue}; f sends 1 and 2 to red and 3 to blue, while g(p)=blue and g(q)=red. List P. Hint for question 1 Group elements by their key in Z. Full solution for question 1 The red x-values 1 and 2 match q, giving (1,q) and (2,q). The blue x-value 3 matches p, giving (3,p). No other pair has equal key values, so P={(1,q),(2,q),(3,p)}. 2. Explanation. Suppose T={t}, u(t)=1 and v(t)=p in the preceding example. Can a mediator T→P with projections u and v exist? Hint for question 2 Check the compatibility equation before seeking a pair. Full solution for question 2 No. f(u(t))=f(1)=red but g(v(t))=g(p)=blue. The pair (1,p) is not in P. More generally, composing a hypothetical mediator with the commuting projection square would force f∘u=g∘v, contradicting this calculation. Where the proof ends In Set, a pullback is the set of exactly those pairs with equal images under f and g. The pointwise argument proves both the square and the unique mediator for every compatible cone. It does not turn every informal “join” into a pullback, nor assert that every category has all limits. The arrow direction and the compatibility equation are the checks to carry into a new example.

title: Free construction and forgetful map
summary: Extend generator maps uniquely to free-monoid homomorphisms.
text: How can a set freely generate an operation? Give me a set X of letters. All finite words in those letters, including the empty word, form a monoid under concatenation. A choice of an image in a monoid M for each letter extends uniquely to a monoid homomorphism on all words. This correspondence is the concrete content of the free-monoid/underlying-set adjunction. Background capsule. A monoid is a set M with an associative binary operation · and an identity e. A homomorphism φ:M→N preserves the operation and identity: φ(x·y)=φ(x)·φ(y), φ(e M )=e N . Let F(X) be finite words on X, with concatenation and empty word ε. For a function r:X′→X, F(r):F(X′)→F(X) replaces each letter x′ by r(x′), preserving order. Let U(M) be M considered only as a set; U sends a monoid homomorphism to its underlying function. The function i:X→U(F(X)) sends each letter to its one-letter word. Hom Mon and Hom Set mean sets of homomorphisms and functions of the indicated type. Choose images of two generators Worked example. Let X={a,b} and M={0,1} with addition modulo 2, whose identity is 0. Choose h:X→U(M) by h(a)=1 and h(b)=0. The induced homomorphism ĥ:F(X)→M evaluates a word by adding its letter values. Thus ĥ(ε)=0, ĥ(a)=1, ĥ(b)=0, ĥ(aba)=1+0+1=0 mod 2, and ĥ(abb)=1+0+0=1. Splitting a word into two pieces does not change the total sum, so ĥ respects concatenation. Evaluation from letters to words Word Letter values ĥ(word) ε none 0 ab 1, 0 1 aba 1, 0, 1 0 bbb 0, 0, 0 0 There are four functions X→M: each of a and b can independently map to 0 or 1. The universal property says there are correspondingly four monoid homomorphisms F(X)→M, since a homomorphism is forced by its values on the one-letter words. This finite count concerns the maps ; the free monoid F(X) itself is infinite. Existence, uniqueness and the bijection Exact statement and full extension proof. For any set X and monoid M, restriction along i gives a bijection Hom Mon ( F ( X ) , M ) ≅ Hom Set ( X , U ( M ) ) Given h:X→U(M), define ĥ(ε)=e and ĥ(x 1 …x n )=h(x 1 )···h(x n ) in that order. Associativity makes this expression unambiguous, and ε maps to e. A concatenated pair of words has exactly the first word's letters followed by the second's, so ĥ(uv)=ĥ(u)·ĥ(v). Thus ĥ is a monoid homomorphism with U(ĥ)∘i=h. Conversely, if φ:F(X)→M is a homomorphism, it sends ε to e and each word x 1 …x n to φ(x 1 )···φ(x n ). Its values on single letters therefore determine it uniquely. Restricting an extension returns h, and extending a restriction returns φ. These operations are inverse bijections. The bijection is natural in X and M. For r:X′→X, extension of h∘r equals ĥ∘F(r):F(X′)→M, since both send a word x′ 1 …x′ n to the ordered product h(r(x′ 1 ))···h(r(x′ n )). If k:M→N is a homomorphism, k∘ĥ equals the extension of U(k)∘h, because both multiply the sequence k(h(x j )). These identities also hold on ε by preservation of identities. This is the named adjunction F⊣U. General adjunction machinery, including units and counits for arbitrary functors, is beyond this proof. There is a crucial failure case: if a proposed word map sends ε to 1 in M={0,1} under addition mod 2, it cannot be a monoid homomorphism, even if it seems to preserve some nonempty concatenations. Preservation of identity is part of the definition. Extend and test 1. Calculation. With X={a,b} and M=({0,1}, addition mod 2), choose h(a)=1, h(b)=1. Compute ĥ(abba) and ĥ(ε). Hint for question 1 Add one copy of each letter's assigned value, retaining repetitions. Full solution for question 1 The word abba has four letters, each valued 1, so ĥ(abba)=1+1+1+1=0 mod 2. The empty word is the monoid identity, so ĥ(ε)=0. These answers also follow by grouping abba as ab·ba: both halves evaluate to 0. 2. Explanation. Why can two homomorphisms F(X)→M that agree on every one-letter word never disagree on a longer word? Hint for question 2 Write a longer word as a concatenation of one-letter words. Full solution for question 2 For w=x 1 …x n , the homomorphism law forces φ(w)=φ(x 1 )···φ(x n ) and the same formula for ψ. Their factors agree letter by letter, hence their products agree. Both send ε to the identity. Therefore φ and ψ agree on every word. The universal arrow The one-letter inclusion i:X→U(F(X)) is universal: every function h:X→U(M) factors uniquely as U(ĥ)∘i. Our proof covers all sets X and all monoids M, not only the two-letter example. It does not say every construction called “free” is a word monoid. The distinctive data are the categories, the forgetful functor and the hom-set correspondence, with the arrow directions intact.

title: Know an object by its maps
summary: Prove a finite contravariant Yoneda instance and state the general scope.
text: What do arrows into an object reveal? To probe an object A, record all maps X→A for each possible X. A map u:Y→X turns a probe X→A into a probe Y→A by precomposition. That reversal is the reason this construction is contravariant. We will prove the Yoneda correspondence for a two-object category, then state the general result with its exact typing. Background capsule. A locally small category has a set Hom C (X,A) of arrows for each pair of objects, even if the class of all objects is large. A contravariant functor F:C op →Set sends u:Y→X in C to F(u):F(X)→F(Y). The represented functor H A =Hom C (−,A):C op →Set sends u to precomposition: h:X→A becomes h∘u:Y→A. A natural transformation H A ⇒F is a compatible family of functions, one for each X. A complete two-object probe Worked example. Let C have objects 0 and 1, identities, and one nonidentity arrow a:0→1. Choose A=1. Then H 1 (0)={a} and H 1 (1)={1 1 }. Precomposition along a maps 1 1 to a. Define a contravariant F by F(1)={r,s}, F(0)={x,y}, and F(a):F(1)→F(0) with r↦x, s↦y. Identities act as identities. All natural maps from H 1 to F Chosen t∈F(1) Component at 1 Component at 0 r 1 1 ↦r a↦x s 1 1 ↦s a↦y The component at 0 is forced: naturality at a requires its value on a to be F(a) applied to the value of the component at 1 on 1 1 . Thus there are exactly two natural transformations, corresponding to the two members of F(1). Notice the direction F(a):F(1)→F(0); writing F(0)→F(1) here would reverse the wrong way. Statement, finite proof and general boundary Exact general statement. For a locally small category C, an object A and F:C op →Set, the contravariant Yoneda lemma gives a bijection Nat ( Hom C ( − , A ) , F ) ≅ F ( A ) Full proof for our finite C. A component at 1 is a function from the singleton {1 1 } into {r,s}, so it chooses t=r or t=s. Naturality for a says η 0 (a)=F(a)(η 1 (1 1 )). This uniquely fixes the component at 0. Conversely, each choice t produces the component pair in the table; the equation holds at a, and identities commute automatically. Hence the association η↦η 1 (1 1 ) is a bijection in this finite category. General proof sketch, not a full proof here. The same candidate map sends η to η A (1 A ). Given t∈F(A), the expected inverse has component at X sending h:X→A to F(h)(t)∈F(X). Naturality follows from contravariant functoriality, and applying the formula to 1 A recovers t. A complete general treatment checks the family and inverse maps across every object and arrow, including any set-theoretic size conventions for a large C. We have stated that route; the bounded proof above checks every case in one finite C. A tempting but ill-typed variant is Nat(Hom C (A,−),F) with this contravariant F. Hom C (A,−) is covariant, so the displayed natural-transformation set is not defined as written: its two functors have different domains. The variance is mathematical content, not decoration. Follow the variance 1. Calculation. Replace F(a) by the constant map r↦x, s↦x. List the two natural transformations H 1 ⇒F. Hint for question 1 Choose η 1 (1 1 ) first, then use naturality to force η 0 (a). Full solution for question 1 For t=r, η 1 (1 1 )=r and η 0 (a)=x. For t=s, η 1 (1 1 )=s and η 0 (a)=x. They remain distinct because their components at 1 differ, even though the components at 0 coincide. 2. Explanation. Why is a proposed map F(a):F(0)→F(1) inconsistent with F:C op →Set when a:0→1 in C? Hint for question 2 In C op , a points from 1 to 0. Full solution for question 2 The arrow a:0→1 becomes a op :1→0. A covariant functor on C op must send it to a function from F(1) to F(0). A function F(0)→F(1) has the opposite type and cannot act on t∈F(1) to make η 0 (a). One precise window In the two-object category, a natural map from arrows into 1 to F is wholly determined by its value on the identity of 1, and every such value works. The general Yoneda lemma asserts this for every locally small C and contravariant Set-valued F; its full general proof is beyond this article. When writing a new instance, check whether both functors live on C or C op before trying a naturality square.

title: Put processes side by side
summary: Prove interchange for Cartesian products of functions in Set.
text: Can two functions run side by side? Functions compose in sequence: f followed by g. They can also act in parallel on pairs of inputs. In Set, the parallel operation is Cartesian product: (f×f′)(a,a′)=(f(a),f′(a′)). The central law says doing two steps in each lane agrees with doing the first steps in parallel, then the second steps in parallel. Background capsule. For f:A→B and g:B→C, g∘f:A→C acts right to left. For f′:A′→B′ and g′:B′→C′, Cartesian products A×A′, B×B′ and C×C′ are sets of ordered pairs. The map f×f′ has type A×A′→B×B′. This typing is necessary for composing it with g×g′. A monoidal category adds such a parallel operation, a unit object and coherent associativity and unit isomorphisms; we study the concrete Cartesian instance. Two lanes, one input pair Worked example. Let A={0,1}, B={u,v}, C={red,blue}; set f(0)=u, f(1)=v, g(u)=red, g(v)=blue. In the other lane let A′={p,q}, B′={2,3}, C′={even,odd}; set f′(p)=2, f′(q)=3, g′(2)=even, g′(3)=odd. Starting at (1,q), first f×f′ gives (v,3), then g×g′ gives (blue,odd). Doing each lane's composite first gives ((g∘f)(1),(g′∘f′)(q))=(blue,odd). Both routes through the paired process Input f×f′ (g×g′)∘(f×f′) (g∘f)×(g′∘f′) (0,p) (u,2) (red,even) (red,even) (1,q) (v,3) (blue,odd) (blue,odd) Those rows illustrate the law but do not prove it for all four input pairs, let alone arbitrary sets. The next calculation proves it pointwise for an arbitrary pair. Check that regrouping respects processes For a numerical example, take three copies of Z and functions f(n)=n+1, g(n)=2n and h(n)=−n. Begin at ((2,3),4) in (Z×Z)×Z. Applying (f×g)×h produces ((3,6),−4); the associator then gives (3,(6,−4)). Alternatively, first regroup to (2,(3,4)) and then apply f×(g×h). The answer is again (3,(6,−4)). The same calculation with arbitrary a,b,c gives (f(a),(g(b),h(c))) along either route. Thus the regrouping bijection is compatible with the processes, rather than just a convenient encoding of elements. Its inverse restores the original parentheses. The order of the three entries stays fixed: an associator changes grouping, while swapping two lanes would use another specified map. The singleton unit has an equally concrete role. Inserting its sole element beside a gives (a,∗), and the right unitor removes it uniquely. The empty set cannot replace the singleton: for a nonempty A, A×∅ has no elements and cannot be bijective with A. The unit requirement concerns a reversible way to add a trivial lane, not merely a small-looking set. Interchange and the associator Exact statement and full interchange proof in Set. For typed functions as above, ( g × g ′ ) ∘ ( f × f ′ ) = ( g ∘ f ) × ( g ′ ∘ f ′ ) At an arbitrary (a,a′)∈A×A′, the left side first produces (f(a),f′(a′)) and then (g(f(a)),g′(f′(a′))). The right side gives exactly that pair by definition. The domain and codomain of both sides are A×A′ and C×C′, so pointwise equality proves the equation as a function equality. The product of identity functions is the identity on A×A′, since (id A ×id A′ )(a,a′)=(a,a′). These are the functorial laws of ×:Set×Set→Set. Parallel composition is associative up to a specified bijection , not literal equality of nested pair expressions. The canonical associator α A,B,C :(A×B)×C→A×(B×C) sends ((a,b),c) to (a,(b,c)); the reverse regrouping is its inverse. The unit is a chosen singleton set 1={∗}. The left unitor λ A :1×A→A sends (∗,a) to a, and the right unitor ρ A :A×1→A sends (a,∗) to a. These are bijections, not equalities of sets in a raw ordered-pair implementation. Together with × they give the Cartesian monoidal structure. We have defined the isomorphisms and proved interchange; the general coherence theorem for all regrouping diagrams is deferred. A common failure is to place g′:B′→C′ in the first lane after f:A→B. Unless B=B′ with suitable types, g′∘f is undefined. Parallel notation cannot repair a broken sequential type. Another failure is declaring ((a,b),c) literally the same ordered pair as (a,(b,c)); the associator relates them, but their nesting differs. Check two kinds of structure 1. Calculation. Using the functions above, calculate both sides of interchange at (0,q). Hint for question 1 First lane: 0→u→red. Second lane: q→3→odd. Full solution for question 1 (f×f′)(0,q)=(u,3), and (g×g′)(u,3)=(red,odd). Separately, (g∘f)(0)=red and (g′∘f′)(q)=odd, so their product also gives (red,odd). 2. Explanation. Are (A×B)×C and A×(B×C) literally the same pair construction? Give the appropriate comparison and its inverse. Hint for question 2 Track the parentheses of one element. Full solution for question 2 With ordinary nested ordered pairs, ((a,b),c) and (a,(b,c)) have different nesting, so the constructions are not being identified literally. The associator sends ((a,b),c)↦(a,(b,c)); its inverse sends (a,(b,c))↦((a,b),c). The two maps undo one another on every triple. Parallel composition has laws Cartesian product makes Set a concrete setting for sequential and parallel processes. Interchange was proved for arbitrary typed functions; associativity and unit were displayed through explicit bijections. General monoidal coherence remains outside this lesson. When applying a “side by side” picture elsewhere, first state the tensor's action on objects and arrows and check that the necessary associator and unit maps exist.

title: A curve has a speedometer
summary: A bent path is longer than its chord. Compute arc length from a smooth parametrization and explain regularity.
text: Question and background How can a ruler measure a curved road? A chord between two points underestimates the trip whenever the road bends. We can break the trip into many short chords, then ask what their lengths approach as their endpoints become close. This article gives that limit a calculable form for a continuously differentiable curve. Local capsule. A parametrized curve is a vector-valued function γ(t)=(x(t),y(t)), with t in an interval [a,b]. Its derivative γ′(t)=(x′(t),y′(t)) is the velocity vector. The Euclidean norm ||(u,v)||=√(u²+v²) is the vector's length. A definite integral adds continuously varying contributions. “Regular” means γ′(t) is never zero; that condition matters for a unit tangent, although a C¹ curve can have finite length even with a stationary point. Time and distance are distinct. Equal changes in t need not cover equal pieces of a path. Indeed, speed is the norm ||γ′||, so the clock has to be weighted by speed when we calculate distance. The method works for a curve in three dimensions as well: add a z′(t)² term under the square root. A worked example Worked example. Take γ(t)=(3cos t,3sin t), from t=0 to t=π/2. This draws one quarter of a circle of radius 3. Differentiation gives γ′=(-3sin t,3cos t), so ||γ′||=√(9sin²t+9cos²t)=3. Every unit of parameter covers three units of distance. Integrating over a parameter interval of length π/2 gives L=3π/2. A two-chord approximation uses the points at 0, π/4 and π/2. Each chord has length 3√(2−√2), giving 6√(2−√2), approximately 4.592. The true arc length 3π/2 is approximately 4.712. Refinement shortens the gaps between the polygon and the curve. The numerical comparison illustrates the limit; it is not by itself a proof of convergence for every curve. Notice that the endpoint displacement is √18, about 4.243. It is smaller than the two-chord route and the arc. The endpoint difference answers a different question from distance traveled. A curve that doubles back may even have zero displacement while accumulating positive length. The statement and its boundary Exact statement. If γ:[a,b]→ℝⁿ is continuously differentiable, its arc length, defined as the supremum of lengths of inscribed polygonal paths, equals the speed integral below. Regularity is not required for this equality. The formula does require the derivative and enough continuity for the usual integral argument. L ( γ ) = ∫ a b ‖ γ ′ ( t ) ‖ d t Why does speed enter? On a short interval [tᵢ,tᵢ₊₁], differentiability says γ(tᵢ₊₁)−γ(tᵢ) is approximately γ′(tᵢ)Δt. The corresponding chord is therefore approximately ||γ′(tᵢ)||Δt. Summing suggests a Riemann sum for the integral. A complete convergence proof needs uniform control of these errors over all sufficiently fine partitions; continuous differentiability on a closed interval supplies it. We use that standard result here and do not pretend the one-line approximation proves it. The triangle inequality explains a useful lower bound: L≥||γ(b)−γ(a)||. Straight travel attains it. Curving or reversing generally makes the inequality strict, even though the same endpoints are retained. Try it yourself Exercise 1. a slanted path. For γ(t)=(2t,3t), 0≤t≤2, compute its length and compare with endpoint displacement. Hint for exercise 1 Differentiate each coordinate; the speed is constant. Full solution to exercise 1 γ′=(2,3), so speed is √(2²+3²)=√13. Therefore L=∫₀²√13 dt=2√13. The endpoints are (0,0) and (4,6), whose difference has norm √(16+36)=2√13. Equality is expected for a straight path traversed without backtracking. Exercise 2. a deceptive clock. Let η(t)=(t²,0), −1≤t≤1. Why is the endpoint difference insufficient, and what is the path length? Hint for exercise 2 Speed is |2t|. Split the integral at zero. Full solution to exercise 2 Both endpoints are (1,0), so displacement is zero. But η moves from x=1 to x=0 and back. Its speed is |2t| and L=∫₋₁⁰(−2t)dt+∫₀¹2t dt=1+1=2. The velocity vanishes at t=0, so this curve is not regular there; nevertheless the C¹ length formula still applies. What to carry forward Keep the pairing of a curve and its speed: the integral records accumulated travel, while the endpoint vector records displacement. A zero-speed instant need not destroy length, but it prevents defining a unit tangent at that instant. Piecewise smooth paths can be measured by adding lengths of pieces; corners require separate treatment of tangent directions. For a next step, change the clock on the same geometric trace. The geometry should stay put even when the speed formula changes. Curvature will ask a second question: how quickly does the direction of motion rotate per unit of distance?

title: Different clocks, same curve
summary: Walk the same path at a different speed. Verify arc-length invariance under smooth increasing reparameterization.
text: Question and background Suppose two walkers follow exactly the same route, with one taking twice as long. They report different velocities at matching clock readings but should agree on the route's length. Reparameterization is the mathematical way to separate the path from the timing. Local capsule. A curve γ(u) has speed ||γ′(u)|| and length ∫||γ′(u)||du. An increasing function u=φ(t) changes the clock; the composite β(t)=γ(φ(t)) visits γ's points in the same order. The chain rule says β′(t)=γ′(φ(t))φ′(t). Substitution in an integral says du=φ′(t)dt when φ′ is positive and φ takes the new endpoints to the old ones. Here “same curve” means same ordered trace, including how many times it is traversed. Equality of point sets alone is weaker: a trip once around a circle and a trip twice around it have the same image but different lengths. A worked example Worked example. Let γ(u)=(cos u,sin u) for 0≤u≤π, the upper semicircle. Its speed is one and its length π. Now use φ(t)=2t on 0≤t≤π/2. Then β(t)=γ(2t)=(cos 2t,sin 2t), and β′=(-2sin 2t,2cos 2t) has speed two. The new time interval has half the duration, so the length is ∫₀^{π/2}2 dt=π. The instantaneous readings change while their accumulation does not. For a nonconstant clock, φ(t)=πt² on 0≤t≤1 also traverses this semicircle in the correct order. Its derivative 2πt vanishes at t=0. The composite's speed is 2πt, and ∫₀¹2πt dt=π. This example shows a subtle distinction: strict positivity of φ′ is a convenient hypothesis for a regular new parameter, but a smooth monotone clock with an isolated pause still gives the same length by substitution. At t=0 the second clock has no unit velocity vector. We can still calculate its length, but a curvature formula requiring nonzero speed cannot be used at that time without changing parameter or taking a limit. Reverse a clock carefully Return to the unit upper semicircle γ(u)=(cos u,sin u), with 0≤u≤π. Set φ(t)=π−t for 0≤t≤π. The new path is β(t)=(−cos t,sin t), beginning at (−1,0) and ending at (1,0). Differentiation gives β′=(sin t,cos t), so its speed is one and its length is π. The original path traverses from right to left; the new one traverses from left to right. Here φ′=−1. The chain rule changes the velocity's sign, but taking a norm changes that factor to |−1|=1. If we omitted the absolute value and integrated −1, we would obtain a negative “length,” exposing the mistake immediately. In substitution language the old integration limits reverse as well. Length is unchanged by a single reversed traversal, while an oriented tangent and signed turning depend on which way the path is followed. Keep those geometric outputs separate when changing parameters. The statement and its boundary Exact statement. Let γ:[a,b]→ℝⁿ be C¹ and let φ:[c,d]→[a,b] be a C¹ increasing bijection with φ(c)=a, φ(d)=b and φ′>0. Then β=γ∘φ has the same length as γ. The proof is a direct chain-rule and substitution calculation: L ( γ ∘ φ ) = ∫ c d ‖ γ ′ ( φ ( t ) ) ‖ φ ′ ( t ) d t = L ( γ ) The norm of a scalar multiple normally gives an absolute value: ||γ′(φ(t))φ′(t)||=||γ′(φ(t))|| |φ′(t)|. We removed the bars only because φ′ is positive. If φ is decreasing, the same norm argument and reversed endpoints still preserve length for a single traversal; orientation changes. If φ oscillates, the new route may retrace parts and length is counted again. Thus merely saying “the images coincide” misses a key hypothesis. This argument proves an equality of integrals. It does not establish that every arbitrary continuous curve has a smooth regular parameter, nor does it make a stopped clock regular. Try it yourself Exercise 1. a slower line. Start with γ(u)=(3u,4u), 0≤u≤1. Put φ(t)=t/3 for 0≤t≤3. Find both speeds and lengths. Hint for exercise 1 Compute β(t)=γ(t/3) before differentiating. Full solution to exercise 1 γ′=(3,4), so ||γ′||=5 and L(γ)=5. The new curve is β(t)=(t,4t/3), so β′=(1,4/3) and ||β′||=5/3. Over three time units its length is ∫₀³5/3 dt=5. The speed is one third, the duration three times as long. Exercise 2. same image, different trip. Compare γ(u)=(cos u,sin u), 0≤u≤2π, with δ(t)=(cos 2t,sin 2t), 0≤t≤2π. Do their point sets and lengths agree? Hint for exercise 2 Count complete revolutions, then integrate constant speeds. Full solution to exercise 2 Both images are the unit circle. γ runs around once with speed one, so L(γ)=2π. δ runs around twice with speed two over the same interval, so L(δ)=4π. The map φ(t)=2t takes [0,2π] to [0,4π], not to γ's original parameter interval; it fails the endpoint hypothesis for a single traversal. What to carry forward Reparameterization preserves the length of one ordered traversal when the new clock covers the same old interval exactly once. The chain rule explains why a higher speed is balanced by a shorter time. A pause can preserve length but break regularity, while a repeated lap increases length even if a plot looks identical. The next step is signed curvature , which measures turning per unit arc length. Its formula should be invariant under an increasing regular clock change; a decreasing change reverses the sign because it reverses the oriented traversal.

title: How sharply does a curve turn?
summary: A circle and a straight line differ by turning rate. Calculate signed curvature of regular plane curves and its value for a circle.
text: Question and background A straight road does not turn; a small roundabout turns faster per metre than a large one. Signed curvature describes this local turning of an oriented plane curve. It keeps track of left versus right turns, which an ordinary radius alone cannot record. Its unit is inverse length, so changing metres to centimetres changes the numerical value but not the geometric bend. Local capsule. For vectors v=(v₁,v₂) and w=(w₁,w₂), det(v,w)=v₁w₂−v₂w₁. A C² curve γ(t) has velocity γ′ and acceleration γ″. It is regular where ||γ′||>0. Its unit tangent is T=γ′/||γ′||, and arc length s grows at rate ds/dt=||γ′||. Rotate T left through 90 degrees to get N=(-T₂,T₁). Curvature must divide turning by distance, not by clock time. Otherwise a walker who speeds up would seem to make the path itself more curved. That is why the formula below has a third power of speed in its denominator. A worked example Worked example. Take the counterclockwise circle γ(t)=(Rcos t,Rsin t), R>0. Its velocity is (-Rsin t,Rcos t) and acceleration is (-Rcos t,-Rsin t). The determinant det(γ′,γ″)=R², while ||γ′||³=R³. Thus κ=1/R. For a clockwise traversal, γ(t)=(Rcos t,-Rsin t), the determinant is −R² and κ=−1/R. The trace is the same circle; orientation changes the sign. As a contrasting example, γ(t)=(t,0) has γ″=(0,0), hence κ=0. A circle with twice the radius has half the magnitude of curvature. The numerical values match the intuitive scale: a gentle large circle turns less over each unit of distance. For the parabola γ(t)=(t,t²), velocity is (1,2t), acceleration is (0,2), and determinant is 2. Its signed curvature is 2/(1+4t²)^{3/2}. It is greatest at the vertex and tends toward zero as |t| grows. A picture can suggest that trend; the formula gives the exact statement. Compare two points on an ellipse Take γ(t)=(2cos t,sin t). The derivatives are γ′=(−2sin t,cos t) and γ″=(−2cos t,−sin t). Their determinant is 2sin²t+2cos²t=2. The squared speed is 4sin²t+cos²t, always positive, so the curvature formula applies at every parameter value. It gives κ(t)=2/(4sin²t+cos²t) 3/2 . At t=0 the point is (2,0), speed is one, and κ=2. At t=π/2 the point is (0,1), speed is two, and κ=2/8=1/4. The ellipse therefore turns much more sharply at its rightmost point than at its top, even though both locations belong to the same smooth closed curve. Unlike a circle, it has no single constant curvature or radius describing every point. The determinant is the same at the two points; the speed correction creates the different answers. Comparing only accelerations or only the numerators would miss this distinction. Reversing this traversal would negate both signed curvatures while preserving their magnitudes. The statement and its boundary Exact statement. At any point where a plane curve γ is C² and regular, its signed curvature for the left normal N is: κ = det ( γ ′ , γ ″ ) ‖ γ ′ ‖ 3 Here is the derivation. Write v=||γ′||. Then T=γ′/v. Differentiating gives dT/dt=γ″/v−γ′v′/v². Taking determinant with T kills the second term because det(γ′,γ′)=0. Therefore det(T,dT/dt)=det(γ′,γ″)/v². Since dT/ds=(dT/dt)/v, we obtain det(T,dT/ds)=det(γ′,γ″)/v³. The derivative of a unit vector is perpendicular to it, so dT/ds=κN and det(T,N)=1. This proves the displayed formula under the stated conditions. An increasing regular reparameterization preserves κ: the numerator and denominator both gain the third power of the positive clock derivative. A decreasing one reverses its sign. If speed is zero, the displayed quotient is undefined; simplification at nearby points cannot silently assign a curvature at the stalled parameter. Try it yourself Exercise 1. a scaled parabola. Find κ at t=0 and t=1 for γ(t)=(t,3t²). Hint for exercise 1 Differentiate twice and compute one determinant. Full solution to exercise 1 γ′=(1,6t), γ″=(0,6), so det(γ′,γ″)=6 and ||γ′||³=(1+36t²)^{3/2}. Thus κ(t)=6/(1+36t²)^{3/2}. At t=0 it is 6; at t=1 it is 6/37^{3/2}. The turn is sharper near the vertex. Exercise 2. a stalled parameter. Consider γ(t)=(t²,t⁴). Can the formula be applied at t=0, even though the trace lies on y=x² for x≥0? Hint for exercise 2 Inspect γ′(0), before substituting into the curvature quotient. Full solution to exercise 2 γ′=(2t,4t³), hence γ′(0)=(0,0). The regularity hypothesis fails and the quotient has zero denominator, so κ is undefined for this parameter at zero. On the regular branch x>0, the graph parameter (x,x²) has curvature 2/(1+4x²)^{3/2}, tending to 2 as x→0⁺. That one-sided limit describes the branch's bend; it does not make the original quotient defined at t=0. What to carry forward Signed curvature is turning per unit distance, with a sign tied to orientation. For a regular C² plane curve it can be computed without first solving for arc length. At a corner there is no single tangent; at a stopped parameter the quotient is undefined. Those are genuine boundaries of this local formula. A moving tangent-normal frame packages the same turning into two differential equations. The frame makes the sign convention explicit and gives another way to reconstruct local geometric information.

title: The moving frame of a plane curve
summary: Carry coordinate axes along a path. Use Frenet equations for a unit-speed plane curve and explain sign conventions.
text: Question and background Imagine carrying two perpendicular arrows along a plane curve. One arrow points forward along the path; the other points left. Even if the arrows keep unit length and remain perpendicular, their directions change. The Frenet equations describe exactly how they rotate. Local capsule. A unit-speed curve γ(s) satisfies ||γ′(s)||=1, so s measures signed progress in units of arc length. Put T(s)=γ′(s). If T=(T₁,T₂), define the left unit normal N=(-T₂,T₁). The dot product T·N is zero and det(T,N)=1. Signed curvature κ is det(T,T′), equivalently the component of T′ along N. All derivatives in this article are with respect to s. The word “normal” can mean a principal normal pointing toward the center of bending, which fails to be defined when κ=0. We instead use the oriented left normal J T, which exists wherever T exists. That convention keeps the equations meaningful even across an inflection point. A worked example Worked example. For a counterclockwise circle of radius R, parameterize by distance: γ(s)=(Rcos(s/R),Rsin(s/R)). Then T=(-sin(s/R),cos(s/R)) and N=(-cos(s/R),-sin(s/R)). Differentiating gives T′=(1/R)N and N′=-(1/R)T. Thus κ=1/R. The normal points inward here because the circle turns left. For clockwise travel along the same circle, γ(s)=(Rcos(s/R),-Rsin(s/R)). At s=0, T=(0,-1) and left normal N=(1,0), which points outward. Now κ=-1/R, so T′=κN still points inward. The sign and normal direction change together. The product remains the physical turning of T. A straight line γ(s)=(s,0) has T=(1,0), N=(0,1), and κ=0. Both frame arrows remain fixed. This case is useful because an approach that divides by κ or insists on a “center of curvature” would fail here, while the oriented-frame equations do not. Catch a derivative taken with the wrong clock Consider β(t)=(2cos 3t,2sin 3t). This is a radius-two circle traversed counterclockwise with speed six. Its unit tangent is T(t)=(−sin 3t,cos 3t), and its left normal is N(t)=(−cos 3t,−sin 3t). Differentiating with respect to t gives dT/dt=3N and dN/dt=−3T. The coefficient three is not the curvature: it measures rotation per unit clock time. Arc length grows at ds/dt=6, so differentiation per unit distance gives dT/ds=(dT/dt)/6=(1/2)N and dN/ds=−(1/2)T. Thus κ=1/2, as expected for a radius-two circle. Equivalently, with an arbitrary regular clock the equations read dT/dt=κ(ds/dt)N and dN/dt=−κ(ds/dt)T for this oriented traversal. The arc-length version removes the speed factor. Before interpreting the coefficient of N as curvature, check which variable appears after the derivative sign. A faster walker changes that coefficient in time without changing the circle. The statement and its boundary Exact statement. For a C² regular plane curve parameterized by arc length, with N obtained from T by a counterclockwise quarter-turn, the frame equations are: T ′ = κ N , N ′ = − κ T Proof: differentiate T·T=1 to get 2T·T′=0. In the plane, a vector perpendicular to T is a scalar multiple of N, so T′=κN, with κ=T′·N=det(T,T′). The rotation J taking (x,y) to (-y,x) is fixed, so N′=J T′=κ JN=-κT. This proves both equations without assuming κ is nonzero. Differentiating T·N=0 provides the same second relation after we know N′ has no N component. These are plane equations. A space curve may require a binormal and torsion, with further regularity and nonzero-curvature caveats. We do not transfer the two-vector plane frame unchanged to three dimensions. Reversing orientation of the parameter reverses signed curvature under this left-normal convention. Try it yourself Exercise 1. read a frame. At one point of a unit-speed curve, suppose T=(3/5,4/5) and κ=-2. Find N, T′ and N′ there. Hint for exercise 1 Rotate T left, then multiply by κ as the equations prescribe. Full solution to exercise 1 N=(-4/5,3/5). Hence T′=κN=(-2)(-4/5,3/5)=(8/5,-6/5). Also N′=-κT=2(3/5,4/5)=(6/5,8/5). Checks: T·T′=24/25−24/25=0 and N·N′=-24/25+24/25=0, as required for unit arrows. Exercise 2. an inflection. Can this left-normal frame exist at a regular point where κ=0? What do the equations say at that point? Hint for exercise 2 The definition N=JT contains no division by κ. Full solution to exercise 2 Yes. Regularity gives a unit tangent T, and rotating it produces N even when κ=0. The equations give T′=0 and N′=0 at that instant. They do not say the arrows are constant on a neighborhood; curvature may change sign across the point. A principal normal defined as T′/||T′|| would be undefined there, which is why the convention matters. What to carry forward The equations are a compact record of oriented turning. They follow from unit length, orthogonality and the chosen left rotation, rather than from a sketch of arrows. The lesson's full proof is restricted to C² unit-speed plane curves; space-curve torsion and global reconstruction lie beyond it. The next part of differential geometry replaces a single moving parameter with two local coordinates on a surface patch . The same habit remains useful: calculate derivative vectors, check they are genuinely independent, and state where the chosen coordinates stop working.

title: A surface needs local coordinates
summary: A globe needs more than one flat map. Define a regular surface patch and identify coordinate singularities on a sphere.
text: Question and background A globe cannot be covered by one ordinary latitude-longitude grid without trouble at the poles. A local surface patch gives two coordinates for a piece of a surface, and its derivatives tell us whether the grid really describes a two-dimensional piece there. Local capsule. A map X(u,v)=(x(u,v),y(u,v),z(u,v)) takes a region of the coordinate plane into space. Partial derivative Xᵤ changes position as u changes with v fixed; Xᵥ does the same for v. Their cross product is perpendicular to both, and it vanishes exactly when they are linearly dependent. For a regular patch, we require a smooth map that is locally one-to-one, with Xᵤ and Xᵥ independent at every point in its domain. Coordinates are names, not the surface itself. A coordinate singularity can reflect a failed naming scheme while the underlying sphere stays smooth. Checking the derivative vectors keeps us from mistaking a grid collapse for a physical spike. A worked example Worked example. For a sphere of radius R>0, use colatitude θ and longitude λ: X(θ,λ)=(Rsinθ cosλ,Rsinθ sinλ,Rcosθ). Restrict 0<θ<π and choose an open longitude interval shorter than 2π. Then Xθ=(Rcosθ cosλ,Rcosθ sinλ,-Rsinθ) and Xλ=(-Rsinθ sinλ,Rsinθ cosλ,0). The two derivatives are orthogonal: their dot product is zero. Their lengths are R and Rsinθ, respectively. Consequently ||Xθ×Xλ||=R²sinθ>0 on the stated domain. This is a regular coordinate patch there. At θ=0 or π, Xλ=(0,0,0): changing longitude no longer changes the pole. The coordinate grid collapses. A different chart centered at the pole can describe a smooth neighborhood, so the sphere itself has no corner at either pole. A simpler patch is a graph X(u,v)=(u,v,f(u,v)). Its derivatives are (1,0,fᵤ) and (0,1,fᵥ); their cross product is (-fᵤ,-fᵥ,1), never zero when f is differentiable. Graphs therefore supply many local patches, including a small neighborhood of a sphere pole written as z=√(R²-u²-v²) on u²+v²<R². The statement and its boundary Exact rank test. A differentiable parametrization X on an open region is regular at a point if its two tangent vectors are linearly independent there. In ℝ³ that is equivalent to: X u × X v ≠ 0 The cross-product equivalence is elementary linear algebra: two vectors have zero cross product exactly when their spanned parallelogram has zero area. For the sphere calculation, orthogonality and the two derivative lengths give cross-product magnitude R²sinθ, which proves the rank claim away from poles. A full surface atlas would also organize overlapping charts and their smooth transition maps. We use the local rank test here, without claiming that one patch covers the entire sphere. Rank alone does not guarantee a globally one-to-one map. Longitudes differing by 2π name the same point, so a complete 0≤λ≤2π strip duplicates a seam even where rank is nonzero. Restricting the coordinate domain avoids that duplication locally. At a true cone tip, by contrast, the surface is not smoothly patchable in this sense; a vanished derivative cannot always be repaired by a new chart. Try it yourself Exercise 1. a graph patch. For X(u,v)=(u,v,u²−v²), calculate Xᵤ×Xᵥ and decide where it is regular. Hint for exercise 1 Use Xᵤ=(1,0,2u) and Xᵥ=(0,1,-2v). Full solution to exercise 1 The cross product is (-2u,2v,1). Its third component is always one, so it never vanishes. Thus every point in any open (u,v) domain is regular. At (0,0), the two tangent directions are (1,0,0) and (0,1,0), and the tangent plane is horizontal. Exercise 2. a coordinate collapse. Consider the cylinder X(u,v)=(cos u,sin u,v). Is u=0 a singularity? What happens if u ranges across a full 2π interval? Hint for exercise 2 Compare nonzero rank with duplicate coordinate names. Full solution to exercise 2 Xᵤ=(-sin u,cos u,0), Xᵥ=(0,0,1), and Xᵤ×Xᵥ=(cos u,sin u,0), with norm one everywhere. In particular u=0 is regular. But u and u+2π name the same cylinder point, so a closed full-period domain repeats a seam. A smaller open angular interval gives a genuine local patch. What to carry forward Two independent derivative directions make a local coordinate grid into a regular surface patch. Coordinate rank failure at a sphere pole and repeated longitudes are different issues: one collapses a derivative, the other duplicates names. Both warn us to restrict or replace coordinates before calculation. The derivative vectors also carry measurements. In the surface metric , their dot products determine lengths of paths drawn in the patch. Nothing about the grid's visual spacing alone tells us those lengths accurately.

title: Measuring on a surface
summary: How long is a route drawn on a curved surface? Compute local length from the first fundamental form of a parameterized surface.
text: Question and background Two routes can look equally long on a flat coordinate map yet have different lengths on a sphere. The first fundamental form repairs that mismatch: it translates small coordinate changes into actual distances along a surface. Local capsule. A regular patch X(u,v) maps two local coordinates into ℝ³; its partial derivatives Xᵤ and Xᵥ are independent tangent vectors. If a route has coordinates u(t),v(t), its spatial velocity is Xᵤu′+Xᵥv′ by the multivariable chain rule. The dot product gives squared length: ||w||²=w·w. We call E=Xᵤ·Xᵤ, F=Xᵤ·Xᵥ, and G=Xᵥ·Xᵥ. These values depend on the chosen coordinates, but the route's physical length does not. This metric is local. To measure a path crossing a chart boundary, split it into chart pieces or use another patch. At a coordinate singularity, the displayed coefficients may be misleading because the two tangent vectors no longer form a valid basis. A worked example Worked example. Use the sphere patch X(θ,λ)=(Rsinθ cosλ,Rsinθ sinλ,Rcosθ), with 0<θ<π and R>0. Its derivative vectors are orthogonal, with ||Xθ||=R and ||Xλ||=Rsinθ. Therefore E=R², F=0, and G=R²sin²θ. For a route at constant θ=θ₀, only longitude changes, and length between longitudes λ₁ and λ₂, along the chosen monotone interval, is Rsinθ₀ |λ₂−λ₁|. At the equator θ₀=π/2, a quarter turn in longitude has length Rπ/2. At colatitude θ₀=π/6, the same longitude change has length Rπ/4, because the latitude circle has radius R/2. A map with equal longitude spacing can hide this difference. The metric coefficient G carries it explicitly. For a meridian, keep λ fixed and vary θ. Then the length is R|θ₂−θ₁|. The coefficients thus recover both familiar circle-arc formulas from one local rule. They also allow routes where θ and λ change together, by integrating the combined squared speed. Why the mixed term matters Use the tilted coordinate grid X(u,v)=(u+v,v,0) on a plane. Its tangent vectors are Xᵤ=(1,0,0) and Xᵥ=(1,1,0). Thus E=1, F=1 and G=2. They are independent, and EG−F²=2−1=1>0, so this is a regular patch. The coordinates are slanted even though the surface is flat. Follow u=t and v=−t for 0≤t≤1. In space, γ(t)=(0,−t,0), a vertical unit segment with speed one. The metric gives the same result: squared speed is 1·1²+2·1·1·(−1)+2·(−1)²=1−2+2=1. Omitting the mixed term would incorrectly give squared speed three and length √3. The negative contribution does not make a squared length negative. It compensates for the overlap of the two nonorthogonal coordinate directions. The full positive quadratic expression, rather than either coefficient separately, measures a tangent displacement. Orthogonal coordinates such as the sphere grid have F=0; general coordinate grids need the cross term. The statement and its boundary Exact statement. For a C¹ regular surface patch and a piecewise C¹ coordinate route c(t)=(u(t),v(t)), its spatial image γ(t)=X(c(t)) has length given by the metric coefficients: ds 2 = E du 2 + 2 F du dv + G dv 2 Derivation: the chain rule gives γ′=u′Xᵤ+v′Xᵥ. Expanding its dot product with itself yields ||γ′||²=E(u′)²+2Fu′v′+G(v′)². Taking the nonnegative square root and integrating in t gives the route length. This is a full derivation from the Euclidean length formula. The shorthand ds² records the same quadratic expression for a tiny coordinate displacement; it is not an ordinary algebraic square of a finite distance between arbitrary points. Because Xᵤ and Xᵥ are independent, E>0, G>0 and EG−F²>0. This positivity makes the quadratic expression strictly positive for every nonzero tangent displacement. At a sphere pole G=0 in these coordinates, and the rank test fails. That is a coordinate failure, not proof that distances vanish near the pole. Try it yourself Exercise 1. a cylinder helix. For X(u,v)=(2cos u,2sin u,v), find E,F,G and the length of c(t)=(t,t), 0≤t≤π. Hint for exercise 1 Find the two partial derivatives and substitute u′=v′=1. Full solution to exercise 1 Xᵤ=(-2sin u,2cos u,0), Xᵥ=(0,0,1). Thus E=4, F=0, G=1. The route has squared speed 4+1=5, hence constant speed √5 and length ∫₀^π√5 dt=π√5. The route circles halfway around while rising by π units. Exercise 2. coordinate units. Why does G tend to zero near a sphere pole, and why is “eastward distance is always zero there” a wrong conclusion for a neighborhood? Hint for exercise 2 Look at the physical radius of a small latitude circle and the exact rank condition at the pole. Full solution to exercise 2 A change of longitude at fixed θ follows a circle of radius Rsinθ, so the squared speed per unit longitude is G=R²sin²θ. As θ→0 this circle shrinks. Exactly at the pole every longitude labels one point and Xλ=0, so longitude is no longer an independent coordinate. Nearby points still have positive distances; we must use a valid chart or compare their spatial positions. What to carry forward The first fundamental form measures tangent lengths through three dot products. It tells us how to compute route lengths once the patch is regular, but it does not by itself choose the shortest route. That question leads to geodesics . Keep checking the coordinate domain. A formula derived in one chart can be trusted where its tangent vectors remain independent. Smooth surfaces often need several overlapping charts, with calculations agreeing wherever both charts describe the same path.

title: Locally straight on a curved surface
summary: Flights follow great circles on an ideal sphere. Define a geodesic by locally stationary length and verify great circles as sphere examples.
text: Question and background On a sphere, the shortest nearby route between two points looks straight to a traveler who stays on the surface, even though it bends in the surrounding three-dimensional space. Such a route is a geodesic. We will verify great circles as examples and be careful about how far “shortest” extends. Local capsule. A surface path γ(s) parameterized by arc length has unit velocity T=γ′. Its acceleration γ″ can be split into a component tangent to the surface and a component normal to it. The tangential component is the intrinsic acceleration ∇ T T. A geodesic has zero tangential acceleration. A locally length-stationary path with fixed endpoints satisfies the same equation under regularity assumptions; deriving that variational equivalence for all surfaces needs a first-variation argument beyond this article. A circle drawn in a plane is curved as a space curve. On a sphere, a great circle can also have nonzero ordinary acceleration. Zero tangential acceleration, rather than zero acceleration in ℝ³, is the right test. A worked example Worked example. Consider a sphere of radius R and the equatorial path γ(s)=(Rcos(s/R),Rsin(s/R),0), parameterized by distance. Then γ′=(-sin(s/R),cos(s/R),0), which has length one. Its acceleration is γ″=-(1/R)(cos(s/R),sin(s/R),0)=−γ/R². At each point γ is a normal vector to the sphere, so γ″ has no tangential component. This proves that the equator is a geodesic. Rotating the whole sphere and the path sends this equator to any great circle. Rigid rotations preserve dot products and tangency, so the same calculation verifies every great circle. This is a direct example proof, not a proof that every sphere geodesic must be a great circle. Now fix colatitude θ₀ other than π/2 and take the latitude circle. Its spatial radius is Rsinθ₀. Its acceleration toward the latitude-circle axis has a component tangent to the sphere except at the equator. Thus the latitude circle is generally not a geodesic, even though it looks like a round and symmetric route on a map. A helical geodesic on a cylinder On the unit cylinder x²+y²=1, let γ(s)=(cos(s/√2),sin(s/√2),s/√2). Its derivative has squared norm (sin²(s/√2)+cos²(s/√2))/2+1/2=1, so s is arc length. The second derivative is γ″=−(1/2)(cos(s/√2),sin(s/√2),0). The vector in parentheses is the outward cylinder normal at γ(s). Thus the acceleration is entirely normal, and the helix satisfies the stated geodesic test. The route looks curved in surrounding space because it winds around the cylinder. Cut the cylinder along a vertical generator and use coordinates (angle,height) on a patch avoiding that seam. Its metric is dθ²+dz². The helix becomes the straight line θ=s/√2, z=s/√2 on the unrolled sheet. This supplies a second interpretation of the zero tangential acceleration. The unrolling is local: angle values separated by 2π describe the same place around the cylinder. Consequently the calculation does not establish that a long helical segment is globally shortest between its endpoints. A different winding choice can produce a shorter connection. The geodesic equation certifies local straightness in the surface metric. The statement and its boundary Exact local test. For a unit-speed C² path γ on a smooth surface, the geodesic equation is: ∇ γ ′ γ ′ = 0 The symbol ∇ here means “take the ordinary derivative and project it onto the tangent plane.” Hence the equation says the ambient acceleration is entirely normal. On a radius-R sphere the outward normal points along γ, which makes the great-circle calculation transparent. A general derivation from stationary length uses a variation γ(s,ε), fixes the endpoints and integrates a first-variation expression by parts. We state that connection and defer its full proof, along with general existence and uniqueness theory. Being geodesic does not imply globally shortest. Two antipodal points on a sphere are joined by infinitely many half great circles of equal length πR. Follow one great circle beyond a half turn and its longer arc between two points is still geodesic locally, but the shorter complementary arc wins globally. For non-antipodal points the shorter great-circle arc is the usual distance candidate; the local equation alone does not establish that global claim. Try it yourself Exercise 1. an equatorial segment. On a sphere of radius 5, find the length of an equatorial arc spanning central angle π/3 and write its acceleration in terms of position. Hint for exercise 1 Use s=R times central angle and the unit-speed great-circle formula above. Full solution to exercise 1 The length is 5π/3. In unit-speed form γ(s)=(5cos(s/5),5sin(s/5),0), so γ″=−γ/25. Since γ points normal to the sphere, this acceleration has no tangential component and the arc satisfies the geodesic equation. Exercise 2. local versus global. A traveler follows a great circle through a central angle 3π/2 between two fixed points. Is that traveled arc globally shortest? Hint for exercise 2 Use the other arc of the same great circle. Full solution to exercise 2 No. The traveled length is 3πR/2. The complementary arc between the same endpoints spans π/2 and has length πR/2. The long arc still has normal acceleration at every interior point and is geodesic there, but its local property cannot defeat the explicit shorter competitor. What to carry forward A geodesic has zero intrinsic acceleration and is locally the surface analogue of a straight route. Great circles pass the test on a sphere. Global minimality requires more information about endpoints and how long the path is followed. Surface paths will also appear in parallel transport . There the question changes: instead of choosing a path, we carry a tangent arrow along an already chosen path and examine what happens after a loop.

title: One curvature, two principal bends
summary: A saddle bends both up and down. Compute Gaussian curvature for sphere and saddle patches and distinguish intrinsic from extrinsic claims.
text: Question and background A sphere bends the same way in every direction, while a saddle bends in opposite ways. Gaussian curvature combines two principal normal bends into one signed number. This article calculates that number on two patches and separates the calculation from a deeper theorem about intrinsic geometry. Local capsule. At a regular surface point choose a unit normal n. Moving along a tangent direction changes n; the negative tangential derivative defines the shape operator S. Its two real eigenvalues k₁,k₂ are principal curvatures under this sign convention. Their product is Gaussian curvature K=det S. Reversing n negates both eigenvalues, so their product remains unchanged. The first fundamental form measures tangent lengths; the second fundamental form involves second derivatives and normal bending. For a patch X(u,v), let E=Xᵤ·Xᵤ, F=Xᵤ·Xᵥ, G=Xᵥ·Xᵥ, and e=n·Xᵤᵤ, f=n·Xᵤᵥ, g=n·Xᵥᵥ. Where the patch is regular, K=(eg−f²)/(EG−F²). We use that local formula with explicit derivatives. A worked example Worked example. First consider the radius-R sphere near its north pole as the graph z=f(x,y)=√(R²−x²−y²). At the pole, fₓ=fᵧ=0, and the tangent vectors are the horizontal coordinate vectors, so E=G=1 and F=0. With the upward normal, second derivatives are fₓₓ=fᵧᵧ=−1/R and fₓᵧ=0. Hence e=g=−1/R, f=0, and K=1/R². Both principal curvatures have the same sign for this orientation. Now take the saddle graph z=x²−y² at the origin. Again E=G=1,F=0 and n points upward. This time e=2, g=−2, f=0. Therefore K=(2)(−2)=−4. The two principal bends oppose each other. If we reversed the normal, the values would be −2 and 2, while K would stay −4. These are point calculations. A surface with variable curvature needs the coefficients recomputed at each point; using the origin's values across the whole saddle would be an error. Calculate the bend of a cylinder For the unit cylinder use X(u,v)=(cos u,sin u,v), on an angular interval shorter than a full turn. Then Xᵤ=(−sin u,cos u,0) and Xᵥ=(0,0,1), giving E=G=1 and F=0. Choose outward unit normal n=(cos u,sin u,0). The second derivatives are Xᵤᵤ=−n, Xᵤᵥ=0 and Xᵥᵥ=0. Dotting them with n gives e=−1, f=0 and g=0 under the convention used above. The quotient formula now gives K=[(−1)·0−0]/[1·1−0]=0 at every point of this patch. One principal direction bends around the cylinder; the other runs along a straight generator and has zero normal curvature. Multiplying the two principal curvatures therefore gives zero, although the cylinder visibly bends in space. Its first fundamental form is du²+dv², the ordinary flat-plane metric on the unrolled coordinate rectangle. This local calculation explains the flat intrinsic curvature without using the unproved general theorem. It does not identify the whole cylinder with the plane: periodicity around the cylinder changes its global topology. The statement and its boundary Exact local formula. For a C² regular patch with its first and second fundamental coefficients defined above, K = k 1 k 2 = e g − f 2 E G − F 2 The matrix of S relative to the coordinate tangent basis is obtained from the inverse metric matrix times the second-form matrix, up to the normal/sign convention chosen for S. Taking its determinant gives the quotient. This is an algebraic derivation of the local formula, and the sphere and saddle substitutions are exact. A full derivation that identifies every shape-operator coefficient from normal differentiation needs additional tensor bookkeeping; we have sketched that step. Gauss's Theorema Egregium says K can be recovered intrinsically from the metric, despite this formula using a normal in ambient space. That surprising theorem is stated here, not proved. Do not infer that any picture of bending alone determines intrinsic curvature. A cylinder visibly bends in ℝ³ yet has K=0 away from any seam, like a flat sheet rolled without stretching. Try it yourself Exercise 1. a scaled saddle. For z=2x²−3y², compute K at the origin with upward normal. Hint for exercise 1 At the origin, the first-form matrix is the identity; find the Hessian entries. Full solution to exercise 1 The first derivatives vanish at the origin, so E=G=1,F=0. The second derivatives are fₓₓ=4, fₓᵧ=0, fᵧᵧ=−6. Thus e=4,f=0,g=−6 and K=(4)(−6)−0=−24. The negative sign reflects opposite principal bends. Exercise 2. a rolled plane. For X(u,v)=(Rcos(u/R),Rsin(u/R),v), explain why its visible bend need not give positive K. Hint for exercise 2 Compute E,F,G and the normal bend along the vertical direction. Full solution to exercise 2 Xᵤ is unit horizontal tangent and Xᵥ=(0,0,1), so E=G=1,F=0. The normal changes as u varies but not as v varies; vertical principal curvature is zero. The other principal curvature has magnitude 1/R, and their product is K=0. The cylinder is extrinsically bent but intrinsically flat locally. What to carry forward Gaussian curvature multiplies the two principal bends and can be positive, negative or zero. The exact point calculations rely on regular C² patches; the general intrinsic-curvature theorem is beyond this article's proof. A zero value at one point does not claim the whole surface is globally flat. Gauss–Bonnet integrates this local quantity over a closed surface and connects it to topology. Applying that theorem requires global hypotheses that no single patch calculation can supply.

title: Curvature adds up to topology
summary: A sphere has a fixed total bend. State Gauss–Bonnet for a compact oriented closed surface and calculate the sphere case.
text: Question and background A sphere can be made larger or smaller, so its curvature at each point changes. Yet the total curvature obtained by integrating over the whole sphere stays fixed. Gauss–Bonnet connects that total with the Euler characteristic, a topological count that does not depend on radius. Local capsule. Gaussian curvature K is the product of principal curvatures of a smooth surface. The area element dA records physical surface area; for a patch it is ||Xᵤ×Xᵥ||du dv. The Euler characteristic χ can be computed from a suitable cell decomposition as V−E+F, with vertices, edges and faces counted once after identification. For a sphere χ=2. A “closed surface” here is compact and without boundary; an oriented surface has a consistent choice of normal direction. Gauss–Bonnet is a theorem about a complete surface under those conditions, not a local identity for any convenient coordinate rectangle. Boundary versions include geodesic-curvature and corner-angle terms. Omitting them changes the answer. A worked example Worked example. On a round sphere of radius R>0, K=1/R² everywhere. Its area is 4πR². Since K is constant, ∫K dA=(1/R²)(4πR²)=4π. A tetrahedral cell decomposition of a sphere has V=4, E=6 and F=4, so χ=4−6+4=2 and 2πχ=4π. The two calculations agree for every positive R. As a second model, a standard embedded torus has χ=0, and Gauss–Bonnet predicts total signed curvature zero. The torus has positively and negatively curved regions, whose integrals cancel. This prediction is conditional on the theorem; a single sketch of a doughnut does not compute the integral. Why does the tetrahedron count apply to a smooth sphere? The boundary of a tetrahedron is topologically a sphere, and Euler characteristic is unchanged under suitable subdivisions. Proving full topological invariance requires more work than counting one model. Here the topological fact χ(S²)=2 is supplied as background, while the round-sphere curvature integral is calculated in full. See the torus cancellation in an integral A round torus with major radius a and tube radius b, where a>b>0, has parametrization X(u,v)=((a+bcos u)cos v,(a+bcos u)sin v,bsin u). Each parameter runs through one full turn, with opposite edges of the parameter square identified. Its first fundamental coefficients are E=b², F=0 and G=(a+bcos u)², so the area element is b(a+bcos u) du dv. The factor a+bcos u stays positive by a>b. With outward normal (cos u cos v,cos u sin v,sin u), the second fundamental coefficients are e=−b, f=0 and g=−(a+bcos u)cos u. The local curvature formula therefore gives K=cos u/[b(a+bcos u)]. Multiplying K by the area element cancels the denominator and leaves cos u du dv. Integrating for 0≤u,v≤2π gives (∫₀ 2π cos u du)(∫₀ 2π dv)=0·2π=0. This computes the cancellation that a doughnut sketch only suggests. The outer region has cos u positive and the inner region negative. The total agrees with 2πχ=0 for a torus, whose usual one-vertex, two-edge, one-face decomposition gives χ=1−2+1=0. These are calculations for the round torus; they still do not prove the theorem for every compact surface. The statement and its boundary Stated global theorem. If M is a compact, oriented, smooth two-dimensional Riemannian manifold without boundary, then: ∫ M K dA = 2 π χ ( M ) The round-sphere calculation above verifies this theorem in one example; it is not a proof for arbitrary M. A general proof may triangulate the surface, relate curvature and boundary turning within pieces, and cancel internal-edge contributions. Carrying that out rigorously needs local Gauss–Bonnet, controlled triangulation and topology. Those steps are deferred. Our exact claims here are the theorem statement with hypotheses, the sphere area and curvature calculation, and the combinatorial χ value for a sphere model. Orientation is stated to fit the standard theorem and its area form. There are formulations for nonorientable surfaces using an unsigned area measure, but we do not silently substitute those. If a surface has a boundary, the displayed formula alone generally fails; it needs boundary curvature and possible corner terms. If a surface is noncompact, convergence and ends must be addressed separately. Try it yourself Exercise 1. scale a sphere. A round sphere has radius 7. Find K, area, total curvature and the Gauss–Bonnet right side. Hint for exercise 1 Use K=1/R², area=4πR² and χ(S²)=2. Full solution to exercise 1 K=1/49 and area=4π·49=196π. Therefore ∫K dA=(1/49)(196π)=4π. The right side is 2πχ=2π·2=4π. Radius cancels because local curvature decreases exactly as area increases. Exercise 2. an invalid shortcut. Someone applies ∫K dA=2πχ to a flat unit disk and concludes 0=2π. Identify the missing hypothesis and the correcting phenomenon. Hint for exercise 2 Does a disk have a boundary? What turns along its circular edge? Full solution to exercise 2 A disk has a boundary, so the closed-surface theorem does not apply. Its interior Gaussian curvature is zero, but its boundary curve has total geodesic curvature 2π in the flat plane. The boundary version gives 0+2π=2πχ(D²), and χ(D²)=1. The original contradiction came from dropping a required boundary term. What to carry forward Gauss–Bonnet turns an integral of local curvature into the topological number 2πχ under precise global conditions. The round-sphere example is a complete calculation; the general theorem is deliberately stated without a full proof. It is useful only when its compactness, orientability and no-boundary hypotheses are checked. For a related consequence, parallel transport around a spherical triangle detects enclosed curvature as a rotation. That application also needs an orientation convention and a warning about rotations counted modulo a full turn.

title: A direction can change after a round trip
summary: Carry an arrow around a spherical triangle. Compute spherical holonomy for one explicit triangle and relate it to enclosed area.
text: Question and background Carry a tangent arrow around a closed route on a sphere while keeping it locally “as parallel as possible.” When you return, the arrow can point in a different direction. The change records curvature enclosed by the loop. We will calculate it for an octant triangle. Local capsule. A tangent vector V(s) lies in the tangent plane along a surface path γ(s). Its covariant derivative ∇ γ′ V is the tangential part of its ordinary derivative in surrounding space. Parallel transport means that tangential part is zero. An arrow may still rotate in ℝ³ because tangent planes themselves turn. Holonomy is the angle between the returned arrow and its starting direction after transport around a closed loop. Angles need orientation. Choose the sphere's outward normal and traverse the boundary so the enclosed region is on the left. With the associated positive orientation, the holonomy angle in our convention equals enclosed curvature modulo 2π. Reversing traversal changes the sign. A worked example Worked example. Let the sphere have radius R. Use three vertices on the positive coordinate axes: A=(R,0,0), B=(0,R,0), C=(0,0,R). Join them by shorter great-circle arcs in the first octant and traverse A→B→C→A. Each side is a quarter great circle of length πR/2. Each interior angle is π/2, because the corresponding coordinate planes meet orthogonally at their axis vertex. The triangle has area one eighth of the whole sphere: (1/8)(4πR²)=πR²/2. The curvature of a round sphere is 1/R². Therefore ∫ over the triangle KdA=(1/R²)(πR²/2)=π/2. The arrow returns rotated by π/2 modulo 2π in the chosen positive sense. There is a second check using spherical excess: three right angles sum to 3π/2, exceeding the Euclidean value π by π/2. On a sphere of constant K=1/R², the geodesic-triangle form of Gauss–Bonnet equates this excess with area/R². The equality explains why the radius cancels; it is not an independent proof of the triangle theorem. Transport one arrow directly The octant also allows a direct check using the definition. Start at A with tangent arrow (0,1,0). On A→B write γ(t)=R(cos t,sin t,0), 0≤t≤π/2, and transport V(t)=(−sin t,cos t,0). This arrow stays unit and tangent. Its derivative is −γ(t)/R, normal to the sphere, so its tangential derivative is zero. At B it equals (−1,0,0). On B→C the route lies in the yz-plane. Keep V=(−1,0,0) constant. It is perpendicular to every radius along that arc and has zero derivative, so it is parallel. At C it is still (−1,0,0). On C→A take γ(t)=R(sin t,0,cos t) and V(t)=(−cos t,0,sin t). The initial arrow matches the preceding leg, and V′(t)=γ(t)/R is normal, giving parallel transport again. At A the returned arrow is (0,0,1). In A's tangent plane, the outward normal is (1,0,0). Rotation from (0,1,0) to (0,0,1) is therefore a positive quarter-turn. This proves the octant's π/2 holonomy directly, including continuity of the arrow at the three corners. The general area–holonomy relation still needs its stated theorem; this special transport calculation does not establish that relation for arbitrary loops. The statement and its boundary Conditional relation. For a positively oriented piecewise smooth simple loop bounding an oriented region D of a sphere of radius R, with parallel transport defined using the sphere's Levi-Civita connection, the returned rotation is: Δθ ≡ Area ( D ) R 2 ( mod 2 π ) This is a holonomy consequence of curvature integration; proving it generally requires the connection form or a Gauss–Bonnet argument for regions with boundary. We invoke that theorem here. For the octant, the three sides are geodesics, so their geodesic curvature is zero. Gauss–Bonnet then relates area curvature to corner turns, producing the π/2 angle found above. A rigorous proof that the arrow's rotation equals that curvature integral is deferred; the area and angle calculations are explicit. Why modulo 2π? A direction after a full turn is indistinguishable from its original direction. Different choices of which spherical region counts as “inside” a loop can differ by the whole sphere's curvature 4π, which is also zero modulo 2π. For a self-intersecting path, a simple unsigned area is inadequate; signed multiplicity and additional care are needed. Try it yourself Exercise 1. change the radius. Repeat the octant calculation for R=3. Find its area, K and expected holonomy angle. Hint for exercise 1 One octant occupies one eighth of 4πR². Full solution to exercise 1 Area=(1/8)(4π·9)=9π/2. Curvature is K=1/9. Their product is (1/9)(9π/2)=π/2. Thus parallel transport around the positively oriented octant returns the arrow rotated by π/2 modulo 2π. Scaling the sphere changes both factors but not this dimensionless angle. Exercise 2. reverse the route. Traverse the same octant boundary A→C→B→A. What happens to the holonomy angle, and why does its magnitude stay the same? Hint for exercise 2 Think of reversing a rotation or the signed orientation of the enclosed region. Full solution to exercise 2 The transport map around a reversed path is the inverse of the original transport map, so its angle is −π/2 modulo 2π. The same geometric region has the same ordinary area and constant curvature magnitude; only the orientation used to assign the signed rotation changes. What to carry forward The octant gives an exact area, an exact spherical excess and a directly verified holonomy calculation. The general transport-curvature relation has been invoked rather than proved. It is safe to use the formula for a simple oriented loop on a round sphere with the stated connection; arbitrary intersecting loops need more careful signed accounting. To revisit the ingredients separately, return to great-circle geodesics and Gauss–Bonnet . The former explains why the octant edges are locally straight; the latter explains why enclosed curvature controls turning.

title: Why a detour cannot be shorter
summary: Prove the direct Euclidean route is no longer than a two-leg detour and identify equality.
text: Can a detour beat a straight route? Put two displacement arrows head to tail. Their combined displacement goes directly from the first tail to the second head. The triangle inequality says the direct distance cannot exceed the total distance walked along the two arrows. This is a statement about every pair of Euclidean plane vectors, including arrows pointing backward or arrows of length zero. Background capsule. A vector u = (a,b) has Euclidean length ||u|| = √(a²+b²). Addition means (a,b)+(c,d)=(a+c,b+d). The dot product u·v=ac+bd satisfies u·u=||u||². The familiar distance between points P and Q is the length of the displacement Q−P. We will derive the one inequality about dot products needed in the proof, so no previous vector theorem is required. An exact three-four-five detour Worked example. Start at (0,0), travel along u=(3,0) to (3,0), then along v=(0,4) to (3,4). The two legs have lengths 3 and 4; the direct displacement u+v=(3,4) has length 5. Thus 5≤3+4. If instead v=(2,0), both legs point the same way: the direct displacement has length 5, exactly the sum 3+2. If v=(−2,0), walking back leaves a direct displacement of length 1 although the walk totals 5. Three routes starting with u=(3,0) Second arrow Direct length Walked length (0,4) 5 7 (2,0) 5 5 (−2,0) 1 5 The table is exact, yet three cases cannot prove a universal claim. It does suggest when equality occurs: arrows in the same direction waste no distance. The next argument turns that observation into a proof for arbitrary real coordinates. A lower bound from the same inequality The inequality also limits how much two lengths can differ. Write u=(u−v)+v. The proved result gives ||u||≤||u−v||+||v||, so ||u||−||v||≤||u−v||. Interchanging u and v gives the opposite difference bounded by the same distance. Together these say | ||u||−||v|| |≤||u−v||. This is the reverse triangle inequality, derived from the original one rather than a new assumption. For u=(3,4) and v=(3,0), the lengths are 5 and 3, while u−v=(0,4) has length 4. Their difference 2 is indeed at most 4. The bound does not assert equality: two points can have nearly equal distances from the origin and still be far apart. For u=(5,0) and v=(−5,0), their lengths agree exactly, but their separation is 10. Remember which pair of endpoints each norm measures before using a length estimate. Why every Euclidean pair obeys the bound Exact statement and full proof. For all u,v in the real coordinate plane, ‖ u + v ‖ ≤ ‖ u ‖ + ‖ v ‖ First prove the needed Cauchy–Schwarz inequality in two dimensions. If u=(a,b) and v=(c,d), expand (ad−bc)²≥0. Rearranging gives (ac+bd)²≤(a²+b²)(c²+d²), hence |u·v|≤||u||||v|| after taking nonnegative square roots. This derivation includes zero vectors; no division by a length has been used. Now expand ||u+v||²=(u+v)·(u+v)=||u||²+2u·v+||v||². Since u·v≤||u||||v||, this is at most (||u||+||v||)². Both sides whose square roots we take are nonnegative, proving the displayed inequality. This is a complete coordinate proof, not an appeal to how straight a drawing looks. When are the two sides equal? The only potentially strict step is u·v≤||u||||v||. For nonzero arrows, equality in the Cauchy–Schwarz calculation requires ad−bc=0, so the arrows are collinear; the positive dot product then says they point the same way. Equivalently v=tu for some t≥0. Equality also holds if either arrow is zero. Oppositely directed nonzero arrows are collinear but generally make a strict inequality: direction matters as much as alignment. Check the route, then test a claim 1. Calculation. Let u=(1,2), v=(2,1). Find the direct length, total walked length, and the slack in the inequality. Hint for question 1 Add coordinates before taking the direct length. Keep radicals exact. Full solution for question 1 u+v=(3,3), so ||u+v||=√18=3√2. Each leg has length √5, making the total 2√5. The slack is 2√5−3√2>0, since their squares are 20 and 18 and both lengths are positive. Equality fails because (1,2) and (2,1) are not positive multiples. 2. Explanation. Someone claims that collinear arrows always give equality. Give a counterexample and identify the missing condition. Hint for question 2 Try a pair pointing in opposite directions. Full solution for question 2 Take u=(3,0), v=(−2,0). They are collinear, but ||u+v||=1 while ||u||+||v||=5. For nonzero arrows equality needs the same direction, meaning a nonnegative scalar multiple, not mere collinearity. What the bound does and does not say A two-leg Euclidean walk can tie the straight route only when its nonzero legs point the same way. The proof used a specific length built from coordinate squares; an arbitrary rule called “length” need not satisfy this inequality. For example, define the invented quantity L(a,b)=|a²−b²|. Then L(1,1)=L(1,−1)=0 but L((1,1)+(1,−1))=L(2,0)=4, violating 4≤0. This rule also assigns zero to nonzero arrows, so it is not a distance. To reason about a new geometry, first state what its distances mean. The triangle inequality is a property to establish, not a consequence of drawing a triangle.

title: A compass bisects an angle
summary: Construct an exact angle bisector from equal-radius arcs and justify it by SSS.
text: Can an unmarked compass halve an angle? Suppose two rays OA and OC form an angle. You can bisect it without reading a number from a protractor. A straightedge draws the joining ray; a compass transfers equal lengths. The exactness comes from congruent triangles, not from pixels appearing symmetric. Background capsule. A circle with centre O and radius r contains precisely points at distance r from O. Two triangles are congruent by side-side-side (SSS) when their three corresponding side lengths agree; then corresponding angles agree. A bisector of a nonzero angle smaller than a straight angle is a ray in its interior that makes the two adjacent angles equal. We assume an ideal straightedge and compass: exact circles, exact intersections and exact lines, with no measurement error. Make two copies of the same triangle Worked example. Choose radius r>0. Draw a circle centred at O, marking its intersections X and Y with the two rays. Thus OX=OY=r. Choose a second radius s large enough that equal circles centred at X and Y meet at a point B inside the angle. Draw those circles and join O to B. The claim is that OB is the bisector. Side pairs in triangles OXB and OYB First triangle Second triangle Reason OX OY First circle radius r XB YB Second circles radius s OB OB Common side For a numerical instance, put O=(0,0), X=(2,0), Y=(0,2), and choose s=2. The inside intersection is B=(2,2): both XB and YB have length two. The drawn ray from (0,0) through (2,2) has direction (1,1), visibly halfway between the coordinate axes. The equal-side table, rather than the visual symmetry of this special instance, is what works for every allowed angle. The congruence argument Exact statement and proof. Let X and Y lie on the two distinct rays of an angle at O with OX=OY>0. Let B be an intersection of equal-radius circles centred at X and Y lying inside the angle. Then ray OB bisects that angle: ∠ X O B = ∠ B O Y OX=OY follows from the first circle. XB=YB follows from the equal radii of the second pair. OB is identical to itself. By SSS, triangles OXB and OYB are congruent, and their angles at O are corresponding angles. Since B was chosen inside the original angle, these two equal angles partition it. Therefore each is exactly half of ∠XOY. There is a small existence condition behind the instructions. X and Y are distinct for a nonzero angle, so the circles of radius s meet in two points when s>XY/2. The perpendicular bisector of XY passes through O because OX=OY. One intersection lies inside the smaller angle when that angle is strictly between 0 and π; select that one. Choosing s=XY/2 makes the circles tangent at the midpoint of XY, which is still inside, but drawing a transverse intersection is easier to specify. At the zero-angle case X=Y and the intended pair of triangles is degenerate. The construction establishes an exact relation in ideal Euclidean geometry. A physical pencil line has width; two displayed circles may have visibly imperfect intersections. Those practical errors do not alter the mathematical claim and cannot serve as its proof. The proof uses SSS and the ability to construct and intersect Euclidean circles. It does not prove that every visually symmetric sketch has equal angles. Use the construction deliberately 1. Calculation. An angle measures 74°. After the construction, what are ∠XOB and ∠BOY? Which equalities justify the answer? Hint for question 1 Find the three matching sides before halving the measure. Full solution for question 1 The first arc gives OX=OY, the equal later arcs give XB=YB, and OB is common. SSS gives ∠XOB=∠BOY. They add to 74° because B lies inside the angle, so each is 37°. 2. Failure test. Suppose the second circles have different radii. Is OB guaranteed to bisect? Construct a concrete numerical counterexample. Hint for question 2 Use X=(2,0), Y=(0,2), and B=(1,2). Compare the two distances from B. Full solution for question 2 XB=√5 while YB=1, so B can be an intersection of circles with those unequal radii.
