OB points in direction (1,2), not (1,1), hence does not split the right angle equally. The SSS argument loses its XB=YB step. Where the certainty lives The compass transfers two pairs of equal lengths, and SSS converts those equal lengths into equal angles. This is a complete Euclidean proof for a nondegenerate angle and the specified inside intersection. A zero angle has no distinct sides to bisect by this recipe; choosing the outside circle intersection would split the reflex region instead. The same method can be repeated to quarter an angle, although it cannot produce every desired numerical angle by straightedge and compass. The important habit is to annotate the equal radii before claiming the pictured ray is a bisector.

title: One parallel axiom, different worlds
summary: Compare the number of parallels in Euclidean, spherical and hyperbolic models with each line definition explicit.
text: How many parallels pass through one point? In a school drawing, a point outside a line has one parallel line through it. That familiar assertion describes Euclidean geometry. Change what counts as a line and how distance is measured, and a different answer can be coherent. The purpose here is to keep each model's objects explicit before comparing counts. Background capsule. In the Euclidean plane, a line extends in both directions without end. Two distinct lines are parallel when they never meet. A geodesic is a locally shortest route for the chosen metric; in the models below it plays the role of a straight line. The sphere uses great circles, intersections of the sphere with planes through its centre. A standard hyperbolic disk model uses circular arcs orthogonal to its boundary circle, plus diameters. The disk boundary is not part of that plane. Three precise cards Lines and intersections in three models Model Lines Through P outside a chosen line Euclidean plane Ordinary infinite straight lines Exactly one disjoint line Sphere, with antipodal points identified for the usual projective incidence model Great circles None: any two meet Hyperbolic plane Complete geodesics Infinitely many disjoint geodesics Worked example. In the Euclidean plane, choose ℓ as y=0 and P=(0,1). Lines through P have equations y=mx+1 except the vertical x=0. If m≠0, y=0 occurs at x=−1/m; the vertical line also meets ℓ at (0,0). Only m=0 gives y=1, which stays disjoint. That is a worked coordinate instance of uniqueness, not a proof of the complete Euclidean axiom from weaker axioms. On a sphere, take the equator as a line and the north pole as P. Every great circle through the poles crosses the equator at two opposite points. In the Poincaré disk, the corresponding picture looks less ordinary: several geodesic arcs through P reach different ideal boundary pairs and can miss a fixed geodesic. Boundary endpoints are infinitely far away in the model metric, so touching a boundary point in the drawing is not an interior intersection. What is an axiom, and what is model evidence? Exact Euclidean claim. In Euclidean geometry, given a line ℓ and P not on ℓ, there exists exactly one line through P disjoint from ℓ. This is Playfair's formulation of the parallel postulate. In the coordinate plane it follows from the slope argument after a rigid change of coordinates places ℓ at y=0. Treating that coordinate plane as a model already assumes Euclidean structure; it does not prove the postulate from Euclid's other axioms. ∃ ! m : P ∈ m ∧ m ∩ ℓ = ∅ The symbols say “there exists exactly one line m” with the stated properties. On the sphere any two great circles come from planes through the origin. Two distinct such planes intersect in a line through the origin; that line hits the sphere at two antipodal points. So no pair of great circles is disjoint. As an incidence comparison this is full reasoning. Yet ordinary spherical great circles have two intersections, unlike some incidence axioms for an abstract line; identifying antipodal points repairs that feature. Also, spherical shortest paths between opposite points are not unique. Those details matter when someone calls the sphere simply “Euclid with a changed postulate.” The hyperbolic claim requires a model theorem. In the Poincaré disk, complete geodesics are orthogonal circular arcs or diameters; there are infinitely many through an exterior point that avoid a given geodesic in the open disk. One can vary their ideal endpoints through an interval. This is model evidence and a sketch, not a proof that the hyperbolic axiom is independent of Euclid's other axioms. Establishing formal independence and consistency needs a precise axiom system and an interpretation theorem. Test the definition before counting 1. Calculation. Let ℓ be y=0 and P=(2,3). Which line through P is Euclidean-parallel to ℓ? Where does y=2x−1 meet ℓ? Hint for question 1 A line parallel to a horizontal line has slope zero. Full solution for question 1 The unique horizontal line through P is y=3, and it never has y=0. For y=2x−1, setting y=0 gives x=1/2, so it meets ℓ at (1/2,0). It does pass through P, since 2·2−1=3, but it is not parallel to ℓ. 2. Explanation. A student says two great circles are parallel because they look nearly horizontal on a map. Give a decisive reason this fails. Hint for question 2 Think of the planes through the sphere's centre that define the two circles. Full solution for question 2 Two distinct centre planes meet in a line through the centre. Its two intersections with the sphere lie on both great circles. Thus the circles meet, regardless of how a map projection draws them. The statement “parallel” requires the spherical line definition, not a resemblance to flat ink lines. A useful comparison boundary Euclidean, spherical and hyperbolic geometry give one, zero and infinitely many disjoint lines through an exterior point under the stated line models. The spherical model needs its antipodal incidence caveat, and the hyperbolic count rests here on the disk-model description. A common failure is to count intersections of drawn arcs at the disk boundary as intersections of hyperbolic lines; boundary points are excluded. The lesson's conclusion is about these specific models, not a derivation of all non-Euclidean geometry from a picture.

title: Where triangle angle sums come from
summary: Prove the Euclidean triangle angle sum and locate the parallel-line step.
text: Why does a flat triangle total 180°? Measure enough paper triangles and their corner angles seem to add to a straight angle. Measurements can motivate the claim, but cannot cover every triangle. A short proof works because Euclidean parallel lines give equal alternate interior angles. Seeing that dependency prepares us to understand why triangles on a sphere or in a hyperbolic plane behave differently. Background capsule. A triangle is formed by three noncollinear points A, B and C joined by straight segments. Write its inside angles as α at A, β at B, γ at C. A straight angle measures π radians, or 180°. When a transversal crosses two parallel Euclidean lines, its alternate interior angles are equal. A line through a point parallel to a given line exists and is unique in Euclidean geometry. The argument below uses existence and the angle equality; both belong to the Euclidean setting. Transfer two corners to the third Worked example. Draw a line through C parallel to AB. Follow that line from left to right. The side CA cuts both the new line and AB, so an angle beside C on the new line equals α by alternate interior angles. Similarly CB makes an angle beside C equal to β. Between them sits γ. These three adjacent angles fill one side of a straight line, so they add to π. For a numerical right triangle with vertices A=(0,0), B=(3,0), C=(0,4), α=π/2. At B, the acute angle has tangent 4/3; at C, the remaining acute angle has tangent 3/4. The two acute angles are complementary because the horizontal and vertical sides are perpendicular, so their sum is π/2. With the right angle the total is π. This instance checks the theorem but the parallel-line argument handles triangles that are not right angled. Where each angle goes in the parallel-line proof Triangle corner Angle at C after transfer Reason α at A Left adjacent angle CA cuts parallel lines γ at C Middle angle Original triangle β at B Right adjacent angle CB cuts parallel lines The exact Euclidean theorem Statement and full proof. For every nondegenerate triangle whose sides are Euclidean straight segments, measured with ordinary Euclidean angles, α + β + γ = π Construct through C a line parallel to AB. Alternate interior angles make its two outer angles on the side containing the triangle respectively α and β. The middle angle is γ. They partition a straight angle at C, whose measure is π. Adding the three parts proves the equation. No particular side lengths or a special drawing orientation enter the reasoning. The proof's logical hinge is the parallel-line angle theorem. In familiar Euclidean foundations it is derived using the parallel postulate, or taken as an equivalent fact within a suitable axiom system. Merely sliding α and β as paper cutouts would hide that hinge. If the “lines” become great-circle arcs on a sphere, there is no parallel through C to AB; the transfer step fails. The octant triangle formed by three mutually perpendicular great circles has three right angles, totalling 3π/2. In constant curvature −1 hyperbolic geometry, a nondegenerate geodesic triangle has angle sum less than π; proving that general result requires more than this Euclidean diagram. Even in Euclidean geometry, the hypothesis “triangle” rules out collinear vertices. If A, B and C lie on one line, the usual three interior angles of a nondegenerate triangle are not defined in the same way. The theorem is not repaired by assigning convenient angles to a collapsed picture. Use the theorem and identify its hinge 1. Calculation. Two angles of a Euclidean triangle are 43° and 68°. Find the third, and decide whether a triangle with 43°, 68°, 80° can be Euclidean. Hint for question 1 Subtract known angles from the straight angle. Full solution for question 1 The third is 180°−43°−68°=69°. The proposed angles 43°+68°+80°=191° do not total 180°, so they cannot be the three interior angles of a Euclidean triangle. 2. Explanation. Someone applies the same transferred-angle proof to a spherical octant triangle. Point to the exact step that fails and give its actual angle sum. Hint for question 2 Can a great circle through one vertex avoid a given great circle? Full solution for question 2 The proof asks for a line through C parallel to AB. Every great circle meets every other great circle, so no such spherical line exists. The octant's three corners each measure π/2, making its sum 3π/2 rather than π. A theorem with an address In a flat Euclidean plane, a parallel through one vertex lets the other two angles be read against a straight angle. The equation α+β+γ=π is exact for nondegenerate Euclidean triangles. It is not a universal definition of triangle: the spherical octant is an explicit failure of that wider claim. When changing geometry, ask what counts as a line and whether the parallel-line angle relation survives. That question is more informative than asking whether the new drawing “looks curved.”

title: Why scale preserves shape
summary: Derive a common side ratio for Euclidean triangles using parallel segments and area.
text: When does changing size keep a triangle's shape? A plan drawing and its built object can have corresponding angles equal while every length changes. Euclidean triangle similarity says the lengths then change by one common factor. We will derive that statement through a parallel segment, so the reason behind the ratio is visible. Background capsule. A ratio a/b requires b≠0. Two Euclidean triangles are similar if their corresponding sides are proportional; corresponding angles are then equal. Conversely the AA criterion says two pairs of equal angles force similarity. The proof below supplies the proportionality step instead of assuming the criterion. It uses the Euclidean parallel-line angle theorem and elementary area: triangles with a shared altitude have areas in the ratio of their bases. All side lengths considered are positive. A smaller triangle inside a larger one Worked example. Take triangle ABC. Choose D on AB and E on AC so that DE is parallel to BC. Suppose AB=9 and AD=6, while AC=12. The scale from the large triangle to ADE is 6/9=2/3. The parallel-line theorem makes ∠ADE equal ∠ABC and ∠AED equal ∠ACB. We should therefore expect AE=(2/3)·12=8. It is tempting to accept the picture, but the intercept argument below makes that ratio exact. Corresponding sides in the nested example Small ADE Large ABC Small/large AD=6 AB=9 2/3 AE=8 AC=12 2/3 DE BC 2/3 One could take measurements from a printed diagram and get 7.9 instead of 8 because of line width. The exact result comes from parallelism, not the physical measurement. Likewise the last row is a mathematical consequence, even when the segment lengths are not labelled numerically. Deriving the intercept ratio Exact statement. If D lies strictly between A and B, E lies strictly between A and C, and DE∥BC in a Euclidean triangle, then AD AB = AE AC = DE BC Here is a local proof of the intercept relation AD/DB=AE/EC. Triangles ADE and BDE share altitude to line AB, so their areas have ratio AD/DB. Triangles ADE and CDE share altitude to line AC, so their areas have ratio AE/EC. Triangles BDE and CDE have the same base DE and equal altitudes because B and C lie on a line parallel to DE. Their areas are equal. Comparing the two ratios therefore gives AD/DB=AE/EC. Add 1 to both sides: (AD+DB)/DB=(AE+EC)/EC, or AB/DB=AC/EC. Equivalently AD/AB=AE/AC after simple cross multiplication. For the DE/BC ratio, parallelism gives equal corresponding angles, so triangles ADE and ABC have matching angles. To avoid circularly invoking AA, use area once more or draw through E a parallel to AB meeting BC at F. DEFB is a parallelogram, hence DE=BF. The just-proved intercept relation applied along sides CA and CB in triangle CAB gives CE/CA=CF/CB. Thus BF/BC=1−CF/CB=1−CE/CA=AE/AC, and therefore DE/BC=AE/AC. This proves all three equalities under the stated assumptions. For two arbitrary Euclidean triangles with two matching angles, use a rigid motion to place their matching angle vertices and rays together. Choose a pair of corresponding sides: if their lengths differ, place the shorter triangle's matching endpoint inside the longer side. Its third side must then run parallel to the longer triangle's third side by the converse of the parallel-angle relation. The nested result yields one common side factor. If the chosen sides are equal, the two triangles coincide by angle-side-angle congruence and the factor is one. This proves AA proportionality without assuming it in the placement step. Find a scale, then challenge a false one 1. Calculation. In triangle ABC, DE∥BC, AD=4, DB=6 and AC=15. Find AE and CE. Hint for question 1 AB=AD+DB. Apply the small-to-large ratio. Full solution for question 1 AB=10, so AD/AB=4/10=2/5. Thus AE/AC=2/5 and AE=(2/5)·15=6. Since E lies on AC, CE=15−6=9. The intercept check is AD/DB=4/6=2/3 and AE/EC=6/9=2/3. 2. Failure test. Two triangles have side lengths (3,4,5) and (6,8,11). A student sees the first two side ratios are 1/2 and declares similarity. Explain. Hint for question 2 Compare the third pair, and check whether the second triple even forms a triangle. Full solution for question 2 The third ratio is 5/11, not 1/2, so there is no single scale. Both are valid triangles because 6+8>11, but matching two side ratios alone does not give AA or all-side proportionality. The included angle between those sides can differ. The condition doing the work Parallel segments in a Euclidean triangle yield equal angle pairs and one common ratio for all corresponding sides. The area proof also explains why merely “looking like” a scaled triangle is weak evidence. AA similarity is a Euclidean result: on a fixed-radius sphere, the angles of a standard convex triangle with shorter great-circle sides determine its side lengths, so there are no differently sized scaled copies with those same angles. Euclidean scaling does not preserve that sphere. The failure case with ratios (3,4,5) and (6,8,11) shows why a partial side match is insufficient. When using a map scale, identify matching vertices and verify the common factor rather than applying one ratio to an unrelated side.

title: The angle at the circumference
summary: Prove the inscribed-angle theorem while tracking which arc a point intercepts.
text: Why does a chord make a half-angle? Fix two points A and B on a circle. Move a point P along one of the arcs between them. The angle APB remains unchanged as long as P stays on that same arc. It equals half the central angle subtending the other arc AB. Stating the arc is essential: on the opposite arc, the angle is supplementary, not identical. Background capsule. A chord joins two circle points. A central angle has its vertex at the circle centre O; an inscribed angle has its vertex P on the circle. Equal radii make triangles OAP and OBP isosceles, so each has equal base angles. A circle's full turn is 2π radians. We take distinct A, B and P, and for the simple half-angle form choose AB's minor arc with central angle θ strictly between 0 and π and P on the major arc. One exact configuration Worked example. Use the unit circle with A=(1,0), B=(0,1), O=(0,0), and P=(−1,0). The central minor angle AOB is π/2. At P, PA points right and PB points northeast, so ∠APB=π/4. Moving P along the major arc changes both rays but preserves that angle. If instead P lies on the minor arc, for example at (√2/2,√2/2), it sees the long arc AB and ∠APB=3π/4. These exact values make the arc restriction more than a technical footnote. Which arc the vertex occupies P location Arc AB seen by P Angle APB Major arc Minor arc of angle θ θ/2 Minor arc Major arc of angle 2π−θ π−θ/2 The two inscribed angles add to π. Thus opposite vertices of a cyclic quadrilateral make supplementary angles, provided the vertices occur in alternating arc order. A screen drawing might obscure which arc is intercepted; marking A, B and P in order resolves the ambiguity. From equal radii to the inscribed-angle theorem Exact theorem with case argument. Let A, B, P be three distinct points on one Euclidean circle, and let θ be the central measure of the arc AB that does not contain P. Then ∠ A P B = θ 2 Draw diameter PQ through centre O, with Q opposite P. In isosceles triangle OAP, let x=∠APO=∠OAP. The angle AOQ is exterior to that triangle at O, so ∠AOQ=2x. Likewise, if y=∠BPO, then ∠BOQ=2y. When PA and PB lie on opposite sides of PQ, ∠APB=x+y and the intercepted central arc measure is 2x+2y. When they lie on the same side, ∠APB is the positive difference |x−y| and the intercepted central arc measure is |2x−2y|. If a ray coincides with PQ, one term is zero. These cases prove the same half relation for every placement of P that does not equal A or B. The “central arc measure” can exceed π; it is the arc not containing P, not automatically the smaller central angle. For P on the major arc and θ<π, the intercepted arc is the minor arc, so the familiar form ∠APB=(1/2)∠AOB follows. For P on the minor arc, the intercepted arc measure is 2π−θ, giving π−θ/2. The proof uses Euclidean exterior-angle and isosceles-triangle facts. It does not establish the same equation for a circle drawn on a sphere using great-circle geodesics. Choose the correct arc 1. Calculation. Minor central angle AOB is 110°. Find APB when P is on the major arc, then when P is on the minor arc. Hint for question 1 First decide whether P intercepts 110° or 360°−110°. Full solution for question 1 On the major arc, P intercepts the 110° minor arc, so APB=55°. On the minor arc, P intercepts the 250° major arc, so APB=125°. These angles are supplementary, as 55°+125°=180°. 2. Failure test. A classmate says that any P on the circle gives APB=55° in the previous setup. Give the error and a counterexample location. Hint for question 2 Put P on the other arc. Full solution for question 2 Take any P strictly on the minor arc AB. It intercepts the 250° major arc, giving APB=125°, not 55°. The formula needs the intercepted arc, so moving P across A or B changes which arc is seen. At P=A or P=B the angle itself is undefined because one ray has zero length. The chord remembers an arc Every inscribed angle is half the measure of the arc it intercepts. For a fixed chord, points on the same open arc see the same opposite arc and hence the same angle. Crossing to the other arc changes the intercepted arc and usually changes the angle to its supplement. The proof is complete for Euclidean circles with distinct points; it uses equal radii and exterior-angle arithmetic. A reliable diagram should label the intercepted arc as well as the central point, because “half the angle at the centre” without that label can give the wrong answer.

title: Straight lines inside a curved disk
summary: Read Poincaré disk geodesics through the model metric and derive radial distance.
prerequisites: basic integration and logarithms (for the optional distance derivation)
text: Why can an arc be straight? In the Poincaré disk model of the hyperbolic plane, many geodesics look like circular arcs on the page. “Straight” means locally shortest according to the model's distance, not straight according to a ruler laid over the screen. The boundary circle marks ideal points infinitely far away; it is excluded from the space. Background capsule. A point is z=(x,y) with x²+y²<1. Write |z|=√(x²+y²), and |dz| for a tiny Euclidean displacement. A metric assigns its length: here the scale factor depends on location. A path's length is the integral of these tiny lengths, or a limit of fine sums. The symbol ln means natural logarithm, the inverse of e x . You can use the exact radial-distance formula below without following its optional integral derivation. A geodesic is a locally distance-minimising path for that metric. Familiar Euclidean circles meet orthogonally when their tangents make right angles at intersection. Walk radially toward the rim Worked example. Follow a radius from the origin to Euclidean radius r. Along that path |dz|=dt, so its hyperbolic length is ∫₀ʳ 2/(1−t²) dt = ln((1+r)/(1−r)). At r=1/2 this is ln 3, about 1.099. At r=9/10 it is ln 19, about 2.944. The Euclidean gaps to the rim are respectively 1/2 and 1/10, yet the hyperbolic distances from the centre grow without bound as r approaches 1. Same radial path, two notions of distance Radius r Euclidean distance from centre Hyperbolic distance from centre 0 0 0 1/2 1/2 ln 3 9/10 9/10 ln 19 The table gives an accessible numerical counterpart to a disk drawing. Points near the boundary may appear compressed into a thin ring, but a radial traveller still has a long hyperbolic journey. A photograph of the disk cannot reveal that metric without its scale rule. The metric and the geodesic rule Exact model definition. On the open unit disk, the curvature −1 Poincaré metric is ds = 2 1 − | z | 2 | dz | , | z | < 1 The radial calculation is a full derivation for that one path: 2/(1−t²)=1/(1−t)+1/(1+t), so integrating gives −ln(1−r)+ln(1+r). Its limit is infinite as r→1. This shows the boundary is infinitely far along radial paths. The model's distance to the boundary is infinite more generally, but that broader statement is not proved solely by one radial calculation. Geodesic identification, with proof boundary. Complete geodesics in this metric are diameters and arcs of Euclidean circles that meet the unit boundary at right angles. A diameter such as the horizontal axis is visibly symmetric under reflection, and the radial length formula shows its natural distance scale. More general orthogonal arcs arise from disk isometries carrying a diameter to an arc. Establishing that these transformations preserve the metric and that every geodesic is of this form requires a derivation beyond this lesson; we use the standard model theorem here rather than claiming the picture proves it. The result concerns complete geodesics; a short portion of one is also geodesic locally. Angles in the disk drawing are Euclidean angles because the metric multiplies every direction at one point by the same positive scale factor. Lengths are not Euclidean: the factor 2/(1−|z|²) changes from point to point. This combination makes the model visually useful and easy to misread. The drawn boundary is neither a geodesic nor a set of ordinary points of the hyperbolic plane. Calculate, then inspect a false shortcut 1. Calculation. Find the hyperbolic radial distance from the origin to radius 3/5. How much farther is that than the distance to radius 1/2? Hint for question 1 Use ln((1+r)/(1−r)); subtract logarithms by dividing their arguments. Full solution for question 1 At r=3/5, the ratio is (8/5)/(2/5)=4, so distance is ln 4. At r=1/2 it is ln 3. The added hyperbolic distance is ln 4−ln 3=ln(4/3), even though the added Euclidean radius is only 1/10. 2. Explanation. A student says a point at radius 0.99 is only Euclidean distance 0.01 from the boundary, so the boundary is nearby in hyperbolic distance. Diagnose the error. Hint for question 2 What happens to the scale factor as |z| approaches one? Full solution for question 2 The student has changed metrics mid-argument. The hyperbolic scale factor 2/(1−r²) diverges near r=1. From the centre to 0.99 the radial distance is ln(199), and as r→1 the radial distance diverges. The remaining radial distance from 0.99 to the boundary is infinite, despite its Euclidean coordinate gap of 0.01. Read the drawing through the metric The disk displays a complete infinite geometry inside a bounded Euclidean circle. Its geodesics are diameters or boundary-orthogonal arcs, and its radial distances grow logarithmically without bound toward the rim. The radial formula was derived here; the general geodesic classification was stated with its model-theorem dependency. A screen circle that merely looks orthogonal is not an exact proof of geodesicity. Before interpreting any diagram, identify its line definition and length rule; then its apparent curvature can be separated from the geometry it represents.

title: Triangle area from missing angle
summary: Apply Gauss–Bonnet to compute area from angle defect at curvature −1.
text: How can missing angle measure area? For a Euclidean triangle the angle sum is π. For a geodesic triangle in a constant curvature −1 hyperbolic plane it is less, and the shortfall equals its area in the model's natural units. This is an exact theorem, but its usual proof invokes Gauss–Bonnet. We will use that theorem with all assumptions visible, check a numerical instance, and distinguish the application from a proof of Gauss–Bonnet itself. Background capsule. Angles are measured in radians. A geodesic triangle has sides that are shortest-path geodesic segments in the specified metric. Gaussian curvature K describes intrinsic bending; the standard Poincaré disk metric has constant K=−1 when lengths use its chosen unit. An area element derived from that metric measures hyperbolic area, which differs from ordinary Euclidean ink area. The triangle must be nondegenerate and have finite vertices in the hyperbolic plane for the direct form used here. A triangle with prescribed angles Worked example. Suppose a hyperbolic geodesic triangle has angles α=π/3, β=π/4, γ=π/6. Their sum is 4π/12+3π/12+2π/12=9π/12=3π/4. The defect is π/4, so its area is π/4 hyperbolic square units at curvature −1. Such an angle triple is possible because all angles are positive and their sum is below π. The number does not mean that a Euclidean drawing of the triangle occupies π/4 square units on paper. Angle ledger for the example Quantity Exact value Euclidean reference total π Hyperbolic angle total 3π/4 Defect π/4 Hyperbolic area, K=−1 π/4 If we keep the same shape in a hyperbolic plane of curvature −1/R², its angle defect remains dimensionless while the natural area scales by R². We must therefore name curvature before converting an angle deficit into an area. Geometry's units are part of the formula. The theorem and its proof dependency Exact conditional statement. For a nondegenerate geodesic triangle T in the complete constant-curvature −1 hyperbolic plane, with interior angles α, β, γ, Area ( T ) = π − ( α + β + γ ) Here is the Gauss–Bonnet route, labelled as a theorem application. For a geodesic triangle, the boundary's geodesic curvature is zero. The local Gauss–Bonnet formula for a topological disk says ∫ T K dA plus the sum of exterior turning angles equals 2π. The exterior turn at each corner is π minus its interior angle, so their sum is 3π−(α+β+γ). Since K=−1 throughout T, the curvature integral is −Area(T). Substituting yields −Area(T)+3π−(α+β+γ)=2π, hence the displayed result. The algebra after invoking Gauss–Bonnet is complete; the general Gauss–Bonnet theorem and the proof that the disk metric has K=−1 are deferred. Positivity of area immediately gives α+β+γ<π for a nondegenerate finite triangle. The converse claim that every positive triple with sum below π is realised by a hyperbolic triangle is a further existence theorem, used as background for the worked example rather than proved here. At curvature K=−1/R², the same substitution gives Area=R²[π−(α+β+γ)]. Replacing R with a number changes the area unit, not the angle deficit. This result does not use the Euclidean formula with a negative correction guessed from a sketch. It requires hyperbolic geodesic sides and hyperbolic area. A curvy region bounded by arbitrary arcs has nonzero geodesic-curvature boundary terms and cannot be put into this triangle formula without adjustment. Apply the right formula to the right object 1. Calculation. A curvature −1 geodesic triangle has angles π/2, π/4 and π/8. Find its angle sum and area. What would its area be at curvature −1/9 if the same angles occur? Hint for question 1 Use eighths of π, then multiply the defect by R²=9 in the second metric. Full solution for question 1 The sum is 4π/8+2π/8+π/8=7π/8. The defect is π/8, so at K=−1 the area is π/8. At K=−1/9, R=3 and the area is 9π/8 square units in that metric. 2. Failure test. A triangle drawn with Euclidean straight segments has angles 50°, 60°, 70°. A student applies the hyperbolic formula and obtains area zero. Explain precisely why that does not determine its Euclidean area. Hint for question 2 Which metric and curvature are hypotheses of the area formula? Full solution for question 2 The angles total 180°, so the numerical defect is zero. But the formula assumes curvature −1 and geodesic sides in that metric. This is a Euclidean triangle with curvature zero. Euclidean triangles with those angles exist at every scale, so their area can vary while their angles remain fixed. The hyperbolic formula cannot be transferred to them. A precise stopping point At curvature −1, a hyperbolic geodesic triangle's area equals its positive angular defect. We derived that equation from Gauss–Bonnet and showed the unit correction for curvature −1/R². We have not proved Gauss–Bonnet or the full disk metric theory here. The Euclidean counterexample exposes the missing hypothesis in any blanket “area from angles” claim. A useful next question is why the sphere reverses the sign: spherical triangles have angle excess , but their own area formula also needs curvature and geodesic sides.

title: Three right angles on a sphere
summary: Verify a spherical octant has three right angles and one-eighth of a sphere’s area.
text: Can a triangle have three right angles? On a sphere, start at the north pole, travel down the prime meridian to the equator, then a quarter of the way around the equator, then back to the pole along a second meridian. The three route segments form a triangle, and each corner is a right angle. The result challenges the habit of treating Euclidean angle sum as part of the word “triangle.” Background capsule. A sphere of radius R consists of points (x,y,z) with x²+y²+z²=R². A great circle is the intersection with a plane through the centre. Its shorter arcs are spherical geodesics. A latitude circle away from the equator is a small circle, not a geodesic. The angle between two curves on a surface is the angle between their tangent directions in the tangent plane at their meeting point. The unit sphere has surface area 4π; radius R has surface area 4πR². Build the octant explicitly Worked example. Use N=(0,0,R), A=(R,0,0), and B=(0,R,0). NA lies in the plane y=0, NB lies in x=0, and AB is a quarter of the equator z=0. All three are great-circle arcs. At A, the equatorial tangent points in the y direction, while the meridian tangent points in the z direction, so the angle is π/2. The same coordinate argument works at B. At N, the two meridians arrive in perpendicular x and y tangent directions, again giving π/2. Exact octant checks Feature Value Reason Angle at N π/2 Perpendicular meridian tangent directions Angle at A and B π/2 each Meridian meets equator orthogonally Angle sum 3π/2 Three right angles Area πR²/2 One of eight congruent octants The area statement can be checked without a surface integral: the three coordinate planes divide the sphere into eight congruent patches, and rotations or reflections exchange them. Each gets one eighth of 4πR². The triangle is one such patch on the positive x,y,z side. Its area is positive even though its angle sum exceeds π. What the octant proves Exact instance and full verification. For N, A and B as above, with shorter great-circle arcs, ∠ N + ∠ A + ∠ B = 3 π 2 Each arc is geodesic because its containing plane passes through the centre. At N the tangent directions to the two meridians are along x and y and are perpendicular. At A the tangent to NA lies in the vertical z direction, while the tangent to AB lies along y; at B the analogous pair is z and x. Dot products of each pair vanish, giving three exact right angles. This proves the displayed angle sum for the octant, not for every spherical triangle. The area follows by eightfold symmetry, as in the table. For a general spherical geodesic triangle on a radius-R sphere, an angle-excess theorem gives Area=R²(α+β+γ−π) for a suitable simple triangle, with conventions about which region and arcs are chosen. Its general proof, often via spherical lunes or Gauss–Bonnet, is deferred here. Our octant confirms the formula in one case: R²(3π/2−π)=πR²/2. A single confirmation is not a derivation of the general theorem. Great-circle segments are essential. If we replace AB with a latitude arc above the equator, that arc is not a geodesic and the simple excess relation no longer applies without a boundary-curvature term. Likewise a spherical “line” can have several shortest routes between antipodal endpoints; choosing the shorter arc avoids that ambiguity for our vertices, which are separated by only a quarter great circle. Reason with tangents and scale 1. Calculation. A sphere has radius 2. Find the three angle measures, their sum, and the area of the octant triangle N-A-B. Hint for question 1 Changing radius changes surface area but not angles. Use one eighth of 4πR². Full solution for question 1 Each angle remains π/2, so the sum is 3π/2. The whole sphere has area 4π·2²=16π, and the octant has area 16π/8=2π. Equivalently πR²/2=π·4/2=2π. 2. Failure test. A traveller follows a circle of latitude at 60° north and calls it a spherical straight line because it looks horizontal on a map. Explain the flaw. Hint for question 2 Does the plane of that latitude circle pass through the sphere's centre? Full solution for question 2 The 60° latitude lies in a plane above the centre, so it is a small circle rather than a great circle. It is not a spherical geodesic. Map horizontality is a feature of the projection, not of shortest-path geometry. The equator is the one latitude that is a great circle. One complete counterexample The octant gives a fully checked spherical triangle with three right angles, angle sum 3π/2 and area πR²/2. It is an explicit counterexample to applying the Euclidean π-sum to all triangles. We have proved this instance from coordinate tangents and symmetry; the general spherical excess theorem remains outside the lesson. To analyze a new spherical route, first confirm that its sides are great-circle arcs. The word “straight” must be read within the surface's metric, not from a flat map.

title: Count area with lattice points
summary: Count interior and boundary lattice points to obtain exact area with Pick’s theorem.
text: Can dots measure a polygon's area? Draw a polygon whose vertices sit on the integer grid. Count grid points strictly inside it and grid points on its boundary. Pick's theorem turns those two whole-number counts into its exact Euclidean area, even if its edges slant. The formula has hypotheses: the polygon must be simple, have lattice vertices, and have no holes in the basic form. Background capsule. A lattice point has coordinates (m,n) with integers m,n. A simple polygon's boundary does not cross itself. Interior points are strictly inside; boundary points include all grid points on edges, not merely the listed corners. The area here is ordinary Euclidean square units for a grid with unit spacing. A triangle with lattice vertices has half-integer area by the determinant or shoelace formula. We will use that observation to sketch why point counting could work. Count a three-by-two rectangle Worked example. Take corners (0,0), (3,0), (3,2), (0,2). Its ordinary area is 3·2=6. Interior lattice points are (1,1) and (2,1), so I=2. The boundary has four points along each horizontal length-three edge and three along each vertical length-two edge, but counting all corners twice would overcount. A compact count is B=2·3+2·2=10. Pick's expression gives 2+10/2−1=6, matching the ordinary area. Exact rectangle count Object Count or area Check Interior lattice points I 2 (1,1), (2,1) Boundary lattice points B 10 2·3+2·2 Geometric area 6 3·2 Pick expression 6 2+10/2−1 A slanted triangle gives a less rectangular check. For vertices (0,0), (2,0), (0,1), area is one. Its only boundary lattice points are (0,0), (1,0), (2,0), (0,1), so B=4 and I=0. Pick gives 0+4/2−1=1. Counting grid points along slanted edges requires care: if an edge changes coordinates by (Δx,Δy), it has gcd(|Δx|,|Δy|) lattice intervals. The formula and a proof sketch Exact theorem. For a simple lattice polygon with connected interior and no holes, A = I + B 2 − 1 A primitive lattice triangle has no lattice points except its three vertices. A substantive lattice lemma says its area is 1/2; half-integrality alone does not prove that lemma. Assuming it, the triangle's Pick expression is 0+3/2−1=1/2. If two lattice polygons are glued along a full edge, their areas add. The boundary and interior counts also combine so that the Pick expressions add: points in the shared edge cease being exterior boundary points and become interior or are handled at its endpoints. One can triangulate a simple lattice polygon and then subdivide triangles that contain lattice points until primitive triangles remain. Each split lowers positive half-integer area, so the process terminates. This indicates a proof route. The primitive-triangle lemma, general triangulation and gluing bookkeeping, including awkward nonconvex cases, are deferred rather than hidden behind a picture. There is a particularly useful boundary count. A segment from (x₁,y₁) to (x₂,y₂) contains gcd(|x₂−x₁|,|y₂−y₁|)+1 lattice points including endpoints. Summing the gcd terms over polygon edges counts each boundary lattice point once because each vertex is the end of one interval and the start of the next. Thus B is the sum of these gcd values. For the rectangle it gives 3+2+3+2=10, agreeing with the direct list. With h holes, the corrected relation for a suitable lattice polygonal region is A=I+B/2−1+h, where B includes inner and outer boundaries. The elementary formula above does not cover holes. The correction reflects topology: an extra boundary component changes the Euler count underlying the gluing argument. Count accurately and catch a missing hypothesis 1. Calculation. Find the area of the lattice triangle (0,0), (4,0), (0,3) using Pick's theorem. First determine B and I. Hint for question 1 Boundary count is gcd(4,0)+gcd(4,3)+gcd(0,3). Compare with base-times-height area. Full solution for question 1 B=4+1+3=8. Count interior rows: at y=1 the points are (1,1) and (2,1); at y=2 only (1,2) lies strictly inside. Thus I=3, and Pick gives A=3+8/2−1=6. The independent base-times-height check is (4·3)/2=6. 2. Failure test. Remove the open unit square 1<x<2, 1<y<2 from the 3-by-3 lattice square, keeping both boundaries. Why does the basic formula give the wrong area? Hint for question 2 Count the outer and inner boundary points, then use h=1. Full solution for question 2 The region's area is 9−1=8. The outer boundary has 12 lattice points and the inner square adds 4, so B=16. No integer lattice points lie strictly in the remaining region, so I=0. Basic Pick gives 0+16/2−1=7, one short. There is one hole, and the corrected expression 0+8−1+1=8 agrees. The missing hypothesis is “no holes.” Count the right dots in the right region Pick's theorem gives exact Euclidean area from I and B for a simple hole-free lattice polygon. The rectangle and slanted triangle are checks; the primitive-triangle argument explains the proof strategy while leaving full triangulation details explicit as deferred work. An edge may contain lattice points between its corners, so use the gcd rule when counts are not obvious. A hole changes the constant term, as the square-ring counterexample shows. Grid plots can help find points, but the polygon's simplicity and boundary components must be established before applying the formula.

title: A walk is a vector
summary: Add and scale plane displacements while separating a path, a location and a vector.
prerequisites: signed numbers and coordinate pairs (refreshed here)
text: Two walks, one displacement You walk three blocks east and one north, then one block west and four north. Where are you relative to your starting point? The route has bends, but its displacement is simply two east and five north. A vector records this net change, independent of the winding route that produced it. Background capsule. Fix horizontal east and vertical north directions, with one block as the unit. An ordered pair (a,b) means a units horizontally and b vertically; negative entries point west or south. A point is a location, while a vector is a displacement. We can draw the same vector with its tail at any point. Coordinates depend on our chosen axes and unit, but the displacement does not. The zero vector (0,0) changes no position. Read the journey by components Worked example. The first leg has displacement u=(3,1), the second v=(−1,4). Starting at (0,0), the first arrival is (3,1); starting there, the second arrival is (2,5). Thus u+v=(2,5). If the second leg is taken first, you reach (−1,4) and then (2,5) again. Addition forgets the route order when only the final displacement matters. One exact journey, read coordinate by coordinate Stage East–west change North–south change First leg u 3 1 Second leg v −1 4 Combined 2 5 Twice the first leg gives 2u=(6,2); its reverse is −u=(−3,−1). A half-leg gives ½u=(3/2,1/2). Scaling a vector changes a displacement, not an absolute destination. If you begin at (7,2), adding u lands at (10,3), yet u still has coordinates (3,1). Why component addition works Exact statement and proof. In the real coordinate plane with fixed horizontal and vertical unit directions, successive displacements (a,b) and (c,d) have net displacement ( a , b ) + ( c , d ) = ( a + c , b + d ) To prove it, start at any point (x,y). The first displacement lands at (x+a,y+b). The second lands at ((x+a)+c,(y+b)+d). Associativity of real-number addition rewrites this as (x+(a+c),y+(b+d)). Subtract the starting coordinates: the net change is (a+c,b+d). This argument does not assume the starting point is the origin. Scalar multiplication is defined componentwise: t(a,b)=(ta,tb). It agrees with repeating a displacement when t is a positive integer, reversing it when t is negative, and dividing it into equal parts for rational t. Real scalars extend the same coordinate rule. For example, 2(u+v)=2(2,5)=(4,10), while 2u+2v=(6,2)+(−2,8)=(4,10). In general t(u+v)=tu+tv because multiplication distributes over addition separately in each coordinate. These laws explain why a translated drawing of an arrow is still the same vector. The starting point can change, but the two differences between head and tail stay equal. In a different rotated coordinate system, the pair of numbers may change; the geometric arrow does not. Later, a basis will make that distinction precise. This lesson proves the coordinate rules in the plane; it does not assert axioms for every abstract vector space. Try two independent checks 1. Calculation. Starting at (5,−2), take displacement p=(−4,3), then twice q=(2,−1). Find the final point and net displacement. Hint for question 1 Compute p+2q first; only then add the starting point. Full solution for question 1 Twice q is (4,−2). Hence p+2q=(−4,3)+(4,−2)=(0,1). From (5,−2) we land at (5,−1). The final point (5,−1) and the net displacement (0,1) answer different questions. 2. Explanation. A friend says the vectors from (0,0) to (2,1) and from (7,−3) to (9,−2) are different because they have different starting points. Decide whether the claim is correct, and say what would change if these were position vectors instead. Hint for question 2 Subtract each arrow's tail coordinates from its head coordinates. Full solution for question 2 The first arrow changes position by (2−0,1−0)=(2,1). The second changes it by (9−7,−2−(−3))=(2,1). They represent the same displacement vector. If the ordered pairs named points or position vectors based at a fixed origin, (2,1) and (9,−2) would indeed name different locations. What the arithmetic remembers Vector addition combines net changes; scalar multiplication repeats, reverses, or resizes one. The component formulas were proved from coordinate displacements and work for any real entries, including negative or zero values. The path itself disappears: a long detour and a straight walk can have the same displacement. This is useful when predicting a destination, but it would be a failure if you used the displacement alone to infer distance traveled. You can stop once you can distinguish a route, a final point, and a net vector. For another use of the same component arithmetic, see how two basis arrows determine a linear map .

title: Why the dot product measures alignment
summary: Compute alignment, signed components and projection onto a nonzero direction.
prerequisites: coordinate pairs and right triangles (refreshed here)
cosine rule (assumed for the angle identity)
text: How much of one direction lies along another? A wind blowing northeast helps a cyclist traveling east, but only part of that wind points down the road. The dot product measures alignment and turns that question into a signed number. Positive means a component along the chosen direction, negative means against it, and zero means perpendicular. Background capsule. A plane vector u=(u₁,u₂) is a displacement. Its length is ||u||=√(u₁²+u₂²), by the right-triangle theorem. For nonzero vectors u and v, let θ be the smaller angle between them, from 0 to π. The dot product is the coordinate calculation u·v=u₁v₁+u₂v₂. A unit vector has length one. We will distinguish the scalar component of u along v from the projected vector itself. A road and a wind Worked example. Let wind u=(3,4) and road direction v=(2,0). The dot product is 3·2+4·0=6. Since ||v||=2, the signed scalar component along the road is (u·v)/||v||=3. The projected vector is ((u·v)/(v·v))v=(6/4)(2,0)=(3,0). Thus the northward component (0,4) contributes nothing to motion along an eastward road. If the road instead points west, v=(−2,0), the scalar component becomes −3: the wind opposes the directed road. Exact projection checks for u=(3,4) Direction v u·v Signed component Projected vector (2,0) 6 3 (3,0) (−2,0) −6 −3 (3,0) (0,2) 8 4 (0,4) The westward direction yields a negative signed component but the same eastward projected vector: multiplying a negative number by a west-pointing unit vector gives an east-pointing vector. This distinction prevents sign mistakes. From coordinates to angles Exact statement. For nonzero u,v in the Euclidean plane, with angle θ between them, u · v = ‖ u ‖ ‖ v ‖ cos θ Here is a complete derivation using the cosine rule, assuming that familiar Euclidean triangle result. Component arithmetic gives ||u−v||²=(u₁−v₁)²+(u₂−v₂)²=||u||²+||v||²−2(u·v). The triangle with sides u, v, and u−v has cosine-rule expression ||u−v||²=||u||²+||v||²−2||u||||v||cos θ. Comparing the two formulas gives the displayed identity. The only deferred part is a proof of the cosine rule itself. Divide by ||v|| to get the signed length of u along v: u·(v/||v||). Divide again by ||v|| to get the coefficient multiplying v, namely (u·v)/(v·v). Therefore proj v u=((u·v)/(v·v))v. Subtract it from u. Its dot product with v is u·v−((u·v)/(v·v))(v·v)=0, so the residual is perpendicular to v. This algebra proves orthogonality without trusting a drawing. The denominator v·v is positive exactly when v is nonzero. If u or v is zero, the coordinate dot product still exists and equals zero. But the angle with a zero vector and projection onto zero are undefined by these formulas. Likewise, a zero dot product with nonzero vectors proves perpendicularity; zero dot product involving a zero vector does not describe a physical right angle. Separate a component from a vector 1. Calculation. Let u=(2,5) and v=(1,2). Find u·v, the signed scalar component along v, the projected vector, and the perpendicular residual. Hint for question 1 Compute v·v before dividing. Keep the square root only in the signed scalar component. Full solution for question 1 u·v=2+10=12 and v·v=1+4=5, so ||v||=√5. The signed scalar component is 12/√5. The projected vector is (12/5)v=(12/5,24/5). Subtraction gives residual (2−12/5,5−24/5)=(−2/5,1/5). Its dot product with v is −2/5+2/5=0, checking perpendicularity. 2. Failure case. Someone writes proj v u=((u·v)/(v·v))v for v=(0,0), then cancels the denominator and concludes the projection is zero. Explain exactly why the calculation fails. Hint for question 2 Evaluate v·v and ask what line the phrase “onto v” identifies. Full solution for question 2 For v=(0,0), v·v=0. The coefficient would require division by zero, so it is undefined. A zero vector also specifies no direction or one-dimensional line onto which to project. Although u·v=0, a zero numerator does not authorize 0/0. One could separately define projection onto the zero subspace to be zero, but that is a different definition and does not rescue this formula. Alignment has a denominator Compute u·v from coordinates, then use the cosine rule to read its sign as alignment. To project onto a direction, first check that the direction vector is nonzero. The scalar component and the projected vector are different outputs; their signs can look different when the chosen direction is reversed. This idea returns in least squares , where the residual is perpendicular to every direction available to a model.

title: When two equations meet
summary: Use reversible row operations to classify and solve 2×2 linear systems.
prerequisites: linear equations and coordinate pairs (refreshed here)
text: Where do two constraints meet? When each equation has at least one nonzero variable coefficient, two linear equations describe two crossing lines, the same line twice, or distinct parallel lines. The corresponding system has one solution, infinitely many, or none. A degenerate equation such as 0x+0y=0 describes the whole plane, while 0x+0y=1 describes no points. Row operations let us decide the solution set without relying on a possibly imprecise graph. Background capsule. A pair (x,y) solves an equation when substituting its coordinates makes the equality true. It solves a system only when it satisfies every equation. The system ax+by=p and cx+dy=q can be abbreviated A(x,y)ᵀ=(p,q)ᵀ, where A has rows (a,b) and (c,d). The superscript T marks a column; it is not an extra variable. A row operation rewrites the equations while preserving their common solution set, provided its inverse is allowed. Eliminate a variable, then check Worked example. Solve x+2y=7 and 3x−y=7. Subtract three copies of the first equation from the second: −7y=−14, so y=2. The first equation then gives x=3. Substitution checks both: 3+2·2=7 and 3·3−2=7. The lines cross at exactly (3,2), because after eliminating y there is no free variable left. Three systems with different solution sets First equation Second equation Elimination result Solutions x+2y=7 3x−y=7 −7y=−14 One: (3,2) x+2y=7 2x+4y=14 0=0 Infinitely many x+2y=7 2x+4y=13 0=−1 None The last two cases look alike on the left side: the second row is twice the first. Their right sides decide whether the lines coincide or stay parallel. A graph may hide that difference if two nearly parallel lines lie close together; exact arithmetic exposes it. Why elimination preserves the answers Exact statement and proof. For a finite system of real linear equations, swapping two equations, multiplying an equation by a nonzero number, or replacing one equation by itself plus a multiple of another preserves the set of simultaneous solutions. We can write the third operation as R j ← R j + t R i ( i ≠ j ) A common solution makes every original equation true. It therefore makes any scaled equation or sum of equations true. Conversely, a swap reverses by swapping back; multiplication by nonzero t reverses by multiplying by 1/t; and the displayed row replacement reverses by subtracting t times the unchanged row i from row j. Thus every solution of the new system also solves the old one. This proves equivalence in both directions for each permitted step. For a 2×2 system, elimination leaves either two pivot variables and one solution, at least one free variable and infinitely many solutions, or an impossible row 0=c with c≠0 and no solution. One zero row may leave one free variable; two zero rows leave two. A free variable in a consistent real system ranges over infinitely many real values. This classification assumes exactly two unknown real numbers; it is not a claim about nonlinear curves, whose intersections behave differently. Why disallow scaling by zero? Multiplying x=1 by zero changes it to 0=0. Every x would satisfy the new equation, although only x=1 solved the original. The missing inverse destroys information. The same care applies when dividing by an expression containing a variable: if it could be zero, a special case must be checked first. Classify as well as solve 1. Calculation. Solve 2x+y=5 and x−y=1. Show a reversible row operation and verify your result in both original equations. Hint for question 1 Add the two rows to remove y, then use either original equation. Full solution for question 1 Replace the first row by its sum with the second: 3x=6, while the second remains x−y=1. Hence x=2 and y=1. Checking gives 2·2+1=5 and 2−1=1. Addition of one row to another is reversible by subtraction, so no solutions were lost. 2. Explain a failure. A proposed solution to x+y=2 and 2x+2y=5 multiplies the first equation by two, subtracts it from the second, obtains 0=1, and then writes x=0,y=1. Diagnose the conclusion. Hint for question 2 Ask whether any pair can satisfy 0=1 and substitute the proposed pair. Full solution for question 2 Subtracting twice the first row gives 0=5−4=1, an impossibility. Therefore the system has no solution. The pair (0,1) fails the first equation already, since 0+1=1 rather than 2. Writing coordinates after a contradiction cannot repair it; the two original lines are distinct and parallel. Arithmetic with geometric meaning A system is about a shared solution. Reversible row operations preserve that set, so elimination can certify a crossing, coincidence, or inconsistency. A tempting divide-by-zero step can erase a case, and a graph alone may miss an exact inconsistency. If you can explain what 0=0 and 0=1 each mean, this is a satisfying stopping point. Kernel and image extend the same reasoning to the dimensions of a linear map.

title: Coordinates depend on a basis
summary: Translate one plane vector between two coordinate systems using an invertible basis matrix.
text: Can a vector have two addresses? A traveler can be located by street coordinates or by distances along two slanted avenues. The location is unchanged; its numerical address depends on the chosen directions. Vector coordinates work the same way. A basis gives a unique address for every vector, and a change-of-basis matrix translates between address systems. Background capsule. In the real plane, vectors add and scale coordinate by coordinate. Two vectors b₁ and b₂ are linearly independent if s b₁+t b₂=(0,0) forces s=t=0. In the plane, two independent vectors form a basis: each vector v can be written uniquely as s b₁+t b₂. Its B-coordinate column is [v] B =(s,t)ᵀ. Standard coordinates [v] E use e₁=(1,0), e₂=(0,1). The column [v] B is an address, not a new physical vector. Translate one address Worked example. Choose b₁=(1,1) and b₂=(1,−1). For v=(4,2), solve s(1,1)+t(1,−1)=(4,2). This gives s+t=4 and s−t=2, so s=3 and t=1. Thus the same v is (4,2) in standard coordinates and (3,1) in basis B. The numbers differ because they count different unit directions. One vector in two coordinate systems Object Standard coordinates B coordinates b₁ (1,1) (1,0) b₂ (1,−1) (0,1) v=3b₁+b₂ (4,2) (3,1) Put the basis vectors into the columns of P=[[1,1],[1,−1]]. Then P(3,1)ᵀ=(4,2)ᵀ. In this example the reverse conversion solves s=(x+y)/2, t=(x−y)/2. Applying it to (4,2) returns (3,1). That reversible formula is possible because the two column vectors are independent. What the conversion formula says Exact statement and proof. Let B=(b₁,b₂) be an ordered basis of R², let E be the standard basis, and let P be the matrix whose columns are the E-coordinates of b₁ and b₂. Then P is invertible and [ v ] B = P − 1 [ v ] E Proof: if [v] B =(s,t)ᵀ, the definition of coordinates says v=s b₁+t b₂. Since the columns of P are b₁ and b₂ in standard coordinates, matrix multiplication gives [v] E =P[v] B . Independence says Pz=0 only for z=0. In the 2×2 case this means its determinant is nonzero, so P has an inverse. Apply that inverse to both sides. The formula translates from standard coordinates to B coordinates; reversing the arrow uses P, not P⁻¹. A basis must be ordered: swapping b₁ and b₂ swaps coordinate entries. It must also be independent. If one chooses c₁=(1,1) and c₂=(2,2), then (2,2)=2c₁+0c₂=0c₁+1c₂, so the coordinates are not unique. P has proportional columns and no inverse. That is a concrete failure of the formula's hypothesis. For a linear map T, an extra distinction appears: the matrix for T in B-coordinates is P⁻¹AP if A is its standard matrix and input and output both use B. This follows by converting B-input to standard with P, applying A, and converting back with P⁻¹. It does not say A and P⁻¹AP act identically on raw coordinate pairs; their inputs use different address systems. Switch addresses deliberately 1. Calculation. For B=((2,0),(1,1)), find [v] B when v=(5,3), then reconstruct v from your answer. Hint for question 1 Write s(2,0)+t(1,1)=(5,3). The second coordinate gives t immediately. Full solution for question 1 The equations are 2s+t=5 and t=3. Thus 2s=2 and s=1, so [v] B =(1,3)ᵀ. Reconstruction gives 1(2,0)+3(1,1)=(5,3), exactly the original vector. The column matrix P=[[2,1],[0,1]] is invertible since its determinant is 2. 2. Explanation. A student chooses C=((1,2),(−1,−2)) and asserts every v has one C-coordinate pair. Find a counterexample to uniqueness and a vector that cannot be represented at all. Hint for question 2 The second candidate basis vector is the negative of the first. Every combination lies on one line. Full solution for question 2 For v=(1,2), both (1,0) and (0,−1) are C-coordinate pairs, since c₂=−c₁. Meanwhile (0,1) cannot equal s(1,2)+t(−1,−2)=(s−t,2(s−t)): a zero first coordinate would force a zero second coordinate. Thus C neither provides unique addresses nor reaches every vector. Keep object and address separate A basis translates geometry into numbers. Put basis vectors in columns to convert new coordinates to old; use the inverse for the return trip. The formula requires an independent pair, and its direction matters. When reading another matrix, ask which basis names its input and output before comparing entries. The eigenvector lesson uses coordinates to find directions with special behavior under a map.

title: Missing dimensions have to go somewhere
summary: Find kernel and image bases and prove finite-dimensional rank-nullity from basis extension.
prerequisites: linear maps, homogeneous systems and basis (refreshed here)
text: Where does a lost dimension go? A shadow of a three-dimensional object lies in a plane. Movement directly toward the lamp may disappear from the shadow, while other movements remain visible. A linear map can similarly make some input directions invisible. Rank-nullity accounts for every input direction: each contributes either to distinct output directions or to the kernel of directions mapped to zero. Background capsule. A linear map T:V→W preserves sums and scalar multiples. Its kernel is ker T={v in V:T(v)=0}; its image is im T={T(v):v in V}. Both are vector subspaces. A basis is an independent list that spans a space, and dimension is the number of vectors in any basis. Rank means dim im T; nullity means dim ker T. We assume V is finite-dimensional. Solving T(v)=0 is a homogeneous linear system. One direction disappears Worked example. Consider T:R³→R² defined by T(x,y,z)=(x+y,y+z). To find the kernel, solve x+y=0 and y+z=0. Let y=t; then x=−t and z=−t. Thus ker T consists exactly of t(−1,1,−1), a one-dimensional line. The direction (−1,1,−1) is invisible: adding it to any input changes neither output coordinate. The image is all of R². Indeed T(1,0,0)=(1,0) and T(0,0,1)=(0,1), two independent outputs; any (a,b) equals T(a,0,b). So rank is two and nullity is one. The input dimension is three: 2+1=3. How input directions behave Input Output Role (−1,1,−1) (0,0) Kernel basis (1,0,0) (1,0) First output direction (0,0,1) (0,1) Second output direction Those three input vectors form a basis of R³: if their combination is zero, the middle coordinate forces the kernel coefficient to zero, and the other coordinates then force both remaining coefficients to zero. Their images explain the dimension count directly. Every input basis can be organized this way Rank-nullity theorem, with proof. For a linear map T:V→W with finite-dimensional domain V, dim ( ker T ) + dim ( im T ) = dim V Take a basis k₁,…,k r of ker T. The finite-dimensional basis-extension theorem lets us add vectors v₁,…,v s so that k₁,…,k r ,v₁,…,v s is a basis of V. This step relies on that standard theorem about independent lists; a proof of basis extension is outside this article. We now prove that T(v₁),…,T(v s ) is a basis of im T. For spanning, expand any input x as a sum of k's and v's. Applying T kills all k terms, so T(x) is a combination of the T(v)'s. For independence, suppose ∑a j T(v j )=0. Then ∑a j v j belongs to ker T, hence equals some combination ∑b i k i . Move one side across. The independence of the full input basis forces every a j =0. Therefore image dimension is s, kernel dimension is r, and input dimension is r+s. The theorem requires a linear map and finite-dimensional domain. It says nothing by itself about the dimension of W; the image can be a proper subspace. A zero map R³→R² has rank zero and nullity three, while the map in our example has rank two and nullity one. One cannot claim “rank plus nullity equals output dimension.” Count visible and invisible directions 1. Calculation. Let S:R³→R² be S(x,y,z)=(x−z,2x−2z). Find a kernel basis, an image basis, rank and nullity. Hint for question 1 Both output coordinates depend only on x−z. Set that equal to zero and choose two free variables. Full solution for question 1 The kernel condition is x=z; y is free. Write (x,y,z)=x(1,0,1)+y(0,1,0), so those two vectors form a kernel basis. Every output is t(1,2), and t=1 is attained at input (1,0,0), so {(1,2)} is an image basis. Rank is one, nullity is two, and 1+2=3, the input dimension. 2. Explanation. A friend sees a map R³→R² and asserts its nullity must be exactly one, because 3−2=1. Give a counterexample and the corrected inequality. Hint for question 2 Try a map sending every input to zero. Rank cannot exceed the output dimension. Full solution for question 2 The zero map R³→R² has image {0}, so rank zero and nullity three. Rank-nullity gives nullity=3−rank. Since rank≤2, nullity≥1, but it need not equal one. Equality requires the image to fill all of R². A dimension ledger To use rank-nullity, solve the homogeneous equations for a kernel basis and identify independent output directions for an image basis. The proof relies on extending a kernel basis, then shows the added vectors have independent images. In finite dimensions no input direction is unaccounted for. For a 2D map, nonzero determinant is one shortcut to rank two and nullity zero; the theorem also handles rectangular matrices where a determinant is unavailable.

title: Directions a map does not turn
summary: Find real 2×2 eigenpairs and understand why rotations need not have real eigenlines.
prerequisites: 2×2 determinant, systems and quadratic equations (refreshed here)
text: Which directions survive a map? A map may stretch a diagonal line while squeezing another. A vector on a special line can emerge on that same line, although its length or direction may change. Such a nonzero vector is an eigenvector. The word “nonzero” prevents every matrix from acquiring the uninformative zero vector as an eigenvector for every number. Background capsule. A real 2×2 matrix A acts on column vectors. Multiplying by a scalar λ scales both coordinates; negative λ reverses the arrow, and λ=0 collapses it. An eigenpair consists of a real number λ and a nonzero real vector v with Av=λv. A nonzero solution of a homogeneous system exists precisely when its 2×2 determinant is zero. For [[a,b],[c,d]], that determinant is ad−bc. Find two stable lines Worked example. Take A=[[3,1],[0,2]], meaning A(x,y)=(3x+y,2y). The vector (1,0) goes to (3,0), so λ=3. The vector (−1,1) goes to (−2,2)=2(−1,1), so λ=2. Neither eigenvector remains fixed in length, but each output lies on its original line. The line rather than a particular arrow is the stable geometric object. Exact actions of A Input Output Eigenvector? (1,0) (3,0) Yes, λ=3 (−1,1) (−2,2) Yes, λ=2 (0,1) (1,2) No: output leaves its line To discover these systematically, form A−λI=[[3−λ,1],[0,2−λ]]. Its determinant is (3−λ)(2−λ). Setting it to zero gives candidate eigenvalues 3 and 2. Solving (A−3I)v=0 gives y=0; solving (A−2I)v=0 gives x+y=0. That recovers both lines. Every nonzero multiple of one listed eigenvector lies on the same eigenline and has the same eigenvalue; there are infinitely many arrows on each line, not just the representative in the table. Use the stable directions for repeated steps For the same matrix A, write an arbitrary vector (x,y) as (x+y)(1,0)+y(−1,1). Expanding the right side gives (x+y−y,y)=(x,y), and the second coordinate determines y uniquely. The two eigenvectors therefore form a basis in this particular example. Applying A repeatedly now multiplies the first coefficient by 3 at each step and the second by 2. After k steps, for any nonnegative integer k, the result is (x+y)3 k (1,0)+y2 k (−1,1). For input (2,1) and k=2 this gives 27(1,0)+4(−1,1)=(23,4). Direct multiplication checks the result: A(2,1)=(7,2) and A(7,2)=(23,4). The decomposition replaces two rounds of matrix arithmetic by two independent scalar powers. It works because these eigenvectors are independent and cover the input plane. A repeated eigenvalue with only one eigenline would not support this calculation for every input; finding one stable direction is not enough. Why the characteristic equation appears Exact statement and proof for real 2×2 matrices. A real scalar λ is an eigenvalue of A exactly when det ( A − λ I ) = 0 , v ≠ 0 , A v = λ v Indeed Av=λv rearranges to (A−λI)v=0. A nonzero solution means that the two columns of A−λI are dependent; in two dimensions, that happens exactly when their determinant is zero. Conversely determinant zero gives dependent columns, hence a nonzero kernel vector. Expanding for A=[[a,b],[c,d]] produces (a−λ)(d−λ)−bc=λ²−(a+d)λ+(ad−bc). This quadratic is the characteristic polynomial. Its real roots, when present, are the real eigenvalues. The argument proves the 2×2 criterion; it does not establish a general theorem about eigenvalues in arbitrary dimension. A real rotation through a quarter-turn R=[[0,−1],[1,0]] is a crucial failure case for an overbroad intuition. Its polynomial is λ²+1, which has no real root. Geometrically every nonzero real vector turns 90 degrees and leaves its line. Over the complex numbers roots i and −i exist, but that is a change of scalar field, not a real eigenline. Even when a matrix has a real eigenvalue, it may lack two independent eigenvectors: [[1,1],[0,1]] has only the line y=0 for λ=1. We have therefore not promised a basis of eigenvectors for every map. Test the line, not just a number 1. Calculation. Find real eigenvalues and one eigenvector for each of B=[[2,0],[1,3]]. Verify by direct multiplication. Hint for question 1 The determinant of B−λI is (2−λ)(3−λ). Solve one homogeneous system per root. Full solution for question 1 Eigenvalues are 2 and 3. For λ=2, (B−2I)(x,y)=(0,x+y), so choose v=(1,−1); Bv=(2,−2)=2v. For λ=3, (B−3I)(x,y)=(−x,x), so choose w=(0,1); Bw=(0,3)=3w. Both vectors are nonzero. 2. Explanation. Someone says every real 2×2 matrix has a real eigenvector because its characteristic polynomial is quadratic. Identify the gap with an explicit matrix. Hint for question 2 A quadratic can have a negative discriminant. Try a quarter-turn. Full solution for question 2 For R=[[0,−1],[1,0]], det(R−λI)=λ²+1. This is positive for every real λ, so no nonzero real v can solve Rv=λv. Being quadratic guarantees complex roots, counted with multiplicity, but does not guarantee real ones. Stable lines have hypotheses Find eigenvalues by det(A−λI)=0, then solve for nonzero vectors and check them in Av=λv. A real matrix can have no real eigenline or too few to form a basis. The singular-value lesson finds useful axes even for a rotation, by studying lengths through AᵀA rather than demanding an eigenline of A itself.

title: The closest answer to an impossible system
summary: Derive normal equations and prove uniqueness of a least-squares fit under full column rank.
prerequisites: dot product, transpose and systems (refreshed here)
text: What is the best answer when the equations disagree? Repeated measurements rarely lie exactly on a proposed line. We can still choose coefficients that make the total squared discrepancy as small as possible. The key geometric fact is that, at the best fit, the leftover error points perpendicular to every change the model can make. Background capsule. For a real m×n matrix A and data column b in Rᵐ, a model prediction is Ax. The residual is r=b−Ax. Its squared Euclidean length is ||r||²=r·r, the sum of squared coordinate errors. Aᵀ is the transpose: rows and columns interchange, and (Au)·v=u·(Aᵀv). The column space of A is all possible model predictions. Full column rank means its n columns are independent, so Az=0 forces z=0. This article proves the normal-equation criterion and uniqueness under that hypothesis. Fit one value to three observations Worked example. Suppose measurements are b=(1,2,6) and the model predicts the same constant c at all three times. Then A is the column (1,1,1)ᵀ, x=c, and Ax=(c,c,c). The squared discrepancy is (1−c)²+(2−c)²+(6−c)². Setting the normal equation AᵀAc=Aᵀb gives 3c=9, hence c=3. The prediction is (3,3,3) and residual is (−2,−1,3). Its dot product with the model direction is −2−1+3=0. Exact residuals for the constant fit Observation Prediction Residual Squared error 1 3 −2 4 2 3 −1 1 6 3 3 9 The total is 14. At c=4, residuals are (−3,−2,2), giving 9+4+4=17. The example suggests that c=3 is better, but checking two candidates is not proof of a global minimum. The argument below supplies that proof for every real c and every full-column-rank matrix. Orthogonality proves the minimum Exact theorem, with proof. If real A has full column rank, there is a unique x̂ minimizing ||b−Ax||² over all x in Rⁿ; it is the unique solution of A T A x ^ = A T b First, full column rank makes AᵀA invertible: if AᵀAz=0, dot with z to obtain ||Az||²=0, so Az=0 and then z=0. A square matrix with trivial kernel has an inverse, hence the equation has a unique solution x̂. Put r̂=b−Ax̂. The equation says Aᵀr̂=0, equivalently r̂·Az=0 for every z. For any alternative x=x̂+z, its residual is r̂−Az. Expanding its squared norm gives ||r̂−Az||²=||r̂||²+||Az||²−2r̂·Az=||r̂||²+||Az||². This is at least ||r̂||², and equality under full column rank requires z=0. That proves the unique global minimum. The orthogonality statement actually survives when columns are dependent: any minimizer has residual perpendicular to the column space, and a fitted prediction is unique. Coefficients may then be nonunique. For A with two identical columns (1,1)ᵀ, coefficients (1,0) and (0,1) give the same prediction; AᵀA cannot be inverted. Thus “solve by (AᵀA)⁻¹Aᵀb” requires full column rank. In serious numerical work, squaring the condition number by forming AᵀA can amplify roundoff; QR or SVD methods are preferred. Our exact derivation does not make a numerical stability claim. Check fit and failure 1. Calculation. Fit a constant c to data (2,4,9). Find c, the residual, its squared norm, and show the residual is orthogonal to (1,1,1). Hint for question 1 The normal equation is 3c=2+4+9. Full solution for question 1 3c=15, so c=5. The prediction is (5,5,5), residual b−Ax=(−3,−1,4), and squared norm 9+1+16=26. The residual dot (1,1,1) is −3−1+4=0. If c changes by t, the new squared error is 26+3t², so 5 is the unique minimizer. 2. Explanation. Let A=[[1,1],[1,1]] and b=(1,1). A student computes AᵀA and tries to invert it to prove a unique coefficient pair. Give all exact fits and explain why this does not contradict the theorem. Hint for question 2 The two columns are equal. Express Ax in terms of x₁+x₂. Full solution for question 2 Ax=(x₁+x₂,x₁+x₂). Every pair with x₁+x₂=1 fits exactly, including (1,0) and (0,1). The columns are dependent and AᵀA=[[2,2],[2,2]] has determinant zero, so it is not invertible. The theorem's full-column-rank hypothesis fails; the prediction (1,1) is still unique, but the coefficient pair is not. Best fit means perpendicular leftover Under full column rank, the normal equations choose one coefficient vector and the Pythagorean identity proves it is the global minimum. The perpendicular residual is an exact geometric certificate, not just a visual impression. If columns repeat or nearly repeat, check rank before claiming unique coefficients or stable floating-point answers. Singular values help reveal which directions a matrix compresses and why fitting can become numerically fragile.

title: Rotate, stretch, rotate
summary: Construct a 2D singular value decomposition conditional on the symmetric spectral theorem.
prerequisites: dot product, eigenvectors and orthogonal matrices (refreshed here)
real symmetric 2×2 spectral theorem (used without proof)
text: Can every planar map be read as simple stretches? A linear map can shear and turn a circle into an ellipse. Singular value decomposition finds perpendicular input directions that emerge as perpendicular output directions, with nonnegative stretch factors. This description works even when the original map has no real eigenvectors or collapses a direction. Background capsule. An orthogonal 2×2 matrix Q preserves dot products: QᵀQ=I. It may rotate or reflect; both count. A diagonal matrix Σ=diag(σ₁,σ₂) scales the coordinate axes by its diagonal entries. A singular value is nonnegative. For a matrix A, AᵀA is symmetric and nonnegative in the sense that vᵀAᵀAv=||Av||²≥0. We use the real symmetric 2×2 spectral theorem: such a matrix has an orthonormal eigenbasis. Its general proof is a named dependency here; the construction below explains what follows from it. An ellipse with exact axes Worked example. Take A=diag(3,1/2). An input on the unit circle can be written (cos t,sin t). Its image is (3cos t,(1/2)sin t), an ellipse with horizontal semiaxis 3 and vertical semiaxis 1/2. Here U=V=I and Σ=A. The right singular vectors are e₁,e₂; their images are 3e₁ and (1/2)e₂. The circle's area π becomes 3/2 times as large, consistent with determinant 3/2. Now compose the stretch with a quarter-turn R=[[0,−1],[1,0]], giving B=R A=[[0,−1/2],[3,0]]. B has the same singular values 3 and 1/2. Its input e₁ goes to (0,3), and e₂ goes to (−1/2,0): the output axes have turned. But B's characteristic polynomial is λ²+3/2, so it has no real eigenvectors. Singular vectors and eigenvectors answer different questions. Input and output principal directions of B Input unit vector Output Output length e₁=(1,0) (0,3) 3 e₂=(0,1) (−1/2,0) 1/2 Build the three factors Exact 2D statement and bounded derivation. Every real 2×2 matrix A admits orthogonal U,V and nonnegative diagonal Σ such that A = U Σ V T Apply the symmetric 2×2 spectral theorem to AᵀA. Choose orthonormal eigenvectors v₁,v₂ with nonnegative eigenvalues λ₁,λ₂, and set σᵢ=√λᵢ. If σᵢ>0, define uᵢ=Avᵢ/σᵢ. Their dot products satisfy uᵢ·uⱼ=(vᵢᵀAᵀAvⱼ)/(σᵢσⱼ), which equals 1 for i=j and 0 otherwise. Thus the nonzero uᵢ are orthonormal. If exactly one σ is zero, choose the remaining output unit vector perpendicular to the first u; if both are zero, A=0 and choose any orthonormal U. For a zero σ, Av=0, so the choice still makes Avᵢ=σᵢuᵢ. Put the vᵢ in V and uᵢ in U. The column equations combine to AV=UΣ, hence A=UΣVᵀ. This is a complete construction conditional on the named symmetric spectral theorem; it is not a proof of that theorem or of the higher-dimensional SVD. The geometric order for an input is Vᵀ first, then Σ, then U. The transpose Vᵀ changes to principal input coordinates; Σ stretches or collapses; U positions the outputs. Because orthogonal matrices preserve lengths, the image of the unit circle has semiaxis lengths σ₁,σ₂. If a singular value is zero, the ellipse degenerates to a segment or point. For a nonzero matrix with two equal singular values, the principal axes are not unique. So the phrase “the unique axes” would be false. Read lengths and limits 1. Calculation. For C=[[0,−2],[1,0]], compute CᵀC, singular values, and the images of the unit coordinate vectors. State the ellipse semiaxis lengths. Hint for question 1 Compute the dot products of C's columns; they are perpendicular. Full solution for question 1 The columns are (0,1) and (−2,0). Thus CᵀC=diag(1,4), with eigenvalues 1 and 4, giving singular values 1 and 2. C e₁=(0,1) has length one, and C e₂=(−2,0) has length two. The image ellipse therefore has semiaxis lengths two and one, along the horizontal and vertical output axes respectively. 2. Failure case.
