For D=diag(2,0), a student says no SVD exists because Av₂/σ₂ divides by zero. Explain how to finish the construction and describe the image of the unit circle. Hint for question 2 Choose an output unit vector perpendicular to the nonzero output direction. Full solution for question 2 DᵀD=diag(4,0), so σ₁=2 and σ₂=0. Take v₁=e₁, v₂=e₂. Then u₁=De₁/2=e₁. Choose u₂=e₂, perpendicular to u₁; no division by zero is required. U=V=I and Σ=diag(2,0) give D=UΣVᵀ. The unit circle maps to {(2cos t,0)}, the segment from (−2,0) to (2,0), not a positive-area ellipse. Axes survive when eigenlines do not The singular values are the square roots of the eigenvalues of AᵀA. They measure principal lengths, while U and V record output and input directions. The derivation relies on the real symmetric spectral theorem, which is deferred here. Zero singular values signal collapse; repeated ones make axes nonunique. A rotation is the sharp counterexample to equating singular vectors with eigenvectors: it preserves all lengths yet may have no real eigenline.

title: Open means room to move
summary: Test openness in the real line with point-dependent neighborhoods and exact endpoint counterexamples.
text: How much room does a point need? The interval (0,1) has no smallest positive point, but every point in it has some room on both sides. That local fact, rather than the appearance of a drawn boundary, is what “open” means for a subset of the real line. We will test it with explicit distances and see why one troublesome point can spoil a set. Background capsule. The real line ℝ contains the usual numbers in order. An interval (a,b) consists of numbers strictly between a and b; [a,b] includes its endpoints. Absolute value |x−y| measures distance. For ε>0, the ε-neighborhood of x is (x−ε,x+ε), the points less than ε away. A subset U of ℝ is open in ℝ when every x in U has an ε-neighborhood contained in U. The ε may depend on x. Work at a point near an edge Worked example. Take U=(2,5) and x=4.9. The left gap is 2.9 and the right gap is 0.1. Choose ε=0.05; then (4.85,4.95) lies in U. The same recipe works for any x with 2<x<5: choose half the smaller of x−2 and 5−x. Both gaps are positive, so this is a positive ε and no point in its neighborhood reaches an edge. Now take [2,5). Its point 2 belongs to the set. For every ε>0, the number 2−ε/2 lies in (2−ε,2+ε) but outside [2,5). No ε can work at 2. The set is therefore not open in ℝ, even though all its other points have room. A single witness is enough to disprove a statement beginning “for every point.” The empty set is open: there is no member at which the condition could fail. All of ℝ is open: ε=1 works at every point. Neither conclusion says that the empty set has a hidden interval or that ℝ has finite edges. The quantifiers and what they permit Exact statement. For U⊆ℝ with its ordinary distance, U open ⇔ ∀ x ∈ U ∃ ε > 0 : ( x − ε , x + ε ) ⊆ U This is the metric definition, so the equivalence sign records terminology, not a theorem needing a separate proof. Notice the order: choose x first and then choose its ε. Requiring one ε to work at all x would reject (2,5), because points can approach 2 arbitrarily closely. Two useful proofs. Every ordinary open interval (a,b) is open by the half-gap construction above. Conversely, if U is open and x belongs to U, the definition supplies an open interval around x lying in U. Taking the union of one such interval for each x recovers exactly U. Thus every open subset of ℝ can be written as a union of open intervals. No finiteness condition is imposed on that union. A set is closed in ℝ when its complement in ℝ is open. The interval [2,5] is closed: its complement is (−∞,2)∪(5,∞), an open union. “Not open” does not mean “closed.” The half-open interval [2,5) is neither: it fails openness at 2, and its complement fails openness at 5. Some sets, including ∅ and ℝ, are both open and closed. The ambient space matters: [2,5) is open relative to [2,∞), because it equals that space intersected with (1,5). For a more irregular set, ℝ without 0 is open. At any x≠0, choose ε=|x|/2; then every point in the neighborhood has the same sign as x. The method is an exact proof; sampling a collection of points would not settle the universal condition. Choose a witness or a counterexample 1. Prove (−3,1)∪(4,∞) is open in ℝ. Give an explicit ε for a point x in either component. Hint for question 1 Stay inside whichever interval already contains x. For the bounded component use both endpoint gaps. Full solution for question 1 If −3<x<1, set ε=min(x+3,1−x)/2; both gaps are positive and the neighborhood stays in (−3,1). If x>4, set ε=(x−4)/2; then x−ε>4, so the neighborhood stays in (4,∞). Every member lies in one of these cases, proving the union open. 2. Is the intersection of all intervals (−1/n,1/n), for positive integers n, open? Compare this with intersections of two open sets. Hint for question 2 Which numbers survive every increasingly narrow interval? Test a positive candidate by choosing n large enough. Full solution for question 2 The intersection is {0}. Zero lies in every interval. If x≠0, choose a positive integer n>1/|x|; then 1/n<|x|, so x is absent. The singleton {0} is not open: for every ε>0, ε/2 belongs to its ε-neighborhood but not to {0}. Two open sets do have open intersection: at a point in both, take the smaller of their two positive neighborhood radii. The failure here involves infinitely many sets. Keep the local test Openness is a claim about every included point and a radius chosen for that point. Endpoints often supply counterexamples, but an open set may have many components or missing points. The discussion used the ordinary real-line distance; in another space, first identify its open neighborhoods. This local test becomes the input for continuity through preimages .

title: Continuity without drawing a curve
summary: Prove the equivalence between metric continuity and open preimages, including relative-domain cases.
text: Can openness detect a jump? A graph can suggest that a function has no jump, but a graph cannot check every point. A precise alternative is to pull each open set in the output space back to the inputs that land in it. Continuous maps always produce an open input set this way. We will prove the equivalence in metric spaces, where distances make both sides explicit. Background capsule. A metric space X has a distance d X (x,y), with positive-radius balls B X (x,r)={z:d X (z,x)<r}. A subset is open if each member lies in some contained ball. For f:X→Y and V⊆Y, the preimage f −1 (V)={x∈X:f(x)∈V}; no inverse function is needed. Continuity at x says: for every ε>0 there is δ>0 such that d X (x,z)<δ implies d Y (f(x),f(z))<ε. Pull back one interval Worked example. Let f:ℝ→ℝ be f(x)=x² and choose V=(1,4). Its preimage is (−2,−1)∪(1,2), since 1<x²<4 means 1<|x|<2. That union is open. For an input near 1.5, a small change stays in the right component; near −1.5 it stays in the left. The preimage is allowed to have disconnected pieces. A function does not need to map an open set to an open set to be continuous; the direction here is specifically preimages of open sets. Compare g(x)=0 for x≤0 and g(x)=1 for x>0. The open output interval (−1/2,1/2) pulls back to (−∞,0], which is not open in ℝ. The point 0 witnesses failure: arbitrarily close positive inputs have output 1. This single open target set proves that g is discontinuous. Both directions of the metric-space theorem Exact statement. For a map f between metric spaces X and Y, continuity at every point is equivalent to open preimages: f continuous ⇔ ∀ V ⊆ Y , V open ⇒ f − 1 ( V ) open in X Forward proof. Suppose f is continuous and V is open in Y. Take x∈f −1 (V), so f(x)∈V. Openness gives an ε-ball around f(x) contained in V. Continuity at x gives δ>0 sending every z in B X (x,δ) into that ε-ball. Thus B X (x,δ) lies in the preimage. As x was arbitrary, the preimage is open. The empty preimage is open vacuously. Reverse proof. Suppose every open preimage is open. Fix x∈X and ε>0. The Y-ball V=B Y (f(x),ε) is open in any metric space: a point y inside has remaining radius ε−d Y (f(x),y)>0, and the triangle inequality keeps its smaller ball inside V. By assumption, f −1 (V) is open and contains x, so some δ-ball about x lies in it. For all z with d X (x,z)<δ, f(z) belongs to V, exactly the ε–δ condition. Since x and ε were arbitrary, f is continuous everywhere. This proof depends on the metric-space definitions and the triangle inequality, but does not depend on a picture or a formula for f. In a general topological space, open preimages are used as the definition of continuity; metric ε–δ language may not exist. Be careful with subspaces: a preimage must be open in its domain . For f:[0,1]→ℝ given by f(x)=x, the preimage of (−1,1/2) is [0,1/2), open relative to [0,1], although not open in the whole real line. Use preimages deliberately 1. For h:ℝ→ℝ, h(x)=|x|, calculate h −1 ((1,3)) and explain why this one calculation alone does not prove continuity everywhere. Hint for question 1 Translate 1<|x|<3 into two signed intervals. Watch the word “every” in the theorem. Full solution for question 1 The preimage is (−3,−1)∪(1,3), an open union. The theorem asks for every open V, so one example is insufficient. Continuity can instead be proved by ||x|−|z||≤|x−z|: given ε>0, δ=ε works at every x. The theorem then guarantees all open preimages are open. 2. Let k(x)=0 when x<0 and k(x)=1 when x≥0. Find an open V whose preimage disproves continuity, and identify the bad input. Hint for question 2 Choose a small interval around the output 1 that excludes 0. Full solution for question 2 Take V=(1/2,3/2). Its preimage is [0,∞), because precisely inputs x≥0 have output 1. This set is not open in ℝ: every neighborhood of 0 contains a negative point. Thus k fails continuity at 0. It is continuous at each nonzero input, since a sufficiently small neighborhood stays on one side of zero. Read the arrow backwards Open-preimage continuity is a global condition built from local neighborhoods. It says something about how output tests pull back to the domain, including its relative topology. It does not say that images of open sets are open. For a stronger notion that preserves shape in both directions, continue to homeomorphisms .

title: When two shapes count as the same
summary: Use cut points to prove that a closed interval and a circle cannot be homeomorphic.
text: Can a line segment become a circle? A segment can be bent almost into a ring. Closing the last gap, however, changes what happens when a point is removed. Topology makes this difference precise with a homeomorphism : a reversible continuous correspondence. The test is stronger than whether two sketches look alike, and it gives a short proof that a closed interval is not a circle. Background capsule. A function is bijective if every point of its target is reached once and only once; then it has an inverse function. A map of metric spaces is continuous when the preimage of each open set is open. A space is connected when it cannot be split into two disjoint, nonempty sets that are open relative to it. An interval of ℝ is connected; we use that standard interval theorem here. A cut point of a connected space X is a point p for which X without p is disconnected. Compare two removals Worked example. In [0,1], remove 1/2. The remaining points split into [0,1/2) and (1/2,1]. Each part is nonempty and open relative to the remaining space: for example, [0,1/2) is the remaining space intersected with (−1,1/2). The two parts cover it without overlap. Thus 1/2 is a cut point. By contrast, removing endpoint 0 leaves (0,1], an interval and therefore connected. On the unit circle S¹={(x,y):x²+y²=1}, remove (1,0). Starting just above that point and walking counterclockwise around the rest reaches any other point without crossing the gap. More precisely, t↦(cos t,sin t) maps the open interval (0,2π) continuously onto S¹ without (1,0). A continuous image of an interval is connected. Every other removed point is the same case after rotation. Hence a circle has no cut point. This argument uses the connected-image theorem, which can be proved directly from open preimages and is developed in the connectedness article. Why a reversible map preserves the test Exact definition. For topological spaces X and Y, a homeomorphism is a bijection f:X→Y such that both f and its inverse are continuous: f : X → Y homeomorphism ⇔ f bijective, f and f − 1 continuous The inverse condition is essential. A continuous bijection may fail to have continuous inverse; for example, the map from [0,2π) onto the circle given by t↦(cos t,sin t) is bijective and continuous, but its inverse jumps near (1,0): points approaching (1,0) clockwise have parameter approaching 2π, while their image approaches parameter 0. This does not contradict the circle argument above, because [0,2π) includes one endpoint and has different local structure there. Invariant proof. If f is a homeomorphism and p∈X, the restriction f:X∖{p}→Y∖{f(p)} is still bijective and continuous; its inverse is the restriction of f −1 . Therefore the punctured spaces are homeomorphic. A homeomorphism carries an open separation in either direction to an open separation, by continuity of the inverse and f respectively. Consequently X∖{p} is disconnected exactly when Y∖{f(p)} is disconnected. Cut points are preserved. Since [0,1] has an interior cut point and S¹ has none, no homeomorphism [0,1]→S¹ exists. This proof is complete once the interval-connectedness and continuous-image facts stated in the capsule are accepted. Those facts are standard and are proved for the latter in connectedness ; a proof of interval connectedness uses the least-upper-bound property of ℝ. We have not classified all one-dimensional spaces or shown every physical bending can be represented by a homeomorphism. Test maps and invariants 1. Is f:[0,1]→[2,5], f(t)=2+3t, a homeomorphism? Give its inverse and check both continuity claims. Hint for question 1 Solve y=2+3t for t. Both resulting formulas are Lipschitz on their domains. Full solution for question 1 f is strictly increasing and maps endpoints 0 and 1 to 2 and 5, so it is bijective onto [2,5]. Its inverse is f −1 (y)=(y−2)/3. For inputs s,t, |f(s)−f(t)|=3|s−t|, so δ=ε/3 proves continuity. For outputs u,v, |f −1 (u)−f −1 (v)|=|u−v|/3, so δ=3ε proves inverse continuity. The relative endpoint topologies are included. 2. Could a letter “Y,” modelled as three closed segments meeting only at one central point, be homeomorphic to [0,1]? Use components after deleting one point. Hint for question 2 Delete the branch point. How many connected pieces remain? Compare deletion of any point of an interval. Full solution for question 2 Removing the center of Y leaves three disjoint open arms, each connected, so there are three connected components. Removing an interior point of [0,1] leaves exactly two interval components; removing an endpoint leaves one. A homeomorphism would restrict to a homeomorphism of the punctured spaces and preserve their component count. No point of [0,1] has a three-component complement, so no such homeomorphism exists. Use properties a map cannot erase A homeomorphism preserves topology in both directions. Cut points distinguish an interval from a circle even when a drawing tempts us to join the interval’s ends. The cut-point test cannot distinguish every pair of spaces; the absence of a cut point alone does not establish a homeomorphism. For another global property preserved by continuous maps, study compactness .

title: Why finite subcovers matter
summary: Prove a closed real interval compact with a supremum argument and exhibit an open cover with no finite subcover.
text: Can infinitely many blankets be reduced to finitely many? Covering each point of a closed interval with a little open neighborhood sounds like an infinite task. Compactness says that, no matter how the neighborhoods were chosen, finitely many already suffice. The statement is about every open cover, not a particular convenient drawing. We will prove the closed-interval case by using the least-upper-bound property of the real numbers. Background capsule. A family {U i } covers a set K if every point of K belongs to at least one U i . An open cover uses sets open in the surrounding space, here ℝ. A finite subcover is a finite selection from that family which still covers K. A bounded nonempty set S of real numbers has a supremum c: c bounds S above and each number below c fails to be an upper bound. This completeness property of ℝ is assumed, not proved here. A cover with endlessly many members Worked example. For each positive integer n, let U n =(−1/n,1+1/n). Every U n contains [0,1], so this infinite family has a one-set subcover. That easy cover does not establish compactness. A more instructive cover of [0,1] is U n =(−1,1−1/n) for n≥2, together with W=(1/2,2). The U n approach 1 without ever containing it, while W covers the right end. In fact U 3 =(−1,2/3) and W together cover [0,1]: their overlap from 1/2 to 2/3 leaves no gap. Contrast (0,1), covered by U n =(1/n,1) for n≥2. Each x in (0,1) lies in some U n , because 1/n eventually falls below x. Any finite selection has a largest index N, hence its union is just (1/N,1) and misses, for example, 1/(2N). This open interval is not compact. The decisive issue is not simply that the original family is infinite; it is whether every such family admits finite reduction. Push a finite cover from left to right Exact statement. A set K is compact when every open cover of it admits a finite subcover. In particular, for real a≤b, ∀ 𝒰 open cover of [ a , b ] ∃ U 1 , … , U n ∈ 𝒰 : [ a , b ] ⊆ ⋃ j = 1 n U j Proof. Fix an arbitrary open cover 𝒰 of [a,b]. Let S consist of those x∈[a,b] for which [a,x] can be covered by finitely many members of 𝒰. Some member covers a, so a∈S. The set S is nonempty and bounded above by b; let c=sup S. Choose U∈𝒰 containing c. Because U is open, there is r>0 with (c−r,c+r)⊆U. By the defining property of a supremum, there is x∈S with x>c−r/2, unless c=a; in that endpoint case take x=a, already in S. A finite selection covers [a,x], and adding U covers [a,c] because the intervals [x,c] lie within (c−r,c+r). Thus c∈S. If c<b, choose y with c<y<min(b+1,c+r/2) and y≤b. The same finite selection plus U covers [a,y], so y∈S, contradicting that c is an upper bound. Therefore c=b, and the finite selection covers [a,b]. The proof works also when a=b: any cover member containing the sole point suffices. Its only substantial external input is the least-upper-bound property. We have not proved arbitrary closed and bounded subsets of higher-dimensional spaces compact. Compactness is preserved by continuous maps: if {V i } covers f(K), then their open preimages cover K; select finitely many and map forward. This short proof shows why compactness matters beyond intervals. The converse fails: a constant map from noncompact ℝ has compact one-point image. Find the finite selection 1. Let U=(−1,0.7), V=(0.4,1.2), W=(0.9,3). Show these three open sets cover [0,1] and find a smaller subcover. Hint for question 1 The overlap of U and V bridges the middle; check both endpoints explicitly. Full solution for question 1 U covers [0,0.7), while V covers (0.4,1]. Their overlap includes (0.4,0.7), so U∪V contains every point of [0,1]. Thus {U,V} is a two-set subcover, and W is unnecessary. Neither U alone covers 1 nor V alone covers 0, so this subcover cannot be shortened further. 2. Give an open cover of [0,1) with no finite subcover, and explain why omitting the endpoint matters. Hint for question 2 Use sets extending slightly left of zero but stopping short of one. Full solution for question 2 Take U n =(−1,1−1/n) for integers n≥2. Any x<1 eventually satisfies x<1−1/n, so the family covers [0,1). A finite selection has largest index N; its union is U N and misses x=1−1/(2N), which still belongs to [0,1). Thus no finite subcover exists. Adding point 1 to the set would also require a cover member reaching that endpoint; in a cover of [0,1], the supremum proof exploits exactly such a neighborhood. Separate the definition from the interval theorem Compactness quantifies over all open covers. The finite-subcover theorem for [a,b] follows from real-number completeness, not from a sketch of finitely many strips. A bounded set can still fail compactness when a limiting endpoint is missing. This global property can help test whether a proposed homeomorphism is possible.

title: A gap you cannot cover up
summary: Prove continuous images of connected spaces are connected and test separations in subspaces.
text: What does “one piece” mean without a picture? Two separated intervals are visibly in two pieces, but pictures are unreliable for complicated spaces. A topological separation replaces visual judgment with two disjoint, nonempty, relatively open sets covering the space. We will use that definition to prove that a continuous map cannot tear a connected domain into a disconnected image. Background capsule. If X is a space and A⊆X, a set W⊆A is open relative to A when W=A∩U for some set U open in X. For f:X→Y, its image f(X) consists of outputs f(x). Continuity means preimages of open sets are open. A separation of X is a pair U,V of disjoint, nonempty open subsets of X whose union is X. A space with no separation is connected . All topologies in the examples are ordinary metric or their subspace topologies. Test two subsets of the line Worked example. Let A=[0,1]∪[2,3]. The sets [0,1] and [2,3] are open relative to A: intersect A with (−1,1.5) or (1.5,4), respectively. They are nonempty, disjoint and cover A, so A is disconnected. Each component separately is connected because it is an interval. For [0,1], try to draw a dividing line at c=1/2. The left part [0,c) and right part (c,1] leave out c. Assigning c to one side destroys openness of that side at c. This is a clue to the interval theorem. A proof uses completeness: if an interval were separated into U and V, take points u∈U and v∈V with u<v, and let c be the supremum of U∩[u,v]. Relative openness of whichever side contains c forces points of that side across the proposed boundary, a contradiction. Details require checking c cannot lie in neither side and using a neighborhood of c; the core fact is the least-upper-bound property. A continuous map may identify different points and even collapse everything to one point. It may not create a separation in its image. For example, f(t)=(cos 2πt,sin 2πt) takes [0,1] continuously onto a circle; it joins the two endpoint images, yet the image is connected. Pull an alleged split backwards Exact statement. For a continuous map f:X→Y of topological spaces, if X is connected, then f(X), with the subspace topology inherited from Y, is connected: ( X connected ∧ f continuous ) ⇒ f ( X ) connected Proof. Suppose instead that f(X) has a separation A,B. Since these are open relative to f(X), write A=f(X)∩O and B=f(X)∩P for open O,P in Y. The sets f −1 (O) and f −1 (P) are open in X by continuity. They are disjoint: no f(x) can lie in both A and B. Both are nonempty because A and B each contain some output of f. They cover X because every output lies in A∪B. This is a separation of X, contradicting its connectedness. Hence the image is connected. The proof uses only definitions and is valid in general topological spaces. The converse is false. A constant map from A=[0,1]∪[2,3] to a one-point space is continuous and has connected image, while A is disconnected. Nor does connectedness mean every two points can be joined by a path in arbitrary spaces; path connectedness is a stronger condition. For intervals and circles in the examples, explicit paths exist. We avoid inferring connectedness merely from a drawing that appears unbroken. Why do intervals stay connected? The supremum argument sketched above can be made exact. Choose u<v on opposite sides, let c=sup(U∩[u,v]). If c∈U, openness of U supplies points of U just right of c (unless c=v, but v∈V), contradicting the bound. If c∈V, openness of V gives a left neighborhood free of U, contradicting the supremum property. Thus neither case works. This proof assumes real completeness; in a rational interval a missing irrational point can produce a separation. Find or forbid a separation 1. Is B=(−2,−1)∪(1,2) connected as a subspace of ℝ? Specify a separation using ambient open sets. Hint for question 1 Choose one ambient interval around each component and intersect with B. Full solution for question 1 Let U=B∩(−3,0)=(−2,−1) and V=B∩(0,3)=(1,2). Both are nonempty and open relative to B, disjoint, and their union is B. They form a separation, so B is disconnected. The gap is expressed by relative openness, not just by its width. 2. A proposed continuous surjection h:[0,1]→{0,1}, with {0,1} carrying the usual subspace topology of ℝ, sends some inputs to each value. Explain why it cannot exist. Hint for question 2 The two singleton subsets of {0,1} are relatively open. Pull them back. Full solution for question 2 The target {0,1} is separated by {0}={0,1}∩(−1/2,1/2) and {1}={0,1}∩(1/2,3/2). Surjectivity makes both preimages nonempty. If h were continuous, those preimages would be disjoint open subsets covering [0,1], separating an interval. Since [0,1] is connected, this is impossible. Carry the hypothesis with the claim A connected domain has a connected image under a continuous map. The theorem does not run backwards and does not say all connected spaces admit paths. The interval-connectedness argument relies on completeness of ℝ; the image theorem needs only topology. These distinctions support the cut-point test for an interval and a circle.

title: Glue edges, change a space
summary: Verify the quotient topology and identify the vertical-edge quotient of a square with a cylinder.
text: What does it mean to glue two edges? Imagine marking matching heights on the left and right edges of a rectangle, then identifying each pair. The result is a cylinder. A quotient space turns this instruction into a set of equivalence classes with a precise topology. We will check the topology rule, construct the cylinder map, and distinguish a genuine mathematical identification from a visual animation. Background capsule. An equivalence relation ∼ on a set X is reflexive, symmetric and transitive. The class [x] is all points equivalent to x; X/∼ is the set of classes. The quotient map q:X→X/∼ sends x to [x]. A preimage q −1 (V) consists of all original points whose classes lie in V. A topology declares which subsets are open; arbitrary unions and finite intersections of open sets must be open, and ∅ and the whole space must be open. Make the cylinder from a square Worked example. Let X=[0,1]×[0,1]. Identify (0,t) with (1,t) for every t∈[0,1], and make no other identifications except those forced by equivalence. For instance, [(0,1/3)] has two representatives, while [(1/2,1/3)] has one. The bottom edge becomes a circle, as does the top edge. The top and bottom are not identified with one another, so the object has two boundary circles rather than being a torus. Define F([s,t])=(cos 2πs,sin 2πs,t), a point of S¹×[0,1]. It is well-defined: the only distinct equivalent representatives have s=0 and s=1 at the same height t, and both give (1,0,t). It is onto because every circle point has an angle s∈[0,1]; it is one-to-one because equal heights and equal circle angles in that range give either equal s or the endpoint pair, already identified. Thus the class set is bijective with the usual cylinder. A neighborhood of a seam point on the cylinder pulls back to two thin strips, one at each vertical edge of the square. Those strips are open relative to the square . This is why a quotient-open set can surround a seam point even though no single interior strip crosses the square’s printed boundary. The quotient topology and its exact guarantee Exact definition. For any topological space X and equivalence relation ∼, declare V⊆X/∼ open precisely when its full preimage is open in X: V open in X / ∼ ⇔ q − 1 ( V ) open in X Verification. The inverse image of ∅ is ∅ and the inverse image of all of X/∼ is X, both open. Preimages commute with arbitrary unions and finite intersections. Therefore the declared open sets obey all three topology axioms. By the same defining rule, q is continuous: every open V downstairs has open preimage upstairs. This is a full verification of the quotient rule, independent of the rectangle example. There is a useful test for maps out of the quotient. If g:X/∼→Y is any map, then g is continuous exactly when g∘q:X→Y is continuous. For an open O⊆Y, the preimage (g∘q) −1 (O) equals q −1 (g −1 (O)); the quotient rule says this is open exactly when g −1 (O) is open. In particular, the map F above is continuous because F∘q is the continuous formula (s,t)↦(cos 2πs,sin 2πs,t). To conclude that F is a homeomorphism, its inverse must also be continuous. One standard route uses two theorems: a closed square is compact, and a continuous bijection from a compact space to a Hausdorff space has continuous inverse. Continuous images of compact spaces are compact, and S¹×[0,1] is Hausdorff. Those general theorems are cited as inputs here; this lesson proves the quotient rule and the explicit bijection, while a full proof of the compact-to-Hausdorff theorem is beyond its scope. The cylinder claim has these hypotheses visible rather than relying on a sketch. Check what is actually identified 1. Under the cylinder relation, list the classes of (0,1/2), (1,1/2), and (1/2,1/2). Decide whether (0,0) and (0,1) are equivalent. Hint for question 1 Only points on opposite vertical edges at the same height are paired. Full solution for question 1 [(0,1/2)]=[(1,1/2)]={(0,1/2),(1,1/2)}. The interior point has singleton class [(1/2,1/2)]={(1/2,1/2)}. The points (0,0) and (0,1) have different heights, so they are not equivalent. Their images under F are (1,0,0) and (1,0,1), on different boundary circles. 2. Suppose someone declares a subset V of X/∼ open whenever it has one open representative region in X. Explain why checking only one representative near a seam is insufficient; state the correct test. Hint for question 2 A class may contain both (0,t) and (1,t). A subset of classes pulls back to all representatives. Full solution for question 2 A set of classes must include or exclude each class as a whole. If V contains [(0,t)], its preimage includes both (0,t) and (1,t); openness must be checked around both in the square’s relative topology. A neighborhood only around (0,t) says nothing about the other representative. The correct condition is that the full saturated preimage q −1 (V), including both seam strips, is open in X. Keep the seam and the topology together A quotient is a set of classes plus the topology determined by full preimages. For the rectangle relation, a continuous bijection to the standard cylinder is explicit, and the usual compact-to-Hausdorff theorem supplies inverse continuity. Identifying the top and bottom as well would define another quotient. No surface-classification theorem follows from this one construction. Return to open sets if relative seam neighborhoods need another look.

title: Can a loop be shrunk?
summary: Construct a based contraction in a convex disk and locate the lifting input behind a punctured-plane obstruction.
text: When can a loop be pulled tight? A loop drawn in a disk can often shrink to its starting point. Around a missing point, the same motion may be impossible without crossing the hole. The formal object is a based homotopy : a continuous family of loops whose common basepoint stays fixed. We will give a complete contraction in a convex disk and a carefully bounded obstruction in the punctured plane. Background capsule. A path in X is a continuous map γ:[0,1]→X. It is a loop based at x₀ if γ(0)=γ(1)=x₀. A homotopy H:[0,1]²→X changes one map continuously into another; the first coordinate s tracks the deformation and the second t tracks a position on the loop. Continuity here means continuity in both variables together. A set C in the plane is convex when every straight segment between its points stays in C. Watch a contraction and an obstruction Worked example. Let C be the closed unit disk centered at 0 and choose the basepoint x₀=(1,0) on its boundary. Any loop γ in C based at x₀ contracts by straight lines toward x₀: H(s,t)=(1−s)γ(t)+s x₀. At s=0 the loop is γ; at s=1 it is constantly x₀. For every s, H(s,0)=H(s,1)=x₀. Convexity keeps all intermediate points inside C. Thus the formula is a full constructive proof for this disk, including loops that cross themselves. Now use X=ℝ²∖{(0,0)} and the loop γ(t)=(cos 2πt,sin 2πt), based at (1,0). Its straight-line contraction toward (1,0) fails: at t=1/2 the starting point is (−1,0), and the segment to (1,0) passes through the deleted origin. This failure of one proposed formula alone does not rule out every conceivable deformation. A winding-number invariant supplies the genuine obstruction, conditional on the angle-lifting fact developed in the next lesson. Try the formula, then audit the whole family First predict what happens halfway through the straight-line contraction. Select the punctured plane and use “See the exact crossing.” Moving beyond s=1/2 produces loops that avoid 0 again, but the whole family has already crossed the deleted point. Compare the winding before and after that crossing. Now select “Contract a retraced loop.” This loop goes once counterclockwise and then follows the same circle backwards; its winding is 1−1=0. Set θ(t)=4π min(t,1−t). The angle formula H(s,t)=(cos((1−s)θ(t)), sin((1−s)θ(t))) stays on the unit circle. Because θ(0)=θ(1)=0, it fixes both endpoints at (1,0), and at s=1 it is constant. This is an explicit valid contraction in the punctured plane even though the straight-line formula for this very same loop hits 0 at s=1/2, t=1/4 and 3/4. A failed formula is not a proof of noncontractibility. Finally select “Check the basepoint trap.” For the once-around loop θ(t)=2πt, reducing the angle keeps every point away from 0, but H(s,1)=(cos(2π(1−s)), sin(2π(1−s))) is not (1,0) when 0<s<1. These slices are open paths, so assigning them a fractional winding number would be a mistake. The formula finishes at a constant yet fails to be a homotopy of loops. The four boundary conditions Exact definition. Based loops γ₀ and γ₁ at x₀ are based-homotopic if there is continuous H:[0,1]²→X satisfying H ( 0 , t ) = γ 0 ( t ) H ( 1 , t ) = γ 1 ( t ) H ( s , 0 ) = x 0 H ( s , 1 ) = x 0 The first two conditions describe start and finish; the last two keep the basepoint fixed throughout. Reversing s reverses a homotopy. Joining two homotopies in time gives another, so based homotopy is an equivalence relation. The joined formula is piecewise continuous because its pieces agree at their common edge; this uses the standard gluing lemma for continuous maps. A free homotopy still requires H(s,0)=H(s,1), so every intermediate path remains a loop, but allows this common endpoint to move. It answers a different question; dropping closure altogether would give a family of paths instead. Obstruction, with boundary named. A loop in the punctured plane has an integer winding number around the origin. For the unit-circle loop above it is 1; for a constant loop it is 0. Winding number remains unchanged under a homotopy that never touches the origin. Therefore those loops cannot be homotopic in X, based or free. The invariance step depends on a continuous lift of angle over the homotopy square, or an equivalent winding theorem. We state that lifting result here rather than pretending the failure of straight-line contraction proves impossibility. We do not compute the full fundamental group of the punctured plane in this article. The basepoint may be anywhere in a convex C, not necessarily at its center. In the contraction formula, t=0 and t=1 both evaluate to (1−s)x₀+s x₀=x₀. This is the often-missed boundary check. If X is not convex, the formula may leave X even when a different homotopy exists; the punctured-plane example needs the winding invariant to settle nonexistence. Check formulas and claims 1. In the convex square C=[−2,2]², based at x₀=(2,0), give a based homotopy from γ(t)=(2cos 2πt,2sin 2πt) to the constant loop. Verify all four boundary conditions. Hint for question 1 Interpolate between γ(t) and x₀, then use convexity of the square. Full solution for question 1 Set H(s,t)=(1−s)(2cos 2πt,2sin 2πt)+s(2,0). At s=0 this is γ and at s=1 it is (2,0). At t=0 or 1, γ(t)=(2,0), so H(s,0)=H(s,1)=(2,0). Both endpoints of every interpolating segment belong to C and C is convex, so H stays in C. Algebraic operations and trig functions make H continuous. 2. Someone argues, “The straight-line formula hits the origin, so the unit-circle loop cannot shrink in the punctured plane.” Identify the logical gap and the missing invariant. Hint for question 2 One failed construction does not rule out every construction. Compare a number assigned to the loop and to a constant loop. Full solution for question 2 The calculation rules out that particular straight-line H, not all continuous H. The unit-circle loop has winding number 1 and a constant loop has winding number 0. If winding number is homotopy-invariant for loops avoiding the origin, no homotopy can connect them. That invariance rests on the angle-lifting theorem, which must be supplied or explicitly assumed; a picture of a loop circling a hole is not a proof by itself. 3. Two loops have exactly the same trace, the unit circle. The first travels counterclockwise once; the second travels counterclockwise once and then retraces clockwise. A student concludes that both are noncontractible in the punctured plane because their pictures surround the same hole. Repair the argument and give an explicit contraction when one exists. Hint for question 3 A loop is a parametrized walk. Follow its angle without resetting it to a principal value; compare the final angle to the initial one. Full solution for question 3 The first loop has winding 1, so homotopy invariance prevents a contraction in the punctured plane. For the second choose θ(t)=4π min(t,1−t); its angle returns to 0, so its winding is 0. The formula H(s,t)=(cos((1−s)θ(t)),sin((1−s)θ(t))) contracts it within the unit circle. The triangular θ is continuous at t=1/2, both endpoints have θ=0, and s=1 gives (1,0) throughout. Here the formula proves existence; zero winding alone would not be a general proof in an arbitrary space. Distinguish construction from obstruction Convexity gives an explicit contraction and all basepoint checks. A deleted origin calls for a homotopy invariant; the winding argument uses a named lifting result. The winding-number lesson computes that invariant on polygonal examples and spells out its proof boundary.

title: Count turns without trusting a picture
summary: Compute turns for polygonal loops avoiding the origin and isolate the lifting theorem behind homotopy invariance.
text: Count turns even when a loop crosses itself A loop can travel twice around a missing point, reverse direction, or cross its own trace. Counting visible intersections with a ray can fail when the loop touches the ray at a vertex. A continuous angle, followed without resetting at 2π, gives a stable count. This lesson computes it for polygonal loops avoiding the origin and states exactly what is needed to extend the count to arbitrary continuous homotopies. Background capsule. A polygonal loop is a finite sequence of nonzero plane vertices v₀,…,v m =v₀, joined by straight segments; we require every segment to avoid 0. The argument of a nonzero point is an angle θ with coordinates r(cos θ,sin θ), where r>0. Angles differing by 2π describe the same point. An unwrapped angle records a continuous real value along a path instead of jumping from near 2π back to 0. Winding is oriented: counterclockwise counts positively. Follow a square all the way around Worked example. Take vertices (1,1), (−1,1), (−1,−1), (1,−1), then back to (1,1), in that order. Starting with angle π/4, the unwrapped angles at the successive vertices are π/4, 3π/4, 5π/4, 7π/4 and 9π/4. Each edge avoids the origin. The total change is 9π/4−π/4=2π, so the winding number is 1. Reversing the vertex order produces change −2π and winding −1. Now traverse that same square twice. The final unwrapped angle is 17π/4, giving change 4π and winding 2. The trace on paper is still just one square; the parametrized walk matters. If the loop travels once counterclockwise and then retraces clockwise, the changes cancel and winding is 0. Such a loop may cross itself or repeat edges; repeated points do not invalidate the calculation as long as the path never touches the origin. A useful boundary check is the segment from (1,0) to (−1,0): it passes through the origin. Its endpoint angles tempt a half-turn assignment, but winding is undefined for a loop using that segment in the punctured plane. The exclusion is a mathematical hypothesis, not a numerical inconvenience. Why the total is an integer Exact statement for polygonal loops. Choose a continuous real angle θ(t) along each origin-avoiding edge, matching values at shared vertices. Then wind ( γ , 0 ) = θ ( 1 ) − θ ( 0 ) 2 π ∈ ℤ Why can an edge use a continuous angle? A straight segment missing 0 cannot sweep an angle of π or more relative to the origin without crossing the opposite ray; equivalently, the normalized segment stays inside one open semicircle after choosing a suitable viewing direction. A continuous angle branch exists there. Begin with any angle at v₀ and, edge by edge, choose the branch that starts at the preceding endpoint. At the final vertex the physical point equals v₀. Therefore its final angle differs from its initial angle by an integer multiple of 2π. Changing the initial angle by 2πk changes both endpoint angles equally, leaving the quotient unchanged. This proves that the polygonal count is well-defined. For computation, add the signed angle changes of the edges, each chosen continuously along the edge. The square gives four increments of π/2. This method is exact for symmetric coordinates, and numerical approximations need an error check near an edge through 0. A tiny change of a path that crosses 0 can change winding; a deformation required to avoid 0 cannot. Homotopy boundary. For an arbitrary continuous loop γ in ℝ²∖{0}, the map γ(t)/|γ(t)| into S¹ has a continuous real angle lift once a starting angle is chosen. For a continuous homotopy of such loops, the lift can be chosen continuously over the parameter square. Then Δθ(s)/(2π) varies continuously with s but is always an integer. A continuous integer-valued function on an interval is constant, proving homotopy invariance. The angle-lifting theorem is the external input; its general proof is deferred to covering-space theory. The polygonal edge construction above alone does not establish it for every homotopy. Compute and inspect the hypotheses 1. A polygonal loop goes through (2,0),(0,2),(−2,0),(0,−2),(2,0) in order. Find its winding around 0. What happens if the route is reversed? Hint for question 1 Use unwrapped vertex angles 0, π/2, π, 3π/2, 2π. Full solution for question 1 Each edge stays away from the origin and changes angle by π/2. The total change is 2π, hence wind=1. Reversing the route changes every signed increment, so Δθ=−2π and wind=−1. Both loops have the same geometric diamond as an unparametrized trace, but opposite orientations. 2. A proposed homotopy shrinks the square from the worked example by H(s,t)=(1−s)γ(t). Does homotopy invariance force a contradiction? Locate the failed hypothesis exactly. Hint for question 2 Inspect the final parameter s=1 and the target space ℝ²∖{0}. Full solution for question 2 At s=1, H(1,t)=0 for every t, so H is not a map into ℝ²∖{0}. The invariance theorem applies only to homotopies whose image avoids 0 at every (s,t). There is no contradiction: the proposed formula is a homotopy in ℝ², where winding about a deleted origin is not an invariant of paths allowed to hit that origin. A number with a clear domain For an origin-avoiding polygonal loop, angle increments yield an integer independent of the starting branch. Extending this to arbitrary continuous loops and homotopies uses the stated angle-lifting theorem. Winding distinguishes some loop classes but a value of zero by itself is not a general claim about all spaces. The circle group lesson makes the integer into a composition law.

title: Loops around the circle form integers
summary: Show that circle-loop concatenation corresponds to integer addition, conditional on path and homotopy lifting.
text: Why circle loops add like integers Start at 1 on the unit circle. Walking around once, twice, or in reverse produces loops that cannot all be continuously deformed into one another while keeping the starting point fixed. Their based-homotopy classes form a group, and the number of turns identifies that group with the integers. We will prove the group-law correspondence while stating the path-and-homotopy lifting lemma on which the classification rests. Background capsule. A based loop γ:[0,1]→S¹ has γ(0)=γ(1)=1, where S¹={z∈ℂ:|z|=1}. Two loops represent the same class if a continuous homotopy between them keeps both endpoints at 1. Concatenation γ*η traverses γ during the first half of the time and η during the second. Reversing a loop gives an inverse class; the constant loop gives the identity. These assertions about the fundamental group follow from routine reparametrization homotopies, whose full formulas are outside this lesson. Lift a walk to a line Worked example. Use p:ℝ→S¹, p(u)=e 2πiu . The real numbers 0, 1 and −1 all map to 1. The loop γ n (t)=e 2πint , for integer n, lifts to the straight real path u n (t)=nt starting at 0. Its endpoint is n. For n=2 the lift climbs from 0 to 2 while the circle image goes around twice; for n=−1 it descends to −1 and traverses clockwise. The integer endpoint keeps information that the circle endpoint alone loses. For two loops, first lift γ from 0 to m. To lift η after γ, begin its real lift at m rather than 0. Since adding an integer does not change p, the second portion ends at m+n. For example, one counterclockwise circuit followed by one clockwise circuit has lift endpoint 1+(−1)=0. Its class is the identity, even though the parametrized loop visibly moved. The classification, conditional on lifting Exact statement. With basepoint 1 and concatenation as group operation, π 1 ( S 1 , 1 ) ≅ ( ℤ , + ) [ γ ] ↦ γ ~ ( 1 ) Here γ̃ is the unique lift of the based loop γ with γ̃(0)=0. The required lifting lemma says that for any path α in S¹ and any chosen u₀ with p(u₀)=α(0), there is a unique continuous lift α̃ through p starting at u₀. It also says that a homotopy of paths lifts continuously once a lift of its initial path is specified; for our based homotopies the lift along the basepoint edge stays at 0. We use this lemma without proving it. It is a covering-space theorem, not a fact supplied by the appearance of a spiral. Proof given that lemma. A based loop ends at 1, so its lift endpoint is an integer. A based homotopy lifts continuously over the square. As the homotopy parameter s varies, the lift endpoint is a continuous integer-valued function of s, hence constant. Therefore the integer depends only on the homotopy class. The concatenation calculation above proves that the map from classes to integers preserves the operation: endpoint(γ*η)=endpoint(γ)+endpoint(η). Every integer occurs, since γ n has lift u n (t)=nt. To show injectivity, suppose γ and η have lifts u and v starting at 0 and ending at the same integer n. The formula H(s,t)=p((1−s)u(t)+s v(t)) is a continuous based homotopy between them: at t=0 both lifts are 0, and at t=1 both are n, which p sends to 1. Thus equal integers give equal classes. The map is bijective and operation-preserving, completing the conditional proof. The lifting lemma is exactly the deferred part. Without it, we can classify the explicit γ n examples but cannot assign a continuous lift to every possible circle loop or guarantee invariance under every based homotopy. The same integer is the winding number of the loop around 0, but the group statement concerns based classes and their concatenation. Use the lift endpoint 1. Let α(t)=e 6πit and β(t)=e −4πit . Find their classes as integers and the class of α*β. Give lift endpoints, not only a drawing. Hint for question 1 Write each exponent as 2πi times an integer multiple of t. Full solution for question 1 α(t)=e 2πi(3t) lifts to 3t and represents 3. β(t)=e 2πi(−2t) lifts to −2t and represents −2. The concatenation lift runs from 0 to 3, then from 3 to 3−2=1. Therefore [α*β] corresponds to 1. Its visible route may overlap itself, but the lift endpoint records the net turn. 2. Suppose two based loops γ and η have lifts u,v with u(0)=v(0)=0 and u(1)=v(1)=−2. Construct a based homotopy and state which assumption allowed you to speak of u and v. Hint for question 2 Interpolate the real lifts, then apply p. Check both time endpoints. Full solution for question 2 Set H(s,t)=e 2πi((1−s)u(t)+s v(t)) . At s=0 it is γ and at s=1 it is η. At t=0 the exponent is 0, and at t=1 it is −2, so both endpoints map to 1 for every s. Continuity follows from continuity of u and v. The path-lifting lemma for p supplied those real lifts; the interpolation itself then proves the homotopy. State the theorem with its input Lift endpoints turn loop concatenation into integer addition, and equal endpoints yield an explicit homotopy. The full classification of all circle loops depends on path and homotopy lifting, which this lesson assumes. This is a proof-based window into the fundamental group, not a computation of fundamental groups for arbitrary spaces. Revisit based homotopy for the boundary conditions or winding for polygonal calculations.

title: Two players, four outcomes
summary: Read a four-cell two-player payoff table, separating each player’s score from a group welfare claim.
text: What does a payoff table actually say? Two friends independently choose a path through a tiny maze. Each can take the upper path U or the lower path L. A table records the points each receives for every pair of moves. It describes a stipulated game: who moves, which choices are possible, and which score follows. It does not tell us what the friends will choose. First learn to read one cell without silently treating the first number as a shared reward. Background capsule. A table has rows and columns. An ordered pair (a,b) keeps its order: here a is the row player's score and b is the column player's score. A payoff is a numerical representation of a player's preference among outcomes in this model. Higher means that player prefers the outcome; adding the two scores is meaningful only if an extra assumption makes their scales comparable. We assume choices are simultaneous, so neither player sees the other's current move before choosing. Read four outcomes, one player at a time Maze points (row player's score, column player's score) Column U Column L Row U (3,2) (0,4) Row L (2,0) (1,1) Worked example. If both choose U, the row player gets 3 and the column player gets 2. If row chooses U while column chooses L, the outcome is (0,4). The row player's score falls from 3 to 0 when column switches from U to L; the column player's score rises from 2 to 4. If row alone switches from U to L while column stays U, compare (3,2) with (2,0). That move changes both scores, but row chooses according to the first coordinate. The column player's score is a consequence of the move, not row's payoff. A payoff table can be read from either player's viewpoint. With row fixed at U, column compares its second-coordinate scores 2 under U and 4 under L, so L is preferable. With row fixed at L, column compares 0 under U and 1 under L, again preferring L. No probability was needed. We merely held one action fixed and compared the two available outcomes. A table is a function on pairs of actions Let S R = {U,L} and S C = {U,L}. The notation u R (r,c) means row's payoff when actions are r and c. Likewise u C (r,c) is the column payoff. A cell records both functions at the same input: u ( r , c ) = ( u R ( r , c ) , u C ( r , c ) ) Exact claim and scope. Under this two-player, two-action description, the table exhausts all four pure action profiles because 2 × 2 = 4. The proof is enumeration: row has two choices and each can be paired with either of column's two choices. This is a description of outcomes, not a theorem about behavior. If a friend can choose a third path, the four-cell table omits possibilities. If points are merely labels that fail to reflect preferences, comparing numbers will not predict preferred outcomes. A higher payoff can mean a greater prize or simply a stipulated rank; the interpretation must be supplied by the game designer. Changing every row-player payoff by the same positive scaling and shift preserves row's ordering of cells. Yet subtracting or adding both players' payoffs to pronounce one outcome “best for the group” needs a welfare rule. The table alone does not give one. In this example (U,U) sums to 5 and (L,L) sums to 2, but sum maximization is a separate criterion. Test your reading 1. Calculation. The column player chooses U. What are row's two possible payoffs, and which row move does row prefer? Then repeat when column chooses L. Hint for exercise 1 Stay in one column, and compare only the first coordinate. Full solution to exercise 1 When column chooses U, row's payoff is 3 from U and 2 from L, so row prefers U. When column chooses L, row's payoff is 0 from U and 1 from L, so row prefers L. The favored row move changes with column's choice, so the table alone does not support saying “row always chooses U.” 2. Interpretation. Someone says that (U,U) must occur because its scores add to the largest total. Identify two assumptions that statement would need, and show one reason it can fail as a prediction of independent moves. Hint for exercise 2 Ask whose preference a sum measures and whether each player would want to stay at (U,U). Full solution to exercise 2 The claim would need a rule that adds the two players' scores on comparable scales, and a mechanism or agreement that makes players choose the sum-maximizing pair. Without these, column sees a profitable unilateral switch from U to L when row uses U: its payoff rises from 2 to 4. Thus (U,U) is not stable under independent payoff-seeking, even though 3 + 2 = 5 is the largest sum in the table. A statement about welfare and a statement about incentives answer different questions. What the grid gives you A payoff cell names one outcome and assigns a separate score to each player. To compare moves, hold the other player's choice fixed and inspect only the decision maker's coordinate. In this example, that calculation is enough to see that row's preferred move depends on column's move, while column prefers L in either row. The next lessons formalize those comparisons as dominance and best response. Failure case. The grid has no entry for communication, uncertain scoring, or a third action. Conclusions drawn from its four cells are conditional on the two-action simultaneous game as stated. A payoff matrix is a precise small model, not a survey of all possible human motives.

title: A move that wins every comparison
summary: Check every opposing action to distinguish strict dominance, weak dominance and equality.
text: Can one move beat another in every case? Suppose two players submit puzzle pieces at the same time. A player may prefer one piece no matter which piece the opponent submits. That is a dominance claim. It is stronger than “this move wins when the opponent chooses left,” because it checks every possible opposing action. We will separate strict dominance, weak dominance, and equal payoffs by doing all the comparisons. Background capsule. A payoff pair (a,b) lists row's points first and column's second. To compare row actions, hold the column action fixed and compare first coordinates. To compare column actions, hold the row action fixed and compare second coordinates. “At least as good” means ≥; “better” means >. The opponent's action is not a probability here: each case is checked separately. Where the strict and weak cases split Payoffs (row, column) in a two-action puzzle Column X Column Y Row A (4,3) (2,2) Row B (1,3) (2,0) Worked example. For row, A gives 4 instead of 1 when column chooses X, and 2 instead of 2 when column chooses Y. Thus A is never worse and sometimes better: A weakly dominates B. It does not strictly dominate B because against Y the two row payoffs tie. For column, the relevant comparisons run across each fixed row. Against row A, X gives column 3 while Y gives 2. Against row B, X gives 3 while Y gives 0. Thus X strictly dominates Y. The equal 3s down the X column compare different row actions and are not a tie in either choice comparison. Notice that two players' dominance statements use different coordinates even though they use the same grid. If the lower-right second coordinate changed from 0 to 5, column Y would beat X against row B (5 > 3), while X would still beat Y against row A (3 > 2). A single changed cell can reverse an “every case” claim. This is why checking just a favored diagonal is inadequate. The quantifier matters Let s and t be two actions of player i, and x an action of the opponent. The exact definition of weak dominance is: ∀ x : u i ( s , x ) ≥ u i ( t , x ) , ∃ x : u i ( s , x ) > u i ( t , x ) Strict dominance replaces “≥ for every x, > for some x” with “> for every x.” In a finite table the proof is exhaustive comparison: each column (for row) or row (for column) supplies one required inequality. Equal payoffs in every case do not count as weak dominance under the definition used here, because there is no strict improvement anywhere; the actions are payoff equivalent. Some texts use “weakly dominates” for the all-≥ condition alone. Stating the convention avoids a verbal disagreement hiding a mathematical one. Boundary. A dominant strategy is an action that dominates each alternative action. With only two actions, comparing that pair suffices. If there are three actions, beating one alternative does not establish dominance over the third. Strict dominance does not require a guess about the opponent's probabilities; it is robust to every pure opposing action and therefore to every mixture of them. Weak dominance may leave a tie under some mixtures, so a player can rationally use the other action in those cases. Make the comparisons yourself 1. Calculation. In the displayed table, decide whether row A strictly or weakly dominates row B. Then decide whether column X strictly or weakly dominates Y. Hint for exercise 1 Write two payoff inequalities for each player; include the equality cases. Full solution to exercise 1 Row sees 4 > 1 against X and 2 = 2 against Y. So A weakly dominates B, but not strictly. Column sees 3 > 2 against A and 3 > 0 against B. So X strictly dominates Y. The equal pair in the lower-left cell concerns row? No: column compares the second numbers within each row, not across rows. Against A, column compares 3 with 2; against B, 3 with 0. Thus the initial glance at equal 3s in the X column was irrelevant to column's decision. 2. Counterexample. Change only row's payoff at (B,Y) from 2 to 5. Does A still weakly dominate B? Explain by checking both opponent actions. Hint for exercise 2 A single failed ≥ inequality destroys weak dominance. Full solution to exercise 2 Against X, row still gets 4 from A and 1 from B, so A is better. Against Y, row now gets 2 from A and 5 from B, so B is better. Neither A nor B weakly dominates the other: each is preferable in one opposing case. A statement about one column cannot be generalized to all columns. A durable comparison, with a limit Strict dominance survives every opposing action with a strict payoff gain. Weak dominance under our convention survives with at least one gain and no losses. The table's column X is strictly dominant for column; row A is merely weakly dominant for row. This language characterizes payoffs, not moral virtue or an empirical guarantee of what a person will select. Failure case. If a player has an unlisted action, or the payoff table leaves out a relevant future consequence, an apparent dominant move can disappear when the game is modeled more fully. With the stated finite actions and scores, however, the displayed inequalities settle the claim exactly.

title: Stable choices are not always nicest
summary: Locate pure Nash equilibria by checking all unilateral deviations, including inefficient and multiple equilibria.
text: Would either player change course alone? Two players choose one of two routes through a puzzle. A pair of choices is stable in a narrow sense if neither player could earn more points by switching their own route while the other keeps theirs. This is a pure Nash equilibrium. Stability under unilateral moves does not mean both players are happy with everything, or that the outcome is best for their combined scores. Background capsule. A payoff pair (a,b) gives row's points first and column's second. A unilateral deviation changes exactly one player's action while fixing the other's. A best response is an action that gives a player the highest payoff against the fixed opposing action; ties produce more than one best response. “Pure” means a definite action, not a lottery over actions. We will check the finite table directly. Mark the best responses Crossing puzzle payoffs (row, column) Column L Column R Row T (4,4) (0,5) Row B (5,0) (1,1) Worked example. If column plays L, row prefers B because 5 > 4. If column plays R, row again prefers B because 1 > 0. Thus B is row's best response to either column action. If row plays T, column prefers R because 5 > 4. If row plays B, column again prefers R because 1 > 0. Their best responses meet at (B,R), giving (1,1). To check it directly, row switching alone to T would get 0 rather than 1; column switching alone to L would get 0 rather than 1. No single player profits by moving. At (T,L), both receive 4, which each prefers to 1. Yet row could earn 5 by changing to B while column holds L. Column could earn 5 by changing to R while row holds T. So (T,L) fails the equilibrium test despite being better for both players than (B,R). The example is a stipulated incentives puzzle; it is not a claim that people cannot coordinate or that one outcome is ethically preferable. What the equilibrium inequality proves For a profile s* = (r*,c*), the pure Nash condition is that every player i and every available alternative action a i satisfy: u i ( s ∗ ) ≥ u i ( a i , s − i ∗ ) The subscript −i means “all the other players,” held at their proposed actions. In the displayed two-action game, there is one alternative for each player at each cell. At (B,R), the two comparisons 1 ≥ 0 and 1 ≥ 0 establish equilibrium. They are sufficient because all unilateral alternatives have been exhausted. This proof is for the finite displayed game; it does not assert an equilibrium for every pure-action game. A best-response method reaches the same conclusion: mark row's payoff maximum in each column and column's maximum in each row. A cell marked for both is an equilibrium. This can reveal multiple equilibria or none. For example, in matching pennies, row gains by matching while column gains by mismatching. Whatever pure pair is chosen, one of them wants to switch. Randomized strategies require a separate model. Check stability rather than appearances 1. Calculation. For the displayed table, test (T,R). Identify who can profit by switching alone and state the gain. Hint for exercise 1 Hold row T fixed to test column; hold column R fixed to test row. Full solution to exercise 1 At (T,R) the payoffs are (0,5). If row switches to B while column stays R, the payoffs become (1,1): row's own score increases from 0 to 1. If column switches to L while row stays T, column's score falls from 5 to 4, so column would not switch for payoff gain. Because row has a profitable deviation, (T,R) is not an equilibrium. One profitable deviation is enough to reject a candidate. 2. Construction. A coordination game pays (2,2) at (A,A), (1,1) at (B,B), and (0,0) at the two mismatches. Find every pure Nash equilibrium and explain why the higher-payoff one need not be the only equilibrium. Hint for exercise 2 At each matching cell, compare a unilateral switch to a mismatch. Full solution to exercise 2 At (A,A), either unilateral switch yields 0 instead of 2, so both stay: equilibrium. At (B,B), either switch yields 0 instead of 1, so both stay: another equilibrium. At (A,B), row can change to B and earn 1 rather than 0; column can change to A and earn 2 rather than 0. At (B,A), analogous improvements exist. Thus exactly the two matching cells are equilibria. Nash checks unilateral incentives at a given cell; it does not select the cell with the largest common payoff. A local test of incentives Pure Nash equilibrium is a complete check of one-player deviations. The crossing puzzle has a single equilibrium (B,R), while the coordination construction has two. Neither fact alone predicts which outcome real players reach. To interpret a game outside the page, the actions, information, and payoffs would need evidence. Failure case. A game can lack a pure equilibrium, as matching pennies does. The absence of a marked cell is not a counting error when every candidate has a profitable unilateral deviation; it motivates the mixed-strategy question.

title: Why randomize a move?
summary: Solve an asymmetric zero-sum two-action game by indifference and verify both mixtures.
text: When every fixed move can be exploited One player hides a token under a left or right cup; another guesses. The hider gains points when the guess is wrong and loses points when it is right; the stakes depend on the side. The guesser receives the opposite payoff. If both choose fixed sides, one of them wishes to change. Randomizing can make the opponent indifferent and remove that predictable weakness. We will solve a deliberately asymmetric two-action game and then check its support conditions. Background capsule. A mixed strategy assigns probabilities to actions, totaling one. Expected payoff is the probability-weighted average of possible payoffs. If an action has positive probability in an equilibrium mix, it must be a best response to the opponent's mix. With two supported actions, this means equal expected payoffs. The rule is necessary, but equality alone is not sufficient if an omitted action does better; we check all available actions. An uneven hide-and-seek table Hider payoff; guesser receives its negative Guess L Guess R Hide L −2 1 Hide R 2 −1 Worked example. Matching the hiding side gives the guesser a gain and the hider a loss. The size differs by side. Let p be the probability that the hider selects L. Against guess L, the hider expects −2p + 2(1−p) = 2−4p. Against guess R, the hider expects p − (1−p) = 2p−1. The guesser tries to minimize these hider values. To make the guesser indifferent, set 2−4p = 2p−1, giving p = 1/2. Both guess choices then give hider expected payoff 0. Now let q be the probability of guess L. If hider chooses L, its expected payoff is −2q + 1(1−q) = 1−3q. If hider chooses R, it gets 2q − 1(1−q) = 3q−1. Setting these equal gives q = 1/3 and common payoff 0. Thus the equilibrium candidates are hider (1/2,1/2) and guesser (1/3,2/3). Each probability lies in [0,1], and each player has only two actions. Every pure action now gives that player the same payoff, so neither can improve unilaterally by changing its mix. Why indifference identifies the mix For player i's two supported actions a and b against opponent mixture σ −i , the equal-payoff condition is: E [ u i ( a , σ − i ) ] = E [ u i ( b , σ − i ) ] Why? If a had higher expected payoff, moving probability from b to a would improve the player's expected score, contradicting equilibrium. Conversely, when both possible pure actions are tied at the maximum, any mixture of them is a best response. In this two-action example there are no hidden third actions to inspect. The two indifference equations determine the opponent's probability, not one's own directly: hider's p makes guesser indifferent, and guesser's q makes hider indifferent. Proof boundary. This derivation checks a particular finite zero-sum table. It is not a proof of the general existence theorem for all finite games. A proposed solution with p outside [0,1] is not a mixed strategy; in such a case the correct equilibrium may be on the boundary with a pure action. If a third action existed, it would need an inequality check against the common supported payoff. Calculate and test a mixture 1. Calculation. For the displayed game, suppose the guesser uses q = 1/2. Find the hider payoff from each pure hide action and its preferred move. Hint for exercise 1 Substitute q into 1−3q and 3q−1. Full solution to exercise 1 Hide L gives 1−3(1/2) = −1/2. Hide R gives 3(1/2)−1 = 1/2. The hider should choose R rather than mix with positive probability on L. Thus q = 1/2 cannot be the guesser's component of a fully mixed equilibrium in this game; the balanced guess probability is 1/3. 2. Explanation. A student solves only 2−4p = 2p−1 and reports “the equilibrium is p = 1/2.” What remains to be found and checked? Hint for exercise 2 Which player does this equation make indifferent? Full solution to exercise 2 The equation equates the hider's payoffs against the two pure guesses, making the guesser indifferent between guesses because its payoffs are the negatives. It finds the hider's mixing probability p = 1/2, but it leaves the guesser's mixing probability q unknown. Equating the hider's pure-action payoffs gives 1−3q = 3q−1, so q = 1/3. Both are valid probabilities; all pure actions have payoff 0 at the pair. These checks establish the claimed equilibrium for the two-action game. Randomness as an incentive condition A mixture is not chosen because half-and-half seems fair. Its probabilities solve the other player's best-response problem. Here the hider uses 1/2 on L and the guesser uses only 1/3 on L because losses from a left-side match are larger. The expected zero payoff is a property of this scoring model. Failure case. Merely drawing actions randomly does not guarantee equilibrium. At guess probability 1/2, the hider exploits the imbalance by always hiding R. Strategic randomization requires the indifference and probability checks together.

title: What changes when play repeats?
summary: Derive the discount threshold for one grim-trigger equilibrium in an infinitely repeated game.
text: Does tomorrow change today's choice? In a one-round puzzle, each player may have an incentive to take a short-term bonus even when mutual restraint would pay both more. If the same pair plays indefinitely and notices past actions, losing future cooperation can outweigh that one-round bonus. This lesson calculates one precise threshold. It does not claim cooperation always emerges in repeated interactions. Background capsule. A payoff pair lists row's score first and column's second. A discount factor δ between 0 and 1 weights one point next round as δ points now, a point two rounds ahead as δ², and so on. The geometric sum 1+δ+δ²+··· equals 1/(1−δ) for 0 ≤ δ < 1. We assume both players observe past actions, know the payoff table, and can condition future actions on that history. A club's recurring choice One-round payoffs (row, column); C is cooperate, D is defect Column C Column D Row C (3,3) (0,5) Row D (5,0) (1,1) Worked example. In one round, D strictly dominates C: against C it gives 5 rather than 3, and against D it gives 1 rather than 0. So (D,D) is the unique one-round Nash equilibrium. Now suppose each player promises to play C until anyone plays D, after which both play D forever. This is a grim trigger strategy. If both comply forever, each obtains 3+3δ+3δ²+··· = 3/(1−δ). If row defects today while column cooperates, row gets 5 today. Column observes the defection, so both use D in every later round; row then gets 1 each round. Its total is 5+δ/(1−δ). Cooperation is at least as attractive as this one-time deviation exactly when 3/(1−δ) ≥ 5+δ/(1−δ), or 3 ≥ 5−4δ, hence δ ≥ 1/2. At δ = 0.6, cooperation pays 7.5 while deviation pays 5+1.5 = 6.5. At δ = 0.4, cooperation pays 5 while deviation pays 5+2/3, so the threat does not deter. Discounting and the incentive boundary The repeated payoff under a path of one-round payoffs u t is: V = ∑ t = 0 ∞ δ t u t , 0 ≤ δ < 1 Exact claim. In this infinitely repeated, perfectly observed game, the specified grim-trigger profile is a subgame-perfect equilibrium when δ ≥ 1/2. The cooperative-path calculation checks the tempting one-time defection. After a defection, both use D forever; D is each player's best response to D in the one-round game, so no player gains by deviating during punishment. At any cooperative history the same comparison applies after discounting to that date. A finite sequence of deviations cannot do better than the best one-time deviation at its first point of difference; the standard one-shot deviation reasoning completes this bounded check. There is an important boundary. If a publicly known final round exists, the last round has no future punishment, so both choose D there; backward reasoning then unravels the proposed cooperation in the earlier rounds under these assumptions. If monitoring is noisy, a false signal can start punishment, and this simple threshold no longer describes the incentives exactly. A larger discount factor is not a moral improvement; it changes the present value of future points. Change the patience parameter 1. Calculation. Evaluate the two totals at δ = 1/2. Is cooperation strictly better than a one-time deviation? Hint for exercise 1 Use 3/(1−δ) and 5+δ/(1−δ). Full solution to exercise 1 Cooperation yields 3/(1/2) = 6. Defecting now and then receiving 1 forever yields 5+(1/2)/(1/2) = 6. The player is indifferent. That suffices for no profitable deviation, so grim trigger can still be an equilibrium at equality, but the threat is not strictly deterrent. The alternative always-D profile also remains an equilibrium. 2. Boundary case. Suppose the club announces that it will play exactly two rounds, and both players know this. Can the same grim-trigger reasoning support C in round one? Explain within this payoff model. Hint for exercise 2 Start from the second and final round, then return to round one. Full solution to exercise 2 In round two, no later payoff can punish D, and D gives each player a higher current payoff against either action. So both choose D regardless of the first-round history. Knowing the second-round outcome cannot depend on today's cooperation, each compares only first-round payoffs. D again strictly dominates C. Therefore (D,D) is played in both rounds in the standard complete-information equilibrium analysis. The infinite-horizon threat relied on indefinitely many future consequences. A threshold, not a general promise Repeating the same stage game can alter incentives because actions today affect future play. Under exact observation, infinite repetition and grim-trigger punishment, δ ≥ 1/2 sustains the displayed cooperative path. The one-round game still rewards defection, and the repeated game still admits always defecting. We have established one equilibrium construction, not a unique prediction. Failure case. A known last round removes the endless punishment stream. Unknown payoffs, missed observations, or forgiveness rules would change the calculation and deserve their own specified model.

title: The group can prefer A to B to C to A
summary: Count three pairwise votes that form a cycle despite coherent individual rankings.
text: Can the group chase its own tail? Three club members rank three possible book covers, A, B and C. Each person's list is internally consistent: if they put A above B and B above C, they put A above C. Yet the group's pairwise majority comparisons can form a circle. Counting this example shows why “let the majority settle each pair” does not always produce a complete ranking with a top choice. Background capsule. A ranking A > B > C means A is preferred to B, B to C, and therefore A to C by that individual. In a pairwise contest between A and B, a voter supports whichever of those two appears higher on their ballot, even if their favorite is C. With three voters there is no pairwise tie if everyone ranks each pair strictly. We assume one ballot per voter, equal weights, and no abstentions. Count all three pairs Three complete ranked ballots Voter First Second Third 1 A B C 2 B C A 3 C A B Worked example. For A versus B, voters 1 and 3 rank A above B; voter 2 ranks B above A. Thus A beats B, 2–1. For B versus C, voters 1 and 2 rank B above C, while voter 3 ranks C above B. Thus B beats C, 2–1. For C versus A, voters 2 and 3 rank C above A, while voter 1 ranks A above C. Thus C beats A, 2–1. Every contest has a clear majority, yet the winners form A > B > C > A. This is an exact tally from the displayed ballots. Each voter ranks transitive preferences, so the cycle does not arise from any voter contradicting themselves. It appears only after taking the three separate majority votes. If an agenda asks A against B first and then that winner against C, C beats A in the final. If it asks B against C first and then that winner against A, A beats B in the final. The agenda can matter even though the ballots are unchanged. Why the cycle blocks a top-ranked option Writing x ≻ M y when a strict majority ranks x above y, the displayed profile establishes: A ≻ M B , B ≻ M C , C ≻ M A A strict ranking that is transitive cannot contain this loop: from A above B and B above C, transitivity would require A above C, contrary to C above A. The proof of the cycle consists of the three 2–1 counts; the proof of its incompatibility with a transitive ranking is that one contradiction. This is a counterexample to the universal claim that pairwise majority always yields a transitive social ranking. It is not a proof that every ballot profile cycles. A Condorcet winner would beat every other option head to head. None exists here: A loses to C, B loses to A, and C loses to B. Other profiles can have a Condorcet winner. For instance, if all three voters rank A first, A defeats both B and C regardless of their lower ranks. The pairwise rule answers a different question from plurality, which counts only first places; in our cyclic profile plurality yields a three-way first-place tie. Work from the rankings 1. Calculation. Change voter 3's ballot to A > C > B, leaving the other two ballots as shown. Count all pairwise contests. Is there still a cycle? Hint for exercise 1 For each pair, list the voters who place the first named option above the second. Full solution to exercise 1 A beats B by voters 1 and 3 versus voter 2, so 2–1. A beats C by voters 1 and 3 versus voter 2, also 2–1. B versus C is supported by voter 1 for B, voters 2 and 3 for C, so C beats B 2–1. The majority order is A > C > B, a transitive ranking. A is the Condorcet winner. One changed ballot can remove the cycle. 2. Explanation. In the original profile, a member proposes “choose the winner of A versus B, then compare it with C.” Who wins? What if the club first compares B versus C, then the winner with A? Hint for exercise 2 Use the three pairwise results already counted; the final ballot is another head-to-head contest.
