Full solution to exercise 2 First A beats B, then C beats A, so C wins the first agenda. In the second agenda B beats C, then A beats B, so A wins. These results do not alter any voter's ranking; they reflect the cycle plus a sequential elimination rule. The claim concerns these two agendas on this particular profile, not all sequential elections. Majority needs a rule for cycles Pairwise majority is decisive on each pair in this three-voter example, but the separate decisions do not combine into a transitive whole. A club that wants one winner must specify what happens with a cycle, a tie, or a chosen agenda. Different specifications can produce different winners while using the same sincere ballots. Failure case. A 2–1 cycle is possible here because the rankings are split in a particular way. It is not inevitable. A common first choice defeats every rival, and the modified exercise produced a clear top option. The lesson identifies a limitation of unrestricted pairwise majority, not a universal defect of voters.

title: Scoring ranked choices changes the winner
summary: Compare plurality and Borda counts on the same complete rankings, with ties declared.
text: Does counting second place change a winner? A club must select one mural color from Amber A, Blue B and Coral C. Each member submits a complete ranking. Plurality counts only first places. Borda scoring gives points for every rank: with three options, 2 points for first, 1 for second, 0 for third. The same ballots can choose different winners, so a counting rule is a substantive part of the decision. Background capsule. A ranked ballot lists each of the three colors exactly once. A plurality score is the number of first-place votes. A Borda score is the sum of assigned rank points. “Winner” means highest score under the named rule. We declare ties when the maximum score is shared; this page never silently breaks a tie by alphabetical order. Each voter has weight one and rankings are strict. Use the same five ballots twice Complete mural-color rankings Number of voters Ranking 2 A > C > B 1 B > C > A 2 C > B > A Worked example. Plurality gives A two first places, B one, and C two. Thus plurality declares a tie between A and C. Borda counts all positions. The two A > C > B ballots give A 4 points and C 2. The B > C > A ballot gives B 2 and C 1. The two C > B > A ballots give C 4 and B 2. Totals: A = 4, B = 4, C = 7. C is the unique Borda winner. The totals add to 15, matching five ballots × (2+1+0) points each; that checksum helps catch counting mistakes. To show an outright plurality-versus-Borda reversal, add one more A > B > C voter. Plurality now gives A three first places, C two, B one, so A wins. Borda adds 2 to A and 1 to B, producing A = 6, B = 5, C = 7, so C still wins. The sixth voter did not create a tie: the rules disagree on a unique winner. Define the score before judging it For candidate c and voters v, let p v (c) be 2, 1 or 0 according to c's position on v's ballot. Then: B ( c ) = ∑ v p v ( c ) Exact claim. On the six-ballot profile, plurality uniquely elects A and Borda uniquely elects C under the stated point convention. The proof is the displayed rank counts and sums. The result is about these ballots and rules; it is not a theorem that Borda always chooses C-like compromises or that plurality always fails. Both methods discard information: plurality ignores lower ranks, while Borda converts ordinal positions into a fixed point spacing that voters may not feel. For m options a common Borda convention assigns m−1 down to 0. Adding the same constant to every rank's points changes all candidate totals equally and leaves winners unchanged for a fixed number of complete ballots. Changing the gaps between ranks can change winners. If voters omit options or share ranks, additional scoring rules are required. We do not apply this formula to incomplete or tied ballots. Count and interpret 1. Calculation. Use the six-ballot profile after adding one A > B > C voter. Change the single B > C > A ballot to B > A > C. Recalculate plurality and Borda winners. Hint for exercise 1 First places stay the same. Only A and C exchange their Borda positions on that ballot. Full solution to exercise 1 Plurality remains A = 3, B = 1, C = 2, so A still wins. In Borda, the changed ballot gives A one point instead of zero and C zero instead of one. Starting from A = 6, B = 5, C = 7, the totals become A = 7, B = 5, C = 6. A now wins Borda too. A change in lower ranks can change the Borda winner while leaving plurality unchanged. 2. Explanation. A member argues that Borda's winner must be the option that beats each other option by pairwise majority. Does the score definition guarantee this? Give a numerical reason to doubt that implication. Hint for exercise 2 One score adds all rank points; a head-to-head count considers one opponent at a time. Full solution to exercise 2 No. The Borda total measures assigned rank points across all ballots, whereas a pairwise majority asks how many voters rank c above a particular rival. The six-ballot profile illustrates the distinction: C scores 7 against A's 6. A is ranked above C by the two A > C > B voters and the added A > B > C voter, while C is ranked above A by the B > C > A voter and the two C > B > A voters. Their head-to-head contest is tied 3–3. Thus C wins Borda but is not a strict Condorcet winner, because C does not beat A head to head. A Borda score alone therefore cannot certify a Condorcet winner. Rules answer different questions Plurality counts first-place support; Borda rewards position across full rankings. On the six-ballot example A wins plurality and C wins Borda. The calculation is decisive only after the rule, completeness requirements and tie convention are set. A real club should decide those before seeing a disputed tally. Failure case. With incomplete rankings or equal ranks, the 2–1–0 tally lacks a defined treatment. Also, no scoring formula proves that its winner meets every possible fairness criterion. The next question is which criteria a chosen rule actually satisfies.

title: What Arrow’s theorem actually assumes
summary: State Arrow’s ranked social-ordering impossibility conditions and illustrate one IIA failure.
text: What exactly becomes impossible? A fictional club wants a rule that turns every member's ranking of at least three designs into one group ranking. Arrow's theorem says no rule of this particular kind can satisfy a specified collection of appealing conditions on every possible preference profile. The theorem is often made too vague: it is neither a proof that ballots are useless nor a statement that every rule fails every condition. To understand its force, specify the input, output and axioms. Background capsule. A ranking is an ordering of options. A weak ordering can include ties, but must be complete and transitive: any two options can be compared, and x ≥ y together with y ≥ z implies x ≥ z. A profile is a list of one ranking per voter. A social welfare function maps each allowed profile to a social ordering of the same alternatives. We use a finite set of at least two voters and at least three options; the rankings contain only order information, not intensity of preference. Why conditions pull against each other Worked example. Consider three voters with A > B > C, B > C > A, and C > A > B. A beats B 2–1, B beats C 2–1, and C beats A 2–1. Pairwise majority honors each local majority but gives a cycle, so it fails the social-ordering requirement on this profile. A dictator rule avoids cycles by copying one person's coherent ranking, but then it fails non-dictatorship. A rank-points rule can produce a complete group order, yet it may violate independence of irrelevant alternatives, abbreviated IIA. Here is a direct IIA test for Borda's 2–1–0 scores. Five voters have the same A-versus-B views in two profiles: three rank A above B; two rank B above A. In profile P, three submit A > C > B and two submit B > A > C. Borda totals are A = 8, B = 4, C = 3, so A ranks above B. In profile Q, those three submit C > A > B and the other two submit B > C > A. Totals are C = 8, B = 4, A = 3, so B ranks above A. No voter changed their A-versus-B comparison. Only C moved. Therefore this Borda social comparison violates IIA on these two profiles. The computation diagnoses one rule; it is not a proof of Arrow's full impossibility theorem. State the theorem with its domain For a fixed finite set of at least three alternatives and at least two individuals, suppose a social welfare function takes every profile of complete, transitive individual rankings and returns a complete, transitive social ranking. Require weak Pareto: unanimous strict preference for x over y forces social x above y. Require IIA: if each person's comparison of x with y is unchanged between two profiles, the social comparison of x with y is unchanged. Then the rule must be dictatorial: some fixed individual always determines every strict social pairwise comparison. Equivalently, no such rule also satisfies non-dictatorship. ( UD ∧ SO ∧ P ∧ IIA ) ⇒ D ( | X | ≥ 3 ) Proof boundary. The example above proves only that Borda violates IIA. The majority cycle proves only that pairwise majority can fail social ordering. Neither proves that every possible rule fails one of the conditions. The general implication requires a separate argument, commonly using decisive coalitions or pivotal voters to show that Pareto and IIA force one individual to determine every pair. This article states that theorem from the cited mathematical-philosophy reference and illustrates its assumptions; it does not present a complete proof of the universal quantification over rules. One must not silently switch from a complete group ranking to a rule that returns only one winner. Winner-only methods answer a related but different formal question. Likewise restricting allowed preference profiles, permitting extra intensity information, or relaxing IIA changes the mathematical setup. Those are possible design choices, not counterexamples to a theorem with its hypotheses intact. Identify the exact violation 1. Calculation. Recompute A's and B's Borda scores in profile Q. Explain which voter-level A/B comparisons changed from profile P. Hint for exercise 1 Each C > A > B ballot gives A one and B zero; each B > C > A gives B two and A zero. Full solution to exercise 1 The three C > A > B ballots contribute A = 3, B = 0. The two B > C > A ballots contribute A = 0, B = 4. Thus Borda places B above A, 4 to 3. In P, the three A > C > B voters still ranked A above B, and the two B > A > C voters still ranked B above A. No A/B pairwise comparison changed at all. The social A/B reversal therefore violates IIA. 2. Scope check. A club uses a rule only when all voters rank A at the top. If it finds a non-dictatorial rule satisfying Pareto and IIA on that restricted set, has it refuted Arrow's theorem? Hint for exercise 2 Ask whether the rule accepts every possible coherent preference profile. Full solution to exercise 2 No. Requiring every voter to put A first excludes many coherent profiles, including the majority cycle shown above. That violates unrestricted domain, one of the theorem's hypotheses. The rule may work well for that narrower domain, but it does not supply a social welfare function meeting all Arrow conditions for every ranking profile. A theorem's conclusion need not hold after one of its assumptions is removed. A precise limit on a precise task Arrow's result concerns aggregation of unrestricted ordinal rankings into a complete and transitive social ranking, while satisfying weak Pareto, IIA and non-dictatorship. The theorem exposes a tradeoff among those requirements. A practical club can choose and explain a rule according to its priorities; it should not claim that the rule has every axiom simultaneously. Failure case for a casual slogan. “No fair election exists” has no defined meaning of fair and confuses ranked social welfare functions with all conceivable voting procedures. Our Borda profiles illustrate one exact axiom failure, while the theorem supplies the general impossibility only under its stated domain and output requirements.

title: Sincere ballots can be unstable
summary: Calculate one profitable plurality misreport under a fixed tie priority and identify its limits.
text: Can a voter prefer to report a false favorite? In a cover election, a ballot can express a voter's true ordering or serve as a move in a game. Suppose the rule counts only first places, and a voter cares about which cover wins. If a false first place changes the winner from their worst option to their middle option, the voter has a profitable manipulation of that rule at that profile. This lesson constructs one, with the tie convention declared before the ballots are counted. Background capsule. A true preference A > B > C means the voter likes A best and C least. A report is the ranking they submit, which may differ. Under plurality, only each ballot's first-ranked option earns one vote. We choose the winner with most votes; if top counts tie, the fixed priority A, then B, then C breaks the tie. A manipulation exists when a voter can submit a report that selects an outcome they strictly prefer to the outcome under truthful reporting, with every other report held fixed. One voter changes the outcome Five sincere rankings before the strategic change Voters True ranking and initial report First-place votes 1 and 2 A > B > C Two for A 3 and 4 B > C > A Two for B 5 C > B > A One for C Worked example. With all five reporting sincerely, plurality counts A = 2, B = 2, C = 1. The announced priority breaks the A/B tie in favor of A. Voter 5 truly ranks C > B > A, so A is their least desired result. If only voter 5 reports B > C > A instead, the first-place counts become A = 2, B = 3, C = 0. B wins without a tie. Voter 5 prefers B to A, so this misreport is profitable for them. It does not elect their top choice C; it avoids their worst outcome in this particular setting. The strategic claim depends on what the other four ballots are, how the rule counts, and how the tie is broken. If priority favored B over A, sincere voting would already elect B and this particular misreport would not strictly improve the outcome. If one of voters 1 or 2 changed, the first-place arithmetic would change. These are features of the constructed example, not assumptions about actual club members. Formalize the deviation Let F(r i ,r −i ) be the winner chosen by the rule from voter i's report and the fixed reports of everyone else. Let ≻ i be i's true strict preference. A profitable manipulation at a profile is a report r i with: F ( r i , r − i ) ≻ i F ( t i , r − i ) Here t i is the truthful ranking. In the example, the left side is B and the right side A, and voter 5 ranks B above A. That is a complete proof of manipulability for this plurality rule with this tie priority: a single counterexample suffices to refute “truthful reporting is always best.” It does not show that every voter at every profile can manipulate, nor that the misreport is guaranteed to work when the other ballots are unknown. Strategic voting is related to game theory because a ballot is an action and the election outcome determines payoff according to a voter's preferences. It is related to social choice because the counting rule maps profiles to outcomes. A voter may lack information about others or value truthful expression for reasons not in this outcome-only model; such motives would require a richer payoff description. Check incentives under changed rules 1. Calculation. Keep the five truthful rankings but change the fixed tie priority to B, then A, then C. What wins with sincere ballots? Does voter 5's B > C > A report strictly improve the winner for them? Hint for exercise 1 The sincere first-place counts remain 2, 2, 1; apply the new tie rule. Full solution to exercise 1 Sincere plurality still ties A and B at two each, but B now wins by the revised priority. Voter 5's misreport gives B three first-place votes, so B wins again. Since the selected cover is B in both cases, the misreport does not strictly improve the outcome. A change to tie handling removes this particular profitable deviation. 2. Explanation. Does the five-voter example prove that no election rule can make truthful voting safe? State exactly what it proves and what a broader theorem would require. Hint for exercise 2 Distinguish one counterexample to one rule from a universal statement about all rules. Full solution to exercise 2 It proves that plurality with priority A > B > C is manipulable: there exists a profile and a voter for whom a false report changes A to the more preferred B. A claim about every rule would require additional hypotheses and a proof covering all eligible rules and profiles. The displayed arithmetic concerns one named rule. It also says nothing about how likely that profile is in real elections. What a strategic ballot demonstrates The profitable deviation is visible in both a count and a preference comparison. Sincere reports yield A by tie priority; voter 5's misreport yields B; voter 5 truly prefers B to A. Specifying those three facts prevents “strategic” from becoming a vague label for any unusual ballot. Failure case. Under a different tie convention the same reports do not improve the outcome. Under uncertain opponents' ballots the voter may not know which report helps. This is a finite counterexample about possible incentives under a stated rule, not a behavioral forecast.

title: Dots, lines, and what a graph forgets
summary: Describe a network by a vertex set, edge pairs, and a symmetric adjacency list while identifying what a simple graph leaves out.
text: What survives when a map is redrawn? A transit map often straightens a winding line and moves stations to make labels fit. The drawing may change radically while the list of directly connected stations stays fixed. Graph theory studies that list of connections. It can answer whether a route exists, but the drawing alone cannot tell us travel time, compass direction, or distance. Background capsule. A finite set is a collection in which each named object occurs once. An unordered pair {a,b} records two objects without choosing a first one. For this lesson a simple undirected graph has a finite vertex set V and an edge set E consisting of unordered pairs of distinct vertices. There are no loops from a vertex to itself and no duplicate edges. We call two vertices adjacent when their pair belongs to E. These conventions matter: other graph models allow arrows, loops, or several edges between the same two vertices. Suppose a tiny museum has rooms A, B, C, D, with doors AB, AC, BC, and CD. Can we describe exactly the same door network without a floor plan? Yes: record the four pairs and nothing about where a room sits on paper. Turn doors into a checkable ledger Worked example. For the museum, let V={A,B,C,D} and E={{A,B},{A,C},{B,C},{C,D}}. The adjacency list says A: B,C; B: A,C; C: A,B,D; D: C. This is a worked conversion: every edge appears in the lists of both endpoints. Conversely, read only the entries after A, then the previously unseen entries after B and C, and recover exactly the four unordered pairs. Recording both directions does not create eight doors; AB and BA name the same edge. Two descriptions of the museum network Room Adjacent rooms Direct door pairs contributed A B, C AB, AC B A, C BC is new C A, B, D CD is new D C No new pair Place A at the top of a page or at the bottom: the ledger stays the same. Even a line crossing in a sketch need not be a station or junction. Only an explicitly named vertex creates a meeting point. This is why an adjacency list is often safer than an artistic map when deciding what the mathematical object is. A precise object and its limits Definition. For a finite simple undirected graph, its edges satisfy the following containment, where the notation on the right means all two-element subsets of V: G = ( V , E ) , E ⊆ { { u , v } : u , v ∈ V , u ≠ v } Representation claim. An adjacency list that names every vertex, lists only vertices in V, contains no self entry, and lists v beside u exactly when it lists u beside v determines one such graph. To justify it, form E by taking the unordered pair {u,v} from each list entry. Symmetry makes the reverse entry the same pair; excluding self entries prevents loops. Every pair in E appears in the list by construction, so moving from pairs to lists and back loses no connection information. This is a complete argument under the finite, simple, undirected convention. Consider instead two different corridors between A and B. The simple graph records only {A,B}, so it cannot distinguish one corridor from two. A multigraph gives those corridors separate edge identities. Likewise, a one-way escalator requires a directed edge. If walking length matters, assign edge weights as additional data. The choice of model follows the question; adding distance to a drawing without declaring weights does not make a shortest-distance claim valid. A graph can still carry an isolated vertex. If room E has no doors, E belongs to V and its adjacency list is empty. Leaving E off the list changes the graph, even though no edge mentions it. This small detail becomes consequential when counting components or asking whether every room is reachable. Build and challenge a model Exercise 1. A club has four members P,Q,R,S. P knows Q and R; Q knows S; R and S know no one else. Treat knowing as mutual. Give V, E, and a complete adjacency list. How many members have no contacts? Hint for exercise 1 Write each unordered pair once, then put each partner in both endpoint lists. A member can have an empty list. Full solution to exercise 1 V={P,Q,R,S} and E={{P,Q},{P,R},{Q,S}}. The lists are P: Q,R; Q: P,S; R: P; S: Q. All four members have at least one contact, so the number with no contacts is zero. The phrase about R and S rules out an RS edge; it does not erase their listed contacts. Exercise 2. A diagram shows two lines crossing without a dot at the crossing. One person reports five vertices, another reports four. Explain the disagreement and give one piece of model data that would settle it. Hint for exercise 2 Ask whether the crossing is meant to be a place where a route may change from one line to the other. Full solution to exercise 2 The geometric crossing alone does not define a vertex. If it is a junction, name it, add it to V, and split each passing edge into edges incident with it; five vertices may then be correct. If the lines merely cross on the page, there are four vertices and no transfer there. An explicit vertex list and edge list, or a statement that the crossing is a junction, settles the model. A graph drawing by itself can be ambiguous. Keep the connections, state the convention A simple graph is its named vertices and unordered edge pairs. The adjacency list is another exact record of those pairs when it is symmetric and includes isolated vertices. A drawing helps the eye, but shape and apparent intersections do not add mathematical connections. Stop here if you can translate between edge sets and adjacency lists and can say which real-world facts this simple model discards. To inspect a route next, use walks, trails, and paths .

title: Every edge has two ends
summary: Double-count edge incidences to prove the degree-sum identity and the even number of odd-degree vertices.
text: Why odd handshake counts cannot stand alone At a small meeting, each handshake involves two people. If everyone remembers how many hands they shook, could exactly one person report an odd number? This is a graph question once each person is a vertex and each handshake between distinct people is an edge. We assume any pair shakes hands at most once, so the graph is simple and undirected. Background capsule. A graph is a finite vertex set V together with a set E of unordered pairs of distinct vertices. The degree of v, written deg(v), is the number of edges touching v. An isolated vertex has degree zero. A finite sum such as Σ deg(v) adds the degrees for every v in V exactly once. We will count the same collection of edge ends in two ways. Neither a picture nor a real party is required for the proof. Use a four-person example: AB, AC, BC, and CD occur. The degree counts are A:2, B:2, C:3, D:1. Their sum is 8, while there are 4 edges. The two odd counts are C and D. Is this ratio and parity pattern forced in every finite simple graph? Count endpoint tokens Worked example. Give one token to each endpoint of an edge. AB deposits one at A and one at B; AC deposits one at A and one at C; BC deposits one at B and one at C; CD deposits one at C and one at D. The token piles are 2,2,3,1, exactly the degrees. Counting by piles gives 2+2+3+1=8. Counting by the four edge deliveries gives 4·2=8. This worked example makes the counting mechanism visible without relying on a diagram. The same eight edge ends counted two ways Edge Endpoints receiving a token AB A and B AC A and C BC B and C CD C and D Try adding an isolated person E. The edge count stays four and the degree sum gains zero. Try adding edge AD instead. Both A and D gain one degree, so the degree sum gains two. The pattern survives both changes for a reason we can state exactly. The handshaking identity Theorem. Every finite simple undirected graph G=(V,E) satisfies ∑ v ∈ V deg ( v ) = 2 | E | . Complete proof. Count ordered incidences (v,e) in which vertex v is an endpoint of edge e. Fixing v first yields deg(v) incidences, and summing over all vertices gives the left side. Fixing e first yields precisely two incidences because a simple edge has two distinct endpoints. There are |E| edges, giving the right side. Both procedures count the identical finite set of incidences, so the totals agree. This proof does not require connectedness. Parity consequence. The number of odd-degree vertices is even. Degrees at even-degree vertices sum to an even number; the complete sum 2|E| is even. A sum of an odd number of odd integers would be odd, because pairing odd summands makes even sums and leaves one odd summand. Therefore the odd-degree summands must occur in an even number. In the four-person example, C and D form such a pair. There is an important failure of the converse. Knowing that the number of odd-degree vertices is even does not determine the edges, or even whether the graph is connected. Two disjoint triangles have six vertices of degree two and no odd-degree vertices, yet there is no route from one triangle to the other. Also, if a problem records a loop, the simple-graph convention is broken. In the usual multigraph convention a loop contributes two to degree, and the handshaking identity still holds; counting a loop as one degree while keeping the same formula would be inconsistent. State the convention before applying it. Audit two degree reports Exercise 1. A simple graph has six vertices with degrees 3,2,2,1,1,1. How many edges does it have? Does the parity consequence object to the list? Hint for exercise 1 Add all six degrees and divide by two. Count how many of the six entries are odd. Full solution to exercise 1 The degree sum is 3+2+2+1+1+1=10, so the handshaking identity gives |E|=10/2=5. Four entries are odd: 3 and the three 1s. Four is even, so parity does not rule the list out. Indeed a graph with edges AB, AC, AD, BE, CF has degrees 3,2,2,1,1,1 when the vertices are A,B,C,D,E,F respectively. Exercise 2. Someone claims a network of five people has degree counts 4,3,2,2,0. Can these be degrees of a simple undirected graph? Explain without trying every edge set. Hint for exercise 2 Use parity first. Then consider what a vertex of degree four means among five vertices. Full solution to exercise 2 The sum is 11, which is odd, while every edge contributes two. Therefore the list is impossible. There is a second contradiction: degree four means that person is adjacent to all other four, including the supposedly isolated degree-zero person. Either reason is sufficient. The degree-sum test is necessary, not a guarantee that every even-sum list can be built. Use parity as a quick necessary test Every edge has two ends, so the total degree is twice the edge count and the odd-degree vertices come in an even number. These are exact results for finite undirected graphs under a consistent degree convention. They can reject an impossible report quickly; they do not reconstruct a graph from degrees alone. The same local counting will help decide when an edge-by-edge route is possible in Euler trails .

title: Three ways through a network
summary: Classify routes by repeated edges and vertices, and show that any connected pair has a simple path.
text: Did you retrace a street or revisit a junction? A courier can pass through a junction twice without using the same street twice. Another courier can cross one street repeatedly. Those routes satisfy different constraints. Graph theory names the distinction so a route requirement can be tested before anybody plans an itinerary. Background capsule. A finite simple undirected graph has named vertices and unordered pairs of distinct vertices called edges. A vertex sequence v₀,v₁,…,vₖ is a walk when each consecutive pair is an edge. Its length is k edges, even when a vertex repeats. We use the common convention that a trail is a walk with no repeated edge, while a path has no repeated vertex. A one-vertex sequence is a length-zero path. In a simple graph, a path also cannot repeat an edge. Use a square A–B–C–D–A with diagonal A–C. The edge set is AB, BC, CD, DA, AC. We can now classify routes from their written sequences, rather than trusting a picture. Check the sequence, one edge at a time Worked example. The sequence A,B,C,A,D uses AB, BC, CA, AD. Every edge exists and occurs once, so this is a trail. Vertex A occurs twice, so it is not a path. Sequence A,B,C,B is a walk, because AB, BC, CB all exist, but BC and CB are the same undirected edge, so it is not a trail. Sequence D,C,B,A has three existing and distinct edges and four distinct vertices, so it is a path and a trail. Route log on the square with diagonal AC Vertex sequence Repeated edge? Repeated vertex? Strongest label A,B,C,A,D No Yes, A Trail A,B,C,B Yes, BC Yes, B Walk D,C,B,A No No Path The word “strongest” here means the most restrictive definition satisfied. A path is still a trail and a walk. If a route starts and ends at the same vertex, some texts call it a closed walk; in a simple graph, a cycle has at least three edges and no other repeated vertices. We will always state the edge and vertex rules rather than rely on an ambiguous everyday meaning of “path.” How the definitions fit together For a path, all vertices in its sequence are distinct, giving the local mathematical condition v i ≠ v j whenever i ≠ j . Read that as “different positions in the list contain different vertices.” The notation vᵢ is the vertex at position i; the starting position is zero. The path condition automatically prevents edge repetition: if the same undirected edge appeared twice, both its endpoint vertices would also appear twice. This proves the inclusion every path is a trail, and every trail is a walk . The square examples show that neither inclusion reverses: a trail can revisit A, and a walk can retrace BC. Another useful exact claim is that whenever a walk connects distinct vertices s and t, there is a path from s to t. Take a connecting walk of the smallest possible length; one exists because walk lengths are nonnegative integers. If it repeated a vertex at positions i and j with i<j, delete the portion from after i through j. The retained sequence still joins consecutive vertices: the vertex before the removed part is the same at both ends. We obtain a shorter s–t walk, contradicting minimality. Thus the shortest chosen walk has no repeated vertex. This is a complete finite argument; it says existence of a path, not that an arbitrary walk is a path. Do not confuse “shortest” here with travel time. Length counts edges. If one street takes 90 minutes and two others take 5 minutes each, the one-edge route has shorter graph length but longer travel time. Weighted shortest paths need edge costs and a different optimization question. A route may also be impossible: if the graph has two disconnected pieces, no walk, trail, or path crosses between them. Classify, then simplify Exercise 1. On edges AB, BC, CA, CD, DE, classify B,A,C,B,C,D,E as a walk, trail, or path. Give the edge sequence and identify any repetition. Hint for exercise 1 Remember that CB and BC are the same edge in an undirected graph. Full solution to exercise 1 The edge sequence is BA, AC, CB, BC, CD, DE. All are listed edges, so the sequence is a walk. CB and BC both name edge BC, used twice; hence it is not a trail. B and C also repeat, so it is not a path. A valid shorter path from B to E is B,C,D,E, using BC, CD, DE. Exercise 2. A student says, “If no street is used twice, no junction can appear twice.” Test the statement on a triangle with vertices P,Q,R and an extra edge P–S. Hint for exercise 2 Travel around the triangle, return to P, then leave for S. List every edge. Full solution to exercise 2 The route P,Q,R,P,S uses PQ, QR, RP, PS exactly once each, so it is a trail. P appears at the start and again before S, so it is not a path. This single counterexample refutes the student's universal claim. A trail forbids repeated edges, while a path forbids repeated vertices. Match the route word to the constraint Write a route as a vertex sequence and check consecutive adjacency first. Then check repeated edge identities for a trail and repeated vertices for a path. Every connected pair admits a path because loops can be removed from a shortest connecting walk. That fact does not solve a visit-every-edge puzzle: such a puzzle asks for a special trail, developed in Euler trails .

title: Can every bridge be crossed once?
summary: Use degree parity and connectedness to decide whether a route can traverse each edge once.
text: Can one walk use every bridge exactly once? An inspector must cross each bridge once. Revisiting an intersection is allowed; reusing a bridge is not. An Euler trail uses every edge once; if it ends where it started, it is an Euler circuit. Isolated vertices have no bridge to inspect. Background capsule. We use a finite simple undirected graph. Degree counts incident edges; a trail repeats none. Two vertices are connected when a walk joins them. An Euler route requires all nonisolated vertices in one connected component, because one continuous walk must reach every edge. Consider bridges AB, BC, CA, and CD: a triangle with a tail. Degrees are A:2, B:2, C:3, D:1. Route D,C,A,B,C uses every edge once and ends at the odd-degree vertices. When is that pattern enough? Pair arrivals with departures Worked example. At an internal vertex of a trail, every arrival along an unused edge is followed by departure along another unused edge. The used incident edges therefore come in pairs. At a start different from the end, the first departure is unpaired. At the final vertex, the last arrival is unpaired. Since an Euler trail uses all edges, these used-edge counts equal the graph degrees. Worked trail D,C,A,B,C Vertex Degree Role in trail D 1 Start: one departure C 3 Arrive from D, depart for A, finally arrive from B A 2 One arrival and one departure B 2 One arrival and one departure The table checks one graph; a construction must establish the general case. Two separate triangles have all degrees even but cannot share one continuous edge-covering route. Connectivity matters. The precise Euler criterion Theorem. Suppose a finite undirected graph has at least one edge and all its nonisolated vertices belong to one connected component. It has an Euler trail exactly when its number of odd-degree vertices is zero or two. It has an Euler circuit exactly when that number is zero. In the two-odd case every Euler trail begins and ends at those odd vertices. Euler trail ⇔ # { v : deg ( v ) odd } ∈ { 0 , 2 } Necessity, proved here. Pair every arrival with a departure at each internal occurrence of a vertex. If start and finish differ, only their first departure and final arrival remain unpaired; hence those two vertices are odd and all others even. If start and finish agree, their unmatched-looking first and last edges pair too, so every degree is even. A route using all edges also forces all nonisolated vertices into one connected component. Sufficiency, construction proof. If all degrees are even, start at a nonisolated vertex and follow unused edges until stuck. A different endpoint is impossible: earlier visits there used arrival–departure pairs, and the current arrival makes used degree odd. Even total degree leaves an unused exit. Thus the trail closes. Its edges remove pairs of incidences, leaving all unused degrees even. If edges remain, connectedness gives an unused edge incident with the closed trail: take one already touching it, or follow a path toward an unused edge and take the first edge leaving the traced vertices. Starting there, build another closed trail from unused edges and splice it into the first. Each splice consumes edges, so finiteness ends the process. With two odd vertices s,t, add one temporary edge between them (a parallel edge if needed), construct the all-even circuit, then remove that edge to open it into an s–t trail. To spell out the splice, write the existing closed trail as a prefix ending at the chosen shared vertex followed by a suffix back to its start. Insert the entire new closed trail between that prefix and suffix. Its last vertex equals its first, so both joins are legal, and it uses only previously unused edges. The combined sequence is therefore a closed trail containing every edge of both old sequences exactly once. If edges remain, repeat; each repetition consumes at least one, so the finite edge set guarantees completion. In the two-odd construction, rotate the resulting circuit to begin with the temporary edge and then delete that first edge. All remaining edges form a trail between the odd endpoints. The temporary parallel edge has its own identity, so removing it leaves any original edge between the same endpoints intact. Zero edges form a degenerate case: depending on whether a length-zero route counts, an edgeless graph may be called Eulerian. We excluded it in the theorem to keep the inspection question meaningful. Degree parity alone remains insufficient when nonisolated components are disconnected. Decide and certify Exercise 1. Edges are AB, BC, CD, DA, AC. Decide whether an Euler trail exists and give one if it does. Can it be a circuit? Hint for exercise 1 Count degrees of A,B,C,D, then begin at an odd vertex. Full solution to exercise 1 A and C each have degree three; B and D each have degree two. The graph is connected, so a trail exists but no circuit does. A,B,C,D,A,C uses AB, BC, CD, DA, AC exactly once and ends at C. A circuit would start and end together, forcing all degrees even, so it is impossible. Exercise 2. A network consists of triangle PQR and separate triangle XYZ. A planner says all degrees are two, so there is an Euler circuit. Diagnose the claim. If the only permitted edit is adding simple edges between the two triangles, find the minimum number of additions that creates an Euler circuit. Hint for exercise 2 The cross edges must connect the components while adding an even number of incidences to every affected vertex. What is the smallest nonempty even-degree simple graph using only cross edges? Full solution to exercise 2 The triangles are disconnected, so no route uses all six original edges. Added cross edges must give every vertex even additional degree. Any nonempty finite graph with all nonisolated degrees even contains a cycle: follow edges without repeating one until a vertex repeats. Cross edges form a simple bipartite graph, whose shortest cycle has four edges. Thus at least four additions are necessary. Add PX, PY, QX, QY: they form a four-cycle of cross edges, giving P,Q,X,Y two extra incidences each. The resulting graph is connected and all-even, so it has an Euler circuit. Four additions suffice and are minimal. Parity and connection work together For a nonempty finite edge set in one connected nonisolated component, zero odd vertices permit a closed edge-once route; two permit an open one; any other number forbids both. The parity proof explains the obstruction, and edge splicing establishes existence. A drawing of two disconnected even-degree cycles is the simplest reminder to check connectivity. For routes minimizing edge count rather than covering every edge, continue to shortest paths .

title: Why a tree has one fewer edge than vertices
summary: Use leaf deletion to prove the tree edge count and the unique-path property.
text: Why does a branching network have one fewer link? A family connection chart that branches without rejoining has a route between any two people and no cycle. It is a tree . If there are seven people in such a connected chart, six links suffice; adding another link creates a cycle. The edge count is useful, but it is the structure that makes the count true. Background capsule. A simple undirected graph has vertices and unordered edges. A path uses distinct vertices; a cycle is a closed route of at least three edges with no repeated vertex except the common start/end. A graph is connected when each pair of vertices has a path. A tree is a finite connected graph without cycles. A leaf is a degree-one vertex. Induction proves a statement for every positive integer by checking a base case and showing the n-case leads to the (n+1)-case; we will show the actual deletion step rather than invoking induction as a slogan. Consider edges AB, BC, BD, DE, DF on vertices A through F. The network is connected, has no cycle, and contains leaves A,C,E,F. It has six vertices and five edges. We can remove F and its one edge DF, leaving another tree. Repeating that action reveals the edge formula. Peel leaves, preserve the routes Worked example. In the example, delete F–D, then E–D, then C–B, then D–B, then A–B. At each stage with at least two vertices, there is a leaf to remove. The remainder stays connected: a path between any two remaining vertices could not have passed through a deleted leaf as an internal stop, because that leaf had only one incident edge. It stays acyclic because deletion cannot create a cycle. Eventually one vertex and no edges remain. One leaf-deletion ledger Stage Vertices left Edges left Original 6 5 After F 5 4 After E 4 3 At one vertex 1 0 Why is a leaf guaranteed? Take a longest path in a finite tree. At one end, any neighbor other than the next vertex on the path would either already lie on the path, making a cycle, or extend the path, contradicting its longest status. Thus that end has degree one. The same is true of the other end when the tree has at least two vertices. Count links and identify the unique route Theorem. Every finite tree with n≥1 vertices has exactly n−1 edges: | E | = | V | − 1 . Complete induction proof. A one-vertex tree has zero edges. Suppose the claim holds for every tree with n vertices. A tree T with n+1 vertices has a leaf by the longest-path argument. Delete that leaf and its incident edge. The remaining graph is connected and acyclic, hence a tree with n vertices. By the induction hypothesis it has n−1 edges. Restoring the one deleted edge gives n edges, which is (n+1)−1. This covers every finite positive size. Another exact tree property is uniqueness of the path between any two vertices. Connectedness gives at least one path. If two distinct simple paths joined u and v, follow them to the first point at which they split and then to a point where they meet again. Those two distinct segments form a cycle, contradicting the tree definition. This proof establishes the path property for trees. Conversely, if there is exactly one path between each pair, the graph is connected by the existence part, and a cycle would give two paths between vertices on it. Thus a finite graph is a tree exactly when every pair of vertices has a unique simple path. Failure case. The equation |E|=|V|−1 by itself does not guarantee a tree. Take a triangle on A,B,C and an isolated vertex D: there are four vertices and three edges, yet the graph is disconnected and has a cycle. The formula becomes a tree test when accompanied by a structural hypothesis, such as connectedness or acyclicity, but proving those strengthened converses requires an argument. A cycle can also appear in a connected graph after one new edge joins two vertices already linked by a path: the new edge plus the old path closes a cycle. Use structure before the formula Exercise 1. A connected acyclic network has nine vertices. How many edges? What happens if one new edge joins two previously nonadjacent vertices? Hint for exercise 1 Apply the tree formula, then use the unique existing path between the endpoints of the new edge. Full solution to exercise 1 It is a tree, so it has 9−1=8 edges. The endpoints of any new edge already have one path between them. The new edge together with that path forms a cycle. The resulting connected graph has nine edges and is no longer a tree. Exercise 2. A report gives V={A,B,C,D,E} and edges AB,BC,CA,DE. It has |E|=|V|−1. Is it a tree? Give two independent reasons. Hint for exercise 2 Inspect the three edges among A,B,C, then try to walk from A to D. Full solution to exercise 2 No. AB,BC,CA make a cycle A–B–C–A, violating acyclicity. Also A and D belong to separate components, violating connectedness. Its four edges and five vertices satisfy the numerical equation, demonstrating that the equation alone does not characterize trees. One link per new vertex A finite tree begins with one vertex and gains each further vertex through one link without creating a cycle. The leaf-deletion proof makes |E|=|V|−1 exact, and the absence of cycles explains why each pair has a unique path. Stop here if you can verify the tree hypotheses before using its count. A tree can also arise while exploring a network layer by layer in breadth-first search .

title: Shortest routes as a proof problem
summary: Trace breadth-first search and justify shortest edge-count distances in an unweighted graph.
text: When is the first discovered route truly shortest? Suppose a contact network records one link for each direct introduction. You want a route from S to T using as few introductions as possible. Breadth-first search, or BFS, explores all vertices one link away before moving to two links away. Its first arrival at T is shortest in number of edges . The phrase “in number of edges” is essential; a costly one-step trip may take longer than a cheap two-step trip. Background capsule. A graph here is finite, simple, and undirected. A path has no repeated vertices. The distance dist(s,v) is the smallest number of edges on an s–v path; unreachable vertices have infinite distance. A queue removes the item added earliest, called first-in-first-out. BFS starts with source s in the queue, marks it distance zero, then repeatedly removes a vertex and discovers each not-yet-discovered neighbor at distance one greater. Each new vertex receives a predecessor, the vertex from which it was first discovered. Use edges SA, SB, AC, BC, BD, CT, DT. Which route from S to T has fewest edges? We can inspect the queue and obtain a certificate of distance, rather than guess from the drawn positions. Trace the queue and layers Worked example. Process neighbors alphabetically. Start queue [S], with dist(S)=0. Remove S and discover A,B at distance one, giving [A,B]. Remove A and discover C at distance two, giving [B,C]. Remove B; C is already discovered, and D is new at distance two, giving [C,D]. Remove C and discover T at distance three, giving [D,T]. The predecessor chain T←C←A←S yields S,A,C,T, three edges. First discoveries in the worked graph Vertex Distance label Predecessor S 0 None A, B 1 S C 2 A D 2 B T 3 C S,B,D,T is another shortest route. BFS need not return a unique path; neighbor order changes predecessor choices, while the distance label remains three. The table is a finite illustration. We need an argument for every unweighted graph. Why layers certify edge-count distance Theorem. In a finite unweighted graph, BFS started at s labels each reachable vertex v with its shortest edge-count distance: label ( v ) = dist ( s , v ) . Proof. Every label assigned by BFS follows a predecessor chain back to s. A vertex labeled k has a chain with k edges, so its true distance is at most k. For the reverse bound, assume an s–v path with r edges. We show by induction along that path that each vertex at path position i gets a label at most i. The start has label zero. When the predecessor at position i is processed, the next vertex is either already discovered with a label no larger than i+1, or it is discovered then with label at most i+1. The queue processes vertices in nondecreasing label order: while vertices of layer i are removed, new vertices enter at layer i+1 behind the remaining layer-i entries. Thus the next vertex cannot have been first discovered earlier with a larger label. At the endpoint, label(v)≤r for every path length r; in particular label(v)≤dist(s,v). Combine both inequalities to obtain equality. Unreachable vertices are never discovered, since every discovery extends a path from s. This proof identifies where FIFO order is used. For the worked graph, no path of one or two edges can reach T because T's neighbors C and D are both at layer two. This is an alternative local certificate of the distance-three answer. A BFS predecessor edge for each discovered non-source vertex forms a tree on the reachable component: every vertex has one parent at a smaller layer, so there is no cycle, and the predecessor chain reaches s. Failure case. Suppose S–T is one edge of weight 100, while S–A and A–T have weights 2 each. BFS says S–T is one edge and therefore shortest by edge count; its cost 100 exceeds the two-edge path's cost 4. The theorem does not apply to weighted total cost. A weighted shortest-path algorithm needs an explicit cost rule and its own proof. Also, changing a queue into a stack can destroy the layer order and the first-discovery guarantee. Compute a layer and test a claim Exercise 1. Starting at P, run BFS on edges PQ, PR, QS, RT, ST, TU, processing neighbors alphabetically. What are the distance labels and one shortest P–U path? Hint for exercise 1 Put Q and R at layer one, then examine their new neighbors in queue order. Full solution to exercise 1 Start P:0. Q and R are discovered at 1. Processing Q discovers S:2; processing R discovers T:2. Processing S finds T already discovered. Processing T discovers U:3. Therefore the labels are P0, Q1, R1, S2, T2, U3. The predecessor chain gives P,R,T,U, a path of three edges. No path of two edges reaches U because its only neighbor is T at layer two. Exercise 2. Edges XY, XZ, ZY have travel times 9, 2, 2 respectively. A friend claims BFS from X gives the fastest route to Y. Evaluate the claim and identify what BFS does prove. Hint for exercise 2 Compare the direct route's edge count and weight with the route through Z. Full solution to exercise 2 BFS discovers Y through direct edge XY at distance one, correctly proving it has the fewest edges. That route takes 9 units. X,Z,Y uses two edges but costs 2+2=4, so it is faster. The friend's claim confuses edge count with weighted travel time; the BFS theorem only covers the former. State what “shortest” measures BFS labels unweighted graph vertices by minimum number of edges from a source. The queue's layer order and the predecessor chain together certify the result. Equal-length paths may coexist, and weights change the optimization problem. If you want to connect this exploration to graph structure, the predecessor links make a tree rooted at the source; trees explains its unique-route property.

title: Scheduling by colouring conflicts
summary: Turn conflicts into colours, prove the greedy degree bound, and distinguish a valid colouring from an optimal one.
text: How many meeting slots avoid conflicts? Several meetings share participants. If two meetings share someone, they cannot run at the same time. Make each meeting a vertex and connect conflicting meetings by an edge. Assigning time slots becomes a vertex colouring : adjacent vertices must receive different colours, with each colour representing one slot. The number of colours is a model result, subject to the assumption that every relevant conflict was entered. Background capsule. We use a finite simple undirected graph. The neighbors of vertex v are vertices adjacent to it, and its degree is the number of those neighbors. The maximum degree Δ(G) is the largest degree in the graph. A proper colouring gives every vertex one colour and gives adjacent vertices different colours. The chromatic number χ(G) is the smallest number of colours in any proper colouring. You can check one proposed colouring edge by edge; proving it uses the minimum possible number requires a lower bound too. For meetings A,B,C,D, suppose AB, AC, BC, and CD are conflicts. The first three form a triangle. At least three slots are needed because each pair among A,B,C conflicts. Can three suffice when D conflicts only with C? Construct a schedule and a lower bound Worked example. Assign A to slot 1, B to slot 2, C to slot 3, and D to slot 1. Every listed conflict has different endpoint slots: AB is 1/2, AC is 1/3, BC is 2/3, and CD is 3/1. Therefore χ(G)≤3. The triangle forces at least three colours, so χ(G)≥3. Together these bounds prove χ(G)=3 for this particular graph. Worked conflict schedule Meeting Conflicts with Slot A B,C 1 B A,C 2 C A,B,D 3 D C 1 Notice that D can share A's slot despite being two steps from A through C. Graph colouring forbids equal colours at edge endpoints, not at all vertices connected by any path. Requiring distinct slots for an entire connected component would solve a much stricter, usually unnecessary problem. Why degree gives a safe upper bound Theorem. Every nonempty finite simple graph admits a proper colouring with at most Δ(G)+1 colours: χ ( G ) ≤ Δ ( G ) + 1 . Complete greedy proof. Fix any order of the vertices. Work through that order, giving the current vertex the lowest numbered colour among 1 through Δ+1 not used by its already coloured neighbors. It has at most deg(v)≤Δ neighbors in total, so at most Δ colours can be forbidden. At least one of Δ+1 remains. Previously coloured adjacent pairs already had different colours, and the new vertex differs from every previously coloured neighbor. Induction over the order proves the final colouring is proper. The argument establishes an upper bound, not that this chosen order minimizes colours. For our four-vertex example Δ=3 at C, so the theorem guarantees at most four colours. The explicit schedule improves that to three, and the triangle proves optimality. A greedy order can use more colours than necessary. In the path with edges AB, BC, CD, a poor order A,D,B,C gives colours 1,1,2,3 under lowest-available greedy colouring: C sees B with colour 2 and D with colour 1. Yet A,C can use colour 1 and B,D colour 2, so χ=2. This concrete failure prevents interpreting the algorithm's output as an optimality certificate. There is another modelling boundary. If a meeting needs two slots, or if slots have different capacities, ordinary vertex colouring does not encode that alone. The theorem assumes one colour per vertex and conflicts represented exactly by edges. It remains useful as a quick guarantee, even when a better tailored schedule uses fewer than Δ+1 slots. Check the bound and the model Exercise 1. Four meetings form a cycle of conflicts AB,BC,CD,DA. Find Δ, give a colouring with as few slots as possible, and justify optimality. Hint for exercise 1 Try giving opposite vertices the same colour. One edge already shows that one colour cannot work. Full solution to exercise 1 Every vertex has degree two, so Δ=2 and the theorem promises at most three colours. Give A,C slot 1 and B,D slot 2. Each edge joins opposite slots, so χ≤2. Since AB is an edge, A and B need distinct colours, hence χ≥2. Therefore χ=2, better than the general upper bound of three. Exercise 2. A planner colours a graph with no edge between X and Y but puts them in different slots, then says the colouring must be invalid because the slots differ. Explain the error. Can two nonadjacent vertices always share a colour in some optimal colouring? Hint for exercise 2 A proper colouring imposes a one-way constraint only on adjacent pairs. For the last question, consider a graph where X and Y each have other neighbors. Full solution to exercise 2 Different slots never violate the proper-colouring condition; only equal slots on an edge violate it. Nonadjacency permits equal colours locally but does not promise that X and Y share one in every optimal schedule. In the path X–A–B–Y, X and Y lie on opposite sides of its unique two-colouring, so any optimal two-colouring gives them different colours despite their nonadjacency. A three-colouring could put them together, but it would not be optimal. This distinguishes a local permission from a global guarantee. A schedule needs both construction and proof Conflicts become edges, slots become colours, and a proper colouring can be checked directly. The greedy argument always supplies at most Δ+1 slots. To claim the minimum, pair an explicit schedule with a lower bound such as a triangle or an edge. Greedy order can waste colours, and missing conflict edges make a schedule claim unreliable. For another use of graph structure in a practical assignment, see matching people to tasks .

title: A formula for flat networks
summary: Derive Euler’s formula for finite connected plane embeddings and identify the hypotheses behind the face count.
text: Why does a flat map satisfy one equation? Draw a connected network on a sheet so that edges meet only at named vertices. The lines divide the sheet into regions, including the unbounded region outside the drawing. Count vertices V, edges E, and faces F. Their counts obey Euler's formula V−E+F=2. It is tempting to count any crossings as faces, but the equation's drawing assumptions are part of the theorem. Background capsule. A finite simple graph has vertices and undirected edges. A plane embedding is a drawing of that graph in the plane in which edge curves have no crossings except at common endpoints. A face is a connected region left after the embedded edges are removed; the outside region counts as one. A tree is connected and has no cycle. We use the proved elementary property that a finite tree has V−1 edges. A spanning tree is a tree using every vertex of a connected graph, obtained by keeping enough edges for connectedness and deleting cycle edges. Start with a square A–B–C–D–A. It has V=4, E=4, F=2: the inside and outside. Add diagonal AC, drawn inside. Now E=5 and F=3, because the old inside face splits into two. Both counts give 2. What makes that pattern hold beyond the square? Start with a spanning tree Worked example. For the square with diagonal, one spanning tree uses AB, BC, CD. It has four vertices, three edges, and only one face, the outside: a tree's arcs do not enclose a region. Add DA along its plane curve. Its endpoints were already connected through A–B–C–D, so the new edge closes a cycle and divides one existing face into two. Counts change from (4,3,1) to (4,4,2). Add AC along the already specified crossing-free curve inside the square; it splits the interior face. Counts become (4,5,3). Euler count ledger for the square with a diagonal Stage V E F V−E+F Spanning tree 4 3 1 2 Add DA 4 4 2 2 Add AC 4 5 3 2 A graph drawn with crossings may still be planar if its edges can be redrawn to remove those crossings. The theorem concerns an actual crossing-free embedding. Counting regions in a drawing with an unmarked crossing creates a different plane graph if that crossing is treated as a vertex, and creates no vertex there if the edges merely pass over one another. Euler's formula with its drawing assumptions Theorem. For a finite connected plane graph, with F counting the outside face, V − E + F = 2 . Proof through edge deletion. In the given embedding, repeatedly delete an edge lying on a cycle until none remains. Such an edge is not a bridge, so deleting it preserves connectedness. In a plane embedding it borders two distinct faces; removing it merges exactly those faces, decreasing both E and F by one. The quantity V−E+F is unchanged. When no cycle remains, the connected graph is a tree. A plane tree has F=1: without a cycle there is no bounded face; equivalently, its complement remains connected. It has E=V−1 by the tree theorem, so V−E+F=V−(V−1)+1=2. Restoring the deleted edges preserves the quantity. The plane-topology step that deletion merges exactly two faces is named here; it follows from the Jordan curve separation associated with an edge on a cycle. We use that standard plane fact rather than claiming to prove the Jordan curve theorem from scratch. This is a graph theorem about an embedding, not just an arithmetic coincidence. A disconnected plane graph with two separate triangles has V=6, E=6, F=3 (two interiors and one shared exterior), giving 3 rather than 2. More generally, a plane graph with c connected components has V−E+F=c+1, but the proof of that extension needs component bookkeeping. The connectedness hypothesis cannot be omitted. One consequence can test planarity: a connected simple planar graph with V≥3 has E≤3V−6. Each face boundary has at least three edge occurrences, and each edge borders two faces, so 3F≤2E. Substitute F=2−V+E into that inequality to obtain E≤3V−6. The face-boundary count needs the simple graph and connectedness assumptions; bridges count twice along their face boundary. This necessary bound does not prove a graph planar when it passes. Count with the outside face Exercise 1. A connected crossing-free drawing has V=8 and E=11. How many faces does it have? If one new edge is drawn inside an existing face between nonadjacent boundary vertices, without crossing any edge, what are the new counts? Hint for exercise 1 Rearrange V−E+F=2. A valid new noncrossing chord splits one face. Full solution to exercise 1 F=2−8+11=5, including the outside. The new edge leaves V=8, raises E to 12, and splits one face, raising F to 6. The check is 8−12+6=2. This answer assumes the chord's interior lies in that face and its endpoints are distinct existing vertices. Exercise 2. Someone draws two disjoint triangles and reports V=6, E=6, F=2 because each triangle has an inside. Explain the face-count error and why the connected theorem still cannot be used. Hint for exercise 2 Count the region outside both triangles. Then inspect connectedness. Full solution to exercise 2 There are three faces: two distinct interiors plus the one unbounded outside region. Thus 6−6+3=3. The graph has two connected components, violating the theorem's hypothesis; the value 3 agrees with the component extension c+1=2+1. Treating the shared outside as absent caused the original F=2 error. The outside counts too For a connected crossing-free plane drawing, deleting cycle edges preserves V−E+F until a spanning tree gives the value two. The proof uses an explicit plane separation fact and does not apply to arbitrary crossing drawings or disconnected graphs as stated. This is a stopping point for a finite, planar result; studying surfaces changes the equation. To revisit why the terminal graph has V−1 edges, use trees .

title: Pairing people and tasks
summary: Flip an augmenting path to enlarge a bipartite matching by one assignment.
text: Can each volunteer take a distinct task? Suppose volunteers can perform only some tasks. Giving each chosen volunteer a different suitable task is a matching problem. A quick first assignment may leave someone unmatched even when a better assignment exists. An alternating route can rearrange earlier choices without dropping anybody already assigned. Background capsule. A bipartite graph has its vertices divided into two sets, here people L and tasks R, with edges only between the sets. An edge means a person can do a task. A matching M is a set of edges with no shared endpoints. An unmatched vertex has no incident edge in M. A path alternates between edges outside M and edges in M when successive edges switch status. An augmenting path begins and ends at unmatched vertices and alternates, starting and ending with edges outside M. In a bipartite graph the endpoints lie on opposite sides if the path is intended to add one assignment. Take volunteers A,B,C and tasks 1,2,3. Allowed pairs are A–1, A–2, B–1, C–2, C–3. If we first assign A–1 and C–2, volunteer B remains unmatched, but the choices can be rearranged. How? Flip an alternating path Worked example. The path B–1–A–2–C–3 uses, in order, an unchosen edge B–1, chosen edge A–1, unchosen A–2, chosen C–2, and unchosen C–3. Its endpoints B and task 3 are unmatched. Remove the chosen path edges A–1 and C–2, then add B–1, A–2, C–3. The new matching assigns all three volunteers to distinct tasks. Two existing assignments changed, but the total count rose from two to three. Assignments before and after the flip Person Before After A 1 2 B Unassigned 1 C 2 3 Every newly used pair was an allowed edge. Every internal vertex on the path trades one matched incident edge for one formerly unmatched edge; the endpoints each gain an incident matched edge. Vertices outside the path keep their previous status. This is a finite local operation, not a claim that every unmatched volunteer can always be accommodated. Why augmentation increases a matching Theorem. If P is an augmenting path for matching M, flipping membership of its edges yields another matching M′ with exactly one more edge: | M ′ | = | M | + 1 . Complete local proof. An augmenting path has an odd number 2k+1 of edges, alternating outside M, inside M, and so on. Therefore it has k edges of M and k+1 edges outside M. Remove its k matched edges and add its k+1 unmatched edges. Each internal path vertex loses one matched incident edge and gains one, while each unmatched endpoint gains one. Because P is a simple path, no vertex is used twice along it, and edges outside P are unaffected. Thus no vertex receives two matching edges and M′ is a matching. Its size changes by −k+(k+1)=1. The worked three-person example has k=2. There is a stronger exact criterion, often called Berge's lemma: a matching is maximum in size exactly when it has no augmenting path. The forward direction is immediate from the theorem. For the reverse direction, compare M with a larger matching N and inspect their symmetric difference, the edges belonging to exactly one of them. Every vertex there has at most one edge from each matching, so components are alternating paths or even cycles. Since N has more edges than M, some component has more N edges and must be an alternating path beginning and ending with N edges. That path augments M. For completeness, a nontrivial component of the symmetric difference has degree at most two at every vertex. If it has a degree-one vertex, start there and follow the unique unused continuation. No branching is possible. The finite walk ends at another degree-one vertex and covers the whole component, because an unvisited attachment would create degree at least three. Thus it is a path, including a single isolated edge as the shortest case. If every vertex has degree two, following edges closes into a cycle; again no other vertex can attach without degree three, so that cycle is the component. Adjacent edges must come from different matchings, making every cycle even with equal contributions from M and N. Paths have either equal contributions or one extra edge of one matching. Since N is larger overall, at least one path has one extra N edge. Both its end edges belong to N, and its endpoints have no incident M edge, so it is an augmenting path for M. This completes the reverse implication. Failure case. If B can do only task 1 and A can also do only task 1, no matching assigns both, no matter how cleverly we rearrange. One task cannot be paired with two people. Hall's theorem gives a complete condition for matching every person, but its general proof lies beyond this lesson. The augmenting path method does not claim every instance has a perfect assignment. Repair or reject an assignment Exercise 1. People P,Q and tasks x,y allow P–x, P–y, Q–x. Current matching is {P–x}. Find an augmenting path and the resulting matching. Hint for exercise 1 Start at unmatched Q and alternate through x and P toward the unmatched task. Full solution to exercise 1 Q–x–P–y is an augmenting path: Q–x is outside the matching, x–P is inside, and P–y is outside. Flip its edges, removing P–x and adding Q–x and P–y. The resulting matching has two edges and assigns both people. It is maximum because only two people and two tasks exist. Exercise 2. People U,V,W can each do only tasks r or s; every person can do both. Can an augmenting path make a matching of size three? Explain the obstruction in the model. Hint for exercise 2 Count the task vertices available as distinct partners. Full solution to exercise 2 No. A matching uses each task at most once, and there are only two task vertices, so any matching has size at most two. For example {U–r,V–s} already reaches that bound; W has no augmenting path ending at an unmatched task because neither task is unmatched. The fact that every person is individually qualified for either task does not create a third distinct task. Reassignment can create room A matching is a set of compatible, nonoverlapping pairs. On an augmenting path, alternating chosen and unchosen edges lets internal vertices keep one partner while both endpoints gain one, so the matching grows by exactly one. Capacity remains a real constraint, and local improvement does not guarantee a full assignment. To test whether two drawings encode the same assignment network, see graph isomorphism .

title: Same network, different drawing
summary: Verify an explicit graph isomorphism and use invariants to reject false matches.
text: Are these two diagrams the same network? A social network can be redrawn with people in new positions and with different labels. If every relationship is preserved, it is the same abstract graph. Deciding this requires more than checking that the pictures look alike; one must exhibit a vertex correspondence that preserves edges and nonedges. Background capsule. A finite simple graph has a vertex set and unordered edge pairs. A function f from V(G) to V(H) assigns each vertex of G one vertex of H. It is a bijection when each vertex of H is used exactly once. The degree of a vertex counts its neighbors. An isomorphism is a bijection that carries adjacency in both directions: u and v are adjacent in G exactly when f(u) and f(v) are adjacent in H. Degrees are therefore preserved, but matching degrees alone may not settle the question. Let G have vertices A,B,C,D and edges AB,BC,CD,DA. Let H have vertices 1,2,3,4 and edges 12,24,43,31. The drawings could place their vertices very differently. Are they the same four-cycle under relabelling? Exhibit the map and check every pair Worked example. Try f(A)=1, f(B)=2, f(C)=4, f(D)=3. Then AB maps to 12, BC to 24, CD to 43, and DA to 31, precisely H's four edges. The map uses all four H vertices once, so it is bijective. Because both graphs have four edges, sending the four distinct edges of G onto H's entire edge set also assures that no nonedge of G can map to an edge of H. We can check the two nonedge pairs directly: AC maps to 14, absent in H; BD maps to 23, also absent. Thus the correspondence is an isomorphism. Pair audit for the four-cycle example Pairs in G Mapped pairs in H Status AB, BC, CD, DA 12, 24, 43, 31 Edges in both AC, BD 14, 23 Nonedges in both Moving vertices in a drawing or bending an edge does not change this pair audit. Adding a vertex at a crossing, however, changes the vertex and edge sets unless it was already a named junction. Isomorphism concerns the abstract pair structure, not the style of the sketch. What a certificate must preserve Definition and test. Graphs G and H are isomorphic when there is a bijection f:V(G)→V(H) satisfying { u , v } ∈ E G ⇔ { f ( u ) , f ( v ) } ∈ E H . Why degrees must match. Fix u in G. The isomorphism maps each neighbor v of u to a neighbor f(v) of f(u), and the inverse bijection maps every neighbor of f(u) back to a neighbor of u. Thus it gives a one-to-one correspondence between the two neighbor sets, so deg(u)=deg(f(u)). Consequently the sorted degree lists of isomorphic graphs agree. This is a complete necessary-condition proof and gives a fast way to reject many proposed isomorphisms. Failure of the converse. A six-cycle C₆ and two disjoint triangles each have six vertices, six edges, and every vertex has degree two. Their degree lists are identical. But C₆ is connected, whereas the two triangles form two components. An isomorphism would map any path in one graph to a path in the other, so it preserves connectedness. Therefore these graphs are not isomorphic. Matching degrees is necessary, not sufficient. The same example shows edge count alone is even weaker. For a larger finite graph, finding f may take systematic search. First compare counts, degree lists, and connected components; if these agree, propose an explicit bijection and verify every unordered pair, or use adjacency tables under a common vertex order. A successful map is a compact certificate. Failure to find one by casual inspection is not proof of nonisomorphism; a differing invariant is one route to a rigorous rejection. Give a map or a disproof Exercise 1. Graph K has edges ab,bc,cd on vertices a,b,c,d. Graph L has edges 13,34,42 on vertices 1,2,3,4. Give an isomorphism and check its edges. Hint for exercise 1 The degree-one endpoints a,d must map to degree-one endpoints in L; trace the path between them. Full solution to exercise 1 L is path 1–3–4–2. Set f(a)=1, f(b)=3, f(c)=4, f(d)=2. Then ab maps to 13, bc to 34, and cd to 42, exactly L's edges. The four images are distinct and cover L's vertices. Both graphs have three edges; this edge correspondence covers all L edges and hence also preserves nonedges. So f is an isomorphism. Exercise 2. Two graphs each have five vertices and four edges. One is the path P₅; the other is a star with one center joined to four leaves. Can they be isomorphic? Hint for exercise 2 Write each sorted degree list. Full solution to exercise 2 The five-vertex path has degree list 2,2,2,1,1. The star has degree list 4,1,1,1,1. An isomorphism preserves each vertex degree, so the differing lists rule one out. Equal vertex and edge counts alone could not settle the question. Relabel by relationships, not appearance An isomorphism is a bijection that preserves both edges and nonedges. An explicit verified map proves sameness; a differing invariant such as degree or connectedness proves difference. Equal degree lists by themselves cannot certify sameness, as the six-cycle and two triangles show. This completes a bounded test for finite graphs; it does not promise a quick visual method for every large instance. For the underlying graph definition, return to graph basics .

title: How surprising is a symbol?
summary: Derive positive-probability self-information and its independent-event addition law.
text: How many bits is a surprise? A fictional printer chooses one glyph from a fixed alphabet on each turn. A circle appears on half the turns; a star appears on one eighth. Which arrival tells you more about what happened? We can answer without pretending that a symbol carries a fixed number of bits in every setting. The answer depends on the probabilities in the specified source. If the printer changes its habits, the same star may carry a different amount of information. Background capsule. A probability lies between zero and one. Independent turns multiply probabilities: an event with chance one half followed by another independent event with chance one half has chance one quarter. A base-two logarithm asks what power of two produces a number: log₂ 8 = 3 and log₂(1/8) = −3. We use bits because doubling the odds against an event adds one to its surprise. Probabilities here are stipulated, not estimated from a sample. A small printer with unequal glyphs Worked example. Suppose circle has probability 1/2, square 1/4, triangle 1/8, and star 1/8. These sum to one, so they define a complete distribution. Circle has surprise −log₂(1/2) = 1 bit. Square has 2 bits. Triangle and star each have 3 bits. A surprising event is one to which the model assigned a small probability; it need not be emotionally surprising to a reader. Surprise under the stipulated printer model Glyph Probability Surprise Circle 1/2 1 bit Square 1/4 2 bits Triangle 1/8 3 bits Star 1/8 3 bits Imagine four independent turns, with circle then circle then star then square. Under this model the sequence probability is (1/2)(1/2)(1/8)(1/4) = 1/128. Its surprise is 7 bits. Adding the individual surprises gives 1 + 1 + 3 + 2 = 7 as well. The agreement is the reason a logarithm is useful for describing successive independent observations. The measure and its boundary For an outcome x assigned positive probability p(x), define its self-information in bits by the following formula. The base matters: base ten gives decimal digits of surprise, and natural logarithms give nats. Numerical values in different units must not be compared without conversion. I ( x ) = − log 2 p ( x ) Exact claim. If X and Y are independent and the observed pair (x,y) has positive probability, then I(x,y) = I(x) + I(y). Independence gives p(x,y) = p(x)p(y). Applying log₂(ab) = log₂ a + log₂ b and changing signs proves the claim. If observations are dependent, use their joint probability: the sum of separate surprises can be wrong. For example, if a second glyph always repeats the first, seeing circle twice has probability 1/2, so the pair has 1 bit of surprise, not 2. A possible outcome with probability zero never occurs under the stipulated model. Formally −log₂ 0 has no finite value; one may describe its limiting surprise as infinite, but cannot insert that infinity into an ordinary observed finite calculation. An outcome with probability one has zero surprise. These edge cases describe the model, and an impossible observed glyph would signal that the model or observation rule needs reconsidering. Calculate and challenge the model Exercise 1. A four-color wheel has probabilities 1/2, 1/4, 1/8, and 1/8. What is the surprise of the sequence second color then fourth color if spins are independent? Give both its probability and bit value. Hint for exercise 1 Multiply the two probabilities, then ask which power of two is their reciprocal. Full solution to exercise 1 The sequence probability is (1/4)(1/8) = 1/32. Since 32 = 2⁵, −log₂(1/32) = 5 bits. Adding the individual values, 2 + 3, checks the result. It would be incorrect to add probabilities or to give 5 bits without the independence assumption. Exercise 2. A machine emits a fair bit and then repeats that bit exactly. A reader says the observation 00 has surprise 2 bits because it contains two zeroes. Test the claim and explain the source of any difference. Hint for exercise 2 List all possible two-character outputs of the machine and their probabilities. Full solution to exercise 2 Only 00 and 11 are possible, each with probability 1/2. Therefore I(00) = −log₂(1/2) = 1 bit.
