The second zero is completely determined after the first, so multiplying two marginal probabilities of 1/2 would assume independence that the machine lacks. Outputs 01 and 10 have probability zero in this model and cannot be given ordinary finite surprise values. What this measure can say Self-information describes how unlikely a specified outcome was under a specified distribution. For the printer, the star carries 3 bits and the circle 1 bit; for a different printer those numbers may change. This is a measure of an event, not yet the average uncertainty before observing a turn. That average is entropy, which weights each event's surprise by its probability. The distinction also matters for coding: a rare symbol can merit a long codeword, while a common one merits a short one. As a stopping check, choose two events whose probabilities multiply to 1/16 and verify that their surprises add to 4 bits. Then ask whether the multiplication is licensed by independence. The MIT information and entropy text develops the logarithmic measure for specified probability models; our printer and exercises are original finite examples. A frequency table from a short run would be evidence about the printer, but it would not automatically equal the stipulated distribution used here.

title: Average surprise in a mystery bag
summary: Compute finite Shannon entropy and prove the binary maximum.
text: How uncertain is the next draw? Before a mystery bag produces its next tile, we know its rules but not its outcome. A bag with equally likely red and blue tiles feels less predictable than one that gives red almost every time. Entropy makes this comparison precise by averaging the surprise of each possible draw. The same formula also tells us the ideal average number of bits associated with the source, although it does not promise a code with exactly that length for each individual symbol. Background capsule. For a finite list of outcomes, an expected value is a probability-weighted average: multiply each value by its chance and add. The surprise of a positive-probability event is −log₂ p bits. We take 0 log₂ 0 to mean its limit, zero, because p log₂ p tends to zero as p approaches zero from above. That convention lets an impossible outcome contribute nothing to an average; it does not give an observed impossible event finite surprise. Three bags with two colors Worked example. Bag A has a fair red-blue split, 1/2 each. Each observed color has 1 bit of surprise, so the average is 1 bit. Bag B has red chance 3/4 and blue chance 1/4. Red contributes (3/4)log₂(4/3), about 0.311 bit, while blue contributes (1/4)·2 = 0.5 bit. Its entropy is about 0.811 bit. Bag C always produces red. Red has zero surprise, and the impossible blue contributes zero to the average, giving entropy zero. Entropy for the stipulated binary bags Bag Red chance Blue chance Entropy in bits A 1/2 1/2 1 B 3/4 1/4 about 0.811 C 1 0 0 The blue tile in B is more surprising than either tile in A, but B's overall uncertainty is lower because blue is uncommon. Do not confuse the largest possible single surprise with its weighted average. If a finite sample from B happens to contain three red and one blue tile, its sample frequencies happen to match the model; a different four-draw sample need not. Average surprise and a binary maximum H ( X ) = − ∑ x p ( x ) log 2 p ( x ) Exact finite claim. For a binary source with probabilities p and 1−p, entropy lies between 0 and 1 bit. Its maximum 1 occurs at p = 1/2; its minimum 0 occurs at p = 0 or 1. For 0 < p < 1, differentiating h(p) gives h′(p) = log₂((1−p)/p). It is positive below 1/2 and negative above 1/2, proving the interior maximum. Continuity with the zero-term convention gives the endpoint values. This derivation uses calculus only for the maximum; the entropy calculation itself requires no calculus. The word bit specifies base two. Changing to natural logarithms multiplies every entropy by ln 2 and changes the unit to nats. For a larger alphabet, the analogous maximum is log₂(number of possible symbols) under a uniform distribution; that general statement needs a separate concavity argument, so the derivative just given proves only the binary case. Entropy measures uncertainty under known probabilities; it does not by itself measure meaning, value, or the accuracy of a guessed probability model. Work with averages Exercise 1. A source emits A with chance 1/2, B with 1/4, and C or D with 1/8 each. Calculate its entropy exactly in bits. Identify the contribution from A separately. Hint for exercise 1 The four surprises are 1, 2, 3, and 3 bits. Multiply by the matching probabilities. Full solution to exercise 1 The weighted terms are (1/2)·1 = 1/2, (1/4)·2 = 1/2, and two copies of (1/8)·3 = 3/8. Their sum is 1/2 + 1/2 + 3/8 + 3/8 = 7/4 bits. A alone contributes 1/2 bit. Averaging the four surprises without weights would give 9/4 bits and answer a different question. Exercise 2. A reader claims that adding a symbol with probability zero must increase entropy because the alphabet is larger. Take a fair binary source and add a third symbol that never occurs. Find the new entropy and assess the claim. Hint for exercise 2 Use the zero-term convention and keep the original two probabilities unchanged. Full solution to exercise 2 The new distribution is (1/2, 1/2, 0). Its entropy is (1/2)·1 + (1/2)·1 + 0 = 1 bit, exactly as before. Merely naming an impossible symbol does not create uncertainty. The three-symbol upper bound log₂ 3 applies when three symbols can carry positive probability, with equality only for a uniform distribution across those three. Stop at a bounded interpretation Entropy is average self-information for a specified random variable. It is zero when its outcome is certain and, for a binary variable, at most one bit. It may be a noninteger even though a single fixed binary codeword has an integer length. The relation between entropy and actual average code length requires coding assumptions, treated in the prefix-code lesson. If a model is learned from a small sample, substituting its frequencies into the entropy formula introduces sampling error and often downward bias; that issue has its own lesson. To test understanding, explain why a 1% event can be very surprising while the binary source containing it has low entropy. The rare event contributes only one hundredth of its large surprise to the average. The MIT information and entropy text supplies the standard finite-source definition and coding context. All bag numbers, table entries, and exercises on this page are original calculations from stipulated distributions.

title: Two clues can repeat information
summary: Derive the finite entropy chain rule with zero-probability rows handled.
text: Do two clues double uncertainty? Imagine two clue cards shown together. Each card may be red or blue. If the second is an exact copy of the first, observing two cards reveals no more than observing one. If their colors are chosen independently, the pair may carry twice as much uncertainty. Joint entropy records uncertainty about the complete pair, while conditional entropy records what remains unknown about one card after the other is revealed. Background capsule. A joint probability p(x,y) is the chance of one particular pair. Summing a row gives the marginal chance p(x). If p(x) > 0, the conditional chance p(y|x) = p(x,y)/p(x). Entropy is the probability-weighted average of −log₂ probability, in bits. Conditional entropy H(Y|X) averages the entropy of Y separately within each positive-probability X group, weighted by the chance of that group. No conditional distribution is required for an X value that never occurs. Two complete pair tables Worked example. In a copying game, the pair RR has probability 1/2 and BB has probability 1/2; RB and BR are impossible. Each single card is fair, so H(X) = H(Y) = 1 bit. The pair has only two equally likely outcomes, hence H(X,Y) = 1 bit. Once X is known, Y is certain: H(Y|X) = 0. Now consider independent fair cards. All four pairs have probability 1/4, so the pair has entropy 2 bits. Knowing the first card leaves one full bit about the second. Pair probabilities in the copying and independent games Pair Copying Independent RR 1/2 1/4 RB 0 1/4 BR 0 1/4 BB 1/2 1/4 A less extreme game makes X fair and copies it with probability 3/4, switching with probability 1/4. Its table is RR = BB = 3/8 and RB = BR = 1/8. Each marginal is still fair. Given either value of X, the conditional distribution of Y is (3/4, 1/4), so H(Y|X) = h₂(1/4), about 0.811 bit. The joint uncertainty is about 1.811 bits. The table sums to one and makes the calculation reproducible without a diagram. Why the chain rule holds H ( X , Y ) = H ( X ) + H ( Y | X ) Exact claim and derivation. For any finite joint distribution, the identity holds with the convention that zero-probability pairs contribute zero. For every positive pair, p(x,y) = p(x)p(y|x), so −log₂ p(x,y) = −log₂ p(x) − log₂ p(y|x). Weight by p(x,y) and sum over positive pairs. The first sum collapses to H(X) because the joint row sums to p(x). The second becomes the weighted conditional entropy. A row with p(x) = 0 contributes nothing and needs no conditional division. Interchanging X and Y gives H(X,Y) = H(Y) + H(X|Y). Conditional entropy is nonnegative, since each positive-probability surprise is nonnegative. Thus H(X,Y) ≥ H(X), but equality can hold when Y is determined by X. Separately adding H(X)+H(Y) equals joint entropy only when the variables are independent. For the copying game, that naive sum is 2 bits while the actual joint entropy is 1. The algebra proves the finite identity; it does not decide whether real clues follow the assumed table. Use the table before the formula Exercise 1. X is a fair bit. Y equals X with probability 3/4 and flips it with probability 1/4, independently of X. Write the four joint probabilities, then calculate H(X), H(Y|X), and H(X,Y). Hint for exercise 1 Split each half-probability X row into a 3/4 copy branch and a 1/4 flip branch. Full solution to exercise 1 RR and BB each have probability (1/2)(3/4) = 3/8; RB and BR each have (1/2)(1/4) = 1/8. H(X) = 1 bit. Each X row gives Y probabilities 3/4 and 1/4, hence H(Y|X) = h₂(1/4) ≈ 0.811 bit. The chain rule gives H(X,Y) ≈ 1.811 bits. Directly summing two 3/8 terms and two 1/8 terms confirms it. Exercise 2. Let X always equal 0, and let Y be fair. Someone attempts to compute p(Y=1|X=1). Is this conditional probability needed for H(Y|X)? Find both H(Y|X) and H(X,Y). Hint for exercise 2 Inspect the probability of the proposed conditioning event before dividing. Full solution to exercise 2 P(X=1) = 0, so p(Y=1|X=1) is undefined under the ordinary ratio definition. The X=1 row has zero weight and is unnecessary. Given X=0, Y is fair, so H(Y|X) = 1 bit. H(X) = 0 because X is certain, and the chain rule gives H(X,Y) = 0 + 1 = 1 bit. Know what the extra clue adds Joint entropy counts uncertainty in a pair. The chain rule assigns the first variable its ordinary entropy and the second only its uncertainty after the first is known. In the copying game, the second card contributes zero; in the independent game, it contributes a full bit. This distinction leads to mutual information, the amount of uncertainty removed by seeing another variable. It also matters for compression of repeated or correlated symbols, where treating the pair as two unrelated letters may waste code length. As a stopping check, ask whether the phrase “two bits from two binary cards” specifies enough to calculate joint entropy. It does not: a joint table or an independence assumption is needed. The MIT information and entropy text supports the entropy and conditional-information identities. Our card games provide finite tables that show exactly where the hypotheses enter.

title: How much does one clue reveal?
summary: Compute information from a joint law and contrast it with linear correlation.
text: How useful is a noisy clue? A hidden card is red or blue, equally likely. A lamp tries to indicate its color but sometimes gives the wrong signal. Seeing the lamp usually helps, yet it does not remove all uncertainty. Mutual information measures how much uncertainty about the hidden card is removed on average by observing the lamp. It is a property of their joint probability law, not of a single favorable prediction or a causal effect of the lamp on the card. Background capsule. Entropy H(X) is average surprise in bits. Conditional entropy H(X|Y) averages the remaining surprise in X after Y is known, using the probability of each Y outcome as its weight. For positive probabilities, p(x|y)=p(x,y)/p(y). A joint table must sum to one. If a conditioning value has probability zero, its conditional fraction is undefined and its row contributes no weight to conditional entropy. A lamp that is right three quarters of the time Worked example. Let X be the fair hidden color and Y the displayed lamp color. Conditional on either hidden color, the lamp displays the correct color with probability 3/4 and the wrong color with probability 1/4. The four joint chances are 3/8 for red-red, 1/8 for red-blue, 1/8 for blue-red, and 3/8 for blue-blue. The lamp itself is fair: its red and blue column sums are each 1/2. Given a red lamp, the hidden card is red with probability (3/8)/(1/2)=3/4; a blue lamp gives the mirror calculation. Hidden card and lamp joint probabilities Hidden X Lamp red Lamp blue Red 3/8 1/8 Blue 1/8 3/8 Before the lamp, H(X)=1 bit. After the lamp, each conditional distribution is (3/4,1/4), whose entropy is about 0.811 bit. Consequently the reduction is 1−0.811≈0.189 bit per use. That small number does not mean the lamp has only a 19% chance of being correct. Its accuracy is 75%; information and classification accuracy answer different questions. The amount revealed on average I ( X ; Y ) = H ( X ) − H ( X | Y ) Exact finite identity. The chain rule gives H(X,Y)=H(Y)+H(X|Y)=H(X)+H(Y|X). Rearranging shows I(X;Y)=H(X)+H(Y)−H(X,Y)=H(Y)−H(Y|X), so the measure is symmetric even though one conditional description may be easier to calculate. Expanding entropy also gives I(X;Y)=Σ p(x,y)log₂[p(x,y)/(p(x)p(y))] over positive joint cells. That is a KL divergence between the joint law and the product of its marginals. Since finite KL divergence is nonnegative, mutual information is nonnegative and equals zero exactly when the variables are independent. The KL lesson proves the needed inequality; this paragraph identifies the boundary of our derivation. Mutual information can be positive when ordinary numerical correlation is zero. For numerical variables, covariance is Cov(X,Y)=E[XY]−E[X]E[Y]; correlation divides that covariance by the product of their positive standard deviations. Let X be uniform on −1,0,1 and set Y=X². Y is determined by X, so I(X;Y)=H(Y)>0. Yet E[X]=0 and E[XY]=E[X³]=0, giving covariance and correlation zero. Both standard deviations are positive here. Correlation measures a particular linear association; mutual information detects this nonlinear dependence. Conversely, a high measured value from a tiny empirical table may be sampling bias rather than strong population dependence. The exact paired-sample investigation derives the two-observation estimator law and shows bias in either direction. Two kinds of dependence Exercise 1. A fair bit X is copied perfectly to Y. Compute H(X), H(X|Y), and I(X;Y). Repeat when Y is an independent fair bit. Hint for exercise 1 Ask whether Y fixes X in each case. If it does not, calculate the remaining fair-bit entropy. Full solution to exercise 1 In perfect copying, H(X)=1 bit and X is known once Y is observed, so H(X|Y)=0 and I(X;Y)=1 bit. With independent fair bits, seeing Y leaves X fair: H(X|Y)=1 bit and I(X;Y)=0. Both cases have H(X)=H(Y)=1; marginals alone cannot distinguish them. Exercise 2. X is uniform on −1,0,1 and Y=X². Find the distribution and entropy of Y, then explain why a zero covariance would not imply zero mutual information here. Hint for exercise 2 Y is zero once and one twice among the three equally likely X values. Full solution to exercise 2 P(Y=0)=1/3 and P(Y=1)=2/3. Thus H(Y)=−(1/3)log₂(1/3)−(2/3)log₂(2/3)≈0.918 bit. Because Y is determined by X, H(Y|X)=0, so I(X;Y)=H(Y)≈0.918 bit. Meanwhile E[X]=0 and E[XY]=E[X³]=0, so covariance is zero. The dependence is real and nonlinear. What the clue does and does not prove Mutual information is average reduction in uncertainty under a specified joint law. In the lamp model it is about 0.189 bit, while the lamp's correct-output probability is 3/4. It does not name a causal direction: the same joint table fits descriptions in which the card causes the lamp or both respond to a shared mechanism. Nor can a small sample table reveal a population information value exactly. The next coding lessons use known source weights; the estimation lesson returns to finite samples. Check the stopping condition by computing the marginal probabilities before any conditional entropy. If a table fails to normalize, all later information calculations are suspect. The MIT information and entropy text supports conditional information and the entropy identities. The lamp and square examples are original finite illustrations.

title: Make a code no symbol can confuse
summary: Test a binary prefix code and its Kraft length condition.
text: Can a stream be decoded without separators? A tiny message uses four symbols, but we send only zeroes and ones. If A is coded as 0 and B as 01, the start of 01 looks like A; a reader cannot decide immediately whether the first 0 is a complete symbol. A prefix-free code avoids that ambiguity by ensuring that no complete codeword begins any other codeword. It provides a clean way to concatenate symbols and decode them one at a time. Background capsule. A binary tree branches left on 0 and right on 1. A codeword is the path from the root to a symbol's leaf; its length ℓ is its number of bits. For source weights p(x), the average length is L=Σp(x)ℓ(x). Entropy H(X) is average surprise in bits. A code's length is measured in actual bits per symbol, while entropy is an ideal lower-bound quantity under the coding assumptions. A four-glyph note Worked example. Use weights A:1/2, B:1/4, C:1/8, D:1/8. Assign A→0, B→10, C→110, D→111. The word 010110 encodes A, B, C: read 0 as A, then 10 as B, then 110 as C. Every codeword ends at a leaf, so the parser knows where to stop. The average length is (1/2)·1+(1/4)·2+(1/8)·3+(1/8)·3=7/4 bits per symbol. The entropy is also 7/4 bits because the probabilities are powers of two matching the lengths. A prefix code and its source weights Symbol Weight Codeword Length A 1/2 0 1 B 1/4 10 2 C 1/8 110 3 D 1/8 111 3 The lengths have Kraft sum 2⁻¹+2⁻²+2⁻³+2⁻³=1. By contrast, the proposed lengths (1,1,2) for three distinct symbols have sum 1/2+1/2+1/4=5/4. No binary prefix tree can realize those lengths: two one-bit codewords already occupy both root branches, leaving no branch for a third symbol. Tree space and the Kraft condition ∑ x 2 − ℓ ( x ) ≤ 1 Exact claim. Every finite binary prefix-free code with nonempty finite codewords satisfies this inequality. Choose a depth D at least as large as every codeword length. A leaf at depth ℓ occupies 2^(D−ℓ) of the 2^D possible depth-D bit strings extending it. Prefix-free leaves occupy disjoint groups, so their counts sum to at most 2^D. Divide by 2^D to obtain the displayed inequality. The converse also holds for positive integer lengths: if their Kraft sum is at most one, some binary prefix code has those lengths. The tree-packing construction for the converse is beyond the counting proof here; the inequality alone does not make an arbitrary assignment of bit strings prefix-free. A prefix-free code has unique immediate decoding because no leaf lies above another leaf; reading reaches exactly one symbol at a leaf, then restarts. A code can be uniquely decodable without being prefix-free, so do not reverse that claim. For a fixed distribution and a binary prefix code, the average length obeys H(X)≤L; this coding lower bound needs a separate proof. Zero-probability symbols may be omitted only if the protocol explicitly excludes them. If the protocol must encode them, they still need distinct codewords even though they add zero to the weighted average. Test a code and a length claim Exercise 1. Consider A→00, B→01, C→1 with source weights 1/4,1/4,1/2. Is the code prefix-free? Decode 10100 and find its expected length and Kraft sum. Hint for exercise 1 Read from left to right until you hit one of the three complete words, then restart. Full solution to exercise 1 Neither 00 nor 01 begins another listed word, and 1 begins neither of them, so the set is prefix-free. Parse 1|01|00 to obtain CBA. Lengths are 2,2,1, so L=(1/4)2+(1/4)2+(1/2)1=3/2 bits per symbol. Kraft sum is 1/4+1/4+1/2=1. The string could not be parsed as 10|100 because neither fragment is a codeword. Exercise 2. A designer requests lengths 1,2,2,2 for four binary symbols. Can a prefix-free code have exactly those lengths? Calculate the obstruction and explain it as tree occupancy. Hint for exercise 2 Compute 2⁻¹+3·2⁻² before trying to draw a tree. Full solution to exercise 2 The Kraft sum is 1/2+3/4=5/4>1, so no such binary prefix-free code exists. A one-bit leaf uses half of all sufficiently long extensions. Three depth-two leaves would use three quarters more. Their disjoint occupied fractions would exceed the entire set of bit strings, which is impossible. What a valid code guarantees Prefix freedom guarantees that a concatenated stream can be parsed from left to right without separators. The Kraft sum checks whether a proposed collection of lengths can fit into a binary tree; the counting argument proves necessity for an existing code. It does not say that a valid tree is best for particular source probabilities. The next lesson chooses lengths by a greedy algorithm and states precisely when that algorithm is optimal. Our four-glyph example reaches entropy because its dyadic weights fit code lengths exactly, which is a special convenience. Before moving on, distinguish three questions: Are the bit strings prefix-free? Are proposed lengths realizable by some prefix code? Is a realizable code optimal for the stated weights? The MIT discrete applied mathematics Huffman notes support the tree and coding results. The glyph code and parsing exercises here are original.

title: Why common symbols get short codes
summary: Build a prefix code, then compare optimal letter and pair codes under an explicit source model.
text: Which symbols should receive short codewords? Huffman's algorithm repeatedly joins the two least likely symbols or subtrees, building a binary tree upward. For a known finite distribution it minimizes mean binary-prefix-code length per chosen unit, a letter or predeclared block. It does not minimize every message's length or construction time. Background capsule. In a binary prefix tree, each source symbol occupies a leaf, and its codeword length is the leaf depth. The average length is L=Σp(x)ℓ(x). Entropy is H(X)=−Σp(x)log₂p(x), with zero terms interpreted by continuity. Weights may be unnormalized positive counts because scaling every weight by the same factor leaves merge order unchanged; divide by their total for a bit-per-symbol average. Merge a four-symbol source Worked example. Let A, B, C, D have probabilities 1/2, 1/4, 1/8, 1/8. First join C and D to form a node of weight 1/4. Now the available weights are A:1/2, B:1/4, CD:1/4. Join B and CD to form weight 1/2. Finally join A with BCD. Assign left branch 0 and right branch 1 at each merge. One resulting code is A→0, B→10, C→110, D→111. Its average length is 7/4 bits, equal to the entropy of this dyadic distribution. One Huffman merge sequence Step Merged weights New weight 1 1/8 and 1/8 1/4 2 1/4 and 1/4 1/2 3 1/2 and 1/2 1 For a fair three-symbol source, each symbol has probability 1/3. Merge two 1/3 weights, then join 2/3 with the remaining 1/3. The depths are 1,2,2, giving L=5/3 bits. Entropy is log₂3≈1.585 bits, so there is a gap of about 0.082 bit. Individual prefix codewords cannot have fractional lengths; equality with entropy is not promised for a single-symbol binary code. Change the unit before comparing the rate Now use only letters A and B, independently drawn with the same probabilities on each draw: P (A)=3/4 and P (B)=1/4. This is an iid letter source. A one-letter binary prefix dictionary needs two nonempty words, so each has length at least one. A→0, B→1 attains one bit per letter and is optimal for that coding unit. Instead agree in advance to split letters into nonoverlapping pairs from a known start. A pair is now one source unit. The decoder knows the dictionary, the block alignment and the exact encoded bitstream boundary. Prefix-free codewords identify successive pairs without separators. This comparison concerns complete two-letter blocks; an odd final letter and any framing or codebook metadata need a separate agreed protocol and cost calculation. Independence gives pair probabilities P (AA)=9/16, P (AB)=3/16, P (BA)=3/16 and P (BB)=1/16. The optimization now has four leaves, rather than two. One resulting dictionary is AA→0, AB→10, BA→110, BB→111. Its expected length is (9×1+3×2+3×3+1×3)/16=27/16 bits per pair . Divide by two letters per pair to get 27/32 bits per original letter . Predict first. Does pairing help iid fair letters? Can expected savings coexist with a longer BB codeword? Change the stipulated probabilities and inspect the exhaustive comparison; these controls do not estimate an unknown source. The greedy claim and its limits H ( X ) ≤ L Huffman < H ( X ) + 1 Exact setting. The algorithm is optimal among binary prefix codes for a finite alphabet with strictly positive known probabilities, one codeword per symbol, and average weighted length as objective. A one-symbol source is a convention-sensitive edge case: with an empty codeword its optimal length and entropy are zero; if the protocol requires a nonempty word, the displayed strict upper bound fails at H=0. For at least two positive symbols, the standard bound applies. Zero-weight symbols can be removed from the source alphabet when the protocol excludes them. Why choose the two smallest weights? In a full optimal tree, deepest leaves can be taken as siblings. Swapping a deeper high-weight leaf with a shallower low-weight leaf cannot increase weighted length, so the two lightest symbols can occupy a deepest sibling pair in some optimum. Contract that pair into one pseudo-symbol of combined weight. Every original leaf below it gains one bit, adding exactly the combined weight to total weighted length. An optimal reduced tree therefore expands to an optimal original tree, and repeating the argument gives the greedy recursion. This is the exchange and contraction proof sketch; it assumes the prefix-tree objective above, not arbitrary uniquely decodable schemes with external constraints. The entropy bound follows from the general prefix lower bound and a comparison with Shannon lengths ⌈−log₂p(x)⌉, whose Kraft sum is at most one and whose mean is strictly below H+1 when all probabilities are positive and there are at least two symbols. Huffman does no worse than those lengths. The proof says nothing about compressing an unknown source from a handful of observed symbols without model uncertainty. An exhaustive proof for four positive-weight leaves For the pair weights 9,3,3,1, Huffman merges 1+3=4, then 3+4=7, then 7+9=16. The sum of the merged weights is 27: each merge adds one bit of depth to exactly its descendant leaves. Dividing by total weight 16 gives the expected 27/16 bits per pair. We can independently prove optimality here without relying on the greedy theorem. Any prefix tree with a node having only one child can suppress that edge and shorten every affected positive-weight word. An optimal tree can therefore be full: each internal node has two children. A full four-leaf tree splits at the root into either two leaves on each side, giving depths (2,2,2,2), or one leaf and three leaves, giving depths (1,2,3,3) in some order. These are the only depth patterns. For a fixed pattern, larger weights belong at smaller depths. If a larger weight lies deeper than a smaller one, exchanging them changes cost by the negative of their weight difference times their depth difference. Thus an exchange cannot worsen cost when putting the larger weight shallower. The balanced pattern costs 2 bits per pair. The best comb pattern costs (9×1+3×2+3×3+1×3)/16=27/16<2. This proves the proposed pair code is optimal. The exact instrument also checks every ordered shape and label assignment: two shapes for a one-leaf/three-leaf split on the left, two with that split reversed, and one balanced shape, for five ordered shapes. Each has 24 permutations of the four distinct pair labels, making 120 cases. Some cases share the same length vector; equal probabilities do not merge the distinct labels AB and BA. The finite search corroborates the classification proof. It does not replace a general proof for arbitrarily many symbols. The existing single-symbol code-tree lab explores the merging algorithm with its own alphabet. Setting its four weights to 9,3,3,1 gives the same weighted-length problem as this pair example, with different source labels. Dividing by two is justified here because a leaf represents two original letters; it is not a universal conversion for a four-leaf tree. Expected length and entropy are different quantities The original one-letter optimum of 1 bit remains correct for its two-leaf problem. The pair code improves the per-letter rate because it solves a different problem. At the worked source, letter entropy is about .811278 bits and the pair rate is .84375, so the code still lies above its entropy lower bound. The mean saving relative to the one-letter code is 1−27/32=5/32 bit per letter. BB takes three bits instead of two: expected savings do not promise savings for every realized message. Huffman's optimality uses the actual distribution of its chosen units; those units need not be independent for the one-unit weighted-length comparison. Here iid letters justify multiplying their probabilities to obtain the pair distribution. If letters are dependent, their marginals alone do not determine that distribution. Question 4 keeps the same marginals while changing the answer. Optional: what increasing block size guarantees under iid letters For a fixed block length b , let L b be the optimal expected prefix length per block. Assume a finite letter alphabet with at least two positive probabilities, iid letters, a known dictionary and fixed block framing. Each block probability is a product of its letter probabilities. Its negative logarithm is the sum of the letters' negative logarithms. Taking expectations gives H (block)= bH (letter). Apply the standard prefix entropy bound to the block alphabet, then divide by b : H ( X ) ≤ L b b < H ( X ) + 1 b The strict upper inequality follows from the Shannon-length comparison above; the alphabet assumptions exclude the convention-sensitive single-positive-symbol case. Thus optimal expected rates can approach letter entropy as block size grows. This does not say every successive block size must improve the rate or that a particular finite message gets shorter. For dependent letters, the general block bound uses their actual joint block entropy; the identity H (block)= bH (letter) need not hold. Allow about 15 additional minutes for this optional argument. Build and assess a tree Exercise 1. For weights 2,3,5,10, build a Huffman merge sequence and give one set of codeword lengths. Calculate average length using probabilities obtained by dividing by 20. Hint for exercise 1 Join 2 and 3 first. Track how many joins each original weight passes through. Full solution to exercise 1 Join 2+3=5, then join that 5 with the original 5 to make 10, then join the two 10s. The weight-10 symbol has depth 1, original weight 5 has depth 2, and weights 2 and 3 have depth 3. Weighted length is (10·1+5·2+3·3+2·3)/20=35/20=1.75 bits per symbol. One code is 10→0, 5→10, 3→110, 2→111. Exercise 2. Three symbols are equally likely. Could a binary prefix code give every symbol a one-bit word? What does Huffman's expected length show about entropy as an achieved code length? Hint for exercise 2 A binary root has only two one-bit branches. Full solution to exercise 2 Three one-bit words cannot fit: their Kraft sum would be 3/2>1. Huffman uses lengths 1,2,2 and has average 5/3 bits. Entropy is log₂3≈1.585 bits, which is lower but not the achieved one-symbol mean. Longer block codes can approach entropy per symbol under the iid and framing assumptions above; that is a different coding setup. Change the distribution, dependence and protocol 3. Fresh iid source. Let independent letters have probabilities P (A)=4/5 and P (B)=1/5. Derive the pair weights, an optimal prefix dictionary and the expected rate per pair and per original letter. Compare the two possible depth patterns. Hint for exercise 3 The integer pair weights sum to 25. Merge the smallest two weights, or assign the largest weights to the shallowest depths of a comb. Full solution to exercise 3 The weights for AA,AB,BA,BB are 16,4,4,1 over 25. Merges are 1+4=5,4+5=9,16+9=25. The comb dictionary 0,10,110,111 has mean (16+8+12+3)/25=39/25 bits per pair, or 39/50=.78 bits per letter. A balanced tree costs 2 bits per pair, so the comb is optimal by the four-leaf classification. The one-letter optimum is still 1 bit per letter. 4. Same marginals, dependent letters. A known source independently chooses each aligned block as AA with probability 3/4 or BB with probability 1/4. Every letter position still has marginal probabilities 3/4 and 1/4. What is the optimal pair dictionary and per-letter rate? Does it violate the entropy lower bound? Explain exactly which strings this dictionary can represent. Hint for exercise 4 The actual block alphabet contains two positive-probability symbols, not four. Compute the block entropy before dividing by two. Full solution to exercise 4 The known block law is (3/4,0,0,1/4), not the iid product law (9,3,3,1)/16. The dictionary AA→0, BB→1 is prefix-free and optimal, at 1 bit per pair or 1/2 bit per original letter. Block entropy is H (3/4,1/4)≈.811278 bits per pair, so the lower bound per letter is about .405639, below the achieved .5. The iid identity that would give twice the one-letter entropy is inapplicable. With known block alignment, concatenations of these codewords represent sequences of AA and BB blocks. The dictionary has no codeword for AB or BA. Their zero probabilities justify excluding them only because this source model is known; it is not a lossless dictionary for arbitrary A/B strings. An encoder that must accept out-of-model blocks needs an agreed fallback or a different dictionary, whose costs must be included. 5. Finite-file audit. Return to the iid 3/4 source. The receiver already knows the dictionary and that the source file contains three letters. Agree to code the first pair with the worked pair dictionary, then code the last letter by A→0, B→1. Find the expected payload length. Which costs and assumptions prevent identifying 27/32 with the exact rate of every finite file? Hint for exercise 5 There is one complete pair and one leftover letter. The receiver's known original letter count identifies when to switch dictionaries. Full solution to exercise 5 The expected payload is 27/16+1=43/16 bits for three letters, or 43/48 bits per letter. A realized payload still has an integer length and may be longer or shorter than its mean. Knowing the original count and both dictionaries makes the final-letter switch unambiguous. If those facts must be transmitted, their framing, length and codebook overhead also count. Alternatively padding requires an agreed way to recover the original length and a new calculation for the padded final block. The ideal 27/32 rate describes complete iid pairs, not all finite-file protocols or every individual message. Keep the optimization target visible Huffman merging is a precise algorithm for minimizing weighted leaf depth among finite binary prefix trees with known positive weights. Ties may yield different trees with the same optimum expected length. The bounds compare that optimum with entropy, and the fair three-symbol example shows why a strict gap can remain. A source with correlations across symbols may benefit from coding blocks or a different model; a code optimized for the wrong weights need not be optimal for the actual source. To check mastery, build a tree and then compute the weighted mean from its leaf depths rather than just reporting the merge list. The MIT discrete applied mathematics Huffman notes support the greedy method and the source-coding bounds. Our numeric weights, codewords, and exercises are original finite examples.

title: A message through a fickle switch
summary: Compute the error and remaining uncertainty of a stipulated binary symmetric channel.
text: What survives a fickle bit switch? Suppose a device accepts a zero or one, then flips it with a fixed chance ε. A displayed bit is evidence about the input, but the amount of evidence depends on both the device and the distribution of inputs. A channel transition rule alone does not specify how uncertain the input was. This lesson computes error and remaining uncertainty for the binary symmetric channel, a small mathematical model rather than a design for a practical communication system. Background capsule. Conditional probability P(Y=y|X=x) describes output Y once input X is fixed. A joint probability is input chance times transition chance. Entropy H(X) is average surprise in bits, and H(X|Y) measures uncertainty in X after the output is seen. The binary entropy function h₂(t)=−t log₂t−(1−t)log₂(1−t), with zero terms defined by continuity, is the entropy of a Bernoulli outcome. We assume a single channel use unless explicitly discussing repeated uses. Follow a fair input through the switch Worked example. Set ε=1/4, so the output agrees with the input with probability 3/4. Let the input be fair: P(X=0)=P(X=1)=1/2. The joint table has 00 and 11 each at 3/8, and 01 and 10 each at 1/8. The output is also fair because each output column totals 1/2. Seeing Y=0, the posterior input distribution is X=0 with 3/4 and X=1 with 1/4. The same uncertainty holds after Y=1, with the labels reversed. Fair input and a channel with flip probability one quarter Input Output 0 Output 1 0 3/8 1/8 1 1/8 3/8 The chance that output differs from input is 1/8+1/8=1/4. H(X)=1 bit and H(X|Y)=h₂(1/4)≈0.811 bit, so the output reveals about 0.189 bit about the input on average. If the input were always zero, the channel would still flip it on one quarter of uses, but H(X)=0 and there would be no uncertainty about the input to remove. The transition rule and the input law play different roles. The exact error statement P ( Y ≠ X ) = ε Exact hypotheses. For each possible input bit x, the binary symmetric channel has P(Y≠x|X=x)=ε and P(Y=x|X=x)=1−ε, with 0≤ε≤1. Then total probability gives P(Y≠X)=ΣₓP(X=x)ε=ε, for any input distribution. With a fair input specifically, symmetry makes Y fair and gives H(X|Y)=h₂(ε) and I(X;Y)=1−h₂(ε). These latter identities are not asserted for arbitrary input weights. At ε=1/2, output is independent of input and mutual information is zero. At ε=1, output always flips, yet perfectly reveals input after reversing the bit; a large raw mismatch rate does not necessarily mean little information. The displayed error rate assumes that the receiver guesses input by copying output. For ε>1/2 a receiver that knows the channel should invert the output, so the best single-bit decision error is min(ε,1−ε) for a fair input. The algebra above describes one channel use and exact stipulated probabilities. Independence of errors across multiple uses has not been assumed or proved, and no coding theorem or capacity claim follows from this table alone. Keep the input law in view Exercise 1. The switch flips with ε=1/8 and the input is fair. Find P(Y≠X), H(X|Y), and I(X;Y). Exact expressions using h₂ are enough; explain each quantity. Hint for exercise 1 Symmetry makes the output fair and the posterior error fraction one eighth. Full solution to exercise 1 P(Y≠X)=1/8 by the channel rule. H(X|Y)=h₂(1/8)=−(1/8)log₂(1/8)−(7/8)log₂(7/8)≈0.544 bit. Because H(X)=1 bit, I(X;Y)=1−h₂(1/8)≈0.456 bit. The first number is an error probability, while the latter two are average uncertainties in bits. Exercise 2. A channel always flips, ε=1. The input is fair. A reader says this channel conveys no information because every output is wrong. Compute H(X|Y) and identify the mistaken assumption. Hint for exercise 2 If Y is always the opposite of X, can you recover X from Y? Full solution to exercise 2 Knowing Y determines X by reversing the bit, so H(X|Y)=0 and I(X;Y)=H(X)=1 bit. P(Y≠X)=1 remains true, but “wrong” here means only that copying Y as the input fails. A receiver informed of the deterministic flip decodes perfectly. The reader treated mismatch with an unadjusted guess as equivalent to lost information. One use, one clear model The symmetric switch has error chance ε regardless of the input law. The amount of input information carried by its output depends on that law; for fair inputs it is 1−h₂(ε) bits per use. Neither number describes all practical noise. Real channels can have asymmetric errors, memory, uncertain parameters, or constraints on the input. A channel table is an explicit mathematical assumption to test against those conditions, not a guarantee about hardware. A useful stopping check is to write a complete joint table from an input distribution and the transition probabilities, then verify that all four cells sum to one. That same table supports conditional probabilities, entropy, and mutual information without changing denominators silently. The MIT information and entropy text supports the finite channel and information framework. The switch arithmetic and exercises here are original.

title: The cost of a wrong probability model
summary: Calculate directional KL divergence with its support condition and log-loss meaning.
text: How costly is a mistaken probability model? A stipulated source has law P, but a predictor or code uses Q. KL divergence measures its excess expected log loss over using P. Averaging Q's predictions under P differs from averaging P's predictions under Q: direction matters. Background capsule. A distribution on a finite alphabet assigns nonnegative probabilities summing to one. Log₂ converts ratios to bits; log₂(a/b) is positive when a>b and negative when a<b. Individual terms in a KL sum can therefore be negative, even though the complete sum is nonnegative. Support means the symbols with positive probability. We define 0 log₂(0/q)=0 when q is positive; when p>0 and q=0, the divergence is infinite. Compare two guesses for a coin-like source Worked example. Let P=(1/2,1/2) and Q=(3/4,1/4) for symbols A and B. Under P, using Q gives average log loss −(1/2)log₂(3/4)−(1/2)log₂(1/4)=about 1.208 bits per draw. Using P gives H(P)=1 bit. The extra is about 0.208 bit. Algebraically, D(P||Q)=(1/2)log₂(2/3)+(1/2)log₂2=(1/2)log₂(4/3), the same result. Directional divergences for two distributions Quantity Exact expression Approximate bits D(P||Q) ½ log₂(4/3) 0.208 D(Q||P) ¾ log₂(3/2)+¼ log₂(1/2) 0.189 The second row uses Q as the averaging law and P as the model. Its value differs, so KL divergence is asymmetric. It is not a metric distance. A second obstruction is support: if P assigns B positive chance but Q assigns B zero, a draw of B has infinite log loss under Q, making D(P||Q)=∞. A finite observed run without B cannot erase that model-level possibility. The formula and Gibbs inequality D KL ( P ∥ Q ) = ∑ x p ( x ) log 2 p ( x ) q ( x ) Exact claim. For finite distributions, D(P||Q)≥0, with equality exactly when P=Q, provided divergence is interpreted as infinite if Q vanishes on positive P support. To see the finite case, use ln u≤u−1 for u>0, with equality only at u=1. For each x with p(x)>0, set u=q(x)/p(x). Then −p(x)ln(q(x)/p(x))≥p(x)−q(x). Sum over positive-P symbols. Their p masses total one, while their q masses total at most one, so the right side is nonnegative. Divide by ln2 to change nats to bits. Equality forces q=p on positive support and leaves no q mass elsewhere. This is Gibbs inequality in a finite setting; an infinite value already satisfies nonnegativity. When support makes it finite, cross-entropy H(P,Q)=−Σp log₂q=H(P)+D(P||Q). This is expected log loss under P, not a guaranteed sample penalty: chance can favor Q on one run. Asymmetry also prevents using KL as a metric in triangle-inequality arguments. Optional investigation: when does merging symbols lose no KL? Change the observation, keep both laws Grouping reveals a symbol's block but hides its identity. Does that strictly reduce KL between two stipulated laws? Apply the same deterministic grouping to both; this is neither Bayesian updating nor estimation from data. Extra background. A map g gives each symbol a block label. For a block B, add its original probabilities separately under the two laws: p B =Σ i∈B pᵢ and q B =Σ i∈B qᵢ. These are the coarse laws P g , Q g . When the corresponding block mass is positive, divide by it to obtain the conditional distribution of the hidden symbol inside that block. Each law has its own normalizer. Use new four-symbol laws P=(3,3,1,1)/8 and Q=(2,2,2,2)/8. Their symbol likelihood ratios P/Q are (3/2,3/2,1/2,1/2). The full divergence is c=(3/4)log₂(3/2)−1/4≈0.188722 bits. A grouping 12 | 34 retains only whether the symbol is in {1,2} or {3,4}; grouping 13 | 24 instead retains membership in {1,3} or {2,4}. Both discard the original symbol. Predict before inspecting. Which grouping keeps equal likelihood ratios together? Check both blocks' conditional laws under P and Q before deciding whether KL is preserved. For 12 | 34, P g =(3/4,1/4) and Q g =(1/2,1/2). Both within-block conditional laws are uniform under both models. The retained KL is c and the discarded contribution is zero. For 13 | 24, the two coarse laws are identical and fair, giving retained KL zero. Within either crossed block, P has conditional law (3/4,1/4) while Q is uniform: each conditional divergence is c, weighted by P(block)=1/2. The discarded total is c. Preserving KL need not recover the symbol or preserve every information quantity. In the first grouping, within-block laws agree, so hidden detail supplies no additional log-likelihood evidence distinguishing P and Q. Noninvertibility need not strictly reduce KL. The exact decomposition First assume finite D(P||Q). On a finite alphabet, this means qᵢ>0 wherever pᵢ>0. Every p B >0 then has q B >0. Define P B (i)=pᵢ/p B and Q B (i)=qᵢ/q B for every symbol in that block. For each positive-pᵢ cell, split its log ratio as log₂(pᵢ/qᵢ)=log₂(p B /q B )+log₂(P B (i)/Q B (i)). Multiply by pᵢ and sum inside each block. The first part becomes p B log₂(p B /q B ); the second becomes p B D(P B ||Q B ). Let F=D(P||Q) be the full divergence, C=D(P g ||Q g ) the coarse divergence, and L=Σ B:p B >0 p B D(P B ||Q B ) the weighted within-block divergence. Summing the split gives the exact identity F = C + L Each complete conditional divergence is nonnegative by the Gibbs inequality proved above, so L≥0 and C≤F. This is deterministic data processing for KL. Individual terms need not be nonnegative: in the preserving example the coarse sum has terms (3/4)log₂(3/2) and −1/4. The conclusion concerns their total and the complete conditional divergences. Equality requires every active block. With finite divergence, C=F exactly when P B =Q B as complete vectors in every block with p B >0. Every weight there is positive, so their nonnegative sum vanishes exactly when every conditional divergence vanishes. Equivalently, pᵢ=(p B /q B )qᵢ for every i in each active block. This includes zero-pᵢ coordinates. Merely checking constant ratios on positive-P cells can miss Q mass elsewhere in that block. One matching inspected block cannot establish this all-block statement. Zero masses and infinite divergences: which quantities exist? A zero-P cell contributes zero, including pᵢ=qᵢ=0; do not evaluate log(0/0). A block with p B =0 is omitted from L. Its P-conditional is not needed, whether q B is positive or zero. Common-null blocks require neither conditional. Inside a positive-P block, however, Q's mass on zero-P cells still matters when comparing the complete vectors. If every positive-P block is Q-positive, the coarse divergence C is finite even if F is infinite. All required conditionals exist. A positive-P/zero-Q cell inside one such block gives an infinite conditional divergence, and the identity means ∞=finite+∞. The sum uses only positive p B , never 0·∞. With finite C, equality is still equivalent to all active conditional laws matching; infinite F cannot equal finite C. If some p B >0 has q B =0, both F and C are infinite, and Q's conditional in that block is undefined. State the support failure directly. Do not form that conditional, subtract ∞−∞, or call equal infinity labels a no-loss certificate. The finite-coarse equality criterion is not asserted there. The extended inequality still holds because both sides are infinite. Boundary calculations outside the controls Laws and grouping Fine and coarse KL Reason P=(1,0), Q=(1/2,1/2); one block F=1, C=0, L=1 The complete conditional vectors differ, despite a single positive-P coordinate. P=(1/2,1/2,0,0), Q=(1/4,1/4,1/2,0); 12 | 3 | 4 F=C=1, L=0 Only block 12 is active. Skip P's block-3 conditional and both common-null block-4 conditionals. P=(1/2,0,1/2), Q=(0,1/2,1/2); 12 | 3 F=∞, C=0, L=∞ The coarse laws agree, but the first conditional divergence is infinite. P=(1/2,1/2,0), Q=(0,1/4,3/4); 1 | 23 F=C=∞; no residual is formed Q's block-1 conditional is undefined. Block 23 also mismatches; infinity equality is not a preservation certificate. Source scope. Polyanskiy and Wu, MIT 6.441 notes, Definition 2.2, Theorem 2.2 and Corollary 2.2, printed pages 21–22 , develops conditional divergence, the chain rule and deterministic data processing. Its §3.1 equality discussion on page 32 assumes finite output divergence. The finite proof, explicit support split, inspector fixtures and changed task here are independently derived; no unrestricted equality claim is imported into ∞=∞. Check direction and support Exercise 1. Let P=(1/2,1/2) and Q=(3/4,1/4). Compute D(P||Q) and D(Q||P) to three decimals. Which distribution supplies weights in each sum? Hint for exercise 1 Write each log ratio before rounding; reverse both the weights and the ratio for the second quantity. Full solution to exercise 1 D(P||Q)=½log₂((1/2)/(3/4))+½log₂((1/2)/(1/4))=½log₂(4/3)≈0.208 bit, weighted by P. D(Q||P)=¾log₂((3/4)/(1/2))+¼log₂((1/4)/(1/2))=¾log₂(3/2)−¼≈0.189 bit, weighted by Q. Their inequality demonstrates asymmetry without relying on a picture. Exercise 2. P=(0,1) and Q=(1/2,1/2). Find both directional divergences. Explain why one can be finite while the other is infinite. Hint for exercise 2 In the reverse direction, Q assigns positive chance to a symbol that P forbids. Full solution to exercise 2 D(P||Q)=1·log₂(1/(1/2))=1 bit; the P-zero first term contributes zero. But D(Q||P)=∞ because Q gives the first symbol probability 1/2 while P gives it zero, so the required log ratio has zero denominator. The two directions average over different supports, not merely different numerical weights. A changed task: nonuniform reference weights inside each block Exercise 3. Keep grouping 12 | 34 fixed throughout. Let Q=(1/6,1/3,1/4,1/4) and P=(1/4,1/2,1/8,1/8). (a) Find both coarse laws and all block conditionals. Does grouping preserve KL? (b) Replace P by P′=(1/8,5/8,1/8,1/8). Show that the coarse laws remain fixed, identify the changed conditional and derive its exact additional divergence and an approximate value. (c) Why can inspecting only block 34 fail to establish a global no-loss conclusion? (d) For this Q and grouping, find every generating law R that loses no KL, including zero-mass blocks. If R's coarse masses must be (3/4,1/4), how many no-loss laws remain? These changed laws are outside the controls. Hint for exercise 3 Normalize separately by each law's own block mass. For equality, compare every cell in every active block. Weight conditional KL by the generating law's block mass. For (d), let a be R's first block mass and allocate it in Q's conditional proportions; handle a=0 or 1 without conditioning on a zero-R block. Full solution to exercise 3 (a) A nonuniform reference can still lose nothing. Q's coarse masses are (1/2,1/2), while P's are (3/4,1/4). In block 12, P's conditional is ((1/4)/(3/4),(1/2)/(3/4))=(1/3,2/3), and Q's is ((1/6)/(1/2),(1/3)/(1/2))=(1/3,2/3). In block 34 both are (1/2,1/2). Symbol ratios are (3/2,3/2,1/2,1/2). Every active conditional KL is zero; full and coarse divergence both equal c=(3/4)log₂(3/2)−1/4≈0.188722 bits. (b) Same coarse laws, different hidden detail. For the fixed grouping 12 | 34, P′ still gives (3/4,1/4), so coarse KL remains c. Its first conditional becomes (1/6,5/6), whereas Q's remains (1/3,2/3). The second conditional still matches. The first conditional divergence is d=(1/6)log₂(1/2)+(5/6)log₂(5/4)=(5/6)log₂(5/4)−1/6≈0.101607 bits. Multiply by P′(12)=3/4 to obtain the discarded total r=(3/4)d=(5/8)log₂(5/4)−1/8≈0.076205 bits. Thus full D(P′||Q)=c+r≈0.264927 bits. Direct fine-alphabet calculation confirms (1/8)log₂(3/4)+(5/8)log₂(15/8)−1/4=c+r. The unchanged-coarse statement uses that fixed grouping. Under the crossed grouping, Q's coarse masses would be (5/12,7/12), P's (3/8,5/8), and P′'s (1/4,3/4), so the generating coarse law would change. (c) One inspected term cannot certify the sum. Block 34 contributes zero for both P and P′, but block 12 contributes positive r for P′. Equality requires matching complete vectors in every positive-generating-mass block. (d) Characterize every no-loss law. Q's conditional proportions force R=(a/3,2a/3,(1−a)/2,(1−a)/2) for 0≤a≤1. For 0<a<1 both conditional rows match. At a=0 the first R block has zero mass and is skipped; at a=1 the second is skipped. In either endpoint the remaining active block matches, and fine=coarse=1 bit. Conversely the equality criterion forces those proportions in every active block, while a zero block has all cell masses zero. Requiring coarse masses (3/4,1/4) fixes a=3/4 and gives the original P as the unique no-loss law. P′ has the same block totals but fails the conditional requirement. Use divergence in its proper direction KL divergence is nonnegative extra expected log loss when Q predicts outcomes actually generated under P. Its support condition can turn it infinite, and reversing arguments changes the question. In information theory, mutual information is KL divergence between a joint law and the product of its marginals; this supplies a proof of nonnegativity for that measure. In data analysis, both P and Q may be estimated, which adds uncertainty and can create misleading infinities from zero empirical counts. Those are model-estimation questions, not defects in the finite identity. At a stopping point, state which law generates observations before writing D(P||Q). The MIT information and entropy text supports the information-divergence framework. The two-symbol distributions, directional calculations, and exercises on this page are original.

title: The tiny sample looks too predictable
summary: Enumerate entropy estimates, then use paired data to show mutual-information bias can have either sign.
text: Why can a tiny sample look too predictable? The entropy formula assumes a probability distribution. In practice we may have only a few draws and replace unknown probabilities with observed frequencies. That plug-in estimate can be useful, but its exact value is random and tends to understate true entropy in a finite sample. A sample that misses a rare symbol assigns it zero frequency, even when the source gives it positive probability. We can see the bias without relying on a simulation by enumerating every sample in a tiny fair-bit experiment. Background capsule. For n draws, the empirical frequency p̂(x) is count(x)/n. Entropy in bits is H(P)=−Σp(x)log₂p(x), with 0 log₂0 treated as zero. The plug-in estimate uses the same function with p̂. Bias means E[estimate]−target, where expectation averages over all possible samples under a fixed source law. It is distinct from the error in a particular realized sample, which may be above or below the target. Enumerate two fair-bit draws Worked example. Let the true source emit independent fair bits. Its true entropy is 1 bit. Draw twice. The ordered samples 00, 01, 10, and 11 each have probability 1/4. For 00 or 11, empirical frequencies are (1,0) or (0,1), yielding plug-in entropy zero. For 01 or 10, frequencies are (1/2,1/2), yielding 1 bit. The average estimate over the four equally likely samples is (0+1+1+0)/4=1/2 bit. Thus bias is 1/2−1=−1/2 bit in this deliberately small case. All two-draw samples from a fair independent bit source Sample Empirical frequencies Plug-in entropy 00 (1,0) 0 bit 01 (1/2,1/2) 1 bit 10 (1/2,1/2) 1 bit 11 (0,1) 0 bit Nothing about a particular 00 sample proves the source deterministic. It records only two observations. If we instead drew one bit, the empirical distribution would always be a point mass and estimated entropy always zero. The sample size, alphabet, and independence assumption matter to any uncertainty report. The estimator and its bias boundary H ^ = − ∑ x p ^ ( x ) log 2 p ^ ( x ) Exact claim. If n independent draws come from a fixed finite distribution P, the ordinary empirical plug-in entropy satisfies E[Ĥ]≤H(P). One way to see the direction is that entropy is concave in its probability vector and E[p̂]=P, so Jensen's inequality gives E[H(p̂)]≤H(E[p̂])=H(P). The enumeration above proves the numerical bias for n=2 without requiring Jensen's inequality. Strictness depends on the source and sample size; a deterministic source has entropy and estimated entropy zero, so no negative bias occurs there. Concavity is the named proof boundary here: the binary maximum lesson shows the shape in two categories, but a general finite-alphabet Jensen proof needs the full concavity result. Bias alone does not supply a confidence interval or tell how far a particular estimate is from truth. For a large alphabet relative to n, unseen symbols can be common and the plug-in value especially fragile. A correction formula or bootstrap would require its own assumptions; we do not silently add one to this two-draw calculation. A difference of biased estimates: exact two-pair investigation (35–45 additional minutes) The entropy result concerns one concave functional. Does it tell the direction of bias when three estimated entropies are combined? The mutual-information lesson gives I(X;Y)=H(X)+H(Y)−H(X,Y). Subtracting the third entropy means three downward-bias statements do not determine the sign of the resulting bias. We can settle a small case exactly. Each observation is a pair (X,Y), with both coordinates binary. Its four possible values are 00, 01, 10, 11, with fixed source probabilities a,b,c,d, respectively. These sum to 1 and may include zeros. Take two independent observations from this same joint source. Independence between observations does not require independence of X and Y within an observation. Form one empirical joint table from those two pairs, then obtain both empirical marginals by summing that table's rows and columns. Define Î=Ĥ(X)+Ĥ(Y)−Ĥ(X,Y), always using that same data. These are bits per paired observation; Î is not divided by the number of observations. Using separately collected or mismatched marginal samples would no longer evaluate mutual information of this empirical joint law. Predict the bias. For independent fair X and Y, must Î always be zero? For a fair X copied perfectly to Y, must Î always be one? Compare the two sources, then inspect a repeated pair and two pairs with both coordinates changed. The known source and the inspected record play different roles. Prove the complete two-observation law There are sixteen ordered records, each weighted by the product of its two source probabilities. If the two observed pairs are identical, all three empirical entropies are zero. If exactly one coordinate changes, that coordinate has empirical entropy one, the unchanged coordinate has entropy zero, and the empirical joint entropy is one; hence Î=0. If both coordinates change, each empirical marginal is fair and the joint table has two equally weighted cells. Then Î=1+1−1=1 bit. Thus Î equals one precisely for records (00,11), (11,00), (01,10), and (10,01). Their source probabilities are ad, da, bc and cb. Every other record gives zero. Consequently P ( I ^ = 1 ) = E [ I ^ ] = 2 ( a d + b c ) The other mass is P(Î=0)=1−2(ad+bc). Numerical equality between a probability and the expected bit value occurs because this estimator takes only the values zero and one. They remain different quantities with different units. This finite n=2 identity is not a general formula for arbitrary sample sizes. Bias can point in either direction Independent fair bits. Here (a,b,c,d)=(1,1,1,1)/4 and true I=0 exactly. The mean estimate is 2(1/16+1/16)=1/4 bit, so bias is +1/4. A record such as (00,11) has empirical information one despite zero population information. A fair bit copied perfectly. Here (a,b,c,d)=(1,0,0,1)/2 and true I=1 exactly. The mean estimate is 2(1/4)=1/2 bit, so bias is −1/2. Repeated records (00,00) and (11,11) each give zero and each have source probability 1/4. The source's dependence is perfect even though those empirical marginals are constant. The quarter-error lamp. The existing joint law (3,1,1,3)/8 gives mean estimate 2(9/64+1/64)=5/16 bit. True information is 1−h₂(1/4)≈0.188722 bit, so bias is approximately +0.123778 bit. The source's logarithmic value and this difference are rounded; the estimator law and its expectation are exact fractions. Here h₂(p)=−p log₂p−(1−p)log₂(1−p). The source information is a fixed target, the estimate is a function of a record, and bias averages its errors across the fixed source's records. Even a possible record with zero empirical cells cannot establish zero source probabilities. In the copying model, off-diagonal source cells really are zero by assumption: records containing them are impossible and have no weight in the estimator law, although the empirical statistic can still be evaluated on that hypothetical record. Paninski's Estimation of Entropy and Mutual Information , Section 3.3 and Section 4, distinguishes entropy's downward bias from mutual-information bias of either sign. That paper's default logarithms are natural; the finite calculations here use log₂ and are derived locally in bits. We infer no correction method or confidence interval from these two-observation laws. Audit a small sample Exercise 1. A fair binary source is sampled three times. Calculate the plug-in entropy for 000 and for 001. Which sample proves the source is fair? Hint for exercise 1 Turn each sample into frequency counts, then use the entropy formula. Keep the true law separate. Full solution to exercise 1 For 000, p̂=(1,0), so Ĥ=0. For 001, p̂=(2/3,1/3), so Ĥ=−(2/3)log₂(2/3)−(1/3)log₂(1/3)≈0.918 bit. Neither sample proves fairness: both have positive probability under the stipulated fair source, and the same finite samples could occur under many other positive-probability laws. Exercise 2. A claimed theorem says “Every plug-in entropy estimate is below the true entropy.” Use the two-draw fair-bit enumeration to test the wording, then state the correct average claim. Hint for exercise 2 Look at the 01 and 10 rows and compare each value with the true one-bit entropy. Full solution to exercise 2 The 01 and 10 estimates equal the true entropy, so “below” is already false if interpreted strictly. With other nonuniform sources, a balanced observed sample can even exceed the true entropy. The supported statement is about expectation under repeated independent samples: E[Ĥ]≤H(P). In this fair two-draw case, the expectation is 1/2 bit, below the target 1 bit by 1/2 bit. Transfer tasks for the optional mutual-information investigation Exercise 3. A fresh independent source. X is Bernoulli(1/4), Y is Bernoulli(2/3), and X and Y are independent. Take two iid paired observations. Derive the four source probabilities in the order 00,01,10,11, then find the full two-point law of Î, its expectation and its bias. Why must the sixteen records not be averaged with equal weights? Hint for exercise 3 Form products of the X and Y probabilities. Weight each ordered record by the product of its two joint probabilities, then use the proved two-observation characterization. Full solution to exercise 3 The joint probabilities are (3/4×1/3, 3/4×2/3, 1/4×1/3, 1/4×2/3)=(3,6,1,2)/12. Independence gives true I=0 exactly. The probability of Î=1 is 2[(3/12)(2/12)+(6/12)(1/12)]=24/144=1/6. Hence P(Î=0)=5/6, E[Î]=1/6 bit and bias=+1/6 bit. As a second check, the chance that the two X values differ is 2(1/4)(3/4)=3/8; the chance that the Y values differ is 2(2/3)(1/3)=4/9. The X sequence and Y sequence are independent under this source, so both differences occur with probability (3/8)(4/9)=1/6. The sixteen ordered records are not equiprobable because their source-cell product weights vary; for example, (01,01) has probability 1/4 while (10,10) has probability 1/144. Exercise 4. The pairing still matters when the marginals agree. Now change the sample size to three. Compare the paired records A=(00,00,11) and B=(00,01,10). Show that both empirical X and empirical Y have one-frequency 1/3 in each record. Compute their empirical joint entropies and mutual informations, and give their exact information difference. Does the n=2 estimator formula apply? Hint for exercise 4 For A, two joint cells have frequencies 2/3 and 1/3. For B, three joint cells each have frequency 1/3. Compute all three entropies from each record's own joint table. Full solution to exercise 4 A has joint counts (2,0,0,1), while B has (1,1,1,0). Their row and column counts are both (2,1), so all empirical marginal entropies equal h₂(1/3)=log₂3−2/3. For A, the joint entropy is also h₂(1/3), giving Î_A=h₂(1/3)=log₂3−2/3≈0.918296 bit. For B, the joint entropy is log₂3, giving Î_B=2h₂(1/3)−log₂3=log₂3−4/3≈0.251629 bit. Their difference is exactly 2/3 bit. Same marginals leave different joint pairings possible. These are individual three-observation statistic values, not their sampling expectations. The n=2 two-point law and expectation formula do not apply to n=3. Report what the data actually support The plug-in formula evaluates entropy at sample frequencies. It is easy to compute, but a tiny sample may miss possible outcomes, and its downward bias is an average statement rather than a guarantee for each data set. Here all four two-draw outcomes were enumerated, making both the target and bias transparent. For real measurement, report sample size, how observations were obtained, the assumed alphabet, and uncertainty about the estimated probabilities. Do not present a histogram from a few draws as the true source distribution. A useful stopping question is whether a zero empirical count means an impossible symbol. It does not without a model assumption or enough evidence; count zero and probability zero are different statements. The MIT information and entropy text supports the entropy definition. Archer, Park and Pillow's JMLR paper, Section 2.1, identifies the empirical plug-in estimator and its negative bias in undersampled data. The finite-sample enumeration here is original; the general bias direction is tied explicitly to concavity rather than inferred from that single example. The optional paired-data investigation shows why subtracting entropy estimates can produce mutual-information bias in either direction, and why the empirical marginals must come from the same joint sample.

title: What and, or, and not actually say
summary: Use all four truth assignments to evaluate conjunction, inclusive disjunction, and negation, then prove a De Morgan equivalence.
text: A dinner invitation with three possible replies A host writes, “Come if you can bring tea or biscuits.” A guest bringing both seems welcome, yet everyday “or” sometimes means “choose one.” Logic cannot settle the host’s intention; it can make the two readings precise. We will use the inclusive or : at least one of the two statements is true, possibly both. If the host really meant exactly one, that needs a different rule. A proposition is a sentence with a definite truth value in a specified situation. Let P mean “the guest brings tea” and Q mean “the guest brings biscuits.” Their truth values may change between situations, but within one row of a truth table each is either true (T) or false (F). The connectives and , or , and not make new propositions from them. A question or an unfilled instruction is not yet a proposition. Our small goal is to evaluate these three connectives in all possible cases. The four rows below exhaust the possibilities for two truth-valued inputs. This is a local prerequisite capsule: you need only distinguish a statement from its truth value and read T and F. No earlier lesson is required. Make every case visible Worked example. First suppose the guest brings tea but no biscuits. P is true and Q false. “Tea and biscuits” is false because one requirement is missing; “tea or biscuits” is true because tea is present; “not tea” is false. Repeat this reasoning row by row. All valuations of P and Q P: tea Q: biscuits P and Q P or Q not P T T T T F T F F T F F T F T T F F F F T The first row is the useful surprise: bringing both satisfies inclusive or. The last row shows why “not P” alone does not imply Q. If the guest brings neither, tea is absent but biscuits are absent too. A truth table is a ledger of stipulated meanings, not a survey of how people usually speak. One equivalence, proved by cases Exact statement. For any two propositions P and Q, the negation of their conjunction has the same truth value as the disjunction of their negations: ¬(P ∧ Q) ≡ (¬P ∨ ¬Q). The symbol ≡ here means equality of truth value under every assignment, not that the two printed strings are identical. ¬ ( P ∧ Q ) ≡ ( ¬ P ∨ ¬ Q ) Complete proof. If both P and Q are true, P ∧ Q is true, so its negation is false; neither ¬P nor ¬Q is true, so the right side is false. In each of the other three rows, at least one input is false. Hence P ∧ Q is false and its negation true; the false input supplies a true negation on the right. Both sides agree in all four possible rows. This proof relies on the stated two-valued propositional semantics. It makes no claim about vague predicates such as “tall” before a truth condition is fixed. The nearby false rule ¬(P ∨ Q) ≡ (¬P ∨ ¬Q) fails when P is true and Q false. The left side is false, since at least one item is present; the right side is true, since biscuits are absent. To deny “tea or biscuits,” the guest must bring neither. The correct right side uses and : ¬P ∧ ¬Q. Two valuations to solve 1. Let P be false and Q true. Evaluate (P ∨ Q) ∧ ¬P, showing each intermediate truth value. Hint for question 1 Work from the parentheses and the negation before applying and. Full solution to question 1 P ∨ Q is T because Q is T. ¬P is T because P is F. Therefore T ∧ T is T. In the dinner story, biscuits without tea satisfy “at least one” and “no tea.” 2. A colleague claims ¬(P ∧ Q) means “neither P nor Q.” Give a row that disproves this and write the correct reading. Hint for question 2 Try one true input and one false input. Full solution to question 2 Take P=T and Q=F. Then P ∧ Q=F, so ¬(P ∧ Q)=T. But “neither P nor Q” is false because P is true. The negated conjunction means “at least one of P and Q is false”; neither means ¬P ∧ ¬Q. For an extra check, build the four rows for “exactly one”: (P ∨ Q) ∧ ¬(P ∧ Q). It is true only in the middle two rows. This formula records a specific rule the host could have chosen. It is not interchangeable with inclusive or whenever both inputs are possible. Keep the words tied to a table Conjunction needs both inputs true; inclusive disjunction needs one or both; negation reverses a truth value. A four-row table can prove an equivalence involving two propositions because it covers every assignment to them. It can also refute an alleged equivalence with a single differing row. The table says nothing about whether a real invitation uses inclusive or; that is a question of what the speaker intended. A satisfying stopping point is the De Morgan equivalence and one counter-row. When you meet an if–then sentence, the same table method will expose a different surprise: an implication is false in only one row.

title: The surprising truth of if–then
summary: Find the single false row of material implication and distinguish its contrapositive from its converse.
text: What does a promise say on a dry day? Consider a rule posted beside an outdoor event: “If it rains, the event moves indoors.” On a rainy day with the event still outside, the rule has plainly failed. On a dry day, an indoor event might happen for another reason; the rule itself has not been broken. Formal logic uses that narrow sense of violation for the connective material implication . Let P stand for “it rains” and Q for “the event moves indoors.” P is the antecedent and Q the consequent. A proposition has a fixed true or false value in each situation. The symbols ¬, ∨, and → mean not, inclusive or, and if–then. A local prerequisite: inclusive or is true whenever either input is true, including when both are true. We will not assume that a rule caused its conclusion; causation requires information beyond this truth table. We will determine exactly when P → Q is false, compare it to ¬P ∨ Q, and distinguish a valid contrapositive from an invalid converse. The ordinary event gives a concrete interpretation, but the proof applies to any two propositions. Inspect the one violating row A rain rule in all four circumstances P: rain Q: move indoors P → Q Reason T T T Rule met T F F Rain with no move violates it F T T Rule makes no demand F F T Rule makes no demand Worked example. The last two rows often sound odd when described as “true promises.” Here “true” means the specified truth-functional sentence has no violating row. It does not mean someone made a good forecast, gave a causal explanation, or intended the dry-day outcome. A contract can add exceptions and time conditions; our P and Q suppress those details. For a worked instance, suppose it does not rain and organizers move indoors to repair the field. P=F and Q=T. The posted rule P→Q is true under material implication. “If indoors, then rain,” written Q→P, is false in precisely this instance. The direction matters. Why implication equals not-P or Q Exact statement. For two-valued propositions P and Q, P → Q is logically equivalent to ¬P ∨ Q. The equivalence describes truth values under every assignment, not a causal mechanism. P → Q ≡ ¬ P ∨ Q Complete proof by cases. If P is false, ¬P is true, so ¬P ∨ Q is true regardless of Q; the rule has no violated requirement, so P→Q is true. If P is true, ¬P is false, and the disjunction has exactly Q’s truth value. The rule also has Q’s truth value: a true antecedent requires a true consequent. Thus the expressions agree for both choices of P and both choices of Q. The contrapositive ¬Q → ¬P is equivalent to P → Q. Using the same violation test, ¬Q → ¬P is false exactly when ¬Q is true and ¬P false—that is, Q false and P true. That is the original false row. By contrast the converse Q→P has its false row when Q true and P false. The dry-day indoor event above disproves equivalence with the converse. Reversing an arrow is not a proof step. Separate implication from converse 1. Take P=F and Q=F. Evaluate P→Q, Q→P, and ¬Q→¬P. Explain why the agreement here proves little. Hint for question 1 Check whether an implication has a true antecedent and false consequent. Full solution to question 1 All three are true: P→Q and Q→P have false antecedents, while ¬Q→¬P is T→T. One row of agreement cannot prove equivalence. The contrapositive agrees in every row by the case argument; the converse fails in a different row. 2. A shop says, “If a customer has a receipt, we issue a refund.” A customer receives a refund without a receipt. Has the stated implication been violated? Does that case refute its converse? Hint for question 2 Use P=“has receipt” and Q=“gets refund.” Full solution to question 2 Here P=F and Q=T. P→Q is true: the rule requires a refund only when a receipt is present. The converse Q→P is false because the customer gets a refund but has no receipt. A real shop may have more policies; this evaluates only the single formal sentence. Try inventing one ordinary-language sentence whose intended meaning includes time, cause, or probability. Its material implication translation may be too weak. That limitation is useful: formalization starts by choosing precisely what the symbols say. The arrow has one failure mode P→Q fails only when P holds and Q does not. Its truth table is exactly that of ¬P∨Q, and its contrapositive is equivalent. The converse is a different claim. The result has a complete four-case proof under classical propositional semantics; it does not settle conversational implications or causation. Stop when you can identify a violating row and distinguish all three sentences. The next useful move is to put “for every” or “there exists” before a rule, where the domain and the order of quantifiers become part of its meaning.

title: Every person has a book: whose book?
summary: Use a people-book relation to distinguish individual witnesses from one witness that works for everyone.
text: Every person has a book: whose book? At a tiny book club, Ada has read Atlas and Ben has read Beacon. Is it true that every member has read a book? Yes. Is there a book every member has read? No. Moving “a book” in front of “every member” changes the claim. Logic records the difference by the order of its quantifiers. A domain tells us what each variable ranges over. Let X={Ada, Ben} be people and Y={Atlas, Beacon} be books. Let R(x,y) mean “person x has read book y.” The relation R is simply a set of permitted person-book pairs. The symbol ∀ means “for every” and ∃ means “there exists.” These definitions are the local prerequisite capsule; no theory of relations is assumed. We compare ∀x∈X ∃y∈Y R(x,y) with ∃y∈Y ∀x∈X R(x,y). A witness for an existential claim is a specific object that makes it true. A counterexample to a universal claim is a specific object for which it fails. Keep those jobs separate as you read the grid. Read the rows, then the columns Who has read which book? Person Atlas Beacon Ada Yes No Ben No Yes Worked example. For the first sentence, choose a book separately after choosing each person. Ada’s witness is Atlas; Ben’s is Beacon. Every row contains a Yes, so the first sentence is true. For the second sentence, choose one book first and hold it fixed. Atlas fails on Ben; Beacon fails on Ada. No column contains two Yes entries, so the second sentence is false. Now add a third book, Common, read by both. Both sentences become true: Common is one witness for all members. The changed table shows the stronger claim can hold; the original table shows it need not follow from the weaker one.
