Finite models are valuable because a single model can refute a proposed general equivalence. An implication and its limit Exact statement. If X and Y are nonempty sets and R is any relation on X×Y, then ∃y∈Y ∀x∈X R(x,y) implies ∀x∈X ∃y∈Y R(x,y). The reverse implication is not valid in general. ( ∃ y ∀ x R ( x , y ) ) → ( ∀ x ∃ y R ( x , y ) ) Complete proof of the forward implication. Assume one y₀ works for every x. Pick any x from X. The same y₀ is a witness for that x, so ∃y R(x,y) holds. Because x was arbitrary, the first-then-second quantifier sentence follows. The two-row table above is a complete countermodel to the converse: it satisfies the right side and falsifies the left side. The nonempty assumption avoids a separate issue about choosing witnesses over an empty person domain. In classical semantics, if X is empty, ∀x∈X ∃y R(x,y) is vacuously true, while ∃y∈Y ∀x∈X R(x,y) depends on whether Y has a member. For the forward implication, an actual y witness still suffices even when X is empty. We restrict to a familiar club so that the worked meaning is concrete. A common failure is to use a different y for each x while writing one y outside ∀x. That silent switch is exactly what the order forbids. Draw rows and columns if the symbols feel slippery: every row needs a Yes versus one column needs Yes everywhere. Find the witness or the failed row 1. Let X={Iris, Jo} and Y={Red, Blue}. Iris likes Red and Blue; Jo likes Blue only. Evaluate both quantified sentences and name witnesses. Hint for question 1 Look for a Yes in each row, then for one all-Yes column. Full solution to question 1 Both are true. Iris has Red or Blue as a witness and Jo has Blue, so every row succeeds. Blue is a common witness: both Iris and Jo like it. The first sentence permits different witnesses, but a shared witness happens to exist here. 2. Construct a two-person, two-book relation in which ∀x∃y R(x,y) is false. State which person fails and whether ∃y∀x R(x,y) can nevertheless be true. Hint for question 2 Give one person an empty row. Full solution to question 2 For example, let only Ada have read Atlas and let Ben have read no book. Ben’s row has no Yes, so ∀x∃y R(x,y) is false. No book is read by Ben, so no common book exists either; ∃y∀x R(x,y) is false. It cannot be true when the first statement is false, by the proved implication. You can reverse the roles of the two people and rename the books; the explanation must still identify the empty row. The exercise checks the implication as well as the grid reading. Who gets to choose when? In ∀x∃y, the choice of y may depend on x. In ∃y∀x, one y must serve every x. A common witness supplies individual witnesses, so the second form implies the first. The diagonal two-person table proves the converse fails. That is a complete proof plus a complete finite countermodel, not merely a visual suggestion. The stopping point is the ability to produce the witness or failure for a sentence in a named domain. Negating quantified sentences is the natural next step, but it requires care with both the quantifier and the predicate.

title: Negating an everyone claim
summary: Negate universal, existential, and nested claims by naming the exact failure pattern.
text: One missed train is enough An announcement says, “Every train on the board departed on time.” To show it false, you need one listed train that did not depart on time. Saying “every train was late” would be far stronger. This small difference is the heart of negating quantifiers. Let D be the set of trains on a particular board and P(x) mean “train x departed on time.” ∀x∈D P(x) says every listed train has the property; ∃x∈D P(x) says at least one does. Negation, written ¬, reverses the truth of the whole sentence. A predicate such as P(x) is not a complete proposition until x is assigned or quantified. This is the local prerequisite capsule. We will prove the two basic negation laws from meanings, then apply them to a sentence with two nested quantifiers. The board is a finite worked model; the laws themselves do not rely on finiteness. We assume ordinary classical true-or-false semantics throughout. A small timetable audit Departures on the board Train On time? A Yes B No C Yes Worked example. The universal claim fails because B is a counterexample. Its negation, “there exists a listed train that was not on time,” is true with witness B. But “no listed train was on time” is false because A and C were on time. If someone instead claims “at least one train was not on time,” its negation says “every train was on time”; there is no need to find a single on-time train to negate existence. For a nested example, let P(x,y) mean person x received message y, with x ranging over members and y over messages. Negating “each member received some message” requires a member for whom every possible message fails. One missed message for one member is too weak; that person could have received a different message. Switch the quantifier, negate the inside Exact laws. For any specified domain D and predicate P, ¬∀x∈D P(x) is equivalent to ∃x∈D ¬P(x), and ¬∃x∈D P(x) is equivalent to ∀x∈D ¬P(x). Both laws also work when D is empty under classical semantics. ¬ ∀ x P ( x ) ≡ ∃ x ¬ P ( x ) Semantic proof. “Not all members have P” is true exactly when the universal sentence has a failing member. Such a member is a witness to ¬P, proving the first equivalence in both directions. “There is no member with P” is true exactly when each member fails P, proving the second. For an empty domain, every universal sentence is true and every existential sentence false; the two equivalences still agree. The proof is about quantified truth conditions, not a mere pattern of swapping symbols. Apply the laws one layer at a time: ¬[∀x∈X ∃y∈Y R(x,y)] ≡ ∃x∈X ¬[∃y∈Y R(x,y)] ≡ ∃x∈X ∀y∈Y ¬R(x,y). A common invalid negation is ∃x∃y ¬R(x,y). That says only that someone lacks one relation to one object. In a two-person, two-book club where each has read exactly one different book, such a missing pair exists, yet every person has read some book. The invalid negation would report failure where there is none. If the domains themselves are constrained by extra conditions, keep those conditions inside the translation. For example “every train on the board” quantifies over that board, not over every train in the world. Changing the domain changes the claim even if the symbols look similar. Negate all the way inward 1. Negate “some integer is both even and positive” in symbols and plain English. Hint for question 1 Negate ∃n∈ℤ [E(n)∧P(n)]; then use the propositional De Morgan law. Full solution to question 1 The negation is ∀n∈ℤ ¬[E(n)∧P(n)], equivalently ∀n∈ℤ [¬E(n)∨¬P(n)]. In words, every integer is either not even or not positive. The original statement is true, for example at n=2, so its negation is false. 2. A club claims ∃b∈B ∀m∈M Read(m,b). Write its exact negation and explain a witness pattern in a two-book club. Hint for question 2 First deny the outer existential, then the inner universal. Full solution to question 2 The negation is ∀b∈B ∃m∈M ¬Read(m,b): for each book there is a member who has not read it. If Ada alone read Atlas and Ben alone read Beacon, Ben witnesses the failure for Atlas and Ada witnesses it for Beacon. The member may depend on the book. Check that your final negation has no ¬ in front of a quantifier and no unnegated predicate when the original was positive. That mechanical check helps, but the witness explanation is what establishes meaning. A negation names a failure Negating ∀ seeks one failure; negating ∃ says all candidates fail. For nested claims, move inward one quantifier at a time and preserve the order of choices. The timetable witness and club countermodel show why “some missing pair” is weaker than “one person lacks every pair.” A good stopping point is a correct symbolic negation plus a plain-language witness pattern. This lesson proves the classical semantic laws; it does not replace the need to state a domain or clarify an ambiguous everyday sentence.

title: A set is its members, not its drawing
summary: Test membership and subset claims, and prove equality by two inclusions.
text: A playlist is its songs, not their order Two friends share playlists. One writes [jazz, folk, ambient]; the other writes [ambient, jazz, folk, jazz]. As ordered lists these differ, but as sets of styles they agree: each contains exactly jazz, folk, and ambient. Set language ignores order and duplicate occurrences. That choice makes membership, rather than a drawing or a list position, the decisive test. Write x∈A when x is a member of set A. Write A⊆B when every member of A is also a member of B; equality A=B means precisely the same members. Braces such as {jazz, folk} describe a set by listing its members. The empty set ∅ has no members. These definitions are the local prerequisite capsule; no Venn diagram convention is needed. Our goal is to test subset and equality claims in finite examples and prove the two-inclusion criterion. We will also distinguish an element from a one-element set: jazz is not the same object as {jazz}. The latter is a set whose member is jazz. Audit membership rather than positions Worked example. Let A={jazz, folk, ambient} and B={ambient, jazz, folk, jazz}. Repeating jazz adds no new member. To verify A⊆B, check jazz, folk, and ambient in B. To verify B⊆A, check every distinct member of B in A. Both tests pass, so the sets are equal. A visual overlap might suggest the same result, but the membership ledger is the argument. Membership check for two playlists treated as sets Style In A? In B? jazz Yes Yes folk Yes Yes ambient Yes Yes A different pair shows why one inclusion is insufficient. Let C={jazz, folk} and D={jazz, folk, ambient}. Every member of C occurs in D, so C⊆D. But ambient∈D and ambient∉C, so D⊄C and C≠D. The same witness, ambient, refutes both reverse inclusion and equality. Equality has two directions Exact statement. For any sets A and B, A=B if and only if A⊆B and B⊆A. Here A⊆B abbreviates the universal claim “for every x, if x∈A then x∈B.” The universal claim ranges over objects in the setting under discussion; it is not inferred from how shaded regions look. A = B ⇔ ( A ⊆ B ∧ B ⊆ A ) Complete proof. If A=B, each member of either is a member of the other, giving both inclusions. Conversely, assume A⊆B and B⊆A. Choose any object x. If x∈A, the first inclusion gives x∈B. If x∈B, the second gives x∈A. Therefore x∈A exactly when x∈B, for every x. By the membership definition of set equality, A=B. This argument is valid for finite or infinite sets, provided ordinary extensional sets are meant. A common type error is to infer {jazz}∈A from jazz∈A. If A is a set of styles, it may contain jazz but not the singleton set {jazz}. In A={jazz, folk}, jazz∈A is true, while {jazz}∈A is false. The singleton is instead a subset : {jazz}⊆A. The symbols ∈ and ⊆ ask different questions. The empty set is a subset of every set. There is no member of ∅ that can violate “every member of ∅ lies in A.” This is a proof by the absence of counterexamples, not a claim that ∅ contains a hidden object. Whether ∅ is an element of A depends on A’s actual membership. Check both directions 1. Let A={1,2,3}, B={x∈ℤ:1≤x≤3}, and C={1,2}. Decide A=B and C=A, giving membership reasons. Hint for question 1 List the integers between 1 and 3 inclusive; then look for a member missing from C. Full solution to question 1 B has exactly 1, 2, and 3, so every member of A lies in B and every member of B lies in A; hence A=B. C⊆A, but 3∈A and 3∉C, so A⊄C and C≠A. 2. For S={∅,{∅}}, classify ∅∈S, {∅}∈S, and {∅}⊆S. Hint for question 2 There are exactly two members of S; then inspect the one member of {∅}. Full solution to question 2 Both ∅∈S and {∅}∈S are true because the roster explicitly lists both objects. Also {∅}⊆S is true: its only member, ∅, belongs to S. The expressions have different meanings even though all three happen to be true here. If the second roster feels strange, read each pair of braces from the inside out. Membership checks one object; subset checks every member of one set against another. That distinction prepares the power set, which is itself a set of subsets. Membership is the final check A set is fixed by its members. Order and repetition in a roster do not change it; two inclusions prove equality. A missing element gives a concrete counterexample to an inclusion. The proof of the two-inclusion rule is general, while a finite roster is a convenient worked case. Stop when you can explain why jazz∈A and {jazz}⊆A are different sentences. The power set takes this one step further by treating all subsets of A as members of a new set.

title: Why n objects have 2^n subsets
summary: Pair subsets of a finite set with binary strings to prove the 2-to-the-n counting rule.
text: Include it or skip it Suppose a lunch menu has three optional extras: olives, herbs, and lemon. A selection can include any collection of these extras, including none and all three. The question “How many selections?” becomes a set question once order is irrelevant and each extra may be chosen at most once. For a set A, its power set ℘(A) is the set of all subsets of A. A subset may be empty or equal to A. If A has n distinct members, choose a fixed order a₁,…,aₙ only for bookkeeping. To each subset S assign a binary string whose ith bit is 1 when aᵢ∈S and 0 otherwise. A binary string is a sequence of 0s and 1s. This is the local prerequisite capsule. We will prove that this correspondence is a bijection and therefore |℘(A)|=2ⁿ for a finite n-member set. “Bijection” means a pairing in which every object on either side has exactly one partner. The proof is finite; infinite power sets need a separate argument and are not described by an ordinary finite exponent. Write the eight selections Worked example. Take A={o,h,l}, abbreviating olives, herbs, lemon. Fix the order o,h,l. The string 101 means include olives and lemon but skip herbs; it corresponds to {o,l}. The string 000 corresponds to ∅, and 111 corresponds to A itself. Every subset of a three-element menu Bits Subset 000 ∅ 001 {l} 010 {h} 011 {h,l} 100 {o} 101 {o,l} 110 {o,h} 111 {o,h,l} The eight rows are not just a pattern to extrapolate. Each selection has one membership answer for each of the three distinct extras, so it produces one row. Conversely, each row tells us exactly which extras to include, so it produces one subset. This two-way recovery is the reason no selection is counted twice and no selection is missed. The finite power-set theorem Exact statement. If A is a finite set with |A|=n, where n is a nonnegative integer, then |℘(A)|=2ⁿ. For n=0, A=∅ and ℘(A)={∅}, which has one member, matching 2⁰=1. | ℘ ( A ) | = 2 n Complete finite proof. List the distinct elements as a₁,…,aₙ. Define F(S) as the length-n string with bit i equal to 1 exactly when aᵢ∈S. If F(S)=F(T), each aᵢ is in S exactly when it is in T, so S=T; thus F is injective. Given any binary string b₁…bₙ, take S={aᵢ:bᵢ=1}; then F(S) is that string, so F is surjective. Hence F is bijective. There are two independent bit choices in each of n positions, making 2ⁿ strings, and therefore 2ⁿ subsets. A failure case appears if the menu allows two servings of the same extra. The set {o,o} is just {o}; it cannot record “two olives portions.” With three possible quantities 0, 1, or 2 per extra, the choices would be 3³, assuming independent limits, and their objects would be quantity vectors rather than subsets. The theorem’s distinct, include-or-skip assumptions matter. Another easy confusion is ∅ versus {∅}. The first has no members; the second has one member, namely the empty set. For A=∅, the power set is {∅}, not ∅. This boundary case tests whether “all subsets” includes the empty subset, as it must. Encode and count 1. Let A={a,b,c,d} in that order. What subset corresponds to 0101? How many subsets include a but exclude d? Hint for question 1 Fix the first and fourth bits, then count the free middle bits. Full solution to question 1 0101 corresponds to {b,d}. For subsets with a included and d excluded, the bits are 1??0. Each ? is independently 0 or 1, yielding 2²=4 subsets: {a}, {a,b}, {a,c}, and {a,b,c}. 2. Someone claims a two-element set A has only three subsets because “choosing none is not a choice.” Refute the count and explain the boundary case. Hint for question 2 List the subsets of {u,v}. Full solution to question 2 For A={u,v}, ℘(A)={∅,{u},{v},{u,v}}, which has four members. The empty set is a legitimate subset because every member of ∅ lies in A vacuously. Excluding it changes the problem to counting nonempty subsets, which would give 2²−1=3. The listing and binary strings agree on every case because the inverse construction recovers each subset. A count alone would not show that correspondence; it could accidentally count the wrong objects. A subset is a string of decisions For a finite set of n distinct objects, each subset corresponds to one length-n binary string, so there are exactly 2ⁿ subsets. We proved both directions of the pairing and checked n=0. This result concerns finite n; a separate diagonal argument later shows an important difference for an infinite collection of binary decisions. A satisfying stopping point is to encode a subset and decode it again. That reversible translation is a simple example of the bijections used throughout mathematics.

title: When can a function be undone?
summary: Separate collisions from unused targets and prove when a two-sided inverse exists.
text: Can a coat-check ticket be undone? A coat check assigns each deposited coat one ticket code. If two coats receive the same code, a clerk holding that code cannot tell which coat to return. If a promised code is never used, a rule that goes from every possible code back to a coat has another problem. These are two distinct obstacles to reversing a function. A function f:A→B assigns each input in set A exactly one output in set B. A is the domain; B is the codomain. The function is injective if different inputs never share an output, and surjective if every object in B occurs as an output. A function that is both is bijective . The identity id_A sends each a∈A to itself. This is the local prerequisite capsule; no graph of a function is required. We will prove that f has a two-sided inverse g:B→A exactly when f is bijective. The word two-sided matters: g(f(a))=a for every input and f(g(b))=b for every target. Merely recovering some observed inputs is a weaker claim. Three small ticket systems Worked example. Let A={coat 1, coat 2} and B={red, blue}. If f sends coat 1 to red and coat 2 to blue, then g(red)=coat 1 and g(blue)=coat 2 reverses the assignment. Both directions work: g(f(coat 2))=coat 2 and f(g(red))=red. Three functions from two coats to ticket codes Codomain Assignments What fails? {red, blue} Both coats → red Collision: no left recovery {red, blue, green} 1 → red, 2 → blue Unused green: no right recovery {red, blue} 1 → red, 2 → blue Nothing: two-sided inverse exists In the collision row, any proposed g(red) can name only one coat; it cannot satisfy both g(f(coat 1))=coat 1 and g(f(coat 2))=coat 2. In the unused-code row, any proposed g(green) must be one of the two coats, but its f-image is red or blue, never green. This separates injectivity from surjectivity even for tiny finite sets. A two-sided inverse is exactly a bijection Exact statement. For sets A and B and a function f:A→B, there exists a function g:B→A satisfying g∘f=id_A and f∘g=id_B if and only if f is bijective. Empty-set boundary cases follow the same definitions: a function between two empty sets is bijective and is its own inverse. g ∘ f = id A , f ∘ g = id B Complete proof, forward direction. Suppose such a g exists. If f(a₁)=f(a₂), apply g to both sides: g(f(a₁))=g(f(a₂)), hence a₁=a₂. So f is injective. For any b∈B, b=f(g(b)), so b is an output of f. Thus f is surjective. Complete proof, reverse direction. Suppose f is bijective. For each b∈B, surjectivity supplies at least one a with f(a)=b, and injectivity makes that a unique. Define g(b) to be this unique a. Then g(f(a))=a by uniqueness, and f(g(b))=b by construction. The two equations hold for every a and b, so g is a two-sided inverse. This argument is about functions on sets; a numerical formula is not required. The failure case “same formula, different codomain” is instructive. Let f:{1,2}→{1,2,3} with f(x)=x. It is injective but not surjective because 3 is unused, so it has no two-sided inverse from the entire codomain. If the codomain were {1,2}, the assignment would be bijective. Naming the domain and codomain is part of a function claim. Optional clinic: does a whole set come back unchanged? Two different questions about a function Fix f:A→B. For a selected input set S⊆A, its image f(S)={f(s):s∈S} collects the outputs it reaches. For a selected target set T⊆B, its preimage f −1 (T)={a∈A:f(a)∈T} collects all inputs reaching T. This set preimage exists even if f has no inverse function. The braces matter: f(a) is an element, f({a}) is a singleton set, and f −1 ({b}) is the set of every possible input for b. An unreachable b has an empty preimage, not an undefined set. The preimage does not select one preferred input from a collision. Sending S forward and then taking its preimage can therefore add inputs. Starting with T, taking its preimage and sending that forward can instead remove targets that were never reached. Map I: A={a,b,c}, B={0,1,2,3}, with a↦0, b↦1, c↦2. Inputs are distinct; target 3 is unused. Map O: A={a,b,c,d}, B={0,1,2}, with a↦0, b↦0, c↦1, d↦2. Inputs a,b collide; every target is reached. The input round trip fills complete fibers Define C(S)=f −1 (f(S)). Membership gives the exact formula C(S)={a∈A: there exists s∈S with f(a)=f(s)}. Indeed a∈C(S) means f(a)∈f(S), which by the image definition means some s∈S has the same output. If a∈S, take s=a. This proves S⊆C(S) ; no selected input can be lost. The fiber above a reached target b is f −1 ({b}), the entire group of inputs sharing that output. C(S) includes every member of each fiber touched by S. Hence C(S)=S exactly when S already contains every touched fiber in full . Empty S and all of A satisfy that condition even for a noninjective function. For map O, {a,c} grows to {a,b,c}, while {a,b,c} is recovered exactly; neither result changes the collision a,b. A second application adds nothing: f(C(S))=f(S), because every newly included input has an output already reached by S, and S⊆C(S). Thus C(C(S))=C(S). This is saturation by equal-output classes, rather than a recovery of the original individual inputs. The equivalence-class lesson supplies the grouping idea; the quotient lesson already requires full saturated preimages at a seam. This calculation gives that whole-fiber requirement a finite set test. The output round trip keeps only reached targets Define R(T)=f(f −1 (T)). Its exact value is R(T)=T∩f(A) . If b∈R(T), some a∈f −1 (T) has f(a)=b, so b lies both in T and in the full image f(A). Conversely, if b∈T∩f(A), an a with f(a)=b exists; that a belongs to f −1 (T), so b∈R(T). The two membership implications prove the identity. Consequently R(T)=T exactly when every selected target is reached , or T⊆f(A). No target outside T can be added. For map I, {1,3} shrinks to {1}; selecting {1,2} instead gives exact recovery even though the full codomain still contains unused 3. The continuity lesson already develops preimages of intervals; here the question is what survives both operations, before making any topological claim. “This set” and “every set” have different strength f is injective if and only if C(S)=S for every S⊆A. If f is injective, f(a)=f(s) forces a=s, so C adds no member. Conversely, suppose every S is recovered and f(a)=f(a′). For S={a}, the equal output puts a′ in C({a})={a}, forcing a′=a. This proves injectivity. f is surjective if and only if R(T)=T for every T⊆B. If f(A)=B, the output identity gives R(T)=T∩B=T. Conversely, apply the assumed recovery to T=B: it gives B=R(B)=f(A). Thus f reaches its full codomain. Both universal recovery conditions together are equivalent to bijectivity, agreeing with the original inverse theorem. Success for one selected set does not establish either universal condition. These arguments cover finite and infinite sets and do not choose representatives for every fiber. If A=∅, the sole input subset is ∅ and the empty function is injective; every output subset recovers exactly only when B=∅. A function from a nonempty A to empty B does not exist. The two finite maps in the inspector illustrate the theorem; they do not prove the assertion for arbitrary functions. For a finite map with r reached outputs there are 2 r recovered input subsets: choose whether to include each whole nonempty fiber. There are also 2 r recovered target subsets: choose any subset of the reached outputs. For map I this gives 8/8 input selections and 8/16 target selections; for O it gives 8/16 input selections and 8/8 target selections. The total selection counts include empty and full sets. Empty S and full A always recover, but full target B recovers exactly when the map is surjective: it fails for I and succeeds for O. The classical image/preimage definitions and round-trip criteria are developed in Hammack, Book of Proof , §12.6, printed pp.242–243 , including exercise 12. The examples, inspector and changed task here are original. Whole-class saturation is also an existing closure construction; this clinic specializes it to equal-output classes and pairs it with target recovery. The controls inspect only the two stated maps, using exact membership; no samples or numerical tolerances decide an equality. Focus a table region to scroll it with arrow keys on a narrow screen. Test both recovery directions 1. Let f:{0,1,2}→{a,b,c} send 0↦b, 1↦c, 2↦a. Write its inverse and verify both equations at one input and one code. Hint for question 1 Reverse each arrow, then compose. Full solution to question 1 The inverse g sends a↦2, b↦0, c↦1. For input 1, g(f(1))=g(c)=1. For code a, f(g(a))=f(2)=a. Each of the three outputs appears once, so the same checks cover all inputs and codes by the definition. 2. For f:ℤ→ℤ given by f(n)=2n, decide injectivity and surjectivity; explain whether a two-sided inverse ℤ→ℤ exists. Hint for question 2 Odd integers are possible codomain values. Full solution to question 2 If 2m=2n, then m=n, so f is injective. It is not surjective onto ℤ because no integer maps to 1: 2n=1 has no integer solution. Therefore no two-sided inverse ℤ→ℤ exists. On the codomain of even integers, an inverse g(2n)=n does exist. Do not confuse an inverse function with the preimage of a set. Preimages can be formed for any function; a two-sided inverse function exists exactly under the proved bijection condition. Optional exercise 3: new function, clipped domain and whole intervals Write an attempt before revealing a hint or answer. This task changes both the map and the kinds of sets; it is outside the inspector's controls. Let q:[−2,1]→[0,9] be q(x)=(x+1)², with S=[−1,1/2] and T=[1/4,25/4]. Find the full image q([−2,1]). Decide injectivity and surjectivity onto the declared codomain, supplying witnesses. Calculate q(S) and q −1 (q(S)). Give exactly the additional inputs, with endpoint status. Why can no original input be lost? Calculate q −1 (T) and q(q −1 (T)). Give exactly the lost targets, with endpoint status. Why can no unselected target be added? Define the different function q₊:[−1,1]→[0,4] with the same formula. Find its inverse, check both compositions on their domains, and recompute the two round trips for S and T′=T∩[0,4]. Does this make the original q invertible? Hint for exercise 3 Put u=x+1, keeping its allowed interval. A condition L≤u²≤U produces two signed intervals before you intersect with the declared domain. A boundary already in S or already recovered is not an added or lost member. On q₊'s domain, x+1≥0, so the principal square root returns x+1. Full solution to exercise 3 (a) For x∈[−2,1], u=x+1 ranges over [−1,2], so 0≤u²≤4. Every y∈[0,4] is attained by x=√y−1∈[−1,1]. Thus the full image is [0,4] , rather than the declared [0,9]. The allowed target 9 is unreachable, so q is not surjective. Also q(−2)=q(0)=1 at distinct allowed inputs, so q is not injective. (b) On S, u∈[0,3/2], so q(S)=[0,9/4]. Pulling that back imposes |x+1|≤3/2, giving [−5/2,1/2] before the domain restriction. Intersect with [−2,1] to obtain q −1 (q(S))=[−2,1/2] . The added set is [−2,−1) : −2 is newly included, while −1 was already selected. No s∈S can be lost, since its own output belongs to q(S). The set touched fibers without containing all their permitted inputs. (c) The inequality 1/4≤(x+1)²≤25/4 gives [−7/2,−3/2]∪[−1/2,3/2] before restricting the domain. Therefore q −1 (T)=[−2,−3/2]∪[−1/2,1] . The first interval maps to [1/4,1] and the second to [1/4,4], so q(q −1 (T))=[1/4,4] . This is exactly T∩q([−2,1]). The lost set is (4,25/4] : 4 is reached and kept; 25/4 was selected and is lost. No unselected output can be added because membership in the preimage required the output to belong to T. (d) For q₊, x+1∈[0,2], where squaring is one-to-one and reaches [0,4]. The inverse is r:[0,4]→[−1,1], r(y)=√y−1 . For x∈[−1,1], r(q₊(x))=√((x+1)²)−1=x because x+1≥0. For y∈[0,4], q₊(r(y))=(√y)²=y. Here S remains allowed and q₊ −1 (q₊(S))=[−1,1/2]=S. Restate the target selection in the new codomain as T′=[1/4,4] ; its preimage is [−1/2,1] and its image returns exactly T′. Restricting the input domain and changing the codomain makes a different, bijective function. It does not repair the original q's collision or fill its missing targets. Preimages of arbitrary ambient target sets can also be defined; the named target selections here are explicitly subsets of each current codomain. Reversal needs no collisions and no gaps Injectivity lets a code identify at most one input; surjectivity ensures every target code identifies at least one. Together they make exactly one, giving a two-sided inverse. We proved both implications for arbitrary sets and used finite tickets to display the two failure modes. Stop when you can name the domain and codomain and test both properties. The same concern about unique representatives will reappear when a relation groups objects into classes.

title: Grouping by an equivalence relation
summary: Prove same-weekday congruence is an equivalence relation and understand its classes.
text: Different dates, one weekday A community hall runs an event every seven days. Two dates can be different numbers but occupy the same place in this weekly cycle. We want a rule that groups dates correctly without accidentally putting a date in two incompatible groups. Use integers to label days, with day 0 some chosen Monday. Say a~b when 7 divides a−b; in other words a−b=7k for some integer k. A relation is a rule that can hold between pairs of objects. A relation is an equivalence relation when it is reflexive (a~a), symmetric (a~b implies b~a), and transitive (a~b and b~c imply a~c). These definitions and integer divisibility form the local prerequisite capsule. Our goal is to prove that same-weekday relation meets all three conditions and to see how its equivalence classes form a partition. The calendar story motivates the rule, but the proof is arithmetic about all integers, including negative day labels. Three dates in one class Worked example. Days 2, 9, and −5 are in the same weekly position. The differences 9−2=7 and 2−(−5)=7 are divisible by 7; also 9−(−5)=14. If day 2 was a Wednesday under our starting convention, then so are day 9 and day −5. The labels can be arbitrarily far apart; the relation records only remainder modulo 7. Membership in the class of day 2 Day b b−2 7 divides b−2? −5 −7 Yes 2 0 Yes 9 7 Yes 10 8 No The equivalence class [2] is all b with b~2, not just the three displayed dates. A finite table illustrates membership; it does not enumerate infinitely many members. Day 10 belongs instead to class [3], since 10−3=7. Every integer lies in one of the seven remainder classes [0] through [6]. Why same weekday is an equivalence relation Exact statement. On ℤ, the relation a~b defined by 7|(a−b) is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive. Consequently its classes are either identical or disjoint and partition ℤ into seven classes. a ∼ b ⇔ 7 | ( a − b ) Complete proof of the three properties. Reflexivity: a−a=0=7·0, so a~a. Symmetry: if a−b=7k, then b−a=7(−k), so b~a. Transitivity: if a−b=7k and b−c=7ℓ, add the equations to get a−c=7(k+ℓ), so a~c. Each step uses only that integers are closed under negation and addition. For the partition claim, every a belongs to [a] by reflexivity. If a class [a] and [b] share some c, then c~a and c~b. Symmetry gives a~c, and transitivity gives a~b. For any x~a, transitivity with a~b yields x~b; the reverse direction follows by symmetry. Thus [a]=[b]. Classes that meet cannot be partly overlapping. Division with remainder gives every integer a exactly one remainder r in {0,…,6}; hence exactly seven different classes occur. The last statement uses the standard integer division algorithm, stated here but not reproved. A failure case shows why all three tests matter. Define aRb on integers by a≤b. This relation is reflexive and transitive, but not symmetric: 2≤3 while 3≤2 is false. The “class” of 2 under this rule would not behave like a same-weekday group. Merely seeing overlapping arrows in a drawing cannot establish equivalence. Test a rule, then a class 1. For relation a~b when 5 divides a−b, decide whether −7 and 8 are related, and list three other integers in [−7]. Hint for question 1 Compute the difference, then add or subtract multiples of 5. Full solution to question 1 8−(−7)=15=5·3, so they are related. Examples in [−7] include −12, −2, and 3, because each differs from −7 by a multiple of 5. The full class is {−7+5k:k∈ℤ}. 2. On ℤ define aRb when a and b have the same sign, with zero called neither positive nor negative. If “same sign” means both positive or both negative, is R an equivalence relation? Hint for question 2 Check reflexivity at zero first. Full solution to question 2 No. For a=0, neither “both positive” nor “both negative” holds for (0,0), so 0R0 is false. Reflexivity fails. One could repair the rule by putting zero in its own class, but that would be a different relation requiring a fresh check of all three properties. A correct classification states the underlying set and the exact rule. Otherwise a special case such as zero can be silently lost. In the weekday relation, every integer, including zero and negative labels, passes reflexivity. A relation earns its classes The divisible-difference rule for seven-day cycles is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive. Those properties make its classes disjoint or identical, and integer remainders supply seven of them. We proved the relation properties and the class-overlap implication; the standard division algorithm supplies the exact count of seven. Stop when you can test all three properties on a proposed grouping rule and exhibit a member of a class. This finite-cycle grouping is distinct from the infinity question of whether every infinite collection can be listed.

title: Why no list catches every binary sequence
summary: Construct a binary sequence missing from any proposed enumeration of all infinite binary sequences.
text: A list that misses a diary Imagine an infinite yes/no diary: one answer for each day, with 1 for yes and 0 for no. Each answer is called a bit . Could someone list every possible diary in rows numbered 1, 2, 3, …? The rows may be infinite themselves, and the proposed list may be clever. Cantor's diagonal idea constructs one diary that differs from each listed row on a particular day. The short infinity discovery matched positive whole numbers with positive evens. The bijection lesson checked that matching for collisions and missed targets. Here the target is different: the collection of all infinite binary diaries. We will show that every proposed numbered list misses a target. A diary is a rule for every day Here ℕ = {1, 2, 3, …}; days and rows start at 1. A binary sequence is an infinite diary whose every entry is 0 or 1. Writing s : ℕ → {0, 1} says that the rule s assigns one of those two bits to each positive whole-number day. Its day- n entry is s n . The subscript identifies a position; it is not a multiplier. A numbered list is another rule: give it a row number and it supplies a whole diary. An enumeration covers every diary in the target collection. Repeated rows are allowed. A set is countable if it is finite or can be completely listed in positive whole-number positions. An infinite set that cannot be completely listed is uncountable . These words describe mathematical lists, not how long a person would take to write them. A finite grid can show the construction, but the proof must give a difference from every numbered row, including rows far beyond the picture. Choose a different answer on one day per row Worked example. Suppose a proposed list begins with the four diaries below. The diagonal uses day 1 of diary 1, day 2 of diary 2, and so on. A star marks each chosen entry. Build a new diary by replacing each chosen 0 with 1 and each chosen 1 with 0. Only the first four days and rows are shown. A star marks a diagonal entry to flip. Diary Day 1 Day 2 Day 3 Day 4 Row 1 0* 1 1 0 Row 2 1 1* 0 0 Row 3 0 0 0* 1 Row 4 1 1 1 0* New diary 1 0 1 1 The chosen entries are 0, 1, 0, 0, so the new diary begins 1, 0, 1, 1. It differs from row 1 on day 1, row 2 on day 2, row 3 on day 3, and row 4 on day 4. Two diaries are identical only if every day's answer agrees; one differing day is enough to rule out a match. Before going on, point to the entry that rules out row 3. It is the third day: row 3 has 0, while the new diary has 1. The later entries in either diary cannot undo that difference. The full construction applies the same instruction to every positive row number. Later rows determine later bits; the four displayed rows do not determine the entire new diary. Turn the construction into a proof Read the row and day separately Write a r,c for the entry in row r , day c . For example, a 2,3 is row 2's day-3 bit, which is 0 in the table. The comma separates the two positions. Write d n for day n of the new diary. Then a n,n means the diagonal entry: row n , day n . The notation {0, 1} ℕ names the set of all infinite binary sequences: all functions from ℕ to {0, 1}. Here the superscript names a collection of functions; it is not ordinary numerical exponentiation. A surjective list would reach every member of this collection. Exact statement. There is no surjective function from ℕ onto {0, 1} ℕ . In words, no list with positive whole-number row labels contains every infinite binary diary. d n = 1 − a n , n Read this as “the new bit on day n is one minus row n 's bit on that day.” Subtracting from one flips a binary bit: 1 − 0 = 1, and 1 − 1 = 0. Allow any proposed complete list. Suppose rows 1, 2, 3, … contain every infinite binary diary. We make no assumption about how the list was ordered, and rows may repeat. Define a valid new diary. For every positive whole number n , set d n = 1 − a n,n . Every row has an entry on every day. Each chosen entry is 0 or 1, so its opposite is an allowed bit too. The rule therefore specifies a whole infinite binary diary d . Rule out whichever row is named. Choose any row number k . On day k , that row contains a k,k , while d contains its opposite. The diaries differ on that day, so d is not row k . The letter k stands for an arbitrary positive row number, rather than just a row we drew. Contradict completeness. The same reasoning rules out every numbered row. Yet d is a valid binary diary, so a list containing every such diary would have to include it. This contradiction defeats the assumption that the proposed list was complete. Because the list was arbitrary, no complete list exists. The rule defines each bit without requiring us to calculate all bits in time. The finite picture alone would show only four differences. The proof goes further by choosing any row number k and naming the day that defeats it. Thus the collection of infinite binary sequences is uncountable. Boundary: finite strings are different. All finite binary strings can be listed: the empty string first; then 0 and 1; then 00, 01, 10, 11; then all length-three strings, and so on. Each length contributes a finite block. Any particular finite string has only finitely many earlier blocks and entries before it, so it reaches a numbered position. Trying the diary proof here can fail because a finite string in row n might have no day- n entry. Alternatively, padding all strings with zeros creates a different target: diaries eventually equal to zero. A diagonal diary need not belong to that restricted target. Name the differing day 1. Calculate. A proposed list begins row 1 = 000…, row 2 = 101…, row 3 = 110…. What are the first three new bits, and where does the new diary differ from each displayed row? Hint for question 1 Read day 1 of row 1, day 2 of row 2, and day 3 of row 3. Then flip those three bits. Full solution to question 1 The chosen entries are 0, 0, 0. In particular, row 2 has second bit 0 and row 3 has third bit 0. The new diary begins 111…. It differs from row 1 on day 1, row 2 on day 2, and row 3 on day 3. Later rows determine its later bits; the displayed prefix does not tell us those bits. 2. Explain. Someone suggests that the new diary might be row 10,000, because the picture showed only four rows. Which day rules out that suggestion? Hint for question 2 Use the proposed row number as a day number too. Full solution to question 2 Day 10,000. The construction chooses the opposite of row 10,000's answer on that day. The two diaries therefore differ there, regardless of their earlier answers. The rule applies to that row just as it applies to the first four. 3. Change the list. Put the missing diary at the front of the old list, shifting every old row down one. Have you made a complete list? Hint for question 3 The new list has a new diagonal. Apply the construction to that list rather than reusing the old diagonal. Full solution to question 3 You have included the particular diary previously shown to be missing. But the proof applies to any numbered list, including the new one. Flip the new list's diagonal to construct a diary that differs from each of its rows. That new diary is absent. The theorem does not say one fixed diary is missing from every list; the constructed diary depends on the list being challenged. One day defeats each row No enumeration of infinite binary diaries is complete. On day n , choose the opposite of row n 's answer. Then whichever row k someone names, day k proves the new diary is different. The finite table shows the construction; the arbitrary row number makes the proof infinite. A useful place to stop is explaining that argument without the subscripts. On another evening, the diagonal sequence lab lets you change a finite display and check each differing position. Its finite rows illustrate the construction; they do not establish the infinite claim by themselves.

title: The collection that cannot be a set
summary: Derive Russell’s contradiction from unrestricted comprehension and identify the assumption it rejects.
text: A filing rule turns on itself Imagine a registry that is meant to contain exactly those registries that do not list themselves. Ask whether this new registry lists itself. If it does, its rule says it should not. If it does not, its rule says it should. This is a warning about which membership conditions are allowed to define sets. Write x∈S when x is a member of set S, and x∉S when it is not. Unrestricted comprehension is the proposed principle that every property P(x) determines a set {x:P(x)} of all objects satisfying it. Here we pretend that the universe ranges over all sets and use the property x∉x. Contradiction means deriving a proposition and its negation from an assumption. These are the local prerequisites; familiarity with a formal axiomatic set theory is not required. Our bounded claim is that unrestricted comprehension is inconsistent with ordinary classical membership reasoning. We will derive the contradiction carefully. We will not infer that everyday finite sets fail or present a full replacement axiom system. Try both answers Worked example. Under the unrestricted rule, form R={x:x∉x}. To decide whether an object y belongs to R, inspect whether y belongs to itself. For ordinary small sets whose members are numbers, this self-membership question usually has an easy negative answer. The decisive test, however, is y=R. Since R is purportedly a set in the same universe, the rule must answer for R too. Both possible answers for the proposed set R Assume Apply the defining rule Conflict R∈R Members of R are exactly sets not in themselves, so R∉R Yes R∉R R satisfies “not in itself,” so R∈R Yes The table is not a computer program caught in an endless loop. It displays a logical inconsistency in the assumption that this particular property defines a set in the unrestricted universe. The two cases exhaust true and false under classical logic. Changing an example registry or adding more ordinary members cannot repair the self-membership condition. The contradiction is conditional Exact statement. In classical logic, the schema “for every property P, there exists a set S such that for every x, x∈S iff P(x)” is inconsistent when x ranges over all sets and P(x) may be x∉x. This is Russell’s paradox. The derivation rejects that unrestricted schema, not the use of sets in a restricted theory. R ∈ R ⇔ R ∉ R Complete derivation within the assumed schema. Instantiate comprehension with P(x) meaning x∉x. It supplies a set R satisfying, for every set x, x∈R iff x∉x. Substitute x=R. Then R∈R iff R∉R. If R∈R is true, the right side says it is false. If R∈R is false, the biconditional says the right side is true and therefore R∈R is true. No classical truth value works. Thus the assumption that such an R exists must be rejected. The proof boundary matters. This argument does not prove that a familiar set such as {1,2} is inconsistent, nor that every collection described in words is a set. A standard restricted idea is separation : given an already existing set A, form {x∈A:P(x)}. Its result is drawn from A rather than from an alleged set of every set. We mention the restriction to locate the issue; proving a whole axiomatic system consistent is far beyond this article. A nearby failure is the “barber who shaves exactly the villagers who do not shave themselves.” If the barber is a villager, the condition contradicts itself; if the barber is outside the village, there may be no contradiction. The domain is crucial. Likewise Russell’s derivation requires R to be among the objects over which the comprehension condition quantifies. Hiding that assumption makes the paradox seem like a trick of grammar. Locate the assumption that breaks 1. Suppose a finite set A={1,2,3}. Define B={x∈A:x is even}. Compute B and explain why checking whether B∈B does not recreate Russell’s contradiction. Hint for question 1 The membership rule for B applies only to x already in A. Full solution to question 1 B={2}. Because B is a set and A contains only the numbers 1, 2, 3, B∉A in this setup. The definition says x∈B iff x∈A and x is even; substituting x=B makes the right side false because B∉A. No equation B∈B iff B∉B follows. The extra domain condition prevents the unrestricted self-membership equivalence. 2. A speaker says, “Russell’s paradox proves there are no infinite sets.” Identify the faulty inference and state what the derivation actually rules out. Hint for question 2 Find the assumption used in the derivation. Full solution to question 2 The derivation assumes unrestricted comprehension over all sets for the property x∉x. It shows that schema cannot hold in classical set theory. It does not use finiteness or infinity of R, and it does not rule out particular infinite sets such as the natural numbers in standard axiomatic theories. The contradiction concerns an unrestricted formation rule. Both questions force attention to the quantifier domain. The self-membership substitution is legal in either definition, but restricted separation adds the condition R∈A; without it, the biconditional does not force a contradiction. A condition does not always define a set If every property defined a set over all sets, the property x∉x would define R and force R∈R iff R∉R. That is a complete conditional contradiction. It identifies an invalid formation principle; it does not invalidate the ordinary operations with specified sets used earlier in this topic. The stopping point is to name the assumption and the substitution x=R. A deeper study of axiomatic set theory asks which restricted formation and existence principles can be adopted, but this lesson makes no consistency claim about an entire system.

title: How to read a definition without fear
summary: Classify even integers by finding valid integer witnesses, and see why the witness domain matters.
text: What does the word require? A definition is a test with exact conditions. A number being called even does not mean that it looks familiar, ends in a preferred digit, or appeared in a list of examples. It means that the number can be written as twice an integer. The phrase “an integer” matters: halves such as 3/2 do not qualify as witnesses. Today the task is small and complete: decide whether given integers satisfy a definition, and explain each answer by showing either a witness or why no witness is possible. Background capsule. Integers include negative whole numbers, zero, and positive whole numbers. A witness is a value that makes an existential condition true. The symbol ∃ means “there exists,” and ⇔ means “if and only if”: both directions of the statement are required. We will use arithmetic and these meanings locally; no previous proof course is needed. Look for the hidden integer Worked example. The formal definition is that an integer n is even exactly when there is an integer k with n = 2 k . For 18, choose k = 9; the equality 18 = 2·9 is a certificate that anyone can check. For −14, choose k = −7. Negative values do not require a new rule. For 0, choose k = 0. The witness need not be positive. Now try 19. Solving 19 = 2 k would require k = 19/2, which lies strictly between 9 and 10 and is not an integer. Thus 19 is not even. Notice the different jobs: to establish evenness we produce one admissible witness; to establish failure we rule out every admissible witness. A guess such as “I tried k = 9 and it failed” is insufficient, because another integer might work. Reading the same definition three ways Claim Required witness Decision 18 is even 9, since 2·9 = 18 True −14 is even −7, since 2·(−7) = −14 True 19 is even 19/2 is not an integer False The two directions of a definition n is even ⇔ ∃ k ∈ ℤ : n = 2 k Read the line aloud “An integer n is even if and only if there is an integer k such that n equals two times k .” The set symbol ℤ names all the integers; ∈ means “belongs to,” and the colon means “such that.” Writing 2 k is shorthand for 2 × k . The letter k is a name for the witness you need to find, rather than another fact you are expected to know. It can change with n : 18 uses 9, while −14 uses −7. The definition does not ask for one witness that works for every integer. Exact claim. For every integer n , this equivalence is the criterion for evenness. The forward direction says that if n is even, an integer witness exists. The reverse direction says that whenever an integer witness exists, n is even. Here the equivalence is a definition, not a theorem discovered by testing. It licenses both uses without requiring a further proof of the vocabulary. The calculations above justify particular classifications by substitution and by showing why 19/2 is outside the allowed set. A useful change of words is “2 divides n .” Divisibility by 2 is itself defined through an integer multiplier, so it states the same condition. But changing the domain changes the question. If k were allowed to be any real number, every integer would equal 2 times some real number, including 19 = 2·9.5. The integer restriction therefore carries the mathematical content. A frequent failure is to quote the formula while silently widening the set from which the witness is chosen. We have classified three integers and stated the general criterion. We have not yet proved broad facts about sums or products of even numbers. Such a proof starts by introducing witnesses for the inputs and then constructs a witness for the result; the direct-proof lesson develops that move. Use the witness test Exercise 1. Decide whether −22 and 23 are even. Supply an integer witness for any true claim and explain a false one without relying on a last-digit rule. Hint for exercise 1 Divide each candidate by 2 and check whether the quotient is an integer. Full solution to exercise 1 −22 = 2·(−11), and −11 is an integer, so −22 is even. If 23 = 2 k , then k = 23/2 = 11.5. No integer equals 11.5, so the required witness does not exist and 23 is not even. Exercise 2. Someone writes, “Every integer is even because n = 2( n /2).” Locate the exact mistake, then decide whether 0 is even. Hint for exercise 2 Ask whether the parenthesized value always belongs to ℤ. Full solution to exercise 2 The displayed arithmetic equality is true, but n /2 need not be an integer; for n = 1 it equals 1/2. That is a counterexample to the proposed argument and claim. For n = 0, the choice k = 0 is an integer and 0 = 2·0, so 0 is even. Keep the domain attached To use a definition, identify its subject, its conditions, and the set from which each variable may come. A single witness establishes an “exists” statement; a missing witness must be justified across the full permitted domain. The even-number example is complete at this scale. Next, direct proof will use two witnesses to make a new one, while testing a conjecture will explain why examples alone cannot establish a statement about every integer.

title: One counterexample ends a universal claim
summary: Use a smallest counterexample to refute a universal prime claim and distinguish testing from proof.
text: How many successes are enough? A pattern can be beautiful and false. Suppose a friend tries the formula n ² + n + 3 and gets the primes 3 and 5 for the starting values 0 and 1. It is tempting to announce a formula that always gives primes. Before doing that, we must fix the claim’s domain and understand what a finite check can establish. Our precise claim is: “For every nonnegative integer n , n ² + n + 3 is prime.” We will test it one input at a time. Background capsule. A prime is an integer greater than 1 whose positive divisors are exactly 1 and itself. “For every” asks for all members of the stated domain, whereas “there exists” asks for at least one. A counterexample to a universal claim is one admissible input for which its asserted conclusion is false. We use elementary multiplication and divisibility; the lesson itself supplies the logic. Keep an honest test ledger Worked example. Evaluate the proposed expression at n = 0: it is 3, prime. At n = 1 it is 5, prime. At n = 2 it is 9 = 3·3, composite. The first two successes are accurate observations. The third row is an admissible input that contradicts the “every” claim. A computer could test a million more values, but those results would not erase the row at 2. For this claim, the smallest nonnegative counterexample is 2 because we checked the only smaller domain members, 0 and 1. Testing a universal prime claim n n²+n+3 Prime? 0 3 Yes 1 5 Yes 2 9 = 3·3 No The optional experiment can search more claims, but this table already contains the complete refutation. A different claim might survive every tested input and still fail later. Keep “tested through N ” separate from “proved for all n .” The logic of one failing input Translate the symbols first Here ℕ means {0, 1, 2, …}, the nonnegative integers. Some books start ℕ at 1, so always check the convention. The symbol ∀ means “for every,” ∃ means “there exists,” ∈ means “belongs to,” and ¬ means “not.” P ( n ) is a name for a claim about n , with a yes-or-no answer. The line below says: “The claim that every allowed input works is false if some allowed input fails.” You can use that sentence without memorising the notation. ∀ n ∈ ℕ , P ( n ) is false if ∃ k ∈ ℕ : ¬ P ( k ) Exact theorem of logic. A universal statement is false exactly when at least one value in its domain fails the predicate. In our worked claim, let P ( n ) mean “ n ² + n + 3 is prime.” The choice k = 2 lies in the domain, and P (2) is false because 9 has divisor 3. This is a complete disproof of that universal statement. It is not a proof that the formula is always composite or that other polynomial formulas fail; the result is limited to the stated claim. Why can passing cases not do the opposite job? A list of tests has a last index. The universal claim includes inputs beyond it. Unless another argument covers them, the ledger says nothing about those inputs. Even a list of 0 through 1000 has no logical bridge to 1001 or to every later number. Testing is still valuable: it can reveal a counterexample, suggest a theorem, or catch arithmetic mistakes in a proposed proof. Its output must be described accurately. One repair is to narrow the claim to a finite set we really checked: “For n = 0 or 1, the expression is prime.” That statement is true and the two calculations prove it by exhausting its domain. Another repair might be a new infinite statement with a valid argument, but we cannot conjure it from two rows. A counterexample changes what we are entitled to say. Refute, then repair Exercise 1. Test “For every positive integer n , n ² + 1 is odd.” Find the smallest counterexample and justify that it is smallest. Hint for exercise 1 Start at the first positive integer and check parity explicitly. Full solution to exercise 1 At n = 1, n ² + 1 = 2, which is even because 2 = 2·1. Since 1 is the smallest positive integer, it is automatically the smallest counterexample. No search over later inputs is needed. Exercise 2. A claim says “Every integer n with n ² = 1 equals 1.” Refute it, then state a true finite replacement and justify it. Hint for exercise 2 Factor n ² − 1 and remember negative integers. Full solution to exercise 2 n = −1 is an admissible counterexample: (−1)² = 1 but −1 ≠ 1. The repaired statement is “An integer with n ² = 1 is either −1 or 1.” Indeed ( n − 1)( n + 1) = 0, and a product of two integers can be zero only if at least one factor is zero. Solving gives the two stated values; both square to 1. Give each result its proper scope A single valid counterexample completely refutes a universal claim. A finite run of successful checks establishes only its tested cases unless the domain itself is finite and exhausted. The smallest-counterexample label also needs a domain and verification of all earlier inputs. This is the useful stopping point. To turn a revised pattern into a theorem, map its assumptions and conclusion before choosing a proof method.

title: What a proof actually owes
summary: Trace assumptions through justified implications and catch a false converse.
text: Where does the conclusion come from? A persuasive argument can quietly use an assumption it never earned. A proof map makes that gap visible. Its boxes hold the given facts, the intermediate claim, and the exact destination; its arrows must carry reasons. We will map a familiar integer claim: if an integer is divisible by 6, then it is even. The destination is deliberately modest, so attention can go to the reasoning rather than difficult arithmetic. Background capsule. “ a divides b ” means that b = ak for some integer k . An implication P ⇒ Q promises that whenever P holds, Q holds. To show an integer is even, produce an integer j such that it equals 2 j . These are all the ingredients needed here; a proof map is a reading and writing aid, not a formal deduction calculus. Label every arrow Worked example. Take any integer n divisible by 6. By the definition of divisibility, n = 6 k for some integer k . Rewrite 6 k as 2(3 k ). Because integers are closed under multiplication, 3 k is an integer. It is the witness required by the definition of evenness. Thus n is even. The proof has a start, a bridge, and a destination, and each transition names its licence. Map for “divisible by 6 implies even” Place Statement Reason Given 6 divides n Hypothesis Witness n = 6k for integer k Definition of divisibility Bridge n = 2(3k), with 3k integer Algebra and closure Goal n is even Definition of evenness The bridge matters more than the picture. If the table merely drew an arrow from “6 divides n ” to “even” with no witness, the reader would have to invent the missing argument. A map can also expose a false claim. Try reversing the arrow: 2 is even, but 6 does not divide 2, so “even implies divisible by 6” is false. Composition of valid implications Letters can stand for whole claims Here P , Q , and R name statements, rather than numbers to calculate. Read P ⇒ Q as “if P is true, then Q is true.” For example, P could mean “6 divides n ” and R could mean “ n is even.” The long arrow in the middle says that the two implications on its left justify the implication on its right. None of these arrows promises a reverse direction. P ⇒ Q , Q ⇒ R ⟹ P ⇒ R Exact claim. For propositions P , Q , and R , two valid implications P ⇒ Q and Q ⇒ R give P ⇒ R . To prove it, suppose P holds. The first implication gives Q ; the second then gives R . That is the whole logical justification. In the integer example, the first arrow translates divisibility to a witness; the second reshapes that witness into one for evenness. Proof maps have a boundary. They show dependencies, but they do not make an invalid arrow valid. Every arrow still needs a definition, a prior theorem, or a proved calculation. In particular, the map cannot turn P ⇒ Q into Q ⇒ P . That reversed statement is the converse , and it needs its own proof or counterexample. Our n = 2 example refutes the converse immediately. Nor may a map change its variable midway without saying so. The original claim concerns any integer divisible by 6. If the calculation were done only for n = 12, it would establish one instance, not the universal theorem. The phrase “take any integer n satisfying the hypothesis” and the symbolic witness keep the proof general. Audit the arrows Exercise 1. Map a proof that every integer divisible by 10 is divisible by 5. Name the witness at each step. Hint for exercise 1 Start with n = 10 k , then factor 10 as 5·2. Full solution to exercise 1 Let n be any integer divisible by 10. Then n = 10 k for an integer k . Rewriting gives n = 5(2 k ). Since 2 k is an integer, it witnesses that 5 divides n . The map is hypothesis → integer witness → factorization → conclusion. Exercise 2. Someone argues, “If a number is divisible by 4, it is even. Therefore every even number is divisible by 4.” Identify the arrow error and give a counterexample. Hint for exercise 2 Write the given implication and the claimed implication in opposite directions. Full solution to exercise 2 The given arrow is divisible by 4 ⇒ even, whereas the claim reverses it to even ⇒ divisible by 4. Reversal is not licensed by implication. The integer 2 is even because 2 = 2·1, but 2/4 is not an integer, so 4 does not divide 2. This is a counterexample to the claimed converse. Keep the arrows honest A proof map is useful when every node is a precise claim and every arrow has a checkable reason. We completely proved the divisibility example and the general rule for chaining implications; we did not build a formal logic system. If you want to construct the witness in a new setting, the direct-proof lesson makes that technique the main event. If an arrow reverses, test its converse separately.

title: A first direct proof with even numbers
summary: Build a witness to prove that the sum of any two even integers is even.
text: Can two witnesses make a third? Adding 4 and 8 gives 12: two even integers have made another even integer. That sounds obvious after a few examples, but a proof must handle every pair of even integers, including zero and negative values. The useful move is to unpack “even” twice, then build the witness demanded by the conclusion. This lesson gives a complete direct proof of one theorem and a pattern that can be reused carefully elsewhere. Background capsule. An integer x is even exactly when x = 2 a for some integer a . Integers are closed under addition: if a and b are integers, so is a + b . “Direct proof” means start from the hypothesis and reach the conclusion through justified steps. These facts, plus elementary algebra, are all we require. Work one pair, then remove its special numbers Worked example. Take −8 and 14. The first is 2(−4), the second is 2·7, and their sum is 6 = 2·3. The result is even. The calculation suggests something general: the witnesses −4 and 7 add to the result’s witness 3. The special pair helps us see a construction, but it cannot by itself prove a statement about every pair. We now replace the two numerical witnesses by arbitrary integers. Where the witness comes from Input Evenness witness Result −8 −4 −8 + 14 = 2(−4 + 7) = 2·3 14 7 A common failure is to write “the sum of two even numbers is even” as the middle step. That is exactly the claim being proved, so it supplies no reason. Another is to choose one witness for both inputs. The numbers need not share a half; use separate names until the algebra combines them. The complete direct proof 2 a + 2 b = 2 ( a + b ) Theorem. For all even integers x and y , the sum x + y is even. Take the given inputs. Let x and y be any even integers. “Any” means we keep their values unspecified; we are not choosing a random pair or limiting ourselves to 4 and 8. Unpack the two definitions. There are integers a and b such that x = 2 a and y = 2 b . They get separate names because the inputs may have different halves. Rewrite the sum. Substitution gives x + y = 2 a + 2 b . Taking out the common factor 2 gives 2( a + b ), as in the displayed equality. Check the new witness. Adding two integers gives an integer, so a + b is allowed as a witness. We have written the sum as two times an integer. By the definition of evenness, x + y is even. The proof uses the hypotheses only to obtain witnesses. It does not assume what it needs to establish. Its generality comes from taking arbitrary x and y , not from checking many examples. The algebraic factorization is the bridge from input witnesses to output witness. One can also show the sum of three even integers is even by applying this theorem twice, but that extra inference needs the first sum to count as an even integer. Be cautious when changing the conclusion. “The sum of an even and an odd integer is even” is false: 2 + 3 = 5. A proof that blindly factors a 2 would fail because an odd integer has the form 2 b + 1, leaving an extra 1. That failure case shows why definitions must be unpacked exactly. A guided first step. With the same inputs, fill the gap: x − y = 2( ___ ). What else must you say before calling the difference even? Check the missing step The gap is a − b , since 2 a − 2 b = 2( a − b ). Subtracting integers gives an integer, so this is an allowed witness. The difference is even. Identifying the expression and checking that it is an integer are separate parts of the argument. Build new witnesses Exercise 1. Prove directly that the product of two even integers is even. Use separate witnesses and identify the witness for the product. Hint for exercise 1 Write x = 2 a and y = 2 b ; factor one 2 from their product. Full solution to exercise 1 Let x = 2 a and y = 2 b with integers a , b . Then xy = 4 ab = 2(2 ab ). Since 2 ab is an integer, it is the required witness. Therefore xy is even. Exercise 2. Is the converse “if x + y is even, then both x and y are even” true? Explain with a specific pair. Hint for exercise 2 Try two odd integers. Full solution to exercise 2 No. Take x = 1 and y = 3. Their sum is 4 = 2·2, even. Neither input is even: their halves are 1/2 and 3/2, not integers. The theorem has not failed; its converse makes a different claim. A complete little proof Direct proof starts with arbitrary inputs meeting the hypothesis, unpacks their definitions, and constructs what the conclusion requires. Here the constructed witness is a + b . The result is a theorem for all even integer pairs, while the numerical pair was only a guide. For a claim whose forward direction is awkward, contrapositive proof offers another route.

title: Proving backward by contrapositive
summary: Prove that an integer with an even square is even by establishing its odd-square contrapositive.
text: What can a square reveal? If an integer’s square is even, must the original integer be even? Trying a few squares suggests yes, but a proof needs to cover every integer. Directly starting with an even square does not immediately give a useful expression for its square root. The contrapositive changes the starting point: assume the integer is not even, hence odd, and show its square is not even. This lesson proves that precise parity claim and keeps the contrapositive separate from the converse. Background capsule. An even integer has form 2 k ; an odd integer has form 2 k + 1, for an integer k . Every integer is exactly one of these types, as division by 2 leaves remainder 0 or 1. For propositions P and Q , the contrapositive of P ⇒ Q is ¬ Q ⇒ ¬ P . These statements have the same truth value; we will also show why. Square an odd witness Worked example. Consider −3. It is odd because −3 = 2(−2) + 1. Its square is 9 = 2·4 + 1, also odd. The same algebra works for every odd integer: write n = 2 k + 1, then expand. The square equals 4 k ² + 4 k + 1 = 2(2 k ² + 2 k ) + 1. The parenthesized value is an integer, so the result is odd. This is more than a list of checked squares; the integer k was arbitrary. Contrast two nearby claims. “If n ² is even, then n is even” is our target. “If n is even, then n ² is even” is its converse; it also happens to be true, but for a different reason. For a general implication, the converse need not be true. For example, “divisible by 4 ⇒ even” holds, while “even ⇒ divisible by 4” fails at 2. Reverse and negate both parts n 2 even ⇒ n even ⇔ n odd ⇒ n 2 odd Theorem. For every integer n , if n ² is even then n is even. Proof by contrapositive. Suppose n is not even. Since every integer is even or odd, n = 2 k + 1 for some integer k . Expanding gives n ² = 4 k ² + 4 k + 1 = 2(2 k ² + 2 k ) + 1. Its coefficient inside the parentheses is an integer. Therefore n ² is odd, hence not even. We have proved the contrapositive, which establishes the original implication. Why is that logical move legitimate? An implication P ⇒ Q fails only in the case P true and Q false. Its contrapositive ¬ Q ⇒ ¬ P fails in exactly the same case: ¬ Q is true and ¬ P is false precisely when Q is false and P true. This truth-condition argument proves their equivalence for any propositions. Our parity algebra then proves the relevant contrapositive; both parts are needed. The formula is an exact integer proof, including negative k . It does not say every square is odd. If n = 2, its square is 4, so such a claim fails immediately. Always retain the hypothesis when reporting the conclusion. Worked example: a product with an odd square Suppose an integer n satisfies n ² = 46 k + 1 for some integer k . Can n be even? The right side is 2(23 k ) + 1, so the square is odd. To answer directly from an even-input assumption, write n = 2 j . Then n ² = 4 j ² = 2(2 j ²), which is even. That contradicts the odd-square condition. Therefore n is odd. This argument uses the contrapositive of “even input implies even square,” rather than our theorem's converse without explanation. The algebra above supplies the needed forward implication. For n = 1, choosing k = 0 shows the hypothesis can actually hold. Checking that instance is useful, but the witness calculation proves the conclusion whenever the stated hypothesis holds. Choose the correct direction Exercise 1. Prove by contrapositive: if n ² is divisible by 3, then n is divisible by 3. You may use that every integer has remainder 0, 1, or 2 after division by 3. Hint for exercise 1 Square the two possible nonzero remainder forms modulo 3. Full solution to exercise 1 If 3 does not divide n , then n = 3 k + 1 or 3 k + 2. In either case its remainder modulo 3 is 1 or 2. The notation ≡ means “has the same remainder”: 1² ≡ 1 and 2² ≡ 4 ≡ 1 (mod 3). Thus the square has remainder 1, so 3 does not divide n ². This proves the contrapositive and therefore the original claim. Exercise 2. Write the contrapositive and converse of “If 6 divides n , then 2 divides n .” State which follows automatically and refute the other if needed. Hint for exercise 2 Reverse both clauses for the converse; reverse and negate both for the contrapositive. Full solution to exercise 2 The contrapositive is “If 2 does not divide n , then 6 does not divide n ”; it follows automatically from the true original statement. The converse is “If 2 divides n , then 6 divides n .” It is false at n = 2: 2 divides 2 but 6 does not. The arrow that is safe to turn Contrapositive proof reverses and negates both parts of an implication. In the square example, odd input gives odd square by a complete algebraic argument, so even square forces even input. The converse is a separate claim even when it happens to hold. Continue with induction when the statements themselves form a sequence indexed by the positive integers.

title: Induction is a chain with a base
summary: Prove the sum of the first n positive integers with an explicit base and inductive step.
text: How do you prove every row length? The sum 1 + 2 + 3 + ··· + n appears whenever a task adds one more item at each stage. For the first few lengths the totals are 1, 3, 6, and 10. They match n ( n + 1)/2, but matching examples cannot certify every positive n . Mathematical induction supplies the missing bridge: prove the first case, then prove that any established case gives the next one. Background capsule. The positive integers are 1, 2, 3, and so on. Let S n mean 1 + ··· + n . An induction hypothesis is permission to use the target formula for one earlier index during the step; it is not permission to assume the formula at the index being proved. We need only algebra, the meaning of a sum, and that order of positive integers. See what a new last term does Worked example. At n = 4, the sum is 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10, while 4·5/2 = 10. Going from length 4 to length 5 adds exactly 5, giving 15 = 5·6/2. In symbols, the move is S n+1 = S n + ( n + 1). This identity is true from the definition of the sum, before we substitute any formula. The question for an induction proof is whether the proposed expression transforms correctly under that move. The optional builder can display several bases and steps. Any finite run is an illustration of the symbolic proof below. Its crucial output is the separation between “assume the formula at n ” and “derive it at n + 1.” A falling-domino picture is similarly useful but cannot replace the arithmetic step. Base, permitted hypothesis, step S n = ∑ j = 1 n j = n ( n + 1 ) 2 A name for a sum The large ∑ means “add up.” Its lower label starts j at 1, its upper label stops at n , and the j to its right is the term to add. At n = 3, it means 1 + 2 + 3. In S n , the small n is a label telling us which sum we mean; it is not multiplication by n . You may read S n as “the sum through n .” Theorem. For every positive integer n , S n = n ( n + 1)/2. Verify the start. At n = 1, the sum is 1 and the proposed formula gives 1·2/2 = 1. Both sides agree. State the permitted assumption. Fix any positive integer n . For this step, suppose the formula is true at n : S n = n ( n + 1)/2. We must now derive the next case from this assumption. Add the new last term. By the definition, S n+1 = S n + ( n + 1). Substituting the assumed formula gives n ( n + 1)/2 + ( n + 1). Combine and factor. Write the added term as 2( n + 1)/2, so both terms have denominator 2. Their numerators have the common factor n + 1. Factoring gives the expression below, exactly the proposed formula at n + 1. n ( n + 1 ) + 2 ( n + 1 ) 2 = ( n + 1 ) ( n + 2 ) 2 The base case and the step together prove the theorem by induction. Why is assuming the earlier case allowed? The step is an “if … then …” claim: if the formula holds at n , then it holds at n + 1. We temporarily take the “if” part as given to prove that implication. We are not assuming that every case is true. The separately verified base makes the implication useful: case 1 gives case 2, which gives case 3, and so on. The logical induction rule is sound because any alleged first positive integer where the formula fails would be greater than 1, since the base succeeds. Its predecessor would satisfy the formula by being earlier than the first failure; the proven step would then force the alleged failure to satisfy it too. That contradiction explains why a base and a universal step reach all positive integers. A false start illustrates the boundary. Writing “assume S n+1 = ( n + 1)( n + 2)/2” in the step assumes the very target. A valid step alone is also insufficient. Consider the claim “ n ≥ 2” for every positive integer. Its step works: if n ≥ 2, then n + 1 ≥ 2. But its base at 1 fails, and the universal claim is false. Starting at 2 would prove only the cases from 2 onward. Always check both obligations and where the route starts. Run both obligations Exercise 1. Prove by induction that 2 + 4 + ··· + 2 n = n ( n + 1) for all positive integers n . Hint for exercise 1 The next sum adds 2( n + 1). Factor n + 1 after substitution. Full solution to exercise 1 For n = 1, both sides equal 2. Suppose the sum through 2 n equals n ( n + 1). Adding 2( n + 1) gives ( n + 1)( n + 2), which is the target at n + 1. The base and step prove the claim for all positive n . Exercise 2. A proposed induction for 1 + ··· + n = n ² says: “At 1 it works. Assume the formula at n + 1; then it works at n + 1.” Find a counterexample and the logical error. Hint for exercise 2 Test n = 2, then inspect which index is assumed in the step. Full solution to exercise 2 At n = 2, 1 + 2 = 3 whereas 2² = 4, so the claim is false. The step assumes its own target at n + 1 instead of assuming the earlier case at n and deriving the next case. The true base cannot rescue a circular step. One verified start, every justified step The sum formula is proved for all positive integers by a base and a valid transition. Checking many rows, or watching many dominoes fall, would not supply that transition. This lesson uses ordinary induction with one immediately previous case. Strong induction permits all earlier cases when a construction needs more than one.

title: When the next step needs every earlier step
summary: Prove existence of prime factorizations by applying earlier cases to both smaller factors.
text: When one predecessor is not enough Every integer at least 2 can be made by multiplying primes. A small factor tree makes the claim plausible: 84 = 2·2·3·7. But why can no larger integer get stuck with a composite factor that never reaches primes? The proof needs access to potentially different smaller factors, not just the immediately preceding integer.
