Strong induction makes exactly that permission explicit. Our goal is existence of a prime factorization; uniqueness is a separate theorem and will not be smuggled into the conclusion. Background capsule. A prime is an integer greater than 1 with no positive divisors except 1 and itself. A composite integer greater than 1 can be written as ab with integers 1 < a , b < n . A prime factorization is a product of one or more primes, with repetitions allowed. Strong induction assumes a property for all earlier indices from the base through n when proving it for n + 1. Follow both branches of a factor tree Worked example. For 84, choose 84 = 6·14. The factor 6 becomes 2·3 and 14 becomes 2·7, yielding 84 = 2·3·2·7. Another first split, 84 = 4·21, gives 2·2·3·7. The two trees illustrate that a composite can split into two strictly smaller integers. Their ends are prime. They do not by themselves show that every integer has such an ending, nor do they prove that all factor trees give the same multiset of primes. The decreasing size is the useful measure of this construction. Every nonprime branch has children at least 2 and smaller than its parent. Since positive integers cannot decrease forever, repeated splitting must stop at primes. That intuition can be organized into a precise strong-induction proof with a base and a step. The optional induction display separates the available earlier cases from the new target. An observed finite set of factor trees is only illustration; the proof below covers all integers at least 2. Use exactly the smaller factors you need n = a b , 1 < a , b < n Theorem. Every integer n ≥ 2 is a product of primes. Base. The integer 2 is prime, so it is a one-factor product of primes. Strong-induction step. Suppose every integer from 2 through n has a prime factorization. Consider n + 1. If it is prime, its one-factor product suffices. If it is composite, write n + 1 = ab with 1 < a , b < n + 1. Both a and b are integers between 2 and n , so the induction hypothesis supplies a prime factorization for each. Multiplying those products gives a prime factorization of n + 1. The base and step prove existence for every integer at least 2. Why not assume only the factorization of n ? If n + 1 = ab , neither a nor b need equal n . At 85 = 5·17, knowledge solely about 84 would not directly factor either child. Strong induction collects the earlier claims we actually need. It is logically equivalent in power to ordinary induction but often matches recursive structures more cleanly. This proof establishes existence only. It never compares two different factorizations. The familiar uniqueness assertion requires a divisibility result such as Euclid’s lemma: a prime dividing a product divides one factor. Without that extra argument, two trees ending in the same primes are examples, not a uniqueness proof. Keep the theorem’s conclusion exactly as strong as its reasoning. Trace the dependencies Exercise 1. Factor 90 by first splitting it as 9·10, then explain which earlier values the induction step would invoke if the target were 90. Hint for exercise 1 Both 9 and 10 are smaller than 90; factor each separately. Full solution to exercise 1 Since 9 = 3·3 and 10 = 2·5, we get 90 = 3·3·2·5, a product of primes. A strong-induction proof at 90 may invoke the already established factorization claims for 9 and 10, among all integers from 2 through 89. Knowledge only about 89 would not directly supply those two branches. Exercise 2. Someone claims the proof above also establishes uniqueness because every splitting process ends. Explain why that inference fails. Hint for exercise 2 Termination says a tree ends, but what would compare two different trees? Full solution to exercise 2 Termination and the induction proof ensure that each tree produces some prime product. They do not show that two distinct first splits produce the same prime factors. For 12, both 2·6 and 3·4 end in 2·2·3, but this one agreement is not a general proof. A comparison needs an additional prime-divisibility argument; uniqueness remains outside this theorem. Existence is enough for this stop Strong induction lets the step use any earlier cases, which fits a factorization split into two smaller pieces. We proved that every integer at least 2 has at least one prime factorization. We did not prove uniqueness, and a drawn factor tree is only a sample. For another way to rule out outcomes by tracking what a process preserves, visit invariants and reachability .

title: An invariant says what cannot happen
summary: Use a preserved remainder to rule out an unreachable state after any sequence of legal moves.
text: Can a sequence of moves reach the goal? Imagine a counter displaying an integer. The legal moves add 4 or subtract 6. It starts at 1. Can it ever display 10? A search may fail to find a route, but a failed search does not establish impossibility unless it somehow covers every possible route. A conserved property can. Both legal changes are even, so the display stays odd. Since 10 is even, it is unreachable. We will prove this exact statement, then distinguish it from claims of reachability. Background capsule. A state is the current displayed integer. A legal move changes it by +4 or −6, with no restriction on intermediate values. A finite sequence of legal moves is a route from the start state. An invariant is a property true at the start and preserved by every legal move; induction then makes it true after any finite number of moves. Here the relevant property is oddness, equivalently remainder 1 upon division by 2. Watch what changes and what does not Worked example. From 1, one +4 move reaches 5; one −6 move reaches −5. Further moves might reach 9, −1, 3, and many other values. Every displayed value in that short search is odd. Write a state as 2 k + 1. Adding 4 gives 2( k + 2) + 1, and subtracting 6 gives 2( k − 3) + 1. Both new coefficients are integers. This symbolic check covers both move types at every state, not just the ones in our sample. As a failure case for careless invariant use, alter the rule by allowing +3 once. From 1, that move reaches 4, an even state, so oddness is no longer preserved. An invariant depends on the exact move list. A property that survives most moves is not enough to rule out a goal reachable by an exceptional move. Prove preservation before declaring impossibility Let I(s) name the remainder of state s upon division by 2: I ( s ) = s mod 2 This defines I for every integer state: it is 0 for an even state and 1 for an odd state. Negative states use the same nonnegative remainders; for example −5 = 2(−3) + 1, so I(−5) = 1. The claim to prove is that I(s) = 1 along every legal route from 1 , not that every possible state has remainder 1. Theorem. Starting at 1 and using only moves +4 and −6, every reachable state is odd; in particular 10 is unreachable. Proof. The start state 1 is odd. Suppose a state after some number of moves is odd, so it equals 2 k + 1 for an integer k . The next state is either 2( k + 2) + 1 or 2( k − 3) + 1, both odd. By induction on the number of moves, every reachable state is odd. Since 10 = 2·5 is even, no legal route can reach it. This proof handles routes of every finite length and either choice at each step. The theorem is one-way: reachability implies oddness. It does not say every odd integer is reachable. Indeed, the two moves change the state by multiples of 2, and here a stronger analysis happens to show more, but we have not supplied it. A particularly clear counterexample to the converse under a modified move set is a counter that starts at 1 and permits only +4: all reachable states are odd, yet 3 is not reachable. Preservation is an obstruction, not a route-construction algorithm. There is also a useful general pattern. For a positive integer m , if every legal change is divisible by m , then the state’s remainder modulo m stays fixed. To justify it, write a change as m q ; adding it does not change the remainder class. This general claim is proved by the same one-move check and induction. The modulus and legal changes must be stated before applying it. Find and test an invariant Exercise 1. A counter starts at 2 and each move adds 6 or subtracts 9. Prove that 4 is unreachable. Hint for exercise 1 Both move sizes are multiples of 3. Compare the start and goal remainders modulo 3. Full solution to exercise 1 The start state 2 has remainder 2 modulo 3. Adding 6 or subtracting 9 changes a state by a multiple of 3, so its remainder stays 2 after every move, by induction on the number of moves. The goal 4 has remainder 1 modulo 3. Therefore no sequence of allowed moves reaches 4. Exercise 2. With the original +4/−6 moves from 1, a friend says “7 is odd, so it is reachable.” Does that conclusion follow? Find a route if one exists, and explain the logical issue. Hint for exercise 2 Try two +4 moves, one −6 move, then another +4 move. Check the final state and consider the direction of the invariant statement. Full solution to exercise 2 Yes, 7 is reachable: 1 → 5 → 9 → 3 → 7 uses +4, +4, −6, +4. But oddness alone did not prove it; the invariant only says reachable ⇒ odd. We needed an explicit legal route to establish reachability. The friend’s inference reversed a one-way implication even though this particular goal happens to be reachable. A conserved fact blocks a destination To use an invariant, prove the start has it, prove every legal move preserves it, and show the goal lacks it. The argument then rules out every finite route. A search table cannot do that by itself, and the invariant alone cannot construct a route to a compatible goal. Existence and uniqueness similarly separates two claims that are easy to blur.

title: Existence and uniqueness are two jobs
summary: Separate quotient–remainder existence from a complete proof of uniqueness.
text: Finding an answer and ruling out rivals When dividing 23 objects into boxes of 5, we can fill four boxes and leave 3 objects. That gives 23 = 5·4 + 3. A mathematical statement about quotient and remainder has two jobs: show that a suitable pair exists, and show that no different suitable pair exists. We will carry out a small construction for one number, then prove existence and uniqueness for any integer dividend and any positive divisor. The existence argument uses well-ordering: every nonempty set of nonnegative integers has a least member. Background capsule. The division form is a = bq + r , where a , q , and r are integers, b is a positive integer, and 0 ≤ r < b . The last inequality selects the standard remainder; without it, many pairs solve the equation. Absolute value | x | is the nonnegative distance of x from 0. These definitions and integer arithmetic suffice for the uniqueness proof. Build one pair, then try to build another Worked example. For 23 and divisor 5, repeated subtraction gives 23 − 5 − 5 − 5 − 5 = 3, so q = 4 and r = 3. This is an explicit existence witness for this case. The tempting alternative 23 = 5·3 + 8 fails the bound because 8 is not less than 5. Likewise 23 = 5·5 − 2 fails because the remainder is negative. The bound is not decoration; it selects the canonical pair. Worked example: a negative dividend. For dividend −7 and divisor 5, the equation is −7 = 5(−2) + 3. The remainder remains between 0 and 4 even though the dividend is negative. Choosing −7 = 5(−1) − 2 would violate the standard remainder condition. These examples show how the convention works; they do not prove that an admissible pair exists for every integer. Candidate quotient–remainder pairs for 23 divided by 5 q r Equation? Bound? 4 3 23 = 20 + 3 Yes 3 8 23 = 15 + 8 No 5 −2 23 = 25 − 2 No Why a valid pair exists and is unique a = b q + r , 0 ≤ r < b Uniqueness theorem. For a fixed integer a and positive integer b , at most one integer pair ( q , r ) satisfies this equation and bound. Proof. Suppose both a = bq + r and a = bq′ + r′ meet 0 ≤ r , r′ < b . Subtract the equations: b ( q − q′ ) = r′ − r . The right side has absolute value less than b , since both remainders lie in the interval from 0 to b − 1. The left side is an integer multiple of positive b . Its only possible value with absolute value less than b is 0. Thus q − q′ = 0, and then r′ − r = 0. The pairs are identical. This argument proves at most one , not at least one . Existence proof. Let S be the set { a − bq : q ∈ ℤ, a − bq ≥ 0}. It is nonempty: take q = −| a |. Because b ≥ 1, the resulting value a + b | a | is nonnegative. By well-ordering, S has a least member r , obtained from some integer q . Thus a = bq + r and r ≥ 0. If r ≥ b , then r − b = a − b ( q + 1) would be a smaller nonnegative member of S, contradicting minimality. Therefore r < b . This supplies an admissible pair for every integer dividend; combined with the uniqueness proof, it proves exactly one pair exists. Well-ordering is the explicitly used integer principle. If the bound is removed, uniqueness is false: 23 = 5·4 + 3 and 23 = 5·3 + 8 are distinct solutions. The algebra alone does not isolate a remainder. This counterexample explains exactly which hypothesis the proof uses. Check both obligations Exercise 1. Find the standard quotient and remainder for −17 divided by 6. Check the equation and remainder bound explicitly. Hint for exercise 1 Look for a multiple of 6 just below −17, so the remainder is nonnegative. Full solution to exercise 1 −17 = 6(−3) + 1. Thus q = −3 and r = 1. The equality holds because −18 + 1 = −17, and 0 ≤ 1 < 6. This constructs a valid pair for this input; the uniqueness theorem says there is no other valid pair. Exercise 2. A student writes 31 = 7·4 + 3 and 31 = 7·3 + 10 and calls this a counterexample to uniqueness. Explain the error and give the unique standard pair. Hint for exercise 2 Check the upper bound on each proposed remainder. Full solution to exercise 2 Both equations are arithmetically true, but the second has remainder 10, which violates 0 ≤ r < 7. The first pair ( q , r ) = (4, 3) meets both conditions, so it is the standard pair. The uniqueness theorem applies only to pairs satisfying the complete definition. Two jobs, one precise conclusion We constructed quotient–remainder pairs in examples, used well-ordering to prove a valid pair always exists, and proved that no two valid pairs can exist for fixed inputs. If a claim says “exactly one,” ask separately where its object comes from and why competitors are impossible. Infinite bijections use a related discipline: check both halves of a function claim.

title: Finite examples and infinite claims
summary: Prove that positive integers and positive even integers have equal cardinality by a bijection.
text: Can a proper part match the whole? Number hotel rooms 1, 2, 3, and so on. Move the guest in room n to room 2 n . Every guest gets a new even-numbered room, no two guests collide, and every even-numbered room receives someone. The even rooms are a proper subset of all rooms, yet this assignment matches the two collections exactly. That is the first surprising feature of infinite sets we will prove, without claiming that every infinite set behaves the same way. If you came from the short infinity discovery , this is the same doubling rule. Here we give names to its two checks and see why the stated target collection matters. Two checks for a matching Let ℕ + = {1, 2, 3, …}, the positive whole numbers; the plus sign excludes zero. Let E = {2, 4, 6, …}, the positive evens. A function assigns one allowed output to every allowed input. Its domain is the input collection, and its codomain is the stated target collection. Injective means no collisions: different inputs never share an output. Surjective means no gaps in the target: every member of the codomain is reached. A bijection passes both checks. The notation f ( n ) means the output of the rule f at input n , rather than multiplication. Make a pairing, then check its coverage Worked example. The first five pairs under f ( n ) = 2 n are 1 ↦ 2, 2 ↦ 4, 3 ↦ 6, 4 ↦ 8, and 5 ↦ 10. The table suggests a regular matching, but its first five rows cannot cover infinitely many inputs or outputs. The general rules do that. If two inputs a and b have the same output, 2 a = 2 b , so a = b . For any even positive output e , the definition of E says e = 2 k for some positive integer k ; choose that k as input. A finite glimpse of the infinite pairing Input n Output 2n 1 2 2 4 3 6 4 8 5 10 Finite intuition suggests that a proper subset has fewer members; for finite sets it does. The hotel pairing shows why that test does not transfer to infinite sets without modification. One still has to specify the two sets exactly: “all integers” and “positive even integers” would require a different pairing. Prove both directions of the match f : ℕ + → E , f ( n ) = 2 n Read the display as “ f takes positive whole numbers to positive evens, and its output at n is twice n .” The arrow between the sets specifies the domain and codomain. Theorem. The function f is a bijection from the positive integers onto the positive even integers. Every input gets an allowed output. For any positive whole number n , twice n is positive and even. Thus the rule really does take inputs in ℕ + to outputs in E . No collisions: injectivity. Suppose two inputs a and b have the same output. Then 2 a = 2 b . Divide by two to get a = b . So different inputs cannot collide. No missed target: surjectivity. Choose any positive even number e . By the meaning of even, e = 2 k for some positive whole number k . Input k therefore has output e . In symbols, e ∈ E means “ e belongs to E .” Both matching checks hold. The proof covers every allowed input and target, not just the five rows in the table. We say two sets have the same cardinality when a bijection pairs them. Therefore ℕ + and E have the same cardinality, even though 1 lies in the first set and not the second. “Same cardinality” does not mean “same members”; that distinction prevents a common misunderstanding. This is a claim about the specified infinite sets and a specified map. It does not settle whether the real numbers can be listed by positive integers; Cantor’s diagonal argument addresses that different question. One failure case is the rule g ( n ) = 4 n from ℕ + to E . It is injective but not surjective onto all positive even integers: 2 has no positive whole-number input giving it as output. Solving 4 n = 2 would require n = 1/2. Such an input, when it exists in the domain, is called a preimage . If we changed the codomain to {4, 8, 12, …}, the same rule would be surjective. The rule and the target collection both belong to the claim. Check collision and coverage Exercise 1. Let O = {1, 3, 5, …}. Show that h ( n ) = 2 n − 1 is a bijection from ℕ + to O . Hint for exercise 1 Solve 2 a − 1 = 2 b − 1, then express an arbitrary positive odd output in the same form. Full solution to exercise 1 If h ( a ) = h ( b ), then 2 a − 1 = 2 b − 1, so a = b ; this proves injectivity. Every positive odd integer o equals 2 k − 1 for a unique positive integer k , so h ( k ) = o ; this proves surjectivity. Thus h is a bijection. Exercise 2. Is j ( n ) = n + 1 a bijection from ℕ + to ℕ + ? Give a precise failure if not. Hint for exercise 2 Which positive integer cannot appear as an output? Full solution to exercise 2 The map is injective: a + 1 = b + 1 implies a = b . It is not surjective onto ℕ + , because output 1 would require input 0, which is outside the domain. Therefore it is not a bijection between the stated sets. One pairing, checked completely The rule n ↦ 2 n , read “ n is sent to twice n ,” pairs every positive integer with exactly one positive even integer and covers every target. That proves equal cardinality for these sets despite proper containment. A finite table is a picture, not the proof; injectivity and surjectivity are the proof obligations. For another evening, the binary-diary diagonal argument asks whether every infinite collection can be listed this way. It recalls the notation before proving that one particular collection cannot. For a different use of existence and uniqueness, try quotients and remainders .

title: A model begins with a question
summary: Estimate how many paper tiles cover an imagined wall mural. Choose variables, assumptions, units and a checkable output.
text: How many tiles does a mural need? A community room plans a paper-tile mural on a rectangular panel. The first useful question is not “What is the answer?” but “What decision must the answer support?” Here it is the number of square tiles to prepare. We can build a compact model that exposes the assumptions behind that number, checks the units, and leaves room to revise it. Background capsule. Area of a rectangle is width times height. A metre multiplied by a metre gives a square metre (m²). A centimetre is one hundredth of a metre, so 20 cm is 0.20 m. An approximation sign means a quantity is estimated under chosen assumptions; it does not excuse an unexplained step. We need multiplication, division, rounding upward, and these unit facts. Suppose the panel is 3 m wide and 2 m high. Tiles are 20 cm squares. We assume complete coverage, negligible grout, no overlap, and no cuts wasted at the boundary. Each assumption is a proposed description of the task, not a mathematical truth. A useful model note records them before anyone buys material. Make the estimate checkable Worked example. The panel area is 3 × 2 = 6 m². A tile side is 0.20 m, so its face area is 0.20 × 0.20 = 0.04 m². Dividing gives 150 tiles. In this particular example the dimensions divide exactly: 3/0.2 = 15 tiles along the width and 2/0.2 = 10 along the height. Their product is also 150. This second calculation tests the first rather than adding a new assumption. Mural model: quantities and units Quantity Value Role Panel width 3 m Input Panel height 2 m Input Tile side 0.20 m Input Tiles 150 Output under assumptions If the panel is instead 3.1 m wide, the raw area ratio is 6.2/0.04 = 155. But a grid of whole 20 cm tiles needs 16 columns and 10 rows, or 160 tiles, if cut pieces are not reused. The area ratio now understates procurement. The choice between area and grid models depends on whether reusable cuts, seams, and a partial edge are allowed. A drawing or small physical trial would resolve that design detail. What the formula actually says Let W and H be panel dimensions in metres and let a be tile side in metres. Under full coverage with no waste, the continuous area estimate is N area ≈ W H a 2 The numerator and denominator are both in m², so their quotient has no physical unit; a count is dimensionless. This dimensional check is exact. The approximation between the quotient and the number of physical tiles depends on the coverage assumptions. For an axis-aligned grid using whole tiles and no reuse of offcuts, the count is instead ceiling(W/a) × ceiling(H/a), where ceiling rounds up to the next integer. That expression is exact for that specified grid rule, but not necessarily the cheapest cutting plan. A modelling cycle has distinct moves: frame the decision, choose variables, state assumptions, compute a consequence, compare against a check, and revise. For this mural, count dimensions independently and try a paper mock-up at the edge. If the check disagrees, locate which assumption failed. “The model was wrong” is less useful than “the continuous-area assumption omitted a partial column.” This is a bounded claim about a toy rectangular panel. It does not predict labour, price, colour arrangement, breakage, or a curved wall. Those may matter to the real decision and would require measured inputs and perhaps another model. Test the model 1. Calculate. A 2.4 m by 1.8 m panel receives 30 cm square tiles. Find both the area estimate and the whole-tile grid count. Explain their agreement or difference. Hint for question 1 Convert 30 cm to 0.30 m; compare the panel dimensions with multiples of that side. Full solution to question 1 Panel area is 2.4 × 1.8 = 4.32 m². Tile area is 0.30² = 0.09 m². The quotient is 4.32/0.09 = 48. The width fits 2.4/0.3 = 8 and the height fits 1.8/0.3 = 6, giving 8 × 6 = 48 whole tiles. There is no partial boundary in this case, so the two rules agree. 2. Diagnose. The tile side is reported as “20” without a unit, while the panel is 3 m by 2 m. A teammate computes 6/400. What went wrong, and what check would you request? Hint for question 2 Inspect the units of numerator and denominator before dividing. Full solution to question 2 Six has unit m²; 400 would have square units of an unspecified tile-side unit. Dividing them is not a meaningful count until the units match. If “20” means centimetres, convert to 0.20 m and use 6/0.04 = 150. I would ask for the tile specification, then verify dimensions by counting 15 columns and 10 rows on a scaled drawing. A useful stopping point A model earns trust through a visible decision, assumptions, units and a check, not through a complicated equation. The area quotient was exact arithmetic yet only an approximate procurement model. Its failure at a partial edge shows why a boundary case is useful. Next, scale a room drawing to see how dimensions change at different powers, or vary assumptions to find which input drives the answer.

title: Build a miniature gallery that scales
summary: Scale a room drawing while estimating paint area. Separate length, area and volume scaling.
text: What grows when a miniature gallery grows? A designer doubles every length in a scale drawing of a cubic display booth. The floor and walls look twice as wide, yet paint and enclosed air do not merely double. The distinction matters when a sketch becomes a materials estimate. We will derive the different scaling rules from multiplication of dimensions and use them to catch a common budgeting mistake. Background capsule. A scale factor s means every corresponding length in a similar shape becomes s times its old length. Area multiplies two lengths; volume multiplies three. Squaring s means s × s, and cubing means s × s × s. A square metre is an area unit, a cubic metre a volume unit. Similarity is the key assumption: if only one direction changes, these powers need adjustment. Imagine a 1 m by 1 m by 1 m open-front cube. Its back and four side panels are each 1 m², so painted interior area is 5 m². Its enclosed box volume is 1 m³, ignoring the open front for this volume calculation. The labels “paint area” and “volume” answer different material questions. Double, then compare Worked example. Scale every dimension of the booth by s = 2. Each panel is now 2 m by 2 m and has area 4 m². Five such panels need 20 m² of paint area, four times the original 5 m². The box dimensions are 2 m by 2 m by 2 m, so volume is 8 m³, eight times the original. No calculus is needed: two or three factors of 2 explain the answer. A similar open-front cube at two sizes Measure Original Scaled by 2 Ratio Edge 1 m 2 m 2 Painted area 5 m² 20 m² 4 Box volume 1 m³ 8 m³ 8 Suppose paint covers 10 m² per litre. At the original size the ideal amount is 5/10 = 0.5 L; at double size it is 20/10 = 2 L. Packaging and coats could change a purchase order, but the area calculation is the relevant starting quantity. Multiplying the original paint by eight would confuse volume with painted surface. Derive the powers of scale For a rectangular object with lengths L, W and H, scaling all three by the same positive dimensionless s produces sL, sW and sH. The area of a corresponding rectangular face changes from LW to (sL)(sW) = s²LW. The volume changes from LWH to (sL)(sW)(sH) = s³LWH. Therefore, for similar shapes whose relevant pieces all follow that scale, L new = s L old , A new = s 2 A old , V new = s 3 V old These are exact consequences of the geometric scaling rule. They do not assert that every practical quantity scales this way. Paint thickness, door sizes, worker hours and structural support may stay fixed or follow other rules. Nor does a room with only its width doubled become a similar room. If length and height remain 1 m while width becomes 2 m, the floor doubles and volume doubles, rather than growing by factors of four and eight. The units provide another check. A unitless s² multiplies an old area in m² and leaves the result in m². Applying s³ to paint area gives a number in m² but a physically unjustified factor; unit consistency is necessary, not sufficient, for a good model. We also need the right geometry and purpose. Scale a new display 1. Calculate. A similar sculpture has original height 0.8 m, surface area 3 m² and volume 0.4 m³. Its new height is 1.2 m. Find the scale factor, new area and new volume. Hint for question 1 Divide the heights first, then use its square and cube. Full solution to question 1 The factor is 1.2/0.8 = 1.5. The area factor is 1.5² = 2.25, giving 3 × 2.25 = 6.75 m². The volume factor is 1.5³ = 3.375, giving 0.4 × 3.375 = 1.35 m³. The outputs retain their original area and volume units. 2. Challenge the rule. A rectangular wall is 4 m wide and 3 m high. Only its width grows to 6 m. Does the old area get multiplied by (6/4)²? Compute the actual new area and identify the missing hypothesis. Hint for question 2 Write area as width times height; check whether both factors changed. Full solution to question 2 The old area is 4 × 3 = 12 m². The new area is 6 × 3 = 18 m², factor 1.5. Squaring 1.5 would predict 27 m², which is false. Uniform scaling of both width and height is missing. The altered wall is a stretch in one direction, not a similar copy. Where the shortcut stops Length, area and volume carry one, two and three scaled dimensions respectively. The proof is simply the product of the dimensions under a common factor. The shortcut fails when different directions scale differently or when the outcome is governed by a separate process. For the mural question, tile count tracks area only if tile size and waste assumptions stay fixed. Sensitivity checks show what happens when one of those assumptions moves.

title: Which assumption matters most?
summary: A toy mural budget depends on tile size and waste. Vary one input at a time and compare output change.
text: Which mural assumption moves the answer? Two people disagree about a mural estimate. One worries that tile side length was measured inaccurately; the other worries about wasted pieces. “Both matter” is true but too vague for a purchasing decision. A sensitivity check changes an input by a declared amount while holding the other inputs fixed, then compares the output. It is a question about the chosen model, so its conclusions must retain that scope. Background capsule. A function y = f(x) gives an output for an input. A percentage change divides a change by its starting value: from 20 to 22 is 2/20 = 10%. A derivative is a limiting rate of change for very small input changes. We can do finite comparisons without derivatives and use a derivative only to explain a local approximation. Counts can be rounded for purchasing after the model calculation. Let a rectangular panel have fixed area A in m². Square tiles have side a in metres. Let w be the fraction of extra tiles ordered for breakage, with w ≥ 0. Our continuous procurement estimate is N(A,a,w) = (A/a²)(1+w). We assume full coverage, a stable waste fraction, and the same tile size throughout. Compare changes on the same scale Worked example. Set A = 6 m², a = 0.20 m, and w = 0.10. The baseline is 6/0.04 × 1.10 = 165 estimated tiles. Raise waste from 10% to 20% while keeping a fixed: the output is 150 × 1.20 = 180, an increase of 15 tiles or about 9.09% of the baseline. Raise tile side from 0.20 to 0.22 m while keeping waste at 10%: the output is 6/(0.22²) × 1.10 ≈ 136.36, a decrease of 28.64 or about 17.36%. One-at-a-time changes to the continuous estimate Case Input varied Estimated N Change from 165 Baseline None 165 0 More waste w = 0.20 180 +15 Larger tiles a = 0.22 m 136.36 −28.64 These changes are not equally sized in relative terms. Waste rate doubles, but the whole factor (1+w) changes from 1.1 to 1.2, only 9.09%. Tile side grows 10%, and the count falls by about 17.36%. The table does not show which input is more uncertain in reality; it shows model response to these specific scenarios. Local sensitivity and its boundary For a positive differentiable output y = f(x), its local elasticity to x is (x/y)(dy/dx). It approximates the percentage change in y caused by a small percentage change in x. Holding A and w fixed gives derivative dN/da = −2A(1+w)/a³ and therefore E a = a N d N d a = − 2 The result is exact for this continuous formula wherever A, a and 1+w are positive. It predicts that a very small 1% increase in side length gives about a 2% decrease in estimated count. For a 10% increase, the exact factor is 1/(1.1²) ≈ 0.8264, a 17.36% decrease rather than 20%. Local derivatives need not match large moves. Actual purchases also require integer counts, layout and availability. Those introduce jumps that the smooth formula omits. For waste, it is clearer to vary the multiplier q = 1+w. Its elasticity is +1: a 1% change in q gives a 1% change in N exactly. An extra ten percentage points of w is not a 10% change in q. Naming the denominator prevents a misleading sensitivity statement. Choose a useful check 1. Calculate. With A = 8 m², a = 0.25 m and w = 0.05, find N. Then raise a by 4% and find the exact count ratio, holding A and w fixed. Hint for question 1 New a is 1.04 times old a; the ratio cancels A and 1+w. Full solution to question 1 Baseline N = 8/0.0625 × 1.05 = 128 × 1.05 = 134.4. The new side is 0.26 m. The ratio new/old is (0.25/0.26)² = 1/1.04² ≈ 0.9246. Thus new N ≈ 124.26. The continuous estimate falls about 7.54%, compared with the local elasticity prediction of about 8%. 2. Interpret. A supplier can only sell packs of 20 tiles. Is the smooth elasticity −2 still the exact sensitivity of packs purchased? Use the baseline 165 tiles and a small decrease to 163 as a counterexample. Hint for question 2 Convert each tile estimate to a whole number of packs by rounding up. Full solution to question 2 For 165 tiles, ceiling(165/20) = 9 packs. For 163, ceiling(163/20) = 9 packs. The continuous estimate changes, but pack count does not. At a threshold such as 160 to 161 tiles, packs jump from 8 to 9. A derivative of the smooth N does not describe this stepped purchasing rule; use scenario calculations around thresholds. Answer a scoped question Sensitivity ranks the consequences of stated input changes within a stated model. It cannot tell us input uncertainty unless we measure or specify that uncertainty. The tile-side elasticity is a precise local property of A(1+w)/a²; the finite table reveals its limits and the pack example exposes a discontinuity. The next practical step is to check the layout and waste assumptions against a small trial, then update the model and repeat the comparison.

title: Two tones make a slow pulse
summary: Two nearby notes produce a rhythmic beat. Use superposition to predict beat frequency.
text: Why do two steady tones seem to pulse? Imagine two clean sine-wave tones, one at 440 cycles per second and one at 444. Each alone has steady amplitude. Add them and the result grows and shrinks in a repeating pattern. A mathematical identity predicts that pattern exactly for the stipulated signals. Whether a listener hears a particular beat depends on the sound source, room and hearing, so the algebra and the perceptual claim must be kept separate. Background capsule. Frequency f in hertz (Hz) means cycles per second. A sine wave sin(2πft) repeats after 1/f seconds because its angle advances 2π radians in one cycle. A radian is a unitless angle measure; π is approximately 3.14159. The identity sin(A)+sin(B)=2sin((A+B)/2)cos((A−B)/2) follows from the sine addition formulas. We need that identity and the idea that waves add point by point. Assume equal amplitudes, zero initial phases, frequencies f₁ and f₂ measured in Hz, and time t in seconds. Superposition means the displacement or ideal signal at time t is y(t)=sin(2πf₁t)+sin(2πf₂t). No instrument timbre or phase drift is included. Follow the slow factor Worked example. For 440 Hz and 444 Hz, the identity gives y(t)=2sin(884πt)cos(4πt). The first factor has average frequency 442 Hz: it changes very rapidly. The cosine factor changes slowly, from +1 through zero to −1 and back. Its signed period is 0.5 seconds because cos(4π(t+0.5))=cos(4πt). But loudness follows the magnitude of that factor: |cos(4πt)| has peaks every 0.25 seconds. Thus the familiar beat-peak rate is 4 per second, the 4 Hz difference. Envelope magnitude for the equal-amplitude 440/444 Hz model Time (s) |cos(4πt)| Interpretation 0 1 Peak possible amplitude 2 0.125 0 Exact cancellation 0.25 1 Next peak The table describes the envelope, not the instantaneous signal. At t=0, both sine terms are actually zero even though the envelope has its maximum possible magnitude. Sampling the carrier at t=0 alone would therefore not reveal the peak. This distinction helps interpret waveform pictures: envelope bounds the rapid oscillation. Check another time scale. If the second frequency moves from 444 Hz to 442 Hz while the first stays at 440 Hz, the difference becomes 2 Hz. Envelope peaks are now half a second apart and the first cancellation occurs after a quarter second. The signed cosine takes a full second to repeat. Changing the difference changes the slow pattern even though the carrier remains near 440 Hz. This is a direct consequence of the same identity, with time still measured in seconds. Identity, envelope and limits Applying the addition identity with A=2πf₁t and B=2πf₂t yields sin ( 2 π f 1 t ) + sin ( 2 π f 2 t ) = 2 sin ( π ( f 1 + f 2 ) t ) cos ( π ( f 1 − f 2 ) t ) This is an exact identity for all real t and frequencies. For positive difference Δf=|f₁−f₂|, |cos(πΔft)| peaks whenever πΔft is an integer multiple of π, so successive peaks are 1/Δf seconds apart. The signed cosine itself takes 2/Δf seconds to return to the same sign. Calling Δf the beat frequency refers to peaks in the magnitude envelope, not the signed modulation frequency. If amplitudes differ, A sin(2πf₁t)+B sin(2πf₂t) need not cancel completely. A useful squared envelope is A²+B²+2AB cos(2πΔft), which has minimum magnitude |A−B|. Our zero troughs therefore rely on equal amplitude. Real sound also has harmonics, reverberation and auditory effects; the ideal signal is a controlled mathematical model, not a prediction of perceived loudness for every listener. Compute and question 1. Calculate. Two equal-amplitude waves have frequencies 300 Hz and 305 Hz. Give the average carrier frequency, beat-peak rate, time between envelope peaks and first cancellation time after t=0. Hint for question 1 Use Δf=5 Hz and find when |cos(πΔft)| first reaches zero. Full solution to question 1 The average frequency is (300+305)/2=302.5 Hz. Difference Δf=5 Hz, so beat peaks occur 5 times per second, separated by 1/5=0.2 s. First cancellation occurs when π(5)t=π/2, giving t=0.1 s. The carrier is rapid while this envelope changes slowly. 2. Find the failed assumption. Two waves have equal frequencies of 400 Hz but amplitudes 1 and 0.6. Will they produce periodic complete silence under the zero-phase model? Hint for question 2 Combine the sine terms directly when their frequencies and phases agree. Full solution to question 2 The sum is 1.6sin(800πt), a single 400 Hz tone with constant amplitude 1.6. There is no slow beat because Δf=0. The signal crosses zero each carrier half-cycle, but that is not periodic cancellation of an envelope. If the frequencies differed, unequal amplitudes would leave envelope minimum |1−0.6|=0.4 rather than silence. Keep the two meanings of period apart Superposition and a trigonometric identity give an exact envelope for ideal equal-amplitude sine waves. Its magnitude peaks at the frequency difference; its signed cosine needs twice as long to return to the same sign. A waveform image or optional sound can illustrate this, but the algebra carries the claim. For a related model of oscillation with a physical approximation, visit the pendulum sketch .

title: Rules, randomness and repeatability in art
summary: Generate a field of dots with a chosen seed. Distinguish deterministic rules, random draws and aesthetic interpretation.
text: Can a rule make a repeatable dot picture? Consider a square canvas on which a program places ten dots. It uses a named rule and a saved seed. Two runs with the same seed and implementation should give the same picture; different seeds usually differ. That repeatability is useful when discussing an artwork, but the picture alone does not prove that its dots are uniformly random or visually pleasing. Those are separate questions. Background capsule. A coordinate pair (x,y) locates a point: x is horizontal and y vertical. The unit square has 0≤x≤1 and 0≤y≤1. A uniform point on that square assigns probability equal to area; for example, the left half has probability 1/2. “Independent and identically distributed” (iid) means each dot follows the same distribution and one dot does not change another's stipulated chances. A computer seed initializes a deterministic pseudorandom algorithm; repeatability does not make its output physically random. Our model is a design recipe: draw n coordinate pairs independently from the uniform distribution on the square, then render them as dots. The distribution is a declared ideal rule; an actual implementation needs a specified generator and seed if another person is to reproduce exact coordinates. Count a feature before judging the picture Worked example. Choose n=10. Let K be the number of dots in the left half, x<0.5. Each dot independently lands there with probability 0.5, so K has a binomial distribution under the ideal model. Its expected value is 10×0.5=5, but an actual picture can have 3 or 8. The chance that all ten land in the left half is (1/2)¹⁰=1/1024. Rare is not impossible; a clustering event is not automatically a broken generator. Three possible dot features under the stipulated rule Feature Exact probability Why First dot left 1/2 Half the area First two left 1/4 Independent product All ten left 1/1024 Ten independent factors Suppose the artist chooses a seed after viewing fifty previews and selects the one with the most balanced left and right halves. The exhibited image no longer represents an unselected draw from the original distribution. The seed still reproduces it, but the selection rule changes what can be inferred from the final image. A model note should say how many candidates were viewed and what criterion selected the display. State the probability model exactly For each i from 1 to n, let (Xᵢ,Yᵢ) be a pair sampled uniformly on [0,1]², independently across i. For any rectangle R inside the square, the model assigns P((Xᵢ,Yᵢ)∈R)=area(R). In particular, with L the left half, P ( K = k ) = ( 10 ! k ! ( 10 − k ) ! ) ( 1 2 ) 10 Here 10! means 10×9×…×1 and k ranges from 0 to 10. The coefficient counts which k of the ten labelled draws land left; independence gives the factor (1/2)¹⁰ for each such pattern. This is a finite probability derivation under the iid hypothesis. It does not certify that a particular software generator satisfies ideal independence, or that a human eye finds the arrangement balanced. A fixed seed yields a fixed sequence for a fixed algorithm and version. For transparent reproduction, record both. A seed alone is insufficient if the generator changes. If the design enforces a minimum distance between dots, draws become dependent; the simple binomial law for arbitrary regions may fail. Such a rule can be artistically useful, but it is a different model and deserves its own probability calculation. Separate rule, draw and judgement 1. Calculate. Four iid uniform dots are placed in the square. What is the chance that none falls in the top quarter, y>0.75? What is the expected number there? Hint for question 1 For one dot, the region has area 1/4, so outside has chance 3/4. Full solution to question 1 Each dot avoids the top quarter with probability 3/4. Independence makes the chance that all four avoid it (3/4)⁴=81/256≈0.3164. Each dot contributes expected count 1/4, so the expected number is 4×1/4=1. Expectation one does not mean every picture has exactly one top-quarter dot. 2. Explain a failure. A designer redraws any dot that lies within 0.1 units of an earlier dot. Are the final dots iid uniform? Is saving a seed still useful? Hint for question 2 Ask whether the allowed position for a later dot depends on earlier positions. Full solution to question 2 The later dot's accepted positions exclude discs around earlier dots, so its final distribution depends on their coordinates. Independence fails and uniformity over the full square fails near excluded regions. A saved seed and specified redraw algorithm can still reproduce the image, but the iid uniform formula no longer describes the accepted dots. What repeatability establishes A seeded generative rule makes a result reproducible under a specified algorithm; probability statements depend on the sampling rule, including any selection or rejection steps. Visual quality is an aesthetic judgement, not a theorem following from uniformity. This small exercise illustrates the broader modelling cycle : record the question, assumptions, mechanism, output and an honest check.

title: A rumor on a small fictional network
summary: Colored markers move across a drawn friendship graph. Compare network structure under an explicit transmission rule.
text: How can a marker travel through a drawn network? Draw four fictional people A, B, C and D as vertices and connections A–B, A–C and C–D as edges. Put an active marker on A. We can stipulate a one-step spreading rule and calculate exactly what it predicts. The drawing is a toy mechanism for comparing structures; its probabilities are not measured facts about friendship or rumour sharing. Background capsule. A graph is a set of vertices with edges connecting chosen pairs. A neighbour of v is a vertex joined to v by an edge. A probability p is between 0 and 1; chance of failure for an event with chance p is 1−p. If events are independent, the chance they all fail is the product of their individual failure chances. Conditional independence means this multiplication holds after the present active set and edge probabilities are fixed. Use a synchronous rule: in each step, every active vertex tries independently to activate each currently inactive neighbour once; an activation takes effect at the next step, and active vertices stay active. Set every edge attempt probability to p=1/2. These timing and independence choices define the model. Work through a small graph Worked example. At time 0, only A is active. At time 1, A tries B and C separately. The four patterns (neither, B only, C only, both) each have probability 1/4 because the two Bernoulli attempts are independent. D cannot activate at time 1: it is connected to C, which only becomes active at the end of the step. This is a useful timing check against an implementation that accidentally allows within-step cascades. Exact first-step outcomes with p=1/2 New active vertices Probability Total active None 1/4 1 B only 1/4 2 C only 1/4 2 B and C 1/4 3 The expected total active after one step is (1+2+2+3)/4=2. A single simulated run can yield any of the four totals; it is an illustration of the rule, not a forecast. At the next step, the attempts depend on which vertices activated at time 1. To compute probabilities correctly, condition on that current state rather than pretending all second-step trials occur in the same scenario. The product rule and its hypothesis Let Iₜ be the active set at the start of step t. For an inactive vertex v, let Aₜ(v) be its active neighbours. If each u in Aₜ(v) independently makes a Bernoulli attempt with probability pᵤᵥ, then P ( v stays inactive at step t+1 | I t ) = ∏ u ∈ A t ( v ) ( 1 − p u v ) The product over an empty set is 1: if no active neighbour can try, v certainly stays inactive under this rule. If two active neighbours each have p=1/2, v avoids both attempts with probability (1/2)²=1/4, so it activates with probability 3/4. That conclusion is exact only given the conditional independence assumption. If one shared event makes both people forward or both remain silent, their failures are correlated; multiplying two marginals can be wrong. Also, the formula concerns one step given Iₜ. It does not say eventual activation probabilities equal a simple product. Loops and repeated opportunities change those questions. A simulation with fixed seed and finite repetitions estimates the behaviour of this specified toy process; it cannot validate the social assumptions or establish causality. Check the mechanism 1. Calculate. An inactive vertex has two active neighbours. Their independent attempt probabilities are 0.2 and 0.4. Find its chance of staying inactive and of activating next step. Hint for question 1 Both attempts must fail for the vertex to stay inactive. Full solution to question 1 The two failure chances are 0.8 and 0.6. Their independent product is 0.8×0.6=0.48, so the activation chance is 1−0.48=0.52. The result lies between 0.4 and 0.6, as expected when a second opportunity is added but neither opportunity is certain. 2. Counterexample. Two active neighbours always act together: with probability 1/2 both send a marker, otherwise neither does. Each marginal attempt chance is 1/2. What is the true chance the target stays inactive, and what would the independent formula incorrectly give? Hint for question 2 List the only two possible joint outcomes. Full solution to question 2 Neither sends with probability 1/2, so the target stays inactive with probability 1/2. Multiplying marginal failure chances would give (1/2)(1/2)=1/4, which is wrong because failures occur together. This directly identifies conditional independence as a necessary hypothesis for the product formula. What the network model can say An explicit graph, clock and attempt rule produce checkable one-step probabilities. Structural comparisons can then be made inside that rule, with independent attempts clearly named. The same picture under a different timing or correlated-attempt rule can produce different results. Stress-testing these assumptions is the job of model validation , and it still cannot turn a fictional graph into a real social forecast.

title: A swinging sketch and a linear model
summary: A drawn pendulum decorates a digital clock. Compare small-angle linear oscillator with nonlinear pendulum.
text: When does a swinging sketch act like a sine wave? A digital-clock illustration shows a weight swinging on a light string. It is tempting to animate its angle with a perfect sine wave. That can be a defensible approximation for small swings, but it is not the exact law of a pendulum. We can state the physical assumptions, derive the nonlinear equation, and see precisely where the linear shortcut enters. Background capsule. Angle θ is measured in radians; 0 is straight down. A dot or prime indicates a time derivative: θ′ is angular velocity in radians per second and θ″ is angular acceleration in radians per second squared. For a sine wave θ(t)=θ₀cos(ωt), differentiating twice gives θ″=−ω²θ. The familiar small-angle relation sin θ≈θ works when |θ| is small in radians. Radians are dimensionless, so sin θ and θ can be compared. Assume a point mass m on a massless rigid string of length L, no friction, constant gravitational acceleration g, and motion in one vertical plane. These idealizations omit air resistance, a bulky weight and support motion. We ask about the angle over time, not the sound of the clock. Compare two amplitudes Worked example. For L=1 m and g=9.81 m/s², the linear model has angular frequency √(g/L)≈3.13 radians per second and period 2π√(L/g)≈2.006 s. This period is independent of amplitude inside that approximation. The restoring acceleration in the exact model, however, uses sin θ rather than θ. At θ=0.1 rad, sin(0.1)≈0.09983, only about 0.17% below 0.1. At θ=1 rad, sin(1)≈0.84147, about 15.85% below 1. The difference in restoring acceleration is much larger at the bigger angle. Restoring-term comparison Angle θ (rad) sin θ Relative gap (θ−sin θ)/θ 0.1 0.09983 0.17% 0.5 0.47943 4.11% 1.0 0.84147 15.85% This table checks the force term at selected positions; it is not itself a period calculation. The nonlinear trajectory accumulates differences over time, and its exact period requires a separate argument. A good model note says “small angle” and checks a specific range instead of treating the linear period as universal. Derive the boundary of the approximation The tangential gravitational force is −mg sin θ, where the minus sign points toward θ=0. Tangential acceleration on a circular path of radius L is Lθ″. Newton's second law gives mLθ″=−mg sin θ. Cancelling positive m and dividing by L yields the exact ideal-pendulum equation. Replacing sin θ by θ gives the linear approximation: θ ″ + g L sin ( θ ) = 0 ⇒ θ ″ + g L θ ≈ 0 The arrow marks approximation, not logical equivalence. Taylor's theorem gives sin θ=θ−θ³/6+R₅ with |R₅|≤|θ|⁵/120 for real θ. Thus the first omitted term is cubic; for |θ|≤0.2 rad, |sin θ−θ|/|θ|≤θ²/6≤0.00667, about 0.67%, using the alternating-series or standard Taylor bound. This bounds the restoring-term error at a position, not the trajectory error over arbitrarily long times. The linear equation has solution θ(t)=C cos(ωt)+D sin(ωt), ω=√(g/L), because differentiating twice returns −ω² times the function. Constants C and D come from initial angle and angular velocity. The exact nonlinear pendulum generally has an amplitude-dependent period, so the linear formula is a purposeful local approximation. Use and challenge the approximation 1. Calculate. With L=2 m and g=9.8 m/s², find the linear angular frequency and period. Check the units. Hint for question 1 g/L has units s⁻²; its square root has units s⁻¹. Full solution to question 1 g/L=9.8/2=4.9 s⁻², so ω=√4.9≈2.214 s⁻¹. The period is 2π/ω≈2.838 s. The radian angle is dimensionless; ωt must be dimensionless, which agrees with ω in inverse seconds. This period belongs to the linear small-angle model. 2. Explain a failure. Someone uses sin θ≈θ at θ=π/2 to predict restoring acceleration. Compare the exact and linear magnitudes in units of g/L and say whether the table's small-angle evidence justifies this use. Hint for question 2 Compute sin(π/2) and compare with π/2. Full solution to question 2 The exact magnitude is (g/L)sin(π/2)=g/L. The linear model gives (g/L)(π/2)≈1.571g/L, an overestimate of about 57.1% relative to exact. π/2≈1.57 rad is far outside the checked small range, so using the approximation here is unjustified. Both models still point toward the bottom, but their magnitudes differ substantially. A precise place to stop The ideal pendulum equation follows from Newton's law under stated mechanical assumptions. The sine-wave solution follows only after a small-angle replacement. We bounded the local restoring-term error; we did not prove a long-time path error bound. For a complementary exact trigonometric signal identity with a different modelling boundary, see two-tone beats .

title: A curve can fit and still mislead
summary: Fit several curves to invented gallery visitor counts. Distinguish interpolation, extrapolation and mechanism.
text: Can a perfect curve still be a poor story? A tiny gallery records visitor counts over three opening days: 10, 12 and 14. Two simple formulas can fit those points exactly yet disagree about a fourth day. That makes the data useful for exploring interpolation, held-out prediction and mechanism. No invented visitor table proves how real galleries behave; it only lets us see what a fitted formula does and does not establish. Background capsule. A function f(x) predicts an output at input x. A residual is observed minus predicted, y−f(x), in the output's units. Interpolation predicts inside the observed input range; extrapolation predicts beyond it. A held-out observation is set aside before fitting and used afterward to assess predictions. A good training fit means small residuals on used data; it cannot by itself establish a causal explanation. Let x be day number and y visitors per day. Our training observations are (1,10), (2,12), (3,14). Hold day 4 aside; suppose its recorded count is 16. We will compare two models fitted only to days 1–3. Two formulas, one training table Worked example. The straight-line rule f(x)=8+2x hits all three training points and predicts f(4)=16. A second rule g(x)=8+2x+5(x−1)(x−2)(x−3) also hits them, because the cubic product is zero at x=1,2,3. At x=4 the product is 3×2×1=6, so g(4)=16+30=46. Both have zero training residual at every observed training day. Against the held-out count 16, f has residual 0 and g has residual −30 visitors. Training fit and a predeclared holdout Day Observed Line f Cubic g Use 1 10 10 10 Training 2 12 12 12 Training 3 14 14 14 Training 4 16 16 46 Holdout The line predicts this held-out day better, but a single held-out day cannot prove the line's mechanism. Perhaps opening hours, advertising or weather change. If we inspect many candidate curves and repeatedly choose the one that does best on day 4, day 4 has become part of model selection; it is no longer an untouched test. A fresh future day would then be needed for a new honest check. What a residual proves For observations (xᵢ,yᵢ) and a named prediction rule f, define r i = y i − f ( x i ) This subtraction is exact and has the units of y. Zero residual means the formula equals that observed number at that input; it says nothing by itself about unobserved inputs. The cubic construction is a direct proof: any multiple c(x−1)(x−2)(x−3) added to the line fits all three training points, and different c values can make arbitrarily different day-4 predictions. Data at finitely many x values do not uniquely determine a general function without restricting the model class. A held-out error checks predictive performance under the split and conditions used. If future days differ in an important way, even a good holdout result may fail to transfer. Causal explanation is a stronger claim: to say opening-hours changes caused counts to rise, we would need a design addressing competing causes, not a regression line through daily totals. The formula g is mathematically valid; its term has no justified gallery mechanism in this example. One can prefer a simpler rule as a tentative prediction when data are scarce, but “simpler” is a modelling choice, not a theorem that the line is true. State the use: estimate a nearby day under stable conditions, with an error check and a limit note. Audit the fit 1. Calculate. On a separately held-out day 5, the observed count is 18. Find the predictions of f and g above, their residuals, and each model's absolute error. Hint for question 1 At x=5 the cubic product is 4×3×2=24. Full solution to question 1 f(5)=8+10=18, residual 18−18=0 and absolute error 0. g(5)=18+5×24=138, residual 18−138=−120 and absolute error 120 visitors. These numbers compare the two rules on this example's fifth day; they do not guarantee future performance. 2. Explain a boundary. A colleague refits the cubic coefficient after seeing day 4 so that g(4)=16, then calls day 4 an independent validation. Why is that claim incorrect? Hint for question 2 Ask whether the held-out value influenced the chosen model. Full solution to question 2 Setting the coefficient using day 4 makes that observation part of fitting. It is no longer held out, even if it was hidden during an earlier step. A fair validation would use a new observation not used to select the coefficient or model class. The revised rule might still predict well, but day 4 cannot be counted as independent evidence for it. Fit, prediction and explanation are different claims A residual describes a particular observation and formula exactly. A holdout checks a prediction under a chosen split. Neither establishes why visitor counts changed. The cubic's perfect training fit and poor held-out result provide a concrete counterexample to equating fit with reliability. Model validation combines this check with units, boundaries and sensitivity.

title: Stress-test a model before sharing it
summary: Predict supplies for a fantasy festival from sparse pilot data. Run unit, boundary, sensitivity and held-out checks, then write a limitation note.
text: What should be checked before sharing a supply estimate? A fictional festival prints paper maps. A planner predicts how many maps each session will need from registered groups. A formula may be easy to calculate and still fail because its units, boundary behaviour or tested conditions are wrong. Validation is a set of question-specific checks; it is not a certificate that the model will always work. Background capsule. A residual is observed minus predicted in the output's units. Absolute error removes the sign, so positive and negative mistakes cannot cancel. Mean absolute error (MAE) averages those magnitudes. A held-out set consists of observations excluded from choosing the formula and its parameters. Sensitivity asks how prediction changes when an input changes, holding others fixed. Sampling variation means a finite set of sessions need not represent all future sessions. Suppose a simple rule predicts maps M(g)=3g+5 for g registered groups: three maps per group plus five spare maps. Its units are maps because 3 has units maps/group and 5 has units maps. We assume group sizes and map pickup habits are similar across sessions; we do not know that they are. Run four different checks Worked example. First, units: at g=10 groups, M=35 maps, not 35 groups. Second, boundary: at g=0, the rule predicts 5 maps. That can make sense if staff need spares; if no session runs without groups, the boundary is outside the intended domain and should not be treated as evidence. Third, sensitivity: increasing g by one always adds exactly three predicted maps. If observed large groups vary widely in size, this fixed slope is suspect. Fourth, hold out two sessions before choosing the rule. Suppose the held-out observations are g=10 with 37 maps and g=20 with 61 maps. Predictions are 35 and 65. Residuals are +2 and −4 maps; absolute errors are 2 and 4. MAE is (2+4)/2=3 maps. The signed mean residual is −1 map, which hides some cancellation. The MAE is a more direct description of typical magnitude in these two cases, though two cases are too few for a reliable future-error estimate. Invented held-out sessions Groups Observed maps Predicted maps Residual 10 37 35 +2 20 61 65 −4 These data are invented to demonstrate the check. A real sharing note would state dates, selection method, and whether the next festival resembles the held-out sessions. No residual table alone tests those conditions. Define the score and its limits For n>0 held-out cases, with observed yᵢ and a prediction ŷᵢ made without using case i to select the model, define eᵢ=yᵢ−ŷᵢ and MAE = 1 n ∑ i = 1 n | y i − y ^ i | This is an exact summary of those n errors. It is measured in the same unit as y, here maps. The qualification about model selection matters: if we tune 3 and 5 using the two “held-out” counts, their errors are training errors. The resulting score is optimistic as an independent check. An honest evaluation keeps the observations untouched until the rule is fixed, or explicitly labels a resampling design. MAE also discards direction and distribution. A model that misses one large session badly can share the same MAE as one with several small misses. For planning stock, underprediction may cost more than overprediction, so a separate asymmetric decision rule may be needed. Even low held-out MAE shows association under a data setting, not causality. It does not prove registered groups cause map demand in the simple three-per-group way. A useful validation memo gives domain (perhaps 1–30 groups), units, assumptions, boundary check, sensitivity, the held-out error table, and what changes would trigger revision. That is a reproducible claim about this model and evidence, not an all-purpose seal of approval. Write a defensible check 1. Calculate. Another fixed model predicts 12, 17 and 22 maps for three held-out sessions. The observed counts are 10, 20 and 21. Find residuals, MAE and signed mean residual. Hint for question 1 Subtract prediction from observation for each case, then average magnitudes separately from signed values. Full solution to question 1 Residuals are 10−12=−2, 20−17=+3 and 21−22=−1 maps. Absolute errors are 2, 3 and 1, so MAE=(2+3+1)/3=2 maps. The signed mean is (−2+3−1)/3=0. Zero signed mean does not mean zero error; opposite signs cancel. 2. Find the boundary failure. A linear rule M(g)=3g+5 is used to predict maps for g=−2 and gives −1 map. What does this show, and how should the intended domain be stated? Hint for question 2 Ask whether a negative number of registered groups is meaningful. Full solution to question 2 g=−2 is not a meaningful group count, so −1 map is outside the model's intended input domain. State g as a nonnegative integer, and preferably the observed range, for example 1–30 registered groups. Within that range predictions are positive, though positivity alone does not validate the slope or intercept. New conditions require fresh checks. Validation is a report of checks Units, boundaries, sensitivity and held-out residuals test different parts of a model. The score MAE is exact for the cases used, but its usefulness elsewhere depends on how they were chosen and whether conditions transfer. A transparent limitation note is part of the answer. For a sharp example of how a perfect training fit can fail a holdout, read a curve can fit and still mislead .

title: Reading a landscape without seeing the mountain
summary: A few contour lines can reveal steepness and direction.
text: A map of height without a picture of the hill A contour joins points with the same height. If a walker follows it, does the height change? If the walker instead crosses it, what can the map tell us about the change? We can answer exactly for the landscape f(x,y)=x²+2y², and learn where a contour map stops short of measuring slope. Background capsule. A point (x,y) records east and north coordinates. Squaring removes signs: x² is the same at x and −x. A level set of f at height c is the collection of points satisfying f(x,y)=c. A displacement (a,b) means moving a units east and b units north. The derivative of a one-variable function measures a limiting height change per unit of that movement; a two-variable slope must also specify a direction. Walk around and across an oval Worked example. At height 2 our level set satisfies x²+2y²=2. Its east and west tips are (±√2,0); its north and south tips are (0,±1). At (1,1/√2) the same equation holds, so these points all lie on one oval. Moving among them changes position but leaves height at 2. The axes have different spans because a unit of northward distance contributes twice as much squared height as a unit eastward distance. Now start at (1,0), where height is 1. An eastward step of length h changes height to (1+h)², a difference of 2h+h². A northward step of the same length changes it to 1+2h², a difference of 2h². At h=1/10 those changes are 21/100 and 2/100. Near this point eastward movement has a first-order effect; northward movement has only a second-order effect. A table of exact heights says more than an oval drawn at arbitrary scale. Two equal coordinate steps from (1,0) Step New height Change (1/10,0) 121/100 21/100 (0,1/10) 102/100 2/100 What the level equation proves Exact statement. For every c>0, the level set is an ellipse with horizontal semiaxis √c and vertical semiaxis √(c/2). Divide its equation by c to obtain x²/c+y²/(c/2)=1. At c=0 there is only the origin; at c<0 there are no real points because both squares are nonnegative. This algebra proves the shape and intercepts, assuming ordinary Cartesian coordinates with equal physical units on both axes. f ( x , y ) = c ⟺ x 2 c + y 2 c / 2 = 1 For a smooth path r(t)=(x(t),y(t)) kept on one contour, f(r(t))=c at every t; therefore its derivative is zero wherever the path is differentiable. This is an exact claim about travel along a level set. It does not say that every move from a point has zero slope. In fact, at (1,0), moving east by h produces (2h+h²)/h=2+h, tending to 2, while moving north produces 2h²/h=2h, tending to zero. Beware a tempting visual shortcut. The distance between contours of heights 1 and 2 depends on which route crosses them, on whether the heights were sampled at equal increments, and on the scale of the map. Close drawn curves suggest rapid change only after those choices are fixed. A finite gap is an average change, not a derivative at a point. The next lesson extracts all first-order directions from a gradient. Use the level equation 1. Calculation. Find the intercepts of the height-8 contour. Starting at (2,0), compare the height changes from steps (1/4,0) and (0,1/4). Hint for question 1 Set one coordinate to zero for intercepts; substitute the two new points directly. Worked solution for question 1 x²+2y²=8 gives (±2√2,0) and (0,±2). At (2,0) height is 4. East gives (9/4)²=81/16, a rise of 17/16. North gives 4+2(1/4)²=33/8, a rise of 1/8. The east step rises more. 2. Explanation. A map draws the height-1 and height-4 contours. A reader says their spacing alone determines the directional derivative at (1,0). Give two reasons this fails. Hint for question 2 Ask what direction and what limiting operation a derivative requires. Worked solution for question 2 A directional derivative specifies a direction: at (1,0) the east and north derivatives are 2 and 0. It also takes a limit as the step shrinks to zero. Two separated contours provide only finite changes. Their drawn spacing additionally depends on map scaling, so it cannot supply either missing ingredient. What the map lets you conclude A level equation locates exactly where the height agrees, and its algebra reveals the shape for this quadratic landscape. Equal-length steps can still produce very different height changes. Stop once you can distinguish a level from a slope and calculate a finite difference before claiming a limiting one. As a failure case, a constant function has every point on one level set and zero slope everywhere; our oval geometry does not apply to it. Continue with the gradient when you want a rule for all directions at once.

title: A compass that points uphill
summary: One arrow summarizes every first-order directional change.
text: Which way is steepest? On a smooth landscape, a single vector can predict first-order height change in any direction. It is called the gradient. Its direction is the fastest uphill direction among unit steps, with a precise exception at flat points. Background capsule. A partial derivative f x freezes y and measures the limiting eastward rate; f y freezes x and measures the northward rate. The dot product (a,b)·(c,d)=ac+bd combines components, and a unit vector u has length √(u 1 ²+u 2 ²)=1. A directional derivative is the limit [f(p+hu)−f(p)]/h as h tends to zero. Here differentiability means one linear approximation works for every sufficiently small displacement, with an error small compared with displacement length. Try a compass on an oval hill Worked example. Take f(x,y)=x²+2y² at p=(1,1). Freezing y gives f x =2x; freezing x gives f y =4y. Thus ∇f(p)=(2,4). North gives rate 4; east gives 2. Northeast along u=(1/√2,1/√2) gives (2+4)/√2=3√2, about 4.24. The gradient's own unit direction is (1/√5,2/√5), and the predicted rate there is 2/√5+8/√5=2√5, about 4.47. Check the prediction at a finite h. Along u=(1/√5,2/√5), direct expansion yields f(p+hu)−f(p)=2√5 h+(9/5)h². At h=1/10, the actual increase exceeds the linear prediction by 9/500. A larger step has a larger quadratic correction. The derivative is the coefficient left after dividing by h and letting h shrink; it is not a promise that finite steps have exactly linear effect. Normalize before comparing. The vector (1,2) has length √5, so its dot product with (2,4) is 10. That number describes change per unit of the parameter in p+t(1,2), which travels √5 distance units per parameter unit. Dividing the direction by √5 gives rate 2√5 per unit distance. Without this normalization a longer direction vector would appear steeper simply because the walker travels farther. Steepest-direction comparisons require equal travel lengths. The theorem and its condition Exact statement. If f is differentiable at p, then for any unit vector u, D u f(p)=∇f(p)·u. If ∇f(p) is nonzero, the maximum over unit directions is ||∇f(p)||, attained only when u points along the gradient; the minimum is its negative, in the opposite direction. If the gradient is zero, every directional derivative is zero, and no unique uphill direction exists at first order. D u f ( p ) = ∇ f ( p ) · u ≤ ‖ ∇ f ( p ) ‖ For the first claim, write f(p+h)=f(p)+L(h)+o(||h||), where L is linear. The coordinate directions identify L(h)=f x h 1 +f y h 2 . Replace h by tu, divide by t, and take the limit. The inequality follows from Cauchy–Schwarz. Equality with positive sign requires aligned nonzero vectors. This proves the steepest direction statement; a contour sketch is only an illustration. Existing partial derivatives at a point do not by themselves guarantee the shared approximation used above. The partials counterexample has both partials at its origin but is discontinuous there. Therefore the differentiability condition belongs in the statement. At the origin of our quadratic, ∇f=0 even though every nonzero displacement raises height; the first-order compass is silent about this second-order bowl. One more useful check is to compare two unit directions that differ only by sign. Their directional derivatives are opposites because the dot product is linear in u. This does not mean walking a finite distance in opposite directions changes height by exactly opposite amounts: quadratic terms can raise both endpoints, as they do at the bottom of a bowl. The gradient describes the first-order part only. Check the compass 1. Calculation. For g(x,y)=3x²+y² at (1,−2), find the derivative along (3/5,4/5) and the steepest ascent rate. Hint for question 1 Compute the two partials first, then dot with a unit direction. Worked solution for question 1 ∇g=(6x,2y), so ∇g(1,−2)=(6,−4). The supplied vector has length 1. Its derivative is 6(3/5)−4(4/5)=2/5. Cauchy–Schwarz gives maximum √(36+16)=2√13, reached along (3,−2)/√13. 2. Explanation. At (0,0), g has gradient zero. Does that prove nearby heights equal g(0,0)? Hint for question 2 Look at g(h,0) and the order of its change. Worked solution for question 2 No. g(h,0)=3h²>0 for h≠0, while g(0,0)=0. Zero gradient says the first-order directional rate vanishes; it does not say the quadratic or higher-order change vanishes. The origin is actually a strict minimum here. One vector, with a boundary For a differentiable landscape, the gradient packages every first-order directional rate, and its length is the largest such rate for unit motion. The same claim can fail without differentiability. A practical stopping point is to compute the gradient, normalize a requested direction, and check what approximation the formula assumes. If a finite step disagrees, inspect the neglected higher-order term before doubting the derivative.

title: Partial derivatives can miss a cliff
summary: Checking only east and north can hide what happens diagonally.
text: Two clear directions, one hidden cliff Suppose a function has an eastward and a northward derivative at a point. Have we learned its behavior on every approach? No: two axes are only two of infinitely many paths. A sharp counterexample lets us separate partial derivatives, directional derivatives, continuity, and a total derivative. Background capsule. For f(x,y), the partial at the origin in x is the limit [f(h,0)−f(0,0)]/h; the y partial uses (0,h). Continuity at the origin requires f(x,y) to approach f(0,0) along every path, not only axes. Total differentiability requires f(h,k)=f(0,0)+L(h,k)+o(√(h²+k²)) for one linear map L. That condition implies continuity because both L(h,k) and its smaller error tend to zero. Walk the axes, then the diagonal Worked example. Define f(x,y)=xy/(x²+y²) away from the origin and f(0,0)=0. On either coordinate axis the numerator is zero, so f(h,0)=f(0,h)=0. Both partial derivatives at the origin exist and equal zero. A test limited to those directions would suggest a flat surface. Along the diagonal x=y=t≠0, however, f(t,t)=t²/(2t²)=1/2. The value stays one-half no matter how close t gets to zero, while f(0,0)=0. Along x=−y=t, the value is −1/2. Thus there is no single two-variable limit at the origin and no continuity there. For an explicit exact-value table, t=1, 1/10, or 1/1000 always gives zero on the axes and one-half on the main diagonal. More decimal sampling cannot repair that disagreement. Approaches to the origin, for any nonzero t Point Value (t,0) 0 (0,t) 0 (t,t) 1/2 (t,−t) −1/2 Try changing the declared central value. Assigning f(0,0)=1/2 would match the diagonal limit, but the axes would still have values zero. Assigning any other constant also leaves at least two disagreeing path limits. The discontinuity cannot be repaired by redefining only the origin. This is different from a removable one-variable hole, where all approaching values already share a common limit and only the value at the missing point needs correction. What exactly fails? Exact conclusion. Both coordinate partial derivatives exist at the origin, but f is neither continuous nor totally differentiable there. In fact, for a nonaxis unit direction u=(a,b) with ab≠0, f(tu)=ab/(a²+b²)=ab for every t≠0. The quotient [f(tu)−0]/t=ab/t has no finite two-sided limit. On the axes it is zero. Even directional differentiability fails in most directions. f ( t , t ) = t 2 2 t 2 = 1 2 ≠ f ( 0 , 0 ) The proof of noncontinuity needs only the diagonal sequence t=1/n. If continuity held, values on that sequence would approach zero; instead every value is one-half. Since differentiability implies continuity, noncontinuity rules out differentiability. This is an implication argument, not merely a claim based on a plot. A common sufficient condition goes the other way: if both partials exist in a neighborhood and are continuous at the point, then f is differentiable there. That is a separate theorem; this example violates its continuity premise. Do not misread the counterexample as saying partial derivatives are useless. They correctly describe coordinate-axis rates, but they cannot alone license the gradient-dot-direction formula or a tangent plane. The example is bounded between −1/2 and 1/2 away from the origin, because 2|xy|≤x²+y². Boundedness therefore does not rescue continuity. The obstruction is persistent directional disagreement: as the distance to the origin tends to zero, diagonal values remain fixed away from the declared value. This also shows why a numerical grid that omits the diagonal could misleadingly suggest a smooth center. Test the hidden path 1. Calculation. For the same f, compute f(t,2t) and decide whether continuity at the origin is possible. Hint for question 1 Cancel t² only after declaring t≠0. Worked solution for question 1 f(t,2t)=2t²/(t²+4t²)=2/5 for every t≠0. As t→0 the path limit is 2/5, different from f(0,0)=0. Thus continuity is impossible even without considering the main diagonal. 2. Explanation. A student finds f x (0,0)=f y (0,0)=0 and writes f(h,k)=o(√(h²+k²)). Locate the unjustified step.
