Hint for question 2 Ask whether axis estimates control points where both h and k are nonzero. Worked solution for question 2 The partial limits only give f(h,0)=o(|h|) and f(0,k)=o(|k|). They give no estimate for f(h,k) when both coordinates vary. Along h=k=t, f=1/2, and [f(t,t)]/√(2t²)=1/(2√2|t|), which diverges. The proposed remainder estimate is false. Use the correct level of evidence Coordinate partials answer two restricted limit questions. Continuity requires every approach, and differentiability requires one linear approximation with a uniform small remainder. This example proves the separation exactly. To continue, ask which additional local conditions guarantee differentiability; continuous partial derivatives near the point are a standard sufficient route, while an isolated point's partials are not.

title: Why polar coordinates need an extra r
summary: Equal steps on a polar grid do not enclose equal areas.
text: Why a polar cell widens as it moves outward In a polar grid, an angular change of one degree covers a longer arc far from the center than near it. That geometric fact becomes the factor r in polar area integrals. We will calculate it locally, check it with an exact annular sector, and mark the origin where polar coordinates cease to be one-to-one. Background capsule. Polar coordinates describe a point by distance r≥0 and angle θ: x=r cosθ, y=r sinθ. A determinant of two planar vectors gives their signed parallelogram area; its absolute value is area. A double integral adds values times tiny area cells. The one-variable identity ∫r dr=r²/2 will suffice for the disk example. Check an annular sector exactly Worked example. Take radii a and a+Δr, with a>0, and an angle width Δθ measured in radians. The sector area of radius R is R²Δθ/2, because it is Δθ/(2π) of a circle of area πR². Subtract two sectors: the annular area is [(a+Δr)²−a²]Δθ/2 = (aΔr+(Δr)²/2)Δθ. Divide by ΔrΔθ; as Δr shrinks, the ratio tends to a. Thus an infinitesimal rectangle in (r,θ) coordinates corresponds to physical area approximately rΔrΔθ, with a precise limiting factor. For a disk of radius 2, integrate the factor: ∫ from θ=0 to 2π and r=0 to 2 of r dr dθ = (2π)(2)=4π. If we omitted r, we would get 4π coincidentally for this radius? The incorrect integral would be ∫1 dr dθ=4π too! Choose radius 3 to expose the error: correct area 9π; omitting r yields 6π. Agreement at radius 2 is an accidental numerical collision, not evidence for the wrong element. Check a ring rather than a disk. The annulus 1≤r≤2 with a full turn has area ∫₀²π∫₁²r dr dθ=2π(4−1)/2=3π. This agrees with subtracting the inner disk area π from the outer disk area 4π. The angular interval has unchanged length, but the radial integral weights outer strips more heavily because each strip wraps around a longer circle. Using just dr dθ would incorrectly assign area 2π. Compute the local area multiplier For Φ(r,θ)=(r cosθ,r sinθ), the derivative sends a small radial displacement to (cosθ,sinθ) and a small angular displacement to (−r sinθ,r cosθ). Their determinant is r(cos²θ+sin²θ)=r. Therefore the local area multiplier is |det DΦ|=r for r≥0. d x d y = | det D Φ | d r d θ = r d r d θ Proof boundary. The determinant calculation proves the local linear area factor, and the sector calculation verifies it exactly in this geometry. A sufficient change-of-variables statement is this: if Φ:U→V is a C¹ diffeomorphism between open planar sets, D is a compact Jordan-measurable subset of U, and g is continuous on Φ(D), then ∫∫ over Φ(D) of g(x,y) dA equals ∫∫ over D of g(Φ(r,θ))|det DΦ(r,θ)| dr dθ. We invoke that theorem rather than prove its general form. The polar map is a diffeomorphism only after restricting to r>0 and an open angular interval with no seam duplication. At r=0 every angle names the same point; at a full-turn seam two angles name the same ray. To integrate a bounded disk, apply the valid change of variables away from those exceptional sets and pass to the limit. The origin and seam have area zero, so continuous bounded integrands are unaffected. This does not claim a diffeomorphism through either exception. Orientation matters for signed determinants. If angle runs clockwise, the signed determinant changes sign; physical area still uses an absolute value. For any integrand, r multiplies the integrand after substituting x and y. For example x²+y² becomes r², so its disk integral is ∫∫r³ dr dθ, not ∫∫r² dr dθ. Integrate with the right cell area 1. Calculation. Compute ∬ over the disk x²+y²≤4 of (x²+y²) dA. Hint for question 1 Use r² for the function and another r for the area factor. Worked solution for question 1 The disk is 0≤r≤2, 0≤θ<2π. Thus the integral is ∫₀²π∫₀² r³ dr dθ = (2π)[r⁴/4]₀²=(2π)(4)=8π. The origin causes no singularity in this integrand. 2. Explanation. A student argues that because det DΦ(0,θ)=0, the disk's area must be zero. Explain the confusion. Hint for question 2 A local factor at one radius does not describe all radii. Worked solution for question 2 The determinant vanishes only at r=0. For every r>0 the local factor is positive and grows with r. Integrating r from 0 to the disk radius accumulates those nonzero annular contributions. The single origin has zero area; it does not make the entire disk collapse. What to keep The extra r measures how a unit angular increment stretches with distance from the origin. It is a Jacobian factor, supported both by a determinant and by annular-sector area. The limitation is coordinate singularity at the origin and seam duplication at a full turn. For a routine disk integral, use a half-open angular range, include r, and check dimensions: dr has length, r dθ has length, so their product has area.

title: The same region, two ways to slice
summary: A difficult integral can become simple when its slices turn sideways.
text: Turn the slices sideways An integral over a triangular region may look hard because its first set of bounds cuts vertically. The same points can be listed horizontally. Reversing integration order is a geometric re-description of the region, followed by a theorem that permits the two iterated calculations to agree for a continuous integrand. Background capsule. In ∫₀¹∫ₓ¹ f(x,y) dy dx, the inner integral holds x fixed and moves y from x to 1; the outer integral then moves x from 0 to 1. Inequalities define a region without reference to drawing scale. For a continuous function on a closed bounded region, its double integral can be computed by either standard slicing order when bounds describe the same region. Describe one triangle twice Worked example. The first bounds say 0≤x≤1 and x≤y≤1. Combine them as 0≤x≤y≤1. To choose y first, y can run from 0 to 1, and for that y, x can run from 0 to y. Hence the other order is ∫₀¹∫₀ʸ f(x,y) dx dy. No region has moved; only the order of enumeration has changed. For f(x,y)=y, the original order gives ∫₀¹ [y²/2] from y=x to 1 dx = ∫₀¹(1−x²)/2 dx=1/3. The reversed order is shorter: ∫₀¹∫₀ʸ y dx dy=∫₀¹ y² dy=1/3. Reversing is especially useful when the new inner antiderivative is simpler, but the region description should come before the algebra. Slices of the same triangle Fixed coordinate Outer range Inner range x 0≤x≤1 x≤y≤1 y 0≤y≤1 0≤x≤y Check a typical slice before integrating. At x=1/4 the original region contains y between 1/4 and 1; at y=1/4 the reversed region contains x between 0 and 1/4. These are different line segments through the same triangular set. A bound depending on the inner variable would not describe a fixed slice: while integrating dx, its endpoints may depend on y, which is being held constant, but cannot still depend on the moving x. Reading one slice aloud often reveals an impossible or reversed inequality before an antiderivative obscures it. The equality and its scope Exact statement. If f is continuous on the compact triangle D={(x,y):0≤x≤y≤1}, then both iterated integrals below exist and equal ∬ D f dA. This is a standard Fubini-type result for such a region, not a consequence of symbol swapping alone. We use that theorem here and prove the equality directly for polynomial examples by calculation. ∫ 0 1 ∫ x 1 f ( x , y ) d y d x = ∫ 0 1 ∫ 0 y f ( x , y ) d x d y The bounds can be justified without a drawing: from 0≤x≤1 and x≤y≤1 we immediately get 0≤y≤1 and 0≤x≤y. Conversely the latter inequalities imply the former. So the two descriptions are logically equivalent point by point. Once that is established, continuity on this bounded set supplies the integrability needed to exchange the order. A failure case lies outside these hypotheses. For unbounded regions or singular integrands, separately existing iterated integrals need not be equal without absolute integrability or an appropriate theorem. Even on the triangle, changing bounds to 0≤x≤1−y would define a different triangle. A sketch can catch such mistakes, but a check of inequalities is decisive. There is a simple area check for the bounds: setting f=1 makes either iterated integral equal the triangle’s area, 1/2. In the first order, each vertical slice has length 1−x, whose integral is 1/2. In the reversed order, each horizontal slice has length y, also integrating to 1/2. This check cannot prove equality for every f, but it catches many wrong bound reversals quickly. Rebuild the bounds 1. Calculation. Reverse ∫₀¹∫ₓ¹ x dy dx and evaluate it in both orders. Hint for question 1 The triangle is unchanged; hold y fixed in the reversed version. Worked solution for question 1 The reversed integral is ∫₀¹∫₀ʸ x dx dy=∫₀¹ y²/2 dy=1/6. Originally, integrating dy gives ∫₀¹ x(1−x) dx=[x²/2−x³/3]₀¹=1/6. Both routes agree. 2. Explanation. Someone replaces the inner x bound with 0≤x≤1−y. Find a point included in the correct region but excluded by the proposed one. Hint for question 2 Choose y near 1 and x below y but larger than 1−y. Worked solution for question 2 The point (x,y)=(3/4,1) satisfies 0≤x≤y≤1, so it lies in D. The proposed bound requires x≤1−y=0 and excludes it. The proposed region has a different diagonal boundary; it cannot be a reversal of the original integral. A reliable stopping rule Translate nested bounds into simultaneous inequalities, decide the new outer interval, then solve the remaining inequalities for the new inner coordinate. The equality of integrals follows for continuous f on this compact triangle. If the integrand is singular or the region unbounded, check a suitable convergence theorem before exchanging order; the geometric bounds alone do not settle that question.

title: Does a round trip cost any work?
summary: Two routes between the same places can have different totals.
text: Does the route affect the work? A force field assigns an arrow to each point. The work along a route adds the force component in the direction of travel. In some fields only endpoints matter; in others two routes between the same endpoints have different totals. The distinction is calculable, not merely visual. Background capsule. A parametrized path r(t)=(x(t),y(t)), a≤t≤b, lists positions in travel order. Its velocity is r′(t)=(x′(t),y′(t)). The dot product F·r′ measures the field component along motion, with a sign: moving against a force contributes negative work. A scalar potential φ has gradient ∇φ=(φ x ,φ y ); its change between endpoints can be found by ordinary substitution. Two routes through one field Worked example. Let F(x,y)=(y,x), from A=(0,0) to B=(1,1). The direct route r(t)=(t,t), 0≤t≤1, has F(r(t))=(t,t) and r′=(1,1). The dot product is 2t, so work is ∫₀¹2t dt=1. Take a broken route: first (t,0), 0≤t≤1, then (1,t), 0≤t≤1. On the horizontal leg F=(0,t), velocity (1,0), and work is 0. On the vertical leg F=(t,1), velocity (0,1), and work is ∫₀¹1 dt=1. Total work is again 1. This agreement has a reason: F=∇(xy), so a potential φ(x,y)=xy increases from 0 to 1 on both routes. Contrast G(x,y)=(−y,x). On the direct route, G(t,t)=(-t,t), orthogonal to (1,1), so work is zero. On the broken route the horizontal leg again gives zero, but the vertical leg gives G(1,t)=(-t,1) dotted with (0,1), so work is one. Same endpoints no longer guarantee same work. Separate route shape from traversal speed. Reparameterize the direct segment as r(s)=(s²,s²), 0≤s≤1. For F=(y,x), substitution gives F(r(s))=(s²,s²) and r′(s)=(2s,2s), so the work is ∫₀¹4s³ ds=1 again. The walker starts slowly and speeds up, but follows the same oriented segment once. The velocity factor in the integral compensates for that changed timing. Reversing orientation changes the answer's sign; a change of speed preserving orientation does not. Merely integrating the field values without the velocity would lose this distinction. Parameter formula and endpoint rule Exact statement. For a continuous field F along a piecewise C¹ path r, its line integral is defined by the parameter formula below. If φ is C¹ on an open set containing the entire path and F=∇φ there, then the line integral equals φ(r(b))−φ(r(a)). This follows from the chain rule on each smooth path piece; intermediate endpoint terms cancel when the pieces are added. ∫ C F · d r = ∫ a b F ( r ( t ) ) · r ′ ( t ) d t Why does the formula reflect work? Partition the path into short segments Δr. Over one segment a continuous force is approximately F(r) and work approximately F(r)·Δr. Summing and refining gives the parameter integral because Δr≈r′(t)Δt. That motivation does not by itself prove all limiting details; the displayed integral is the precise definition we use. Reversing a path reverses its integral: the velocity changes sign under reversed parametrization. In a gradient field, a round trip has zero work because start and end coincide. The converse needs conditions. A field can have zero scalar curl wherever defined and still give nonzero circulation around a hole; see the punctured-plane example . Checking curl locally is insufficient for a global potential on an arbitrary domain. Compute and interpret work 1. Calculation. Let H(x,y)=(2x,2y) and r(t)=(t,t²), 0≤t≤1. Compute work and then identify a potential. Hint for question 1 Substitute the path first; r′=(1,2t). Worked solution for question 1 H(r(t))=(2t,2t²), so H·r′=2t+4t³. Its integral is [t²+t⁴]₀¹=2. A potential is φ=x²+y², whose endpoint change is φ(1,1)−φ(0,0)=2. The two methods agree. 2. Explanation. A path from A to B has work 3 in a continuous field. What is the work along exactly the same path traversed backward? Does this establish path independence? Hint for question 2 Track the sign of velocity; then ask whether another geometric route was tested. Worked solution for question 2 The reversed path has work −3, because its displacement direction is reversed at each point. This says nothing about other routes from A to B. Path independence requires every pair of admissible routes between the endpoints to have the same work, or equivalently every closed admissible loop to have zero circulation. A path calculation with a test Parametrize each piece, substitute F, dot with velocity, and integrate with travel direction intact. If you can exhibit a C¹ potential on the whole region containing the route, endpoint subtraction replaces the calculation. If you have only a zero-curl calculation, first inspect the domain for holes and the path for singularities before claiming a potential.

title: The hole that curl cannot see
summary: A field can have zero curl everywhere it exists and still do work around a loop.
text: A local test misses a global loop A field can have zero curl at every point where it exists and still circulate around a missing point. This is the cleanest warning about the domain condition in the familiar “zero curl implies conservative” rule. We will calculate both sides exactly, then identify the hypothesis the shortcut omitted. Background capsule. For F=(P,Q), scalar curl in the plane is Q x −P y . Circulation around a parametrized loop r(t) is ∫F(r(t))·r′(t)dt. A gradient field F=∇φ has zero circulation on every closed loop in its domain by the endpoint rule. A simply connected region has no hole that prevents a loop from being shrunk continuously to a point while staying inside the region. Circle the excluded origin Worked example. On U=ℝ²\{(0,0)}, define F(x,y)=(-y/(x²+y²),x/(x²+y²)). The denominator is positive at every point of U. Traverse the unit circle counterclockwise with r(t)=(cos t,sin t), 0≤t≤2π. Since x²+y²=1 there, F(r(t))=(-sin t,cos t)=r′(t). The dot product is exactly 1. Therefore the circulation is ∫₀²π1 dt=2π. Reverse the orientation and the result is −2π. A circle of radius R>0 gives the same counterclockwise answer: F(R cos t,R sin t)=(-sin t/R,cos t/R), while r′=R(-sin t,cos t), so the dot product remains 1. A circle missing the origin cannot be continuously contracted through the origin while remaining in U. That missing point is where the field would become undefined, not an ordinary point with an unmeasured curl. Inspect an annulus explicitly. Take 1≤√(x²+y²)≤2. The positive boundary of this region consists of the radius-two circle counterclockwise and the radius-one circle clockwise. Their circulations are 2π and −2π, adding to zero, exactly matching the integral of zero curl over the annulus. The inner boundary is essential. Keeping only the outer circle would describe a different boundary and would quietly fill the missing disk. This calculation distinguishes a legitimate use of Green's theorem on a region avoiding zero from an illegitimate use on the full disk. Compute the curl and find the omitted premise Write s=x²+y². Then Q=x/s and P=−y/s. Quotient differentiation gives Q x =(s−2x²)/s²=(y²−x²)/s². Similarly P y =(-s+2y²)/s²=(y²−x²)/s². Their difference is zero at every point of U. Thus zero curl and nonzero circulation coexist without contradiction. ∮ | r | = 1 F · d r = ∫ 0 2 π 1 d t = 2 π Exact boundary. On a simply connected open planar domain, a C¹ field with Q x −P y =0 has a potential; this is a standard theorem we state, not prove in full here. Our punctured plane is not simply connected. More directly, if our F had a globally single-valued C¹ potential on U, the endpoint rule would force the unit-circle integral to be zero, contradicting 2π. So no such potential exists. Locally, away from a branch cut, the polar angle θ has gradient F. But θ jumps by 2π after one full turn; it cannot be a globally single-valued continuous potential on U. Do not apply Green's theorem to the filled unit disk: F is undefined at its center, violating the theorem's smoothness condition on a neighborhood of the region. On an annulus the inner and outer boundary circulations cancel with their induced opposite orientations. Check the topology and sign 1. Calculation. Compute the circulation along r(t)=(2 cos t,−2 sin t), 0≤t≤2π. Hint for question 1 This path runs clockwise; either compute the dot product or reverse a known circle. Worked solution for question 1 F(r(t))=(sin t/2,cos t/2), while r′=(-2 sin t,−2 cos t). Their dot product is −sin²t−cos²t=−1. Integration from 0 to 2π gives −2π. The radius does not alter the magnitude. 2. Explanation. A student integrates the zero curl over the unit disk and concludes its boundary circulation is zero. Identify the exact invalid premise. Hint for question 2 Check where the vector field is defined. Worked solution for question 2 The disk contains (0,0), where x²+y²=0 and F is undefined. Green's theorem requires the field and relevant partial derivatives throughout an appropriate neighborhood of the filled region. Integrating a formula valid only off the origin over the disk does not meet that condition; the direct boundary integral is 2π. Local curl is not the whole story The computation establishes zero curl on U and circulation 2π around a counterclockwise loop. A global potential would contradict the latter. Stop with the domain-aware rule: inspect both derivatives and where the field exists. A loop avoiding a singularity can still enclose it, and enclosure can change the circulation even when every point on the loop is regular.

title: A boundary remembers the whole interior
summary: Interior edges cancel, leaving a theorem on the outside.
text: Why a boundary can remember an interior Green's theorem turns circulation around a planar boundary into a double integral of local rotation inside. On a rectangle, the identity follows from the one-variable fundamental theorem twice. This proof exposes why the boundary must be counterclockwise and why inner edges cancel when rectangles are tiled. Background capsule. A field F=(P,Q) contributes P dx+Q dy along a moving path. The scalar curl is Q x −P y . Counterclockwise orientation means the region stays to your left as you walk its outer boundary. A C¹ function has continuous first partial derivatives, allowing us to apply the one-variable fundamental theorem and exchange ordinary integrations on a rectangle. Walk around a unit square Worked example. Let P=−y and Q=x on D=[0,1]×[0,1]. Along the bottom edge y=0, travel right: P dx=0. Along the right edge x=1, travel up: Q dy=1 dy, total 1. Along the top edge y=1, travel left from x=1 to 0: P dx=−1 dx, and the reversed x bounds give another 1. Along the left edge x=0, travel down: Q dy=0. Total circulation is 2. Inside, Q x =1 and P y =−1, so curl is 2 everywhere. The area is 1, giving double integral 2. This match is exact. Clockwise travel would give −2 on the boundary, while the right side would remain +2 unless we also changed the orientation convention. A theorem statement that omits orientation is incomplete. Follow one shared contribution. Divide the unit square at x=1/2 for the worked field (−y,x). The shared vertical edge contributes ∫₀¹(1/2)dy=1/2 when it is the right edge of the left rectangle. As the left edge of the right rectangle it contributes ∫₁⁰(1/2)dy=−1/2. Their sum is exactly zero, while each rectangle's curl integral is 2 times area 1/2, hence 1. Adding gives the original circulation 2. Cancellation concerns the same geometric edge with opposite traversals; it does not require the field itself to vanish there. Prove the rectangular case Take D=[a,b]×[c,d], with P,Q continuously differentiable on an open neighborhood. Bottom and top contributions from P are ∫ₐᵇP(x,c)dx and −∫ₐᵇP(x,d)dx. Together they equal −∫ₐᵇ∫꜀ᵈP y (x,y)dy dx by the fundamental theorem. Right and left contributions from Q are ∫꜀ᵈQ(b,y)dy and −∫꜀ᵈQ(a,y)dy, together ∫꜀ᵈ∫ₐᵇQ x (x,y)dx dy. Continuous partials allow both to be written as integrals over D, yielding the formula. ∮ ∂ D P d x + Q d y = ∬ D ( Q x − P y ) d A Proof boundary. We have proved the axis-aligned rectangular case. If two rectangles share an edge, one counterclockwise walk traverses that edge upward and the other downward; their line integrals cancel because reversing a path reverses its integral. This explains a route toward more general regions, but passing to curved boundaries requires approximation and regularity arguments not supplied here. For a standard piecewise smooth planar region and C¹ field on its neighborhood, Green's theorem holds with the correctly oriented boundary; holes add clockwise inner boundaries. A counterexample to careless use is the vortex field F=(-y/(x²+y²),x/(x²+y²)) on a disk centered at the origin. It has zero curl wherever defined yet nonzero unit-circle circulation because it is undefined inside. The missing smoothness condition blocks Green's theorem on that disk. Check edges and hypotheses 1. Calculation. On D=[0,2]×[0,1], let P=0 and Q=x². Compute both sides of Green's formula. Hint for question 1 Only the vertical edges contribute to the line integral. Worked solution for question 1 On the right edge x=2, Q=4 and upward dy from 0 to 1 contributes 4. On the left x=0, Q=0. The horizontal edges have P=0, so the boundary total is 4. Inside, Q x −P y =2x; integrating ∫₀¹∫₀²2x dx dy gives 4. 2. Explanation. Two adjacent counterclockwise rectangles share a vertical edge. Why does that edge disappear from the boundary integral of their union? Hint for question 2 Describe the travel direction on each copy of the shared edge. Worked solution for question 2 The right edge of the left rectangle is walked upward; the left edge of the right rectangle is walked downward. The same field is evaluated at the same points, but dr changes sign, so the two line integrals are negatives and sum to zero. The remaining edges trace the outer boundary. A proved case and a wider theorem For a rectangle with a C¹ field, boundary circulation equals integrated scalar curl by two applications of the fundamental theorem. Tiling gives an exact cancellation pattern for interior edges. Stop by checking orientation and whether the field is smooth on the whole filled region. For irregular boundaries or holes, invoke the general theorem only with its geometric and domain hypotheses intact.

title: Count the flow through a box
summary: Tiny sources inside a region determine its net outward flow.
text: Count what flows out of a box A three-dimensional field can send material through a closed surface. Divergence measures local net source strength, and the divergence theorem equates its volume total with outward flux. For a rectangular box, the equality is a direct cancellation of opposite faces through the one-variable fundamental theorem. Background capsule. F=(F₁,F₂,F₃) assigns a vector to each point. A face has an outward unit normal n: on the right x=b it is (1,0,0), on the left x=a it is (−1,0,0). The product F·n is signed flux per area. A triple integral sums over volume. Divergence is ∂F₁/∂x+∂F₂/∂y+∂F₃/∂z. A C¹ field has continuous first partial derivatives. Six faces, one source count Worked example. Choose the unit cube 0≤x,y,z≤1 and F=(x,y,z). On the right face x=1, F·n=1, so flux is 1. On the left face x=0, F·n=−x=0. The top y=1 and front z=1 faces each contribute 1, while their opposite zero-coordinate faces contribute 0. Total outward flux is 3. The divergence is 1+1+1=3 throughout the cube. Volume is 1, so its integral is 3. This field expands away from the origin; arrows alone suggest outward flow, but the face-by-face signs and areas give the exact total. If F were constant, opposite faces would contribute equal and opposite flux, and divergence would be zero. Prove the box identity Let V=[a,b]×[c,d]×[e,f] and F be C¹ on a neighborhood. Pair the x faces. Their net contribution is ∫꜀ᵈ∫ₑᶠ[F₁(b,y,z)−F₁(a,y,z)] dz dy. By the one-variable fundamental theorem, the bracket equals ∫ₐᵇ ∂F₁/∂x dx. Hence the pair contributes ∭ V ∂F₁/∂x dV. The y pair similarly gives ∭∂F₂/∂y, and the z pair ∭∂F₃/∂z. Add the three pairs. ∯ ∂ V F · n d S = ∭ V ( ∂ x F 1 + ∂ y F 2 + ∂ z F 3 ) d V Proof boundary. This establishes the rectangular-box theorem. Subdividing a larger box cancels shared-face flux because the outward normals of neighboring cells are opposites. A standard sufficient general statement is: if V is a bounded solid with closed piecewise C¹ boundary and F is C¹ on an open neighborhood of its closure, then the outward flux through ∂V equals the volume integral of div F. Corners are allowed as lower-dimensional boundary pieces under this formulation. Passing from boxes to curved faces and proving this general statement requires a separate limiting argument; we state it rather than claim our box proof establishes it. The neighborhood condition ensures the derivatives used in the volume are defined right up to the boundary. Sign matters. The theorem uses outward normals; inward normals would negate the left side. It also needs a closed boundary. Flux through only five faces of a cube can differ from the volume integral because the missing face may carry nonzero flow. A singular field inside a volume may defeat the smoothness hypothesis, even if its divergence vanishes wherever it is defined. For a box with side lengths L, W, and H, a constant divergence c integrates to cLWH. That units check matters: divergence has flux per unit volume, so multiplying by volume returns flux. A single face flux instead depends on its area and on the field component normal to that face. Confusing these quantities can produce a numerically plausible answer with the wrong geometric meaning. Balance a different box 1. Calculation. For F=(2x,0,−z) on V=[0,2]×[0,1]×[0,3], compute outward flux by faces and by divergence. Hint for question 1 Only the x and z face pairs contribute; each face area differs. Worked solution for question 1 At x=2, F·n=4 on area 1·3=3, giving 12; at x=0 it is zero. At z=3, F·n=−3 on area 2·1=2, giving −6; at z=0 it is zero. The y faces contribute zero. Total is 6. Divergence is 2−1=1, and the box volume is 2·1·3=6, so the volume integral is 6. 2. Explanation. Why can a constant field have nonzero flux through one face but zero net flux through a closed box? Hint for question 2 Pair opposite faces and compare their normals. Worked solution for question 2 The same constant component meets equal-area opposite faces, but their outward normals have opposite signs. Their signed contributions cancel pairwise. Divergence of a constant field is zero, consistent with zero total closed-surface flux. A single face does not include its cancelling partner. Sources inside, flux outside For a C¹ field on a box, opposite-face differences integrate the corresponding partial derivatives. Add all directions to obtain divergence and total outward flux. This is a proof for boxes and a template for understanding the general theorem, whose curved-surface passage needs more work. Keep the entire closed boundary and its outward orientation in the calculation.

title: The same circulation from different surfaces
summary: A loop can be spanned by different surfaces yet give the same answer.
text: One loop, different spanning surfaces A circle can bound a flat disk or a curved cap. Stokes' theorem says circulation around the oriented loop equals the normal component of curl integrated over a suitable spanning surface. The boundary orientation must match the surface normal, and the field must be smooth where the chosen surface lies. Background capsule. For F=(P,Q,R), curl is (R y −Q z , P z −R x , Q x −P y ). A surface normal n gives a positive side. Looking from the tip of n toward the surface, the compatible boundary direction is counterclockwise. A surface integral of curl·n dS adds local rotation through tiny oriented area patches. The cross product of tangent vectors gives an oriented area element for a parametrized surface. Compute the disk and its rim Worked example. Let F(x,y,z)=(-y/2,x/2,0), and let S be the unit disk z=0 with upward normal (0,0,1). Its boundary is r(t)=(cos t,sin t,0), 0≤t≤2π, traversed counterclockwise from above. On the boundary, F=(-sin t/2,cos t/2,0) and r′=(-sin t,cos t,0). Their dot product is 1/2, so circulation is ∫₀²π1/2 dt=π. The curl is (0,0,1), constant everywhere. On the upward disk curl·n=1, and the disk has area π, so the surface integral is π. Reverse the normal to downward and the induced positive rim direction becomes clockwise; both integrals become −π. If one changes only the normal but keeps the old rim traversal, the signs disagree because the orientations are incompatible. Calculate the cap's flux directly as a check. Away from its equator, the upper hemisphere is the graph z=√(1−x²−y²). Its upward oriented area vector is (−z x ,−z y ,1) dx dy. Dotting this with curl F=(0,0,1) leaves dx dy, so integration over the projected unit disk gives π. The graph derivatives become unbounded at the equator; one can calculate first on projected radius ρ<1 and let ρ increase to 1. The result depends on projected oriented area, explaining why the hemisphere's larger surface area does not produce a larger flux for this vertical curl. The theorem and what this example establishes General statement. For an oriented piecewise smooth surface S with piecewise smooth boundary and a C¹ field on a neighborhood of S, Stokes' theorem equates circulation around the induced oriented boundary with the flux of curl through S. For our planar disk, the identity reduces to Green's theorem because the vertical component of curl is Q x −P y . The direct calculations above verify this example; they are not a proof for every curved surface. ∮ ∂ S F · d r = ∬ S ( ∇ × F ) · n d S To see a second spanning surface without integrating a difficult normal, use the upper hemisphere x²+y²+z²=1, z≥0, with outward/upward normal. Its boundary is the same unit circle, counterclockwise when viewed from above. Since F is smooth throughout both surfaces and Stokes applies to each, both curl fluxes equal the same boundary circulation π. For arbitrary admissible fields, this same-boundary conclusion invokes the general theorem for the curved cap; the graph calculation above additionally verifies the cap value directly for our selected constant curl. The two surfaces need not have equal area or matching normals point by point. A failure case is a field singular on one proposed spanning surface. The punctured-plane vortex can be integrated along a circle, but an attempt to span it with a disk through the origin violates smoothness. Choosing a different surface does not allow a hidden singularity to be ignored; verify a valid field neighborhood and compatible orientation first. Trace the orientation 1. Calculation. Replace F by G=(-y,x,0) on the upward unit disk. Compute circulation and curl flux. Hint for question 1 G is twice the worked field. Worked solution for question 1 Along the rim, G(r(t))=(-sin t,cos t,0)=r′(t), so the integrand is 1 and circulation is 2π. Curl G=(0,0,2), so upward flux is 2 times disk area π, also 2π. 2. Explanation. A student chooses the downward normal but walks the rim counterclockwise from above, then reports opposite signs as a failure of Stokes. Repair the setup. Hint for question 2 Use the right-hand orientation rule to choose the boundary direction. Worked solution for question 2 Downward normal induces clockwise rim travel when viewed from above. Reverse the boundary path, giving circulation −π for the worked field. Curl flux with downward normal is also −π. Keeping counterclockwise travel pairs the boundary of one orientation with the surface of the other and does not match the theorem. The loop carries its orientation For the smooth field and upward disk, both sides equal π. A different valid spanning surface inherits the same boundary total through the general theorem, not because its area equals the disk's. Stop by checking three items in order: the field is defined and C¹ near the surface, the surface normal is chosen, and the boundary traversal matches it. Those checks prevent most apparent sign paradoxes.

title: Divisibility as a witness
summary: Use integer witnesses to prove divisibility rules and test seductive false converses.
text: What does it mean for a count to fit exactly? A maker packs screws in trays of six. An order of 42 screws fills seven trays; an order of 43 leaves one screw. The distinction is more useful than the familiar phrase “goes into”: it asks for a whole-number witness. For integers a and b , a divides b , written a ∣ b, means that some integer k satisfies b = ak. We call k a witness. Thus 6 ∣ 42 has witness 7. The definition permits negative integers: −6 ∣ 42 has witness −7. It also permits zero as the number being divided: every nonzero a divides 0, with witness 0. The background here is only multiplication of integers. There is no need yet to factor a number into primes. We will make one exact claim about chains of divisibility, then notice why some tempting variations fail. The tray picture helps when counts are positive, but the integer definition is what makes the general statement precise. Keep track of the witnesses Worked example. Suppose 4 ∣ 12 and 12 ∣ 60. The first statement has witness 3 because 12 = 4·3; the second has witness 5 because 60 = 12·5. Combining them gives 60 = (4·3)·5 = 4·15. The new witness is 15, so 4 ∣ 60. The numerical work is a model for the proof, but the proof must work with unspecified integers. Witnesses, including a sign change Claim Witness equation Conclusion −3 ∣ 18 18 = (−3)(−6) True 5 ∣ 0 0 = 5·0 True 0 ∣ 5 5 = 0·k has no solution False 0 ∣ 0 0 = 0·k for any integer k True under this definition Some texts reserve the word “divisor” for a nonzero number even while using the same witness relation. We will say explicitly when a nonzero divisor is needed, especially before a division algorithm. A zero row in the table is therefore a useful test of the definition rather than a practical tray arrangement. A small theorem from one substitution Transitivity of divisibility. For any integers a, b and c, if a ∣ b and b ∣ c, then a ∣ c. By the two hypotheses, there are integers r and s with b = ar and c = bs. Substitute the first equality into the second: c = (ar)s = a(rs). Integers are closed under multiplication, so rs is an integer witness. That completes the proof; no assumption that a, b or c is positive was used. a ∣ b ∧ b ∣ c ⇒ c = a ( r s ) ⇒ a ∣ c A related rule follows from the same definition: if a ∣ b and a ∣ c, then a divides b+c and b−c. Write b = ar and c = as. Their sum is a(r+s), and their difference is a(r−s). This explains why adding a multiple of a to a number does not alter whether that number is divisible by a. It will power the remainder steps of the Euclidean algorithm . Failure case. Reversing the transitivity claim does not work. Although 4 ∣ 60, choosing 7 as a supposed middle number gives neither 4 ∣ 7 nor 7 ∣ 60. More concretely, “a divides b+c, so a divides both b and c” is false: 3 ∣ (1+2), yet 3 divides neither 1 nor 2. A sum can create a multiple by cancellation of remainders. Find a witness, then test a claim 1. Show that −4 divides 28 and 28 divides 84. Give a witness for −4 ∣ 84 obtained by multiplying your first two witnesses. Hint for question 1 Write each target as the stated divisor times an integer, keeping the minus sign on the first multiplier. Full solution to question 1 28 = (−4)(−7), so the first witness is −7. Also 84 = 28·3, giving witness 3. Substitution yields 84 = (−4)(−7·3) = (−4)(−21). The product −21 is the requested witness, and the two negative signs correctly make 84 positive. 2. A proposed rule says: if 6 divides the product xy, then 6 divides x or 6 divides y. Find a counterexample with positive x and y, and explain the missing condition. Hint for question 2 Split the factors 2 and 3 between the two numbers. Full solution to question 2 Take x = 2 and y = 3. Then xy = 6, so 6 ∣ xy with witness 1. But 6 ∤ 2 and 6 ∤ 3 because neither has a whole-number quotient by 6. A prime divisor has a product rule of this form; 6 is composite, and its required factors can live in different factors of xy. We have only refuted the proposed general rule, not proved the prime version here. Carry the witness with the claim Divisibility is an existence statement: find an integer k for b = ak. A proof can manipulate that witness, as transitivity did, while a counterexample can show no such integer exists. Watch the zero case whenever an argument later divides by a number. A remainder table is the next useful step: it finds the greatest positive number dividing two inputs by repeatedly preserving their common divisors.

title: The ancient algorithm hiding in rectangles
summary: Compute gcd by a decreasing remainder ledger and prove each step preserves common divisors.
text: How large can an exact square tile be? A 252-by-198 rectangle can be covered with equal square tiles of side 18, but can a larger integer side work? A tile side must divide both dimensions. The greatest common divisor , gcd(a,b), is the greatest positive integer dividing both integers when at least one is nonzero. If a divides b, an integer k satisfies b = ak. That is the only definition from divisibility needed here; it is repeated so this page stands alone. For any integers a and positive b, division with remainder gives a = qb+r with integers q and r satisfying 0 ≤ r < b. A quotient and remainder are unique under that range condition. The Euclidean algorithm repeats this division until the remainder is zero. The square-cutting picture suggests the operations for positive sides, while the remainder equations explain why the final answer is exact. Run the ledger Worked example. For the rectangle, 252 = 1·198+54. A 198-square leaves a 54-wide strip. Next 198 = 3·54+36, so three 54-squares leave a 36 strip. Finally 54 = 1·36+18 and 36 = 2·18+0. The last positive remainder is 18. A physical cut can be awkward to draw accurately, so the table retains every numerical obligation. Euclid's divisions for 252 and 198 Dividend Divisor Quotient Remainder 252 198 1 54 198 54 3 36 54 36 1 18 36 18 2 0 Check the answer before trusting the procedure: 252/18 = 14 and 198/18 = 11, both whole numbers. The algorithm says more than that 18 works; it says no greater common divisor exists. This is what the invariant below establishes. The common divisors do not change Remainder theorem. If a = qb+r, every common divisor of a and b also divides r = a−qb. Conversely, every common divisor of b and r divides a = qb+r. The two pairs therefore have exactly the same common divisors. When b is positive and 0 ≤ r < b, this gives: gcd ( a , b ) = gcd ( b , r ) That proof uses only the fact that a divisor of two integers divides any integer sum or difference of their multiples. It explains each row of the ledger. At the last row, gcd(36,18) = gcd(18,0) = 18 because every positive divisor of 18 divides zero, and 18 is the largest positive divisor of itself. Termination. Every nonzero remainder is a nonnegative integer strictly smaller than the previous positive divisor. There cannot be an infinite strictly decreasing sequence of nonnegative integers: after at most finitely many such decreases, zero appears. This is a proof of termination, though it does not yet give a sharp count of steps. For inputs with signs, first replace them by absolute values. If one input is zero, gcd(a,0)=|a| for a ≠ 0; gcd(0,0) is left undefined here because there is no greatest positive common divisor. Failure case. Rounding a quotient to the nearest integer can yield a negative remainder, breaking the displayed 0 ≤ r < b convention. For example 19 = 2·10−1 is true but is not the division step used here; the correct row is 19 = 1·10+9. The equality of gcds still holds for any integer q, but the decreasing-remainder termination argument needs a controlled remainder. A picture of rectangles alone cannot supply that guarantee. Worked example: a zero endpoint reached early Find gcd(84,28). The very first division is 84 = 3·28 + 0, so the procedure stops with answer 28. There is no requirement to manufacture several nonzero remainders. Every common divisor of 84 and 28 divides 28, while 28 itself divides both numbers. Thus 28 really is the greatest positive common divisor. Compare gcd(28,84). Its first quotient is zero: 28 = 0·84 + 28. This legal row simply puts the smaller positive number second, after which the previous division applies. A zero quotient is allowed; a zero divisor is not. If the original input is (−84,28), absolute values give the same positive answer. Keeping these cases in the ledger prevents a rule about attractive rectangles from silently replacing the integer algorithm. Do the arithmetic and defend it 1. Compute gcd(119,34) with all remainder equations. State which row shows that the answer divides both original inputs. Hint for question 1 Subtract multiples of 34 from 119 until the remainder is below 34. Full solution to question 1 119 = 3·34+17 and 34 = 2·17+0. Hence gcd(119,34)=gcd(34,17)=17. The final row shows 17 divides 34; the first row then gives 119 = 3·34+17, also a multiple of 17. The invariant, rather than only these checks, excludes a larger common divisor. 2. A friend stops at the first nonzero remainder and says gcd(252,198)=54. Locate the precise error. Hint for question 2 Check whether 54 divides the previous divisor 198. Full solution to question 2 The first remainder 54 need not be a common divisor. Here 198 = 3·54+36, so 54 does not divide 198. The invariant only says gcd(252,198)=gcd(198,54), not that the gcd equals 54. Continue until the remainder is zero; the last positive remainder is 18. A repeated equality with a stopping rule Euclid's algorithm is trustworthy because each row preserves the entire set of common divisors and because the positive remainders decrease. The last positive remainder is therefore the gcd. Retain the quotient ledger: reversing its equations in Bézout's identity will express that gcd as a signed combination of the starting numbers.

title: A gcd as a linear combination
summary: Reverse Euclid's ledger to construct Bézout coefficients and understand the coprime case.
text: Can two pack sizes make exactly one unit? Imagine movements of 26 units forward and 15 units backward. Can some signed combination land at 1? Negative coefficients are allowed: they stand for reversing a movement, not for ordering a negative number of physical packs. An expression 26x+15y with integer x and y is an integer linear combination . The smallest positive number attainable this way is connected to gcd(26,15). Here is the local refresher. A common divisor of a and b divides both. The Euclidean algorithm replaces (a,b) by (b,r) whenever a = qb+r and 0 ≤ r < b; the pair has the same common divisors, and positive remainders decrease until zero. Bézout's identity states that the gcd can be written as one of these integer linear combinations. We will construct the coefficients and prove why this always succeeds, rather than treating the coefficients as a lucky guess. Reverse a remainder ledger Worked example. Divide: 26 = 1·15+11; 15 = 1·11+4; 11 = 2·4+3; 4 = 1·3+1; 3 = 3·1+0. The final nonzero remainder is 1, so gcd(26,15)=1. To express that 1 using only the original inputs, reverse the equalities. Start with 1 = 4−3 and replace 3 by 11−2·4, giving 1 = 3·4−11. Replace 4 by 15−11 to get 1 = 3·15−4·11. Finally replace 11 by 26−15: 1 = 7·15−4·26. Backward expression for the last remainder Stage Expression for 1 Last step 4 − 3 Replace 3 3·4 − 11 Replace 4 3·15 − 4·11 Replace 11 7·15 − 4·26 Checking the numerical certificate is easy: 7·15−4·26 = 105−104 = 1. The hard part is knowing such a certificate must exist for any pair not both zero. Why back-substitution always works Bézout's identity. For integers a and b, not both zero, there exist integers x and y such that ax+by=gcd(a,b), where gcd is positive. Apply Euclid to |a| and |b|. The initial two numbers are integer combinations of themselves: |a|=1·|a|+0·|b| and |b|=0·|a|+1·|b|. If two successive ledger values are such combinations, their remainder, the first minus an integer multiple of the second, is another. Induction through the finite ledger makes the last nonzero remainder a combination. Euclid proved that remainder is the gcd. Change coefficient signs as needed to return from |a|,|b| to a,b. a x + b y = gcd ( a , b ) This is a complete existence proof assuming the division algorithm for integers, which supplied the quotient and remainder. It does not say that x and y are unique. For our example, x = −4, y = 7 works; so does x = 11, y = −19, because 26·11+15·(−19)=1. The coefficient pair changes while the gcd does not. Failure case. If gcd(a,b)=d>1, no integer combination can equal 1. Every ax+by is divisible by d, while 1 is not. For example 14x+21y is always divisible by 7. Its best positive target is 7, obtained as 21−14. The conclusion “we can always make one unit” therefore needs the coprimality condition d=1. The identity itself remains true for noncoprime inputs. Worked example: reaching a multiple of the gcd Which integer targets can 18 x + 30 y reach? Euclid gives 30 = 18 + 12 and 18 = 12 + 6, so 6 = 18 − 12 = 2·18 − 30. To reach 24, multiply this certificate by 4: 24 = 8·18 − 4·30. The chosen coefficients are integers, and direct multiplication checks 144 − 120 = 24. More generally, multiplying the certificate for 6 by any integer t reaches 6 t . Conversely, both 18 and 30 are divisible by 6, so every integer combination is divisible by 6. Together these two arguments characterize all reachable targets as the multiples of 6. Finding one Bézout certificate therefore supplies more information than finding just one small successful target. The coefficients need not be nonnegative; imposing that additional constraint would change the problem. Build and interpret two certificates 1. Find integers x,y with 35x+12y=1 using remainder equations, then check your result by multiplication. Hint for question 1 Start with 35=2·12+11 and 12=1·11+1. Express the last remainder using the two earlier equations. Full solution to question 1 Euclid gives 35=2·12+11 and 12=1·11+1. Thus 1=12−11=12−(35−2·12)=3·12−35. Hence x=−1 and y=3. Direct check: 35(−1)+12(3)=−35+36=1, so gcd(35,12)=1. 2. Someone claims 18x+30y=5 has an integer solution because 5 is small. Decide whether this is possible and provide a reachable positive target. Hint for question 2 Compute the gcd before searching for coefficients. Full solution to question 2 gcd(18,30)=6 because 30=1·18+12, 18=1·12+6, and 12=2·6. Every integer combination 18x+30y is divisible by 6, so it cannot equal 5. A reachable positive target is 6: 6=2·18−30, using x=2 and y=−1. The failure concerns target 5, not the validity of Bézout's identity. Keep the coefficients, not just the gcd The Euclidean algorithm computes a gcd; its reverse ledger produces a certificate ax+by=gcd(a,b). This certificate will tell us exactly when multiplication has an inverse on a modular clock. It does not by itself claim uniqueness of the coefficients or any efficient cryptographic security. For practical calculation, checking the final equality catches a surprising number of sign mistakes.

title: When division works modulo m
summary: Prove that a multiplicative inverse modulo m exists exactly for a coprime multiplier.
text: Can a clock multiplication be undone? On a seven-position clock, multiplying a position by 3 sends 0,1,2,3,4,5,6 to 0,3,6,2,5,1,4. Every output appears once. Multiplying by 3 is reversible: multiplication by 5 reverses it because 3·5=15 has remainder 1 modulo 7. On an eight-position clock, multiplying by 2 sends both 0 and 4 to 0. That collision makes reversal impossible. The question is to predict the difference without trying every position. Local background: a ≡ b (mod m) means m divides a−b, with m a positive integer. The gcd of a and m is their greatest positive common divisor. Bézout's identity says that integers u,v satisfy au+mv=gcd(a,m); it follows by reversing the Euclidean remainder equations. We will use that identity and show the exact condition for an inverse. The clock picture is for intuition; the divisibility definition is what supports a proof. Find one inverse and one collision Worked example. Take a=5 and m=12. The Euclidean ledger is 12=2·5+2, then 5=2·2+1. Reverse it: 1=5−2·2=5−2(12−2·5)=5·5−2·12. Thus 5·5 ≡ 1 (mod 12), so the inverse of 5 is also 5. For example, if 5x ≡ 7 (mod 12), multiply both sides by 5: 25x ≡ 35, hence x ≡ 11 (mod 12). Check 5·11=55 ≡ 7. Multiplying residues modulo 8 by 2 Input 0 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 Output 0 2 4 6 0 2 4 6 No output in that row is 1, so 2 has no inverse modulo 8. The table is a finite check for one modulus. The next argument covers every modulus m≥2 and every integer a. The coprimality test Inverse criterion. An integer a has a multiplicative inverse modulo m≥2 exactly when gcd(a,m)=1. If the gcd is 1, Bézout supplies integers u,v with au+mv=1. Reducing modulo m removes mv, giving au ≡ 1; u is an inverse. Conversely, suppose au ≡ 1. Then m divides au−1, so au−mv=1 for some integer v. Any common divisor of a and m divides the left side and therefore divides 1. Their greatest common divisor is 1. Both directions are proved. ( ∃ u ∈ ℤ : a u ≡ 1 ( mod m ) ) ⇔ gcd ( a , m ) = 1 An inverse is unique as a residue: if au ≡ av ≡ 1, multiply the first equation by v and the second by u to obtain u ≡ v. Or use the inverse to cancel a from au ≡ av. That cancellation only works when a has an inverse. More generally, multiplication by a permutes all m residues exactly when gcd(a,m)=1. If an inverse exists, equal outputs ax ≡ ay imply x ≡ y, so the finite map is one-to-one and onto. If d=gcd(a,m)>1, the distinct residues 0 and m/d both map to 0 because a(m/d)=(a/d)m. Failure case. From 2x ≡ 2 (mod 8), cancelling 2 would claim x ≡ 1 (mod 8). Yet x=5 also works: 2·5=10 ≡ 2. Dividing a congruence by a noninvertible number can lose solutions. One may reduce the modulus carefully in some problems, but ordinary cancellation modulo the original m is invalid. Worked example: solving a congruence with a negative inverse Solve 4 x ≡ 3 (mod 9). The identity 1 = 9 − 2·4 says that −2 is an inverse of 4 modulo 9. Its standard nonnegative representative is 7, since −2 and 7 differ by 9. Multiplying by −2 gives x ≡ −6 ≡ 3 (mod 9). Check the candidate: 4·3 = 12 = 9 + 3. Every integer 3 + 9 t satisfies the original congruence, because multiplying the added term by 4 still gives a multiple of 9. Conversely, multiplying any alleged solution by the same inverse forces that residue. Thus the answer is one residue class, containing infinitely many integers. A negative coefficient from back-substitution is a valid inverse; discarding it because it is negative would discard a useful certificate. Use a certificate rather than a guess 1. Find the inverse of 7 modulo 20 and solve 7x ≡ 9 (mod 20). Hint for question 1 20=2·7+6 and 7=6+1; reverse those equations. Full solution to question 1 1=7−6=7−(20−2·7)=3·7−20, so 3 is an inverse of 7 modulo 20. Multiplying 7x ≡ 9 by 3 yields x ≡ 27 ≡ 7 (mod 20). Check: 7·7=49 ≡ 9. The solution is unique modulo 20 because multiplication by 7 is reversible. 2. Explain why 6 has no inverse modulo 15 and exhibit two distinct inputs with the same output after multiplication by 6. Hint for question 2 The gcd is 3. Try inputs differing by 15/3. Full solution to question 2 gcd(6,15)=3, so an inverse would force the impossible equation 6u−15v=1, whose left side is divisible by 3. Inputs 0 and 5 are distinct modulo 15, while 6·0 ≡ 0 and 6·5=30 ≡ 0. The collision shows directly why a reversible multiplication map is impossible. Reversal needs a gcd of one Bézout gives an inverse exactly for numbers coprime to the modulus. It also exposes the obstruction when a shared factor produces collisions. This is the gate for solving simultaneous clock conditions and for choosing a toy public-key exponent. Tables are good checks, while the two-direction argument establishes the general rule.

title: Two clocks can locate one moment
summary: Construct and prove the unique simultaneous residue class for two coprime moduli.
text: Can two clocks specify one moment? A machine reports that an event happened at position 2 in a three-step cycle and position 4 in a five-step cycle. One answer is 14: it leaves remainder 2 on division by 3 and remainder 4 on division by 5. Are there other answers, and what makes the pair of readings reliable? This lesson handles two positive coprime moduli m and n, meaning gcd(m,n)=1. Recall locally that x ≡ a (mod m) says m divides x−a. An inverse of n modulo m is a number u with nu ≡ 1 (mod m); one exists exactly when gcd(n,m)=1, by Bézout's identity. We need just that inverse fact and ordinary divisibility. The theorem gives a single residue class modulo mn, not a unique integer in all of Z: adding mn changes neither reading. Find the meeting point without scanning forever Worked example. For x ≡ 2 (mod 3) and x ≡ 4 (mod 5), write x=4+5t. The first condition becomes 4+5t ≡ 2 (mod 3), or 1+2t ≡ 2. Thus 2t ≡ 1 (mod 3). Since 2·2 ≡ 1 (mod 3), multiply by 2 to find t ≡ 2 (mod 3). Choose t=2: x=14. Choosing t=2+3k yields x=14+15k, so all displayed solutions have the same residue modulo 15. Two readings across one full fifteen-step cycle Candidate mod 3 mod 5 Both requested? 4 1 4 No 9 0 4 No 14 2 4 Yes 19 1 4 No; repeats the cycle Checking four candidates is an illustration, not a proof of the general construction or uniqueness. The algebra below gives both and explains the role of coprimality. Construction and uniqueness Two-modulus Chinese remainder theorem. For any integers a,b and positive coprime m,n, there is exactly one residue class modulo mn satisfying x ≡ a (mod m) and x ≡ b (mod n). Write x=b+nt. The remaining condition is nt ≡ a−b (mod m). Since gcd(n,m)=1, choose u with nu ≡ 1 (mod m). Taking t ≡ u(a−b) (mod m) constructs a solution. This proves existence, and it is constructive once the inverse is known. x ≡ b + n u ( a − b ) ( mod m n ) For uniqueness, let x and y satisfy both readings. Then m divides x−y and n divides x−y. Because gcd(m,n)=1, their product mn divides x−y. To justify that last step without hiding it, write x−y=mk. Since n divides mk and n is coprime to m, Bézout gives integers r,s with rm+sn=1. Multiply by k: k=rmk+snk. Both terms on the right are divisible by n, so n divides k. Hence x−y=mnℓ. Thus x and y are the same residue modulo mn. This proves exactly the theorem claimed. Failure case. Coprimality cannot be omitted. Conditions x ≡ 0 (mod 4) and x ≡ 1 (mod 6) conflict: every multiple of 4 is even, but every number congruent to 1 modulo 6 is odd. Conditions x ≡ 0 (mod 4) and x ≡ 2 (mod 6) do have solutions, such as 8, yet uniqueness is modulo 12, the least common multiple, rather than modulo 24. The general noncoprime theorem needs a compatibility test; this lesson proves only the coprime case. Worked example: a negative reading on one clock Find the least nonnegative integer satisfying x ≡ −1 (mod 4) and x ≡ 1 (mod 5). Write x = 1 + 5 t . Modulo 4, the first condition becomes 1 + t ≡ −1, hence t ≡ 2. Taking t = 2 gives x = 11. Indeed 11 − (−1) = 12 is divisible by 4, and 11 − 1 = 10 is divisible by 5. The moduli are coprime, so uniqueness is modulo 20. All solutions are 11 + 20 k for integer k ; the representative 11 is the only one between 0 and 19. Negative readings are ordinary residue labels. Replacing −1 by 3 modulo 4 describes exactly the same condition, without changing the solution class. Solve and test a boundary 1. Solve x ≡ 3 (mod 4), x ≡ 2 (mod 7), giving the least nonnegative answer and the full solution class. Hint for question 1 Set x=2+7t and solve 7t ≡ 1 (mod 4). Full solution to question 1 Set x=2+7t. Modulo 4 this is 2+3t ≡ 3, so 3t ≡ 1. Since 3·3 ≡ 1 (mod 4), t ≡ 3 (mod 4). Choosing t=3 gives x=23. Every solution is 23+28k because changing t by 4 changes x by 28. Checks: 23=4·5+3 and 23=7·3+2. 2. Decide whether x ≡ 1 (mod 6), x ≡ 3 (mod 9) is solvable. Explain without trying a large list of numbers. Hint for question 2 Both moduli are divisible by 3. Compare the requested residues modulo 3. Full solution to question 2 The first condition forces x ≡ 1 (mod 3), because 6 is divisible by 3. The second forces x ≡ 0 (mod 3), because both 9 and 3 are divisible by 3. A number cannot have two different remainders modulo 3, so no solution exists. This is a counterexample to using the coprime formula without its hypothesis. One class from two compatible clocks For coprime m and n, one modular inverse builds a simultaneous solution and divisibility proves it unique modulo mn. The result is exact even when a or b is negative. A finite timeline can check a specific answer, but cannot replace the construction and uniqueness argument. The noncoprime situation needs its own compatibility condition and is outside this theorem.

title: A prime modulus makes a striking pattern
summary: Prove Fermat's little theorem by permuting and cancelling the nonzero residues.
text: Why does a power come back to one? Compute powers of 2 modulo 7: 2, 4, 1, 2, 4, 1, and so on. In particular 2 6 leaves remainder 1. This pattern is part of a theorem about every prime modulus, though six is not the first returning exponent for 2. The theorem says that for a prime p and an integer a not divisible by p, a p−1 ≡ 1 (mod p). It does not identify the shortest cycle for each a. Here is the local background. A prime p>1 has only positive divisors 1 and p. Congruence modulo p means that p divides a difference. A nonzero residue is one of 1 through p−1. If p does not divide a, then gcd(a,p)=1 and multiplication by a has an inverse modulo p: Bézout gives au+pv=1. We will use that fact to prove multiplication by a rearranges, or permutes , the nonzero residues. No infinite sequence experiment is required. Watch a permutation on six residues Worked example. Let p=7 and a=3. Multiply each nonzero residue by 3 and reduce modulo 7. The list 1,2,3,4,5,6 becomes 3,6,2,5,1,4. Every number from 1 to 6 appears exactly once, in another order. The product of the original list is 720. The product of the new list is also 720, but it is also 3 6 ·720 modulo 7. Since 720 ≡ 6 (mod 7) and 6 has an inverse, cancelling it gives 3 6 ≡ 1 (mod 7). Multiplication by 3 modulo 7 r 1 2 3 4 5 6 3r mod 7 3 6 2 5 1 4 The table verifies a particular case. To turn it into a general proof, we must explain both why no outputs collide and why cancellation of the product is allowed. Permute, multiply, cancel Fermat's little theorem. If p is prime and p does not divide a, then a p−1 ≡ 1 (mod p). Because p is prime and does not divide a, gcd(a,p)=1; hence a has an inverse modulo p. If ar ≡ as (mod p), multiply by that inverse to obtain r ≡ s (mod p). Thus a·1, a·2, …, a·(p−1) are distinct nonzero residues. There are p−1 of them, so they are exactly the nonzero residues in some order. Multiplying these congruences gives the same product on both sides: a p − 1 ( p − 1 ) ! ≡ ( p − 1 ) ! ( mod p ) Here (p−1)! means 1·2·…·(p−1). None of those factors is divisible by p, so their product is coprime to p and has an inverse modulo p. Cancel it to obtain the theorem. This is a complete proof given the elementary inverse criterion, which follows from Bézout. The primality hypothesis matters at two points: it ensures each nonzero residue has an inverse and allows cancellation of the product. Failure case. Replacing “prime” by “any integer” fails. With modulus 8 and a=3, gcd(3,8)=1, yet 3 7 ≡ 3 (mod 8), since powers of 3 alternate between 3 and 1. The exponent m−1 is not generally valid for composite m. The converse also fails as a primality test: 2 340 ≡ 1 (mod 341) even though 341=11·31. The latter numerical fact can be checked by repeated squaring; it illustrates why a passing Fermat-style test alone does not certify primality. Use the theorem and test its limits 1. Compute 5 101 modulo 13 without multiplying 101 copies of 5. State why the theorem applies. Hint for question 1 13 is prime, so group the exponent into multiples of 12 and a remainder. Full solution to question 1 Because 13 is prime and 13 does not divide 5, Fermat gives 5 12 ≡ 1 (mod 13). Since 101=8·12+5, 5 101 ≡ 5 5 . Now 5²=25 ≡ −1 (mod 13), so 5⁴ ≡ 1 and 5⁵ ≡ 5. The requested residue is 5. The theorem reduces the exponent; the final small power is calculated separately. 2. A student argues that 7 10 ≡ 1 (mod 11) proves 11 is prime. Identify the logical error and test 3 7 modulo 8. Hint for question 2 Distinguish a theorem's “if” direction from its converse; then square 3 modulo 8. Full solution to question 2 The theorem says prime modulus implies the congruence for eligible bases; one successful congruence cannot reverse that implication. Independent divisibility checks show 11 is prime, but the proposed proof does not. Modulo 8, 3²=9 ≡ 1, so 3 7 =(3²)³·3 ≡ 3, not 1. This composite modulus directly fails the naive replacement of p by m. The permutation is the proof For prime p, multiplying nonzero residues by a number not divisible by p rearranges them. Multiplying and cancelling that rearranged list proves a p−1 ≡ 1. The theorem is a reliable exponent reduction under its hypotheses, not a complete primality test and not a promise of the shortest period. Repeated squaring makes large residual powers efficient to compute.

title: Huge powers with few multiplications
summary: Compute modular powers from exponent bits and prove a binary exponentiation invariant.
text: How do you calculate a huge power with a short ledger? To find 7 45 modulo 13, multiplying 7 forty-four times is tedious. The exponent has binary expansion 45=32+8+4+1. Five successive squares of 7 give the powers with exponents 2,4,8,16,32, and the selected ones can be multiplied. This method is called repeated squaring, or binary exponentiation. Local background: modulo a positive integer m, numbers with the same remainder may replace one another in sums and products. Binary digits represent an integer as a sum of distinct powers of two. For example 13=8+4+1, written 1101 in base two. The method works for any integer base a, any modulus m≥2, and any nonnegative exponent e. Negative exponents need a modular inverse, which may not exist, so they are outside this lesson. Follow every square Worked example. Start with 7 modulo 13. Squaring gives 7²=49 ≡ 10. Square that residue: 7⁴ ≡ 10²=100 ≡ 9. Again, 7⁸ ≡ 9²=81 ≡ 3. Then 7¹⁶ ≡ 3²=9 and 7³² ≡ 9²=3. For exponent 45=32+8+4+1, multiply the selected residues: 7 45 ≡ 3·3·9·7. Reduce in stages: 3·3·9=81 ≡ 3 and 3·7=21 ≡ 8 (mod 13). Thus the answer is 8. Squares of 7 modulo 13 Exponent 1 2 4 8 16 32 Residue 7 10 9 3 9 3 Use for 45? Yes No Yes Yes No Yes The table is a trace, not the correctness reason. The reason is that every squaring doubles the represented exponent and every selected multiplication adds that exponent to the running total. A loop invariant for every bit Set result =1, base =a modulo m, and remaining =e. Repeatedly inspect whether remaining is odd. If it is, replace result by result·base modulo m. Then replace base by base² modulo m and remaining by its integer half, discarding any fractional part. Stop when remaining=0. The exact invariant is result·base remaining ≡ a e (mod m). It holds initially. If remaining=2q, no result multiplication occurs, and after squaring base and setting remaining=q the product stays result·(base²) q . If remaining=2q+1, the extra base is moved into result and the same calculation applies. At the end base 0 =1, so result is the required residue. result · base remaining ≡ a e ( mod m ) The remaining exponent falls from e to floor(e/2) each round, so a positive e reaches zero after floor(log₂ e)+1 rounds. Each round uses one modular square and, for a 1 bit, one more modular multiplication. This is a count of arithmetic operations; multiplying very large integers also has a bit-level cost, which this simple count does not measure. For e=0 the loop runs zero times and returns 1, consistent with a⁰=1 even when a is divisible by m. Failure case. Squaring alone does not assemble an exponent such as 45, since 45 is not a power of two. Multiplying every square in the table would compute the sum 1+2+4+8+16+32=63 instead. The selected binary digits determine which powers join the result. Another common mistake is to halve an odd exponent without moving one copy of the base to result; that silently changes the target exponent. Compute and check the invariant 1. Compute 3 29 modulo 11 by repeated squaring. Show the binary decomposition and chosen residues. Hint for question 1 29=16+8+4+1. Successively square 3, reducing modulo 11 each time. Full solution to question 1 The residues for exponents 1,2,4,8,16 are 3,9,4,5,3: indeed 9²=81 ≡ 4, 4²=16 ≡ 5, and 5²=25 ≡ 3. Select 16,8,4,1 for 29: 3 29 ≡ 3·5·4·3=180 ≡ 4 (mod 11), since 180=16·11+4. A direct check using Fermat is possible but not needed for the algorithm. 2. Start the loop for a=4, e=5, m=7. After processing the first odd bit, state result, base and remaining, and verify the invariant numerically. Hint for question 2 Multiply result by the old base before squaring that base. Then floor(5/2)=2. Full solution to question 2 Initially result=1, base=4, remaining=5. Because 5 is odd, result becomes 4. Square base: 4²=16 ≡ 2 (mod 7), and set remaining=2. The new invariant reads 4·2²=16 ≡ 2 (mod 7). The original target 4⁵ also has residue 2: 4² ≡ 2, 4⁴ ≡ 4, and 4⁵ ≡ 4·4=16 ≡ 2. Both sides agree. Each bit pays for one doubling Repeated squaring keeps the intended power intact while reducing the remaining exponent by roughly half. A binary ledger of squares and selected multiplications computes a modular power in a number of modular operations proportional to its exponent's bit length. This is an algorithmic correctness claim, not a cryptographic security claim. The method will keep the arithmetic manageable in a small RSA demonstration .

title: A toy lock with arithmetic keys
summary: Run and justify a tiny RSA round-trip for coprime messages, with its proof boundary and security limits.
text: A small public lock made of congruences Suppose you publish two numbers, n=55 and e=3, and keep a third number d=27 private. Someone encodes the message number 7 by computing 7³ modulo 55. You then raise that result to the 27th power modulo 55 and recover 7. This is a toy RSA calculation: its tiny factors are obvious, so it illustrates arithmetic only. It gives no security guarantee. Here is the necessary local background. The primes p=5 and q=11 give n=pq=55 and φ=(p−1)(q−1)=40. We choose e=3 coprime to 40; d=27 satisfies ed=81=1+2·40. Congruence x ≡ y (mod n) means n divides x−y. Fermat's little theorem says that if p is prime and p does not divide a, then a p−1 ≡ 1 (mod p). We will use this theorem and the elementary fact that if coprime 5 and 11 both divide a difference, their product 55 divides it. The proof below is explicitly for messages coprime to 55. Follow one complete round-trip Worked example. The published operation is c ≡ m e (mod n). For m=7, c=7³=343 ≡ 13 (mod 55), because 343=6·55+13. The private operation gives c d ≡ 13 27 (mod 55). Repeated squaring keeps that manageable. Powers of 13 with exponents 1,2,4,8,16 have residues 13,4,16,36,31 modulo 55. Since 27=16+8+2+1, multiply 31·36·4·13 modulo 55. In stages 31·36=1116 ≡ 16; 16·4=64 ≡ 9; 9·13=117 ≡ 7. The recovered residue is the original 7. Toy key and one message Quantity Value Role p,q 5, 11 Small prime factors n,φ 55, 40 Modulus and key-construction number e,d 3, 27 Exponent pair, 3·27 ≡ 1 mod 40 m,c 7, 13 Message and encoded residue The trace checks one message. Correctness for every message in the stated class needs a theorem, and the exponent equation alone does not prove it without relating 40 to the two prime moduli. Why the chosen messages return Scoped RSA correctness claim. Let p and q be distinct primes, n=pq, φ=(p−1)(q−1), and choose positive e,d with ed ≡ 1 (mod φ). For every integer m with gcd(m,n)=1, decrypting the encoded residue yields m modulo n: (m e ) d ≡ m (mod n). Write ed=1+kφ. Because m is coprime to n, neither p nor q divides m. Fermat's theorem gives m p−1 ≡ 1 (mod p). Since φ is a multiple of p−1, m kφ ≡ 1 (mod p), and therefore m ed ≡ m (mod p). The same reasoning with q−1 gives m ed ≡ m (mod q). The two distinct primes are coprime, so their product n divides m ed −m. This completes the proof for coprime messages. m e d ≡ m ( mod p q ) The exact proof boundary matters. A stronger theorem handles messages sharing a factor with n by considering the zero case separately modulo each prime, but we have not established that extension here. Nor have we shown why a real implementation hides its factors, resists chosen-message attacks, pads messages, or manages keys. Those are engineering and cryptographic questions beyond this numerical model. Even within the toy, if e is not coprime to φ, a modular inverse d may not exist. For example e=2 has gcd(2,40)=2, so no integer d makes 2d ≡ 1 (mod 40). Failure case. Using the wrong private exponent breaks the round-trip. If d=3 instead of 27, then ed=9 is not 1 modulo 40. For m=7, the encoded residue remains 13, but 13³=2197 ≡ 52 (mod 55), not 7. The exponent congruence is a real condition, not a decorative key label. Test the key condition and the computation 1. With the same key (n,e,d)=(55,3,27), encode m=2. Explain why the correctness proof applies, and give the recovered residue without evaluating a 27th power directly. Hint for question 1 First calculate 2³ modulo 55. Then check gcd(2,55) and the relation 3·27=1+2·40. Full solution to question 1 The encoded residue is c=2³=8. Since gcd(2,55)=1 and 3·27=81=1+2·40, the scoped theorem applies: c 27 ≡ 2 81 ≡ 2 (mod 55). For a direct modular check, 8² ≡ 9, 8⁴ ≡ 26, 8⁸ ≡ 16, and 8¹⁶ ≡ 36. Multiplying the residues for 27=16+8+2+1 gives 36·16·9·8 ≡ 2 (mod 55). The theorem and the trace agree. 2. A proposed public exponent is e=6 for n=55. Can it use the same construction with φ=40? Explain precisely, without claiming that every other exponent fails. Hint for question 2 Look for an integer d with 6d−40k=1 and test the gcd of 6 and 40. Full solution to question 2 gcd(6,40)=2. Every integer of the form 6d−40k is even, so it cannot equal 1. Thus 6 has no inverse modulo 40, and this key-construction rule cannot supply a d for e=6. This says nothing against choices such as e=3, which do have an inverse; it identifies the exact obstruction for the proposed exponent. Arithmetic correctness is a narrow promise For coprime messages, the relation ed ≡ 1 modulo (p−1)(q−1), Fermat's theorem at each prime, and divisibility by both primes explain the round-trip. The small numbers let you inspect every step, including a bad exponent. They do not demonstrate secrecy. The satisfying stopping point is the exact correctness proof for this stated class of messages; real RSA requires additional mathematical and implementation safeguards.

title: Why a computer loses a tiny number
summary: Adding a small quantity to a large one can change nothing. Explain finite precision using a small decimal floating-point model.
text: When adding changes nothing Suppose a calculator stores only three significant decimal digits. It shows 100 as 1.00 × 10² and 0.04 as 4.00 × 10⁻². Their exact sum is 100.04, but rounding that sum to three significant digits returns 100. The addition occurred; the stored result cannot distinguish it from the original number. This small model makes finite precision visible without pretending that ordinary computers store decimal digits in exactly this way. Background capsule. In scientific notation, a nonzero number is a significand times a power of ten. Three significant digits preserve, for example, 1.23 × 10² but not every number between 123 and 124. Rounding to nearest chooses a representable neighbor; a tie needs a stated rule. Here we use ties to even, although none of the main examples is a tie. “Exact” below means the mathematical real-number operation before rounding; fl denotes the stored result. Work the gaps between stored numbers Worked example. Near 100, consecutive positive three-digit numbers in this toy system are 100, 101, 102, and so on. Their spacing is 1. Thus 100 + 0.04 = 100.04 rounds back to 100. Repeating the rounded addition twenty-five times still gives 100, although adding twenty-five copies of 0.04 in exact arithmetic gives 101. The repeated calculation rounds after every addition; the exact sum rounds only once. The order of operations matters. Computation Exact intermediate Stored result 100 + 0.04 100.04 100 (100 + 0.04) + 0.04 100.04 after the first stored step 100 100 + (25 × 0.04), then round 101 101 A second experiment starts at 1.00. Here the spacing is 0.01; adding 0.004 rounds back to 1.00, whereas adding 0.006 rounds to 1.01. The same absolute increment may be visible at one scale and invisible at another. The number of significant digits, not a fixed absolute error, is the useful first description. A precise statement about one rounded operation fl ( a + b ) = a can hold even when b ≠ 0 The statement is existential, not a law for every pair. It follows in our toy system because any exact result strictly within half a spacing of a representable number rounds back to that number. At 100 the half-spacing is 0.5, so 0.04 vanishes when added once. At a power-of-ten boundary the neighboring spacings can differ, and ties require the rounding rule. These qualifications matter when predicting particular outputs. In a normalized base-ten system with three significant digits and an unbounded exponent, rounding a nonzero real result to nearest gives relative error at most about 0.005: half a unit in the last place divided by the leading scale. This simple bound concerns one rounded result. Real hardware normally uses binary formats with finite exponent ranges, subnormal numbers, infinities, and exceptional values. Near underflow a uniform small relative-error promise may fail; overflow can produce no finite result at all. Even away from those boundaries, a sequence of individually small rounding errors can accumulate or cancel in complicated ways. One helpful alternative for the toy repeated sum is to accumulate the small terms first: 25 × 0.04 = 1.00, then 100 + 1.00 = 101. This is a particular repair, not a universal rule that “small first” always wins. Reordering may affect other problems differently, and a stored 0.04 must itself be representable in the chosen format for this exact toy calculation. Test the model Exercise 1. With three significant decimal digits and rounding to nearest, evaluate fl(10.0 + 0.04) and fl(10.0 + 0.06). State the local spacing and explain both answers. Hint for exercise 1 List the neighboring stored values near 10.0 before rounding either exact sum. Solution to exercise 1 The stored values are 10.0, 10.1, 10.2, and so forth, so spacing is 0.1. Exact sums are 10.04 and 10.06. The first lies 0.04 above 10.0 and rounds to 10.0; the second lies 0.04 below 10.1 and rounds to 10.1. Neither is a tie. Exercise 2. Someone argues that because each rounded addition loses less than 0.05 near 10, one hundred such additions must have total error less than 0.05. Give a counterexample using 10.0 and repeated 0.04. Hint for exercise 2 Ask whether later additions start from the exact partial sum or the already rounded value. Solution to exercise 2 Each stored step computes fl(10.0 + 0.04) = 10.0, so one hundred steps still store 10.0. The exact total is 10.0 + 100(0.04) = 14.0. The final error is 4.0, much larger than 0.05. The per-operation observation does not bound a chain by the same single-step amount; errors from repeated loss can add systematically. What you can trust A floating-point format represents a discrete set of values, whose spacing changes with scale; actual hardware formats have finitely many such values, while our toy model allowed unbounded exponents. A rounded operation can discard a nonzero contribution, and repeating it can make an error much larger than the error of one operation. The toy model proves those claims exactly within its own rules. It does not predict the final bits of a particular machine calculation without knowing its format, rounding mode, and evaluation order. Next, cancellation shows a different way a seemingly simple expression loses information. Driscoll and Braun’s Fundamentals of Numerical Computation , cited in the lesson metadata, supplies the wider setting for finite arithmetic and algorithmic error; the toy table and exercises here are original.

title: Two equal formulas, unequal answers
summary: Algebraically identical expressions can behave differently on a machine. Rationalize √(1+x)−1 to reduce cancellation.
text: An exact identity with unequal numerical behavior For a small positive x, the square root of 1 + x is just above 1. Subtracting 1 then asks a finite-precision calculator to recover a tiny difference between nearly equal stored numbers. This is cancellation: leading digits agree and disappear. We can compute the same real number through a different formula whose intermediate subtraction is absent. Background capsule. The square root symbol denotes the nonnegative root. For x ≥ −1, √(1+x) is real.
