Multiplying (a−b)(a+b) gives a²−b². “Relative error” means absolute error divided by the magnitude of the nonzero exact answer; it can become large even when absolute error looks small. We use a three-significant-decimal-digit, round-to-nearest toy format for a transparent example, and reserve actual binary-machine claims for qualitative discussion. Calculate the same quantity twice Worked example. Take x = 0.004, exactly representable in our toy format. The exact square root √1.004 is about 1.00199800399. In a strict three-digit calculation, 1+x first rounds from 1.004 to 1.00; its square root is 1.00. Even if the square-root function instead receives the exact 1.004, its output rounds to 1.00. The direct expression therefore stores 1.00 − 1.00 = 0. Yet the exact answer is positive, about 0.001998. A zero result here is a property of the sequence of rounded operations, not of the function. Now calculate x/(√(1+x)+1). The rounded root is again 1.00. Its sum with 1 is 2.00, and 0.004/2.00 gives 0.00200. The exact answer is about 0.001998, so the stable result differs by about 0.000002, roughly 0.1% of the answer. The direct result has 100% relative error. This table uses the exact mathematical value as reference, evaluated from the rationalized identity to the displayed precision; it does not use the unstable direct toy result as “truth.” Route for x = 0.004 Toy stored answer Exact answer, rounded for display √(1+x) − 1 0 0.00199800399 x/(√(1+x)+1) 0.00200 0.00199800399 Derive the repair and its boundary 1 + x − 1 = x 1 + x + 1 Multiply the left side by (√(1+x)+1)/(√(1+x)+1). Its numerator becomes (1+x)−1 = x. For every real x ≥ −1 the denominator is at least 1, so division is valid; at x = 0 both sides equal zero. For small positive x the denominator is near 2 and involves addition of positive quantities, which avoids the destructive subtraction. The quotient still undergoes rounding, but it retains the size of the desired result. Why does the direct method suffer? If the computed square root differs from the exact root by an absolute amount e, then subtraction leaves desired answer plus e. As x approaches zero, the desired answer is approximately x/2, so the ratio |e|/(x/2) can be large. This explanation assumes a nonzero absolute rounding error at the root step; when the root happens to be exactly representable, that source of error disappears. It is a sensitivity analysis of the expression , not evidence that the mathematical function itself is badly conditioned. Indeed, near x = 0 the function tends smoothly to zero with slope 1/2. The rationalized formula also has limits. If x is so tiny that its input representation underflows to zero, neither formula can reconstruct the lost input. If 1+x overflows, the square-root path can fail. Complex x needs different branch conventions. The identity remains true over its stated real domain; its numerical advantage is particularly relevant for small positive or negative x where 1+x is near 1. Use algebra as a numerical tool Exercise 1. Rationalize √(9+t)−3 for real t ≥ −9, and calculate its value at t = 0.006 using three-significant-decimal-digit arithmetic. Compare the direct and rationalized routes. Hint for exercise 1 Multiply by the sum of the two terms. Round the square root before the following arithmetic. Solution to exercise 1 The exact identity is √(9+t)−3 = t/(√(9+t)+3), because the denominator is at least 3. At t = 0.006, the strict three-digit addition first rounds 9.006 to 9.01; √9.01 still rounds to 3.00. Direct subtraction stores zero. The rationalized denominator rounds to 6.00, giving 0.006/6.00 = 0.00100. The exact value is about 0.000999833, so the latter retains useful digits. Exercise 2. Does rationalizing prove that every output for every real x ≥ −1 is more accurate on every computer? Identify a boundary case and explain precisely what the identity does establish. Hint for exercise 2 Separate equality of real formulas from rounding and input representation. Solution to exercise 2 No. At x = 0 both exact formulas give zero, and a typical correctly rounded calculation of either does too; there is no strict improvement. At x = −1, direct √0−1 gives −1 exactly in many formats, while the quotient −1/(0+1) also gives −1. More generally underflowed input, overflow, and implementation details can affect either route. The proof establishes exact real-number equality for x ≥ −1. The small-x rounding analysis explains a common advantage under the stated model, not a universal ranking. Choose an expression with useful intermediates Equivalent algebraic formulas need not have equivalent finite-precision behavior. For small x, x/(√(1+x)+1) avoids subtracting two nearly equal numbers and usually preserves the tiny answer. When the answer itself is zero, relative error is undefined, so report absolute error or exact equality instead. Conditioning versus stability separates a problem’s inherent sensitivity from errors introduced by a particular computation. The numerical-method context is supported by the source in this lesson’s metadata; all toy calculations here follow the declared format.

title: A bad problem or a bad algorithm?
summary: An accurate calculation cannot repair data that determine the answer weakly. Distinguish conditioning from computational stability with scalar examples.
text: Where did the error come from? An answer can be unreliable for two different reasons. The input may genuinely determine the answer weakly: a slight change in measured data causes a large output change. Or a chosen sequence of calculations may amplify rounding even though the exact problem is tame. The first is conditioning of a problem at a particular input; the second is stability of an algorithm. Treating them as synonyms hides which repair is possible. Background capsule. If x and f(x) are nonzero, the relative input change is |Δx|/|x| and the relative output change is |f(x+Δx)−f(x)|/|f(x)|. The derivative f′(x) is the limit of output change divided by input change as Δx tends to zero. We use absolute values to compare magnitudes, and discuss finite perturbations separately from derivatives. Two questions, two diagnoses Worked example. First take f(x) = 1/(x−1) at x = 1.01. The exact answer is 100. If the measured input is 1.011 instead, the exact answer becomes about 90.909. The input changed by roughly 0.099% relative to 1.01, yet the output changed by about 9.09%. No perfectly accurate algorithm can tell whether the intended input was 1.01 or 1.011. The answer’s sensitivity is part of the problem. Second take g(x) = √(1+x)−1 near x = 0.004, with the input accurately specified. Its exact answer changes moderately with x in absolute terms, but a three-digit direct calculation returned zero in the cancellation lesson . Rationalizing returned a useful result. Here the algorithmic expression is the main culprit. “Ill-conditioned input” would be the wrong diagnosis for this example when absolute output error is the quantity that matters. These examples also warn against a scale-free label. The relative condition of g near zero is roughly 1, even though g(0)=0 makes relative output error undefined exactly at zero. For f near 1, both absolute and relative output sensitivity are large. State the input, output and error measures before declaring a problem well or badly conditioned. Derive local relative sensitivity κ f ( x ) = x f ′ ( x ) f ( x ) Assume f is differentiable at x and x ≠ 0, f(x) ≠ 0. Write f(x+Δx)−f(x) = f′(x)Δx + r(Δx), where r(Δx)/Δx tends to zero. Divide the output change by f(x), and divide the input change by x. To first order the ratio of relative changes has magnitude |xf′(x)/f(x)|. This is a local limiting factor, not a finite-error inequality. A finite guarantee needs a bound on derivatives over the full perturbation interval and assurance that no singularity is crossed. For f(x)=1/(x−1), differentiation gives f′(x)=−1/(x−1)². Thus κ_f(x)=|x/(x−1)|; at 1.01 it is 101. This predicts that an input perturbation of about 0.1% may create about a 10% relative output perturbation. The finite example gives 9.09%; first-order prediction is close but not identical. At x=1 the function is undefined, and κ has no value there. At x=0 the displayed relative condition formula is also not the right measure, even if f(0) is defined. Algorithmic stability asks a different question: did the computed output accurately solve a nearby input problem, or at least remain close to the exact output under justified bounds? A backward-stable result may still have a large forward error when the problem is ill-conditioned. Conversely, a well-conditioned problem can receive a poor answer from an unstable expression. The labels require an explicit computational model; the exact f above alone does not certify any implementation. Make the diagnosis Exercise 1. For f(x)=x² with x≠0, calculate κ_f(x). Predict the first-order relative output change when the input increases by 1%, then compute the exact change. Hint for exercise 1 Differentiate x², then compare (1.01x)² with x². Solution to exercise 1 f′(x)=2x, so κ_f(x)=|x·2x/x²|=2. The first-order prediction is a 2% output increase. Exactly, ((1.01x)²−x²)/x² = 1.0201−1=0.0201, or 2.01%. The extra 0.01 percentage point is the quadratic term in the finite perturbation. Exercise 2. A program for f(x)=1/(x−1) returns 100 exactly for stored input 1.01. A laboratory later reports the physical x only within ±0.001. Is the program’s exact arithmetic enough to certify the physical answer as 100 ± 1? Give the actual endpoint range. Hint for exercise 2 Evaluate f at 1.009 and 1.011; f decreases on this interval. Solution to exercise 2 No. The admissible physical interval is [1.009,1.011]. Since f′ is negative there, its exact range is [1/0.011,1/0.009] ≈ [90.909,111.111]. That range extends about 9.091 below and 11.111 above 100, so ±1 is unsupported. Better arithmetic cannot remove the uncertainty in measured input. Ask which promise you need A condition number measures local response of an exact problem under a specified perturbation and error scale. Stability describes how faithfully an algorithm handles that problem in a finite arithmetic model. A small residual, a small backward error, and a small forward error are different promises. Near zeros or singularities, relative measures may be undefined or huge; use a meaningful absolute or finite-interval bound instead. The next bisection lesson gives a bracket whose width certifies positional uncertainty under explicit continuity and sign assumptions.

title: A root you can trap
summary: Repeated halving turns uncertainty into a certified interval. Run bisection and choose iterations for a requested bracket width.
text: Certify a root by trapping it A numerical root is a point r where f(r)=0. A calculator may print many digits for a proposed root, but the digits alone do not prove a root lies nearby. Bisection offers a different output: an interval known to contain at least one root, provided a continuous function has opposite signs at its endpoints and those signs are determined reliably. Every step halves the uncertainty without needing a derivative. Background capsule. A continuous function cannot move from a negative value to a positive value across an interval without taking zero somewhere; this is the intermediate value theorem. The midpoint of [a,b] is (a+b)/2, and its width is b−a. “Bracket” means endpoints with opposite signs, or an endpoint that is already a root. The promise concerns a root’s location, not which root is found if several occur. Trap √2 with exact signs Worked example. Set f(x)=x²−2 on [1,2]. Here f(1)=−1 and f(2)=2, so some root lies inside. The midpoint is 1.5; f(1.5)=0.25 is positive, leaving [1,1.5]. Next midpoint 1.25 gives f(1.25)=−0.4375, leaving [1.25,1.5]. Next midpoint 1.375 gives −0.109375, leaving [1.375,1.5]. The width is now 0.125. These decimals are exact terminating rational calculations; no uncertain sign is concealed. Halvings Certified bracket Width 0 [1,2] 1 1 [1,1.5] 0.5 2 [1.25,1.5] 0.25 3 [1.375,1.5] 0.125 If we report the midpoint of the final bracket as an approximation, its absolute error from some enclosed root is at most half the width, or 0.0625. The midpoint is 1.4375, and √2 is indeed closer, but the certificate does not need to know √2’s decimal expansion. To obtain width at most 0.001 from an initial width 1, choose n with 2⁻ⁿ ≤ 0.001; ten halvings suffice because 1/1024 < 0.001. Why the interval promise persists b n − a n = b 0 − a 0 2 n Assume f is continuous on the original closed interval and its endpoint values have opposite signs. At a midpoint m, either f(m)=0 and the task is finished, or its sign agrees with exactly one endpoint sign. Retain m and the endpoint of opposite sign. Continuity remains valid on this smaller closed interval, so the intermediate value theorem again places a root inside. Its width is exactly half the previous width. Induction proves the displayed width formula and bracket invariant for every completed step. The width certificate is independent of a small residual. A nearly flat function such as f(x)=10⁻⁹(x−100) can have a tiny residual far from 100. Bisection certifies a location because it encloses a root, not because |f(m)| is small. If f is not continuous, opposite signs do not suffice: f(x)=−1 for x<0 and +1 for x≥0 has opposite endpoint signs on [−1,1] but no zero. If endpoint signs are produced by uncertain rounded arithmetic, an apparent bracket may be false. Interval arithmetic or exact rational evaluations can help certify signs; ordinary displayed decimals do not automatically do so. A bracket does not establish uniqueness. For example, x³−x changes sign over [−2,2] and has three roots there. A monotonicity proof, as for x²−2 on [1,2], supplies uniqueness when needed. Make a certificate Exercise 1. For f(x)=x²−3 on [1,2], perform two bisections with exact midpoint signs. Give the final bracket and a midpoint error bound. Hint for exercise 1 Evaluate f(3/2), then f at the midpoint of the retained half. Solution to exercise 1 f(1)=−2 and f(2)=1. At 3/2, f=9/4−3=−3/4, so retain [3/2,2]. Its midpoint is 7/4; f=49/16−48/16=1/16, so retain [3/2,7/4]. The width is 1/4; midpoint 13/8 is within 1/8 of an enclosed root. Since f increases on this positive interval, the root √3 is unique there. Exercise 2. A student claims f(−1)<0<f(1) proves a root exists on [−1,1], without saying anything about continuity. Construct a function violating the conclusion and say exactly which proof step fails. Hint for exercise 2 Use a jump across zero and keep every function value away from zero. Solution to exercise 2 Define f(x)=−1 for x<0 and f(x)=1 for x≥0. Its endpoint signs are opposite, but f never equals zero. The intermediate value theorem cannot be applied because f is discontinuous at zero. Halving intervals around the jump gives small widths but certifies no root. A guarantee with visible assumptions For a continuous function with reliable opposite endpoint signs, bisection keeps a root in a shrinking bracket. After n halvings the bracket width is the initial width divided by 2ⁿ, and its midpoint has at most half that positional error relative to an enclosed root. This is a strong guarantee but can be slow. Newton’s method can accelerate near a suitable simple root, while losing this global bracket promise unless guarded.

title: Newton's method can leap the wrong way
summary: A fast root finder can converge beautifully or fail spectacularly. Compute Newton steps and diagnose a cycle or zero derivative.
text: A tangent makes a bold guess Imagine standing at x on a curve and drawing its tangent line. The tangent’s intersection with the horizontal axis suggests a new root estimate. Repeating that construction is Newton’s method. Near a well-behaved simple root it often gains digits rapidly; away from such a root its steps may escape, cycle, or be undefined. The same formula supports both stories, so a reliable use needs hypotheses and a stopping check. Background capsule. A derivative f′(x) is a tangent slope. The linear approximation near x is f(x)+f′(x)(t−x). A simple root r satisfies f(r)=0 and f′(r)≠0. “Residual” means |f(x)|; “root error” means |x−r|. They can differ greatly when the function is nearly flat. Compare a success with a cycle Worked example. For f(x)=x²−2, the Newton step from x=1.5 is 1.5−0.25/3 = 17/12 ≈1.416667. One more step gives about 1.414216, already close to √2. Because the derivative 2x is nonzero near positive √2, this is the favorable local setting. A bisection bracket [1,2] would need many halvings to achieve comparable decimal width, though every retained interval carries a location guarantee. Now take g(x)=x³−2x+2, starting at x=0. Here g(0)=2 and g′(0)=−2, so Newton gives x=1. At x=1, g(1)=1 and g′(1)=1, so Newton returns x=0. The iteration cycles forever: 0, 1, 0, 1, … . The function does have a real root between −2 and −1, since g(−2)=−2 and g(−1)=3. Newton’s failure from this starting point says nothing about root nonexistence. Function and start First step Second step Interpretation x²−2 at 1.5 1.416667 ≈1.414216 Rapid local approach x³−2x+2 at 0 1 0 Two-cycle Derive the step and its local rate x n + 1 = x n − f ( x n ) f ′ ( x n ) Set the tangent approximation f(x_n)+f′(x_n)(t−x_n) equal to zero and solve for t. The division requires f′(x_n)≠0. This construction is not an assertion that the tangent’s intercept is a root. For the local claim, suppose f is twice continuously differentiable near a simple root r. Taylor’s theorem about x_n gives 0=f(r)=f(x_n)+f′(x_n)(r−x_n)+(f″(ξ)/2)(r−x_n)² for some ξ between r and x_n. Rearranging and comparing with the Newton step yields x_{n+1}−r = [f″(ξ)/(2f′(x_n))](x_n−r)², with sign according to the expansion. Continuity and f′(r)≠0 ensure the denominator stays bounded away from zero near r, while f″ is bounded there. Hence |e_{n+1}| ≤ C|e_n|² for sufficiently close iterates. This is a local quadratic error bound, not a global promise or a claim that each step doubles digits under every rounding model. At a multiple root, f′(r)=0 and the proof fails. For f(x)=x², Newton from nonzero x gives x/2, only linear convergence to zero. At a point with f′(x)=0 and f(x)≠0, the step is undefined. In floating point a derivative too small to divide safely is also a practical stop condition. A small residual needs a separate derivative or bracket bound before it certifies root location. Inspect the steps Exercise 1. Starting at x₀=2, take two Newton steps for f(x)=x²−3. Keep fractions for the first step and give the second as a fraction. Hint for exercise 1 Use x_{n+1}=(x_n+3/x_n)/2. Solution to exercise 1 x₁=(2+3/2)/2=7/4. Then x₂=(7/4+12/7)/2=(49/28+48/28)/2=97/56≈1.732143. The positive root is √3≈1.732051. These steps suggest convergence but do not replace a bracket or the local hypotheses in the proof. Exercise 2. For f(x)=x³−2x+2, verify the 0↔1 cycle and explain why |f(1)|=1 cannot be treated as a positional error bound. Hint for exercise 2 Compute f and f′ at both iterates, then recall the root lies to the left of −1. Solution to exercise 2 At 0, f=2 and f′=−2, yielding 1. At 1, f=1 and f′=1, yielding 0. Repetition is exact. The real root is in (−2,−1), so the iterate 1 is more than 2 units from it despite residual 1. Even a much smaller residual would require a sensitivity or bracket argument to become a location certificate. Speed needs a guard Newton’s tangent step has a local quadratic error bound near a simple root under smoothness and a sufficiently close initial guess. Neither the formula nor a finite table proves global convergence. A cycle, zero derivative, or small misleading residual is a reason to return to a reliable bracket or to use a guarded hybrid. The derivation and examples are original; the cited numerical-method text supplies wider context.

title: Why a smaller step can give a worse derivative
summary: Approximation and rounding pull a computation in opposite directions. Balance truncation and roundoff in a finite difference.
text: When shrinking h makes the answer worse The derivative is a limit as h approaches zero, so it is tempting to choose the smallest positive h a machine can hold. A forward difference, however, subtracts two nearby computed function values and divides by h. Its mathematical approximation error generally shrinks with h; its sensitivity to evaluation and rounding errors grows like 1/h. A finite step can therefore be better than a tinier one. Background capsule. The forward difference is D_h f(x)=[f(x+h)−f(x)]/h for h≠0. Taylor’s theorem writes f(x+h)=f(x)+hf′(x)+(h²/2)f″(ξ) when f is twice continuously differentiable between x and x+h. A unit roundoff u describes the scale of one relative arithmetic rounding error away from underflow and overflow. We distinguish exact function evaluations from computed ones. An exact truncation error you can see Worked example. Take f(x)=x² at x=1. Exact arithmetic gives D_h f(1)=[(1+h)²−1]/h=2+h. The true derivative is 2, so the truncation error is exactly |h|. At h=0.1 the answer is 2.1; at h=0.001 it is 2.001. This side of the story favors smaller h. Now use a toy device that rounds function values to four significant decimal digits before subtraction. At h=0.001, f(1+h)=1.002001 rounds to 1.002, while f(1)=1.000; the difference quotient is 2.000. At h=0.0001, f(1+h)=1.00020001 rounds to 1.000, so the quotient is zero. The input 1+h must also be represented accurately enough in an actual implementation; this toy example isolates output rounding to show the mechanism. h Exact D_h Four-digit rounded-value D_h 0.01 2.01 2.00 0.001 2.001 2.00 0.0001 2.0001 0 At h=0.01, 1.0201 rounds to 1.020, so the displayed toy quotient 2.00 is correct. The table is a demonstration under declared rules, not an empirical universal error curve for binary floating point. Balance two different error mechanisms | D h f ( x ) − f ′ ( x ) | ≤ M 2 | h | If |f″(t)|≤M throughout the segment from x to x+h, Taylor’s theorem gives the displayed exact-arithmetic truncation bound. It does not include rounding. Suppose separately that computed values have absolute errors at most ε_f each, and that h itself and the subtraction/division are exact for this simplified analysis. The difference of two evaluation errors has magnitude at most 2ε_f, so the computed quotient error relative to the exact quotient is at most 2ε_f/|h|. Together we obtain M|h|/2 + 2ε_f/|h|. This bound is minimized at |h|=2√(ε_f/M) when M, ε_f>0. The exact constants depend on the arithmetic and function evaluator; the result is a model choice, not a magic step size. In an idealized floating-point model, ε_f is often on the order of u times the scale of f(x), giving the familiar schematic C₁h+C₂u/h. If f(x)≈0, if input x+h rounds to x, if function data are noisy, or if f″ changes rapidly, that schematic needs revision. Centered differences have a different truncation order under stronger smoothness assumptions and a different balance. Automatic differentiation or analytic derivatives may avoid this finite-difference tradeoff where available. Choose a step with a reason Exercise 1. For f(x)=x³ at x=1, derive the exact forward difference and its exact error for positive h. Hint for exercise 1 Expand (1+h)³ before dividing by h. Solution to exercise 1 D_h=[(1+3h+3h²+h³)−1]/h=3+3h+h². Since f′(1)=3 and h>0, the exact error is 3h+h². Its leading behavior is proportional to h, but the h² term remains visible for larger steps. Exercise 2. A model bound is E(h)=h+10⁻⁶/h for h>0. Find its minimizing h and the bound there. Explain why setting h=10⁻¹² is worse according to this model. Hint for exercise 2 Differentiate E or use the arithmetic-geometric mean inequality. Solution to exercise 2 E′(h)=1−10⁻⁶/h², so the minimum occurs at h=10⁻³ and equals 0.001+0.001=0.002. At h=10⁻¹², the second term alone is 10⁶, dwarfing the truncation term. This is a bound within the stated error model; actual error can be smaller through cancellation or different evaluation behavior. A finite difference is a computation The derivative’s limiting definition does not prescribe the smallest machine step. Smoothness bounds control mathematical truncation; an explicit arithmetic or data-error model controls the amplification of subtraction errors. State both before selecting h. The related cancellation lesson explains the lost digits, while conditioning helps distinguish noisy input data from an unstable formula.

title: Counting area with a known error
summary: Rectangles improve when curvature is taken seriously. Apply composite trapezoidal quadrature with a certified smooth-function bound.
text: An area estimate with an error ceiling Dividing an interval into more trapezoids often improves an integral estimate, but a numerical pattern alone does not say how far the answer is from the true area. For a function with bounded second derivative, the composite trapezoidal rule has a provable error ceiling. Curvature supplies the missing information: a straight line is integrated exactly, while bending creates the gap. Background capsule. The definite integral ∫ a b f(x)dx is signed accumulated area. A trapezoid over [s,t] has area (t−s)[f(s)+f(t)]/2. For n equal subintervals, h=(b−a)/n and nodes x_j=a+jh. A twice continuously differentiable function has a continuous second derivative; on a closed interval its maximum absolute second derivative exists. Estimate the integral of a parabola Worked example. Take f(x)=x² on [0,1]. The exact integral is 1/3. With n=2, nodes 0, 1/2, 1 have heights 0, 1/4, 1. The composite trapezoidal estimate is (h/2)[f(0)+2f(1/2)+f(1)] = (1/4)(0+1/2+1)=3/8. Its actual error is 3/8−1/3=1/24≈0.04167. Here f″(x)=2 everywhere. The standard bound gives (b−a)h²·2/12 = (1/4)/6 = 1/24. Equality occurs for this quadratic, so the bound is sharp in this example. With n=4, h=1/4, the bound becomes 1/96, exactly one-quarter as large. It is reasonable to expect second-order behavior for this smooth case; that expectation is backed by the bound, not merely by a plot. Panels Step h Trapezoidal estimate Actual absolute error Certified bound 2 1/2 3/8 1/24 1/24 4 1/4 11/32 1/96 1/96 The 4-panel estimate is 11/32: using the heights 0, 1/16, 1/4, 9/16, 1 gives (1/8)[0+2(1/16+1/4+9/16)+1]=(1/8)(11/4)=11/32. Where the h² bound comes from | E T | ≤ ( b − a ) h 2 12 max a ≤ x ≤ b | f ″ ( x ) | On one panel [s,t] of length h, let L(x) be the line through the endpoint values of f. The interpolation remainder for a twice continuously differentiable f is f(x)−L(x)=f″(ξ_x)(x−s)(x−t)/2 for some ξ_x in the panel. This follows by applying Rolle’s theorem twice to f−L minus a multiple of (x−s)(x−t); it is an exact pointwise statement, though ξ_x may vary with x. Taking absolute values and using |f″|≤M gives |f(x)−L(x)|≤(M/2)(x−s)(t−x). Integrating that nonnegative parabola over the panel gives Mh³/12. The integral of L is the trapezoid area. Summing n panel bounds gives nMh³/12 = (b−a)Mh²/12. This proves the displayed inequality. It assumes exact function values and exact arithmetic for the quadrature sum. Rounding and uncertain measurements add other error terms. A finite difference of successive estimates can suggest an observed rate, but it does not certify the unknown integral without a theorem or independent enclosure. The hypothesis matters. For f(x)=√x on [0,1], f″ is unbounded near zero, so the displayed global M does not exist. The trapezoidal rule still produces numbers, but this particular C² certificate cannot be invoked. Discontinuities and singular integrands call for separate analysis or adapted methods. Use the bound correctly Exercise 1. For f(x)=x² on [0,2] with n=4 equal panels, find T₄, the exact integral, and the bound. Check whether equality holds. Hint for exercise 1 Use nodes 0, 1/2, 1, 3/2, 2 and M=2. Solution to exercise 1 Here h=1/2. The endpoint heights are 0 and 4, interior heights 1/4,1,9/4. Thus T₄=(1/4)[0+2(1/4+1+9/4)+4]=(1/4)(11)=11/4. The exact integral is [x³/3]₀²=8/3. Their difference is 11/4−8/3=1/12. The bound is (2)(1/4)(2)/12=1/12, again equality for a quadratic. Exercise 2. On [0,1], suppose |f″|≤6. How many equal panels suffice for a trapezoidal error at most 0.0005? Explain what would change if the sampled f values each had unknown error up to 0.01. Hint for exercise 2 Solve 6/(12n²)≤0.0005; then consider the weighted average of sample errors. Solution to exercise 2 The exact-arithmetic bound is 1/(2n²). Requiring it ≤1/2000 gives n²≥1000, so n≥32 suffices. If every sampled value may differ by 0.01, the trapezoidal weights are nonnegative and sum to interval length 1, giving an additional possible error of 0.01. Thus the 0.0005 total-error certificate is lost regardless of n unless those data errors are reduced or otherwise controlled. A theorem, with its domain attached The composite trapezoidal error is at most (b−a)Mh²/12 when f is C² and M bounds |f″|. The proof is a one-panel interpolation error summed across the interval. A singular endpoint, unreliable function samples, or rounding changes the error budget. For a complementary lesson about choosing a step when rounding competes with approximation, see finite differences .

title: More points can make an interpolant worse
summary: High-degree polynomial fitting can oscillate near the edges. Compare equally spaced and Chebyshev nodes on Runge's function.
text: Why extra sample points can hurt Polynomial interpolation passes exactly through chosen data. One might expect that adding points always improves the curve between them. Runge’s function, f(x)=1/(1+25x²) on [−1,1], is a famous warning: high-degree interpolation at equally spaced nodes can swing badly near the ends. Node placement can matter more than the sheer number of nodes. This lesson gives a concrete small calculation and the error formula that explains where the danger enters. Background capsule. Through n+1 distinct nodes x₀,…,x_n there is exactly one polynomial p_n of degree at most n matching the sampled values. Its maximum error is max over the interval of |f−p_n|. Chebyshev–Lobatto nodes are cos(jπ/n), j=0,…,n; they cluster near ±1. The exact interpolating polynomial is a mathematical object. A computed one also incurs finite-precision errors. Compare degrees and node choices Worked example. For n=2, both equally spaced nodes and Chebyshev–Lobatto nodes happen to be −1,0,1, so they give the same interpolant. We can calculate it exactly: f(0)=1 and f(±1)=1/26. Symmetry makes p₂(x)=1−(25/26)x². At x=1/2, the true value is 1/(1+25/4)=4/29≈0.13793, while p₂(1/2)=1−25/104=79/104≈0.75962. The discrepancy is about 0.62168 despite exact agreement at all three nodes. For n=4, the equally spaced nodes are −1, −1/2, 0, 1/2, 1; Chebyshev–Lobatto nodes are −1, −√2/2, 0, √2/2, 1. Symmetry makes both quartics of the form 1+ax²+bx⁴. Matching f(1)=1/26 and f(1/2)=4/29 gives the uniform-node polynomial 1−(3225/754)x²+(1250/377)x⁴. Matching f(1)=1/26 and f(√2/2)=2/27 instead gives the clustered-node polynomial 1−(1925/702)x²+(625/351)x⁴. This supplies a reproducible comparison without relying on a plot. Degree and nodes Interpolated value at x=0.9 Absolute error against f(0.9)=4/85 2, shared nodes −1,0,1 23/104 ≈ 0.221154 ≈ 0.174095 4, equally spaced −109/377 ≈ −0.289125 ≈ 0.336183 4, Chebyshev–Lobatto −11/208 ≈ −0.052885 ≈ 0.099943 At this one interior point, adding equally spaced nodes makes the error almost twice as large, while the clustered nodes reduce it. That is a finite counterexample to “more nodes always improve every point,” not a proof of any whole-interval or asymptotic comparison. Clustering controls a key node-product factor near the endpoints, but it does not assert that every finite Chebyshev interpolant beats every equally spaced one at every x. The node product and what it does not prove f ( x ) − p n ( x ) = f ( n + 1 ) ( ξ ) ( n + 1 ) ! ∏ j = 0 n ( x − x j ) For f with n+1 continuous derivatives, this pointwise remainder holds for x in the interval and some ξ depending on x and the nodes. One proof subtracts from f−p_n a multiple of the node product chosen to make the difference zero also at x; repeated Rolle’s theorem then produces the derivative value. At a node, both sides vanish without needing the quotient construction. The node product is small near a node but can be large between sparse edge nodes. Chebyshev-type clustering controls its maximum far better than equally spaced placement for high degree. The formula alone does not prove convergence as n grows: the derivative f^(n+1), its factorial ratio, and the product all change with n. For Runge’s function, complex singularities at ±i/5 limit polynomial approximation behavior, and equally spaced interpolation is known to diverge near interval endpoints as degree grows. A complete asymptotic proof needs additional estimates beyond this lesson. Trefethen’s cited author-hosted approximation text treats the Chebyshev-centered theory. Our exact degree-two calculation demonstrates that matching sample values does not control between-node error; it does not itself prove divergence. Interpolating noisy data raises another issue. The interpolant fits noise exactly at the nodes and may amplify it elsewhere through its interpolation weights. More nodes are not automatically helpful when the data themselves are uncertain. Piecewise low-degree interpolation is another practical response, with its own smoothness and error analysis. Optional 35–45 minute investigation: how much can node errors grow? A different error, with an explicit budget Keep the original three nodes −1,0,1 and Runge data (1/26,1,1/26). Suppose each recorded value differs from its exact value by at most ε=1/100. This is an absolute error budget, not a percentage and not a probability model. The nodes themselves are exact. Let p be the exact polynomial through the original data and p̃ the exact polynomial through the recorded data. Can |p̃−p| exceed 1/100 between nodes, even though both polynomials interpolate their own data exactly? Extra background. Three distinct nodes determine one polynomial of degree at most two: the difference of two candidates would have three distinct zeros. The cardinal polynomial ℓⱼ equals one at node j and zero at the other two. Thus p(x)=Σⱼyⱼℓⱼ(x). If data change by eⱼ, linearity gives δp(x)=p̃(x)−p(x)=Σⱼeⱼℓⱼ(x). No differentiability assumption on an unknown underlying function is needed for this data-to-interpolant identity. Predict before inspecting. Compare a common positive error (+ε,+ε,+ε) with the fixed record (−ε,+ε,+ε), chosen to align contributions at x=1/2. Will the latter still be worst at x=−1/2? Moving the probe below keeps the entire recorded error vector fixed. Build the weights and prove the sharp bound For three distinct nodes t₀,t₁,t₂, construct ℓⱼ(x)=∏ k≠j (x−tₖ)/(tⱼ−tₖ). Substituting any node verifies its zero-or-one values. The same interpolation uniqueness gives Σⱼℓⱼ(x)=1, because both sides interpolate constant data. For nodes −1,0,1, the weights are ℓ₀=x(x−1)/2, ℓ₁=1−x² and ℓ₂=x(x+1)/2. Define Λ(x)=Σⱼ|ℓⱼ(x)|, the Lebesgue function for these nodes. The triangle inequality gives an exact absolute data-error bound: | δp ( x ) | ≤ ε ∑ | ℓ j ( x ) | = ε Λ ( x ) Why sharp? At a specified target x, choose eⱼ=ε when ℓⱼ(x)>0 and eⱼ=−ε when ℓⱼ(x)<0. Zero weights can receive any admissible error. All nonzero products then contribute positively, attaining δp=εΛ. Negating the errors attains the negative bound. These optimizing signs can depend on the target; they need not describe one record that attains the envelope everywhere. “Attained” in the instrument means |δp|=εΛ, including a negative signed δp. On [0,1], ℓ₀≤0 and ℓ₁,ℓ₂≥0, so Λ(x)=1+x−x²=5/4−(x−1/2)². Reflection gives Λ(x)=1+|x|−x² on [−1,1]. Therefore its exact continuous-interval maximum is 5/4, attained at ±1/2. The sharp full-interval bound is consequently ε·5/4=1/80. This proves a statement about every real x in the interval, not only the seventeen displayed probes. Continuity on the closed interval supplies a maximizing point; choosing errors for that point proves sharpness of the full-interval bound too. One fixed record need not attain every pointwise envelope Probe (ℓ₀,ℓ₁,ℓ₂) Λ δp for fixed (−ε,+ε,+ε) −1 (1,0,0) 1 −ε: absolute bound attained −1/2 (3/8,3/4,−1/8) 5/4 ε/4=1/400, below 1/80 0 (0,1,0) 1 ε 1/2 (−1/8,3/4,3/8) 5/4 5ε/4=1/80 1 (0,0,1) 1 ε The fixed right-target record gives δp=ε(1+x−x²). A different record (+ε,+ε,−ε) attains the positive envelope on the negative half. By contrast, a common offset (+ε,+ε,+ε) gives δp=εΣℓⱼ=ε everywhere. This is not a statement about all unequal same-sign errors. At every node Λ=1; checking only nodes would miss amplification between them. Keep three error questions separate The certificate bounds p̃−p, not the total error from an underlying function. Here at x=1/2, the original p value is 79/104. The right-target errors add 1/80, giving p̃=803/1040. The true Runge value remains 4/29. Hence f−p=−1875/3016 while f−p̃=−19127/30160: the new data error reinforces the pre-existing approximation error at this point. Other signs could partially cancel it. For a continuous underlying f on the closed interval, write f−p̃=(f−p)−(p̃−p). Thus the maximum total error is at most the maximum noiseless approximation error plus ε times the maximum Λ. A computed evaluation would require a third, separately justified, arithmetic-error term. Smaller Λ alone does not prove smaller total error for every function or every record, and exact arithmetic cannot remove uncertain input data. This is an absolute sensitivity bound; it never divides by a possibly zero output as a relative condition number would. The quadrature lesson already bounds data errors using nonnegative weights, and finite differences amplify evaluation errors by 2ε f /|h|. Here the new issue is a spatially varying sum of absolute signed interpolation weights, with a constructive sharp bound over a continuous interval. Trefethen's authored Lebesgue-function note in the sources defines this data-to-interpolant viewpoint. Our three-node calculations are derived here. Scope. Three distinct fixed nodes, exact arithmetic and bounded value errors are essential to the stated model. No random noise, confidence band, noisy-node analysis, high-degree asymptotic theorem or numerical algorithm certification follows. The optional timing is an unpiloted estimate, separate from the original 30-minute lesson. Check what the nodes guarantee Exercise 1. For f(x)=1/(1+25x²) and nodes −1,0,1, derive p₂ and compute the signed error f(1/2)−p₂(1/2) exactly. Hint for exercise 1 Use symmetry to write p₂(x)=1+cx², then fit x=1. Solution to exercise 1 From 1+c=1/26, c=−25/26. Thus p₂=1−25x²/26. At 1/2, f=4/29 and p₂=79/104. The signed error is 4/29−79/104=(416−2291)/3016=−1875/3016≈−0.62168. Interpolation is exact only at the three nodes. Exercise 2. A plot at degrees 8 and 12 shows smaller maximum error for Chebyshev nodes. Does it prove convergence for every degree? State what additional type of argument is required, and one situation where neither plot is enough. Hint for exercise 2 Separate finite observations from a bound uniform in all sufficiently large n. Solution to exercise 2 No. Two finite cases cannot establish a limit over all n. One needs an asymptotic error bound, for example by controlling approximation error and interpolation amplification or the remainder uniformly as n grows. If sample values contain unknown noise, even an exact-arithmetic plot of noiseless f does not bound the error for the measured data; noise amplification needs its own estimate. Optional exercise 3: change both the nodes and the true function Exercise 3. Use nodes (−1,−1/2,1), the exact quadratic f(x)=x²+x, and node-value errors bounded by ε=1/50. Work on [−1,1] in exact arithmetic. These nodes and function are outside the controls. (a) Derive the three cardinal polynomials. At x=1/4 find their weights, the sharp pointwise error bound, an attaining record and the perturbed value. (b) Find the complete piecewise Λ and its exact global maximum and maximizing points. Would node-only checks establish that bound? (c) For your fixed attaining record from (a), find the signed perturbation at x=−3/4. Does it attain the local bound there? Supply a record that does. (d) Bound total error from this f and explain why the unchanged Runge example needs another term. Does a larger Λ maximum rank every record or every function's total error? Hint for exercise 3 Build each ℓⱼ to be one at its own node and zero at the other two. Its sign can change only at those zeros. Since Σℓⱼ=1, subtract twice the negative weight to obtain Λ on each interval. Complete the square to find each maximum. Choose error signs at the specified target. A degree-two polynomial is interpolated exactly by three distinct nodes. Fully worked answer to exercise 3 (a) The weights are ℓ₀=(x+1/2)(x−1), ℓ₁=4(1−x²)/3 and ℓ₂=(x+1)(x+1/2)/3. At x=1/4 they are (−9/16,5/4,5/16), summing to one with absolute sum 17/8. The sharp bound is (17/8)(1/50)=17/400. Errors (−1/50,+1/50,+1/50) attain its positive sign. The exact f data are (0,−1/4,2), so recorded data are (−1/50,−23/100,101/50). The noiseless interpolant is f itself, with f(1/4)=5/16; the perturbed value is 5/16+17/400=71/200. Thus p̃−f=17/400 and f−p̃=−17/400. (b) On [−1,−1/2], ℓ₂≤0 while ℓ₀,ℓ₁≥0, so Λ=1−2ℓ₂=2/3−x−(2/3)x²=25/24−(2/3)(x+3/4)². Its maximum there is 25/24 at −3/4. On [−1/2,1], ℓ₀≤0 while ℓ₁,ℓ₂≥0, giving Λ=1−2ℓ₀=2+x−2x²=17/8−2(x−1/4)². Its maximum there is 17/8 at 1/4. Both pieces equal one at the common boundary. Because 17/8>25/24, the global maximum is 17/8 and its unique maximizing point is 1/4. All three nodes have Λ=1, so checking only nodes misses that maximum. (c) At x=−3/4 the weights are (7/16,7/12,−1/48), and Λ=25/24. The fixed record (−ε,+ε,+ε) gives δp=ε(−7/16+7/12−1/48)=ε/8=1/400. Its magnitude is below the local bound (25/24)ε=1/48. A different fixed record (+ε,+ε,−ε) attains the positive bound there. A pointwise sharp envelope can require different errors at different targets. (d) Since f is degree two, its noiseless interpolant equals f everywhere. Therefore maximum total error is at most (17/8)(1/50)=17/400, and the record in (a) attains it at 1/4. Runge's noiseless interpolation error is nonzero, so its total error requires that separate term. The larger constant describes a larger worst case, not every record: zero errors give zero data perturbation, and a common offset gives exactly ε under either node set. It does not rank total errors for every function. Place points for the space between them Interpolation matches nodes exactly, while error between nodes depends on smoothness and node geometry. Chebyshev clustering mitigates endpoint trouble for high-degree polynomial interpolation, but finite tables are evidence of behavior only for the tested degrees. The remainder formula has explicit differentiability assumptions; an asymptotic claim needs more work. Continue with quadrature error for a different use of interpolation that yields a full finite bound.

title: A decaying equation with an exploding computation
summary: The numerical solution can grow while the exact solution shrinks. Derive Euler's stability restriction on a decay equation.
text: A decaying model, a growing calculation The equation y′=−λy describes exponential decay when λ>0. Yet a numerical method can turn that decay into alternating growth if its time step is too large. This apparent contradiction is not a failure of the differential equation: the discrete update has its own dynamics. Forward Euler makes the distinction especially clear because both the exact solution and the computed sequence have simple formulas. Background capsule. An ordinary differential equation specifies a derivative; y′ is the rate of change of y with time. For y′=−λy and y(0)=y₀, the exact solution is y(t)=y₀e^(−λt). A geometric sequence y_n=qⁿy₀ tends to zero for every finite y₀ exactly when |q|<1. A step h>0 places grid time t_n=nh. We first use exact arithmetic to isolate method stability. Try three time steps Worked example. Set λ=2, y₀=1. Forward Euler uses the current slope −2y_n over one step: y_{n+1}=y_n−2hy_n=(1−2h)y_n. At h=0.25 the factor is 0.5, so values are 1, 0.5, 0.25, 0.125: positive decay. At h=0.75 the factor is −0.5, giving 1, −0.5, 0.25, −0.125: decay in magnitude with alternating signs, even though the exact solution remains positive. At h=1.25 the factor is −1.5; values 1, −1.5, 2.25, −3.375 grow in magnitude while e^(−2t) decreases. Step h Euler factor 1−2h First three updates Long-run behavior 0.25 0.5 0.5, 0.25, 0.125 Decays without sign flips 0.75 −0.5 −0.5, 0.25, −0.125 Decays with sign flips 1.25 −1.5 −1.5, 2.25, −3.375 Grows in magnitude At h=0.25 the first Euler value is 0.5, while the exact value at t=0.25 is e^−0.5≈0.60653. Stability has not made the first step exact. Conversely, a single step can happen to look plausible even when the repeated update is unstable. Report both the time grid and the quantity compared. Derive the stability interval y n + 1 = ( 1 − h λ ) y n , | 1 − h λ | < 1 Euler replaces a short interval of the solution curve by a tangent step: y_{n+1}=y_n+h(−λy_n). By induction, y_n=(1−hλ)ⁿy₀. For nonzero y₀, decay of this geometric sequence to zero is equivalent to |1−hλ|<1. With real λ,h>0, that inequality is equivalent to 0<hλ<2. At hλ=2, values alternate without shrinking; at hλ>2, their magnitudes grow. At hλ=1, the numerical value reaches zero after one step, which is stable but generally inaccurate at that time. For fixed final time T and h=T/n tending to zero, (1−λT/n)ⁿ tends to e^−λT. This gives convergence for this scalar problem in exact arithmetic as the step is refined. Stability at one fixed h and convergence as h→0 are different questions. Local truncation error is of order h² per step for smooth solutions, yielding first-order global accuracy over fixed T under suitable bounds. That accuracy claim does not mean a large stable step is acceptable for a requested tolerance. Finite precision introduces another layer: repeated multiplication may underflow or accumulate error. The scalar restriction 0<hλ<2 does not automatically cover nonlinear equations, systems with complex eigenvalues, or arbitrary stiff models. A system requires analysis of its update matrix and relevant norms or spectra. The exact exponential decay model is a useful test equation, not a full ODE solver certification. Separate stability from accuracy Exercise 1. For y′=−4y, y₀=2, classify h=0.2, h=0.5, and h=0.6 by long-run Euler behavior, and give y₂ for each. Hint for exercise 1 Compute q=1−4h and y₂=2q². Solution to exercise 1 At h=0.2, q=0.2 and y₂=2(0.04)=0.08; the sequence decays. At h=0.5, q=−1 and y₂=2; it alternates without decay, the boundary case. At h=0.6, q=−1.4 and y₂=2(1.96)=3.92; its magnitude grows. Exact y(t)=2e^−4t decays for every t≥0. Exercise 2. A student chooses h=1/λ because Euler then gives zero after one step and calls the result “exact.” Explain the error at t=h and why the method is nevertheless stable for this test equation. Hint for exercise 2 Compare 0 with y₀e^−1 and inspect the update factor. Solution to exercise 2 At h=1/λ, q=0, so y₁=0 and all later Euler values are zero. But the exact solution at t=h is y₀e^−1, so the absolute first-step error is |y₀|/e, nonzero unless y₀=0. Since |q|=0<1, the numerical sequence does decay to zero; it is stable in the scalar long-run sense but not exact at finite time. Check the discrete dynamics For scalar decay with λ>0, forward Euler’s repeated values decay precisely when 0<hλ<2. Positivity requires the stronger 0<hλ≤1 for nonnegative initial data. Neither property by itself gives a tight finite-time error. A graph of points can reveal trouble, while the factor calculation proves the threshold. Quadrature error gives a contrasting example of a finite-step numerical certificate.

title: Fit a line without squaring the trouble
summary: Two least-squares methods can amplify errors differently. Form a small least-squares problem and explain the numerical appeal of QR.
text: Fit without needlessly magnifying sensitivity When more observations than unknowns are available, their equations may be inconsistent. Least squares chooses coefficients that minimize the sum of squared residuals. A familiar route forms AᵀA and solves the normal equations. A QR factorization instead uses orthogonal coordinates before solving a triangular system. Both yield the same exact full-rank solution, but AᵀA can square the matrix’s condition number in finite precision. Background capsule. For A with m rows and n columns, m≥n, and b with m entries, the residual is r=Ax−b. Its Euclidean norm squared is the sum of component squares. A matrix has full column rank when its columns are linearly independent. In a thin QR factorization A=QR, Q has n orthonormal columns (QᵀQ=I) and R is invertible upper triangular. The 2-norm condition number κ₂(A) is the ratio of largest to smallest singular value for full-rank A. A two-measurement fit Worked example. Suppose a one-parameter model predicts the same value x for observations 1 and 3. Then A is the column [1,1]ᵀ and b=[1,3]ᵀ. The objective is (x−1)²+(x−3)². Expanding gives 2x²−8x+10, whose derivative 4x−8 vanishes at x=2. The residual is [1,−1]ᵀ and has norm √2. Here Q=[1/√2,1/√2]ᵀ and R=[√2]. The QR equation Rx=Qᵀb becomes √2x=(1+3)/√2=2√2, so x=2. The residual is orthogonal to Q: Qᵀ[1,−1]ᵀ=0. That geometry explains why no movement along the column of A can reduce the residual further. For a sensitivity warning, consider columns a₁=[1,0]ᵀ and a₂=[1,ε]ᵀ with small positive ε. They are nearly parallel, so separating their coefficients from measured data is inherently delicate. Forming AᵀA gives [[1,1],[1,1+ε²]]. Its determinant is ε², much smaller than typical entries. In a short-precision calculation, 1+ε² may round to 1 and the computed normal-equation matrix can appear singular. QR does not remove the intrinsic coefficient sensitivity, but it avoids creating this squared-conditioning intermediate. Route Exact core equation Numerical concern Normal equations AᵀAx=Aᵀb Condition number squares Thin QR Rx=Qᵀb Requires a stable QR implementation and full rank Derive the reduction and condition identity A = Q R , R x = Q T b , κ 2 ( A T A ) = κ 2 ( A ) 2 For full-rank A=QR, decompose b into QQᵀb plus the perpendicular residual (I−QQᵀ)b. Orthogonality gives ||Ax−b||² = ||Rx−Qᵀb||² + ||(I−QQᵀ)b||². The second term does not depend on x, and invertible R lets us set the first term to zero. This proves Rx=Qᵀb gives the unique least-squares minimizer. Equivalently, its residual is orthogonal to every column of A, yielding normal equations in exact arithmetic. The eigenvalues of AᵀA are the squares of A’s positive singular values. Therefore the ratio of largest to smallest eigenvalue, which is κ₂ for this symmetric positive definite matrix, equals (σ_max/σ_min)² = κ₂(A)². This is an exact matrix identity for full-column-rank A. It indicates why errors in constructing and solving normal equations can be magnified. It is not a universal numerical error bound saying that QR always delivers a particular number of correct digits; implementation, scaling, data error and rank thresholds matter. If A is rank deficient, R is not invertible and the coefficient minimizer is not unique. If columns are nearly dependent, QR can still produce a large coefficient error from small perturbations in b because the original problem is ill-conditioned. A small residual alone does not establish accurate coefficients. Stable Householder QR is common; classical Gram–Schmidt without care may lose orthogonality in finite precision. This lesson’s exact derivation assumes an exact Q and R and labels the implementation issue separately. Read the geometry and the arithmetic Exercise 1. Fit a common value x to observations 2, 2, and 5. Give A, Q, R, the QR equation, solution and residual norm. Hint for exercise 1 A is a column of three ones; its norm is √3. Solution to exercise 1 A=[1,1,1]ᵀ, Q=A/√3 and R=[√3]. Then Qᵀb=(2+2+5)/√3=3√3, so √3x=3√3 and x=3. The residual Ax−b=[1,1,−2]ᵀ has squared norm 1+1+4=6 and norm √6. Its components sum to zero, confirming orthogonality to A. Exercise 2. For A with columns [1,0]ᵀ and [1,ε]ᵀ, ε>0, calculate AᵀA and its determinant. If arithmetic rounds 1+ε² to 1, what false conclusion might the normal-equation matrix suggest? Hint for exercise 2 Compute each column dot product and then the 2×2 determinant. Solution to exercise 2 AᵀA=[[1,1],[1,1+ε²]], whose determinant is (1)(1+ε²)−1=ε²>0. The exact A is full rank. If 1+ε² rounds to 1, the stored matrix becomes [[1,1],[1,1]] with determinant zero, falsely suggesting rank deficiency. This illustrates an intermediate arithmetic failure; it does not claim QR makes the original near-dependence disappear. Preserve geometry before solving Thin QR turns a full-column-rank least-squares problem into a triangular solve by separating the component of b in the column space of A from its orthogonal remainder. Forming AᵀA squares the 2-norm condition number and can squander precision. QR is a numerical choice, not a cure for uncertain data or genuinely near-dependent columns. Revisit conditioning versus algorithm to name those two limits separately.

title: The best box from a sheet of card
summary: Optimize an ideal open box from a square sheet by modeling its feasible cuts and checking a derivative sign.
text: What should be cut away to make more room? A rectangular sheet can become an open box by cutting a square from each corner and folding up the sides. Larger cuts make taller walls, but also shorten the base. The interesting choice is the cut size, not merely the final shape. We shall optimize an ideal volume and say exactly where that model applies. Background capsule. Let the sheet have length L and width W, both positive, and let x be the side of each removed square. After folding, the base dimensions are L−2x and W−2x and the height is x. Volume is the product of these three lengths. A feasible choice keeps all lengths nonnegative, so 0≤x≤min(L,W)/2. At either endpoint a dimension is zero. A derivative f′(x) measures the limiting slope of a function; interior maxima of differentiable functions can occur where that slope is zero, but endpoints require separate attention. A square sheet with exact arithmetic Worked example. Take L=W=12 centimetres. The ideal volume is V(x)=x(12−2x)², for 0≤x≤6. At x=1 the volume is 100 cubic centimetres; at x=2 it is 128; at x=3 it is 108. These values suggest a maximum near 2, but three samples cannot certify the whole interval. Expand V(x)=144x−48x²+4x³. Differentiating gives V′(x)=144−96x+12x²=12(x−2)(x−6). On (0,2), both factors are negative, so the derivative is positive. On (2,6), one factor is positive and the other negative, so it is negative. Volume rises to x=2 and then falls. At x=0 and x=6 it equals zero. Thus x=2 is the unique global maximum on the feasible interval, with base 8×8 and height 2. The word ideal matters. Card has thickness; folds and seams consume material; a real box may need a lid. The model answers a clean geometric question, not a manufacturing specification. Changing the objective to, say, usable interior volume changes the calculation. Model first, certify second The central model is V ( x ) = x ( L − 2 x ) ( W − 2 x ) , 0 ≤ x ≤ min ( L , W ) 2 Exact statement. For a square sheet of side s>0, the ideal volume V(x)=x(s−2x)² on [0,s/2] has its unique maximum at x=s/6, of value 2s³/27. To prove this, differentiate: V′(x)=(s−2x)(s−6x). The first factor is nonnegative throughout the interval and positive before its right endpoint. The second changes sign from positive to negative at s/6. So V increases until s/6 and decreases afterward. Substitution gives (s/6)(2s/3)²=2s³/27. Continuity on the closed interval guarantees some maximum; the sign argument locates it and establishes uniqueness. This proof applies to square sheets and zero-thickness geometry. For a general rectangle, expand and solve a quadratic derivative, then keep only critical values inside its own feasible interval. A root outside that interval is no physical cut. The derivative test is a candidate finder; comparison with boundaries and feasibility is part of the solution. Do not infer that "more wall height gives more volume." On a 12-centimetre sheet, increasing x from 2 to 3 raises height by half but lowers volume from 128 to 108. Likewise, a cubic polynomial outside the feasible interval may have other behavior irrelevant to the box. Check the choice 1. Calculation. An 18-by-18 sheet is folded in the same way. Find the best cut and ideal volume. Hint for question 1 Use the square-sheet result with s=18, and calculate the remaining base side. Full solution for question 1 The maximizing cut is s/6=3 centimetres. Each base side is 18−2·3=12 centimetres. The volume is 3·12²=432 cubic centimetres, matching 2·18³/27=432. The endpoints 0 and 9 give zero, so this interior value beats them. 2. Model check. Someone cuts x=5 from a 10-by-14 sheet and reports a large box because the walls are tall. Explain the error and compare x=1 and x=2. Hint for question 2 Check both base dimensions and the permitted interval before comparing volumes. Full solution for question 2 The feasible interval is 0≤x≤5. At x=5 the 10-centimetre side becomes 10−10=0, so the box has zero volume. At x=1, V=1·8·12=96 cubic centimetres. At x=2, V=2·6·10=120. Thus x=2 beats x=1, but this comparison alone does not establish the global optimum of the rectangular problem. A stopping point You can turn a physical choice into a function and a feasible set, then justify a maximum by checking every type of candidate. The square-sheet formula follows from a derivative sign argument; a sketch or a handful of samples would be weaker evidence. For another way to distinguish a best point from a merely flat point, continue to local and global minima .

title: A valley is not always the deepest valley
summary: Separate local and global minima from stationary candidates, with explicit endpoint and counterexamples.
text: Does stopping downhill mean you are done? Imagine standing in a valley. No nearby step descends, yet a deeper valley could lie beyond a hill. Optimization needs words that separate these two claims. A local minimum compares a point with sufficiently nearby feasible points. A global minimum compares it with every feasible point. The chosen domain is part of both definitions. Background capsule. A function f assigns a number to each input x in a domain D. For x* in D, local minimum means that some radius r>0 satisfies f(x*)≤f(x) for all feasible x with |x−x*|<r. Global minimum means f(x*)≤f(x) for all x in D. A derivative is the limit of nearby secant slopes when that limit exists. “Stationary” means f′(x*)=0. We use the derivative only where x* lies inside an open interval of feasible inputs. Three points that look deceptively similar Worked example. Take f(x)=x³−3x on [−2,2]. Its derivative is 3x²−3=3(x−1)(x+1), so stationary candidates are −1 and 1. The derivative is positive before −1, negative between −1 and 1, then positive after 1. Thus −1 is a local maximum and 1 is a local minimum. Values are f(−2)=−2, f(−1)=2, f(1)=−2, and f(2)=2. The local minimum at 1 is global too, but the left endpoint −2 is another global minimizer despite a nonzero one-sided slope there. A stationary point need not be a minimum: −1 is a maximum. For an actual shallow-versus-deep valley, use h(x)=(x²−1)²+x/4 on [−2,2]. On [3/4,1], the derivative h′(x)=4x(x²−1)+1/4 is negative at 3/4 (−17/16) and positive at 1 (1/4). Continuity gives a minimum on that closed interval, and these inward derivative signs rule out both endpoints, so an interior point is a local minimum on the full domain. Yet throughout [3/4,1], h(x)≥x/4≥3/16, while h(−1)=−1/4. This right-hand valley is therefore definitely not global. A local test alone cannot certify the best value. The necessary condition and its limits The exact first-order claim is f ′ ( x * ) = 0 when f is differentiable at an interior local minimum x*. Here is a short proof. For sufficiently small h>0, local minimality gives [f(x*+h)−f(x*)]/h≥0. For h<0, the same numerator is nonnegative but the denominator is negative, so its quotient is ≤0. If both one-sided quotients converge to the same derivative, that number is at once ≥0 and ≤0; hence it is zero. There are three crucial qualifications. At a domain endpoint, only one side is feasible; f(x)=x on [0,1] has a global minimum at 0 despite f′(0)=1 if the formula is extended to the real line. At a corner, the derivative may not exist; |x| has a global minimum at 0 and slopes −1 and 1 on opposite sides. Finally, zero derivative alone is insufficient: x³ is stationary at 0 but takes negative values just left of 0 and positive values just right. On a closed interval [a,b], a continuous function attains a global minimum and maximum. If it is differentiable in the interior, compare values at a, b and every interior stationary or nondifferentiable candidate. This is a complete method only when candidates can actually be found or ruled out. It does not imply that an arbitrary nonlinear problem is easy, nor that an iterative method visiting one valley finds a global answer. Find the gap in a proposed certificate 1. Calculation. Minimize q(x)=x²−4x on [0,5], naming all candidate types and values. Hint for question 1 Complete the square or solve q′(x)=0, then compare endpoints. Full solution for question 1 q′(x)=2x−4, so the only interior stationary point is x=2. Values are q(0)=0, q(2)=−4 and q(5)=5. Since q(x)=(x−2)²−4≥−4 on the whole interval, x=2 is the unique global minimizer; the square completion independently certifies the conclusion. 2. Counterexample. A colleague claims every point satisfying f′(x)=0 is at least a local minimum. Give one smooth counterexample and explain both neighboring sides. Hint for question 2 A cubic can pass through a horizontal tangent without turning. Full solution for question 2 Let f(x)=x³ on the real line. Its derivative 3x² vanishes at x=0. Yet for every r>0, choose a negative x with |x|<r; then x³<0=f(0). Choose a positive x of the same size and x³>0. Therefore 0 is neither a local minimum nor a local maximum, despite stationarity. What the derivative actually buys At an interior smooth local minimum the slope must vanish. That is a filter, not a certificate. You still need feasible-domain checks and a comparison argument. Convexity supplies a special global guarantee; absent that structure, one valley gives little information about another.

title: The special promise of a convex bowl
summary: Prove the local-to-global theorem for convex functions on convex sets and separate uniqueness from existence.
text: When can a nearby best point be best everywhere? A convex landscape has no hidden valley beneath a line segment connecting two points. That geometric condition turns a local minimum into a global one. It is a strong statement about the whole feasible set and the whole function; a bowl-like sketch alone is not enough. Background capsule. A set C is convex if for any x,y in C and 0≤t≤1, the point (1−t)x+ty also lies in C. This is the straight segment from x to y, in one or many dimensions. A function f on C is convex if its value at each segment point does not exceed the weighted average of endpoint values. A local minimum is best in some small neighborhood relative to C; a global minimum is best throughout C. Test a simple bowl exactly Worked example. Take f(x)=(x−3)²+2 on the real line. Its minimum value is visibly 2 at x=3 because a square cannot be negative. For x=1 and y=5, the midpoint is 3: f(3)=2 while [f(1)+f(5)]/2=6. The graph lies below that chord. This one check illustrates the inequality, but does not prove convexity for all pairs. To prove it, set a=x−3 and b=y−3. The identity (1−t)a²+tb²−[(1−t)a+tb]²=t(1−t)(a−b)²≥0 gives the inequality for every x,y and t in [0,1]. The added constant 2 cancels. When 0<t<1 and x≠y, the final term is positive: f is strictly convex. The exact proof works on any interval as well as the whole line. Test a constrained endpoint. Keep the same function but restrict its domain to [4,6]. The unconstrained minimum x=3 is unavailable. For feasible x, x−3≥1 and squaring increases as x increases, so the unique constrained minimizer is x=4 with value 3. Its derivative is 2 rather than zero. This fits the local-to-global theorem because the interval and objective remain convex, while illustrating why an unconstrained stationary equation is insufficient for a constrained problem. Local-to-global, with its hypotheses visible The defining formula is f ( ( 1 − t ) x + t y ) ≤ ( 1 − t ) f ( x ) + t f ( y ) for x,y∈C and 0≤t≤1. Theorem. If C is convex and f:C→ℝ is convex, then every local minimizer x* is global. Proof: suppose some feasible y has f(y)<f(x*). Every segment point z t =(1−t)x*+ty is feasible. Convexity gives f(z t )≤(1−t)f(x*)+tf(y)<f(x*) for every t>0. As t tends to zero, z t approaches x*, contradicting local minimality. The proof uses both convexity assumptions; it does not require differentiability. If f is strictly convex, it has at most one global minimizer on a convex set: two distinct minimizers would have a midpoint with strictly smaller value. Existence is a separate matter. For example, f(x)=x² on C=(0,1) is strictly convex, but its infimum zero is unattained because 0 is excluded. Even an ordinary convex function can have many minimizers, as f(x)=0 on [0,1] shows. For differentiable convex f on an open convex set, the supporting-line inequality f(y)≥f(x)+∇f(x)·(y−x) makes ∇f(x)=0 sufficient for global optimality. That claim assumes convexity and an unconstrained interior point. A constrained optimum can have nonzero gradient, because feasible directions are restricted. Use the promise carefully 1. Calculation. Show f(x)=2(x+1)²+5 is strictly convex and find its global minimizer on [−3,4]. Hint for question 1 Scale the square identity in the example by two; then use nonnegativity. Full solution for question 1 The chord gap is 2t(1−t)(x−y)², positive for distinct x,y and interior t, so f is strictly convex. The square term is nonnegative and vanishes at x=−1, which lies in [−3,4]. Thus f(−1)=5 is the unique global minimum. Convexity also means any established local minimum would have been global. 2. Boundary of the theorem. Give a strictly convex function on a convex feasible set that has no minimizer, and say why this does not contradict uniqueness. Hint for question 2 Remove the point where a square reaches zero. Full solution for question 2 Use f(x)=x² on C=(0,1). The set is convex and the square identity proves strict convexity there. Values approach zero as x→0 from the right, but every feasible x is positive and has f(x)>0. There is no minimizer to be unique; “at most one” allows zero. One guarantee, two separate questions Convexity of both domain and objective makes local optimality global. Strict convexity rules out two distinct minimizers, while compactness or coercivity and suitable continuity may be needed to ensure one exists. Do not apply this conclusion to a disconnected feasible set or a nonconvex objective merely because the nearby graph looks bowl-shaped. Gradient descent asks how to approach a minimizer once the landscape has useful structure.

title: How long should a downhill step be?
summary: Derive the exact fixed-step convergence interval for gradient descent on a positive-definite quadratic.
text: How far should “downhill” go? The negative gradient points in a locally decreasing direction. Yet a step can overshoot the bottom and climb the other side. On a positive quadratic, exact linear algebra says which fixed step sizes converge and how fast. This article proves that narrow result and uses a one-dimensional case so every number can be checked. Background capsule. For a differentiable f on ℝⁿ, ∇f is the vector of partial derivatives. The Hessian is the matrix of second partial derivatives. A symmetric positive-definite matrix Q has vᵀQv>0 for every nonzero v; its eigenvalues λᵢ are positive. For f(x)=½(x−x*)ᵀQ(x−x*)+c, the gradient is Q(x−x*). An iteration chooses a new x from the current x; convergence means its error tends to zero as the iteration count grows. A step that alternates, then a step that explodes Worked example. Let f(x)=(x−2)². Its gradient is 2(x−2). Starting at x₀=0 with α=3/4 gives x₁=0−(3/4)(−4)=3. Then x₂=3−(3/4)(2)=1.5, and x₃=1.5−(3/4)(−1)=2.25. The errors relative to 2 are −2, 1, −1/2, 1/4: each changes sign and halves in magnitude. The objective values fall from 4 to 1 to 1/4 to 1/16. Now take α=5/4. From x₀=0 the first point is x₁=5, farther from 2, with objective 9. The error multiplier is 1−2α=−3/2, so later magnitudes grow. “Negative gradient” describes the initial direction, not the effect of an arbitrary finite stride. The exact quadratic guarantee The update is x k + 1 = x k − α ∇ f ( x k ) Exact statement. For the positive-definite quadratic in the capsule, a constant α with 0<α<2/λ max (Q) makes every starting point converge geometrically to x*. To prove it, write eₖ=xₖ−x*. Substitution gives eₖ₊₁=(I−αQ)eₖ. A symmetric Q has an orthonormal eigenbasis; in each eigenvector direction the scalar error is multiplied by 1−αλᵢ. The stated interval makes −1<1−αλᵢ<1 for every i. Therefore the Euclidean error shrinks at most by ρ=maxᵢ|1−αλᵢ|<1 each step. Induction gives ‖eₖ‖≤ρᵏ‖e₀‖. This is geometric, also called linear convergence of errors; it is not Newton's quadratic convergence. The interval is sharp for a guarantee from every starting point of this fixed positive quadratic: if α=2/λ max , an error component along a largest-eigenvalue direction alternates without shrinking; above it, that component grows. The case α=0 makes no progress. A gradient norm tending to zero here is meaningful because positive definiteness gives a unique minimizer; on a general nonconvex function, small gradient alone does not certify global optimality. A broader smooth descent inequality says that if ∇f is L-Lipschitz, then f(x−α∇f(x))≤f(x)−α(1−Lα/2)‖∇f(x)‖² for 0<α<2/L. This follows by integrating the gradient along the step and bounding its change by L times travel distance. It ensures descent at nonstationary points, but without further assumptions it does not establish convergence to a global minimum. The eigenvalue proof above supplies the stronger conclusion only for its quadratic model. Optional investigation: which minimum does descent select? Allow 20–30 additional minutes. This is an editorial estimate, separate from the 25-minute core lesson; it has not been timed with readers. You will use differentiation, two linear equations and a geometric sequence. The nearest-point argument explains its dot products locally. When several coefficient pairs fit the same data, minimizing a loss leaves a choice unresolved. Question 2 in least squares gives every exact fit on the line x+y=1. Can the descent procedure itself select one point on that line? Investigate the ordinary Euclidean gradient of f ( x , y ) = 1 2 ( x + y − 1 ) 2 Its minimizers form L={(x,y):x+y=1}. The Hessian has both rows equal to (1,1), with eigenvalues 2 and 0. The positive-definite theorem above therefore does not apply. That missing hypothesis alone does not tell us whether these iterates converge. 1. Same loss, different starts Use the fixed step α=1/4. Starting at (2,0), calculate two iterates. Do you expect convergence to (1/2,1/2), another point of L, or no point? What changes from (0,0)? Derive a recurrence for the residual uₖ=xₖ+yₖ−1 and find a quantity that stays unchanged. Then use them to prove a limit and find the exact interval of real fixed steps that guarantees convergence to a minimizer from every start. Also distinguish the loss, gradient norm, distance to L, and distance to the particular minimizer (1/2,1/2). Which must tend to zero? Hint 1 for the two starts Differentiate f. What stays unchanged when each coordinate has the same amount subtracted from it? Hint 2 for the two starts Add the two coordinate updates, then subtract 1. A scalar recurrence uₖ₊₁=ruₖ gives uₖ=rᵏu₀. When does it tend to zero for every u₀? Full solution: residual, invariant and selected limits Put uₖ=xₖ+yₖ−1. The gradient is (uₖ,uₖ), so the coordinate updates are x k + 1 = x k − α u k y k + 1 = y k − α u k From (2,0), u₀=1. The first two iterates at α=1/4 are (7/4,−1/4) and (13/8,−3/8). Adding the updates gives the residual recurrence. Subtracting them shows that vₖ=xₖ−yₖ is an invariant : its value is unchanged at every step. u k + 1 = ( 1 − 2 α ) u k v k + 1 = v k = v 0 Thus uₖ=(1−2α)ᵏu₀. It tends to zero for every start exactly when |1−2α|<1, or 0<α<1. Solving xₖ+yₖ=1+uₖ and xₖ−yₖ=v₀ gives xₖ=(1+uₖ+v₀)/2 and yₖ=(1+uₖ−v₀)/2. Hence throughout this interval, ( x ∞ , y ∞ ) = ( 1 + v 0 2 , 1 − v 0 2 ) At α=1/4 the residual halves each time. From (2,0), v₀=2, so the limit is (3/2,−1/2). From (0,0), v₀=0, so the limit is (1/2,1/2). The direction in which the loss is flat retains information about the start. The loss is uₖ²/2, the gradient norm is √2|uₖ|, and the distance to L is |uₖ|/√2. All three tend to zero for 0<α<1. Distance to a specified minimizer need not: from (2,0), the distance to (1/2,1/2) tends to √2. A statement about “distance to the minimum” must say which distance it means. The interval is an all-start guarantee. At α=1, every nonzero residual alternates without shrinking, producing a two-cycle. At α>1 or α<0, its magnitude grows. At α=0, an off-line start never moves. The exception throughout is u₀=0: a start already on L has zero gradient and stays fixed for every real α. 2. Why that particular point? For 0<α<1, show that the selected point is the unique point of L nearest the start z₀=(x₀,y₀) in Euclidean distance. Why does zero initialization then select the minimum Euclidean norm solution, even though no penalty was added to f? Hint for the nearest-point claim Write the limit as p=z₀−(u₀/2)(1,1). If q and p both lie on L, what is the sum of the coordinates of q−p? Compare that direction with z₀−p. Full solution: perpendicular displacements and Pythagoras The limit formula can be written p=z₀−(u₀/2)(1,1), where u₀=x₀+y₀−1. Its coordinates sum to 1, so p lies on L. For any other q on L, the coordinates of q−p sum to zero. The dot product of two vectors (a,b) and (c,d) is ac+bd; a zero dot product means the vectors are perpendicular. Thus (q−p)·(1,1)=0. Since z₀−p is a multiple of (1,1), the displacements z₀−p and p−q are perpendicular. Expanding the squared length of their sum gives Pythagoras: ‖ z 0 − q ‖ 2 = ‖ z 0 − p ‖ 2 + ‖ p − q ‖ 2 The last term is nonnegative and is zero only when q=p. Therefore p is the unique point of L nearest z₀; f still has infinitely many minimizers. The distance from z₀ to L is ‖z₀−p‖=|u₀|/√2, which also justifies the distance formula used above. For z₀=(0,0), distance from the start is the Euclidean norm ‖q‖=√(qₓ²+qᵧ²). The selected point (1/2,1/2) therefore has the smallest norm of all points on L. This selection comes from the update and initialization, without changing the objective. 3. Change the observation Change only the observation in the loss to f ~ ( x , y ) = 1 2 ( x + 2 y − 1 ) 2 Start again at (2,0). Derive the gradient, a recurrence for uₖ=xₖ+2yₖ−1, and a linear combination of xₖ and yₖ that stays unchanged. Find the all-start convergence interval and the selected limit. Test α=1/4 and α=3/4, both of which were safe in the previous investigation. Include boundary exceptions and explain which point zero initialization selects. Hint for the changed observation The gradient points along (1,2). Which linear combination of the two coordinate updates cancels a displacement in that direction? Add the first update to twice the second to track the residual. Full solution: a new invariant and a new step interval The gradient is (x+2y−1)(1,2). Thus xₖ₊₁=xₖ−αuₖ and yₖ₊₁=yₖ−2αuₖ. The residual and the newly derived invariant vₖ=2xₖ−yₖ obey u k + 1 = ( 1 − 5 α ) u k v k + 1 = v k = v 0 Every start converges to a minimizer exactly when |1−5α|<1, giving 0<α<2/5. From (2,0), u₀=1 and v₀=4. At the limit, solve x+2y=1 and 2x−y=4: the second equation gives y=2x−4, so 5x−8=1. The selected point is (9/5,−2/5). For any start the limit is p=z₀−(u₀/5)(1,2). It lies on the new minimizing line, and every displacement q−p along that line satisfies (q−p)·(1,2)=0. The same Pythagorean proof makes p the unique nearest point to z₀. In particular zero initialization selects the minimum norm point (1/5,2/5). At α=1/4 the residual multiplier is −1/4: residuals alternate and shrink. The first two iterates are (7/4,−1/2) and (29/16,−3/8). At α=3/4 the multiplier is −11/4. From this start the residual magnitude grows, so the iterates diverge and the objective grows by the factor 121/16 each step. Changing the observation requires a new step interval. At α=2/5 a nonzero residual alternates without shrinking. Above 2/5 or below 0 it grows; at α=0 an off-line start stays put. A start already satisfying x+2y=1 stays fixed for every real step size. Saying only that the Hessian is not positive definite would establish none of these conclusions. Choose a stride from the curvature 1. Calculation. For f(x)=3(x+1)², find the fixed-step convergence interval, then calculate two iterates from x₀=1 using α=1/12. Hint for question 1 The Hessian is 6; track error relative to −1. Full solution for question 1 The Hessian eigenvalue is 6, so 0<α<2/6=1/3. Here 1−6α=1/2. Initial error is 1−(−1)=2, so successive errors are 1 and 1/2. Thus x₁=0 and x₂=−1/2. Directly, ∇f(1)=12 and 1−(1/12)12=0, agreeing with the error calculation. 2. Failure check. For the same f, what happens with α=1/3 from x₀=1? Is the failure numerical accident? Hint for question 2 Compute 1−αλ exactly. Full solution for question 2 The error multiplier is 1−(1/3)6=−1. Starting error 2 alternates between 2 and −2, so the iterates alternate between 1 and −3. Both have objective 3·2²=12. This exact cycle is the boundary case of the theorem, not rounding error. What the model proves For a positive-definite quadratic, curvature sets a precise safe interval and an exact contraction factor. Outside that class, a descent inequality may survive while global convergence does not. A step-size plot illustrates behavior but cannot replace the eigenvalue argument. The next challenge is when a feasible region blocks the negative-gradient direction; multipliers describe that geometry.

title: An optimum pressed against a fence
summary: Derive the regular equality-constraint multiplier condition and classify a candidate with a direct certificate.
text: What if the best direction crosses a fence? At an unconstrained smooth minimum, all small directions are available and the gradient must vanish. On a smooth constraint curve, only tangent directions are permitted. The gradient of the objective may be nonzero yet perpendicular to that curve. A multiplier records this alignment; solving its equations finds candidates, which still need classification. Background capsule. For f(x,y), the gradient ∇f=(∂f/∂x,∂f/∂y) points in the direction of steepest local increase. An equality g(x,y)=0 describes a curve when ∇g≠0 nearby; its tangent vectors v satisfy ∇g·v=0. Two nonzero vectors perpendicular to the same one-dimensional tangent line are parallel. A regularity condition such as ∇g(x*)≠0 is essential for the elementary multiplier theorem. The closest point on a line Worked example. Minimize f(x,y)=x²+y² subject to g(x,y)=x+y−4=0.
