The objective is squared distance from the origin, so the closest point should lie where the perpendicular from the origin meets the line. Gradients are ∇f=(2x,2y) and ∇g=(1,1). Setting ∇f=λ∇g gives 2x=λ and 2y=λ, hence x=y. The constraint makes x=y=2 and λ=4. The objective is 8. This candidate is global: write y=4−x, then f(x,4−x)=x²+(4−x)²=2(x−2)²+8≥8. The square completion supplies the certificate; the multiplier equations alone did not. The line is unbounded, but the squared distance grows away from (2,2), so an optimum does exist. Why the gradients align The central necessary condition is ∇ f ( x * ) = λ ∇ g ( x * ) , g ( x * ) = 0 Precise scope. If f and g are continuously differentiable near an interior constrained local optimum x* in ℝ², and ∇g(x*)≠0, then some real λ satisfies the equation. The regularity condition allows a smooth local parametrization of the constraint with a nonzero tangent v. Along that curve, f has a one-variable local optimum, so its tangential derivative ∇f·v is zero. Since ∇g·v is also zero and in the plane both gradients lie in the one-dimensional normal space, they are parallel. This invokes the elementary local-curve theorem under the stated regularity; it is not a claim for arbitrary singular constraint sets. The sign convention is flexible for equality constraints. If one writes L=f−λg, stationarity is ∇f−λ∇g=0. If one writes L=f+μg, then μ=−λ. By contrast, inequality constraints require feasibility, nonnegative multipliers under an agreed ≤0 convention, and complementarity; those additional conditions appear in KKT . Failure case: minimize f(x)=x subject to g(x)=x²=0. The only feasible point, x=0, is certainly both minimum and maximum. But g′(0)=0 while f′(0)=1, so f′(0)=λg′(0) has no solution. Regularity fails, exactly where the theorem said it must hold. Another caution: on the unit circle g(x,y)=x²+y²−1=0, let f(x,y)=x. Then ∇f=(1,0) and ∇g=(2x,2y). The multiplier equations force y=0 because λ cannot be zero, and feasibility gives (1,0) or (−1,0). At (1,0), λ=1/2 and f=1, the global maximum of x on the circle. At (−1,0), λ=−1/2 and f=−1, the global minimum. Equality multipliers may have either sign. Solving the equations without comparing values would leave both candidates unclassified. Classify, then certify 1. Calculation. Minimize x²+4y² subject to x+y=3. Find x,y and the multiplier for L=f−λ(x+y−3). Hint for question 1 Stationarity says 2x=λ and 8y=λ; then use x+y=3. Full solution for question 1 From 2x=8y, x=4y. Thus 5y=3, so y=3/5 and x=12/5; λ=24/5. Substitute x=3−y: f=(3−y)²+4y²=5(y−3/5)²+36/5. Hence 36/5 is the unique global minimum on the entire line. 2. Hypothesis check. Let f(x)=x and constrain x by x²=0. Why is rejecting x=0 because no multiplier exists wrong? Hint for question 2 Describe the feasible set before writing stationarity. Full solution for question 2 The feasible set is the singleton {0}; x=0 is automatically its global minimizer. The multiplier equation would demand 1=λ·0, impossible for any λ. This is no contradiction because the constraint gradient is zero at 0. The necessary-condition theorem explicitly requires a nonzero constraint gradient. A candidate generator with a visible limit At a regular equality-constrained optimum, objective and constraint gradients align. That alignment has no built-in minimum test and can fail to describe optima on singular constraints. Always substitute back, compare candidates and use a separate certificate when possible. For straight-edged feasible regions, linear programs offer a different finite candidate method.

title: Why the best mix often sits at a corner
summary: Solve a bounded two-variable linear program by vertices and an explicit resource bound.
text: Why does the best mixture touch a corner? Suppose two products consume limited resources and yield different value. Each inequality trims the plane to a half-plane; their intersection may be a polygon. A linear objective has straight, parallel level lines. Sliding such a line toward better values suggests a vertex solution, but the claim needs boundedness and a nonempty polygon, and an entire edge can tie. Background capsule. A linear inequality such as x+y≤4 specifies all points on one side of a line. A feasible region is the intersection of all such conditions. A vertex is a corner that cannot be expressed as a nontrivial convex combination of two other feasible points. An objective cᵀx=c₁x+c₂y assigns a number to each feasible point. Maximizing reward is equivalent to minimizing its negative. We use exact arithmetic to check intersections and objective values. A two-resource allocation Worked example. Choose nonnegative x,y with x+y≤4 and 2x+y≤6. Maximize R=3x+2y. The feasible polygon has vertices (0,0), (3,0), (2,2), and (0,4). To find (2,2), solve x+y=4 and 2x+y=6 together: subtract to get x=2, then y=2. The rewards at the four vertices are 0, 9, 10, and 8. So (2,2) has the largest vertex reward, 10. To see why this vertex check covers the interior, decompose any feasible polygon point as a convex combination of its vertices. Its linear reward becomes the same weighted average of the vertex rewards and cannot exceed their maximum. This geometric decomposition is the finite-polygon fact used here. In this example the winner is unique: any mixture involving a vertex with reward below 10 yields less than 10. Check a rejected intersection. The lines x=0 and 2x+y=6 meet at (0,6), but this point violates x+y≤4. It is not a feasible vertex and its reward 12 cannot enter the comparison. Listing intersections of boundary lines is only a candidate step: each point must pass every inequality. The direct bound R≤10 is a useful independent protection against accepting such a spurious answer. A candidate reward exceeding that proven bound signals either infeasibility or an arithmetic mistake, rather than a better allocation. The finite vertex certificate In minimization notation the model is min c T x subject to A x ≤ b Exact claim. If the feasible region in ℝ² is a nonempty bounded polygon, then a linear objective attains its minimum at some vertex. A bounded polygon is the convex hull of its finitely many vertices. If x=Σᵢtᵢvᵢ with tᵢ≥0 and Σᵢtᵢ=1, linearity gives cᵀx=Σᵢtᵢcᵀvᵢ≥minᵢcᵀvᵢ. This proves the claim once the polygon decomposition is established. It does not say every optimum is a vertex. For a tie, maximize x+y over the triangle x≥0, y≥0, x+y≤4. The vertices (4,0) and (0,4) both give 4, as does every point on the edge between them. A statement that "the best mix always sits at a unique corner" would be false. Nor may we ignore unboundedness: maximize x over x≥0; feasible values have no finite maximum. Some unbounded polyhedra have an optimum at a vertex, but the simple bounded-polygon theorem does not decide all such cases. Feasibility itself must be checked first. There is a stronger direct certificate in the worked allocation: 3x+2y=(x+y)+(2x+y)≤4+6=10. The point (2,2) is feasible and reaches both bounds, so no feasible point can do better. This inequality proof is useful even without listing all vertices; it foreshadows dual bounds . Vertices and edges 1. Calculation. Maximize P=2x+y over x,y≥0, x+y≤5, x≤3. List the vertices and identify every maximizer. Hint for question 1 The rectangle cut by x+y≤5 has a top slanted edge. Check where x=3 meets it. Full solution for question 1 The vertices are (0,0), (3,0), (3,2), and (0,5). Their P-values are 0, 6, 8, and 5. Any feasible point is a convex combination of vertices, so P≤8, attained at (3,2). It is the unique maximizer since the other vertices have strictly smaller values. 2. Tie check. Maximize x+y on x,y≥0 with x+y≤5. Is the answer one vertex, two vertices, or more? Hint for question 2 Equality in the constraint gives the best possible objective. Full solution for question 2 The inequality directly gives x+y≤5. Every point (t,5−t), 0≤t≤5, is feasible and attains 5. There are infinitely many maximizers, including vertices (5,0) and (0,5). The vertex theorem promises at least one vertex optimum and is fully consistent with an optimal edge. What a corner proves A bounded feasible polygon makes vertex enumeration a complete finite method for a linear objective. An explicit weighted-constraint bound can certify the answer even more directly. Check emptiness, boundedness and ties before making a claim. In higher dimensions the same finite-vertex principle applies to polytopes, but enumerating vertices can become expensive.

title: A second problem certifies the first
summary: Construct a Lagrangian lower bound, prove weak duality and compute a certified primal-dual gap.
text: Can a different problem prove your answer is good? Finding a feasible choice gives an upper bound on a minimization problem's best value. A Lagrangian dual construction gives lower bounds. If the two meet, the candidate is optimal; if they nearly meet, the gap quantifies what remains unproved. This lesson proves weak duality directly and keeps strong duality separate. Background capsule. Write a primal problem as minimizing f₀(x) subject to fᵢ(x)≤0. A feasible x obeys every inequality. The infimum p* is the greatest lower bound of feasible objective values; it may be unattained. For a real-valued function h, infₓh(x) is a number or −∞. Each inequality receives a multiplier λᵢ≥0. We use the convention L(x,λ)=f₀(x)+Σᵢλᵢfᵢ(x), and define the dual function g(λ)=infₓL(x,λ), with x ranging over the stated base domain. A lower bound you can see Worked example. Minimize x² subject to x≥1. Put the constraint in the agreed form f₁(x)=1−x≤0. For λ≥0, L(x,λ)=x²+λ(1−x). Complete the square: L=(x−λ/2)²+λ−λ²/4, so g(λ)=λ−λ²/4. At λ=1 this gives 3/4. Thus no feasible x can have objective below 3/4, even before we solve the primal. At λ=2, g(2)=1. The feasible candidate x=1 also has objective 1, so lower and upper bounds match. Hence p*=1 and x=1 is optimal. Notice what was checked: λ=2 is nonnegative, x=1 is feasible, and g(2) really is the infimum over all real x, attained at x=1. If we had simply inserted x=1 into L without taking an infimum, we would not have constructed a valid lower bound. Why weak duality never needs convexity The core inequality is g ( λ ) = inf x L ( x , λ ) ≤ p * for λ ≥ 0 Proof with its domain. For any feasible x and nonnegative λ, each λᵢfᵢ(x)≤0. Therefore g(λ)≤L(x,λ)≤f₀(x). Taking the infimum of the rightmost quantity over feasible x yields g(λ)≤p*, provided the feasible set is nonempty and the value is interpreted in the extended-real sense. Convexity was not used. If a feasible candidate x̄ has objective U and a valid λ has finite dual value L b =g(λ), then L b ≤p*≤U. The nonnegative difference U−L b is a certified bound on the candidate's suboptimality. The dual problem maximizes g(λ) over λ≥0. The best dual lower bound d* is at most p*. Equality d*=p* is strong duality , which requires additional conditions. For convex problems with suitable constraint qualification, such as a strictly feasible point under the usual Slater hypotheses, strong duality can hold. This article does not prove that theorem. It proves the elementary inequality that remains valid even for nonconvex objectives. Two failures are easy to avoid. A negative multiplier reverses the direction of a constraint contribution and may make the claimed bound invalid. An infeasible primal candidate does not supply an upper bound on p*. For example, x=0 in the worked problem gives objective zero, but violates x≥1. Reporting a gap 0−g(2)=−1 would reveal the mistake rather than an astonishing improvement. Build and audit a bound 1. Calculation. Minimize (x−1)² subject to x≥2. With constraint 2−x≤0, find g(λ), a dual multiplier matching the feasible candidate x=2, and the gap. Hint for question 1 Complete the square in (x−1)²+λ(2−x), or set its derivative to zero. Full solution for question 1 The minimizer of L over x is x=1+λ/2. Substitution gives g(λ)=λ−λ²/4: indeed the square term λ²/4 and constraint contribution λ(1−λ/2) combine to λ−λ²/4. At λ=2, g=1. Candidate x=2 is feasible and has objective (2−1)²=1. The gap is 1−1=0, certifying optimality by weak duality. 2. Certificate repair. In the original problem minimize x² subject to x≥1, a proposed report uses x=1/2 and λ=2 to claim a negative gap. Locate every relevant number and repair the report. Hint for question 2 Check feasibility before calling an objective an upper bound. Full solution for question 2 x=1/2 violates 1−x≤0 because 1−1/2=1/2>0. Its objective 1/4 is not a primal upper bound. λ=2 is dual feasible and g(2)=1, a valid lower bound. Replace the candidate by x=1, which satisfies the constraint and has objective 1. The corrected gap is 1−1=0. The apparent negative gap came from a nonfeasible candidate, not failure of weak duality. A certificate with honest limits For minimization, feasible choices give upper bounds and nonnegative inequality multipliers give Lagrangian lower bounds after taking the infimum. A zero gap certifies optimality without needing a general strong-duality theorem. A positive gap measures uncertainty about the particular candidate and bound, not necessarily an inherent gap between primal and dual optima. KKT conditions organize when the two sides meet.

title: Constraints that matter and constraints that rest
summary: Check all four KKT conditions and prove their sufficiency for differentiable convex inequalities.
text: Which fences actually hold the answer in place? A constrained optimum may lie on one boundary while another constraint sits slack. Complementary slackness says a strictly slack inequality must receive zero multiplier. Together with stationarity and feasibility, this makes a compact certificate for many convex problems. The directions of the theorem matter: convexity gives sufficiency; necessity needs a constraint qualification. Background capsule. Consider minimize f₀(x) subject to fᵢ(x)≤0, with x in an open Euclidean domain and differentiable functions. A constraint is active if fᵢ(x)=0 and slack if fᵢ(x)<0. The Lagrangian is L=f₀+Σᵢλᵢfᵢ with λᵢ≥0. For convex differentiable h, the supporting inequality h(y)≥h(x)+∇h(x)·(y−x) follows from convexity. A candidate must satisfy all original inequalities before a multiplier calculation can certify anything. One active fence and one resting fence Worked example. Minimize f₀(x)=(x−3)² subject to f₁(x)=x−1≤0 and f₂(x)=−x−2≤0. The feasible interval is [−2,1]. The nearest feasible point to 3 is x*=1, with objective 4. At x=1, the first constraint is active (f₁=0); the second is slack (f₂=−3). Stationarity is 2(x−3)+λ₁−λ₂=0. Taking λ₁=4 and λ₂=0 satisfies it. Both multipliers are nonnegative and λ₁f₁=λ₂f₂=0. There is also an immediate direct proof: for any x≤1, |x−3|≥2, so (x−3)²≥4. The KKT check packages the same optimum into reusable conditions. If we tried λ₂=1, complementarity would fail because λ₂f₂=−3; the resting fence cannot carry a positive multiplier under this certificate. Separate zero multiplier from slackness. Complementarity forces a slack constraint's multiplier to vanish, but the reverse implication fails. Minimize x² subject to x≤0. The optimum x=0 is active, yet stationarity 2x+λ=0 gives λ=0. The unconstrained minimum already lies on the fence, so no positive multiplier is needed. Thus active constraints may carry zero multipliers. A list of positive multipliers can identify supporting restrictions, but it need not list every active boundary. Four conditions and two theorem directions The conditions are f i ( x * ) ≤ 0 , λ i ≥ 0 , λ i f i ( x * ) = 0 , ∇ x L ( x * , λ ) = 0 Sufficiency theorem. Suppose f₀ and each fᵢ are convex and differentiable, and a feasible x* and λ satisfy the four conditions. Because λᵢ≥0, L(·,λ) is convex. Stationarity makes x* a global minimizer of L over the whole unconstrained domain, using the supporting inequality. Complementarity gives L(x*,λ)=f₀(x*). For any feasible y, L(y,λ)≤f₀(y). Combining these facts yields f₀(x*)=L(x*,λ)≤L(y,λ)≤f₀(y), so x* is globally optimal. This proof does not need strict feasibility once a KKT pair has been supplied. Necessity boundary. A convex optimum need not admit multipliers without a qualification. A common sufficient condition for differentiable convex inequalities is Slater's condition: a point in the open domain exists that satisfies every inequality strictly; with affine equalities, it must also satisfy those exactly. Under the full convex-duality theorem, an attained optimum then admits suitable KKT multipliers. We cite that theorem rather than proving separation here. In the one-dimensional example minimize x subject to x²≤0, only x=0 is feasible and optimal, but stationarity would require 1+λ·0=0, impossible. Strict feasibility is absent. Nonconvex stationarity is another trap. Minimize f(x)=−x² without constraints. At x=0 stationarity holds and the empty feasibility/complementarity conditions are automatic, yet 0 is a maximum, and the objective is unbounded below. The convexity hypothesis is what turns a KKT point into a global certificate. Check every condition 1. Calculation. Minimize (x−4)² subject to x≤2 and x≥−1. Find a KKT pair and certify its value. Hint for question 1 Use f₁=x−2 and f₂=−x−1. The closest feasible point to 4 is the right endpoint. Full solution for question 1 Take x*=2, λ₁=4, λ₂=0. Primal residuals are f₁(2)=0 and f₂(2)=−3; dual multipliers are nonnegative. Stationarity is 2(2−4)+4−0=0. Both complementary products vanish. All functions are convex and differentiable, so sufficiency proves x*=2 globally optimal, with objective 4. Directly, x≤2 implies |x−4|≥2. 2. Faulty certificate. For the worked problem, someone offers x=0, λ₁=6, λ₂=0 because stationarity holds. What fails? Hint for question 2 Evaluate both constraint values and their multiplier products at x=0. Full solution for question 2 At x=0, both inequalities are feasible: f₁=−1, f₂=−2. Stationarity is 2(0−3)+6−0=0. But λ₁f₁=6(−1)=−6≠0, so complementarity fails. Indeed f₀(0)=9 exceeds f₀(1)=4. The multiplier was placed on a constraint that is slack at the proposed point. A complete check is a useful proof Primal feasibility, dual feasibility, complementary slackness and stationarity must all be stated under one sign convention. With convex differentiable data they suffice for a global minimum. Claiming they are necessary requires qualification, and claiming sufficiency for a nonconvex objective requires more work. Nonsmooth convex functions retain global certificates through subgradients rather than ordinary derivatives.

title: A minimum with no derivative
summary: Derive the subdifferential of absolute value and prove the median rule for absolute deviations.
text: Can a sharp corner be the best point? The graph of |x| has a clear minimum at zero, although it has no derivative there. A convex subgradient replaces the single tangent slope with every supporting slope. This idea also explains why medians, rather than means, minimize total absolute deviation. Background capsule. For a convex function f:ℝ→ℝ, a number g is a subgradient at x if the line through (x,f(x)) with slope g lies at or below the graph everywhere. The set of all such g is written ∂f(x). The condition 0∈∂f(x) says the horizontal line at height f(x) supports the whole graph, which is exactly global minimality. A median of sorted data a₁≤⋯≤aₙ has at least half the observations on each side; when n is even, every point in [aₙ/₂,aₙ/₂₊₁] is a median. Three observations and an interval of answers Worked example. For data 1, 2, 10, let F(m)=|m−1|+|m−2|+|m−10|. At m=2, the cost is 1+0+8=9. At the mean 13/3, the cost is 10/3+7/3+17/3=34/3, larger than 9. Between 1 and 2, two observations lie to the right and one to the left, so moving right decreases F by one per unit. Between 2 and 10, two lie to the left and one to the right, so moving right increases F by one per unit. The minimum occurs at the median 2. For even data 1, 2, 10, 12, the total absolute deviation is constant on [2,10]. At m=2 it is 1+0+8+10=19; at m=6 it is 5+4+4+6=19; at m=10 it is 9+8+0+2=19. Outside that interval, a move toward it reduces more distances than it increases. The minimizing set can thus be an interval, not a unique point. Supporting slopes and the median proof The defining inequality is g ∈ ∂ f ( x ) ⇔ f ( y ) ≥ f ( x ) + g ( y − x ) for all y At x=0 for f(x)=|x|, the inequality becomes |y|≥gy for every real y. For y>0 this requires g≤1; for y<0, division by a negative reverses the sign and requires g≥−1. Conversely every g in [−1,1] satisfies |y|≥gy for both signs. Thus ∂|·|(0)=[−1,1]. Away from zero the graph is a straight line locally, and the unique subgradient is −1 for x<0 or 1 for x>0. This is a full derivation, not an appeal to a picture. Median theorem. For sorted real data a₁≤⋯≤aₙ, minimizers of Σᵢ|m−aᵢ| are exactly the interval between the lower and upper middle order statistics. One proof pairs the smallest with the largest, the next smallest with the next largest, and so on. For a pair a≤b, |m−a|+|m−b|≥b−a, with equality exactly when m∈[a,b]. For even n, the intersection of the paired intervals is [a n/2 ,a n/2+1 ], the interval from the lower to upper median. For odd n, the paired intervals all contain the middle observation; the unpaired term |m−a (n+1)/2 | forces m to that exact observation. This proves the characterization, including repeated values. Absolute-loss minimizers need not be means. For 1,2,10 the mean is 13/3 and is pulled toward 10. The median result assumes ordinary equally weighted absolute deviations on the real line. Different weights or a restriction to a discrete feasible set require a modified check; do not transfer the answer unexamined. Use slopes that still work at corners 1. Calculation. Find every minimizer of |m−1|+|m−4|+|m−9|+|m−12| and the minimum value. Hint for question 1 Find the interval between the two middle observations and evaluate at one point. Full solution for question 1 The middle observations are 4 and 9, so every m∈[4,9] minimizes the sum. At m=4 the value is 3+0+5+8=16. For any m in the interval, the outer pair contributes 12−1=11 and the inner pair contributes 9−4=5, totaling 16. Outside the interval, the inner-pair contribution increases, so no other point minimizes it. 2. Supporting line. Is g=3/2 a subgradient of |x| at zero? Prove the answer using one test input. Hint for question 2 The support condition must hold for all y; choose a positive y. Full solution for question 2 No. At x=0, g=3/2 would require |y|≥(3/2)y for every y. Taking y=2 gives 2≥3, false. The complete subgradient set is [−1,1], found by testing positive and negative y separately. A derivative is optional for a convex minimum Subgradients express global supporting inequalities. Zero belongs to the subdifferential exactly at a global minimizer of a convex function on the whole line. Pairing absolute distances proves the median result and exposes possible intervals of optima. For nonconvex nonsmooth functions, a local generalized slope of zero is not automatically a global certificate; the convex support inequality is the key.

title: Use curvature to choose a better step
summary: Derive Newton’s model step, prove its exact positive-quadratic behavior and locate failure cases.
text: Can curvature fix a badly scaled valley? Gradient descent uses slope and a chosen step length. Newton's method builds a local quadratic model and solves for that model's minimum. For an actual positive quadratic it can reach the answer in one step; elsewhere it is a local method whose full step may fail. A positive-definite Hessian guarantees a unique model-minimizing Newton step and, away from stationarity, a descent direction. Background capsule. For twice differentiable f:ℝⁿ→ℝ, ∇f(x) is the gradient and H f (x) is the symmetric matrix of second partial derivatives. A quadratic Taylor model around x for displacement p is mₓ(p)=f(x)+∇f(x)ᵀp+½pᵀH f (x)p. Positive-definite H makes its quadratic term strictly upward in every nonzero direction. Solving Hp=−∇f means finding a vector p whose Hessian-weighted image cancels the gradient; it is preferable to explicitly computing a matrix inverse. A narrow quadratic, solved exactly Worked example. Take f(x,y)=½(x−1)²+50(y+2)². Its minimizer is (1,−2). The gradient is (x−1,100(y+2)), and the Hessian is diag(1,100). From (3,0), gradient is (2,200). Newton solves p₁=−2 and 100p₂=−200, so p=(−2,−2). One full update lands at (1,−2), where the objective is zero. A single gradient step with α=1 would instead move to (1,−200), wildly overshooting the steep y direction. The one-step result is not magic: this f equals its quadratic Taylor model exactly everywhere. Newton corrects each eigen-direction by its own curvature scale. That explains the appeal of the method on a narrow valley, but a general function's Hessian changes with location and its local model may mispredict a distant full step. Derive the step, then inspect its assumptions Setting the model gradient with respect to p to zero gives H f ( x k ) p k = − ∇ f ( x k ) , x k + 1 = x k + p k Exact quadratic theorem. If f(x)=½(x−x*)ᵀQ(x−x*)+c with Q symmetric positive definite, Newton's full step from any x lands at x*. Indeed ∇f(x)=Q(x−x*) and H f =Q. The linear system Qp=−Q(x−x*) has unique solution p=−(x−x*), hence x+p=x*. Positive definiteness ensures the target is the unique global minimum. This is a theorem for a quadratic objective; it says nothing about arbitrary nonlinear functions. For a general twice differentiable function, if H(x) is positive definite and ∇f(x)≠0, then the Newton direction is locally descending: ∇f(x)ᵀp=−pᵀH(x)p<0. By differentiability, a sufficiently small positive step t along p decreases f. A full step t=1 may still increase f, so practical algorithms often use line search or a trust region. This paragraph proves local descent from positive definiteness; it does not prove a global convergence theorem. Quadratic local convergence near a suitable nondegenerate minimizer requires stronger smoothness and a sufficiently close start, which we leave as a named advanced result. A simple failure is f(x)=−x². At x=1, gradient −2 and Hessian −2. Newton's equation gives p=−1 and lands at x=0, a maximum . The Hessian was negative, so the quadratic model had no minimum. Another failure is a singular Hessian: for f(x)=x⁴ at zero, both gradient and Hessian vanish, and a unique Newton direction is undefined even though zero is a minimum. Separate model from objective 1. Calculation. For f(x,y)=2(x−3)²+½(y+1)², start at (0,4). Compute the Newton direction and next point. Hint for question 1 The Hessian is diagonal. Divide each negative gradient component by its matching diagonal entry. Full solution for question 1 At (0,4), the gradient is (4(0−3),4+1)=(−12,5), and H=diag(4,1). Solving Hp=−∇f gives p=(3,−5). The next point is (0,4)+(3,−5)=(3,−1), the unique minimizer, with value zero. The exact quadratic theorem explains the one-step finish. 2. Failure check. Apply a full Newton step to f(x)=−x² from x=2. Does the new point minimize f locally or globally? Hint for question 2 Solve (−2)p=−(−4), then classify the new point by nearby values. Full solution for question 2 At x=2, gradient is −4 and Hessian −2, so −2p=4 and p=−2. The full step lands at 0. There f(0)=0 but f(ε)=−ε²<0 for every nonzero ε, so 0 is a strict local maximum, not a local minimum. Globally f has no lower bound on ℝ. The negative Hessian invalidates the model-minimum interpretation. Use curvature with a check Newton's direction minimizes a positive-definite quadratic local model. It exactly solves positive-definite quadratics in one step, but full steps on changing or indefinite curvature require control and classification. A solver for the Hessian system is a tool, not a certificate of global optimality. Compare this with fixed-step descent : each method has a different narrow theorem and a different failure mode.

title: Return to the model: three chances and a remembered draw
summary: A working self-study return with exact ticket laws, a remembered draw and later recording audits. Forty minutes is an uncalibrated editorial estimate.
text: What can three separate checks leave undecided? Suppose every two warning lights pass a chance calculation. Can we multiply all three lights’ chances to predict their joint signal? Write your prediction before opening the worked answer. This return lesson changes the finite models from A test for independence, not a feeling ; it does not change that lesson or its original tasks. Working self-study edition. About 40 minutes is an uncalibrated editorial estimate: roughly 10 minutes to read and reconstruct the example, 15 for the changed tasks, and 15 for a return in another sitting. These tasks and solutions have not been evaluated with learners. A study checkmark records your own activity, not a grade or verified mastery. Preparation return. You need fractions, finite sample spaces and conditional probability. If those feel uncertain, return to the original lesson’s product test and two original cases , or the conditional-probability explanation . Here a word such as 101 records three lights in the fixed order X,Y,Z; 1 means on, 0 means off. An event is a collection of words. P(A) is the sum of their probabilities, and A ∩ B means both events occur. When P(A) is positive, P(B | A)=P(A ∩ B)/P(A). Read the complete ticket law before multiplying Worked example. A machine chooses one of eight labelled tickets uniformly, once. Tickets may display the same word; each ticket, rather than each different word, has chance 1/8. The entire law is below. Let A mean X=1, B mean Y=1, and C mean Z=1. Eight equally likely tickets; rows give the number displaying each word Word XYZ Ticket count Probability 000 2 2/8 001 0 0 010 1 1/8 011 1 1/8 100 1 1/8 101 1 1/8 110 2 2/8 111 0 0 The counts total eight. Summing the rows with each light on gives P(A)=4/8=1/2, P(B)=4/8=1/2 and P(C)=2/8=1/4. For example, A includes 100,101,110,111, with counts 1+1+2+0. Equal ticket probabilities do not mean equal word probabilities. Attempt these before reading on: check every two-event product; then compare the probability of all three with the product of their individual chances. Finally, compare the chance of Z=1 given X=1 with its chance given both X=1 and Y=1. Hint for the ticket calculation For A ∩ B, add 110 and 111. For A ∩ C, add 101 and 111; for B ∩ C, add 011 and 111. The combined clue A ∩ B has positive probability even though 111 has none. Full worked ticket calculation The intersections are P(A ∩ B)=2/8=1/4=(1/2)(1/2), P(A ∩ C)=1/8=(1/2)(1/4), and P(B ∩ C)=1/8=(1/2)(1/4). All three pairs pass. But P(A ∩ B ∩ C)=0, whereas (1/2)(1/2)(1/4)=1/16. The three events are pairwise independent and are not mutually independent. One clue gives P(C | A)=(1/8)/(1/2)=1/4. Both clues give P(C | A ∩ B)=0/(1/4)=0. Neither division has a zero denominator. Dependence on the combined clues is compatible with independence from each clue separately. State exactly which products a claim requires Exact finite statement. Two events are independent when the probability of their intersection equals the product of their probabilities. Three events are pairwise independent when this holds for all three pairs. They are mutually independent when the three pair equalities and the triple equality all hold. The central test for three is therefore: P ( A ∩ B ) = P ( A ) P ( B ) P ( A ∩ C ) = P ( A ) P ( C ) P ( B ∩ C ) = P ( B ) P ( C ) P ( A ∩ B ∩ C ) = P ( A ) P ( B ) P ( C ) The ticket calculation is a complete counterexample to the claim that passing all pairs suffices. A triple equality alone would also leave the pair requirements unchecked. This is a calculation from an exact model, not a conclusion drawn from a few observed records. Replacement describes the bag, not the whole mechanism. Putting a token back restores the contents. It does not specify how the next token is selected. Independent uniform draws from a restored bag do give the product law: for any first labelled token i and second labelled token j, the conditional second-selection probability is 1/N whatever i, hence the joint probability is (1/N)(1/N). Summing over the chosen colour events gives the colour product law. A rule that remembers i can give a different conditional chance, even with the same restored bag and the same unconditional colour chances. Change the procedure, then return without the labels The restored four-token bag Exercise 1. Work through the following changed selection procedure. A bag has four distinct tokens, two red and two blue. Choose the first token uniformly, record its colour and replace it. Then use a fresh fair six-sided die whose result is independent of the first selection. On 1 or 2, select that same labelled token again. On 3,4,5 or 6, select uniformly from all four tokens using fresh randomness independent of the first selection and the die. Record the second colour. The copying branch is deliberately not a fresh uniform draw conditional on the first token. Compute the four colour-pair probabilities, both single-red probabilities and the chance of second red given first red. Does physical replacement justify multiplying the two red probabilities here? Explain which assumption from fresh repeated draws is missing. Hint for exercise 1 Separate the die branches. With probability 1/3 the colours must agree. With probability 2/3 the four colour pairs each have conditional chance 1/4. Include the chance of the first colour in the copying branch too. Full solution to exercise 1 Write A for first red and B for second red. The copying branch contributes (1/3)(1/2)=1/6 to red-red and 1/6 to blue-blue, and nothing to mixed pairs. The fresh branch contributes (2/3)(1/4)=1/6 to each of the four pairs. Thus red-red, red-blue, blue-red, blue-blue have probabilities 1/3,1/6,1/6,1/3. They sum to one. P(A)=1/3+1/6=1/2, and P(B)=1/3+1/6=1/2. But P(A ∩ B)=1/3 differs from their product 1/4, so these events are dependent. Also P(B | A)=(1/3)/(1/2)=2/3. Replacement restored the bag; the memory-dependent selection rule prevented the full procedure from being a fresh uniform draw conditional on the first selection. If the copying branch were removed and every second draw used the fresh uniform rule, each colour pair would have chance 1/4. For another sitting: three recording audits Take a break before this return if you can. Close earlier answers and your notes, then open only the prompt below. There is no enforced delay or hidden answer key: these are public self-study tasks. Record your explanation before using a hint; if you need one, record that too. The protocols are deliberately not labelled with their mathematical classification. Exercise 2. Audit all three records below as one comparison, using the shared hint and solution. Open the fresh recording-audit prompt Record I. Five labelled tokens comprise two gold and three silver. The first selection is uniform and its token is replaced. For every possible first selection, the second selection chooses each of the five labels with probability 1/5. Is the chance of two golds equal to the product of the two single-gold chances? Give the complete colour table and justify its row probabilities. Record II. Keep the five tokens and first selection, including replacement. If the first token is gold, choose the second uniformly from the two gold tokens; if it is silver, choose the second uniformly from the three silver tokens. Answer the same question. Can the single-gold chances distinguish Records I and II? Record III. A device chooses one of sixteen labelled tickets uniformly. In XYZ order its complete word counts are below. A technician proposes replacing this table by multiplying the three single-light probabilities. Decide whether that replacement gives the right chance for every word. Calculate all three two-light intersections and the all-three intersection; do not stop after one successful check. Record III: complete counts out of sixteen tickets XYZ Count 000 4 001 2 010 2 011 0 100 5 101 1 110 1 111 1 Finish with one sentence stating what these exact specifications establish and what a short run of observed records would leave uncertain. Hint for exercise 2 For Records I and II, condition on the first colour before adding over it; replacement by itself supplies no probability. For Record III, check that all counts total sixteen, sum the single-light and intersection counts, and compare each intersection with the corresponding product. One failed required equality is enough to reject the full product proposal. Full solution to exercise 2 Record I. The probability of a first gold is 2/5. The conditional second-gold chance is 2/5 after every possible first label, so gold-gold has chance 4/25. Gold-silver, silver-gold and silver-silver have chances 6/25,6/25,9/25. The two single-gold chances are both 2/5 and their product is 4/25: the events are independent under this specified rule. Record II. A first gold forces a second gold, and a first silver forces a second silver. The colour table in the same order is 2/5,0,0,3/5. Each single-gold chance remains 2/5, but the two-gold chance is 2/5, not 4/25. The events are dependent. The single-position probabilities and physical replacement do not distinguish these two procedures; the joint law does. Record III. The counts sum to sixteen. With A meaning X=1, B meaning Y=1 and C meaning Z=1, their counts are 8,4,4, so P(A)=1/2 and P(B)=P(C)=1/4. The two-light counts are 2,2,1: P(A ∩ B)=1/8=(1/2)(1/4), P(A ∩ C)=1/8=(1/2)(1/4), and P(B ∩ C)=1/16=(1/4)(1/4). All pairs pass. But the all-three chance is 1/16, twice the proposed product (1/2)(1/4)(1/4)=1/32. These events are pairwise independent and not mutually independent. The technician’s proposal fails already on word 111. Indeed, the combined clue A ∩ B gives P(C | A ∩ B)=(1/16)/(1/8)=1/2, while C alone has chance 1/4. These conclusions follow from the complete exact probability models given in the prompts. Counts in a short observed sample would instead be uncertain evidence about an unknown law; matching a few empirical products would not prove the underlying independence claim. Check the reasoning you actually wrote Self-study feedback; each row is a distinct reasoning check Evidence to look for If it is missing Outcomes and weights stated; each complete table totals one If you gave every different word equal weight, return to the ticket counts and count labelled tickets instead. Marginals and intersections computed from the same model If you mixed Record I’s product with Record II’s intersection, rebuild one full colour table before comparing. Every pair checked before a pairwise claim, and the triple checked separately If one successful equality became a claim about all three, list the four required equalities and check each. The selection mechanism explains the conclusion If “the token was replaced” was your whole reason, write the conditional second-selection rule after each first colour. Conditional fractions use a positive clue probability; model conclusions stay distinct from observations If zero triple mass made you call the combined clue impossible, calculate the pair-clue denominator. If a few observations became a proof, restate the exact-law assumption. Mark each applicable row as shown, needs repair, or used a hint. A correct classification without its counts and explanation needs repair. After comparing the answers, close them and reconstruct one failed calculation. These labels are for reflection; they are not a graded attempt, a credential or a measured learning outcome. Repair conditional fractions and evidence for two events Repair a conditional fraction. Work within one specified probability law. P(B | A)=P(A ∩ B)/P(A) requires P(A) to be positive. If P(A)=0, this ratio does not define P(B | A); a zero numerator does not repair the zero denominator. The product test separately compares P(A ∩ B) with P(A)P(B). Restored four-token bag. Let A mean first red and B mean second red. P(A)=1/2 and P(A ∩ B)=1/3, so P(B | A)=(1/3)/(1/2)=2/3. The denominator is positive. This differs from P(B)=1/2: after a first red, the copying branch increases the second-red chance. Record I. Let A mean first gold and B mean second gold. P(A)=2/5 and P(A ∩ B)=4/25, so P(B | A)=(4/25)/(2/5)=2/5. The denominator is positive. This equals P(B)=2/5 under this record's fresh uniform second-selection rule. Record II. Keep those gold events in this record's law. P(A)=2/5 and P(A ∩ B)=2/5, so P(B | A)=(2/5)/(2/5)=1. The denominator is positive. This differs from P(B)=2/5 because the second selection must have the first selection's colour. Repair an observation claim. These calculations follow exactly from the stipulated selection laws. A short observed run instead gives uncertain evidence about a law: a near equality of empirical products does not prove exact independence. An empirical conditional frequency divides the count of A ∩ B by the count of A only when that sample denominator is positive. If no A was observed, this empirical conditional fraction is undefined, not zero. A zero sample count does not establish P(A)=0: a finite run of independent repetitions of a model whose P(A) is strictly between zero and one can contain no A. Keep the model probabilities and sample frequencies distinct before revising your explanation. Keep the model attached to the multiplication Independence concerns specified events under a specified probability law. All pairs can pass while a three-event claim fails. Restoring a bag does not determine the next selection mechanism, and equal single-position chances do not settle a joint probability. Return to the original preparation and examples when the distinction needs another concrete pass. Once you can reconstruct both tables, use the binomial lesson to ask which full-sequence products its derivation needs.

title: A deck, a die, and the sample space
summary: List outcomes for a small game and distinguish an event from one elementary outcome.
text: The question and needed ideas A board game asks you to roll a blue die and a yellow die. You win if their total is seven. What exactly can happen before we call anything a “chance”? The first job is to choose an outcome description precise enough to settle the win condition. Recording the two colors in order works: (blue result, yellow result). Background capsule. A sample space , written Ω, is the set of all elementary outcomes in a specified experiment. An event is a subset of Ω. Here (2,5) is one outcome, whereas “total seven” is an event containing several outcomes. The bars |A| mean the number of members of A. Choosing a coarser description such as “the sum” is possible, but its members are generally not equally likely. Work through the model Worked example. For two fair, independent six-sided dice, Ω contains all 36 ordered pairs (i,j) with i and j each from 1 through 6. Every pair has chance 1/36: the blue die has six equally likely faces, and each yellow result has chance 1/6 regardless of blue. The winning event A contains (1,6), (2,5), (3,4), (4,3), (5,2), and (6,1). It has six members, giving P(A)=6/36=1/6. Here is the full grid: rows are blue results and columns yellow results. Each cell shows the total; a tick marks a winning pair. For seven, the winning cells form a descending diagonal. “Blue 1, yellow 6” is only one of six winning paths. A sum of seven has six pairs producing it, while a sum of two has just (1,1). Before changing the target to eight, predict whether more or fewer cells will match. Then count them. You can also switch the question to doubles or to “blue is greater than yellow.” The 36 possible pairs stay the same; the event being counted changes. If the game adds one reroll, specify when it may be used and whether the reroll replaces one die or both. That change creates a different experiment and sample space; the 1/6 calculation does not settle the new rule. The statement and its limits Read the counting rule in words Ω is the Greek letter omega, used here as a name for all possible outcomes. A names the event we want. The bars in | A | count its members; here they do not mean an absolute value. P ( A ) means “the probability of event A .” So the fraction says “number of matching outcomes divided by number of possible outcomes.” The equal-likelihood assumption is what makes counting enough. Exact statement. If Ω is finite and nonempty, and every elementary outcome has the same probability, then an event A has probability |A|/|Ω|. The disjoint elementary outcomes in A each contribute 1/|Ω|, so adding |A| identical contributions proves the formula. Independence of the dice is one route to equal pair probabilities, but the counting rule itself assumes equal pair probabilities directly. The total probabilities add to one because Ω contains |Ω| such outcomes. A useful check is P(Ω)=|Ω|/|Ω|=1 and P(∅)=0, where ∅ is the empty event with no outcomes. Partitioning Ω into A and its complement (everything outside A) also gives P(not A)=1−P(A), since their counts add to |Ω|. Now consider a bag with two red tokens and one blue token. If you treat “red” and “blue” as two equally likely elementary outcomes, you get the wrong answer 1/2. Label the physical tokens R1, R2 and B; these three have equal draw chances, and the red event contains two of them. Alternatively use the two color outcomes with unequal probabilities 2/3 and 1/3. The mathematical description must match the random procedure. P ( A ) = | A | | Ω | Try two cases Exercise 1. Roll two fair, independent colored dice. What is the chance that the first result is greater than the second? Hint for exercise 1 Count by the first die: how many smaller second results follow each first value? Full solution to exercise 1 For first values 1 through 6, the counts are 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5. Their sum is 15. Each of 36 ordered pairs has chance 1/36, so the event probability is 15/36=5/12. The six ties and 15 reverse-order pairs account for the remaining 21. Exercise 2. An ideal spinner lands uniformly by angle and has three sectors with angles 180°, 90°, and 90°. Is choosing one of three sector names uniformly a valid model? Find the chance of the largest sector. Hint for exercise 2 Compare angular sizes with the full 360° turn. Full solution to exercise 2 No. If the spinner lands uniformly by angle, sector names have probabilities 180/360, 90/360, and 90/360. The largest sector has probability 1/2. A three-name equiprobable sample space would incorrectly give 1/3 because the physical sectors have unequal size. What to carry forward The usable stopping point is to name Ω, name A as a subset, and justify equal likelihood before dividing counts. This lesson proves a finite counting rule, not a rule that every imaginable list of outcomes is uniform. The biased spinner is the failure case. Next, combine overlapping events without counting their shared outcomes twice.

title: Why two chances can overlap
summary: Use the addition rule to count overlapping events once.
text: The question and needed ideas A standard 52-card deck is shuffled, and one card is drawn. You win if it is red or a face card. Red includes hearts and diamonds; face cards are jacks, queens and kings. Adding 26 red cards to 12 face cards sounds plausible, but some red cards are face cards. A card can satisfy both win conditions. Background capsule. “Or” is inclusive here: one or both conditions suffice. A∪B is the union, the outcomes in at least one event. A∩B is the intersection, the outcomes in both. If A and B share no outcomes, they are disjoint , and their probabilities add directly. The fractions in this lesson use a uniformly shuffled deck, making each individual card equally likely. Work through the model Worked example. Let A be red and B be face. There are 26 red cards and 12 face cards. Six cards are both: J, Q and K in each of hearts and diamonds. The sum 26+12 counts these six twice. Remove one copy of the overlap: 26+12−6=32 cards. The winning chance is 32/52=8/13. A disjoint accounting of the winning cards Region Cards Red, not face 20 Both red and face 6 Face, not red 6 Neither 20 The table totals 52 and makes the 32 winners visible as 20+6+6. This partition is more reliable than a diagram whose overlapping areas have no exact scale. It also gives the complement: 20 losing cards, so 1−20/52=32/52. Another worked example: two badges. A box contains ten equally likely numbered tickets. Four tickets carry a star, five carry a circle, and two carry both badges. A ticket wins if it has either badge. Counting four plus five gives nine badge appearances, but the two double-badge tickets each appear twice. Subtract those two extra appearances to obtain seven winning tickets, so the chance is 7/10. The disjoint categories are two star-only, two both, three circle-only, and three neither. They total ten. If someone supplies only the two separate badge counts, the winning chance is not yet determined: the overlap is still needed. The statement and its limits Exact statement. For any two events A and B in one probability space, the union formula holds. Split A∪B into three disjoint pieces: A without B, A∩B, and B without A. Since probabilities of disjoint pieces add, their total equals P(A)+P(B)−P(A∩B). This is a proof from additivity, not a diagram-only argument. The same reasoning works with unequal outcome chances: replace counts by probability masses and partition the event in the same way. It does not require independence. Indeed, independence concerns whether P(A∩B)=P(A)P(B); it is a different condition from disjointness. In this deck example, A and B happen to be independent because (26/52)(12/52)=6/52, but that fact is accidental to these choices. Failure to subtract overlap can even produce a number above one. If A and B are both “card is red,” naive addition gives 1/2+1/2=1 while their union is merely the red event with chance 1/2. The intersection is the same red event, and the formula returns 1/2. P ( A ∪ B ) = P ( A ) + P ( B ) − P ( A ∩ B ) One way to audit the card arithmetic is to count the complement first. A card loses only when it is black and not a face card. Each black suit has ten numbered or ace cards, giving twenty losers and thirty-two winners. This independent route agrees with the three-region partition. When two counting methods disagree, the usual culprit is a shared card or a missing category. The addition rule does not require a deck: a school club could count members who play chess or paint by the same disjoint-region argument, provided each person is counted once in the total. Try two cases Exercise 1. Roll one fair die. Find P(even or at least 5). Hint for exercise 1 List each set and its shared member. Full solution to exercise 1 Even is {2,4,6}, and at least 5 is {5,6}. The overlap is {6}. Their union is {2,4,5,6}, so its chance is (3+2−1)/6=4/6=2/3. Direct enumeration checks the subtraction. Exercise 2. A student says, “If two events are disjoint, they are independent.” Test this with events A={1} and B={2} on a fair six-sided die. Hint for exercise 2 Compare P(A∩B) with P(A)P(B). Full solution to exercise 2 The events cannot occur together, so P(A∩B)=0. Yet P(A)P(B)=(1/6)(1/6)=1/36. The equality required for independence fails. Positive-probability disjoint events are dependent: learning A rules out B. What to carry forward For two events, ask first what “or” includes, then mark the shared outcomes once. The formula does not tell you the overlap automatically; you must calculate or model it. Conditioning asks a different question: after learning one event occurred, which denominator remains?

title: The clue changes the denominator
summary: Condition on events, then compare truthful reporting rules that weight the same possible dice pairs differently.
text: The question and needed ideas A mystery card is drawn uniformly from a standard 52-card deck. Before you see it, the chance that it is a queen is 4/52. Someone then tells you it is a heart. The card is still hidden, but the information changes the relevant group of cards. How likely is a queen now? Background capsule. P(A|B), read “probability of A given B,” is the probability of A after restricting attention to outcomes where B happened. The vertical bar is not division. A∩B means both conditions hold. The conditional fraction uses the probability of B as its denominator; it is meaningful only if B has positive probability. Work through the model Worked example. This first model conditions on the event that the card is a heart, keeping every heart with its original weight; a rule for choosing which clue to announce is introduced later. Let A mean queen and B mean heart. There are 13 hearts. Exactly one is a queen, so among the 13 cards still possible after the clue, one is favorable: P(A|B)=1/13. The original probability 4/52 also equals 1/13, but that coincidence is due to the deck's symmetry. A different clue can change the number dramatically. Suppose the clue is “face card” instead. Twelve cards remain possible and four are queens. Then P(queen|face)=4/12=1/3. The cards outside the clue were removed from the denominator. The queen event did not physically change; the information narrowed the possible cases. Using the original full-deck probabilities gives the same result: P(queen and face)=4/52, P(face)=12/52, and their ratio is (4/52)/(12/52)=4/12. This calculation is useful when outcomes are not naturally counted as equally likely. See the new denominator Now roll a blue die and a yellow die fairly and independently. We condition on the event “at least one die shows six.” This means keeping all pairs that meet that condition, rather than adding a rule that selects or reports particular rolls. Predict the chance of a total of seven before counting the grid. Explain the dice count The six pairs in blue’s row 6 and the six in yellow’s column 6 share (6,6), so only 6 + 6 − 1 = 11 pairs remain. Two of them, (1,6) and (6,1), total seven. The conditional probability is 2/11. Dividing by 36 would keep outcomes the clue has ruled out; dividing by 12 would count (6,6) twice. Try the clue “blue is even” with the same target. Eighteen pairs remain and three total seven, giving 3/18 = 1/6. A clue can change the denominator without changing this event’s probability. The dice were independent before the clue; after the “at least one six” clue, learning that blue is not six forces yellow to be six. Do not assume independence still holds after conditioning. The statement and its limits Exact statement. For events A and B with P(B)>0, conditional probability is defined by the displayed ratio. In a finite equally likely model, it equals |A∩B|/|B| because dividing (|A∩B|/|Ω|) by (|B|/|Ω|) cancels the original total. The new denominator is precisely the number of B outcomes. This derivation explains the card count and extends the idea to models with unequal masses. Rearranging gives the multiplication rule P(A∩B)=P(A|B)P(B). For the queen and face clue, (1/3)(12/52)=4/52. Reversing the condition changes the question: P(face|queen)=1 because every queen is a face card, while P(queen|face)=1/3. The two values generally differ. The boundary is essential. If a six-sided die is known to show seven, B has probability zero in the stated model. P(A|B) is undefined, and no simple “new denominator” exists. One must revise the model, perhaps by allowing a misreported die, before assigning a chance. P ( A | B ) = P ( A ∩ B ) P ( B ) P ( B ) > 0 Conditioning can be checked by reconstructing a full partition. For the face-card clue, the twelve face cards divide into four queens and eight non-queens. The conditional probabilities 4/12 and 8/12 add to one. The other forty cards have no place in this conditional denominator, although they still matter for the probability that the clue itself occurs. This separation is especially useful when comparing two clues: “face” has chance 12/52, while “heart” has chance 13/52; each clue creates its own group of survivors and its own conditional distribution. How did this report reach you? The first dice grid conditions on an event: keep every pair containing a six. Now receive the truthful sentence “at least one die is six” from a specified reporter. Its meaning excludes pairs without a six, but its chance of being sent may vary among the remaining pairs. To find the posterior distribution, we need the reporting rule as well as the sentence. The dice are still fair and independent. In both protocols, also generate an independent fair selector, blue or yellow. That makes 36×2=72 equally likely prior states, each a triple (blue face, yellow face, selector). The receiver knows the protocol and hears only the sentence; neither faces nor selector identity are revealed. Scan both. Inspect both dice and send the report whenever at least one is six. Otherwise send no report. The selector is ignored. Select one. Inspect only the die named by the independent selector. Send the report if that die is six; otherwise send no report, even if the unselected die is six. Do not reveal which die was selected. Both reports are truthful: a reported six guarantees at least one actual six. Truthfulness alone does not give all compatible pairs the same posterior weight. Predict whether changing the protocol will preserve 2/11. Then inspect (1,6), (6,6), and a pair without a six. The face controls inspect possible worlds; they do not change the prior or supply an observed roll. The same 72-state prior gives different report events In the scan protocol, each of the eleven pairs containing a six has two selector states that report. There are 22 reported triples. The two pairs totaling seven, (1,6) and (6,1), supply four of them. Thus P(total seven | report)=4/22=2/11, agreeing with the original event-only grid. In the select-one protocol there are six reports when blue is selected and six when yellow is selected: twelve triples altogether. Only (6,1,blue) and (1,6,yellow) also total seven, giving 2/12=1/6. A particular one-six pair, such as (1,6), reports only for one selector, while (6,6) reports for both. After receiving this report, the ten one-six pairs each have probability 1/12 and the double-six pair has probability 2/12=1/6. The same eleven pair values remain possible, but they are not equally likely. The selector was independent of the dice before reporting. Conditioning on the report couples them: if the pair is (1,6) in the selected protocol, the selector must have been yellow. We average over that hidden selector to obtain the posterior over pairs. Counting all 72 prior triples equally is valid; counting the eleven posterior pair values equally is not valid for this protocol. Weight a world by its chance of producing the report Let W be a finite-valued hidden world, with prior probability p(w). Let R be the event that this exact report is received. Write r(w)=P(R | W=w), its reporting likelihood, for worlds with positive prior probability. The multiplication rule gives P(W=w and R)=p(w)r(w). Summing these joint probabilities gives Z=P(R)=Σ_u p(u)r(u). If Z>0, P ( W = w | R ) = p ( w ) r ( w ) ∑ u p ( u ) r ( u ) For our dice worlds w=(blue,yellow), every prior p(w) is 1/36. Scan likelihood is 1 on any pair with a six and 0 elsewhere. Select-one likelihood is 1/2 on exactly-one-six pairs, 1 on (6,6), and 0 elsewhere. The denominator normalizes these weights. A likelihood such as 1/2 is a chance of sending the report from a fixed world; it is not that world's posterior probability. Exactly when can the report be replaced by its truthful content? Let U be the event described by the sentence. Assume the report is truthful, so r(w)=0 outside U, and assume Z=P(R)>0. Then P(U)>0. The full posterior given R equals the prior conditioned just on U if and only if r(w) is the same positive constant for every world in U having positive prior probability. To prove sufficiency, let that constant be c. Then Z=cP(U), so p(w)r(w)/Z=p(w)/P(U) for w in U and both posteriors are zero outside. Conversely, equality at each positive-prior w in U gives p(w)r(w)/Z=p(w)/P(U). Cancel p(w)>0 to obtain r(w)=Z/P(U), the same positive number for each such world. Zero-prior worlds impose no restriction. If Z=0, the received report cannot be conditioned on by this ratio. This compares every world, hence every event in the full posterior. Agreement for one target event can occur accidentally even when the likelihood is not constant; exercise 4 provides an example. The general observation-mechanism criterion appears in Grünwald and Halpern, Updating Probabilities , Theorem 3.2 (UAI 2002, printed page 190). The finite algebra here proves the special statement we use. The card and original dice counts remain valid for their stated event-conditioning models. If an actual person chooses which truthful clue to announce, that selection is an additional part of the experiment. With an unspecified rule, a truthful sentence alone need not determine a unique posterior. Our two rules make that difference exact without inventing any observed evidence. Try the event and the reporting rule Exercise 1. A fair die is rolled. Given an even result, what is the chance the result is at least four? Hint for exercise 1 Write the outcomes left after the even clue. Full solution to exercise 1 The clue leaves {2,4,6}. The favorable outcomes are {4,6}; hence P(at least four|even)=2/3. In the formula, the intersection has chance 2/6 and even has chance 3/6, yielding (2/6)/(3/6)=2/3. Exercise 2. A bag holds three red and two blue tokens. Is P(red|blue)=P(blue|red) when one token is drawn? Explain. Hint for exercise 2 Can one drawn token have both colors? Full solution to exercise 2 For this single draw, red and blue are disjoint, so both conditional probabilities are zero; each denominator is positive. That equality is a special case, not a general symmetry. If the events were “red” and “striped” and some red tokens were striped, the two denominators could differ. The question must specify the event model before swapping the condition. Exercise 3. A different truthful sentence. Change the report to “at least one die is even.” Keep fair independent dice and an independent fair selector. The scan rule reports iff either die is even. The selected rule reports iff the chosen die is even, concealing its identity. Under each rule, find the report probability and P(total seven | report). Find the posterior probabilities of the individual pairs (1,2) and (2,2). Work from the 72 states or likelihoods; the explorer only covers six-reports. Hint for exercise 3 There are nine odd-odd pairs, eighteen pairs with exactly one even face, and nine even-even pairs. Every total-seven pair has exactly one even face. Each pair has two prior selector states. Full solution to exercise 3 Scan keeps 36−9=27 pairs, each with two reporting selectors, so 54/72=3/4 of prior triples report. All six total-seven pairs contribute both selectors, giving 12/54=2/9. Every compatible pair, including (1,2) and (2,2), then has posterior 1/27. Selected reports for three even blue faces times six yellow faces, plus three even yellow faces times six blue faces: 18+18=36 triples. Its report probability is 36/72=1/2. The six total-seven pairs each report for just their even selector, giving 6/36=1/6. The likelihood for (1,2) is 1/2, giving posterior 1/36; the likelihood for (2,2) is 1, giving 2/36=1/18. The posterior check is eighteen single-even pairs times 1/36 plus nine double-even pairs times 1/18, totaling 1. Exercise 4. One matching answer does not identify a posterior. Keep exercise 3's even-report protocols. Let A be “the blue face is either 1 or 2.” Compute P(A | report) under each. Does agreement show that reporting can be replaced by conditioning only on “at least one even”? Explain using one individual pair. Hint for exercise 4 When blue is 1, three yellow faces are compatible. When blue is 2, all six are compatible. In the selected protocol, count reporting selectors separately for the two blue values. Full solution to exercise 4 Scan gives nine compatible pairs for A out of 27, so P(A | report)=1/3. Selected gives three reporting triples when blue is 1 (yellow must be even and selected), and nine when blue is 2 (six with blue selected, three with yellow selected). Thus P(A | report)=12/36=1/3 as well. This particular event agrees, but the full posteriors differ: (2,2) has probability 1/27 under scan and 1/18 under selected. Nonconstant likelihood fails the full-posterior criterion despite this accidental event equality. What to carry forward Conditional probability uses a positive-probability event and the correct prior weights. Conditioning on a truthful report eliminates incompatible worlds and weights compatible worlds by their chances of producing that report. Constant reporting likelihood makes event-only conditioning valid for the full posterior; truthfulness or one matching event probability does not establish that condition. Specify the prior, any hidden selection and the reporting rule before counting. Continue to Bayes’ update to reason backward from an observed clue to a hidden cause.

title: A test for independence, not a feeling
summary: Check independence through an equality and show how sampling without replacement breaks it.
text: Does the first colour change the second chance? Draw twice uniformly from three red and two blue tokens. Does the first colour inform the second? Specify whether the first token is replaced and the bag mixed between draws. Background capsule. An event is a collection of outcomes. Let A mean “first draw is red” and B mean “second draw is red.” We call them independent if learning whether the first event occurred leaves the chance of the second unchanged. A uniform draw means each token currently in the bag has the same chance of being chosen. Read the symbols in words P ( A ) is the probability of A. A ∩ B means both events occur, here red twice. The bar in P(B | A) reads “given”: second red given first red. Juxtaposed probabilities are multiplied. Before the first-colour clue the probability is unconditional; after it, conditional. Keep the two procedures separate With replacement. Put the first token back and mix. The bag again has three red tokens out of five, whatever the first colour was. A fresh uniform draw gives P ( B | A ) = 3/5. The chance of red twice is (3/5) × (3/5) = 9/25. Without replacement. Keep the first token out. After a red, two red tokens remain among four, so P ( B | A ) = 2/4 = 1/2. The chance of red twice is (3/5) × (2/4) = 3/10. After a blue instead, three of the four remaining tokens are red: a different second-red chance, 3/4. Worked example. The four colour sequences below cover every possible result. They do not have equal chances. Each row multiplies the chance of its first colour by the chance of its second colour after that first draw. Two uniform draws from three red and two blue tokens First, then second Put back Keep out Red, red (3/5) × (3/5) = 9/25 (3/5) × (2/4) = 6/20 Red, blue (3/5) × (2/5) = 6/25 (3/5) × (2/4) = 6/20 Blue, red (2/5) × (3/5) = 6/25 (2/5) × (3/4) = 6/20 Blue, blue (2/5) × (2/5) = 4/25 (2/5) × (1/4) = 2/20 Check each column totals one: 25/25 or 20/20. To find the second-red chance before learning the first colour, add the red-red and blue-red rows. With replacement it is (9+6)/25 = 3/5. Without replacement it is (6+6)/20 = 3/5 too. Both procedures give unconditional second-red probability 3/5. Only the fresh-uniform replacement procedure makes these events independent: without replacement, a first red changes that chance to 1/2. Equal probabilities at two positions do not establish independence. A test that settles the question Exact statement. Events A and B are independent exactly when the chance of both equals the product of their individual chances: P ( A ∩ B ) = P ( A ) P ( B ) In both token procedures, the individual chances are 3/5 and 3/5, whose product is 9/25. With replacement the chance of both is 9/25: the equality holds. Without replacement it is 3/10, which differs from 9/25: the equality fails. For P(A)>0, P(B|A)=P(A∩B)/P(A). Dividing the product equality by P(A) gives P(B|A)=P(B); multiplying recovers it. Reversing A and B gives the corresponding equivalence when P(B)>0. Replacement here includes a fresh uniform draw from the restored bag. Physical replacement alone, particularly without mixing, does not specify that rule. Independence belongs to specified events under a specified probability model; unrelated-sounding descriptions do not establish it. Disjoint events share no outcomes. On a fair die, “one” and “six” are disjoint but dependent: one rules out six, with joint chance 0 versus product (1/6)(1/6)=1/36. Positive-probability disjoint events cannot be independent. Why use the product definition for a zero-chance event? If P ( A ) = 0, the chance of A ∩ B is also zero. The product equality holds for any B . But the conditional fraction would divide by zero, so P ( B | A ) is undefined in this finite model. The product definition covers this edge case without that division. Optional investigation: can every pair pass while the triple fails? Three events require another question The two-event test above settles exactly the two-event question. Now consider three events A, B and C. They are pairwise independent when each of the pairs A,B; A,C; and B,C passes its product test. They are mutually independent when those three equalities hold and the triple also satisfies P(A∩B∩C)=P(A)P(B)P(C). More generally, mutual independence requires the product equality for every nonempty selection of the events. A triple equality alone does not replace the pair tests. Extra background. A bit takes values 0 and 1. Let A={X=1}, B={Y=1}, C={Z=1}. A word such as 101 records the three bits in order. The joint law assigns probabilities to all eight words. A one-bit marginal sums words with that bit fixed; a pair table sums over the third bit. These are exact model probabilities. A classical parity construction Choose X and Y as two independent fair bits, so their four pairs are equally likely. Set Z to 1 exactly when X and Y differ: Z=X xor Y. The resulting complete words are 000, 011, 101 and 110, each with probability 1/4; the other four words have probability zero. This is the classical pairwise-but-not-mutual parity example, also developed using two dice in the MIT source below. Check all three pairs. Reading XY across those four words gives 00,01,10,11. Reading XZ gives 00,01,11,10, and reading YZ gives 00,11,01,10. Each pair therefore has four cells of probability 1/4. Each individual bit is fair, so every pair cell equals (1/2)(1/2). Nevertheless P(X=1,Y=1,Z=1)=0, whereas the product of the three one-bit probabilities is 1/8. Every pair passes; the triple fails. Predict before inspecting. Does one bit leaving Z fair imply two bits do? Do matching one-bit and pair laws force matching count laws? Compare the same word under XOR and independent fair bits; which probabilities fail to factor? Why the combined clue matters Pairwise independence gives P(Z=1|X=1)=1/2 and P(Z=1|Y=1)=1/2. But the combined event X=1,Y=1 has probability 1/4, and XOR makes Z=0 there. Hence P(Z=1|X=1,Y=1)=0. The conditioning event is possible even though the triple 111 is impossible. Independence from either clue separately does not imply independence from their combined information. For binary X,Y,Z, mutual independence of A,B,C is equivalent to factorization of every word probability. Complements follow by subtraction: P(110)=P(A∩B)−P(A∩B∩C)=P(A)P(B)(1−P(C)); P(100)=P(A)−P(A∩B)−P(A∩C)+P(A∩B∩C)=P(A)(1−P(B))(1−P(C)). Permutation gives the other cases, and inclusion-exclusion gives P(000)=(1−P(A))(1−P(B))(1−P(C)). Conversely, summing factorized words gives the pair and triple equalities. The independent preset assigns 1/8 per word; XOR does not. Which conclusions survive the weaker assumption? Let K=X+Y+Z count the ones. XOR permits only K=0 with probability 1/4 and K=2 with probability 3/4. Independent fair bits instead give probabilities (1,3,3,1)/8 for K=0,1,2,3. Both counts have mean 3/2 and variance 3/4. These are different count laws with the same first two moments. The mean needs no independence: linearity gives E[K]=E[X]+E[Y]+E[Z]=3/2. Since each bit squares to itself, K²=X+Y+Z+2XY+2XZ+2YZ. Pairwise independence is enough to give E[XY]=E[XZ]=E[YZ]=1/4, hence E[K²]=3/2+2(3/4)=3 and Var(K)=3−(3/2)²=3/4. Those pair products do not determine P(111) or all the individual word probabilities. The binomial derivation uses the stronger full-sequence product rule: a specified word with k successes has probability pᵏ(1−p)³⁻ᵏ, and adding the words with the same k gives the count law. Matching a mean, variance, or even the whole binomial count law does not establish independence of the underlying trials. A complete binomial count can still hide dependent trials Assign lexicographic words 000,001,010,011,100,101,110,111 the probabilities (1,1,0,2,2,0,1,1)/8. Each bit is fair. Adding by number of ones gives the exact binomial count probabilities (1,3,3,1)/8. But P(X=1,Z=1)=P(101)+P(111)=1/8, not 1/4, so those two bits are dependent. Even the triple probability is 1/8 here: the triple-product equality alone is insufficient. The ordering information discarded by K matters. Source scope. MIT 18.05, Spring 2022, Problem Set 3 solutions, problem 1(a)–(b) gives the pairwise/mutual definitions, classical parity counterexample and warning that a triple equality alone is insufficient. The inspector, count comparison, converse counterexample and biased-family derivation are original. No observed sample proves independence here. Try two cases Exercise 1. A fair six-sided die is rolled twice independently. Let A be “first roll is even” and B be “second roll exceeds four.” Check the product equality. Hint for exercise 1 Count choices for each roll separately. Exceeds four means five or six. Full solution to exercise 1 A has chance 3/6 = 1/2 and B has chance 2/6 = 1/3. Of 36 equally likely ordered pairs, 3 × 2 = 6 satisfy both. Thus P ( A ∩ B ) = 6/36 = 1/6 = (1/2) × (1/3). The events are independent under the stated independent-roll assumption. Exercise 2. One fair die is rolled. Are “even” and “greater than three” independent? Predict first, then list the overlap. Hint for exercise 2 List both sets and count their shared faces. Compare that probability with the product of the two separate probabilities. Full solution to exercise 2 Even is {2,4,6}, and greater than three is {4,5,6}; each has chance 1/2. Their overlap is {4,6}, chance 2/6 = 1/3. Since 1/3 differs from (1/2) × (1/2) = 1/4, they are dependent. Learning “even” makes “greater than three” have chance 2/3 instead of 1/2. A changed task: pairwise independent bits with chance one third Exercise 3. Now X,Y,Z each have success probability 1/3, and every pair is independent. No exchangeability assumption is supplied. Write t=P(111). (a) Derive all eight word probabilities from these constraints, and find the full possible range of t. (b) Derive the law, mean and variance of K=X+Y+Z. At t=0, realize the model using nine equally likely tickets and compare its count law with Binomial(3,1/3). (c) Find exactly when the bits are mutually independent within this constrained family . (d) Compute P(Z=1|X=1,Y=1) throughout the family and compare it with conditioning on X alone. This task is outside the fair-source controls. Hint for exercise 3 Every pair has both-success probability 1/9. Subtract t to get each two-success word, then use a one-bit success probability to get each one-success word. Normalize to get 000. Require every mass to be nonnegative. Add the rows with the same success count; for moments, use K²=X+Y+Z+2XY+2XZ+2YZ. For mutual independence, 111 must have probability (1/3)³, and all the other words must agree too. The combined conditioning event always has probability 1/9. Full solution to exercise 3 (a) Derive, rather than assume, the symmetry. Pairwise independence gives P(X=1,Y=1)=P(X=1,Z=1)=P(Y=1,Z=1)=1/9. Removing 111 leaves P(110)=P(101)=P(011)=1/9−t. For example, the X-success marginal gives P(100)=1/3−P(101)−P(110)−P(111)=1/9+t. The other two marginals similarly give P(010)=P(001)=1/9+t. Normalization leaves P(000)=1/3−t. Thus the constraints themselves force the equal masses in each success-count class: Each listed probability belongs to one individual word, not the entire class Word or class Probability of each word Number of such words 000 1/3−t 1 001,010,100 1/9+t 3 011,101,110 1/9−t 3 111 t 1 Nonnegativity of 111 and the two-success words requires 0≤t≤1/9. These bounds also make every other mass nonnegative, with total 1. They suffice: each pair table in 00,01,10,11 order is (4,2,2,1)/9, the Bernoulli(1/3) marginal products. For example XY=00 has mass (1/3−t)+(1/9+t)=4/9 and XY=11 has (1/9−t)+t=1/9. The displayed words give the remaining cells and pairs. (b) Count and moments. Grouping words gives P(K=0,1,2,3)=(1/3−t,1/3+3t,1/3−3t,t). Linearity gives E[K]=3(1/3)=1; the three pair expectations 1/9 give E[K²]=1+2(3/9)=5/3, hence Var(K)=2/3 throughout. At t=0, nine equally likely tickets realize the law: three labelled 000 and one each of 001,010,100,011,101,110; none is 111. K is uniform on {0,1,2}, unlike Binomial(3,1/3)'s law (8,12,6,1)/27, despite matching mean 1 and variance 2/3. (c) Full independence within this family. Necessarily t=P(111)=(1/3)³=1/27. Conversely this value gives masses 8/27 for 000, 4/27 per one-success word, 2/27 per two-success word and 1/27 for 111. Each factors as (1/3)ᵏ(2/3)³⁻ᵏ, proving mutual independence. Within this constrained family, K is binomial exactly at this same t, since P(K=3)=t. The earlier counterexample prevents extending that converse to arbitrary trial laws. (d) One clue versus two. Pairwise independence gives P(Z=1|X=1)=1/3. The combined clue X=1,Y=1 has probability 1/9>0 throughout, giving P(Z=1|X=1,Y=1)=9t. This ranges from 0 to 1 with fixed marginals, pair tables and count moments: it is 1/3 at t=1/27, forces Z=0 at t=0, and Z=1 at t=1/9. These endpoint conditionals remain defined because their clue has positive probability. One question to take away Check independence by comparing the joint probability with the product of marginals in one model. Reconstruct why the bag's second-red marginal stays 3/5 without replacement. The binomial model needs independence across full trial sequences, beyond one successful pair test.

title: Fair games and expected score
summary: Build a finite weighted mean, then optionally investigate why almost-sure stopping need not preserve it.
text: Can an average be a score nobody gets? Roll a fair die for paper points: six earns eight, odd faces earn two, and other even faces earn zero. Averaging only eight and zero omits a score and its frequency. Write the reward for each face before calculating. Background capsule. A random variable assigns a numerical score to an outcome: here a reward to a die face. Several faces may share a score. Its distribution lists the scores and probabilities. Expected value is their probability-weighted average, which need not be obtainable in one play. A name for the average Write the score as X and its expectation as E[X], “expectation of X.” Lower-case x names a possible score, such as 0, 2 or 8; P(X=x) is its probability. Negative scores represent losses. Build the average from the six faces List the scores. Faces 1 through 6 earn 2, 0, 2, 0, 2, 8. All six faces have equal chances, so their ordinary average is (2 + 0 + 2 + 0 + 2 + 8)/6 = 14/6. Group equal scores. Zero occurs on two faces; two points occurs on three; eight points occurs on one. Their probabilities are 2/6, 3/6 and 1/6, which add to one. Weight each score by its chance. Multiply each score by its probability, then add the contributions below.
