The result is 14/6 = 7/3 points, about 2.33. Score contributions in the carnival game Score Die faces Chance Score × chance 0 2, 4 2/6 0 2 1, 3, 5 3/6 6/6 8 6 1/6 8/6 Worked example. No play scores 7/3 points. Two points is the most likely score, but 7/3 is the mean. Those answer different questions. For 60 independent plays under this same model, the expected total is 60 × 7/3 = 140 points. An actual total may differ; the calculation does not promise a particular sequence of rolls. Averaging score labels gives (0+2+8)/3=10/3, incorrectly assigning equal chances to unequal-frequency scores. With a biased die, even the six-face average fails; use the actual face probabilities. The general rule, read slowly Exact statement. For a random variable with finitely many possible values, its expected value is the sum of each value multiplied by its probability: E [ X ] = ∑ x x P ( X = x ) The symbol ∑ means add, visiting each distinct score x once. Here it gives 0P(X=0)+2P(X=2)+8P(X=8), the table's last column. Unequal probabilities are allowed; equal elementary-outcome chances are unnecessary. Changing every score has a predictable effect. If each play costs two points, subtract two from every payoff. The new mean is the old mean minus two: 7/3 − 2 = 1/3 point. If every payoff doubles, its mean doubles too. In symbols, E [ aX + b ] = aE [ X ] + b , where a and b are fixed numbers. Why does changing the scores work this way? Replace each score x by ax + b in the weighted sum. Distributing gives a sum of ax × its probability and a sum of b × its probability. Pull the fixed a out of the first sum to get aE [ X ]. The second sum is b times all the probabilities added together, which is b × 1. Adding the two parts gives the rule. For finite scores on one experiment, E[X+Y]=E[X]+E[Y]. Weight the combined score at each elementary outcome by its probability, then split each contribution into X and Y parts. Their sums are the individual means. Independence is unnecessary, as exercise 2 demonstrates. If “fair” means zero expected net points, entry cost must equal expected reward. A mean reward alone specifies neither that cost nor reward variability. The optional investigation removes the fixed last toss. It uses geometric series and introduces martingales. Optional investigation: can a fair process finish at one? A paper-score model with a stopping rule Toss an independent fair coin repeatedly for imaginary points, starting at 0. On toss k, add 2 k−1 for heads or subtract it for tails; stop at the first head. Thus amounts begin 1,2,4,…, chosen from past tosses before seeing the next result. Neither amounts nor possible negative scores are bounded. Let T be the index of the first head. Let G n be the accumulated score after at most n tosses, keeping the score fixed after the first head. Thus G 0 =0. For example, H finishes at 1; TH finishes at −1+2=1; TTH finishes at −1−2+4=1. If all of the first n tosses are tails, the current score is −(1+2+⋯+2 n−1 )=1−2 n . Predict first. At a cap of four tosses, what are the two possible scores? If you replace four by twenty, does the negative branch's contribution to the mean become negligible? Keep its probability, score and probability-weighted contribution in separate columns. Two finite facts, then an infinite conclusion The stopped score is a martingale. This means it is integrable at each fixed time and, given the whole history so far, its next conditional mean is its current value. If a head has already occurred, the next score stays 1. Otherwise, after n tails, the next two equally likely scores are 1 and 1−2 n+1 . Their average is 1−2 n , the current score. At any fixed n there are only finitely many scores, so integrability holds. Iterating this one-step equality gives E [ G n ]=0. The stopping time is almost surely finite and has finite mean. The event T > n is exactly n initial tails, with probability 2 −n . These probabilities tend to 0, so P ( T <∞)=1. Also P ( T = t )=2 −t for t ≥1. Counting one unit for each toss that is needed gives E [ T ]=∑ n≥0 P ( T > n )=1+1/2+1/4+⋯=2. All terms in this tail sum are nonnegative. The terminal score is 1 almost surely. A first head at time t adds 2 t−1 after total previous subtraction 2 t−1 −1. Therefore G T =1 on every finite stopping path. Set its value arbitrarily, say 0, on the probability-zero infinite all-tail sequence. The terminal score is integrable and E [ G T ]=1. Almost-sure stopping gives G K →G T almost surely as the deterministic cap K increases. This does not imply convergence of expectations. The exact place where the limiting argument fails At any fixed cap K , the score is 1 with probability 1−2 −K , and 1−2 K with probability 2 −K . The second branch includes paths whose first head comes later; it has not been discarded. The two contributions to the mean cancel: E [ G K ] = ( 1 − 2 − K ) + ( 1 − 2 K ) 2 − K = 0 The rare branch has probability tending to 0 but magnitude tending to infinity. Its negative contribution tends to −1. More decisively, on T ≤ K the current and terminal scores agree; on T > K they differ by exactly 2 K almost surely. The assigned value on the probability-zero infinite all-tail sequence does not affect an expectation. Hence, even at K =0, E [ | G K − G T | ] = 2 K 2 − K = 1 The mean absolute error never shrinks. Thus the convergence is not in L 1 , which means convergence in mean absolute error. In particular, E [lim G K ]=1 while lim E [ G K ]=0. One cannot interchange expectation and this limit. Which optional-stopping assumptions fail? For martingales, sufficient optional-stopping hypotheses include a bounded stopping time; an almost-surely finite stop with a common process bound; finite E[T] with uniformly bounded increments; or uniform integrability of the stopped family. These are alternative sufficient conditions for equality of initial and stopped expectations. No deterministic bound holds: P(T>K)>0 for every K. Scores 1−2 K have no common bound. After n unresolved tails, the next increment has magnitude 2 n , also unbounded. Neither E[T]=2 nor terminal-score integrability supplies the missing hypothesis. Uniform integrability means that the expected absolute contribution from scores above a sufficiently high magnitude cutoff can be made small uniformly over all caps . It fails here. For any cutoff C >1, choose larger and larger K with 2 K −1> C . The no-head branch alone contributes (2 K −1)2 −K =1−2 −K to that absolute tail expectation, approaching 1. There is also no single integrable random variable dominating every | G K |; such a bound would give convergence of expectations by dominated convergence, contrary to the exact calculation. Even the unconditional means of absolute increments are bounded: E | G n+1 − G n |=2 −n 2 n =1. This is weaker than a common bound on their conditional means given the past, which equal 2 n on the unresolved history. It is not the conditional-increment hypothesis in that more general stopping theorem. Bounded stopping gives mean 0 at every finite cap. Passing to the unbounded stop fails without tail control. In the fair-walk lesson , increments are bounded but mean absorption time is infinite; here mean stopping time is finite but increments grow. Check the actual hypotheses in each case. Try two cases Exercise 1. A game gives 5 points with chance 1/4 and loses 1 point otherwise. Find its expected score. Then subtract a two-point entry fee. Can either mean occur as a single-play net score? Hint for exercise 1 The remaining chance is 3/4. Use −1 for the loss. A fixed fee is subtracted on every outcome. Full solution to exercise 1 The mean before the fee is 5 × (1/4) + (−1) × (3/4) = 1/2 point. After the fee it is 1/2 − 2 = −3/2 points. You can check directly: net scores are 3 and −3, so their mean is 3 × (1/4) + (−3) × (3/4) = −3/2. Neither mean is an available single-play score. Exercise 2. Roll one fair die. Let X be its face number and let Y be seven minus that number. Knowing X determines Y , so these scores are dependent. Find the means of X , Y and their sum. Does dependence break the addition rule? Hint for exercise 2 In face order, Y takes values 6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1. What is X + Y on every roll? Full solution to exercise 2 Both scores have mean (1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 6)/6 = 21/6 = 7/2. Their sum is always 7, so its mean is 7 too. Thus E [ X + Y ] = 7 = 7/2 + 7/2. Dependence does not break addition. For example, learning X = 1 forces Y = 6, but the weighted sums still add. Optional tasks: audit the cap, then change the growth rule Three tasks for the stopping investigation Task A: two meanings of “short”. At cap K =3, find the exact score law, expected number of tosses used and expected total of the amounts assigned to those tosses. An amount is counted positively whether the toss adds or subtracts it. Why can the first expectation stay below 2 as the second grows without bound? Hint for task A The third toss is used only after two tails. Count amounts 1, 2 and 4 with their respective probabilities of being used. Full solution to task A The score is 1 with probability 7/8 and −7 with probability 1/8, so its mean is 0. The mean toss count is 1+1/2+1/4=7/4. The mean total amount is 1×1+2×(1/2)+4×(1/4)=3. More generally, toss k is used with probability 2 −(k−1) . Each used amount has expected contribution 2 k−1 2 −(k−1) =1, so the mean total through cap K is K . In contrast, the mean toss count is 2(1−2 −K )<2. Time and score magnitude are different quantities. Task B: change the mathematics. Keep independent fair tosses and stop at the first head, but replace doubling by growth factor 3/2: amounts 1, 3/2, 9/4, …. Rational paper scores are allowed. Derive the score at the first head. What is the probability that the terminal score is positive? Find its mean and explain why it exists. Does the terminal mean still differ from every capped mean? Hint for task B For a =3/2, the subtraction before toss t is (1+ a +⋯+ a t−2 )=2( a t−1 −1), including a zero empty sum when t =1. The first-head probabilities are still 2 −t . Sum a geometric series with ratio 3/4. Full solution to task B The terminal score is H T =2−(3/2) T−1 . The first three possible values are 1, 1/2 and −1/4; later values are more negative. Thus positivity means T ≤2 and has probability 1/2+1/4=3/4. Also E [(3/2) T−1 ]=(1/2)∑ j≥0 (3/4) j =2. The bound | H T |≤2+(3/2) T−1 proves integrability, so subtraction of these expectations is legitimate and E [ H T ]=0. Every capped mean is also 0, by the same one-step fair conditional-mean argument. A terminal score is positive with probability 3/4 here, yet its mean is zero. Let D sum the positive amounts used up to T. Then E[D]=∑ k≥1 (3/2) k−1 P(T≥k)=∑ k≥1 (3/4) k−1 =4. Every absolute capped score is bounded by D, so dominated convergence applies. Unbounded increments alone do not force failure: the stated stopping conditions are sufficient, and this model has another integrable bound. Task C: quantify the changed limit. For the 3/2 rule in task B, first show E | H T |=5/4. Then find E | H K − H T |. Does it tend to zero? You may use independence of future tosses after a fixed initial string of K tails. Hint for task C The positive part has contributions 1×(1/2)+(1/2)×(1/4)=5/8. The mean is 0, so the negative part has the same expected magnitude. On the no-head-by- K branch, let S be the additional waiting time for a head. Full solution to task C The positive and negative parts both have expectation 5/8, hence E | H T |=5/4. After K tails the current score is H K =2−2(3/2) K . The fresh delay S has the original first-head law. Subtracting the two scores gives H T − H K =(3/2) K [2−(3/2) S−1 ] on this branch; the difference is zero on all other branches. Multiplying its conditional absolute mean by probability 2 −K gives E | H K − H T |=(5/4)(3/4) K →0. This is convergence in L 1 , unlike the doubling rule's constant error 1. A good place to stop Separate outcomes, scores and their probability-weighted mean. Explain why the carnival's three score labels cannot be averaged equally. To compare equal-mean games with different spread, continue to variance . A fixed cap and an almost-surely finite stop can have different limiting expectations. Track the rare branch's weighted contribution: its small probability and E[T]=2 did not control the doubling example's score tails.

title: Same average, different surprises
summary: Calculate finite variance and standard deviation, including the shortcut identity.
text: The question and needed ideas Two puzzle machines both average five points. Machine S always awards five. Machine W flips a fair coin and awards zero or ten. Their expected scores agree, but one machine is predictable and the other is not. A single number for the mean hides the difference, so we need a measure of spread around that mean. Background capsule. Write μ=E[X] for the mean. The deviation from μ is x−μ. Simply averaging deviations always gives zero, because positive and negative deviations cancel. Squaring before averaging avoids cancellation. Variance is the expected squared deviation; standard deviation is its nonnegative square root. Scores may be in points, while variance is in squared points. Work through the model Worked example. For S, the only deviation is 5−5=0, so Var(S)=0. For W, the mean is 0(1/2)+10(1/2)=5. Both possible scores differ from five by five; each squared deviation is 25. Thus Var(W)=25(1/2)+25(1/2)=25, and its standard deviation is √25=5 points. The shortcut gives the same answer. E[W²]=0²(1/2)+10²(1/2)=50, and E[W]²=25; their difference is 25. For S, E[S²]=25 and E[S]²=25, giving zero. The shortcut is useful when scores have many values, but the squared-deviation definition is the meaning to remember. A table with rows (0, 1/2, 25) and (10, 1/2, 25) for score, probability and squared deviation makes the calculation transparent. Each row contributes 12.5 to W’s variance. Neither table row is a “typical” outcome in the sense of being close to the mean: the mean itself never occurs. The statement and its limits Exact statement. For a finite distribution, Var(X)=E[(X−μ)²] with μ=E[X]. Expand the square: E[X²−2μX+μ²]=E[X²]−2μE[X]+μ²E[1]. Since E[X]=μ and E[1]=1, this equals E[X²]−μ². This is an algebraic proof of the shortcut; it does not require a bell curve or repeated trials. Variance is never negative because every squared deviation is nonnegative and probabilities are nonnegative. It equals zero exactly when all positive-probability outcomes equal the mean. Adding a constant c leaves the deviations unchanged, so Var(X+c)=Var(X). Scaling scores by a multiplies variance by a²: Var(aX)=a²Var(X). A failure case for “same mean means same game” is S versus W. Also, a large standard deviation does not by itself reveal whether low or high scores are more frequent; different distributions can have the same first two moments. Inspect the underlying probabilities for decisions that depend on tails or worst cases. Var ( X ) = E [ X 2 ] − E [ X ] 2 To interpret the scale, compare a third machine T that awards four or six points with equal chances. It also has mean five, but each deviation is only one point, so Var(T)=1 and its standard deviation is one point. The ordering S, T, W is now visible: zero, one and five standard-deviation points. Variance amplifies large deviations because it squares them. A score ten points from the mean contributes one hundred squared points before weighting, while a score one point away contributes only one. This sensitivity is useful, but it means variance is not a complete description of a distribution. Try two cases Exercise 1. X is equally likely to be 1, 3 or 5. Find its mean, variance and standard deviation. Hint for exercise 1 The mean is the middle value; square each distance from it. Full solution to exercise 1 μ=(1+3+5)/3=3. Squared deviations are 4, 0 and 4. Their average is Var(X)=8/3. The standard deviation is √(8/3), about 1.633, in the original score units. The shortcut checks it: E[X²]=(1+9+25)/3=35/3, minus 3²=9 leaves 8/3. Exercise 2. Define Y=2X+7 for the same X. Calculate Var(Y) and explain why adding seven alone does not increase spread. Hint for exercise 2 Use deviations from E[Y], or the scaling rule. Full solution to exercise 2 E[Y]=2·3+7=13. The values of Y are 9, 13 and 17, with deviations −4, 0 and 4, so Var(Y)=(16+0+16)/3=32/3. Equivalently 2²Var(X)=4·8/3=32/3. The constant seven shifts each value and the mean equally; it changes location, not distances from the mean. What to carry forward Variance measures average squared distance under the stated probabilities, while standard deviation restores the original unit. The identity proved here is exact for finite distributions. It does not say every high-variance game is undesirable; that is a preference question. For repeated independent trials, binomial counts give a useful case with a compact mean and variance.

title: How many successes in ten tries?
summary: Count exactly k successes under fixed-probability independent trials.
text: The question and needed ideas Flip a fair coin ten times and count heads. The event “exactly three heads” contains many sequences: H H H T T T T T T T is one, but so is T H T H T T H T T T. Counting only the first sequence would miss most ways to get the same count. The binomial distribution turns the sequence tree into probabilities for counts. Background capsule. A trial has success or failure. Here success means head. Let X be the number of successes in n trials. The notation C(n,k), also written “n choose k,” counts selections of k trial positions from n. The factorial n! multiplies 1·2·…·n, with 0!=1. A binomial model requires a fixed n, two outcomes per trial, a common success chance p, and independence across trials. Work through the model Worked example. For ten fair flips, a particular sequence with three heads and seven tails has probability (1/2)³(1/2)⁷=1/1024. There are C(10,3)=10·9·8/(3·2·1)=120 choices of head positions. The sequences are disjoint, so P(X=3)=120/1024=15/128, about 0.1172. For a biased coin with p=0.3, the same count probability is 120(0.3)³(0.7)⁷, about 0.2668. The position count stays 120, but each sequence now has probability p³(1−p)⁷. We do not need to enumerate all 1024 sequences to compute it. As a quick boundary check, P(X=0)=(1−p)ⁿ because there is just one all-failure sequence; P(X=n)=pⁿ. For p=0 all mass is at zero, and for p=1 all mass is at n. These extreme cases are valid in the formula with the usual convention that a zero exponent contributes one to the product. The statement and its limits Exact statement. Under the four binomial assumptions, every sequence with k successes has probability pᵏ(1−p)ⁿ⁻ᵏ by independence and common p. There are C(n,k) such sequences: order n distinct positions in n! ways, but divide by k! reorderings of chosen positions and (n−k)! reorderings of unchosen positions. Adding equal probabilities of these disjoint sequences proves the displayed formula. The probabilities for k=0 through n sum to one because those events partition all trial sequences; equivalently their sum is (p+(1−p))ⁿ=1 by the binomial theorem. Writing X as a sum of success indicators I₁+···+Iₙ gives E[X]=np from linearity. Independence makes covariance terms vanish, giving Var(X)=np(1−p); that last variance identity needs a separate indicator calculation and is not inferred merely from the count formula. If you draw tokens without replacement, the conditional chance of success after the first draw changes with what was drawn, and the trials are dependent. The binomial formula is then generally wrong. A fixed number of draws is not enough by itself. P ( X = k ) = ( n ! k ! ( n − k ) ! ) p k ( 1 − p ) n − k Here is the moment calculation in elementary terms. Let Iᵢ equal one when trial i succeeds and zero otherwise. Then E[Iᵢ]=0(1−p)+1p=p, and because Iᵢ²=Iᵢ, Var(Iᵢ)=E[Iᵢ²]−E[Iᵢ]²=p−p²=p(1−p). The count X is I₁+···+Iₙ, so linearity gives E[X]=np. To see its variance, expand (X−np)² as a sum of squared individual deviations plus pairs of cross-products. Independence makes each cross-product have mean E[Iᵢ−p]E[Iⱼ−p]=0 for distinct trials. Only n individual variances remain, yielding np(1−p). Without independence, those cross-products need not vanish. Try two cases Exercise 1. A fair coin is flipped four times. Find the chance of exactly two heads. Hint for exercise 1 Choose two head positions from four. Full solution to exercise 1 C(4,2)=4!/(2!2!)=6. Each two-head sequence has probability (1/2)⁴=1/16. Hence P(X=2)=6/16=3/8. The six sequences can be listed to check the count: HHTT, HTHT, HTTH, THHT, THTH, TTHH. Exercise 2. A bag has two red and two blue tokens. Draw twice without replacement and count red draws. Would a Binomial(2,1/2) model give the correct chance of two reds? Hint for exercise 2 Compare the second-red chance after a first red with 1/2. Full solution to exercise 2 No. The true chance of two reds is (2/4)(1/3)=1/6. A Binomial(2,1/2) formula would give (1/2)²=1/4. After a red is removed, only one of three remaining tokens is red, so independence fails: the conditional red chance changes after the first draw, despite both draw positions having marginal red chance 1/2. What to carry forward The binomial model is a count model for a very specific repeated experiment. Its elegance comes from equal sequence probabilities within each success count. Check the trial mechanism before using it. When n grows, a normal curve can sometimes approximate the count bars, but that later step is never exact for finite n.

title: When a bell curve is a useful sketch
summary: Standardize a binomial count and qualify a normal approximation.
text: The question and needed ideas A long run of success counts often makes a mound of bars. A smooth bell curve can help estimate areas under those bars, but a discrete count cannot literally have a continuous normal distribution. The useful question is when the smooth curve captures a binomial count well enough for the task and when it misses important tail behavior. Background capsule. For a Binomial(n,p) count, μ=np and σ=√[np(1−p)]. The standardized score Z=(X−μ)/σ tells how many standard deviations X lies from its mean. A standard normal variable has mean zero and variance one. Standardization requires 0<p<1 so that σ>0. A continuity correction treats an integer count k as the interval from k−0.5 to k+0.5 on the continuous scale. Work through the model Worked example. Take 100 independent trials with p=1/2. Then μ=50 and σ=5. For X≤60, the continuity-corrected normal sketch uses P(N≤60.5) with N having mean 50 and standard deviation 5. This is P(Z≤(60.5−50)/5)=P(Z≤2.1), approximately 0.9821 from a standard normal table. An exact binomial sum would be ∑ from k=0 to 60 of C(100,k)/2¹⁰⁰; the normal value is an approximation to that exact finite sum. Evaluating the sum gives about 0.9823999, while the corrected normal estimate is about 0.9821356; their difference is roughly 0.0002643 here. This close match belongs to this particular central event and parameter choice, not to every binomial tail. The half-unit correction matters because a bar at 60 covers a width around 60; cutting the smooth curve at 60 would omit half of that represented bar. It still cannot make the approximation exact. A table or calculator can evaluate the finite binomial sum if a precise tail chance matters. Try p=0.02 with n=20. Its mean is 0.4 and most mass sits at zero; the count cannot go negative. A symmetric normal curve centered at 0.4 assigns some area to negative values and misses the skew. That is a visible failure case, despite n being greater than one. The statement and its limits Qualified theorem. For independent Bernoulli trials with one fixed p strictly between zero and one, as n tends to infinity the standardized count converges in distribution to a standard normal variable. This is a special case of the central limit theorem. “Converges in distribution” means probabilities at continuity points of the limiting curve approach the corresponding normal probabilities; it does not make any finite-n distribution exactly normal. Why the standardization? Write X as a sum of n success indicators. Each indicator has mean p and variance p(1−p). Independence makes the sum mean np and variance np(1−p), so subtracting and dividing yields mean zero and variance one. This algebra motivates the scale. A full proof of the central limit theorem requires an additional limiting argument and lies beyond this article; the theorem is stated with its conditions, not proved by a histogram. Common rules of thumb ask both np and n(1−p) to be reasonably large, often around ten, before using a normal approximation. Such thresholds are heuristics, not guarantees of a particular numerical error, especially deep in a tail. If p changes with n toward zero, the fixed-p theorem does not directly settle the accuracy; a Poisson-type approximation may be more suitable. Z = X − n p n p ( 1 − p ) Try two cases Exercise 1. For X∼Binomial(64,1/2), find the mean, standard deviation, and continuity-corrected z cutoff for P(X≤36). Hint for exercise 1 Use μ=np, σ=√[np(1−p)], and include the full bar at 36. Full solution to exercise 1 μ=64/2=32 and variance is 64(1/2)(1/2)=16, so σ=4. The corrected upper boundary is 36.5; its z score is (36.5−32)/4=1.125. Thus a normal sketch estimates P(X≤36) by Φ(1.125), about 0.870. The exact chance remains a finite binomial sum. Exercise 2. For n=30 and p=0.01, explain two reasons a bell curve centered at np is a poor sketch. Hint for exercise 2 Calculate np and consider the left edge of a count. Full solution to exercise 2 np=0.3, so success counts cluster at zero with a long right tail. The count has lower bound zero, while the symmetric normal curve centered at 0.3 gives area to negative values. Also np is far below common heuristic thresholds, indicating strong skew and sparse successes. The fixed-p limiting theorem does not promise accuracy for this small finite n. What to carry forward Use the normal curve as a labelled approximation to a well-specified binomial model, with the mean, spread and continuity correction shown. Exact binomial arithmetic remains the reference for finite counts. The extreme-p example is a boundary, not an exception to probability itself. Return to the exact count formula whenever tail accuracy or model assumptions are in doubt.

title: The missing number in the rationals
summary: Use rational brackets around the positive square root of two to locate the completeness gap.
text: A sequence that asks for a missing number Imagine working only with rational numbers: fractions of integers with nonzero denominators. You can bracket a positive number whose square is 2 as tightly as you like using decimals, yet no rational number fills the gap. This is a useful way to see what the completeness of the real numbers supplies. We will prove the missing-number claim, then say exactly which extra property the real line has. Background capsule. An upper bound of a set is a number at least as large as every member. Its least upper bound , or supremum, is an upper bound smaller than every other upper bound. A sequence is Cauchy if its late terms get arbitrarily close to one another, even before we know its limit. We need only integer divisibility, elementary inequalities, and the fact that between distinct real numbers lies a rational number. We take the existence and least-upper-bound property of the real numbers as axioms here; constructing them from rationals is a separate project. Build rational brackets Worked example. Start with 1² < 2 < 2². Testing tenths gives 1.4² = 1.96 < 2 < 2.25 = 1.5². Testing hundredths gives 1.41² = 1.9881 < 2 < 2.0164 = 1.42². These calculations certify an interval, not an exact decimal representation. At the next stage, divide the current bracket into ten equal rational pieces and keep the pair that straddles the square value 2. After stage n, the bracket width is 10 −n . Its left endpoints increase, its right endpoints decrease, and any two later choices lie at most 10 −n apart. Two finite rational brackets Lower endpoint Upper endpoint Width 1.4 1.5 0.1 1.41 1.42 0.01 The brackets are a concrete worked example of Cauchy behavior in the rationals. Their widths tend to zero, but that fact alone cannot conjure a rational limit. To see why, we need an exact obstruction. Where completeness enters Exact statement. Let S be the set of nonnegative rational x with x² < 2. It is nonempty and bounded above. It has no least upper bound within the rationals. In the real numbers, its supremum exists and is the unique positive real whose square is 2: sup { x ∈ ℚ : x ≥ 0 , x 2 < 2 } = 2 ∉ ℚ First prove irrationality. Suppose the positive square root were p/q in lowest terms, with positive integers p and q. From p² = 2q², p² is even, hence p is even: an odd integer has odd square. Put p = 2k. Then 4k² = 2q², so q² = 2k² and q is also even. Both p and q would share a factor 2, contradicting lowest terms. Thus no rational square is 2. For any rational a ≥ 0 with a² < 2, a slightly larger rational still has square below 2. One explicit choice is a+h with positive rational h smaller than both 1 and (2−a²)/(2a+1), because (a+h)² ≤ a²+h(2a+1) < 2. So no member of S is its maximum. If a rational upper bound b had b² > 2, a sufficiently small rational step left would still have square greater than 2, and would remain an upper bound: for positive x, x² < 2 < (b−h)² implies x < b−h. Thus b would not be least. No rational has square exactly 2, which exhausts the possibilities. This proves the rational failure without assuming the desired real limit. In ℝ the least-upper-bound axiom gives c = sup S. The same small-step arguments show neither c² < 2 nor c² > 2 is possible, so c² = 2. Strict increase of x² on nonnegative numbers makes c unique. The bracket endpoints above converge to c because both surround c and their gap tends to zero. The completeness axiom does real work; the decimal table merely guides it. Test the boundary 1. Construct a bracket. Find two hundredths that bracket the positive solution of x² = 3, and check both squares exactly. Hint Try neighboring hundredths near 1.73; convert each to a fraction with denominator 100 before squaring. Worked solution We have 1.73² = 29929/10000 = 2.9929 < 3 and 1.74² = 30276/10000 = 3.0276 > 3. Thus the solution lies strictly between 1.73 and 1.74. This calculation alone does not prove that its decimal expansion has any particular later digits. 2. Repair a claim. Someone says, “Every bounded increasing sequence of rationals converges in ℚ.” Identify the missing assumption or counterexample. Hint Use lower endpoints of successively finer brackets for √2. Ask what a rational limit would have to square to. Worked solution The lower endpoints are rational, bounded above by 2, and nondecreasing. In ℝ they converge to √2: the bracket gap tends to zero and always contains √2. Were their limit rational, uniqueness of limits in ℝ would make that rational equal √2, contradicting the parity proof. The correct monotone-convergence statement needs completeness of the ambient real numbers; boundedness inside ℚ alone is insufficient. The property behind the gap A list of rational approximations can become arbitrarily self-consistent while its limit lies outside ℚ. Completeness says bounded nonempty real sets have real suprema; it does not say every rational approximation eventually equals its target. The next optional connection is why bounded real sequences contain convergent subsequences , where completeness appears again in nested intervals.

title: A sequence cannot escape a closed box
summary: Construct a convergent subsequence of any bounded real sequence with nested intervals.
text: Can a bounded sequence avoid settling anywhere? The sequence 0, 1, 0, 1, … never converges, but its zero terms form a convergent subsequence. This is not an accident of having only two values. Every bounded sequence of real numbers has some convergent subsequence. We will construct one by repeatedly choosing an interval that contains infinitely many terms. Background capsule. A subsequence keeps terms in their original order, with strictly increasing indices n₁ < n₂ < …. A sequence is bounded if all its values lie between some finite a and b. The nested-interval property says a decreasing sequence of nonempty closed real intervals whose lengths tend to zero has exactly one common point. It follows from completeness: the increasing left endpoints have a supremum, which remains inside every interval. We will use that property explicitly. Keep the busy half Worked example. Consider x n = (−1) n + 1/n for n ≥ 1. All its terms lie in [−1, 2]. Bisect that interval into [−1, 1/2] and [1/2, 2]. Infinitely many terms must lie in at least one half; otherwise the whole sequence would have only finitely many terms. For this sequence, the even terms approach 1 and eventually occupy the right half. Keeping that half, then repeatedly bisecting, concentrates on a cluster near 1. Choosing a term with an index larger than the last chosen index at every stage gives a genuine subsequence, not a rearrangement. There can be a tie: both halves may have infinitely many terms. Either choice works. Closed halves overlap at their shared midpoint, and that causes no problem. The construction asserts a possible convergent subsequence, not a unique one; choosing the negative terms here leads to −1 instead. The invariant in a generic bisection Stage Interval length Terms retained 0 b−a Infinitely many 1 (b−a)/2 Infinitely many k (b−a)/2 k Infinitely many Construct the convergent subsequence Bolzano–Weierstrass in ℝ. If every x n belongs to [a,b] with real a ≤ b, there are indices n₁ < n₂ < … and a real c such that x nₖ → c. [ a , b ] ⊃ I 1 ⊃ I 2 ⊃ ⋯ , | I k | = b − a 2 k → 0 Proof. Put I₀ = [a,b]. Given a closed interval I k containing infinitely many sequence terms, split it into two closed halves. At least one half contains infinitely many terms; choose it as I k+1 . The intervals are nested and their lengths are (b−a)/2 k . By the nested-interval property they share one point c. For each k, choose an index n k larger than n k−1 with x nₖ ∈ I k . Infinitely many terms in I k ensure such an index exists even after finitely many earlier choices. Because both x nₖ and c lie in I k , |x nₖ −c| ≤ (b−a)/2 k . Given ε > 0, choose K large enough that this length is below ε; then all k ≥ K satisfy the limit requirement. If a = b, every term is a and the result is immediate. This is a proof in the real line; we have not shown the analogous statement in an arbitrary metric space. The real-number hypothesis matters. Rational approximations to √2 inside [1,2] form a bounded rational sequence whose convergent subsequences in ℝ must tend to √2. None has a limit in ℚ. That is another face of the rational gap . The theorem also does not claim the original sequence converges: alternating 0 and 1 is a simple failure case. Choose and diagnose subsequences 1. Calculate. For x n = (−1) n + 1/n, give two explicit subsequences and prove their limits. Hint Take even and odd indices separately, then bound the reciprocal terms. Worked solution For n = 2k, x 2k = 1 + 1/(2k) → 1 because 1/(2k) < 1/k → 0. For n = 2k−1, x 2k−1 = −1 + 1/(2k−1) → −1. For any ε > 0, choose K > 1/ε; then the reciprocal errors are below ε for all k ≥ K. The two different limits also prove the full sequence does not converge. 2. Find the flaw. A proposed proof says, “Every bounded sequence has a convergent subsequence because it has an infinite set of distinct values.” Why does this fail, and what repairs it? Hint What if values repeat? Even infinitely many distinct values need a limit point in the domain. Worked solution The constant sequence 3,3,3,… has only one distinct value yet has a convergent subsequence. Conversely, having infinitely many distinct rational values does not ensure a rational accumulation point, as approximations to √2 show. The repair is the nested-interval construction in ℝ: it keeps infinitely many indexed terms at each stage and invokes real completeness for a common point. Boundedness gives one settled thread Repeated bisection and completeness find a convergent subsequence without claiming anything about the whole sequence. A useful stopping test is whether you can identify both the “infinitely many terms” invariant and the real-number property that supplies c. The optional next question is what stronger condition makes all terms approach the same c.

title: One tolerance for the whole interval
summary: Compare a pointwise input tolerance with one shared across an interval.
text: May one input tolerance serve every point? A continuous function responds gently to small input changes near each fixed point. But the required input tolerance can depend on that point. Uniform continuity asks for one tolerance that works simultaneously across the domain. For x² this difference appears as soon as the domain stretches without bound. Background capsule. |u−v| is the distance between real numbers u and v. Ordinary continuity at a means: for each output tolerance ε > 0 there is an input tolerance δ > 0 such that x in the domain and |x−a| < δ imply |f(x)−f(a)| < ε. The δ may depend on a. A function is Lipschitz with constant L if |f(x)−f(y)| ≤ L|x−y| for all domain points. We will prove a concrete Lipschitz bound rather than assume a compactness theorem. Try a shared tolerance Worked example. On [−3,3], take f(x) = x². Factoring gives |x²−y²| = |x−y||x+y|. Since |x+y| ≤ 6 on this interval, an input gap below ε/6 guarantees an output gap below ε. For example, to keep square values within 0.12, δ = 0.02 works everywhere in [−3,3]. At x = 3 and y = 2.99 the output gap is 9−8.9401 = 0.0599, comfortably below 0.12. This one sample does not establish the guarantee; the factorization does. On the entire real line the same δ cannot work. If x is very large, even a modest fixed input change h produces |(x+h)²−x²| = |2xh+h²|. Its size grows with x. The location is what breaks the shared promise, although x² remains continuous at each individual x. Use the bound as a resolution requirement. On [−3,3], any two recorded inputs differing by less than 0.001 have squared outputs differing by less than 0.006. This conclusion is independent of which two inputs occur. It is conservative near zero: the actual change from 0 to 0.001 is only 0.000001. Uniform continuity allows a safe common tolerance to be smaller than the best tolerance at particular points; it asks for reliability everywhere, not equal sharpness everywhere. Put the quantifiers in their places Exact definition. A function f on D ⊆ ℝ is uniformly continuous if ∀ ε > 0 ∃ δ > 0 ∀ x , y ∈ D : | x − y | < δ ⇒ | f ( x ) − f ( y ) | < ε The decisive order is “choose δ, then consider every pair.” For x² on [−M,M] with M > 0, |x+y| ≤ 2M. Choosing δ = ε/(2M) makes |x²−y²| < ε. If M = 0, the one-point domain is trivially uniformly continuous. The same proof works on any bounded interval by enclosing it in some [−M,M]; its endpoints need not be included. This establishes a local result directly. Now fix ε = 1 on D = ℝ. For any proposed δ > 0, choose h = min(δ/2,1/2), so 0 < h < δ. Set y = x+h and take x > 1/(2h). Then |y²−x²| = 2xh+h² > 1. Thus no δ works for all pairs. Notice that choosing x only after seeing δ is legitimate: it disproves the universal-pair part of the definition. This is a full counterexample, not a graph-based impression. Continuity of x² at a fixed a follows separately. If |x−a| < 1, then |x+a| ≤ 2|a|+1. Choose δ = min(1, ε/(2|a|+1)). The bound proves |x²−a²| < ε. This δ depends on a, which is why this pointwise proof does not establish uniform continuity on ℝ. A broader theorem says every continuous function on a compact interval [a,b] is uniformly continuous. Its proof needs compactness; we do not infer it merely from the x² calculation. The unbounded-domain counterexample does not mean every unbounded-domain function fails: f(x)=2x is uniformly continuous on ℝ with δ=ε/2. Domain and growth both matter. Work with the shared δ 1. Calculate. Give an explicit δ for f(x)=x² on [2,5] when ε=0.1, and justify it for every pair in the interval. Hint On [2,5], how large can x+y be? Worked solution Here |x+y| ≤ 10. Take δ = 0.01. If |x−y| < 0.01, then |x²−y²| = |x−y||x+y| < 0.01·10 = 0.1. The strict input inequality gives the strict output inequality even at the maximum possible sum. 2. Diagnose. Is f(x)=1/x uniformly continuous on (0,1)? Supply a decisive pair sequence. Hint Choose points approaching zero whose distance shrinks while reciprocal values separate. Worked solution Take x n =1/(n+1) and y n =1/(n+2), both in (0,1). Their distance is 1/((n+1)(n+2)) → 0, but |1/x n −1/y n | = |(n+1)−(n+2)| = 1. For ε=1/2, every δ is defeated by a sufficiently large n. The missing endpoint zero matters: continuity on an open bounded interval does not automatically give uniform continuity. One promise or many Ordinary continuity lets δ change with the base point; uniform continuity requires one δ for all pairs. On a bounded interval, the x² factorization gives a direct shared bound. On ℝ its growth defeats every shared δ. The optional next link is uniform convergence , which uses a similar “one bound across all x” idea for a sequence of functions.

title: When rectangle sums refuse to agree
summary: Use rational and irrational density to show that all Darboux gaps stay wide.
text: Can every bounded function be integrated by rectangles? For many curves, narrower rectangles make upper and lower area estimates converge. Now imagine a function equal to one at rational inputs and zero at irrational inputs. Both kinds of input occur in every interval, however small. We will show that every upper rectangle is forced to height one and every lower rectangle to height zero. This is a structural obstruction, not a failure to sample enough points. Background capsule. A partition of [0,1] is a finite chain 0=x₀<x₁<…<xₙ=1. On each cell, the lower sum uses the infimum of function values times cell width; the upper sum uses the supremum. A bounded function is Riemann integrable by the Darboux criterion exactly when upper and lower sums can be made arbitrarily close. We use two familiar density facts: every nonempty open interval contains a rational and an irrational. These facts can be proved from the Archimedean property and the irrationality of √2; their full derivation is beyond this local calculation. A partition that changes nothing Worked example. Define D(x)=1 if x is rational and D(x)=0 otherwise. Try the partition 0, 1/4, 1/2, 1. Each cell contains rationals and irrationals, so its supremum is 1 and infimum is 0. The three widths add to 1. Consequently U(P)=1 and L(P)=0. Cutting each cell into a million smaller intervals changes neither local extreme. A finite plot might draw only its rational sample values, or only its irrational ones, depending on how coordinates are represented. Either picture is misleading about the continuous interval. Every cell has the same oscillation Cell Infimum Supremum Contribution to U−L [0,1/4] 0 1 1/4 [1/4,1/2] 0 1 1/4 [1/2,1] 0 1 1/2 The exact Darboux obstruction Statement. For the rational indicator D on [0,1], every finite partition P has lower sum zero and upper sum one: L ( P ) = 0 , U ( P ) = ∑ i n ( x i − x i − 1 ) = 1 Proof. Each partition cell has positive width. Its interior is a nonempty open interval. Rational density supplies a point where D=1, and irrational density supplies a point where D=0. Since D only takes those two values, the supremum on that cell is exactly 1 and the infimum exactly 0. The widths telescope to xₙ−x₀=1. Therefore U(P)−L(P)=1 for every P. In particular, no partition has a gap below 1/2, so the Darboux criterion fails. The function is not Riemann integrable. The same observation shows D is discontinuous at every point. At a rational a, nearby irrational inputs give values zero while D(a)=1; at an irrational a, nearby rational inputs give one while D(a)=0. For ε=1/2, no δ can enforce continuity at either kind of point. This is a direct proof, independent of the more general theorem characterizing Riemann integrability by a null discontinuity set. There is a surprising second integral notion. The rationals in [0,1] are countable and can be covered by intervals of arbitrarily small total length; see countable sets of zero length . Under Lebesgue measure, D equals zero almost everywhere, so its Lebesgue integral is zero. We are not treating “Riemann area” and “Lebesgue area” as interchangeable definitions: one fails to exist here while the other exists. The countable-cover argument supports the Lebesgue conclusion once measure and measurable-function integration are defined. A different dense-set example warns against overgeneralization: a function that is one at only finitely many rational points and zero elsewhere is Riemann integrable with integral zero. Density of all rationals matters in D; merely having some discontinuities does not force failure. Ask what every cell contains 1. Calculate. On [2,5], let E equal 3 at rational inputs and −1 at irrational inputs. Find U(P) and L(P) for every partition P. Hint Each cell has both values. The total width is now 3. Worked solution Every cell has supremum 3 and infimum −1. Thus U(P)=3(5−2)=9 and L(P)=−1(5−2)=−3, independent of the partition. The gap is 12, so E is not Riemann integrable on [2,5]. Changing the number of cells never shrinks that gap. 2. Compare. Let H(x)=1 at x=1/2 and zero elsewhere on [0,1]. Is H Riemann integrable? Hint Put 1/2 inside a very short pair of cells. What happens to the upper sum? Worked solution Yes. Every lower sum is zero. For any ε>0 choose a partition with a cell [1/2−η,1/2+η] of width 2η<ε, along with cells outside it. Only the central cell can have supremum one, so its upper sum is at most 2η<ε. The Darboux gap can therefore be made arbitrarily small and the integral is zero. A single isolated discontinuity is unlike the everywhere-discontinuous D. Sampling cannot repair incompatible bounds The obstruction is exact: every positive-width cell sees both values. A finite numerical trace cannot certify or refute this density property. The Riemann integral fails for D even though a later measure-based integral assigns it zero. This is a useful stopping point before investigating which sets have zero measure.

title: A limit can change the shape of a theorem
summary: Track the moving error peak in xⁿ and prove that uniform limits preserve continuity.
text: When does a limit keep continuity? A sequence of continuous curves can approach a function that jumps. The standard example fₙ(x)=xⁿ on [0,1] crowds its change closer to the right endpoint as n grows. Every fixed x below 1 eventually sees height near zero, yet the value at 1 always stays one. We will locate exactly which convergence condition is missing, then prove a theorem that protects continuity. Background capsule. Pointwise convergence lets the index N required for a given error depend on the input x. Uniform convergence requires one N that works at every input in the domain. The supremum of a set of nonnegative errors is its least upper bound; it need not be attained. A continuous f at a responds to a small input change near a with a small output change. We use the triangle inequality |u+w|≤|u|+|w| and ordinary ε arguments. Follow one fixed point, then move the point Worked example. At x=1/2, fₙ(x)=2 −n tends to zero. At x=0.9 it also tends to zero, though more slowly. At x=1, fₙ(1)=1 for all n. Thus the pointwise limit f is zero on [0,1) and one at 1. It has a jump at the endpoint: inputs x<1 can be arbitrarily close to 1 while f(x)=0 remains one unit from f(1)=1. To test uniform convergence, do not freeze x first. For each n, choose xₙ=2 −1/n , which is strictly below 1 but tends to 1. Then fₙ(xₙ)=1/2 whereas f(xₙ)=0. Every n has an error of at least 1/2. In fact the supremum error is one: for x<1, |fₙ(x)−f(x)|=xⁿ, and values of x arbitrarily close to 1 make xⁿ arbitrarily close to one. The supremum is not attained on [0,1) but it is still one. Fixed and moving inputs tell different stories Input choice Error at stage n As n grows x=1/2 fixed 2 −n Tends to zero xₙ=2 −1/n 1/2 Stays 1/2 Supremum over [0,1] 1 Stays 1 A uniform limit theorem Exact statement. If functions fₙ:D→ℝ are continuous at a∈D and fₙ→f uniformly on D, then f is continuous at a. Here continuity uses points of D near a; no interval or compactness assumption on D is needed. sup x ∈ D | f n ( x ) − f ( x ) | → 0 Proof. Given ε>0, uniform convergence supplies one n so large that |fₙ(x)−f(x)|<ε/3 for all x∈D, including x=a. Keep this n fixed. Continuity of this particular fₙ at a supplies δ>0 such that |x−a|<δ and x∈D imply |fₙ(x)−fₙ(a)|<ε/3. The triangle inequality gives |f(x)−f(a)|≤|f(x)−fₙ(x)|+|fₙ(x)−fₙ(a)|+|fₙ(a)−f(a)|<ε. This proves continuity. The order of choices matters: choose a single n that works for all x, then use continuity of that one function. For xⁿ on [0,1], each fₙ is continuous, but the limit is not continuous. By the theorem, convergence cannot be uniform; our exact supremum calculation directly confirms that. Pointwise convergence alone does not permit the first and third error terms to be controlled using one n while x varies near a. The converse is false. Continuous functions may converge pointwise to a continuous function without uniform convergence. On ℝ, fₙ(x)=x/n tends pointwise to zero, but sup over ℝ of |x/n| is unbounded for each n. The limit is continuous. So uniform convergence is a sufficient condition for preservation of continuity, not a necessary one. On restricted bounded domains the same sequence is uniform; the domain must be stated. Audit a sequence of functions 1. Calculate. Show gₙ(x)=x/(n+1) tends uniformly to zero on [−4,4]. Give an explicit N for ε=0.01. Hint Maximize |x| on the given domain, then bound 4/(n+1). Worked solution For every x∈[−4,4], |gₙ(x)|≤4/(n+1), with equality at either endpoint. Thus the supremum error is 4/(n+1)→0. For strict error below 0.01=1/100, require n+1>400, so N=400 works for all integer n≥400. Indeed 4/401<1/100. The same N controls every x. 2. Diagnose a false proof. “Because fₙ(x)→f(x) for each x and each fₙ is continuous, we may take n large, then move x near a.” What is the missing condition? Hint Ask whether the chosen n still works after x changes. Worked solution Pointwise convergence supplies an index N(x,ε), which may change as x moves. It cannot guarantee a single n controls fₙ(x)−f(x) for all nearby x. The sequence xⁿ on [0,1] defeats the argument at a=1. Uniform convergence supplies an N(ε) valid for all x, allowing the three-term triangle-inequality proof above. Control the error over the whole domain The limit of xⁿ changes continuity because its error peak keeps sliding toward 1. Uniform convergence rules out that sliding peak and transfers continuity by a short ε/3 proof. The next optional investigation is passing limits through integrals , where a different condition—integrable domination—controls a different failure.

title: Infinitely many points can have zero length
summary: Allocate an arbitrarily small interval budget to cover every point of a countable set.
text: How can a dense set take no length? Every interval contains a rational number, yet all rationals together can be covered by open intervals whose total lengths add to less than any positive budget. This statement is about outer measure : it does not depend on being able to draw every interval or on the rationals being sparse. We will construct the cover and explain the gap between countability and length. Background capsule. A set is countable if its elements can be listed as a₁,a₂,…, allowing repetitions; finite sets fit as well. An interval centered at a with radius r has length 2r. A cover is a collection of sets whose union contains the target set. For A⊆ℝ, Lebesgue outer measure m*(A) is the infimum of sums of lengths over countable open-interval covers of A. We use this definition only to establish zero outer measure; full construction of Lebesgue measure and its measurable sets is deferred. Spend half the remaining budget each time Worked example. Suppose the target is the set {1,1/2,1/3,…}. Give the nth listed point an open interval of length ε/2 n , centered there. If ε=1/8, the first interval has length 1/16, the second 1/32, then 1/64, and so on. These intervals can overlap; overlap only makes the union shorter than the sum, never longer. Every listed point is covered, even though infinitely many points cluster at zero. The total offered length is ε because 1/2+1/4+1/8+…=1. To verify the sum without invoking an unproved infinite manipulation, the first N terms sum to 1−2 −N , as multiplication by 2 and subtraction shows. This increases to 1. We may choose ε as small as we like, independently of the number of points. The cover is an exact mathematical collection; no finite drawing can display all its intervals. Zero outer measure for every countable set Exact statement. If A⊆ℝ is countable, then m*(A)=0. Given an enumeration A={a₁,a₂,…} and any ε>0, define Iₙ=(aₙ−ε/2 n+1 ,aₙ+ε/2 n+1 ). Each Iₙ has length ε/2 n , and A ⊆ ⋃ n = 1 ∞ I n , ∑ n = 1 ∞ | I n | = ε Proof. The displayed intervals cover every aₙ by construction, and their lengths sum to ε. By the definition of infimum, m*(A)≤ε for every ε>0. Outer measure is nonnegative, so m*(A)=0. If A is finite, list its points once and use a finite allocation, or repeat points in the infinite enumeration; either way the same bound applies. The result holds even if A is dense, because density concerns whether points occur in each open interval, whereas outer measure concerns total cover length. Why may we call the rationals countable? For each positive denominator q and integer numerator p, p/q is rational. The integer lattice pairs (p,q) with q>0 can be enumerated by increasing |p|+q; each shell is finite. Duplicates such as 1/2=2/4 do not spoil a listing. Therefore ℚ∩[0,1] has outer measure zero. A full proof of density is separate, but countability alone suffices for this length claim. Zero outer measure does not imply countability. The Cantor set is uncountable and has zero outer measure. Nor does measure zero mean empty: a single point already has zero outer measure. Conversely, a dense set need not have zero measure; [0,1] is dense in itself and has length one. The bridge from outer measure zero to ordinary Lebesgue measure zero uses the fact that outer-null sets are Lebesgue measurable, a standard consequence of the measure construction that we are not proving here. Budget and logic checks 1. Calculate. Cover a listed countable set with total interval length at most 0.01 using the alternative allocation 0.03/4 n . Does it work? Hint Use the geometric sum Σ4 −n =1/3. Worked solution Yes. Center an interval of length 0.03/4 n at the nth point. The total is 0.03(1/4+1/16+…)=0.03·(1/3)=0.01. The first N partial sum is (1−4 −N )/3, which justifies the infinite total. Every point is covered regardless of overlap. 2. Repair an inference. “ℚ∩[0,1] has zero measure, so it cannot meet every small interval.” Explain the error. Hint Distinguish total covering length from the existence of a point in each interval. Worked solution The premise is true, but the conclusion is false. Between any two distinct real numbers a<b there is a rational p/q: choose q so large that q(b−a)>1, then an integer p strictly between qa and qb. Thus ℚ is dense. Its enumeration nevertheless admits covers of arbitrarily small total length. Density and measure answer different questions. Many locations, arbitrarily little cover A geometric allocation gives every listed point a place while keeping total length under any budget. This proves a countable set is outer-null, including dense rational sets. It does not classify all null sets or construct the full Lebesgue measure; those are later tasks.

title: An uncountable set with no length
summary: Calculate shrinking Cantor-stage lengths and prove uncountability by binary choices.
text: Remove length without removing every point Start with [0,1]. Remove its open middle third, then remove the open middle third of each surviving interval, and continue forever. The resulting Cantor set has zero length, yet its points cannot be listed in a sequence. We will prove both assertions with separate arguments; finite pictures of the first few stages suggest them but do not establish either infinite claim. Background capsule. A set is countable if its members can be listed a₁,a₂,… . An uncountable set defeats every such list. Outer measure is the infimum of total lengths of countable interval covers; if covers with arbitrarily small total length exist, outer measure is zero. The nested-interval property of ℝ says closed intervals inside one another, with widths tending to zero, share exactly one real point. We use that completeness fact to attach a point to each binary choice sequence. Record the finite stages Worked example. Let C₀=[0,1]. At stage one, C₁=[0,1/3]∪[2/3,1]. At stage two, four closed intervals remain, each of length 1/9. At stage n there are 2 n disjoint closed intervals, each of length 3 −n . Their total length is (2/3) n . For example, C₃ has eight intervals of length 1/27, total 8/27. Define the limiting Cantor set C as the intersection of all Cₙ. Its endpoints survive because we remove open middle thirds. Finite stage length budget Stage n Intervals Each length Total 0 1 1 1 1 2 1/3 2/3 2 4 1/9 4/9 3 8 1/27 8/27 A finite stage still has positive length. The statement about C follows by trapping C inside every stage, whose total length approaches zero. The uncountability argument must use a different invariant: at each stage there remain two choices, left and right. Two proofs with distinct jobs Zero-length statement. The Cantor set has Lebesgue outer measure zero: C ⊆ C n , m * ( C ) ≤ ( 2 3 ) n → 0 Proof of zero outer measure. Each Cₙ is a finite union of closed intervals with total length (2/3) n . The definition of outer measure formally asks for open covers. Enlarge these finitely many intervals by a combined amount less than any η>0, obtaining an open cover of C of total length below (2/3) n +η. Hence m*(C)≤(2/3) n after letting η shrink. Since this holds for every n and the right side tends to zero, nonnegativity gives m*(C)=0. Outer-null sets are Lebesgue measurable in the standard construction, so their Lebesgue measure is also zero. We are relying on that standard measurability result, not proving the full measure construction here. Uncountability statement. Each infinite binary sequence b₁b₂… selects a unique point of C: at stage k retain the left surviving third if bₖ=0 and the right surviving third if bₖ=1. The selected closed intervals are nested and have lengths 3 −k , so completeness gives exactly one common point. Different binary sequences first disagree at some stage; their chosen stage intervals are separated by a removed open middle third, so their points differ. This is an injection from infinite binary sequences into C. It avoids any reliance on potentially ambiguous ternary expansions of endpoints. The infinite binary sequences are uncountable by diagonalization. If they were listed as rows s¹,s²,…, define a new sequence t with its nth bit opposite the nth bit of row n. Then t differs from row n at position n for every n, so it is absent from the list. An injection of this uncountable collection into C proves C uncountable. The conclusion is stronger than merely saying there are infinitely many endpoints; those endpoints form only a countable subset. There is no contradiction with countable sets being null : that theorem gives a sufficient condition, not an equivalence. Length measures geometric coverage, while cardinality counts how many distinct points a set contains. Check the two invariants 1. Calculate. At stage four, how many intervals remain and what is their combined length? Give an open-cover bound for C. Hint Double the interval count and divide each length by three at every stage. Worked solution There are 2⁴=16 intervals, each of length 3⁻⁴=1/81, so total length is 16/81. For any η>0, enlarge the 16 closed intervals slightly so the total extra length is below η. The resulting open intervals cover C and have combined length below 16/81+η. This bound alone is not zero; repeating at arbitrarily large stages proves zero. 2. Diagnose. “At each finite stage the set consists of finitely many intervals; therefore the limit set is finite.” Why is this invalid? Hint Count choices across all stages, not intervals at a fixed stage. Worked solution The number of intervals increases with the stage: no fixed finite list persists. Every infinite left/right sequence selects a point, and two sequences differing at any stage select different points. Diagonalization shows these sequences cannot be listed. A limit of finite-stage descriptions can therefore contain uncountably many points while its total stage lengths tend to zero. Cardinality and length part ways The Cantor set is closed, uncountable, and outer-null. The length proof uses shrinking finite covers; the size proof uses infinitely branching choices and completeness. Neither proof by itself gives the other conclusion. A later measure course studies larger families of such sets and what “almost everywhere” permits.

title: Integrating by sorting heights
summary: Integrate measurable simple functions by the sizes of their value sets.
text: Integrate by grouping values Riemann sums divide the input axis into intervals. The Lebesgue approach can instead ask how much measurable set receives each height. This is easy to compute for a simple function with finitely many values, and it suggests the definition for any nonnegative measurable function. We will calculate a simple integral and state the definition precisely, while leaving construction of Lebesgue measure itself outside this gateway lesson. Background capsule. A σ-algebra is a collection of subsets containing X and closed under complements and countable unions; its members are measurable sets. A measure μ assigns nonnegative sizes to those sets, with μ(∅)=0 and μ of a countable disjoint union equal to the sum of their sizes. The indicator 1 A (x) equals one on A and zero elsewhere. A nonnegative simple function takes finitely many nonnegative values and is measurable when its value sets are measurable. A function f is measurable if {x:f(x)>t} is measurable for each real t. We assume a measure space (X,Σ,μ) is already given. Three heights on one interval Worked example. On X=[0,1] with Lebesgue measure, let s=2 on [0,1/4), s=5 on [1/4,1/2), and s=0 on [1/2,1]. The first two pieces each have length 1/4. Group by value: two units of height over the first quarter contribute 2·1/4=1/2, five units over the next quarter contribute 5·1/4=5/4, and the rest contributes zero. Thus ∫s dμ=7/4. Whether the first and second sets are contiguous is irrelevant; only their measures and assigned values enter this simple-function integral. Simple-function calculation Measurable set Height Measure Contribution [0,1/4) 2 1/4 1/2 [1/4,1/2) 5 1/4 5/4 [1/2,1] 0 1/2 0 We used disjoint value sets. If a simple function has an overlapping representation, refine the sets into disjoint pieces before summing. Standard measure additivity then shows the result does not depend on the particular representation; we do not reconstruct that general well-definedness argument here. From simple functions to a nonnegative integral For s=Σ j=1 m a j 1 Aⱼ with disjoint measurable Aⱼ and aⱼ≥0, define ∫s dμ=Σaⱼμ(Aⱼ), using the convention 0·∞=0 when a zero-height set has infinite measure. For a nonnegative measurable f, define: ∫ f d μ = sup { ∫ s d μ : 0 ≤ s ≤ f , s simple } The supremum is allowed to be +∞. For the worked s itself, the supremum equals 7/4: choosing the simple function s gives at least 7/4, while monotonicity for simple functions bounds every simple t≤s above by ∫s. That monotonicity follows by refining both value partitions into common disjoint measurable pieces and comparing heights piece by piece. This explains why the definition extends the earlier finite calculation rather than assigning a different answer. As a second worked comparison, let f=1 ℚ∩[0,1] . The rational set is countable and Lebesgue null. Its indicator is a simple measurable function. Its integral is 1·μ(ℚ∩[0,1])=0, although the Riemann integral does not exist . This is possible because the new definition uses measured sets of positions, not the supremum in every input interval. The word “layer cake” is sometimes used for the identity ∫f dμ=∫₀∞ μ({f>t})dt for nonnegative measurable f. We can verify it for our finite example without claiming the general theorem: the set where s>t has measure 1/2 for 0≤t<2, measure 1/4 for 2≤t<5, and zero above 5. The area under those height-distribution levels is 2·(1/2)+3·(1/4)=7/4. Proving the identity for arbitrary measurable f needs approximation and a convergence theorem; that proof is beyond this article. For signed functions, the usual integral uses positive and negative parts and requires care when both integrals are infinite. Nothing here declares ∞−∞ meaningful. Likewise, the existence of Lebesgue measure and its countable additivity are assumptions of this gateway, not consequences of a picture or a finite table. Compute and check definitions 1. Calculate. On [0,2], let u=3 on [0,1/2), u=1 on [1/2,3/2), and u=0 elsewhere. Find ∫u and its height-distribution calculation. Hint The two nonzero value sets have measures 1/2 and 1. Worked solution The simple integral is 3·(1/2)+1·1=5/2. For 0≤t<1, {u>t} has measure 3/2; for 1≤t<3 it has measure 1/2; above 3 it has measure zero. The distribution-area calculation is 1·(3/2)+2·(1/2)=5/2. Endpoint choices for t affect only isolated heights and hence do not change the latter ordinary integral. 2. Explain a boundary. Why can we not define ∫v by simply adding a negative coefficient to the nonnegative formula and then allowing arbitrary +∞ and −∞ terms? Hint Consider the arithmetic expression +∞−∞. Worked solution Infinite positive and negative contributions may each diverge, and their difference has no defined value. A signed measurable v is handled by v⁺=max(v,0) and v⁻=max(−v,0); ∫v=∫v⁺−∫v⁻ is defined only when at least one side is finite, and absolute integrability requires both finite. The nonnegative supremum definition alone does not settle this cancellation problem. A precise gateway, not a measure construction Simple functions convert measured value sets into finite sums. The nonnegative Lebesgue integral is the supremum of those sums from below. We have calculated examples and marked the assumed machinery: measurable sets, countable additivity, and extension to signed functions. The next optional question is when limits commute with this integral.

title: When may a limit pass through an integral?
summary: Compare exact spike integrals with the hypotheses that permit interchanging limit and integral.
text: When may a limit move inside an integral? Pointwise convergence says that at each fixed input, function values eventually settle. It does not prevent a thin spike from carrying the same area forever. Dominated convergence adds a single integrable bound to rule out that escape. We will test its hypotheses, prove a useful finite-measure bounded special case using a named lemma, and clearly separate that from the full theorem. Background capsule. “Almost everywhere” means except on a set of measure zero. An integrable function g belongs to L¹ when ∫|g| dμ<∞. A measurable f is one whose threshold sets are measurable. We assume a measure space and the Lebesgue integral from simple-function integration . The full Fatou lemma and its proof are not supplied here; we will not claim a proof of the full dominated-convergence theorem. A spike that keeps its area Worked example. On [0,1], define fₙ(x)=n when 0<x<1/n, and zero elsewhere. For every fixed x>0, eventually n>1/x and then x lies outside the spike, so fₙ(x)=0. At x=0 all values are zero too. Thus fₙ→0 pointwise everywhere. Its integral, however, is rectangle height n times width 1/n, exactly one for every n. The limiting function has integral zero. A plot with fixed pixel spacing may miss the narrow interval entirely, so the exact calculation matters more than the displayed shape. Could there be an integrable g≥|fₙ| for every n almost everywhere? Because there are countably many n, combine their exceptional null sets into one null set. Outside it, on each dyadic band (2 −(k+1) ,2 −k ] with k≥1, the index n=2 k −1 has 1/n>2 −k , so g≥2 k −1 throughout that band. Its integral there is at least (2 k −1)2 −(k+1) ≥1/4. Summing over disjoint bands gives an infinite integral. Thus no common L¹ dominator exists. This direct argument avoids using the theorem we are about to state to verify its own hypothesis. The theorem and one bounded case Dominated convergence theorem. If measurable fₙ converge almost everywhere to a measurable f and there is a measurable g∈L¹ with |fₙ|≤g almost everywhere for every n, then f∈L¹ and lim n → ∞ ∫ f n d μ = ∫ f d μ The notation means limₙ ∫fₙ dμ = ∫f dμ; the limit is of the numerical integrals. In our spike example fₙ and f are measurable and converge pointwise, but the required integrable g is absent. The theorem is a sufficient condition, not a necessary condition for every individual sequence. Bounded finite-measure special case. Suppose μ(X)<∞, all fₙ and f are measurable, |fₙ|≤M for one finite constant M, and fₙ→f almost everywhere. Then |f|≤M almost everywhere. Fix η>0 and let Eₙ={x:|fₙ(x)−f(x)|>η}. Define B N =∪ n≥N Eₙ. The sets B N decrease, and their intersection is null by almost-everywhere convergence. Continuity from above of finite measures gives μ(B N )→0. For n≥N, split the integral of |fₙ−f| over B N and its complement. On the complement the difference is at most η; on B N it is at most 2M almost everywhere. Hence ∫|fₙ−f|≤ημ(X)+2Mμ(B N ). First choose η small, then N large: the right side tends to zero. Therefore |∫fₙ−∫f|≤∫|fₙ−f|→0. This argument uses continuity from above, a standard measure lemma: if A₁⊇A₂⊇… and μ(A₁)<∞, then μ(∩Aₙ)=lim μ(Aₙ). It follows from countable additivity by partitioning A₁ into disjoint losses, but that foundational proof is outside this short gateway. We have proved the special case conditional on that lemma, not the general theorem. For arbitrary integrable g, the usual proof needs Fatou’s lemma or equivalent machinery to control nonconstant tails. The finite-measure condition in the special case matters. On ℝ, hₙ=1 [n,n+1] tends pointwise to zero and is bounded by 1, but ∫hₙ=1. Here μ(ℝ)=∞ and constant 1 is not integrable. This is another honest failure case, distinct from the shrinking spike. Check every hypothesis 1. Classify. On [0,1], let uₙ(x)=xⁿ. Does dominated convergence justify passing the limit through the integral? Compute both sides. Hint Use the constant bound 1 and remember the exceptional endpoint x=1. Worked solution Each uₙ is measurable, 0≤uₙ≤1, and g=1 is integrable on [0,1] with integral one. For x<1, xⁿ→0; at x=1 the limit is one. The limit is zero almost everywhere because {1} is null. Dominated convergence gives ∫uₙ→0, matching the direct integral ∫₀¹xⁿdx=1/(n+1)→0. Its pointwise limit has integral zero. 2. Find the missing assumption. On ℝ, let vₙ=1 [n,n+1] . Which dominated-convergence condition fails, and why does |vₙ|≤1 not fix it? Hint Ask whether the constant function one belongs to L¹(ℝ). Worked solution The functions are measurable and converge pointwise to zero, but 1 has infinite integral over ℝ, so it is not a valid L¹ dominator. In fact no integrable common dominator can exist: if g≥vₙ almost everywhere for each n, countable union of null exceptions aside, g≥1 on every [n,n+1], n≥1. Thus ∫g≥Σ n≥1 1=∞. Each ∫vₙ=1, so the conclusion would fail. A bound must carry finite total mass Pointwise settling is not enough for integral convergence. A shared integrable envelope rules out mass hiding in shrinking or escaping regions. We proved a bounded finite-measure case with a stated measure lemma and applied the full theorem as a named result; the full proof and measure construction belong to a longer course.

title: A corner that defeats the derivative
summary: Compare both sides of a corner and separate continuity from differentiability.
text: What does a corner do to a rate? The graph of |x| is an upright V. It is continuous at zero: its height tends to zero from either direction, matching its value there. Yet a traveller following this height graph changes direction abruptly. Can a single slope describe the graph exactly at the turn? Background capsule. Absolute value |x| is distance from zero, so |x| = x when x ≥ 0 and |x| = −x when x < 0. A secant slope divides change in height by a nonzero horizontal step. A derivative at a is the limit of these slopes as the step tends to zero through both positive and negative values. One-sided limits inspect only one direction. A two-sided limit exists only when the two one-sided limits agree. Try equal steps on opposite sides Worked example. At the origin the base point is (0,0). With step h = 1/4, the second point is (1/4,1/4), and the slope is 1. With h = −1/4, the second point is (−1/4,1/4), and the slope is −1. Shrinking either step to one thousandth changes neither answer. The values do not drift towards one another. Secants through the origin Step h Height |h| Slope |h|/h 1/4 1/4 1 1/1000 1/1000 1 −1/4 1/4 −1 −1/1000 1/1000 −1 The same calculation applies to any positive or negative nonzero step, so the table illustrates an exact fact rather than supplying the proof. Notice the height is always positive but the slope is signed: moving rightwards from a negative x to zero goes downhill. Check a point beside the corner. At a=1/10 choose |h|<1/20. Then a+h is still positive, so [|a+h|−|a|]/h=h/h=1. The small interval around a stays entirely on one straight branch, which proves the derivative there. At zero no positive radius can exclude both branches: every neighborhood contains positive and negative inputs. The issue is therefore local geometry at the chosen base point. Translating the V changes the location of its exceptional point; multiplying its height by a nonzero constant changes the one-sided slopes but does not make them agree. The precise obstruction Statement. The function f(x)=|x| is continuous at zero but has no ordinary derivative there. Its right derivative is 1 and its left derivative is −1. | h | − 0 h = 1 h > 0 − 1 h < 0 Proof. On the positive side, |h|=h, so the quotient is h/h=1. On the negative side, |h|=−h, so the quotient is −h/h=−1. If a two-sided limit L existed, choosing positive steps arbitrarily close to zero would force L=1, while choosing negative steps would force L=−1. One real number cannot equal both. For continuity, however, ||h|−|0||=|h|. Given any tolerance ε>0, every |h|<ε makes the height error less than ε. These are different tests. Elsewhere the graph has an ordinary derivative: for a>0, a sufficiently small neighbourhood stays positive and f(x)=x there, giving slope 1; for a<0 it stays negative and f(x)=−x, giving −1. The corner is one exceptional point, not a claim that absolute value is nowhere differentiable. A function with a derivative at a must be continuous there. Indeed, f(a+h)−f(a)=h[(f(a+h)−f(a))/h], and the bracket approaches a finite derivative while h approaches zero. The converse fails here. The argument presumes a finite derivative and a point in the function's domain; it does not turn an infinite one-sided slope into an ordinary derivative. Test the definition yourself 1. Calculate. Let g(x)=|x−2|. Find the left and right secant slopes at x=2, then decide whether g′(2) exists. Hint for 1 Replace x with 2+h. Divide g(2+h)−g(2) by h. Worked solution for 1 g(2+h)=|h| and g(2)=0. Thus the quotient is |h|/h. For h>0 it equals 1; for h<0 it equals −1. Both one-sided limits exist but differ, so g′(2) does not exist. 2. Explain. The function q(x)=x|x| has a V-shaped ingredient. Is it differentiable at zero? This tests whether the mere appearance of an absolute-value symbol settles the matter. Hint for 2 Write the difference quotient at zero before inspecting signs. Worked solution for 2 q(0)=0, so [q(h)−q(0)]/h=|h| for every h≠0. Since |h| tends to zero from both sides, q′(0)=0. The absolute-value factor is multiplied by x; this flattens the graph enough for a derivative. A visual cue alone is not a proof. A boundary worth remembering The derivative is a two-sided promise about secant slopes. Continuity only controls heights. At a corner, both height limits agree while slope limits disagree. For a nearby positive point, the formula changes back to an ordinary slope of 1; the failure is localized at the meeting point. Next, ask what happens when a change in one quantity drives a second change through a composed function.

title: The chain rule as two magnifying lenses
summary: Multiply local conversion rates through a composition, including when the inner increment vanishes.
text: What happens when one change passes through another? Imagine the temperature of a liquid depends on time, and a sensor's voltage depends on temperature. Voltage changes with time even though its formula names temperature, not time. The chain rule says the two local conversion rates multiply, evaluated at the right places. Background capsule. A composition f(g(t)) first computes g(t), then feeds that result into f. The derivative g′(t) is the limiting ratio of output change to input change. In units, if g maps seconds to degrees and f maps degrees to volts, their derivative product has volts per second. Differentiability means a finite derivative exists at the point in question. We use a local linear approximation with an error small relative to the input change, written o(h): a remainder r(h) is o(h) if r(h)/h tends to zero. Two lenses on one example Worked example. Let temperature be T(t)=20+t² degrees and voltage be V(T)=T³/1000 volts. At t=2, temperature is 24 degrees. The temperature rate is 2t=4 degrees per second. The voltage sensitivity at 24 degrees is 3(24)²/1000=1.728 volts per degree. Multiplication predicts 6.912 volts per second. This is a local rate, not the voltage change over an entire second. Check with a short step h=0.01. The new temperature is 24.0401, an increase of 0.0401, close to 4h=0.04. The voltage change is approximately 1.728×0.0401=0.0692928, with a small curvature correction. Dividing by h gives a slope near 6.912. At smaller steps the correction, after division by h, disappears. The units cancel correctly: volts/degree times degrees/second becomes volts/second. A simpler exact example is f(u)=u² and g(t)=3t−1. At t=2, g=5 and g′=3; f′(5)=10, so the composed rate is 30. Direct expansion, (3t−1)²=9t²−6t+1, has derivative 18t−6=30 at t=2. The rule and a safe derivation Statement. If g is differentiable at t and f is differentiable at g(t), then f∘g is differentiable at t and its derivative is the product below. Both hypotheses matter. No inverse of g is required, and g′(t) may be zero. ( f ∘ g ) ′ ( t ) = f ′ ( g ( t ) ) g ′ ( t ) Derivation. Put y=g(t) and k=g(t+h)−g(t). Differentiability of f at y means f(y+k)−f(y)=f′(y)k+r(k), where r(k)/k→0 as k→0, and define r(0)=0. Differentiability of g gives k=g′(t)h+s(h) with s(h)/h→0. Also k/h→g′(t), so k/h is bounded near zero. Divide the composition's increment by h: f′(y)[k/h]+[r(k)/h]. The first term tends to f′(y)g′(t). If k≠0, the second is [r(k)/k][k/h]→0; if k=0, it equals zero by our definition. This avoids dividing by a possibly zero k. Thus the limit exists and equals the displayed product.
