The rule does not assert that a composition must fail when an ingredient lacks a derivative. For example, f(u)=u² and g(t)=|t| give f(g(t))=t², differentiable even at zero. The stated hypotheses are sufficient, not necessary. Conversely, a numerical product of guessed rates is not evidence that either defining limit exists. Check placement and hypotheses 1. Calculate. For H(t)=(1+t²)³, find H′(2) and explain the units if t is minutes and H is millilitres. Hint for 1 Use g(t)=1+t² and f(u)=u³; evaluate f′ at g(2), not at 2. Worked solution for 1 g(2)=5 and g′(2)=4. Since f′(u)=3u², f′(5)=75. Therefore H′(2)=75×4=300 millilitres per minute. Direct differentiation of (1+t²)³ gives 3(1+t²)²(2t), the same value. 2. Explain. Let f(u)=|u| and g(t)=t². Why is f(g(t)) differentiable at zero even though f′(0) does not exist? Hint for 2 First simplify the composition for real t. Then compute its difference quotient. Worked solution for 2 Since t²≥0, f(g(t))=|t²|=t². Its quotient at zero is h²/h=h→0, so its derivative is zero. The chain-rule hypotheses do not hold because f is not differentiable at g(0)=0. We did not apply the formula; we proved the composition's derivative directly. Multiply local conversions For a differentiable composition, the outer sensitivity is evaluated at the current inner output and multiplied by the inner rate. The local-remainder proof covers inner changes that vanish for some steps. A global change over a large interval can differ from this local prediction; curvature accumulates. The next bridge asks how a continuously changing rate relates to accumulated input.

title: Why accumulation undoes differentiation
summary: Bound a short accumulated strip to prove its derivative equals the current continuous input.
text: If a quantity accumulates, what is its current rate? Let rain fall at a changing rate f(t). The total rain collected by time x is the area under the rate graph from a starting time a to x. A thin additional time interval should add roughly its width times the rate at x. The first fundamental theorem of calculus makes that intuition exact when the input is continuous. Background capsule. A definite integral ∫ from a to b of f(t)dt is the limit of signed rectangle sums when that limit exists. For a nonnegative rate, it is an area; for a rate that changes sign, positive and negative contributions cancel. A derivative of A at x is the limit of [A(x+h)−A(x)]/h for nonzero h approaching zero from both sides. Continuity of f at x says nearby values f(t) are arbitrarily close to f(x). Here a is fixed and x may vary inside an interval where f is integrable. A bowl that fills according to x² Worked example. Take f(t)=t² on [0,2] and define A(x)=∫ from 0 to x of t²dt. The rectangle-sum lesson gives A(x)=x³/3 for x≥0. At x=1, the accumulated amount is 1/3. At x=1.1, it is 1.331/3≈0.443667, an increment of 0.110333. Divide by 0.1 to get an average rate of about 1.10333. The current input at x=1 is exactly f(1)=1. The difference comes from the rate rising across that tenth of an interval. For a symmetric-looking but genuinely one-sided increment h=−0.1, A(0.9)=0.729/3=0.243, and [A(0.9)−A(1)]/(−0.1)=0.90333. The two average rates surround 1. As |h| shrinks, both tend to 1. The sign convention works: a negative increment means going backwards in accumulation, and division by a negative h returns a positive local rate. Do not confuse A(x) with f(x). The first stores everything from the starting point to x; the second is the input right now. Changing the starting point shifts A by a constant but does not change its interior derivative. A theorem from local bounds Statement (first fundamental theorem). Let f be Riemann integrable on an interval containing a and x, and continuous at the interior point x. Define A(y)=∫ from a to y of f(t)dt. Then A is differentiable at x and A′(x)=f(x). A familiar sufficient setup is f continuous on the entire interval. At endpoints, only the appropriate one-sided derivative is claimed. A ( x ) = ∫ a x f ( t ) d t ⇒ A ′ ( x ) = f ( x ) Proof. Additivity of the integral gives A(x+h)−A(x)=∫ from x to x+h of f(t)dt, including h<0 under signed orientation. Subtract f(x)h and divide by h. Given ε>0, continuity at x supplies δ>0 such that |f(t)−f(x)|<ε whenever |t−x|<δ. For 0<|h|<δ, every t between x and x+h satisfies this bound, so the integral of the deviation has absolute value at most ε|h|. The quotient's error is therefore at most ε, for either sign of h. This proves the derivative statement without assuming a graph looks smooth. The second fundamental theorem says something different: if f is continuous on [a,b], F is continuous on [a,b], differentiable on (a,b), and F′=f there, then ∫ from a to b f=F(b)−F(a). It follows here because A is one antiderivative and two antiderivatives differ by a constant on an interval, using the mean value theorem. We do not need this consequence to prove the local statement above. Boundary. Continuity at the point matters. Let f(t)=0 for t<0 and f(t)=1 for t≥0, with A(x)=∫ from −1 to x f(t)dt. At x=0, A is constant to the left and rises with slope 1 to the right; A′(0) does not exist. The integral still exists. Merely being integrable does not force a derivative at every point. Rates from accumulated input 1. Calculate. Define B(x)=∫ from 2 to x (3+t²)dt. Find B(2), B′(2), and B(3). Hint for 1 The interval from 2 to 2 has zero width. For B(3), integrate the constant and t² separately. Worked solution for 1 B(2)=0. The input is continuous, so B′(2)=3+2²=7. For B(3), ∫₂³3dt=3 and ∫₂³t²dt=(27−8)/3=19/3. Thus B(3)=28/3. The average input over [2,3] is 28/3, larger than its initial value 7 because t² increases. 2. Explain. If f(t)=|t| and C(x)=∫ from −1 to x f(t)dt, does the corner in f prevent C′(0)? Hint for 2 The theorem requires continuity of f, not differentiability of f. Worked solution for 2 No. |t| is continuous at zero even though its derivative there fails. Therefore C′(0)=f(0)=0. Directly, for h>0 the added area is h²/2; for h<0 it is the negative of the area over [h,0], namely −h²/2. Dividing by h gives |h|/2 in both cases, which tends to zero. Accumulation remembers; differentiation asks now For an integrable input continuous at x, a short accumulated increment differs from f(x)h by less than any chosen fraction of |h| once h is small enough. That is the precise bridge between area and rate. A jump in the input can break differentiability of the accumulation at the jump. Explore the mean value theorem next if you want a complementary statement: an average change must be attained as a local rate somewhere.

title: The average speed you must have reached
summary: Turn a secant slope into an attained tangent slope by Rolle's theorem.
text: Must an average rate occur somewhere exactly? A vehicle travels 120 kilometres in two hours. Its average velocity is 60 kilometres per hour. If position changed continuously and had an instantaneous velocity at every interior time, must its velocity have equalled 60 at least once? The mean value theorem answers yes, even when the velocity varies wildly. Background capsule. A secant slope between (a,f(a)) and (b,f(b)) is [f(b)−f(a)]/(b−a), with a<b. A derivative f′(c) is the local secant limit at interior c. Continuity on [a,b] includes both endpoints; differentiability is required only on (a,b). A continuous function on a closed bounded interval attains a maximum and minimum. At an interior local maximum or minimum where it is differentiable, the derivative is zero: right-hand secants and left-hand secants have opposite allowable signs, so their common limit is zero. A curving journey Worked example. Take position s(t)=t² kilometres over t from 1 to 3 hours. The change is 9−1=8 kilometres over 2 hours, so average velocity is 4 kilometres per hour. Since s′(t)=2t, at t=2 the instantaneous velocity is exactly 4. This is not an accidental midpoint rule: for this quadratic and interval, algebra happens to put the matching point at the midpoint. Consider instead s(t)=t³ on [0,2]. Average velocity is (8−0)/2=4, while s′(t)=3t². The promised point is t=2/√3≈1.155, not the midpoint 1. The theorem promises existence, not an easy location or uniqueness. If the derivative has a plateau at the average slope, many matching points may occur. In both examples, position is continuous across the closed interval and differentiable in its interior. One cannot simply draw a line parallel to the secant and assume it touches: the proof needs hypotheses and a maximum principle. Subtract the secant, then apply Rolle Mean value theorem. If f is continuous on [a,b] and differentiable on (a,b), with a<b, then some c strictly between a and b satisfies the displayed equality. f ′ ( c ) = f ( b ) − f ( a ) b − a Proof boundary and derivation. First prove Rolle's special case: if q has the same endpoint value and meets the same continuity and differentiability conditions, then q′(c)=0 somewhere inside. If q is constant, any interior c works. Otherwise, the closed-interval extreme-value theorem puts a maximum or minimum different from the common endpoint value at an interior point. Fermat's local-extremum argument in the capsule makes its derivative zero. This derivation invokes the extreme-value theorem; its proof from completeness of the real numbers is outside this lesson. Now put m=[f(b)−f(a)]/(b−a) and q(x)=f(x)−m(x−a). Then q(b)=f(b)−[f(b)−f(a)]=f(a)=q(a). Rolle gives q′(c)=0. Since q′(c)=f′(c)−m, the promised equality follows. The endpoint hypotheses ensure Rolle applies; the interior derivative hypothesis makes the final equation meaningful. Failure case. f(x)=|x| on [−1,1] has equal endpoint values, so its average slope is zero. Its interior derivatives are −1 on the negative side and 1 on the positive side; at zero no derivative exists. There is no c with derivative zero. Continuity alone cannot replace differentiability. A jump at an endpoint can likewise defeat the theorem if closed-interval continuity is dropped. Find and test the promised point 1. Calculate. For f(x)=x²+2x on [0,2], find the average slope and every interior c at which f′(c) equals it. Hint for 1 Compute f(0), f(2), then solve 2c+2=m. Worked solution for 1 f(0)=0 and f(2)=8, so m=(8−0)/2=4. The derivative is 2x+2. Setting 2c+2=4 gives c=1, which lies strictly between 0 and 2. Thus it satisfies the theorem. 2. Explain. A function equals x on [0,1) but is assigned f(1)=3. The average slope on [0,1] is 3. Why is there no contradiction when f′(x)=1 at every interior x? Hint for 2 Check the endpoint limit at x=1 against the assigned value. Worked solution for 2 f(0)=0 and f(1)=3, hence the average slope is 3. On (0,1), f′=1, so it never equals 3. But as x approaches 1 from the left, f(x) approaches 1, not f(1)=3. The function is not continuous on the closed interval, so the theorem's first hypothesis fails. An existence promise with exact conditions Subtract the average-rate line and a zero-derivative point appears through Rolle's theorem. The result certifies that some local rate matches a secant rate; it does not identify a unique point or say the midpoint works. Corners and endpoint jumps show why the hypotheses belong in the statement. A useful next application is comparing derivatives to bound how far a function can change.

title: Substitution is a change of ruler
summary: Track transformed widths and oriented endpoints in definite integration.
text: When you change the input, what happens to the width? Substitution is often presented as replacing symbols in an integral. Its real content is accounting for how a new input changes with the old one. If u=g(t), then a small change in t produces approximately g′(t) times that change in u. The endpoints move too, and their order carries orientation. Background capsule. The chain rule differentiates F(g(t)) as F′(g(t))g′(t). A definite integral from a to b is signed: reversing endpoints changes its sign. For continuous f, the fundamental theorem supplies an antiderivative F(u)=∫ from a chosen base point to u of f(v)dv with F′=f. A continuously differentiable g has a continuous derivative on the interval, enough for the calculations here. No one-to-one condition is required for the formula we will prove. A doubling and a reversal Worked example. Compute ∫ from 0 to 1 of 2t(1+t²)³dt. Choose u=1+t². Then du/dt=2t, exactly the factor outside the cube. At t=0, u=1; at t=1, u=2. The answer is ∫ from 1 to 2 of u³du=[u⁴/4] from 1 to 2=(16−1)/4=15/4. Keeping t endpoints 0 and 1 after changing the integrand to u³ would silently calculate a different integral. Now take g(t)=1−t on [0,1], and f(u)=u². The transformed integrand is (1−t)²(−1). Its integral is −1/3. The right side has endpoints g(0)=1 and g(1)=0, so ∫ from 1 to 0 of u²du=−1/3. The negative derivative and reversed endpoints agree. If the task instead asks for ∫₀¹(1−t)²dt, move the minus sign explicitly: its value is +1/3. The orientation check is useful before any algebra: a positive integrand over increasing t cannot acquire a negative answer merely because a substitution reverses its coordinates. Check the ruler in a small example. Set u=2t on 0≤t≤1 and integrate f(u)=u. The original integral is ∫₀¹(2t)·2 dt=2; the transformed integral is ∫₀²u du=2. Omitting the derivative factor would give 1, exactly half the answer. The interval in u is twice as long as the interval in t, and g′=2 accounts for that stretch. The endpoint calculation and the width calculation are separate parts of the same substitution. The definite substitution formula Statement. Let f be continuous on an interval containing the values g(t) for a≤t≤b, and let g be continuously differentiable on [a,b]. Then the following equality holds, even if g reverses direction or revisits a value: ∫ a b f ( g ( t ) ) g ′ ( t ) d t = ∫ g ( a ) g ( b ) f ( u ) d u Derivation. Set F(u)=∫ from a fixed u₀ to u of f(v)dv. Continuity of f makes F′(u)=f(u). By the chain rule, d[F(g(t))]/dt=f(g(t))g′(t). The integral of this derivative from a to b is F(g(b))−F(g(a)); by the second fundamental theorem, this difference is ∫ from g(a) to g(b) of f(u)du. This proof uses the fundamental theorem and chain rule under the stated regularity. It does not rely on counting stretched rectangles one by one. If g goes forward then backward, some contributions cancel. For example, g(t)=t² on [−1,1] has g(−1)=g(1)=1, so ∫ from −1 to 1 of 2t f(t²)dt=0 for continuous f. The formula captures the signed cancellation. It is not the same as an unsigned area change-of-variables formula, where multiple coverings and absolute values require different bookkeeping. Boundary. Omitting g′ generally fails: ∫₀¹(1+t²)³dt cannot be replaced by ∫₁²u³du, because du is not dt. Likewise, a discontinuous f can fall outside this proof even if a more general substitution result remains true. State the version you use. Keep the limits attached 1. Calculate. Evaluate ∫ from 0 to 2 of 3(3t+1)²dt by substitution. Hint for 1 Set u=3t+1; compute both transformed endpoints. Worked solution for 1 du=3dt, while t=0 gives u=1 and t=2 gives u=7. The integral becomes ∫₁⁷u²du=[u³/3]₁⁷=(343−1)/3=114. The result is positive, as the original integrand is nonnegative. 2. Explain. Let g(t)=t² on [−1,1] and f(u)=1. A learner writes ∫ from −1 to 1 of 2t dt=∫₀¹1du=1. Locate the error and calculate the correct value. Hint for 2 Both t endpoints map to the same u endpoint. Worked solution for 2 g(−1)=1 and g(1)=1, so the transformed integral runs from 1 to 1 and equals zero. Directly, ∫₋₁¹2t dt=[t²]₋₁¹=1−1=0. The learner kept only the forward trip from t=0 to 1 and lost the backward trip from t=−1 to 0. Change the width and the endpoints together The derivative g′ accounts for signed local stretching, and g(a),g(b) account for the new endpoint labels. The proof is an application of chain rule plus fundamental theorem; an invertible substitution is a convenient special case, not a necessary assumption. When solving a fresh problem, write the endpoint map before evaluating the antiderivative.

title: An infinite journey with finite area
summary: Classify power-tail integrals by computing finite cutoffs and taking limits.
text: Can a region stretch forever and still have finite area? The region under y=1/x² from x=1 to the right never ends. Nevertheless, each successive stretch contributes less area. The word “infinite” describes its horizontal extent, not automatically its area. An improper integral answers the area question by first stopping at a finite cutoff and then taking a limit. Background capsule. For finite R>1, ordinary integration gives a number ∫ from 1 to R of f(x)dx. We define ∫ from 1 to infinity of f(x)dx as the limit of those numbers as R→∞, if the limit is finite. If no finite limit exists, the improper integral diverges. For p≠1, an antiderivative of x −p is x 1−p /(1−p); for p=1 it is ln x. The logarithm grows without bound as x→∞. Watch the cutoff move Worked example. For p=2, ∫₁ᴿx −2 dx=[−1/x]₁ᴿ=1−1/R. At R=2 the area is 1/2; at R=10 it is 9/10; at R=100 it is 99/100. Each finite area is less than 1, and the missing tail is exactly 1/R. The limiting area is 1. Area beneath 1/x² through a finite cutoff R Area 1−1/R Area still beyond R 2 1/2 1/2 10 9/10 1/10 100 99/100 1/100 By contrast, for y=1/x, the area through R is ln R. It keeps increasing with no finite ceiling, though very slowly. A plot through x=100 may make the two curves look similarly close to zero. Their total areas behave differently, so a finite window cannot settle convergence. Choose a cutoff for a requested accuracy. For the worked p=2 curve, stopping at R gives 1−1/R, so an absolute tail below 0.001 requires R>1000. This is an exact certificate even though we never draw the infinite remainder. For p=3/2 the tail is 2/√R; the same requirement instead needs R>4,000,000. Both integrals converge, yet their tails decay at very different rates. The yes-or-no convergence classification does not by itself tell us how much finite computation is needed for a desired accuracy. The p threshold Statement. For real p, the improper integral ∫ from 1 to infinity of x −p dx converges exactly when p>1, and then equals 1/(p−1). For p≤1 it diverges to positive infinity. These claims concern this nonnegative power family on this interval. ∫ 1 ∞ x − p d x = 1 p − 1 when p > 1 Proof. For p≠1, integrate only to finite R: ∫₁ᴿx −p dx=(R 1−p −1)/(1−p). If p>1, then 1−p<0, so R 1−p =1/R p−1 tends to zero. The limit is 1/(p−1). If p<1, the positive power R 1−p grows without bound; division by the positive 1−p preserves that divergence. At p=1 the finite expression is ln R, which also tends to infinity. The exceptional logarithm case cannot be obtained by substituting p=1 into the power antiderivative, where its denominator vanishes. Why is the limit a legitimate definition? Every finite cutoff includes only a bounded interval where the integrand is continuous and ordinarily integrable. The infinite interval itself is not an ordinary Riemann interval. Taking the cutoff limit is an additional operation, and its existence must be checked. For nonnegative x −p , finite areas increase with R, so either they approach a finite ceiling or grow without bound; oscillatory signed examples require more care. Boundary. A function can approach zero and still have infinite area: 1/x is the counterexample. The size of individual heights does not answer the accumulation question. Conversely, convergence of this area does not imply that the region has finite horizontal length; its x-range remains unbounded. Classify before calculating 1. Calculate. Find ∫ from 1 to infinity of x −3/2 dx, and find the area beyond R=16. Hint for 1 Here p=3/2. Use the finite cutoff formula to isolate the tail. Worked solution for 1 The total is 1/(3/2−1)=2. The area from 1 to R is 2(1−R −1/2 ), so the remaining tail is 2R −1/2 . At R=16 it is 2/4=1/2; the area through 16 is therefore 3/2. 2. Explain. Does ∫ from 1 to infinity of 1/√x converge because its integrand tends to zero? Hint for 2 Identify p in x −p and compute through finite R. Worked solution for 2 No. Here p=1/2≤1. Its finite integral is [2√x]₁ᴿ=2√R−2, which grows without bound as R→∞. The integrand tends to zero, but the shrinking is too slow for finite accumulated area. Infinity enters only through a limit The p-test threshold follows from a finite antiderivative and a cutoff limit. Convergence means the total area approaches a finite value; it does not mean the curve reaches zero or the region stops. Whenever you see an infinite endpoint, replace it by R, calculate, then justify the limit. A later course may compare less elementary tails with this family.

title: A polynomial approximation with an error receipt
summary: Certify a sine approximation with a derivative bound and an integral remainder.
text: How much can a polynomial approximation miss? A polynomial is easy to evaluate, so it is tempting to replace sin x by x near zero. But “near” is vague until we know how large the error can be. Taylor's theorem attaches a bound to a polynomial built from derivatives. We will make a concrete certified approximation and explain the theorem's hypotheses. Background capsule. The n-th Taylor polynomial of f at a is Pₙ(x)=Σ from k=0 to n of f (k) (a)(x−a) k /k!. Here k! is the product 1·2·…·k, with 0!=1. The residual Rₙ(x)=f(x)−Pₙ(x) is the actual error, which may be positive or negative. A bound on |Rₙ| is a guarantee. We use derivatives and the fundamental theorem; the proof below establishes an integral remainder when f has enough continuous derivatives, while the familiar Lagrange form needs its own theorem. A numerical receipt for sin x Worked example. At a=0, sin 0=0, cos 0=1, the second derivative −sin is zero, and the third derivative −cos is −1. The cubic Taylor polynomial is P₃(x)=x−x³/6. At x=0.5 it gives 0.5−0.125/6≈0.4791667. The true sin(0.5) is about 0.4794255, so the actual error is about 0.0002589. For a certified bound, use the fourth derivative sin x. Its absolute value is at most 1 everywhere, giving |R₃(0.5)|≤0.5⁴/4!=0.0625/24≈0.0026042. This is valid but loose. A tighter receipt notices that the fourth derivative sin t is at most |t| for t between 0 and 0.5, because |sin t|≤|t|; integrating that sharper envelope produces an error ≤0.5⁵/5!≈0.00026042. The observed error lies below it, close to the certificate. The first bound is enough for correctness. The sharper one matters if we promise three decimal places: 0.00026042 is less than 0.0005, so rounding P₃(0.5) to three decimals gives the same rounded result as sin(0.5), provided the rounded value is not near a midpoint. Here P₃ rounds to 0.479 and the error interval stays below 0.479427, so it remains below 0.4795. Where the bound comes from Statement. Suppose f has continuous derivatives through order n+1 on the interval between a and x, and |f (n+1) (t)|≤M there. Then its Taylor polynomial Pₙ at a satisfies the displayed error bound. For x<a, interpret the interval between them with the same absolute length. | f ( x ) − P n ( x ) | ≤ M | x − a | n + 1 ( n + 1 ) ! Integral-remainder proof for x≥a. The fundamental theorem gives the base case R₀(x)=f(x)−f(a)=∫ₐˣf′(t)dt. Suppose R n−1 (x)=1/(n−1)! times ∫ₐˣf (n) (t)(x−t) n−1 dt. Integrate I=1/n! times ∫ₐˣf (n+1) (t)(x−t) n dt by parts: the boundary term is −f (n) (a)(x−a) n /n!, and the remaining integral is R n−1 . Thus I=R n−1 −f (n) (a)(x−a) n /n!=Rₙ. This establishes the formula f(x)=Pₙ(x)+I. Taking absolute values and using |f (n+1) |≤M gives |Rₙ|≤(M/n!)∫ₐˣ(x−t) n dt=M(x−a) n+1 /(n+1)!. Reversing the oriented interval gives the same absolute bound for x<a. This is a derivation under continuous-derivative assumptions, not a proof for every function that happens to have n derivatives at a. For x≠a, under the stated continuous-derivative assumptions, the Lagrange statement also says Rₙ=f (n+1) (ξ)(x−a) n+1 /(n+1)! for some ξ strictly between a and x. At x=a the remainder is zero directly. We do not need to locate ξ or assert it is unique. The integral proof supplies the bound directly. It also reveals that a small bound depends jointly on a small interval and control of a higher derivative. Boundary. Having many derivatives at one point alone gives no uniform M on a surrounding interval. Even derivatives of every order at a do not by themselves guarantee the infinite Taylor series equals f nearby; the next lesson gives an exact counterexample. Compute and certify 1. Calculate. Use P₂(x)=1+x+x²/2 for eˣ at x=0.2. Give a valid error bound using M=e 0.2 <1.23 for the third derivative on [0,0.2]. Hint for 1 Substitute x=0.2 and n=2 into M|x|³/3!. Worked solution for 1 P₂(0.2)=1+0.2+0.04/2=1.22. The bound is 1.23×0.2³/6=1.23×0.008/6=0.00164. Hence e 0.2 lies between 1.21836 and 1.22164; since its third derivative is positive, the integral remainder is positive and the sharper one-sided interval is [1.22,1.22164]. 2. Explain. If |f (4) |≤5 on [0,1], can a cubic Taylor approximation at zero miss f(1) by more than 1/4? Hint for 2 Use n=3, M=5 and |x−a|=1. Worked solution for 2 No, provided f has the required continuous derivatives. The theorem gives |R₃(1)|≤5·1⁴/4!=5/24≈0.2083, which is less than 1/4. The sign of the error is not determined by the absolute derivative bound alone. A receipt has assumptions A Taylor polynomial matches derivatives at its centre; the remainder theorem controls how far that matching reaches when a higher derivative is bounded over the whole interval. A finite-degree error bound says nothing by itself about the limit as degree tends to infinity. To claim an infinite Taylor series recovers a function, show the residual tends to zero.

title: A smooth function its Taylor series misses
summary: Show that all derivatives can vanish at a point while the function stays positive nearby.
text: Can every derivative miss a positive function? Knowing every derivative at a point sounds like complete local knowledge. It is not. We will build a function that is positive on either side of zero yet whose value and every derivative at zero vanish. Its Taylor series at zero is therefore identically zero and disagrees with the function at every nearby nonzero point. Background capsule. A function is smooth if derivatives of every finite order exist and are continuous. It is analytic at zero if it agrees with its Taylor power series on some open interval around zero. Smoothness concerns each fixed derivative; analyticity also requires an infinite sequence of approximations to converge to the function. We write e u for the exponential and use that e y grows faster than any fixed power y m as y→∞. A short proof of the needed estimate appears below. An almost invisible bump at the origin Worked example. Define f(0)=0 and f(x)=exp(−1/x²) when x≠0. This f is positive at every nonzero real x. Yet f(0.5)=e −4 ≈0.0183 and f(0.2)=e −25 ≈1.39×10 −11 . A normal-scale graph near zero may look flat on the axis. That image cannot decide whether f actually vanishes there; the formula says it does not. Start with the first derivative at zero. The quotient [f(h)−f(0)]/h=e −1/h² /h. Its absolute value becomes √y e −y after putting y=1/h². This tends to zero, so f′(0)=0. Away from zero, ordinary chain rule gives f′(x)=2x −3 e −1/x² . This derivative also approaches zero at zero despite its factor x −3 , because the exponential wins. Repeat differentiation: each derivative away from zero is a finite sum of integer powers of x −1 times e −1/x² . The powers become larger, but for each fixed differentiation order there are only finitely many of them. Each term still tends to zero. That is the mechanism behind complete flatness. Why all coefficients vanish Statement. The displayed function is smooth on the whole real line and f (n) (0)=0 for every integer n≥0. Its Taylor series at zero is zero for every x, while f(x)>0 when x≠0. Hence f is not analytic at zero. f ( x ) = e − 1 / x 2 x ≠ 0 0 x = 0 ⇒ f ( n ) ( 0 ) = 0 Dominance lemma. For every fixed q≥0, y q e −y →0 as y→∞. Choose an integer m>q. Since e y ≥y m /m! for y>0 by the positive exponential series, 0≤y q e −y ≤m! y q−m →0. Thus for every fixed positive integer k, |x| −k e −1/x² →0 as x→0 by y=1/x². This is the exact estimate needed; saying “exponentials win” alone would not prove it. Induction. At x≠0, write the n-th derivative as Pₙ(1/x)e −1/x² , where Pₙ is a polynomial. This holds for n=0 with P₀=1. Differentiating once gives e −1/x² [−x −2 Pₙ′(1/x)+2x −3 Pₙ(1/x)], again a polynomial in 1/x times the exponential. The dominance lemma makes this expression tend to zero as x→0. Assume the derivative f (n) (0) is zero. Its derivative at zero is the limit of f (n) (h)/h; that quotient is again a finite sum of negative powers of h times the exponential, so the lemma makes it zero. Induction establishes every derivative at zero and continuity of each derivative there. Every Taylor coefficient f (n) (0)/n! is zero. Therefore every finite Taylor polynomial and the infinite series sum are zero. For any neighbourhood of zero, choose x≠0 inside it: f(x)=e −1/x² >0. The disagreement proves nonanalyticity. This example does not contradict finite Taylor bounds: for each fixed order a suitable residual bound exists, but controlling all orders uniformly as n grows is another question. Use the mechanism, not the picture 1. Calculate. For h(x)=x −4 e −1/x² when x≠0, find its limit at zero and justify it with the lemma. Hint for 1 Put y=1/x², so x −4 =y². Worked solution for 1 h(x)=y²e −y with y→∞. Choose m=3 in the lemma: 0≤y²e −y ≤3!/y=6/y→0. Hence h(x)→0 from both sides. 2. Explain. Does the fact that all Taylor coefficients of f at zero vanish imply f is zero on (−0.1,0.1)? Give an exact witness. Hint for 2 Choose any nonzero number in that interval and inspect the defining formula. Worked solution for 2 No. At x=1/20=0.05, f(x)=e −400 , which is strictly positive, though extremely small. Its Taylor series still gives zero at x=1/20 because every coefficient is zero. The witness disproves equality on the interval without relying on numerical rounding. Smoothness has a strict boundary Each fixed derivative can be perfectly well behaved at zero while the whole infinite Taylor series misses the function. A plotted curve, finite jet of derivatives, or finite Taylor error bound cannot establish analyticity. To recover a function from its power series, one must separately prove that the residual tends to zero as the polynomial degree grows throughout a neighbourhood.

title: Who is missing from the sample?
summary: Separate target population, sampling frame and observed sample.
text: Which club members did the poll actually reach? A club polls only people who attend a meeting. The question is what the observed numbers allow us to say, and where the tempting shortcut fails. Background capsule. A percentage is a part divided by a stated whole. A population is the set about which the question is asked; a sampling frame is the list or mechanism from which people can be contacted. A sample is the people who actually supply data. These three sets need not coincide. Worked example A fictional drawing club has 100 members: 40 attend a Saturday meeting and 60 do not. Of the attendees, 30 prefer pencils; among nonattendees, only 12 do. A meeting-only poll sees 30 pencil votes among 40 responses, giving 75%. The whole club has 42 pencil preferences among 100 members, giving 42%. Both arithmetic statements are true. Only the latter describes all members in this invented census. The 33-point difference arose because attendance and preference were associated. Notice that 30/40 has a complete count of attendees in its denominator, while 42/100 has a complete count of members. The numerators differ because the latter includes twelve pencil preferences among the sixty people who did not attend. Calling both numbers “the club percentage” conceals the change in who was counted. The claim and its conditions pencil replies all replies = 30 40 = 0.75 Write I=1 when a member enters the sample and Y=1 when that member prefers pencils. The observed 30/40 estimates a preference among attendees, P(Y=1|I=1), if every attendee answers honestly. The club-wide quantity is P(Y=1). Equality would need a justified selection condition, such as the special fact that preference has the same rate inside and outside the frame. Simply increasing the number of Saturday respondents does not add absent members. A random draw from the attendees can reduce random fluctuation within that frame while leaving the frame mismatch intact. Nonresponse creates another selection stage: being invited is not the same as answering. Proof boundary and failure case. No universal adjustment follows from the meeting poll alone. If the 60 nonattendees could have any pencil rate from 0% to 100%, the population count could range from 30 to 90, hence the population proportion from 30% to 90%. The observed 75% therefore does not pin down the target. Weighting works only with credible group sizes and within-group measurements or assumptions. If the club selected members with unequal known inclusion chances, an appropriately weighted estimator could target the full membership without making the raw respondent rate equal the population rate. That still requires coverage, measured inclusion chances, and attention to nonresponse. In this example, no such design information is supplied, so the meeting fraction cannot be repaired by a formula alone. Optional 30–40 minute investigation: which denominator makes inverse weighting unbiased? A fixed population and a random sampling design The club example has no stated probability-sampling mechanism. We now supply one for a different, fully specified four-member population. The fixed outcomes are (y₁,y₂,y₃,y₄)=(1,1,0,0), so its fixed mean is ȳ=2/4=1/2. We reveal this small teaching census so we can check the estimators against their target. A real sample would reveal only the included members' outcomes. Extra background. A sampling design gives probabilities to possible subsets. Repeating that design hypothetically keeps every yᵢ fixed and varies which subset is observed. The design expectation E d [Z] is the probability-weighted average of an estimate Z across those possibilities. Its bias is E d [Z]−ȳ. Unbiased means that bias is zero; it does not mean every sample gives the right answer. Here there is no prior or posterior distribution on the outcomes. This expectation is over sample choices. Choose one of four equally likely tickets labelled 12, 12, 13, 24. Ticket 13 means sample members 1 and 3, without replacement, each counted once. The duplicate 12 tickets give the same subset twice as much probability: Pr(S={1,2})=1/2, while Pr(S={1,3})=Pr(S={2,4})=1/4. They do not create four different subsets or count any selected member twice. A member's inclusion chance is πᵢ=Pr(i∈S), obtained by adding the probabilities of all subsets containing that member. Thus π₁=π₂=3/4 and π₃=π₄=1/4. These are not the probabilities of the particular sampled subset. The inclusion chances add to 2, the fixed sample size, rather than to 1. Three estimators with two different denominators Let Ŷ=∑ i∈S yᵢ/πᵢ be the inverse-inclusion weighted total and N̂=∑ i∈S 1/πᵢ the corresponding estimate of population size. We know that the actual population size is N=4. Compare the ordinary sample mean R, the Horvitz–Thompson mean H that divides Ŷ by known N, and the normalized inverse-weight, or Hájek, mean A that divides Ŷ by random N̂. R = 1 2 ∑ i ∈ S y i , H = 1 4 ∑ i ∈ S y i π i , A = ∑ i ∈ S y i / π i ∑ i ∈ S 1 / π i Predict before inspecting. Will all three estimates have design expectation 1/2? For subset 12, does the weight sum equal the known population size? When you inspect another sample, which quantities should change and which must stay fixed? The exact four-ticket averages The raw estimates for subsets 12,13,24 are 1,1/2,1/2, so E d [R]=(1/2)1+(1/4)(1/2)+(1/4)(1/2)=3/4. Members with outcome 1 are more likely to be included. The HT estimates are 2/3,1/3,1/3; their expectation is (1/2)(2/3)+(1/4)(1/3)+(1/4)(1/3)=1/2. The normalized estimates are 1,1/4,1/4, giving E d [A]=1/2+1/16+1/16=5/8. Normalization produces a weighted average between the observed outcomes, but it changes the unbiasedness calculation. Here Ŷ takes values 8/3,4/3,4/3 with expectation 2; N̂ takes values 8/3,16/3,16/3 with expectation 4. The mean of their ratio is 5/8, while the ratio of their means is 2/4=1/2. A random denominator cannot generally be moved outside an expectation. Why the known-size HT mean is unbiased For a general fixed population of N members, assume each inclusion chance πᵢ is known and positive and each included outcome is measured. Let Iᵢ be 1 if member i is included and 0 otherwise. Since E d [Iᵢ]=πᵢ, linearity gives E d [ H ] = 1 N ∑ i = 1 N E d [ I i ] y i π i = 1 N ∑ i = 1 N y i = y ¯ No independence of the inclusion indicators is required. They are dependent here because every sample contains exactly two members. The actual πᵢ, not an arbitrary convenient set of weights, cancel the expectation. This proves a repeated-design property for every fixed outcome vector. It supplies no posterior probability statement after one sample. Accuracy needs a separate calculation. Mean squared error is MSE d (Z)=E d [(Z−ȳ)²]. In this teaching census, the full design gives MSE(R)=1/8, MSE(H)=1/36, and MSE(A)=5/32. Those are exact calculations from the revealed census and all possible samples. They are not variance estimates available from one realized sample. Exercise 3 changes the census and reverses which estimator has the smaller MSE. Coverage boundary. The proof needs πᵢ>0 for every member whose unknown outcome contributes to the target. If some are never observed, no inverse weight can recover their unrestricted outcomes. Also distinguish first-order inclusion πᵢ from pair inclusion πᵢⱼ=Pr(i and j both enter S). Here π₁₄=π₂₃=π₃₄=0. These zeros do not affect the first-order unbiasedness proof, but the usual sample-based unbiased variance formula involving division by πᵢⱼ cannot be used for those pairs. We make no such variance-estimation claim. Source scope. Zong, Zhu and Zou, §2 defines the finite-population HT total; dividing it by known N gives our mean. Their §4.1 constructs a ratio of HT totals; setting the auxiliary variable to one yields A. Oliva-Aviles, Meyer and Opsomer, equation (2.2) names that normalized estimator Hájek. We use its definition, without importing that paper's positive pair-inclusion or asymptotic assumptions. The finite design, calculations and exercises here are original. This fixed-population experiment differs from random hidden-bag draws , where dependence changes a sampling distribution, and from conditioning on a report , where likelihoods change posterior world weights. In the queue observation lesson , normalizing exact inverse-rate probability weights recovers an exact clock law. That identity for complete laws does not claim that a ratio computed from a finite sample is unbiased. Try two checks 1. Calculation. Suppose a club has 80 members, 20 attend, and 16 attending members say yes. Ten of the 60 absent members later say yes in a complete follow-up. Find the meeting rate and the club rate. Hint for exercise 1 Keep the two denominators separate: 20 for the meeting and 80 for the club. Full solution to exercise 1 The meeting rate is 16/20=80%. The complete club count is 16+10=26 yes responses, so the club rate is 26/80=32.5%. The meeting result is 47.5 percentage points higher. 2. Interpretation or counterexample. A second club polls every person on its email list, but the list excludes people who joined by paper form. Does a 100% response rate from the list ensure a representative estimate? Hint for exercise 2 Name the target population, frame, and response set. Full solution to exercise 2 No. The target includes every member, while the frame and response set contain only email-listed members. Perfect response removes nonresponse inside that frame; it cannot reveal the excluded members’ preferences. If paper-form members differ, the frame estimate differs from the club estimate. One further check is to bound the unknown total before accepting a claimed correction. With no data about absent members, at least the 30 known pencil preferences remain and at most all 60 absent people add to them. That yields the 30%–90% range, wide enough to include many different club stories. Two further tasks for the optional weighting investigation 3. Change the fixed population, keep the design. Set (y₁,y₂,y₃,y₄)=(1,0,1,0), still with samples 12,13,24 of probabilities 1/2,1/4,1/4. Without using an explorer preset, find the fixed target and all three estimator values for each sample. Compute each design expectation and MSE. Does an unbiased estimate of this population proportion have to lie in [0,1]? If H is clipped to 1 whenever it exceeds 1, what is its new expectation? Hint for exercise 3 The πᵢ stay unchanged. For sample 13 the weighted numerator is 1/(3/4)+1/(1/4)=16/3. Divide by known 4 for H and by the weight sum 16/3 for A. Square each error around the fixed target before averaging it with the design probabilities. Full solution to exercise 3 The new target is still (1+0+1+0)/4=1/2. In order 12,13,24, R takes values (1/2,1,0), H takes (1/3,4/3,0), and A takes (1/2,1,0). Thus E d [R]=E d [A]=(1/2)(1/2)+(1/4)1=1/2, and E d [H]=(1/2)(1/3)+(1/4)(4/3)=1/2. The raw and normalized estimators happen to be unbiased for this particular population. That does not prove unbiasedness for every fixed population; the original (1,1,0,0) already disproves it. MSE(R)=MSE(A)=(1/2)0²+(1/4)(1/2)²+(1/4)(−1/2)²=1/8. For H, MSE(H)=(1/2)(−1/6)²+(1/4)(5/6)²+(1/4)(−1/2)²=1/4. An unbiased estimator can have larger mean squared error than another estimator. The value H=4/3 is a possible estimate of the fixed proportion, not a probability assigned to an event; known-N inverse weighting is not constrained to be a convex average of observed outcomes. Clipping changes its three values to (1/3,1,0), whose expectation is 1/6+1/4=5/12. Clipping has destroyed unbiasedness. 4. A frame that never reaches two members. Change the design so the only possible sample is 12. The sample reveals y₁=y₂=1. Compare fixed populations (1,1,0,0) and (1,1,1,1). What are their means and inclusion probabilities? Could any estimator using only the observed sample and this design be unbiased for the population mean for every binary outcome vector? Explain rather than assigning infinite weights. Hint for exercise 4 Ask whether either possible population can change the observed data. An expectation over a design with one possible sample is the estimate for that sample. Full solution to exercise 4 The means are 1/2 and 1, while the design has π=(1,1,0,0) in either case. Every possible observation is identical: members 1 and 2 with outcomes 1 and 1. Any sample-only estimator therefore has the same value, and hence the same design expectation, under the two populations. It cannot equal both targets. Even adding independent randomization would give the same distribution under both populations. The missing outcomes are not identified from this frame without extra assumptions; dividing by zero cannot repair that missing information. This is the finite-population version of the original club's frame problem. What you can carry forward Before trusting a percentage, write down who could enter the numerator and denominator. This is a design question before it is a calculation question. The example establishes the possibility of selection bias, not its size in a real club. A useful next step is to plan a sampling frame that covers the target and record how invitation and response occur. The 75% estimate is perfectly accurate for the forty attendees because everyone there was counted. The error appears only when its label silently changes to all members. An honest report can state the narrow attendee result while seeking a better frame for the wider question.

title: One dataset, several histograms
summary: Explain how bin width changes a histogram without changing observations.
text: Can the same times have two different-looking shapes? Rebin a set of puzzle completion times. The question is what the observed numbers allow us to say, and where the tempting shortcut fails. Background capsule. A histogram groups numerical values into consecutive, nonoverlapping intervals called bins. Its vertical axis must name count, proportion, or density. A dotplot keeps each observation visible; a histogram sacrifices that detail to show grouped mass. Endpoints need an explicit convention so a value on a boundary belongs to exactly one bin. Worked example Ten imaginary puzzle times in minutes are 1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 4, 4, 8, 9. With one-minute bins [1,2), [2,3), and so on, the counts are 2, 2, 2, 2, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1. With wider bins [0,5) and [5,10), the counts are 8 and 2. The second picture looks like a steep two-bar decline; the first shows a four-bin shelf, a gap, then two late observations. Neither changed any time. A five-minute boundary at 5 happens to be easy here, but another origin could redistribute observations near edges. For these exact ten values, the two-minute cluster at 8 and 9 is separated from the eight values at 1 through 4 by empty one-minute bins. The broad [5,10) bin absorbs both late observations into one bar. A graph maker should disclose the bin edges so a reader can see that the gap was grouped away. Read a boundary explicitly. In [2,3), the left endpoint is included and the right endpoint is excluded. Both recorded times equal to 2 belong there, while neither time equal to 3 does. The next bin receives those observations instead. This convention prevents one observation contributing to two bars; it also lets someone reconstruct the tally from the displayed edges rather than guessing how boundary values were handled. The claim and its conditions f j = c j n , ∑ j k f j = 1 For equal-width bins, relative frequency is count in the bin divided by total count. The narrow [8,9) bin has one of ten observations, or 10%, and [9,10) has another 10%; [0,5) has eight, or 80%. Check conservation: the bin counts sum to ten because the intervals partition the listed observations. For unequal widths, bar height should be frequency density, count divided by width, if bar area is intended to represent count. Otherwise a broad bin can look deceptively tall merely because it covers more horizontal range. To compare two groups of unequal sample size, relative-frequency or density histograms are more useful than raw counts. Proof boundary and failure case. The partition identity is exact for the recorded data. Claims such as “this population has two modes” are not proved by changing bins in ten observations. Too few bins erase detail; too many make noise look like structure. Always inspect individual points or several reasonable bin widths before describing a smooth distribution. The relative frequencies are 0.2 in each of the four occupied early one-minute bins, 0.1 in [8,9), and 0.1 in [9,10). Their sum is 1.0. The broad [0,5) bin has frequency 0.8. Because its width is five minutes, its density height would be 0.8/5=0.16 per minute, if the plot uses area to represent proportion. Try two checks 1. Calculation. Using the ten times, make bins [0,3), [3,6), [6,9), [9,12). Give counts and relative frequencies. Hint for exercise 1 A time of 3 belongs to [3,6); a time of 9 belongs to [9,12). Full solution to exercise 1 [0,3) contains 1,1,2,2: count 4 and frequency 0.4. [3,6) contains 3,3,4,4: 4 and 0.4. [6,9) contains 8: 1 and 0.1. [9,12) contains 9: 1 and 0.1. Counts total 10 and frequencies total 1. 2. Interpretation or counterexample. Two adjacent bins have widths 1 and 4 minutes and each contains four observations. If bar area is count, what are their heights? Hint for exercise 2 Divide each count by its own width. Full solution to exercise 2 The one-minute bar height is 4/1=4 observations per minute. The four-minute bar height is 4/4=1 observation per minute. Both areas are 4 because height times width gives count; equal raw-count heights would misrepresent the wider bin’s area. A useful check is to place each of the ten raw times in exactly one interval. If a boundary time is counted twice or omitted, the bin-count sum will not equal ten. For a rebinning comparison, keep the same data and change only the interval choice. What you can carry forward A histogram is a choice of measurement display, not a new dataset. State edges, endpoint rule, vertical scale, and sample size. Rebinning can reveal or hide features, so shape claims should survive sensible choices and be supported by more data when they matter. These bins suggest a gap in the recorded ten times, but cannot establish a gap in the underlying population of puzzle completion times. More observations, plus a display of their individual locations, would help decide whether that feature persists.

title: The typical value depends on the question
summary: Contrast mean and median under an outlier.
text: Which song length is typical when one track is very long? One exceptionally long song changes the playlist average. The question is what the observed numbers allow us to say, and where the tempting shortcut fails. Background capsule. The arithmetic mean adds values and divides by their count. The median is the middle ordered value for an odd number of observations, or the average of the two middle values for an even count. Both have the same units as the observations, but answer different questions. Worked example Five invented track lengths are 2, 3, 3, 4, and 8 minutes. The mean is (2+3+3+4+8)/5=20/5=4 minutes. The median is the third ordered value, 3 minutes. Replace the last track by a 28-minute soundscape: the mean becomes 40/5=8 minutes, while the median remains 3. The replacement is one observation, yet it doubles the mean. If the club must budget the total time for all five tracks, the mean is directly tied to total playback time. If it asks for the middle track length, the median says exactly that. In the first playlist the 8-minute track contributes 8/20 of the total duration, or 40%, even though it is only one fifth of the tracks. When it becomes 28 minutes, that one track contributes 28/40=70% of total duration. The mean records that large change in aggregate listening time. The claim and its conditions x ¯ = ∑ i = 1 n x i n Changing one observation by an amount d changes the sum by d and the mean by d/n, provided n stays fixed. In our replacement, d=20 and n=5, so the mean rises by 4 minutes. The median is unchanged here because the changed observation remains the largest; its position does not cross the middle. This does not make medians immune to all changes. Replacing a middle value, changing enough values, or adding observations can move the median. Nor is the largest value necessarily an error: the 28-minute track may be genuine and important to total listening time. Proof boundary and failure case. The formula and shift identity are exact for a finite numeric list. “Robust” is a comparison of sensitivity under specific changes, not a guarantee that the median is the best summary. A bimodal dataset such as 1,1,9,9 has median 5, a value no observation takes. Always look at the distribution as well as a single center. The median’s invariance here is an order-statistic fact: the third value remains 3 because neither the first four values nor their ranks around the middle change. If the 28-minute track instead became 0 minutes, ordering would change to 0,2,3,3,4, and the median would still be 3 by coincidence; other changes can move it. Try two checks 1. Calculation. For four track lengths 2, 2, 4, 12, calculate mean and median. Replace 12 by 20 and recalculate. Hint for exercise 1 For four ordered values, average positions two and three for the median. Full solution to exercise 1 Initially the sum is 20, so the mean is 5; the middle two values are 2 and 4, so the median is 3. After replacement the sum is 28, mean 7, and the middle two remain 2 and 4, so median 3. The 8-minute increase changes the mean by 8/4=2. 2. Interpretation or counterexample. A manager wants to estimate total minutes for 100 plays sampled from the same finite playlist. Which center is linked algebraically to total minutes, and why might the median still be reported? Hint for exercise 2 Multiply each center by the number of observations and compare with the actual sum. Full solution to exercise 2 The mean is linked exactly: sample sum = n times sample mean. The median generally does not reconstruct the sum. The median is still informative about the middle observed duration and can expose that a few long tracks pull the mean away from most tracks. Neither one alone describes the full spread. For even sample sizes, check that the two middle observations are averaged before making a median claim. A list 2,2,4,12 has median 3, which is not itself an observed duration. This is still a meaningful midpoint of the central pair. What you can carry forward Choose a center after stating the task. Use the mean for arithmetic totals and the median for a middle rank; report both when asymmetry matters. An extreme legitimate value changes the mean by a predictable amount, while the median can stay still until ranks near the middle change. The mean and median should be reported with units and sample size. “Typical” without those details can hide whether the question concerns total minutes, a middle track, or a prediction for a future selection from a different playlist.

title: Why two honest polls disagree
summary: Compare sampling protocols with equal marginals, different covariance and a hidden-bag variance floor.
text: Why can two fair samples disagree? Repeated tile samples reveal how a statistic varies. Start with a fixed jar and independent draws, then compare one hidden bag per run with independent bag selection before every draw. The protocols share individual blue probabilities but give different sampling distributions. Background capsule. A parameter is a fixed population or model feature; a statistic is computed from a random sample. Code blue as 1 and other colours as 0; their average is the sample proportion. Independence means one draw does not change another's model probability. Variance averages squared deviation from the mean; standard deviation is its square root. Covariance averages products of centered deviations and vanishes for independent finite-variance draws. Worked example Imagine sampling with replacement from a jar whose blue probability is p=0.4. In five draws, one sample might contain 1 blue tile, giving 1/5=0.2, while another contains 3, giving 3/5=0.6. Neither result changes the jar’s fixed p. Under this model the chance of exactly one blue draw is 5(0.4)(0.6)^4=0.2592. The chance of exactly three is 10(0.4)^3(0.6)^2=0.2304. Both samples are ordinary possibilities, so disagreement alone is no sign that either sampling operation was dishonest. For the five-draw jar, the distribution of the blue count has six possible values, 0 through 5. The sample proportion therefore changes in steps of 0.2. A normal bell curve would be a rough picture at this sample size; the exact binomial probabilities are available and more informative. The claim and its conditions SE ( p ^ ) = p ( 1 − p ) n Let X_i be the zero-one result of draw i. Each has mean p and variance p(1−p). The average p-hat=(X_1+...+X_n)/n has mean p by linearity. For independent draws, covariance terms vanish, so its variance is n p(1−p)/n²=p(1−p)/n. Taking the square root gives its standard deviation, called the standard error here. This derivation is exact for iid Bernoulli draws with replacement. It does not need a normal approximation. In a finite jar sampled without replacement the draws are dependent, and a finite-population correction changes the variance. Proof boundary and failure case. A standard error describes spread of the statistic across hypothetical repetitions under a named design. It is not a bound that every sample must obey. Plugging p-hat into the formula estimates an unknown standard error and adds approximation error. Systematic exclusion from a sampling frame is a separate problem: increasing n shrinks the iid random component but does not repair a biased frame. Expanding Var(X₁+⋯+Xₙ) gives individual variances plus twice each pairwise covariance. Independence removes those terms; dependence can increase or decrease spread. The next experiment specifies that dependence. A hidden bag changes the joint law A bag population has two types, equally likely when a bag is selected: its blue rate P is either 1/4 or 3/4. A draw returns its tile before the next draw. Conditional on the selected rate, draws from that bag are independent Bernoulli trials. Independent selection of a bag means a fresh draw from this population; it may select the same type again. One bag per run. Select a single hidden P, then take all n replacement draws from it. A new hypothetical run starts with a fresh bag choice. Redraw the bag each draw. Independently select a bag before each draw, then take one tile from it. Bag choices and the draw randomness are independent across draws. Either protocol gives a particular draw blue probability (1/2)(1/4)+(1/2)(3/4)=1/2. The population mixture mean μ=1/2 is a fixed parameter. The selected bag rate P is random across runs. A sample proportion from one bag may estimate that bag's rate well while estimating μ poorly. Stating the target is part of stating the problem. Predict before changing n. At n=4, which protocol makes extreme counts more likely? At n=16, can either variance fall below 1/16? Does agreeing on each draw's marginal probability force the same count distribution? Exact count laws, not an observed histogram Let K count blue draws and Y=K/n be their proportion. Conditional on P=p, K has the binomial law. Averaging over the two possible shared bags gives Pr ( K = k ) = 1 2 ( n k ) [ ( 1 4 ) k ( 3 4 ) n − k + ( 3 4 ) k ( 1 4 ) n − k ] Here the stacked n and k mean the binomial coefficient, the number of ways to place k blue draws. The binomial lesson derives it. With a redrawn bag, each draw has a fresh independent rate and fresh draw randomness; after averaging these out, the indicators are independent Bernoulli(1/2). Its count law is therefore Pr(K=k)=C(n,k)/2ⁿ. Shared-bag counts are a mixture of two binomial laws, not a binomial law with their averaged parameter. For n=4, shared-bag probabilities for K=0,1,2,3,4 are (41,60,54,60,41)/256. Redraw probabilities are (1,4,6,4,1)/16. Both have mean count 2. Their equal means conceal different spreads: Pr(K=0 or 4) is 41/128 in the shared protocol and 1/8 in the redraw protocol. The instrument enumerates count probabilities exactly; no observed runs are generated. The covariance that survives averaging For two distinct draws from the shared bag, conditional independence gives E[X_i X_j | P]=P². Thus E[X_i X_j]=E[P²]=5/16. Each marginal mean is 1/2, so Cov(X_i,X_j)=5/16−1/4=1/16. Independence after conditioning on P does not imply independence before conditioning. Seeing blue makes the high-blue bag more plausible, which changes another draw's probability. There are n(n−1) ordered pairs of distinct draws in the variance expansion. Each indicator has marginal variance 1/4. Consequently Var(Y)=[n/4+n(n−1)/16]/n²=(n+3)/(16n). Redraws have zero covariance and Var(Y)=1/(4n). At n=1, both laws and variances agree; a single marginal cannot reveal their different dependence. Separate variation within bags from variation between bags The same calculation has a useful general form. Suppose a shared bag has any finitely supported random blue rate P, with independent replacement draws conditional on P. Let μ=E[P], v=Var(P), and w=E[P(1−P)]. These are fixed features of the bag population. Conditional on P, the sample proportion has mean P and variance P(1−P)/n. Var ( Y ) = E [ Var ( Y | P ) ] + Var ( E [ Y | P ] ) = w n + v This is the law of total variance. To prove it here, write Y−μ=(Y−P)+(P−μ), square, and average. The cross term has expectation zero because E[Y−P | P]=0. The first squared term averages to w/n and the second to v. This finite conditional calculation is also a proof of the displayed identity in this model; it requires neither a bell curve nor a simulated trend. MIT's conditional-expectation lecture gives the general identity and its proof. For our equally weighted bags, w=3/16 and v=1/16. The shared variance is 3/(16n)+1/16: increasing n removes the within-bag contribution but leaves the between-bag floor. With a freshly independent bag for every draw, Var(Y)=μ(1−μ)/n=(w+v)/n instead. At n=16 these are 19/256 and 1/64. The first remains larger than 1/16; the second is smaller. These are variances, not standard errors; take square roots to compare standard deviations. Why one increasingly large bag sample is not consistent for the mixture mean An estimator is consistent for μ if, for every fixed ε>0, the probability that its error exceeds ε tends to zero as the sample size grows. Unbiasedness, E[Y]=μ for every n, is a different statement. Our shared-bag Y is unbiased but is not consistent for μ=1/2. We can prove more than a positive variance floor. Conditional squared error around the selected bag satisfies E[(Y−P)²]=3/(16n). Whenever |Y−1/2|≤1/8, either bag rate is at least 1/8 away from Y. For a nonnegative variable Z, E[Z]≥a Pr(Z≥a), because those outcomes each contribute at least a. Apply this with Z=(Y−P)² and a=1/64 to obtain Pr ( | Y − 1 2 | ≤ 1 8 ) ≤ min ( 1 , 12 n ) → 0 The bound is uninformative when n≤12, but its limit proves Pr(|Y−1/2|>1/8)→1. Meanwhile E[(Y−P)²]→0: Y does approach the chosen bag's rate in probability. More draws within that single bag improve estimation of P, not of the mixture mean μ. This conclusion concerns repeated runs under the stipulated model, not a claim that every finite observed sample lies near a bag rate. A nonzero limiting variance alone would need care for unbounded estimators, since rare extreme errors can keep a variance large. Here Y is bounded, and the direct probability argument establishes the precise failure of consistency. Use the sampling protocol 1. Calculation. For p=0.4 compare the exact standard errors for n=25 and n=100. Hint for exercise 1 Compute p(1−p)=0.24, divide by n, then take square roots. Full solution to exercise 1 At n=25, SE=sqrt(0.24/25)=sqrt(0.0096)≈0.0980. At n=100, SE=sqrt(0.0024)≈0.0490. Quadrupling n halves the standard error under the same iid model. 2. Interpretation or counterexample. A poll samples 1,000 people from a list that omits half the neighborhood. Does the small iid standard-error formula settle accuracy for the whole neighborhood? Hint for exercise 2 Ask which population supplied the observations and whether draws from it represent the target. Full solution to exercise 2 No. The formula can quantify random variation for an iid model of the listed people, if that model is credible. It says nothing about the omitted half’s responses. A narrow sampling distribution around the wrong target may still produce inaccurate neighborhood claims. 3. A two-draw diagnostic. Return to equally likely rates 1/4 and 3/4. Without using the explorer, find both count laws for n=2. Compute the chance of two blue draws under each protocol and the covariance of the two indicators. Why can the one-draw distributions not settle the question? Hint for exercise 3 For a shared bag average p² over its two possible values; for independent bag redraws multiply the two marginal blue probabilities. Use Cov(X₁,X₂)=E[X₁X₂]−E[X₁]E[X₂]. Full solution to exercise 3 The shared-bag law for K=0,1,2 is (5,6,5)/16: Pr(K=2)=[(1/4)²+(3/4)²]/2=5/16, symmetry gives Pr(K=0)=5/16, and the middle mass is 6/16. The redraw law is (1,2,1)/4, with Pr(K=2)=1/4. Each indicator has mean 1/2 in either protocol. Shared covariance is 5/16−1/4=1/16; redraw covariance is zero. Both one-draw distributions are Bernoulli(1/2). Marginal probabilities specify individual draws, while a joint law also specifies how draws depend on each other. 4. A fresh population and a fixed sample budget. A new bag population has rate 1/8 with probability 1/3 and rate 5/8 with probability 2/3. Independently select B bags and take m independent replacement draws from each, with independent randomness across bags. The total N=Bm is fixed at 24. Let Y be the grand proportion across all 24 draws. Assume all draws cost the same and selecting additional bags has no setup cost. Find μ, v=Var(P), and w=E[P(1−P)] for this population. Does treating all 24 indicators as iid follow from their common marginal probability? Derive Var(Y) for general B and m, then compare three designs: 3 bags with 8 draws each, 8 bags with 3 draws each, and 24 bags with 1 draw each. Among equal-size designs with Bm=24, which variance is smallest? Explain what assumption permits the comparison and which term stays fixed. Would extra draws from one already selected bag supply the same information as extra independent bag selections? Hint for exercise 4 Compute E[P²]−μ² and E[P−P²] separately. Each bag mean has variance v+w/m by the conditional calculation above. The B bag means are independent and equally weighted in Y. Average their variances before inserting N=Bm. Full solution to exercise 4 The marginal mean is μ=(1/3)(1/8)+(2/3)(5/8)=11/24. E[P²]=(1+2×25)/(3×64)=17/64, so v=17/64−(11/24)²=1/18. Within-bag variation averages to w=(1/3)(7/64)+(2/3)(15/64)=37/192. As a check, w+v=143/576=μ(1−μ). Common marginals do not make indicators independent: distinct draws within one bag have covariance v=1/18; draws from independently selected bags have covariance zero. Write Y=(Y₁+⋯+Y_B)/B, where Y_b is the proportion within bag b. Each Y_b has variance v+w/m, and the bag means are independent. Hence Var(Y)=B(v+w/m)/B²=v/B+w/(Bm). For N=24 this is 1/(18B)+37/4608. The designs give Fresh population, always 24 total replacement draws Independent bags B Draws per bag m Grand-mean variance 3 8 367/13824 ≈ 0.0265480 8 3 23/1536 ≈ 0.0149740 24 1 143/13824 ≈ 0.0103443 For fixed N, w/N stays fixed while v/B decreases as B grows. Since v>0, the minimum among the allowed equal-size designs occurs at B=24,m=1. This is exactly the independently redrawn-bag protocol, with variance μ(1−μ)/24. It follows under independent bag selection and the stipulated cost model. Bag setup costs, dependence between selected bags, or unequal bag sample sizes require a new design calculation. Extra within-bag draws reduce that bag's draw noise; extra independent bag choices also average the between-bag variation. They are not interchangeable. Repetition rules differ: the fixed jar uses p=0.4 in every run; each shared-bag run first selects P. Specify what is independently repeated before deriving a sampling distribution. What you can carry forward Separate a population parameter, a statistic, and the distribution of that statistic across specified repetitions. The iid square-root law follows from zero covariances. A shared hidden bag preserves each draw's marginal probability while creating positive covariance and a variance floor. Increasing the number of independent bags addresses a different source of uncertainty from increasing draws within one bag. Always name the target and the sampling protocol. A proportion can be unbiased for a mixture mean yet fail to approach it, while successfully approaching its own bag's rate. A standard error reports scale rather than a guaranteed error band; an exact variance calculation does not repair an omitted population or establish that a real sampling procedure matches the model.

title: What a 95% confidence interval covers
summary: Interpret repeated coverage, then construct continuous confidence sets by inverting exact binomial tests.
text: What does the 95% belong to? Many jars have the same hidden color proportion. The question is what the observed numbers allow us to say, and where the tempting shortcut fails. Background capsule. The unknown parameter p is fixed in a frequentist sampling model; a confidence interval is calculated from random sample data. Coverage asks whether the interval contains p across repeated samples generated in the same way. A normal approximation treats a standardized sample proportion as approximately bell-shaped when sample size and success counts are adequate; it is not an exact finite-sample law. Worked example A fictional spinner has an unknown blue probability. In 100 independent spins, 60 are blue, so p-hat=0.60. A simple Wald interval uses p-hat plus or minus 1.96 times the estimated standard error sqrt(0.60×0.40/100)=0.0490. Its endpoints are about 0.504 and 0.696. This calculation says which interval this procedure produced from these data. It does not say the probability that this now-fixed interval contains p is 95% under this frequentist model. If p were exactly 0.5, this particular interval would miss it. The observed interval just clears 0.5 at its lower endpoint. A different count of blue outcomes could shift both endpoints, including one that covers 0.5. This is the random feature in the repeated procedure; the spinner’s underlying p is held fixed in the coverage calculation. The claim and its conditions P p ( p ∈ C ( X ) ) ≈ 0.95 Imagine repeating the 100-spin experiment, calculating a new interval each time, and marking cover or miss against one fixed p. An advertised 95% confidence procedure aims for coverage near 95% over those repetitions, at each p in its claimed range. For the Wald procedure, that number is only approximate and can be poor near p=0 or p=1 or with small n. If exact binomial coverage is crucial, one must choose and verify a different procedure, such as an inversion of binomial tests; the present calculation does not prove uniform 95% coverage. The event “p is inside C(X)” is random before observing X because C(X) depends on X. Proof boundary and failure case. The approximate symbol matters. The usual 1.96 multiplier describes a normal reference distribution, and estimated standard error adds another approximation. For n=10 with zero blue spins, the Wald interval collapses to [0,0], even though positive p could easily produce zero successes. That failure shows why the rule cannot be advertised as exact or reliable at the boundary. Selection of a convenient interval after looking at results can also alter a predeclared coverage claim. For p away from 0 and 1 and sufficiently large n, the approximate normal pivot (p-hat−p)/sqrt(p(1−p)/n) is near standard normal under iid Bernoulli sampling. The central normal region has probability about 0.95 when its absolute value is at most 1.96. To obtain the Wald rule, first replace the unknown p in the standard error by p-hat, then invert the resulting inequality. Inverting the original p-dependent pivot without that plug-in instead yields the score/Wilson construction. The plug-in makes the Wald coverage only approximate, especially near boundaries. Construct an exact procedure by inverting tests (45–60 additional minutes) The Wald example tells us what a convenient approximate rule returns. We now build a different rule from exact binomial tails and prove its coverage. Keep the sampling plan fixed: take exactly two iid Bernoulli trials. Their success count K has probabilities (1−p)², 2p(1−p), p² for 0,1,2. We use a nominal 75% procedure so that its complete three-interval family has manageable exact endpoints. Distinguish a candidate parameter u, a hypothetical observed count k, and the fixed true parameter p used when calculating repeated-sampling coverage. For each candidate u, define the inclusive tails Fᵤ(k)=Pᵤ(K≤k) and Gᵤ(k)=Pᵤ(K≥k). With α=1/4, give each tail a rejection budget α/2=1/8. Reject u only when Fᵤ(k)<1/8 or Gᵤ(k)<1/8. Equality is retained. C ( k ) = { u ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] : F u ( k ) ≥ 1 8 , G u ( k ) ≥ 1 8 } This inversion keeps all real candidates that the test does not reject. It is not a collection restricted to a numerical grid. The instrument's rational controls probe these continuous sets; a parameter between grid points is still included or excluded by the same exact inequalities. Predict before changing the probes. At true p=1/4, which of the three possible intervals misses? Does exact coverage have to equal 75%? Will changing only the candidate u change coverage of the whole repeated procedure at that true p? Derive all three continuous intervals For k=0, Gᵤ(0)=1 and Fᵤ(0)=(1−u)². Retaining F≥1/8 gives u≤1−√(1/8). For k=1, Fᵤ(1)=1−u² and Gᵤ(1)=1−(1−u)²; retaining both gives 1−√(7/8)≤u≤√(7/8). For k=2, Fᵤ(2)=1 and Gᵤ(2)=u², giving u≥√(1/8). Thus Complete confidence-set family, with equality included at every endpoint Observed count Full continuous interval 0 [0, 1−√(1/8)] 1 [1−√(7/8), √(7/8)] 2 [√(1/8), 1] The root expressions are exact. Any decimal values or root positions in a picture are approximations. The acceptance decisions use the inclusive tail probabilities themselves. In particular, a binding tail equal to 1/8 does not reject. Why test inversion proves repeated coverage The argument works for any fixed number n of iid Bernoulli trials and any predeclared 0<α<1, using inclusive binomial tails. Hold the true p fixed. Because Fₚ(k) is nondecreasing in k, the event Fₚ(K)<α/2 is an initial segment K≤j, if it is nonempty. Its probability is Fₚ(j)<α/2. Similarly, Gₚ(k) is nonincreasing in k, so the event Gₚ(K)<α/2 is a terminal segment, with probability below α/2, or it is empty. Their union therefore has probability at most α. The key is an equality of events: p is excluded from C(K) exactly when the test of that same true p rejects. Hence P p ( p ∉ C ( K ) ) = P p ( test of p rejects ) ≤ α So coverage is at least 1−α for every fixed p. We do not bound the chance that any candidate gets rejected; false candidate values are supposed to be removable. There is no extra correction over all the candidate values in this inversion argument. Nor does it assign a probability distribution to the fixed true parameter after observing data. Berkeley's test–confidence-set duality notes state the general event identity. Exact does not mean equal to the nominal percentage At p=1/4, only C(2) misses, with probability p²=1/16, so coverage is 15/16. At p=1/2, all three intervals contain p and coverage is 1. Neither equals the nominal 3/4. The generic theorem supplies a guarantee; we can analyze the full behavior of this small procedure more sharply. Name the four ordered internal boundaries a=1−√(7/8), b=√(1/8), c=1−√(1/8), d=√(7/8). They satisfy 0<a<b<c<d<1. Sum the binomial mass of exactly those counts whose interval contains p: Exact coverage for every real p, not only the displayed grid probes True parameter range Covering counts Coverage 0≤p<a 0 (1−p)² a≤p<b 0, 1 1−p² b≤p≤c 0, 1, 2 1 c<p≤d 1, 2 1−(1−p)² d<p≤1 2 p² Endpoints matter because the procedure retains equality. At a, the binding tail is Gₐ(1)=1/8; at b it is G_b(2)=1/8; at c it is F_c(0)=1/8; at d it is F_d(1)=1/8. Those counts remain included. Put v=√14/2−7/8. The coverage limits and actual endpoint values are: One-sided coverage limits are different from endpoint coverage Endpoint Limit from left Value at endpoint Limit from right a 7/8 v v b 7/8 1 1 c 1 1 7/8 d v v 7/8 Every coverage value is strictly above 7/8. For example, on [0,a), (1−p)²>(1−a)²=7/8, while on [a,b), 1−p²>1−b²=7/8; the right-hand pieces are symmetric. Coverage is 1 on [b,c] and at p=0,1. Its infimum , or greatest lower bound, is 7/8, approached at a from the left, b from the left, c from the right and d from the right. No p attains 7/8, so there is no attained global minimum. These conclusions use the piecewise formula and exact boundaries, not rounded endpoints. By contrast, the finite p=j/20 grid has an attained minimum 351/400 at j=7 and 13. That is an exact result about twenty-one probes, not the infimum across every real p. Keep the generic nominal guarantee ≥3/4, the sharper fixture infimum 7/8, and the finite-grid minimum 351/400 separate. NIST's exact-binomial documentation gives the binomial-tail equations for interval endpoints. The closed intervals, equality convention, complete real-p coverage and changed calculations here are derived locally. No normal approximation or simulated coverage count establishes these guarantees. Try two checks 1. Calculation. For 400 independent trials with 200 successes, calculate the Wald 95% interval to three decimals. Hint for exercise 1 Use p-hat=0.5, estimated SE=sqrt(0.25/400)=0.025. Full solution to exercise 1 The margin is 1.96×0.025=0.049. Endpoints are 0.5−0.049=0.451 and 0.5+0.049=0.549. These numbers are approximate interval endpoints under iid Bernoulli sampling; 95% describes a procedure’s approximate repeated coverage. 2. Interpretation or counterexample. A friend says: “Because the interval is 95%, there is a 95% probability the unknown p lies between my observed endpoints.” Explain the interpretation issue and give the relevant repeated experiment. Hint for exercise 2 Decide what remains random after the data and endpoints are fixed. Full solution to exercise 2 In the stated frequentist model, p is fixed and the observed endpoints are fixed; the containment statement is either true or false, though unknown. The 95% refers to a procedure across fresh iid samples: calculate a new interval each time and count how often it includes the same p. A probability for p after observing data would require an explicit probability model for p and a different analysis. Coverage should be checked across a grid of possible p values because a procedure can work near p=0.5 yet fail near zero. Counting cover/miss marks in a finite simulation illustrates the procedure; a finite run cannot prove exact 95% coverage. Transfer tasks for the exact-inversion investigation 3. Zero successes under a changed fixed plan. Take exactly ten iid Bernoulli trials and observe zero successes. Use the predeclared 95% equal-tailed construction: retain u when both inclusive binomial tails are at least 1/40. Derive the full interval, state whether its endpoints are included, and explain how it differs from the collapsed zero-count Wald interval. Hint for exercise 3 Fᵤ(0)=(1−u)¹⁰ and Gᵤ(0)=1. Solve (1−u)¹⁰≥1/40 for 0≤u≤1. Do not replace the exact root by a rounded value when deciding inclusion. Full solution to exercise 3 The upper-count tail is always 1 and imposes no restriction. The other inequality gives u≤1−(1/40)^(1/10), so C(0)=[0, 1−(1/40)^(1/10)]≈[0,0.308497108]. Both endpoints are included: u=0 passes, and at the upper endpoint the lower-count tail equals 1/40, which is retained. Positive p can produce zero successes. This interval accounts for that possibility, whereas the Wald plug-in standard error at zero successes vanishes and gives [0,0]. The percentage describes repeated use of the fixed procedure, not a posterior probability for the observed interval. 4. Change the requested object to a one-sided bound. Keep the ten-trial plan and zero observed successes, but predeclare a one-sided 95% upper confidence bound. Use the single-tail rule C⁺(k)={u:Fᵤ(k)≥1/20}. Derive the zero-count bound and compare it with exercise 3. Then test candidate u=3/10 under both procedures using its exact zero-count probability. Does a possible miss contradict the one-sided guarantee? Hint for exercise 4 The full 5% rejection budget belongs to the one lower-count tail. Use 1/20 rather than 1/40. Compare (7/10)¹⁰ with both cutoffs by integer cross-products. Full solution to exercise 4 The retained values satisfy (1−u)¹⁰≥1/20, giving C⁺(0)=[0, 1−(1/20)^(1/10)]≈[0,0.258865551]. Equality is retained, so the upper endpoint is included. The upper bound is smaller than the equal-tailed one because the same 5% budget is spent on one tail rather than split between two.
