The general single-tail test-inversion proof gives coverage at least 95% for this predeclared bound across fresh fixed-size samples. For u=3/10, the zero-count probability is (7/10)¹⁰=282475249/10¹⁰. It is strictly greater than 1/40 because 40×282475249>10¹⁰, and strictly less than 1/20 because 20×282475249<10¹⁰. Thus zero successes retains 3/10 in the two-sided interval and excludes it in the one-sided bound. This possible observed miss does not contradict a repeated-sampling guarantee: the event has probability about 0.02825 under p=3/10. Neither the coverage guarantee nor the selected interval assigns a probability distribution to the fixed parameter. What you can carry forward Attach the percentage to the method, sampling model, and parameter range over which coverage was checked. An observed interval reports plausible values by a chosen procedure, with approximation limits. When n is small or p near a boundary, inspect an interval method with demonstrable coverage rather than trusting a convenient symmetric formula. For the 60-of-100 result, report the endpoints and method together: “Wald interval under an iid Bernoulli model.” If a different construction is used, its endpoints and actual coverage behavior may differ even on the same data.

title: A p-value is a conditional probability
summary: Compute a null tail, then count what changes when one accumulating sample is inspected twice.
text: How surprising is this spinner result under a fair-spin model? A supposedly fair spinner lands blue unusually often. The question is what the observed numbers allow us to say, and where the tempting shortcut fails. Background capsule. A null hypothesis specifies a probability model for the data. A test statistic orders possible outcomes by how extreme they are for a predeclared question. “At least as extreme” must therefore be fixed before seeing the data, including the direction of the tail. Binomial counts arise from a fixed number of independent trials with the same success probability. Worked example Suppose ten independent spins of a fair two-color spinner yield eight blue results. Before spinning, the club decides to test only for an excess of blue. Under the null p=1/2, X, the blue count, follows Binomial(10,1/2). The upper-tail p-value is P(X≥8)=P(X=8)+P(X=9)+P(X=10)=(45+10+1)/1024=56/1024≈0.0547. The observed blue fraction is 80%, an effect of 30 percentage points relative to the null value. The p-value and that effect answer different questions. The binomial coefficients 45, 10 and 1 count sequences with eight, nine and ten blue outcomes. Each of the 1024 length-ten color sequences has probability 1/1024 under independent fair spins. This makes the 56/1024 tail directly checkable without a smooth approximation. The claim and its conditions p − value = P H 0 ( X ≥ 8 ) = 56 1024 The calculation conditions on the fair-spinner model and on the planned sampling and tail rule. It sums every null outcome at least as extreme as eight in the chosen direction. It is not P(the spinner is fair | eight blues); assigning probabilities to hypotheses would require a prior and an alternative model. Nor does 0.0547 mean there is a 5.47% chance of these exact eight blue results: the single-count probability is 45/1024. The tail includes counts 9 and 10. If the club instead had prespecified a two-sided rule using |X−5|≥3, symmetry would double this tail to 112/1024≈0.1094. Choosing whichever direction looks favorable after observing the data does not preserve the original test’s error calculation. Proof boundary and failure case. The exact 56/1024 follows from ten iid Bernoulli trials under p=1/2 and a prespecified upper-tail statistic. Dependence among spins, a drifting spinner, optional stopping, or choosing a tail after inspection changes the sampling distribution. A small p-value measures incompatibility with this full model; it does not prove a physical mechanism or quantify practical importance. If the observed count had been seven rather than eight, the same predeclared upper-tail rule would include counts 7 through 10 and yield a larger p-value. The test procedure is a mapping from every possible count to a tail area; interpreting just the observed number without that rule loses the reference distribution. What if the club looks twice? Now change the sampling plan before collecting data. Inspect the same accumulating sequence after 8 spins and after 16. At either look, reject fairness if that look's upper binomial p-value is at most .05. Stop on the first rejection; otherwise finish at 16. This rule has two chances to trigger. The final count includes the first eight spins, so these are dependent looks, even though all individual spins are independent. At the first look, seven or eight blue results trigger: P ( X 8 ≥7)=9/256≈.0351563. Six do not, since the tail is 37/256>.05. At the final look, at least twelve blue trigger: P ( X 16 ≥12)=2517/65536≈.0384064. Eleven do not, since that tail is 6885/65536>.05. Each separate fixed-size test has null rejection probability below .05. Does that settle the probability that either look rejects? Predict first. Let A mean the first threshold is crossed and B the final threshold is crossed. Would you add their probabilities? Multiply them? Count the overlap before choosing. The explorer enumerates the exact model law, not a batch of simulated tests. Count on one shared sample space Under the fair independent-spin null there are 2 16 =65536 equally likely full records. A first-look rejection occupies 9×256=2304 of them: nine qualifying eight-spin prefixes, each with 256 continuations. A final-look rejection occupies 2517. Counting full records after an early rejection is a mathematical device. Those unused continuations need not actually be observed. For the overlap, a prefix with seven blue has eight possible orders, and needs at least five blue among the remaining eight. There are 93 such continuations. The all-blue prefix needs at least four more blue, giving 163 continuations. Thus A ∩ B has 8×93+1×163=907 records. Inclusion–exclusion now gives the actual error of the complete rule: P 0 ( A ∪ B ) = 2304 + 2517 − 907 65536 = 3914 65536 This is about .059723, above .05. It is the probability of any rejection under the stipulated fair null, not the probability that fairness is true after a rejection. Neither adding the two probabilities without overlap nor the independent-tests formula describes this rule. For example, conditional on seven blue at the first look, the final threshold has probability 93/256≈.363281; unconditionally its probability is only 2517/65536. The cumulative looks share the early spins. An exact joint-count formula for any two fixed looks Write the predeclared sizes as n 1 < n 2 . Let i be blue at the first look and j the final blue count. There are C( n 1 , i ) ways to place the early blue and C( n 2 − n 1 , j − i ) ways to place the additional blue. Here C( n , k ) is the binomial coefficient counting choices of k positions out of n . The product, divided by 2 n₂ , is the joint probability. It is zero when the counts cannot occur. Sum these weights over each of the four threshold patterns: early only, final only, both, neither. This calculation uses independence of the two disjoint blocks of spins. It does not assume independence of the two cumulative counts. Equivalently, given the first count i , the additional count is Binomial( n 2 − n 1 ,1/2). This gives the explorer's conditioning probe, including probabilities zero or one when the required additional count is impossible or already assured. The unconditional procedure's error stays fixed while that probe changes. Predeclare an error budget for both looks One simple repair is Bonferroni: allow .025 at each of the two predeclared looks. For a fixed sample size, an upper-tail binomial p-value rejects on a tail whose null probability is at most its cutoff; if no count reaches the cutoff, it never rejects. Therefore each rejection event has probability at most .025. The union bound gives P 0 (any rejection)≤.025+.025=.05, with no independence assumption between the looks. For the 8/16 plan, the corrected boundaries are eight blue and thirteen blue. The early event has 256 full records; the final event has 697. Their overlap is 93: an all-blue prefix followed by at least five more blue. The union is 256+697−93=860 records, or 215/16384≈.0131226. This is below the .05 bound, not equal to it. Discrete counts make the cutoff conservative. A third look or a rule chosen after inspection would need its own analysis; the stated two-look budget does not cover extra opportunities. Repeated fixed-size p-values lose a general .05 guarantee when used this way. They need not exceed .05 for every possible schedule: the changed task below gives a counterexample to that stronger claim. The independent-tests lab addresses a different selection rule, with fresh independent samples for different tests. Its product formula remains appropriate for that model. Optional: a different process with an anytime error bound Can one predeclare a rule valid at arbitrarily many looks? Here is one mathematical construction for these independent spins. Keep the fair null probability 1/2, and fix an alternative probability 3/4 before seeing the sequence. The likelihood ratio after n spins with X n blue is L n =3 Xₙ /2 n , starting at L 0 =1. It is the alternative model's likelihood of that ordered record divided by its null likelihood; it is not a posterior probability. A blue spin multiplies L by 3/2; another color multiplies it by 1/2. Given the entire past under the independent fair null, the next conditional multiplier mean is (1/2)(3/2)+(1/2)(1/2)=1. Values are nonnegative and integrable at every fixed time. Thus L is a nonnegative martingale: its next conditional mean is its present value. This depends on the stated null and the preselected alternative; mechanically dependent or drifting spins need not satisfy it. Predeclare rejection when L first reaches or exceeds 20. Let that crossing time be τ . At any deterministic horizon H , stop the process at the earlier of τ and H . The finite stopped conditional-mean argument gives mean 1. On a crossing it has value at least 20, and elsewhere it is nonnegative, so 1≥20 P 0 ( τ ≤ H ). These crossing events increase as H increases. Taking their probability limit gives P 0 (ever cross 20)≤1/20=.05. This is the relevant case of Ville's inequality. It passes a limit through increasing events, not an unjustified limit through expectations. The bound is an inequality, not a claim that the crossing probability equals .05. This likelihood-ratio rule differs from repeatedly comparing ordinary binomial p-values with .05. For example, seven blue in eight spins has one-sided p-value 9/256<.05, but L 8 =2187/256<20. The rule must be chosen before inspecting the record. Allow about 15 additional minutes for this optional argument. Check the whole procedure 1. Calculation. With five fair independent spins and a predeclared upper-tail test, find the p-value after observing four blue results. Hint for exercise 1 Count outcomes with X=4 or X=5 out of 2^5 equally likely sequences. Full solution to exercise 1 There are C(5,4)=5 sequences with four blues and C(5,5)=1 with five. Thus P(X≥4)=(5+1)/32=6/32=0.1875. That is a null-tail probability, not a probability that fairness is true. 2. Interpretation or counterexample. A club examines the data first, chooses whichever color is overrepresented, and reports that color’s one-sided tail as if planned. What changed? Hint for exercise 2 Compare the set of outcomes that would have triggered a report before and after allowing color choice. Full solution to exercise 2 The reporting rule now allows either color to be selected by the observed imbalance. Its rejection set includes both tails, so a one-direction calculation no longer describes the full procedure. For the ten-spin result eight of either color, the symmetric two-tail probability under the fair null is 112/1024, assuming the absolute-deviation rule was specified. The observed 80% blue is an effect estimate for these ten spins, 30 points above fairness. A small or large null-tail probability does not tell whether that difference would matter for a game. That judgment needs an application and perhaps more precise estimation. A changed schedule needs a fresh count 3. Transfer task. Predeclare looks at 6 and 12 fair independent spins. At either look reject if the upper binomial p-value is at most .05. Find both boundaries and the exact probability of any rejection. Does it exceed .05? Now use Bonferroni's .025 at each look. Do the boundaries change? Explain why the result does not contradict the 8/16 example or the union bound. Hint for task 3 For six spins, compare tails at five and six blue. For twelve, compare tails at nine and ten. Work on all 4096 twelve-spin records. The all-blue six-spin prefix needs at least four further blue to reach ten. Full solution to task 3 The six-spin tails at five and six are 7/64 and 1/64. The twelve-spin tails at nine and ten are 299/4096 and 79/4096. Thus the .05 boundaries are six and ten. The early event has 64 full records and the final event has 79. Their overlap has C(6,4)+C(6,5)+C(6,6)=15+6+1=22. The union has 64+79−22=121 records, giving 121/4096≈.0295410, below .05. The .025 boundaries are also six and ten: 1/64 and 79/4096 are already below .025, while the preceding tails exceed even .05. Bonferroni changes neither rejection set for this schedule. Discreteness can make two different probability cutoffs select exactly the same attainable counts. The uncorrected two-look rule has no general .05 guarantee, but need not exceed .05 on every schedule. The corrected guarantee is ≤.05, not equality or a promise that each boundary must move. 4. Procedure audit. In the original 8/16 plan, someone reports 1−(1−9/256)(1−2517/65536) for the chance of any rejection. Identify the unproved step. Then explain why dividing .05 equally between two predeclared looks does not need that step. Hint for task 4 Write the union as a sum minus an intersection. What intersection is hidden inside the product formula? Full solution to task 4 The product formula substitutes P ( A ) P ( B ) for P ( A ∩ B ), which requires independence. The final count includes the first eight spins, and the exact overlap is 907/65536; it is not that product. Bonferroni instead uses P ( A ∪ B )≤ P ( A )+ P ( B )≤.025+.025. This bound holds regardless of the overlap. What you can carry forward Write the null model, test statistic, tail, and sampling plan before interpreting a p-value. Report the observed effect alongside the tail probability. A p-value is conditional on a model and selection rule; it is neither the probability the null is true nor a stand-alone decision about importance. A valid fixed-size test does not automatically supply a valid repeated-look rule. Count the joint rejection event for the complete plan, or use a predeclared bound that covers its opportunities. A guarantee of at most .05 is not a claim of equality. A fair-spinner null is an idealized model. If spins are mechanically linked or the wheel changes between trials, the equal-probability sequence count fails. The arithmetic remains correct for the stipulated model but stops answering the physical question.

title: The winner from twenty guesses
summary: Explain how selection inflates false discoveries.
text: Why is the best-looking result from twenty tries suspicious? Try twenty patterns in random coin tosses and report the most striking. The question is what the observed numbers allow us to say, and where the tempting shortcut fails. Background capsule. A valid p-value under a true null is super-uniform: P(p≤t)≤t for every t between 0 and 1. A continuous exact null p-value may be Uniform(0,1), making equality hold. Discrete tests, including many binomial tests, usually have jumps and are typically conservative at some thresholds. A family of tests is the set of questions the analyst committed to treat together. Worked example Imagine twenty unrelated patterns in random coin sequences, each tested once. If all twenty nulls are true and each p-value is independent Uniform(0,1), the chance a particular test gives p≤0.05 is 0.05. The chance none does is 0.95^20≈0.3585. So the chance of at least one apparently significant result is 1−0.95^20≈0.6415. A report that names only the smallest p-value hides the twenty chances to find it. The calculation describes a stipulated model, not evidence that any particular selected pattern is false. For twenty tests, the expected number of p-values at or below 0.05 is 20×0.05=1 under the exact uniform true-null model, even though the probability of at least one is about 0.6415. Expectation and probability of any hit are different summaries of the same experiment. A dependence example. Suppose the twenty reported tests are actually copies of one exact uniform null p-value. Then either every copy crosses 0.05 or none does. The chance of at least one crossing is exactly 0.05, rather than 0.6415. Each individual p-value still has the same uniform distribution. What changed is their joint dependence. This calculation shows why counting twenty labels does not establish twenty independent opportunities, while the union bound continues to apply. The claim and its conditions P ( min p i ≤ α ) = 1 − ( 1 − α ) m Independence multiplies the probabilities of twenty no-hit events. Exact uniformity supplies each factor 1−α. If p-values are independent but merely valid super-uniform, each no-hit chance is at least 1−α, making 1−(1−α)^m an upper bound rather than an equality. Without independence, the union bound still gives P(any false rejection)≤mα for m true nulls and valid p-values. Bonferroni therefore tests each of m prespecified hypotheses at α/m to keep familywise false-rejection probability at most α, without needing independence. This bound can be conservative when tests share data or have discrete p-values. Proof boundary and failure case. The displayed equality needs m independent continuous Uniform(0,1) true-null p-values. For discrete binomial tails it is generally not exact. Dependence can make the exact familywise rate larger or smaller than that expression, though the union bound remains valid for individually valid tests. Redefining the test family after seeing which results look good defeats a claim that a prespecified correction protected that family. For dependent tests, write A_i for the event that test i falsely rejects. The union bound P(∪A_i)≤ΣP(A_i) follows without multiplying probabilities. If each valid p-value is compared with 0.05/20=0.0025, the familywise false-rejection probability is at most 0.05. This remains a bound even if several tests are nearly duplicates. Try two checks 1. Calculation. For five independent exact Uniform null p-values, calculate the probability of at least one value at or below 0.1. Hint for exercise 1 Subtract the probability that all five exceed 0.1. Full solution to exercise 1 Each exceeds 0.1 with probability 0.9, so all five do with probability 0.9^5=0.59049. At least one is at or below 0.1 with probability 1−0.59049=0.40951. 2. Interpretation or counterexample. Ten related valid tests use the same data. Give a threshold that ensures familywise error at most 0.05 without an independence assumption, and explain the cost. Hint for exercise 2 Use the union bound on ten events, each with probability at most its threshold. Full solution to exercise 2 Bonferroni uses 0.05/10=0.005 for each prespecified test. Under all true nulls, the probability of any false rejection is at most 10×0.005=0.05, regardless of dependence. The bound may be loose, so a genuine effect can be harder to detect than under a more tailored procedure. In the coin-pattern story, the family must include patterns that were tried but not reported. If the twenty candidate patterns were themselves chosen after exploring data, the effective search could be wider still. The analyst should distinguish prespecified tests from exploration. What you can carry forward Count every tested or selected claim in the relevant family. A selected minimum is expected to be small more often than a single test. Distinguish exact independent-uniform calculations from valid upper bounds, and state the selection rule before treating one attractive result as confirmatory. An individual p-value may be valid for its own predeclared test while the published minimum is a selected statistic with a different distribution. Publishing the tested list, selection rule, and correction lets a reader reconstruct the family being discussed.

title: Same trend, different story
summary: Interpret correlation as association, inspect shape and confounding.
text: Does a shared trend reveal a shared cause? Track umbrella drawings and rainy days on a shared calendar. The question is what the observed numbers allow us to say, and where the tempting shortcut fails. Background capsule. A scatterplot places each paired observation at its two measured values. Correlation r summarizes linear association after centering and scaling both variables. Positive r means larger x values tend to pair with larger y values in a linear sense; it does not specify a mechanism. Both variables must vary for the usual r denominator to be nonzero. Worked example Across four fictional days, a club records rainy-hour counts x=(0,1,2,3) and umbrella sketches y=(1,2,3,4). The averages are x-bar=1.5 and y-bar=2.5. Centered deviations are the same sequence, (−1.5,−0.5,0.5,1.5). The cross-product sum and both squared-deviation sums are 5, so r=5/sqrt(5×5)=1. Yet drawing umbrellas did not cause the rain. The weather plausibly affects both the opportunity or mood to sketch umbrellas and the measured rainy hours. Correlation captures an arrangement of pairs, not an arrow of influence. For the four rainy days, the numerator is 5 because deviations in rainy hours and umbrella sketches have matching signs and magnitudes. The denominator is also 5. The computation is exact for these four paired observations; changing any one pair could change the coefficient substantially. Worked comparison: change the measurement unit. Double every sketch count in the four-day example, giving y=(2,4,6,8). Its mean doubles from 2.5 to 5 and every centered y deviation doubles. The cross-product numerator therefore becomes 10, while the two squared-deviation sums are 5 and 20. The new correlation is 10/√(5×20)=1. The slope and the numerical counts changed, but the standardized linear arrangement did not. This invariance concerns a positive change of scale. Multiplying every y by a negative number would reverse its order and change the correlation's sign. The claim and its conditions r = ∑ ( x i − x ¯ ) ( y i − y ¯ ) ∑ ( x i − x ¯ ) 2 ∑ ( y i − y ¯ ) 2 The numerator adds paired products of deviations. A pair above both averages contributes positively; a pair above one average but below the other contributes negatively. The denominator makes r dimensionless, so changing minutes to hours for one variable without reversing its order does not change r. The Cauchy–Schwarz inequality bounds r between −1 and 1 when both centered sums are positive. Equality at r=1 means all centered pairs lie on a positive-slope line. It does not imply the line is a causal law, that it will hold in new data, or that all possible relationships are linear. Proof boundary and failure case. A single unusual pair can dominate r, and a curved relationship can have r near zero. For example x=(−1,0,1), y=(1,0,1) has a clear U shape but cross-product sum zero and r=0. Scatterplots and context are needed before interpreting the coefficient. No calculation of r from observational pairs alone identifies a causal effect. One possible causal account is that rain encourages umbrella drawings. Another is that a third calendar factor affects both counts, or that the fictional club schedules drawing sessions on rainy days. The same r=1 does not choose among these stories. A design that separates alternatives is needed for a causal question. Try two checks 1. Calculation. For pairs (1,2), (2,4), (3,6), calculate r and state only the supported geometric conclusion. Hint for exercise 1 Check whether centered y deviations are a positive constant times centered x deviations. Full solution to exercise 1 The x deviations are −1,0,1; the y deviations are −2,0,2. Numerator is 4; squared sums are 2 and 8, giving r=4/sqrt(16)=1. The three observed points lie exactly on a positive-slope line. The calculation alone says nothing about causation. 2. Interpretation or counterexample. For x=(−1,0,1) and y=(1,0,1), calculate r and describe what a scatterplot adds. Hint for exercise 2 The means are 0 for x and 2/3 for y; calculate the cross-product sum. Full solution to exercise 2 The cross-product sum is (−1)(1/3)+0(−2/3)+(1)(1/3)=0. The denominator is positive, so r=0. A scatterplot reveals the U shape: y is high at both x extremes and low in the middle. Zero linear correlation has not shown absence of association. The U-shaped counterexample has zero cross-product because the left and right contributions cancel. Its scatterplot still gives a deterministic pattern. This is why a plot should precede the sentence “there is no relationship.” What you can carry forward Read r with a scatterplot, variable definitions, and a plausible data-generating account. A coefficient can efficiently summarize linear arrangement, but cannot replace shape checks, sampling design, or a causal design. Correlation is undefined if every x or every y value is identical, because the denominator is zero. Reporting r=0 in that case would incorrectly suggest evidence about a lack of linear association; there is no variation to assess it.

title: The line misses in patterned ways
summary: Use residual plots to test a linear description.
text: What do the misses tell us about a fitted line? Fit a line to the tempo and length of invented tracks. The question is what the observed numbers allow us to say, and where the tempting shortcut fails. Background capsule. A fitted line predicts y from x as a+bx. A residual is observed y minus predicted y, so a positive residual lies above the line. Ordinary least squares chooses a and b to minimize the sum of squared residuals for the recorded pairs. A residual plot puts each residual against x or fitted value to reveal structure the line did not capture. Worked example Consider five invented pairs x=0,1,2,3,4 and y=2,1,2,5,10. They follow y=2−2x+x² exactly: 2,1,2,5,10. Their mean x is 2 and mean y is 4. The centered cross-product sum is 20, while centered x squared sum is 10, so the least-squares slope is b=2 and intercept a=4−2×2=0. The fitted values are 0,2,4,6,8; residuals are 2,−1,−2,−1,2. That symmetric U pattern is systematic curvature, despite the line passing through the data center. The line y-hat=2x predicts zero at x=0 even though the observed value is 2, and eight at x=4 even though the observed value is 10. The central point at x=2 has residual −2. Reading residuals in x order reveals the U pattern that a mere sum of zero would conceal. The claim and its conditions e i = y i − ( a + b x i ) A small algebra bridge makes the minimization readable without prior calculus: for any number u, changing it to u−h changes its square by (u−h)²−u²=−2uh+h². Applied to each residual, this shows how a small shift in intercept or slope changes the total squared error; at a minimum the linear-in-h part must vanish. At an unconstrained least-squares minimum with an intercept, differentiating S(a,b)=Σ(y_i−a−bx_i)² with respect to a gives Σe_i=0; differentiating with respect to b gives Σx_i e_i=0. Solving yields b=Σ(x_i−x-bar)(y_i−y-bar)/Σ(x_i−x-bar)² when the x values are not all equal, and a=y-bar−b x-bar. These are algebraic properties of the fitted sample, not evidence that errors are independent or that the line predicts well outside the observed x range. A U-shaped residual pattern warns that the mean response is not well described by a straight line over this range. Proof boundary and failure case. Classical standard errors for a simple linear model also require a suitable error model, often independent errors with constant conditional variance; normality is used for exact small-sample t inference. Residual plots can flag curvature, changing spread, or outliers, but cannot certify every assumption or prove independence. The exact parabola here is a constructed failure case for a line. Fitting a more flexible curve may improve in-sample fit while increasing overfitting risk. The normal equations only say the residual vector is orthogonal to the constant column and the observed x column. Curvature can still remain because x² is a different direction of variation. A quadratic fit would represent these five constructed values exactly, but perfect in-sample fit is not a guarantee for new tracks. Try two checks 1. Calculation. For the fitted line y-hat=1+2x, find residuals at (x,y)=(0,2),(1,2),(2,6). What is the sum? Hint for exercise 1 Calculate each fitted value first, then subtract it from y. Full solution to exercise 1 At x=0, fitted 1 and residual 1. At x=1, fitted 3 and residual −1. At x=2, fitted 5 and residual 1. The sum is 1. This line was supplied, not necessarily fitted by least squares with an intercept, so the residual sum need not be zero. 2. Interpretation or counterexample. A least-squares line has residuals that widen in spread as fitted values rise, with no obvious curve in their center. What concern does this raise, and what does the plot not prove? Hint for exercise 2 Think about whether prediction-error variance is constant across the range. Full solution to exercise 2 The widening suggests heteroscedasticity: error variance may increase with fitted value. Standard-error formulas assuming constant conditional variance may then be unreliable. The plot is diagnostic, not proof of a particular variance function; it also cannot establish independence, a causal relation, or reliable extrapolation. If residuals are plotted against fitted values, retain their signs and a visible horizontal zero reference. A run of positive, then negative, then positive residuals suggests the line systematically misses the center relative to the ends. What you can carry forward Use residuals to test what the line leaves behind. Their algebraic sum can be zero by construction while their pattern is plainly nonrandom. Inspect shape, spread, and extreme points before using a line for prediction or inference, and keep causal claims outside a descriptive fit. Prediction beyond x=4 is extrapolation. The original points cannot show whether a quadratic physical mechanism continues there. A residual check diagnoses a mismatch within the observed range; it does not establish a future law.

title: A random walk on a tiny map
summary: Count finite fair-walk paths and endpoints, with parity and biased-step checks.
text: Where can a wandering token land? A token starts at position 0 on a numbered line. At each chime a fair coin independently sends it one step right or left. The process is random, but its possible positions and their chances can be calculated exactly. We shall separate a path , the whole record of moves, from an endpoint , the position after a chosen number of moves. Background capsule. Independent tosses mean that knowing previous tosses does not change the chance of the next one. For a fair coin each specified sequence of three tosses has chance (1/2)³ = 1/8. We add chances for mutually exclusive sequences. A random variable here simply assigns +1 to a right move and −1 to a left move. The subscript on X₃ names the third move; S₃ names the position after three moves. This is a model of a token whose rule never changes. It does not claim real people choose directions independently. Its usefulness is that an exact small calculation tells us what a path drawing should and should not suggest. Count paths before counting endpoints Worked example. After three moves, RRL, RLR and LRR all end at +1. Each has probability 1/8, so P(S₃ = 1) = 3/8. Likewise the three sequences with two left moves end at −1. RRR ends at +3 and LLL at −3. The four endpoint probabilities are 1/8, 3/8, 3/8, 1/8 from left to right. They total one, as they must. Exact distribution after three fair independent moves Endpoint Number of paths Probability −3 1 1/8 −1 3 3/8 +1 3 3/8 +3 1 1/8 A drawn path such as RRL is one possible history, not a representation of all histories. In particular, +1 is more likely than +3 because three paths reach it, not because any individual path to +1 is favored. The token cannot be at 0 after three unit steps: its parity alternates each chime. If an animation shows position 0 at time three, its rule or labels need checking. The sum records every move S n = ∑ i = 1 n X i , X i ∈ { − 1 , + 1 } For n moves, let R be the number of rights. There are n−R lefts, so Sₙ = R−(n−R) = 2R−n. Conversely, an endpoint s requires R = (n+s)/2, which must be an integer between 0 and n. There are “n choose R” sequences with that many rights. Under independent fair moves every sequence has chance 2⁻ⁿ; hence P(Sₙ=s) = C(n,(n+s)/2)2⁻ⁿ for allowed s, and zero otherwise. This is a finite counting identity, not an approximation or a claim about eventual behavior. Hypotheses and boundary. If the chance of right is p at every independent move, a path with R rights has probability pᴿ(1−p)ⁿ⁻ᴿ and the endpoint probability becomes C(n,R)pᴿ(1−p)ⁿ⁻ᴿ. If the token changes its rule after a left move, paths with the same number of rights may no longer have the same probability; then the counting factor alone is insufficient. Independence is what licenses multiplying fixed move probabilities. The expected position of a fair walk is zero because right and left cancel in expectation at every chime. That does not mean the token is likely to be at zero at every time. At odd times it cannot be there at all. Average position across many independent repeats and position in one run are different objects. Check the counting rule 1. Calculation. After four fair moves from 0, what is P(S₄ = 0)? Also give P(S₄ = 4). Hint for question 1 Zero requires the same number of rights and lefts. Four requires all rights. Full solution to question 1 For zero, R = (4+0)/2 = 2. Choose which two of four moves are right in C(4,2) = 6 ways. Each path has probability 1/16, so P(S₄=0)=6/16=3/8. For +4, R=4, leaving only RRRR, so P(S₄=4)=1/16. Notice that an endpoint is not itself one equally likely outcome among five listed positions. 2. Explain a failure. A biased coin moves right with chance 3/4 independently each time. After two moves, compare paths RL and RR. Does the fair-walk endpoint table still apply? Hint for question 2 Multiply the two move chances along each specified path. Full solution to question 2 P(RL) = (3/4)(1/4) = 3/16; P(RR) = (3/4)² = 9/16. LR also has chance 3/16, so the zero endpoint has chance 6/16, while +2 has chance 9/16 and −2 has chance 1/16. The fair table's equal path probabilities of 1/4 do not apply. Counting paths remains useful only after weighting them with the right model. What the little walk establishes A path is a sequence; an endpoint can collect several paths. For a fixed finite number of independent steps, count and weight those paths to obtain exact probabilities. This lesson has not established long-run recurrence, a typical distance, or a hitting time. Those questions need additional arguments and sometimes absorbing boundaries. For the latter, see a walk that stops at an edge . A useful self-check is to recompute the three-step table for p = 1/2 by adding its four entries. The total must be one, and impossible parity values must have probability zero. MIT OpenCourseWare's introduction to stochastic processes develops the random-walk and finite-state language behind this model; the token example and questions here are original.

title: How long until the token reaches an edge?
summary: Solve finite hitting probabilities and mean durations, then investigate how certain stopping can coexist with an infinite expected wait.
text: Which edge arrives first? A token moves independently left or right with probability 1/2 on integer positions 0,…,4, stopping at absorbing edges 0 and 4. Starting at 1, what is the chance of hitting 4 first? Paths can bounce arbitrarily long, so use a recurrence instead of listing them. Background capsule. Conditional probability fixes known information. A first right move from 1 restarts the problem at 2; a left move reaches 0. Total probability multiplies each first-move chance by its subsequent success chance, then adds. The resulting equations use ordinary algebra. Let hᵢ be the probability of eventually reaching 4 before 0 from i. We prove almost-sure absorption on a finite board and calculate expected duration. Removing the right edge in the optional investigation preserves almost-sure stopping but gives infinite mean duration. These are ideal token models. Solve the four-space board Worked example. The boundary values are h₀ = 0 and h₄ = 1. From each interior position a first step lands on a neighbor, giving h₁ = h₂/2, h₂ = (h₁+h₃)/2 and h₃ = (h₂+1)/2. Substitute the first and third equations into the second: 2h₂ = h₂/2 + (h₂+1)/2 = h₂+1/2, so h₂ = 1/2. Then h₁ = 1/4 and h₃ = 3/4. Starting one space from the left edge gives only one chance in four of reaching the far edge first. Fair-walk chance of reaching 4 before 0 Start i 0 1 2 3 4 hᵢ 0 1/4 1/2 3/4 1 The table suggests hᵢ=i/N on a fair board 0,…,N. From 1 an early right move reaches 2, where success still has chance 1/2. The recurrence weights both first moves and their futures, avoiding impressions from a few paths. Why the recurrence has a unique answer h i = p h i + 1 + ( 1 − p ) h i − 1 , h 0 = 0 , h N = 1 For the fair case p = 1/2, rearranging gives hᵢ₊₁−hᵢ = hᵢ−hᵢ₋₁. Thus successive differences are a constant d. Starting from h₀ = 0 gives hᵢ = id; ending at hᴺ = 1 forces d = 1/N. This proves the displayed rule for every finite N ≥ 1, provided each interior move is independently fair and the process stops at the endpoints. From any interior position, N consecutive left moves reach 0 within N steps, with chance at least 2⁻ᴺ. Each fresh N-step block therefore has conditional absorption chance at least 2⁻ᴺ. Survival through k blocks is at most (1−2⁻ᴺ)ᵏ→0. This proves almost-sure absorption and identifies the bounded recurrence solution as the eventual hitting probability. Boundary. Unequal move chances break equal differences: on 0,1,2 with right chance 3/4, h₁=3/4. Reflecting only after the first edge hit leaves first-hit probabilities unchanged. Fixed-time location is a different question with different boundary data. Finite simulations cannot prove eventual absorption or exact fractions. How many chimes should the finite game take? Let T count chimes until first hitting 0 or N; on an edge T=0. Expectation weights durations by probability; see expected scores . For nonnegative integer T, E[T]=∑ t≥0 P(T>t), possibly infinite: a k-step path contributes one at t=0,…,k−1. Nonnegative terms justify the rearrangement without cancellation. Prove finiteness first. The block bound above gives P(T>kN) ≤ (1−2 −N ) k . Within each block of N times, survival is no larger than at its beginning. Therefore E[T] ≤ N∑ k≥0 (1−2 −N ) k = N2 N < ∞. This loose bound is enough to justify manipulating the finite means next; we have not assumed the answer we want to prove. Write e i =E i [T] for the mean from position i. A first step uses one chime, then leaves the same fair problem at a neighbor. Thus e 0 =e N =0 and e i =1+(e i−1 +e i+1 )/2 for 0<i<N. Rearranging gives e i+1 −2e i +e i−1 =−2. Direct substitution shows that e i =i(N−i) satisfies these equations and both boundaries. For uniqueness, subtract any two solutions: their difference has constant neighboring differences and zero values at 0 and N, so every difference is zero. Consequently E i [T]=i(N−i) for a finite fair board. On 0,…,4 the mean is 3 chimes from 1 and 4 from 2. Runs may finish immediately or bounce arbitrarily long. Unlike the hitting-probability recurrence, the duration recurrence has an extra 1 and zero values at both edges. What exactly does a finite recording measure? With recording cap H, duration is min(T,H) and its exact mean is ∑ t=0 H−1 P(T>t), excluding survival at H. Predict how this increases with H and whether it can exceed the finite-board full mean. The calculation counts all possible fair coin histories to the finite horizon, including unused continuations after a token has stopped. It is not a set of sampled runs. On a finite board, condition on each still-active position x at time H: its future mean delay is x(N−x). This gives the exact check E[T] = E[min(T,H)] + ∑ x interior P(X H =x,T>H)x(N−x). The remaining delay is weighted by unconditional active mass, not by a distribution renormalized to survivors. The seeded walk laboratory samples paths recorded for at most 2,000 steps. Its sample mean of min(T,2000) estimates the capped expectation, not necessarily E[T]. Censored paths are still active: calling them absorbed or discarding them changes the measured quantity. Optional: stopping has probability one, but the mean duration is infinite (about 15–25 minutes) Remove the right edge, not just its drawing Now the state space is 0,1,2,…, with absorption only at 0. Start at a fixed positive integer i. Every move before absorption is independently left or right with probability 1/2. Let T 0 be the first hit of 0. There is no rule that reflects or stops the token at the diagram’s right-hand window. Almost-sure absorption. Choose any integer N>i and follow the same coin sequence both on this half-line and on a finite board stopped at 0 or N. On the event that 0 is hit before N, the half-line token also hits 0. The finite result therefore gives P i (T 0 <∞) ≥ 1−i/N for every N>i. Taking N arbitrarily large forces this probability to be 1. “Almost surely” means probability one; it does not say that every conceivable infinite coin sequence hits 0. Infinite expected duration. On that same shared coin sequence, the first hit of either 0 or N occurs no later than the first hit of 0 alone. Thus T 0 ≥ T {0,N} , and nonnegative expectation gives E i [T 0 ] ≥ i(N−i) for every N>i. The right side grows without bound. Hence E i [T 0 ] = ∞, despite T 0 being finite almost surely. We used inequalities for nonnegative durations, not an exchange of a random limit with expectation. Find the invalid line in a tempting expectation argument The stopped position M n =X min(n,T₀) is the token’s location after n chimes, keeping it at 0 once it arrives. For every fixed finite n, its mean remains i. One elementary proof writes M n =i+∑ k=1 n 1 {T₀≥k} ξ k , where ξ k is the fair ±1 move and the indicator is 1 only when a kth move is still needed. Whether that move is needed is determined by the earlier moves, independently of ξ k . Each summand therefore has mean zero. Only a finite sum is being averaged. Almost-sure absorption also gives M n →0 almost surely. It is tempting to write E[lim M n ] = lim E[M n ], but here the two sides are 0 and i. That equality is the invalid step. The terminal position is integrable (it is zero), increments are bounded by one, and the stopping time is almost surely finite. None of those facts, alone or together in this example, supplies a common integrable bound or sufficient control of the whole family’s tails. In particular E[T₀] is infinite. Let s n =P(T₀>n)↓0. Absorbed paths contribute zero while E[M n ]=i, so E[M n |T₀>n]=i/s n →∞ whenever s n >0. Fewer survivors carry the same mean. Bounds M n ≤i+n depend on n; on a finite board, 0≤M n ≤N is one common bound. The optional-stopping theorem has hypotheses; it has not failed. It concerns martingales: processes with integrable values whose conditional next mean, given the past, equals their current value. For a martingale, a bounded stopping time, or an almost-surely finite stop with a common bound on the stopped positions, are useful sufficient cases for preserving the mean. Another sufficient case combines finite expected stopping time with bounded increments. This half-line example lacks the relevant tail control. Full martingale theory is outside this short investigation. Roch’s author-hosted Notes 18, Theorem 18.8 and section 3 states the conditions and develops these stopping-time results. The finite recurrences and comparisons above give the local proofs used here. Use the boundary conditions 1. Calculation. On a fair board with edges 0 and 6, find the chance of reaching 6 first from 2. Then give the chance of reaching 0 first. Hint for question 1 Use hᵢ = i/N and the fact that one of the two edges must eventually be reached. Full solution to question 1 With i=2 and N=6, h₂=2/6=1/3. Absorption occurs with probability one, and the two first-hit events are disjoint and exhaustive. Thus the chance of hitting 0 first is 1−1/3=2/3. Starting closer to 0 gives it the larger chance. 2. Explain a changed rule. On 0,1,2 a move from 1 goes right with chance 2/5. What is the success chance, and which line of the fair proof breaks? Hint for question 2 Both destinations are already absorbing. Write the one-step recurrence. Full solution to question 2 h₀=0 and h₂=1, so h₁=(2/5)h₂+(3/5)h₀=2/5. The fair proof used the average of neighboring values, leading to equal differences. Here the weights are 2/5 and 3/5, so h₁ is not halfway between the boundaries. The first-step recurrence remains valid under the new rule. 3. Duration is a different recurrence. For a fair board with edges 0 and 6, calculate the full mean duration from 2 and from 3. A friend uses e i =(e i−1 +e i+1 )/2 with zero endpoint means and gets zero everywhere. Which term is missing? Hint for question 3 The first move itself takes time even if it lands on an edge. Full solution to question 3 The means are 2(6−2)=8 and 3(6−3)=9 chimes. The correct recurrence is e i =1+(e i−1 +e i+1 )/2. The omitted 1 records the first chime; zero boundary values alone do not distinguish the two questions. 4. Changed start and horizon, on paper. Start at 2 on the fair board 0,…,5 and record at most H=2 chimes. List the four two-coin histories. Find survival at H, mean recorded duration, conditional surviving position, and the exact remaining-delay term. Verify that capped mean plus remaining delay equals the full mean. Hint for question 4 The endpoints are 0,2,2,4; each two-coin history has chance 1/4. Use x(5−x) only for still-active positions. Full solution to question 4 LL reaches 0, LR and RL reach 2, RR reaches 4. Only LL has stopped, so survival is 3/4. No path can reach an edge before time 2; recorded duration is always 2, so its mean is 2. Among survivors, positions 2,2,4 have equal conditional weights, giving mean 8/3. The unconditional future-delay sum is (1/2)·2(5−2)+(1/4)·4(5−4)=3+1=4. Thus 2+4=6=2(5−2), as required. Renormalizing the delay weights to survivors would instead give 16/3, which is the conditional future delay and must be multiplied by survival 3/4 before adding to the capped mean. 5. Optional half-line proof check. A fair half-line walk starts at 2 and stops at 0. Someone argues: “The stopped position is always nonnegative, every increment is bounded, the final position is zero, and stopping happens with probability one. Therefore its initial expected position must be zero too.” Locate the unjustified step. Give an arbitrarily large lower bound for the mean duration using a finite board. Hint for question 5 Compare the expectation at a fixed finite horizon with the expectation of the limiting position. For duration, couple the half-line walk to a board with an arbitrarily distant right edge. Second hint for question 5 At a finite stopped horizon, use fairness to keep the starting mean. For the duration bound, use the same coin sequence on 0,…,N and substitute the starting position into the finite-board exit-time formula before increasing N. Full solution to question 5 Each finite-horizon stopped position has mean 2, while its almost-sure limit has mean 0. Nonnegativity, bounded increments, integrable terminal value and almost-sure stopping do not justify passing expectation through that limit. For every N>2 the half-line duration is at least the exit duration from 0,…,N, so its mean is at least 2(N−2). These bounds are arbitrarily large, proving infinite expectation. A finite expected-time condition needed with bounded increments is absent. 6. Identical finite records, different full means. Start at 1 with fair steps and record H=3 chimes. Compare absorption at 0 or 5, absorption at 0 or 12, and absorption only at 0 on the half-line. Show that every three-coin history has the same recorded positions and duration in all three models. Find each full mean duration. Can even an exact three-chime distribution identify that full mean without knowing the stopping rule? Hint for question 6 The largest position reachable in three steps from 1 is 4. Neither finite right edge can yet be reached. Full solution to question 6 All three rules behave identically until time 3: they absorb at 0, and neither 5 nor 12 is reachable. At H=3 the common surviving mass is 3/8, capped mean is 2, and conditional survivor position is 8/3. Nevertheless the finite full means are 1(5−1)=4 and 1(12−1)=11, while the half-line mean is infinite. An exact finite-prefix law alone does not specify the missing future rule. This does not prevent calculation once the full model is given; it shows why a finite record cannot establish that infinite-time model by itself. What a small recurrence can settle First-step equations settle hitting probabilities hᵢ=i/N and mean durations Eᵢ[T]=i(N−i) on finite fair boards, using different boundary data. A recording cap measures min(T,H). Removing the right edge preserves almost-sure absorption but destroys finite expectation, as the comparison proof shows. Rewrite recurrences when rules change; the free-walk lesson supplies path notation.

title: Memory lives in the state
summary: Test whether a proposed state captures all history needed for the next step.
text: How much history must a state remember? A music box displays Calm or Bright. The displayed state is Markov if, given today, earlier labels do not change tomorrow's distribution. A relevant hidden phase can invalidate that description. The property belongs to a state description and probability rule, not merely to randomness. Background capsule. P(A|B) conditions on positive-probability B. Xₜ is the state at time t; a history records compatible X₀,…,Xₜ₋₁. Given Xₜ, the Markov equality says this history does not alter Xₜ₊₁'s distribution. Successive states need not be independent. We use a discrete-time model: one tick per day. We can make the rule time-homogeneous by using the same next-state probabilities every day, but the Markov property itself does not require constant probabilities across days. Two histories, one visible label Worked example. First define a genuine two-state rule: after Calm, tomorrow is Bright with chance 1/4; after Bright, tomorrow is Calm with chance 1/2. The daily choice uses a new independent random draw. Whether yesterday was Calm or Bright, if today is Calm the chance of Bright tomorrow is 1/4. Past labels may help predict today's label before we see it, but once today is known, they add nothing under this stipulated rule. Now consider a different, entirely deterministic music box whose hidden display sequence repeats Calm, Calm, Bright, Calm, Calm, Bright, and so on. The displayed label Calm occurs twice in each cycle. After the first Calm, tomorrow is Calm; after the second Calm, tomorrow is Bright. Knowing only “today is Calm” is insufficient, while knowing yesterday distinguishes the positions: Bright then Calm identifies the first Calm; Calm then Calm identifies the second. With a uniformly random initial phase, both histories occur with positive probability, so the conflicting conditional predictions are genuine. Two compatible histories in the three-phase cycle Yesterday Today Tomorrow Chance of Bright tomorrow Bright Calm Calm 0 Calm Calm Bright 1 “Calm” is the same visible label in both rows. Thus it cannot support one next-step probability that agrees with both histories. Sampling many sequences would reveal the difference, but the stipulated transition rule already proves it. State the condition precisely P ( X t + 1 = j | X t = i , history ) = P ( X t + 1 = j | X t = i ) The equality must hold for every time, next state and compatible positive-probability history. Zero-probability histories do not supply ordinary conditional probabilities. In the first music box, the next random draw and today's label generate tomorrow, so yesterday cannot change its conditional chance. In the three-phase box, today's label leaves an unresolved phase, and yesterday changes the prediction. This is a direct counterexample, not an inference from a plot. A repair is to call the state (visible label, phase), with phase 0, 1 or 2. The next phase is then determined by the current phase. An even smaller state can be “first Calm,” “second Calm,” or “Bright.” On these three states the rule is Markov and deterministic. Expanding the state can restore the property, but may make a model more complex than the question warrants. Boundary. The Markov property describes one-step conditional distributions. It neither asserts independence of states nor guarantees convergence to a stationary distribution. The deterministic three-phase cycle is Markov after phase augmentation and still cycles forever. Also, a process may be Markov with a rule that changes with t; a single fixed transition matrix then would not represent every day. Optional investigation: when can hidden states safely share a label? One rule that works however the chain started The music-box cycle shows that merging hidden states can create memory. Now ask the positive question: when does a grouped label keep enough information for one common transition matrix, regardless of the initial distribution? Extra background. For a finite time-homogeneous Markov chain, P(x,z) is the probability of moving from hidden state x to hidden state z in one step. Every entry is nonnegative and every row sums to 1. Partition the hidden states into disjoint blocks B₁,…,Bᵣ that cover all states. The visible state Zₜ records only the block containing Xₜ. A grouped transition probability into a block adds all P(x,z) with z in that block. A starting distribution specifies the hidden state at time 0; it is not inferred from a report. We seek one common, time-homogeneous matrix Q that describes Z for every initial hidden distribution . The same Q must remain valid after every positive-probability visible history. Finding a one-step average for one start is a weaker statement. Compare two hidden states inside U Group A and B into visible U, and C into visible V. In the equal-totals model, A's row is (1/2,0,1/2), B's is (0,1/2,1/2), and C's is (1/2,1/2,0). A and B have different hidden destinations but both send probability 1/2 into each visible block. Predict what happens to the next-V probability if the initial law is (w,1−w,0), first at w=0 and then at w=1. Now change only B's row to (0,3/4,1/4). Can one U row still work for both starts? For equal block totals, the common matrix has U row (1/2,1/2) and V row (1,0). For unequal totals, starting at A gives next-V probability 1/2 while starting at B gives 1/4. Both visible starts are U, so one common U row cannot reproduce both. For the mixture (w,1−w,0), its one-step next-V probability is w/2+(1−w)/4=1/4+w/4. Choosing one value of w does not remove the disagreement across starts. The block row-sum criterion Claim. For a fixed finite stochastic matrix P and a fixed partition, one common time-homogeneous grouped matrix Q works for every initial hidden law if and only if, for each source block Bᵢ and target block Bⱼ, the following sum has the same value for every hidden x in Bᵢ: Q i j = ∑ z ∈ B j P ( x , z ) for every x ∈ B i Necessity: start at one hidden state. Suppose that one common Q works for every initial law. Start with probability 1 at x∈Bᵢ. The initial visible block is certainly i, so its probability of moving to j must be Qᵢⱼ. The hidden chain gives that probability as the displayed sum. Starting instead at any x′ in the same block must give the same Qᵢⱼ. Thus the block sums agree. This argument uses point-mass starts, not a stationary mixture. Sufficiency: condition on any compatible history. Suppose the row sums agree, and use their common values to define Q. Its entries are nonnegative and each row sums to 1 because the target blocks partition all hidden destinations. Fix any initial law and any positive-probability visible history ending in block i. Conditional on that history, the hidden state has some probability weights aₓ inside Bᵢ. These weights can depend on the whole history. The hidden Markov property and total probability give Pr ( Z t + 1 = j | history ending at i ) = ∑ x ∈ B i a x Q i j = Q i j The final equality uses ∑aₓ=1. Every possible hidden mixture gives the same next-block row, so the history adds no prediction beyond the current visible block. The matrix is independent of time and the initial law. Histories with probability zero are excluded before forming these conditional probabilities. No stationarity, irreducibility or convergence assumption is needed for this finite proof. This property is called strong lumpability . Wolfer and Watanabe, §3.4, Theorem 3.1 states the row-sum characterization; footnote 8 distinguishes its independence of the starting law. Their paper works with irreducible chains. The elementary finite proof above establishes the precise common-Q statement used here without requiring irreducibility. A special start can still work when the universal criterion fails Failure of the criterion means that one common Q cannot work for every start . It does not say that the grouped process fails to be Markov for every particular start. To make that distinction concrete, use a third matrix P*, separate from both explorer presets: P*: an unequal-row matrix with a family of special starting laws From / to A B C A 1/2 1/4 1/4 B 0 1/4 3/4 C 1/2 1/2 0 A and B have next-V chances 1/4 and 3/4, so the universal row criterion fails. But start with hidden law (p/2,p/2,1−p), for any p∈[0,1]. Whenever the visible state is U at time 0 with positive probability, its hidden conditional mixture is half A, half B. Under P*, that mixture moves to hidden (A,B,C) with probabilities (1/4,1/4,1/2). Conditional on staying in U, it is again half A, half B. If the visible state was V, the hidden state was C, whose next U mixture is also half A, half B. Induction over any positive-probability visible history now preserves this conditional half/half mixture whenever its last block is U. Therefore next V has chance (1/2)(1/4)+(1/2)(3/4)=1/2 after every such U history, and next U has chance 1 after V. The grouped process has Q with rows (1/2,1/2) and (1,0) throughout this family of starting laws. This is an exact all-history argument, not a conclusion from a finite sample of paths. It does not supply the common-Q guarantee for all other starts. Question 4 changes the start while keeping P* fixed. Test the state you were given 1. Calculation. In the two-state random music box, today is Calm. What is the chance of Bright tomorrow? If yesterday was Bright, what is that chance under the same rule? Hint for question 1 Use the stipulated Calm row; ask whether yesterday enters the rule. Full solution to question 1 The Calm row assigns 1/4 to Bright tomorrow. The fresh draw uses today's state and does not consult yesterday, so the conditional chance remains 1/4 after adding “yesterday was Bright.” This equality is the Markov check. It would not follow merely from knowing a marginal chance of Bright on an arbitrary day. 2. Diagnose and repair. In the Calm, Calm, Bright cycle, why is the visible label not a sufficient state? Give a sufficient finite state. Hint for question 2 Compare what happens after the two different Calm positions. Full solution to question 2 A visible Calm can mean the first Calm, followed by Calm, or the second Calm, followed by Bright. Yesterday's label distinguishes them, so the next-state conditional distribution changes with the history. Labeling the three phases “first Calm,” “second Calm” and “Bright” repairs this: each phase has a determined next phase. The augmented process is Markov but periodic. Two further tasks for the optional grouping investigation 3. A new four-state grouping. The following hidden matrix has blocks U={a,b} and V={c,d}. Find a common grouped Q or explain why none works for every initial law. Then make each of two changes separately to the original matrix: move 1/8 of b's self-transition probability to d; or move that same 1/8 to a. Does either change preserve the original quotient? Work from block sums rather than the three-state controls. Four-state transition matrix for question 3; each row sums to 1 From / to a b c d a 1/2 1/4 1/4 0 b 1/4 1/2 0 1/4 c 1/4 1/4 1/4 1/4 d 1/4 1/4 1/4 1/4 Hint for question 3 Compare a's and b's total probabilities of entering {a,b} and {c,d}. Then compare c and d. Moving mass within a target block leaves its total unchanged; moving it across blocks can alter that total. Full solution to question 3 Both a and b have block totals (3/4,1/4), while both c and d have totals (1/2,1/2). Thus Q has U row (3/4,1/4) and V row (1/2,1/2), common to every initial distribution by the theorem. The first change replaces b's row with (1/4,3/8,0,3/8). Its next-V total is 3/8, but a's remains 1/4. Starting at a or b then gives conflicting next-block probabilities, so no common Q works for every initial law. This verdict does not by itself decide every particular start. The second change replaces b's row instead with (3/8,3/8,0,1/4). Its block totals remain (3/4,1/4); the other rows are unchanged. Hence the same Q survives. The criterion compares totals into blocks, not equality of every hidden destination probability. 4. Change the start, keep P*. Use the special-start matrix P* above, but now start at hidden A with probability 1. Compare two visible histories at time 2: UUU and UVU, whose letters give Z₀,Z₁,Z₂. Find each history's probability, its conditional hidden law at time 2, and the conditional chance of V at time 3. Does this start give a Markov grouped process? Explain why the answer does not contradict the half/half family proved above. Hint for question 4 Propagate unnormalized A/B/C probability masses along each history, discarding paths whose visible block does not match. Divide by the history's total mass only at the end. For UVU, the middle hidden state must be C, so its return row helps. Compare predictions for two histories ending in the same visible state at the same time. Full solution to question 4 After UUU, the unnormalized hidden masses at time 2 are (1/4,3/16,0). For example, the B mass comes from A→A→B with probability (1/2)(1/4)=1/8 and A→B→B with probability (1/4)(1/4)=1/16. The history probability is 7/16, so its conditional hidden law is (4/7,3/7,0). Its next-V probability is (4/7)(1/4)+(3/7)(3/4)=13/28. For UVU, A first reaches C with chance 1/4; C then returns to A or B with probability 1/2 each. The terminal masses are (1/8,1/8,0), the history probability is 1/4, and its conditional hidden law is (1/2,1/2,0). Next V therefore has chance 1/2. Both histories have positive probability and end in U at time 2, yet 13/28≠1/2. Earlier visible labels change the next-step prediction, so this start does not give a Markov grouped process, even if a rule were allowed to depend on time. Starting at A is outside the family (p/2,p/2,1−p); the family's hidden-mixture induction is unaffected. No conditional distribution has been formed on an impossible history. What a state promises A Markov state contains enough information for the next-step probability calculation under the chosen model. The test compares histories that reach the same proposed state. A successful one-step test does not by itself validate the model against data, and it says nothing about long-run settling. The transition matrix packages a fixed Markov rule into rows after a state is chosen.

title: A playlist that chooses its next mood
summary: Advance a finite-state distribution with a row-stochastic transition matrix.
text: Move a whole distribution forward A generative playlist has three moods: Calm (C), Bright (B), Tense (T). The current mood affects the next one. We could follow one sampled playlist, but the more useful question is: if many copies start with a known distribution, what fraction is expected in each mood one step later? A transition matrix keeps the three conditional rules together. Background capsule. A probability distribution is a list of nonnegative numbers totaling one. Conditional probability P(next mood j | current mood i) fills one row of a table. We use row vectors: πₜ = (chance of C, chance of B, chance of T) at time t. Multiplying a row distribution by a matrix means that the new chance of state j is the sum over all possible starting states i of πₜ(i)Pᵢⱼ. This is the law of total probability, not a new physical law. Suppose the next mood depends only on the present mood and the same table is used each chime. Those are the time-homogeneous Markov assumptions for this example. One chime in a three-mood playlist Transition chances; each row is the current mood Current Next C Next B Next T C 1/2 1/2 0 B 1/4 1/2 1/4 T 0 1/2 1/2 Worked example. Begin half Calm and half Tense: π₀ = (1/2,0,1/2). The next Calm fraction is (1/2)(1/2)+(0)(1/4)+(1/2)(0)=1/4. Bright gets (1/2)(1/2)+(0)(1/2)+(1/2)(1/2)=1/2. Tense gets 1/4. Thus π₁=(1/4,1/2,1/4). A playlist sampled once will land in exactly one mood. The row vector describes uncertainty over many possible samples, not a song that is partly in all moods. Repeat once more: Calm becomes (1/4)(1/2)+(1/2)(1/4)=1/4; Bright remains 1/2 because every row sends half its chance there; Tense becomes (1/2)(1/4)+(1/4)(1/2)=1/4. The distribution is unchanged after the second chime. This is a particular stationary example, established by multiplication, not by a long animation. The row rule and its boundary π t + 1 = π t P , ∑ j = 1 r P i j = 1 The matrix P has row i equal to the conditional distribution of the next state from i. For any next state j, partition the possibilities by current state: P(Xₜ₊₁=j)=ΣᵢP(Xₜ=i)P(Xₜ₊₁=j|Xₜ=i). This is exactly the jth entry of πₜP. Each row sum equals one, so Σⱼπₜ₊₁(j)=Σᵢπₜ(i)ΣⱼPᵢⱼ=1. Nonnegative entries remain nonnegative. The matrix therefore preserves valid distributions. Under a fixed P, two steps give π₂=π₀P², where P² means two successive uses of the same transition rule. If the rule changes by day, use P₀ then P₁: π₂=π₀P₀P₁. Reversing their order can change the answer. If the displayed mood omits a hidden phase that affects tomorrow, no matrix on these three visible moods may represent the conditional rule; state sufficiency must be checked first. Counterexample to a common claim. Let a two-state matrix send A to B with certainty and B to A with certainty. Its rows normalize and π=(1/2,1/2) is unchanged by multiplication, yet starting at A produces A,B,A,B forever. The existence of a stationary row does not prove that every starting distribution approaches it. Periodicity matters. Advance and audit 1. Calculation. Using the table, begin certainly in Bright. Find the distribution after one chime and the chance of Calm after two. Hint for question 1 The first answer is the Bright row. Weight the second step by that row. Full solution to question 1 Starting in Bright gives π₁=(1/4,1/2,1/4). For Calm on the next step, multiply by the Calm column: (1/4)(1/2)+(1/2)(1/4)+(1/4)(0)=1/8+1/8=1/4. The other second-step entries are 1/2 and 1/4, so normalization also checks the result. 2. Audit a proposed row. Someone writes a Calm row (0.6,0.5,0). Can it be a transition row? Explain and suggest a correction preserving the first entry. Hint for question 2 Rows are conditional distributions and must total one. Full solution to question 2 The entries sum to 1.1, so they cannot be exclusive next-mood probabilities. Keeping 0.6 for Calm and 0 for Tense leaves 0.4 for Bright, giving (0.6,0.4,0). That corrected row is nonnegative and sums to one. It is a different model, so later calculations must use its declared values. Use the table for the question it answers Multiplication advances uncertainty about a state under a fixed, sufficient Markov rule. Row normalization is an immediate arithmetic check. A stationary row is one special distribution that remains fixed; it is not automatically the destination of every start. The next lesson solves for such rows and states when convergence follows.

title: What a Markov chain settles into
summary: Solve a stationary row and separate stationarity from convergence.
text: A fixed distribution need not be a destination A playlist changes Calm (C) to Bright (B) with chance 1/3 and B to C with chance 2/3. A stationary distribution stays unchanged after one chime. Whether every other initial distribution approaches it is a separate question. Background capsule. A row distribution π=(c,b) has nonnegative entries c+b=1. With row convention, one step is πP. A stationary distribution solves πP=π: applying the transition rule leaves its distribution unchanged. A chain is irreducible if every state can eventually reach every other with positive probability. It is aperiodic if its returns are not locked into a common cycle length greater than one. In a finite irreducible aperiodic chain, the distribution from any start converges to its unique stationary distribution; that theorem is stated here, while the two-state calculation below is proved directly. Balance the flows Worked example. The transition rows are C→(2/3,1/3) and B→(2/3,1/3). Remarkably, both rows are identical. Whatever mixture c,b we start with, the next distribution is (2/3,1/3), because c+b=1. Hence π=(2/3,1/3) is stationary, and every start reaches it after exactly one step. Its Calm probability satisfies c=(2/3)c+(2/3)b=(2/3)(c+b)=2/3. For a less instant example, change the rule to C→(3/4,1/4) and B→(1/2,1/2). At equilibrium the flow from C to B, c/4, must equal the flow from B to C, b/2. Thus c=2b and c+b=1, giving c=2/3, b=1/3 again. Starting certainly in C gives Calm probabilities 1, 3/4, then (3/4)(3/4)+(1/4)(1/2)=11/16. These approach 2/3: subtracting 2/3 from the next Calm chance multiplies the difference by 1/4. We can prove convergence directly in this example because repeated multiplication by 1/4 sends any initial error to zero. Second rule: Calm probability at successive chimes from C Time 0 1 2 Limit P(C) 1 3/4 11/16 2/3 Equation, theorem boundary, counterexamples π = π P , ∑ i r π i = 1 These equations define stationarity for a finite transition matrix. A finite chain always has at least one stationary distribution, but it may have several. If irreducible, it has exactly one. If also aperiodic, distributions from every starting state converge to it. For finite chains irreducibility supplies positive recurrence automatically. We use this standard theorem only as a stated boundary; solving πP=π alone is elementary algebra and does not prove the theorem. Periodicity blocks convergence in the two-state alternation A→B, B→A. The stationary row is (1/2,1/2), yet a start at A alternates between (1,0) and (0,1). Reducibility permits nonuniqueness: with P equal to the identity, every starting row is stationary. In that example the distribution does converge—it simply remains where it began—so reducibility alone does not mean failure of convergence. The point is that no single unique long-run row is forced by the equation. Failure case. A ten-chime histogram near (2/3,1/3) does not prove the model equation πP=π. Even under a stationary distribution, individual paths keep changing mood rather than settling into one state. Optional investigation: can a stationary chain keep circulating? Why two-state opposite flows balance For two states, c=cP CC +bP BC rearranges to cP CB =bP BC : opposite stationary flows balance. With more states, excess inflow from one neighbor can leave through another. Total flow balance need not imply pairwise balance. Extra background. In a finite time-homogeneous chain, Pᵢⱼ is the chance of moving from i to j in one step. Start with a stationary row π, so the marginal distribution remains π at every time. The adjacent-pair probability Jᵢⱼ=Pr(Xₜ=i,Xₜ₊₁=j)=πᵢPᵢⱼ is a probability per step. Its row totals and column totals both equal π. We call Jᵢⱼ−Jⱼᵢ the net current from i to j. Detailed balance requires that difference to be zero for every pair. Three states, unchanged occupancies, directional paths Use new labels A,B,C and the transition rows (1/2,1/3,1/6), (1/6,1/2,1/3), and (1/3,1/6,1/2). Each column sums to 1, so π=(1/3,1/3,1/3) is stationary. All entries are positive, and every state has a self-transition. The directional effect below is therefore unrelated to the earlier periodicity or reducibility counterexamples. At stationarity, A→B has pair probability (1/3)(1/3)=1/9, while B→A has (1/3)(1/6)=1/18. The same excess 1/18 circulates along A→B→C→A. Every vertex receives as much total probability as it sends. Nevertheless, the stationary record ABCA has probability (1/3)(1/3)³=1/81, while its reversal ACBA has probability (1/3)(1/6)³=1/648 under the same rule: a ratio of eight. Predict before inspecting. Can the two kernels have the same one-time occupancies but different pair flows? Must every selected word distinguish the directions in a nonreversible chain? Which probability should always match the forward word: its reversal under the same kernel, or under the correctly reversed kernel? Stationarity and detailed balance are different equations Stationarity: ∑ i π i P i j = π j Detailed balance: π i P i j = π j P j i for every i,j Detailed balance implies stationarity: summing its equality over i gives ∑ᵢπᵢPᵢⱼ=πⱼ∑ᵢPⱼᵢ=πⱼ, since the last sum is row j of P and equals 1. The converse fails for the circulating example, whose AB and BA pair flows already disagree. The balanced inspector preset has diagonal entries 1/2 and off-diagonal entries 1/4. It has the same π and holding chances, but each opposite pair flow is 1/12; both three-edge loops then have probability (1/3)(1/4)³=1/192. Derive the reversed transition rule Keep the forward chain stationary. For a currently observed state i with πᵢ>0, the probability that its preceding state was j is the adjacent joint probability divided by the current marginal: P i j * = Pr ( X t − 1 = j | X t = i ) = π j P j i π i This P* is stochastic: its entries are nonnegative and its row-i sum is (∑ⱼπⱼPⱼᵢ)/πᵢ=1 by stationarity. Also πP*=π, because ∑ᵢπᵢP*ᵢⱼ=πⱼ∑ᵢPⱼᵢ=πⱼ. The stationary weights matter. P* equals the transpose of P in our uniform presets, but that shortcut is generally wrong for nonuniform π. Positive-support boundary. If πᵢ=0, conditioning on the stationary event Xₜ=i is undefined by this ratio. Restrict to S={i:πᵢ>0}. This set is closed under P: for j outside S, 0=πⱼ=∑ᵢπᵢPᵢⱼ forces Pᵢⱼ=0 for every i inside S. The reversed kernel and path identities below are defined on that positive stationary support. Zero transition probabilities are permitted there. Reverse the whole path, including its initial weight For a word x₀,…,xₙ, its forward stationary probability is π x₀ times the product of its n transition probabilities. Under P*, the reversed word begins with weight π xₙ . Each reversed transition has factor π xₖ P xₖ,xₖ₊₁ /π xₖ₊₁ . Multiplying those factors cancels consecutive positive π terms: ∏ k = 0 n − 1 π x k π x k + 1 = π x 0 π x n The reversed word's initial π xₙ therefore leaves exactly the forward π x₀ and the original transition factors. This proves Pr π , P ( x 0 , … , x n ) = Pr π , P * ( x n , … , x 0 ) Only positive stationary weights were cancelled, never transition probabilities. An impossible path and its reversed counterpart can both have probability zero. The identity holds for every length and also shows that a stationary forward chain read backward has the Markov path law with initial π and kernel P*. Same-kernel reversibility. The chain is reversible in its stationary law when every word and its reversal have equal probability under the same P . Detailed balance gives P*=P on positive support, so the identity proves that symmetry for all lengths. Conversely, if same-kernel reversal symmetry holds for every word, applying it to two-observation records i,j gives πᵢPᵢⱼ=πⱼPⱼᵢ: detailed balance. Stationarity alone and one accidentally matching word do not establish this property. Initialization boundary. The homogeneous reverse rule above uses the forward stationary law. With a nonstationary initial distribution, let μₜ be the forward distribution at time t. Where μₜ₊₁(j)>0, the backward chance of i given next state j is μₜ(i)Pᵢⱼ/μₜ₊₁(j), generally depending on t. On a fixed finite horizon, the reversed process still has a Markov description with those time-dependent backward rows and initial law μ at the final time. Question 4 demonstrates the distinction. Source scope. Aldous and Fill, Reversible Markov Chains and Random Walks on Graphs , §3.1 and §3.1.1 , gives detailed balance, stationary path symmetry and the reversed-chain definition. Its opening setup is finite and irreducible. Our explicit positive-support calculation needs stationarity but not irreducibility; the examples, inspector and changed tasks are original. No hitting-time result from that chapter is used. Solve and distinguish 1. Calculation. For C→(3/4,1/4) and B→(1/2,1/2), solve for the stationary row using flow balance and normalization. Hint for question 1 Set the C-to-B flow equal to the B-to-C flow. Full solution to question 1 Write π=(c,b). Stationarity requires c/4=b/2, so c=2b. Since c+b=1, 3b=1, b=1/3 and c=2/3. Direct check: new Calm chance (2/3)(3/4)+(1/3)(1/2)=1/2+1/6=2/3; Bright is 1/3. Thus πP=π. 2. Explain a counterexample. A two-state chain swaps A and B with certainty. Find a stationary row and describe the distributions from a start at A. Hint for question 2 After one swap, the two coordinates exchange places. Full solution to question 2 The row (1/2,1/2) is stationary because swapping equal entries changes nothing. From A, the rows are (1,0), (0,1), (1,0),… and have no limit. The chain is irreducible but has period two, so the aperiodicity condition for convergence fails. Stationarity and convergence from a specified start are distinct assertions. Two further tasks for the optional reversal investigation 3. Nonuniform occupancies change the reverse kernel. Use the following four-state matrix and proposed π=(2,1,1,1)/5. Verify stationarity and compute P*. Compare the stationary pair record AB under P with BA under P*. Then find the probabilities of ABCDA under P, ADCBA under the same P, and ADCBA under P*. Is merely transposing P a valid reverse transition matrix? Four-state P for question 3, outside the controls; proposed π=(2/5,1/5,1/5,1/5) From / to A B C D A 5/8 1/4 0 1/8 B 1/4 1/4 1/2 0 C 0 1/4 1/4 1/2 D 1/2 0 1/4 1/4 Hint for question 3 Multiply each row by its π weight and inspect column totals. Use P*ᵢⱼ=πⱼPⱼᵢ/πᵢ, keeping row and column roles explicit. Every complete-record probability includes its own starting π weight. Check whether the proposed transpose even has row sums 1. Full solution to question 3 The weighted column totals are (2/5,1/5,1/5,1/5). For example, the A column gives (2/5)(5/8)+(1/5)(1/4)+(1/5)0+(1/5)(1/2)=1/4+1/20+1/10=2/5.
