Clockwise flows along A→B→C→D→A are all 1/10; the opposite flows are all 1/20. Including stays, each state's incoming and outgoing totals equal its proposed π weight. Thus πP=π, but detailed balance fails. The reverse row from A has P* AB =[(1/5)(1/4)]/(2/5)=1/8. The reverse B→A entry is [(2/5)(1/4)]/(1/5)=1/2. Computing every entry gives Correct reversed P* for question 3 From / to A B C D A 5/8 1/8 0 1/4 B 1/2 1/4 1/4 0 C 0 1/2 1/4 1/4 D 1/4 0 1/2 1/4 The AB record under P has probability (2/5)(1/4)=1/10. The reversed BA record under P* starts with π B , so its probability is (1/5)(1/2)=1/10. Under the original P, BA instead has probability (1/5)(1/4)=1/20. The complete loop ABCDA under P has probability (2/5)(1/4)(1/2)(1/2)(1/2)=1/80. Its reversal ADCBA under the same P has probability (2/5)(1/8)(1/4)(1/4)(1/4)=1/1280. Under P*, ADCBA has probability (2/5)(1/4)(1/2)(1/2)(1/2)=1/80, matching the forward loop as required. Transposing P would give A row (5/8,1/4,0,1/2), whose sum is 11/8. It is not even stochastic. Nonuniform stationary weights must enter the reversal formula. 4. Change the initial law, keep the circulating kernel. Return to the three-state circulating P, but start at A with probability 1 instead of π. Compute Pr(X₀=A|X₁=B) and compare it with the stationary reverse entry P* BA . Then compute Pr(X₁=A|X₂=B). What do these two times establish about using the stationary homogeneous reverse kernel for this start? Hint for question 4 At the first time the earlier state was fixed. At the second time, use μ₁=(1/2,1/3,1/6). Compute the joint probability μ₁(A)P AB and the full marginal μ₂(B) before dividing. Both conditioning events must have positive probability. Full solution to question 4 Since X₀=A certainly and Pr(X₁=B)=1/3>0, Pr(X₀=A|X₁=B)=1. The stationary reverse entry is P* BA =(π A P AB )/π B =1/3; it does not apply to this nonstationary start. At the next time, μ₂(B)=(1/2)(1/3)+(1/3)(1/2)+(1/6)(1/6)=13/36. The joint event X₁=A,X₂=B has probability (1/2)(1/3)=1/6. Consequently Pr(X₁=A|X₂=B)=(1/6)/(13/36)=6/13. The full previous-state row given B at time 2 is (6/13,6/13,1/13). The same backward source state B therefore has previous-A chance 1 at one time and 6/13 at another. This demonstrates time dependence, not a failure of the reversed process to be Markov. On a fixed finite horizon, use the appropriate time-dependent backward rows and the final forward marginal as the reversed initial law. The stationary formula is recovered when every μₜ equals π. What has been proved here We solved two small balance systems and directly proved convergence for one two-state rule through shrinking error. The general finite-chain convergence statement relies on irreducibility and aperiodicity and is supplied as a theorem with its hypotheses, not derived by those examples. When presented with a new transition matrix, first check its rows, then solve πP=π, then inspect communication and period before making a long-run claim.

title: Random arrivals at an imaginary museum
summary: Use a constant-rate Poisson arrival count and test its assumptions.
text: Count arrivals in a fixed interval An imaginary museum sees visitors arriving according to a stipulated model at an average rate of two per hour. What is the chance of exactly three arrivals during one hour? A Poisson process offers one answer when arrivals occur independently in disjoint time intervals at a constant rate, with at most one arrival to first order in a very short interval. The formula is a consequence of that idealized rule, not a universal law of museums. Background capsule. N(t) counts arrivals during an interval of length t, beginning at time zero. The rate λ has units “arrivals per unit time”; λt is a unitless expected count. The factorial k! means k(k−1)…1, with 0!=1. The number e is about 2.718; e⁻ˣ is the decaying exponential, equal to one when x=0. We use independence to multiply probabilities across disjoint small intervals. Time t must be nonnegative and λ positive for the usual nondegenerate process. If λ=0, there are no arrivals and only the k=0 probability is one. Three visitors in one hour Worked example. With λ=2 per hour and t=1 hour, λt=2. The chance of exactly three arrivals is e⁻²2³/3! = (4/3)e⁻², about 0.1804. For zero visitors it is e⁻², about 0.1353. For one visitor it is 2e⁻², about 0.2707. The fact that the expected count is two does not make exactly two certain: P(N(1)=2)=2e⁻², also about 0.2707. Poisson counts with expected count two k Exact probability Approximate probability 0 e⁻² 0.1353 1 2e⁻² 0.2707 2 2e⁻² 0.2707 3 (4/3)e⁻² 0.1804 The displayed rows omit four or more arrivals; their probabilities total less than one. In a two-hour interval at the same rate, λt=4, so we must use four rather than two in the formula. Mixing hours and minutes without conversion would silently change the model. A count histogram from finitely many simulated days may look uneven even when the exact probabilities are fixed. Where the Poisson formula comes from P ( N ( t ) = k ) = e − λ t ( λ t ) k k ! , k = 0 , 1 , 2 , … One exact construction partitions an interval into n tiny cells of width t/n and gives each cell an independent arrival indicator with chance λt/n, for n large enough that this is at most one. The count is binomial: P(Nₙ(t)=k)=C(n,k)(λt/n)ᵏ(1−λt/n)ⁿ⁻ᵏ. For fixed k as n→∞, C(n,k)/nᵏ→1/k!, and (1−λt/n)ⁿ⁻ᵏ→e⁻λᵗ. The limit yields the formula. The limiting construction supports the Poisson count law; it does not by itself prove that a particular real arrival stream follows it. A Poisson process also has independent increments: counts in disjoint intervals are independent. It has stationary increments: their distributions depend on interval lengths, not clock positions. These assumptions imply the same expected count λt in every interval of length t. A rush-hour pattern violates constant rate; arrivals in groups can violate the single-event small-interval behavior or independence. Either makes the simple model questionable. “Random arrivals” alone is too vague to imply a Poisson process. Proof boundary. We derived the marginal count formula from a binomial rare-event limit. The full continuous-time process needs a compatible construction of counts across all intervals. This article uses the usual Poisson-process axioms for those joint statements. A finite observed timeline can help assess fit but cannot verify exact independence or the limit. Keep rate and time together 1. Calculation. A toy counter follows a Poisson process at rate six per hour. Find the chance of no arrivals in ten minutes and of exactly one arrival in ten minutes. Hint for question 1 Ten minutes is 1/6 hour, so find λt first. Full solution to question 1 λt=(6/hour)(1/6 hour)=1. Thus P(N=0)=e⁻¹≈0.3679 and P(N=1)=e⁻¹1¹/1!=e⁻¹≈0.3679. Using t=10 without converting minutes to hours would produce an expected count of 60 and answer a different question. 2. Model check. A museum admits visitors only in buses of exactly ten at scheduled times. Can its one-hour count be described by a Poisson process merely because the bus timing is uncertain? Hint for question 2 Ask whether a tiny interval can contain ten simultaneous arrivals and whether individual arrivals are independent. Full solution to question 2 No. Counts jump by ten when a bus arrives, so the probability of multiple individual arrivals in a short interval is of the same order as a bus arrival. The simple Poisson process assumes single arrivals to first order and disjoint-increment independence. A model for bus arrivals might be Poisson, but the individual visitor count would then be a compound count with multiples of ten, not the displayed Poisson law. What a count model commits to The Poisson formula relates the count k to a dimensionless expected count λt. Its small-interval and independence assumptions are substantive. Next, waiting for the first arrival turns the zero-count probability into a survival probability. The direction of that derivation is exact within the same process model.

title: The next chime has no appointment
summary: Derive exponential first-arrival survival and memorylessness from zero counts.
text: How long until the next chime? In a toy arrival process, visitors appear at constant rate λ and counts in disjoint intervals are independent. Let T be the time from now until the next arrival. Counting zero events before time t is the same event as waiting longer than t. This simple equivalence turns a Poisson count formula into an exponential waiting-time formula. Background capsule. A survival probability P(T>t) is the chance a nonnegative waiting time exceeds t. For a Poisson process, N(t) counts events in the next t time units and P(N(t)=0)=e⁻λᵗ. The rate λ is events per time unit, so 1/λ has units of time. The cumulative probability P(T≤t) is one minus survival. An integral is an area under a curve; here integrating the exponential density would recover cumulative probability, but the zero-count argument needs no integration. We specify the start of waiting independently of future arrivals. A random calendar time in a changing-rate process need not have the same rule. Wait for a model museum visitor Worked example. Suppose λ=2 per hour. The chance of waiting more than half an hour is e^(−2 × 1/2)=e⁻¹≈0.3679. The chance of an arrival within half an hour is 1−e⁻¹≈0.6321. The average waiting time in this model is 1/λ=1/2 hour, but the chance of waiting longer than that average is still about 36.8%. An average is not a deadline. Now suppose half an hour has passed with no arrival. The chance of waiting at least another quarter hour is P(T>3/4 | T>1/2)=e⁻²(3/4)/e^(−2 × 1/2)=e^(−1/2)≈0.6065. It equals the chance of a new wait exceeding a quarter hour. The elapsed half hour changes no future Poisson increment; this is the memoryless property. It can feel odd, but it is an exact consequence of the specified process. Survival probabilities at rate two per hour Wait exceeds Exact Approximate 0 hours 1 1 1/4 hour e^(−1/2) 0.6065 1/2 hour e⁻¹ 0.3679 1 hour e⁻² 0.1353 The rows do not give the chance of an arrival at exactly a listed instant; for a continuous exponential time that chance is zero. They give chances of surviving past the listed durations. Derive survival and memorylessness P ( T > t ) = P ( N ( t ) = 0 ) = e − λ t For s,t≥0, the event T>s+t is contained in T>s. Therefore P(T>s+t | T>s)=P(T>s+t)/P(T>s)=e⁻λᵗ. This also equals P(T>t). The derivation uses the Poisson zero-count law and λ constant; the independent-increments axiom explains why a fresh interval follows the same process rule. It is not a universal property of all waits. The expected wait is 1/λ. One way to see it uses the tail-area identity E[T]=∫₀∞P(T>t)dt for nonnegative continuous T. Substituting e⁻λᵗ yields ∫₀∞e⁻λᵗdt=1/λ for λ>0. The integral evaluates because the antiderivative is −e⁻λᵗ/λ and the exponential tends to zero. This calculation justifies the stated mean under the model; it does not estimate λ from any data. Failure case. Suppose a chime rings at exactly each whole hour and you start just after one. The wait is nearly one hour, whereas starting just before one gives a nearly zero wait. Elapsed clock position matters. Even if the number of chimes per hour averages one, the wait is not exponential and the memoryless equation fails. A variable arrival rate likewise changes the survival calculation to a rate-dependent expression. The simple formula requires the homogeneous Poisson process, not merely an average count. Calculate a wait and test a claim 1. Calculation. Chimes form a Poisson process at rate four per hour. Find P(T>15 minutes) and P(T≤15 minutes). What is the mean waiting time? Hint for question 1 Convert 15 minutes to 1/4 hour before multiplying by the rate. Full solution to question 1 λt=(4/hour)(1/4 hour)=1. Thus P(T>15 minutes)=e⁻¹≈0.3679 and P(T≤15 minutes)=1−e⁻¹≈0.6321. The mean is 1/λ=1/4 hour, or 15 minutes. The mean wait and the 15-minute survival threshold happen to coincide here, but the survival probability is not one half. 2. Conditional wait. At rate four per hour you have already waited 30 minutes. Under the same process, what is the chance of waiting at least 15 more minutes? Explain why “already waited longer than average” does not change it. Hint for question 2 Use the ratio of survival probabilities at 45 and 30 minutes. Full solution to question 2 The ratio is e^(−4 × 3/4)/e^(−4 × 1/2)=e⁻¹≈0.3679. Equivalently, the next 15-minute increment has zero arrivals with chance e⁻¹, independent of the earlier empty interval. A long past wait does not increase or decrease the chance of a chime in the next interval under the homogeneous Poisson assumptions. A scheduled or time-varying process would not support this answer. The count-wait connection “Wait exceeds t” and “zero arrivals in t” name the same event. That is why a Poisson process produces an exponential first wait. The calculation is exact for the model and fragile outside it: rate units, constant intensity and independent increments matter. Read Poisson counts again if the zero-count formula or its assumptions are unclear.

title: Why a short queue sometimes grows
summary: Compare time-weighted and event-weighted observations of one M/M/1 queue, with exact rate recovery and explicit sampling protocols.
text: When does a single-server queue have a steady size? Visitors arrive at rate λ to one artist serving at rate μ when busy. Independent exponential arrival gaps and service times, with arrivals independent of service, define the M/M/1 queue: memoryless arrivals, memoryless service, one server. A stationary distribution exists only for λ<μ. Background capsule. The state n counts people in the system , including the one being served. At n≥1, an arrival increases n by one at rate λ and a service completion decreases n by one at rate μ. At n=0 there is no service completion. A rate is an average event count per unit time, so 1/μ is mean service time. The dimensionless load ρ=λ/μ compares demand with capacity. A stationary distribution is a list πₙ that is unchanged by the queue's stochastic evolution. Assume unlimited waiting space, first-come first-served service, no abandonment, and λ,μ>0. Observation comparisons require λ<μ. At λ=0 the empty stationary clock law exists, but no ongoing arrival/change record can be normalized. Real desks may violate these assumptions. Clock-time fractions and event-record fractions need not agree. A postcard desk at half load Worked example. Let λ=2 arrivals per hour and μ=4 completions per busy hour, so ρ=1/2. In the stationary M/M/1 model the chance of n people in the system is (1−ρ)ρⁿ. Thus P(0)=1/2, P(1)=1/4, P(2)=1/8, P(3)=1/16. The chance of at least three people is ρ³=1/8, since the geometric tail sums to that value. Mean system size is ρ/(1−ρ)=1 person. This is an ensemble or long-run mean under stationarity, not a guarantee that a particular observed line never grows beyond one. Stationary system size at λ=2/hour and μ=4/hour People n 0 1 2 3 Probability 1/2 1/4 1/8 1/16 The tail n≥4 has probability 1/16. Raising arrivals to 3.6/hour with service four/hour gives ρ=0.9 and stationary mean nine. Stability λ<μ alone does not ensure a short queue. Which clock does the recorder use? One recorder counts minutes empty; another records size after every actual arrival or departure, weighting rows equally. Should both find 50% empty? An empty queue changes only at arrivals; a busy queue can also change at departures, shortening visits. The display shows exact equilibrium probabilities, not finite-sample frequencies. Its ≥7 bucket aggregates the full tail; it invents no transition rule. Means include the tail's exact first moment. Balance neighboring states ρ = λ μ < 1 , π n = ( 1 − ρ ) ρ n In a short time Δt, a state n moves upward with probability approximately λΔt; from n+1 it moves downward with probability approximately μΔt. At stationarity, flow across the edge between n and n+1 balances: πₙλ=πₙ₊₁μ. Therefore πₙ₊₁=ρπₙ and recursively πₙ=ρⁿπ₀. For ρ<1, the geometric series Σₙ≥0ρⁿ=1/(1−ρ), so normalization forces π₀=1−ρ. This derives the stationary probabilities within the M/M/1 model. Summing Σnπₙ gives ρ/(1−ρ); it can be obtained by differentiating the finite geometric sum and taking its limit, valid for ρ<1. For ρ≥1 the geometric series cannot normalize, so this irreducible birth-death queue has no stationary probability law. At λ=μ it is critical, with no finite stationary mean; individual paths need not steadily grow. At λ>μ demand exceeds capacity and long-run growth is typical. Finite animations do not prove these asymptotic statements. Failure case. Ten scheduled hourly arrivals and fixed six-minute services both average ten/hour, yet violate memoryless arrivals and service. The geometric M/M/1 law does not follow from mean rates alone. Even at load below one, changing service variability can change waiting behavior. Derive the event-frequency law The geometric probabilities π describe the state at an ordinary stationary clock time, equivalently long-run fractions of elapsed time in this stable model. To count actual state changes, let q n be the rate of leaving state n: q 0 =λ, while q n =λ+μ for n≥1. At 0 no service is completed, because there is nobody to serve. At stationary time fraction π n , exits from n occur at mean rate π n q n . Inflow equals outflow, so after-change frequencies are proportional to these rates. Their total is λπ 0 +(λ+μ)(1−π 0 )=λ(1−ρ)+(λ+μ)ρ=2λ. Therefore: α n = π n q n 2 λ Explicitly α 0 =(1−ρ)/2 and α n =(1−ρ)(1+ρ)ρ n−1 /2 for n≥1. The positive-state probabilities sum to (1+ρ)/2, so the total is one. At λ=2 and μ=4, π 0 =1/2 but α 0 =1/4; π 1 =1/4 but α 1 =3/8. Both recorders can be correct. The second observes busy states more often because more state changes occur there per hour. Summing nα n gives actual-change mean (1+ρ)/[2(1−ρ)], exactly 1/2 above clock-time mean ρ/(1−ρ). At half load these are 3/2 and 1. Each expectation requires its observation law. The mean stationary actual-change rate 2λ does not make changes a homogeneous Poisson process: instantaneous rate depends on emptiness. Equal long-run arrival and departure rates do not establish independence. Berestycki and Sousi, Theorem 2.10 proves the invariant-measure/jump-chain relationship used in our geometric calculation. Recover time weights, with the correct boundary Because α n /q n =π n /(2λ), normalization recovers π; ∑α/q=1/(2λ) hours/change. At half load mean visits last 1/2 hour when empty and 1/6 when busy. Equal visit weights discard this difference; inverse exit rates restore model-mean durations. Finite records need a separate denominator. Consider seven consecutive complete visits with states 0,1,0,1,2,1,0 and durations 10/20,2/20,5/20,8/20,6/20,4/20,10/20 hours. These invented exact values illustrate a record, not a simulation. Each visit begins after an actual change; the next unlisted state is 1. One illustrative record: visits and actual holding times answer different questions Visit State Duration in hours 1 0 10/20 2 1 2/20 3 0 5/20 4 1 8/20 5 2 6/20 6 1 4/20 7 0 10/20 Empty visits form 3/7 of the record; empty elapsed time is (10+5+10)/(10+2+5+8+6+4+10)=25/45=5/9. Using model-mean durations 1/2 and 1/6 instead yields (3/2)/(3/2+4/6)=9/13. Exact stationary-law inverse-rate recovery does not claim that a finite-record estimator equals the fraction based on realized durations. Before an arrival, after an arrival, or at a null tick? Not every event sample has law α. At an external Poisson arrival immediately before it joins , the stationary queue size has law π: Poisson arrivals see time averages, or PASTA. This uses stationarity and a nonanticipating arrival mechanism, with future arrival increments independent of past queue/service history and arrivals independent of service. The arrivals help create the queue, so it would be wrong to call the arrival process independent of the entire queue process. We use PASTA here as a named theorem; Sigman’s continuous-time notes, the PASTA section gives the assumptions and statement. After that arrival, the size has increased by one. Its distribution is therefore π shifted upward: empty probability zero and mean 1/(1−ρ). At λ=2 and μ=4 that mean is 2, rather than the prearrival mean 1 or all-change mean 3/2. Which side of the event is recorded is part of the question. A different construction uses one Poisson clock of rate R=λ+μ. Each tick proposes an arrival with chance λ/R or a service attempt with chance μ/R. At a positive state both proposals change the size. At 0 a service attempt is a null event , leaving the size at 0; it is not a departure. Retaining every tick gives transition probabilities P 00 =μ/R, P 01 =λ/R, and the usual up/down probabilities elsewhere. Direct substitution verifies πP=π. Removing the null ticks gives the actual-change chain and its law α. Thus software that logs all proposed ticks and software that logs only actual changes can produce different histograms for one correct model. Optional: why the kth change from empty does not settle to the event-frequency law Frequency across visits is not a fixed-index distribution Let Y k be the queue size after k actual changes, with Y 0 =0. At every change the size increases or decreases by exactly one. Consequently Y k has the same parity as k. Empty probability is zero at every odd index, whereas α 0 >0 in the stable model. Fixed-index distributions from empty therefore cannot converge to α. In fact their even/odd mass alternates forever. Initialized with α, the jump chain stays distributed as α at every index. From empty, long-run visit proportions still converge to α in this irreducible positive recurrent model. Aperiodicity is required for convergence of fixed-index distributions, not these proportions. The stationarity lesson separates invariance from attraction. Stationary clock-time initialization uses π, not automatically jump-chain law α. Specify clock and initialization separately. The optional fixed-index control starts empty. Uniformized ticks retain a self-transition at 0, avoiding the parity obstruction; deleting null ticks changes that behavior. Calculate and inspect the model 1. Calculation. For M/M/1 rates λ=3/hour and μ=6/hour, find ρ, stationary P(0), P(2), and the mean system size. Hint for question 1 Find the rate ratio first, then use the normalized geometric formula. Full solution to question 1 ρ=3/6=1/2<1. Therefore P(0)=1−ρ=1/2 and P(2)=(1−ρ)ρ²=(1/2)(1/4)=1/8. The mean number in the system is ρ/(1−ρ)=(1/2)/(1/2)=1. These are stationary values; a queue just opened empty has P(0)=1 initially, so the formula does not describe its first instant. 2. Boundary and scope. An artist serves at μ=5/hour while arrivals are λ=5/hour. A colleague substitutes ρ=1 into πₙ=(1−ρ)ρⁿ and concludes every queue length has probability zero. What went wrong? Hint for question 2 Ask whether the infinite geometric series is finite at ρ=1. Full solution to question 2 The stationary derivation normalized Σρⁿ, which diverges at ρ=1. The factor 1−ρ=0 is only the limiting normalization from below, not a probability distribution at ρ=1. Assigning zero to every n sums to zero rather than one. This critical M/M/1 model has no normalizable stationary queue-length distribution; finite-time probabilities still exist and sum to one. 3. Changed load, unchanged reasoning. Use λ=3 and μ=5 per hour. Find the clock-time and actual-change empty probabilities, the corresponding mean sizes, and the prearrival and postarrival means. Recover the clock law’s empty probability by inverse-rate weighting. Hint for question 3 ρ=3/5, q 0 =3, q n≥1 =8, and ∑α/q=1/6 hour per change. Full solution to question 3 Clock empty probability is 2/5 and mean size 3/2. Actual-change empty probability is 1/5 and mean size (1+3/5)/(2(1−3/5))=2. Prearrival mean is 3/2 by PASTA under the stated assumptions; postarrival mean is 5/2. The inverse-rate empty weight is (1/5)/3=1/15. Dividing by the total weight 1/6 gives (1/15)/(1/6)=2/5, recovering clock time. 4. Change speed without changing load. Compare (λ,μ)=(2,4) with (4,8). Which of the observation laws and mean sizes change? What happens to mean holding times at empty and positive states, and to the mean stationary actual-change rate? Does “eight actual changes per hour on average” imply a Poisson change process? Hint for question 4 Separate the ratio λ/μ from the absolute rates. Divide both mean holding times by two, then reconsider which distribution formulas use only the ratio. Second hint for question 4 Keep the same embedded sequence of states while rescaling its clock. Which stationary weights depend only on the rate ratio, and which waiting-time and event-count quantities also depend on the common rate scale? Full solution to question 4 Both loads are 1/2, so π, α, the prearrival and postarrival laws, the uniformized invariant law and inverse-rate recovery all stay the same. Empty holding time falls from 1/2 to 1/4 hour; positive holding time from 1/6 to 1/12 hour. Mean actual-change rate doubles from 4 to 8 per hour. This is a mean rate, not a claim of homogeneous Poisson changes; instantaneous changes remain faster in positive states than at 0. 5. Transfer to a different process. A two-state continuous-time chain moves 0→1 at rate 1/hour and 1→0 at rate 3/hour. Find its clock-time stationary law and its actual-change visit frequencies. Show inverse-rate recovery. Can its fixed jump-index law from 0 converge? Hint for question 5 Balance π 0 ·1=π 1 ·3. Actual changes alternate deterministically between the two states. Full solution to question 5 Balance and normalization give π=(3/4,1/4). The alternating event visits have frequencies α=(1/2,1/2). Weighting by inverse exit rates gives (1/2,1/6); normalization by 2/3 recovers (3/4,1/4). At a fixed jump index from 0, the state is 0 at even indices and 1 at odd ones, so the distributions do not converge. The M/M/1 mean-size difference of 1/2 was specific to that queue law; the rate-weighting principle transfers more broadly. 6. Audit a recorder. One program logs the size just before each Poisson arrival. Another logs after every rate-(λ+μ) proposal tick, including unsuccessful service attempts at 0. A third logs after actual changes only. At λ=2,μ=4, which equilibrium empty fractions should they target? If all start empty, must the first ten rows already have those fractions? Hint for question 6 Identify whether each recorder includes null ticks or shifts the size at arrivals. Keep a stationary law distinct from a short record started empty. Second hint for question 6 For each observation rule, first identify the probability law it samples. Compare the rate-weighted actual-change law with the time-stationary law, and check whether the initial state is already drawn from either law. Full solution to question 6 The first targets 1/2 under the prearrival PASTA assumptions. The second also has invariant empty fraction 1/2 because it retains the null ticks. The third targets actual-change frequency 1/4. Starting empty is not stationary; finite records also fluctuate. None must equal its equilibrium value in ten rows. For the third, even the distribution of a fixed kth row from empty has a parity obstruction, while long-run visit frequencies can still converge. Read load together with assumptions M/M/1 balance requires a specific birth-death model and observation protocol. Clock-time π, actual-change α, and pre/postarrival laws answer different questions; retaining null ticks changes event frequencies. Normalization requires λ<μ and tail size depends on ρ. Finite records and fixed-index distributions need separate interpretation. Revisit violated assumptions; exponential waits supplies the memoryless construction.

title: A family tree that may end
summary: Compare generation growth, eventual extinction and the different trees selected by a finite deadline.
text: Can a family tree end even when it grows on average? Each fantasy creature independently produces 0, 1 or 2 descendants under one shared rule, then leaves. This Galton–Watson process has generation size Zₙ, starting at Z₀=1. Expected generation size and eventual extinction probability ask different questions. Background capsule. If a creature has offspring count K with probabilities p₀,p₁,p₂, its mean is m=0p₀+1p₁+2p₂. Expectation is an average across imagined repeats; it need not describe a typical realized tree. A generating polynomial f(s)=p₀+p₁s+p₂s² packages the offspring probabilities. Extinction means Zₙ=0 at some finite generation; zero then remains zero. Independent, identically distributed reproduction is essential to the formulas below. We will use a toy rule with p₀=1/4, p₁=1/4 and p₂=1/2. Its mean is 5/4, yet extinction still has positive probability. One generation, then the whole future Worked example. From one creature, the first generation has 0, 1 or 2 creatures with the stated probabilities. Its expected size is 0·1/4+1·1/4+2·1/2=5/4. The expected second generation is (5/4)²=25/16, because each of the expected first-generation creatures independently has mean 5/4 children. This does not imply the family grows on every run: it ends immediately with probability 1/4. Let q be the eventual extinction chance from one creature. If the first creature has no children, extinction is certain. If it has one, the chance is q; if two, both independent child lines must die, chance q². Thus q=1/4+(1/4)q+(1/2)q². Rearranging, 2q²−3q+1=0, with roots 1/2 and 1. Which root is the extinction probability? The smaller one: q=1/2. The root 1 appears algebraically for every offspring distribution because f(1)=1, but in a supercritical process it need not be the actual extinction chance. Two different summaries for the toy family Quantity Value Meaning Mean offspring m 5/4 Average children per creature E[Z₂] 25/16 Mean size of generation two Extinction probability q 1/2 Chance of ever reaching zero A finite sample of trees may all grow or vanish. Neither proves eventual extinction probabilities; estimation requires repeated runs. Which extinct trees did the observer collect? Compare trees selected for eventual extinction with trees extinct by generation 2. Predict each collection's ancestor offspring law, especially its zero-child probability. Selection leaves the original reproduction mechanism unchanged. Expectation recurrence and the correct root E [ Z n ] = Z 0 m n , q = f ( q ) Condition on Zₙ=z. There are z parents, each with independent offspring count of mean m, so E[Zₙ₊₁|Zₙ=z]=mz. Averaging over Zₙ yields E[Zₙ₊₁]=mE[Zₙ]; induction gives Z₀mⁿ for a fixed finite initial number Z₀. Independence is not needed for this expectation step alone if conditional means remain m, but it is needed for multiplying child-line extinction probabilities. For extinction, let qₙ be the chance the line is extinct by generation n. Start q₀=0 for one living ancestor. Independence of child lines gives qₙ₊₁=f(qₙ). Because extinction is absorbing, qₙ increases and is bounded by one, so it tends to a limit q. Polynomial continuity makes q=f(q). Iterating from zero selects the smallest fixed point in [0,1]: if r is any fixed point there, induction gives qₙ≤r and hence q≤r. This proves the root selection for the stated finite offspring model. For the toy polynomial f(s)=1/4+s/4+s²/2, iteration starts 0, 1/4, 11/32, and rises toward 1/2. The other root 1 is not selected. In general, m≤1 implies extinction with probability one under the usual nondegenerate finite-mean Galton–Watson assumptions, except the deterministic exactly-one-child rule, where the line never ends. When m>1, extinction can still be positive if p₀>0; the exact value depends on the whole offspring distribution, not just m. Failure case. If siblings' descendants are forced to share a single environmental coin, child lines are dependent. Then the chance both die need not be q², and f(q) need not be the extinction equation. Identical mean offspring alone does not preserve the fixed-point calculation. Selecting eventual extinctions changes the offspring law Let E mean eventual extinction, with probability q >0, and let K be the ancestor's offspring count. Given K = k , all k independent child lines must die out, with probability q k . For no children this probability is 1: there are no child lines to keep alive. Thus P ( K = k , E )= p k q k . Dividing by P ( E )= q gives the selected law: P selected ( K = k ) = p k q k q = p k q k − 1 The probabilities sum to f ( q )/ q =1. For our original law they are (1/2,1/4,1/4), with mean offspring r =0×1/2+1×1/4+2×1/4=3/4. Compare that with the original mean 5/4. This describes a selected set of trees; it is not a causal intervention on the original reproduction mechanism. If q =0, conditioning on extinction by this division is undefined. Why the selected child lines are still independent A root calculation alone does not justify applying the new law to the whole tree. Suppose the ancestor has two children. Write E 1 , E 2 for extinction of their lines, and B 1 , B 2 for any events about their respective subtrees. Original independence makes the probability of both B i ∩ E i events the product of their probabilities. Conditional on both lines becoming extinct, divide by q ². The result is the product of P ( B 1 | E 1 ) and P ( B 2 | E 2 ). So, conditional on the number of children and eventual extinction, their subtrees are independent copies of the original tree conditioned on extinction. With one child there is one such copy; with zero there are none. Apply the same argument recursively at every child. The entire selected tree is therefore a Galton–Watson process with the selected offspring law above, rather than merely having a different ancestor distribution. Total size needs the selected mean Let S = Z 0 + Z 1 +⋯ be the total number of individuals ever born, including the ancestor once. Under the eventual-extinction selected law, generation n has mean r n . If r <1, nonnegative summation gives E [ S | E ] = ∑ n = 0 ∞ r n = 1 1 − r More explicitly, finite partial totals have means 1+ r +⋯+ r n ; monotone convergence permits their nonnegative limit. This proves finiteness when r <1 rather than assuming it while solving an expectation equation. Here the conditional mean total is 4. Unconditionally, however, survival has probability 1/2 and then infinitely many individuals are born, so the original total-size mean is infinite. Do not insert the original mean 5/4 into the subcritical formula. The hypothesis r <1 matters. In the critical zero-or-two example in question 1, extinction is certain and the selected law is unchanged, with r =1. Every selected tree is finite almost surely, yet its mean total size is infinite; question 5 develops the calculation. A finite deadline is a different condition Let E h mean extinction by generation h , with probability q h . The ancestor is alive at generation 0, so q 0 =0. For h ≥1, q h = f ( q h−1 ). A child line now has only h −1 generations in which to die out. Therefore the deadline-selected ancestor probabilities are p k q h−1 k / q h . At h =1 only zero children are possible; use an empty product of 1 for that case. There is no conditional law given E 0 , an event of probability zero. For h =2, q 2 =11/32. The ancestor probabilities are (8/11,2/11,1/11), rather than the eventual law (1/2,1/4,1/4). Any children in this selected tree must themselves have zero children: only one generation remains. Reusing the ancestor's deadline law at each generation would incorrectly allow living grandchildren at the extinction deadline. Child subtrees remain conditionally independent, but their laws use the remaining deadline, which shrinks down the tree. The explorer's three top-level masses concern all original trees : extinct by h , q h ; extinct later, q − q h ; and never extinct, 1− q . They sum to 1. Among eventually extinct trees, the fraction already extinct is instead q h / q , which at h =2 is 11/16. The finite slider illustrates this partition. The fixed-point proof establishes the eventual value; a finite display does not prove it. Optional: exact full-size means within a deadline-selected set At deadline 2, the only possible complete trees have sizes 1, 2 and 3. Their selected probabilities are 8/11,2/11,1/11, so their mean is (8+4+3)/11=15/11. This is a full tree-size mean conditional on extinction by the deadline. It is not the size of a still-living tree with later generations omitted. For a general deadline, define a score equal to S on E h and zero outside it; call its unconditional mean A h . This definition avoids any product of infinity with zero. Start A 0 =0. The root contributes one individual on the event E h , hence contributes q h to the score's mean. With one child, the child-size contribution is p 1 A h−1 . With two independent children, each child's size counts only if the other child line also dies by the remaining deadline. Their combined contribution is 2 p 2 q h−1 A h−1 . Thus A h = q h +( p 1 +2 p 2 q h−1 ) A h−1 , and the selected mean full size is A h / q h . These finite recurrences produce the exact explorer values. For the original law at h =3 they give q 3 =809/2048 and mean full size 1379/809. Allow about 15 additional minutes for this optional recurrence and its check. Mean and extinction are different tasks 1. Calculation. Each creature has zero or two children, each with probability 1/2. Starting from one, find m, E[Z₃] and eventual extinction probability. Hint for question 1 Write f(s)=1/2+s²/2, solve q=f(q), and select the smallest root in [0,1]. Full solution to question 1 m=0·1/2+2·1/2=1, so E[Z₃]=1³=1. The fixed-point equation is q=1/2+q²/2, or (q−1)²=0. Its only root is q=1, so eventual extinction has probability one, despite every generation having expected size one. Rare large surviving trees keep the mean at one. 2. Counterexample. Every creature deterministically has exactly one child. Compare its mean and extinction chance with question 1. Why does mean alone fail to specify q? Hint for question 2 Write the actual generation sizes and its generating function. Full solution to question 2 Here m=1 again, but Zₙ=1 for every generation, so q=0. The generating function f(s)=s makes every s a fixed point; iteration from q₀=0 stays at zero, selecting q=0. In question 1, f(s)=(1+s²)/2 and extinction is certain. Equal means conceal different offspring distributions, so the mean-growth formula cannot determine extinction by itself. Change the reproduction law 3. Transfer to a fresh law. Give zero, one and two children probabilities 3/8,1/8,1/2. Find its original mean and eventual extinction probability. Derive the offspring law among eventual extinctions, then the mean full tree size in that selected set. Why is the unconditional mean full size different? Hint for question 3 Solve 4q²−7q+3=0 and select the smaller fixed point. Apply the selected-law formula before using a geometric total-size sum. Full solution to question 3 The original mean is 1/8+1=9/8. The fixed points are 3/4 and 1, so q=3/4. The selected probabilities are ((3/8)/(3/4),1/8,(1/2)(3/4))=(1/2,1/8,3/8). Their mean is r=1/8+2(3/8)=7/8<1, giving conditional mean total size 1/(1−7/8)=8, including the ancestor. The original tree survives with probability 1/4 and then has infinite total size, so its unconditional mean total is infinite. 4. Change the selection as well. For question 3's law, select trees extinct by generation 2. Find that selection's probability, the ancestor's offspring law and the mean full size. Partition all original trees into extinct by 2, extinct later and never extinct. What fraction of the eventually extinct trees are already extinct by 2? Hint for question 4 Start q₁=3/8 and substitute into f. Conditional on extinction by 2, all of the ancestor's children have zero children, so the full size is 1+K. Full solution to question 4 q₂=3/8+(1/8)(3/8)+(1/2)(3/8)²=63/128. The ancestor's three joint masses with this event are 48/128,6/128,9/128. Normalizing gives (16/21,2/21,1/7). The mean ancestor offspring is 2/21+2/7=8/21, so the mean full size is 1+8/21=29/21, not 8. The three unconditional masses are 63/128,33/128 and 1/4. Among eventual extinctions, the fraction extinct by 2 is (63/128)/(3/4)=21/32. The denominators describe different selected sets. 5. Check the mean hypothesis. Return to the zero-or-two critical law in question 1. Is the mean full tree size finite? How can your answer coexist with almost-sure extinction and a finite realized tree? Hint for question 5 Compute the expected total through generation n before taking its nonnegative limit. Every generation has mean size 1. Full solution to question 5 The partial total through generation n has mean n+1. Its monotone limit is the full total, so the mean is infinite. Since extinction occurs at a finite generation almost surely and each individual has at most two children, every realized extinct tree is finite. Rare large finite trees make its mean infinite. Here q=1 leaves the selected law unchanged, with r=1, so the finite formula 1/(1−r) does not apply. Keep two summaries apart Expected generation size follows a one-line conditional-expectation recurrence. Extinction follows a generating-function recurrence and the smallest fixed point, with independent child lines. A supercritical mean can coexist with a substantial chance of extinction; a critical mean can coexist with either certain extinction or deterministic survival, depending on the offspring law. These are conclusions about the specified toy process, not predictions about real populations. State the selection event before describing a collected tree. Eventual-extinction selection has one new reproduction law throughout the tree; deadline selection has a shrinking horizon down its branches. A finite cutoff does not turn “not extinct yet” into “survives forever.” For total-size means, check the selected mean offspring and count the ancestor.

title: What counts as an algorithm?
summary: A recipe must finish and give the promised dish. Specify input, output, termination, and correctness for a finite procedure.
text: A recipe that earns its name Suppose a library has an unordered stack of returned books and wants to find every copy with a given identifier. “Look until you find it” is incomplete: it may miss a later copy, and if none is present it gives no stopping condition. An algorithm needs a defined input, a defined output, finite steps, and a claim relating them. Here the input is a finite list of identifiers and a target; the output can be the list of all matching positions. Background capsule. A finite sequence has entries numbered 0 through n −1. A function associates an output with each permitted input. A precondition says which inputs are allowed; a postcondition says what the output guarantees. We will assume identifiers can be compared exactly and the input list does not change during a run. These assumptions are part of the specification, not hidden conveniences. Trace a complete scan Worked example. Consider the list [A, B, A, C] and target A. Start with an empty output list and an index i =0. At each step, compare entry i with A, append i if equal, and increment i . Stop when i =4. The successive output lists are [], [0], [0], [0,2], [0,2]. The final result [0,2] refers to positions, not copies of the letter. If the target were D, the same scan would stop and return []. A trace is useful evidence about one run. It is not a proof that every finite list is handled correctly. To make the algorithm precise, include the instruction to stop at i = n before reading an entry. Otherwise the program might access an undefined position. The mathematical specification is “return exactly the indices whose entries equal the target,” not merely “return some match.” A loop invariant does the proof work Claim. For every finite input list of length n , the scan stops after exactly n comparisons and returns all and only matching indices. After i iterations, maintain the invariant: the output contains exactly the matching positions among 0,…, i −1. Initially i =0 and there are no inspected positions, so the empty output satisfies the claim. In the next iteration, the test at position i either appends that index if it matches or leaves the output alone if it does not. Both choices make the invariant true for the longer inspected prefix. This proves preservation without assuming the final answer. Termination requires a separate argument. The nonnegative integer n − i decreases by one on each iteration and cannot decrease forever while remaining nonnegative. At i = n , the invariant covers every valid position. Thus the postcondition follows. The mathematical core is a bounded loop; an actual implementation must additionally handle practical details such as memory limits and identifier equality. Those details do not make the abstract proof false, but they narrow where it applies. A tempting “optimization” is to stop at the first A. That procedure meets a different specification, finding one witness, but it fails the present one on [A,B,A,C]. A successful trace on [B,A,C] would not expose the error. Correctness always refers to a stated contract; the same code can be correct for one contract and incorrect for another. A ( x ) = y Worked example: an empty input still has an answer Run the same scan on the empty list, searching for A. Its length is zero, so the initial state has i = 0 = n . The stopping condition holds before any entry is inspected. Return the empty output list. This is correct because there is no valid position at which a match could occur, and it uses exactly zero comparisons. Now compare a one-entry list [A]. The initial stopping test fails, the comparison at position zero succeeds, and the output becomes [0]. Incrementing the index gives i = 1 = n , so the run ends. Writing the stop test before the access handles both sizes with one rule. An algorithm that assumes a first element exists would have an unstated nonempty-input precondition and would not meet our original contract. Two specification checks 1. Run the scan on [7,4,7,7] with target 7. State its output and the invariant after two iterations. Hint for question 1 After two iterations only positions 0 and 1 have been examined. Full solution to question 1 The output changes from [] to [0], stays [0], then becomes [0,2] and [0,2,3]. At i =2, the matching positions in the inspected prefix [7,4] are exactly [0], so the invariant holds. The final output is [0,2,3]. 2. Replace “increment i ” with “increment i only after a match.” Give a failing input and explain which proof obligation breaks. Hint for question 2 Place a nonmatching entry at position zero. Full solution to question 2 With list [B] and target A, the first comparison fails, i remains 0, and the loop repeats forever. The measure n − i no longer decreases, so termination is unproved and in fact false. The output may remain empty, but a correct answer never arrives. What the proof bought us A finite algorithm is more than a plausible recipe. Its contract says what an answer means; an invariant links each intermediate state to that contract; a decreasing measure establishes a finish. For this scan, those ingredients prove a full result for every finite list under exact comparisons. They do not prove that arbitrary programs terminate. If you want a sharper cost question, binary search studies how an additional sortedness precondition can save comparisons.

title: Why halving a search works
summary: Finding a page in a sorted book takes few questions. Explain binary search invariant and logarithmic comparison bound.
text: Ask about the middle A catalogue sorted by identifier invites a faster search than reading every row. Binary search compares the target with a middle entry, then discards a half that cannot contain the target. Its speed rests entirely on the order guarantee. We will prove a precise version that returns the first position of a target, or reports absence. Background capsule. A list is sorted in nondecreasing order when entry a[i] is at most a[j] whenever i < j . Equal values may appear. An interval [ lo , hi ) contains integer positions starting at lo and stopping just before hi . Its length is hi − lo . We use indices 0 through n −1, and the target can be compared with an entry. A boundary search Worked example. Search [2,4,4,4,9,12] for 4. Set lo =0, hi =6. At each round choose mid =floor(( lo + hi )/2). If a[mid] <4, set lo = mid +1; otherwise set hi = mid . The first midpoint is 3, whose value is 4, so hi becomes 3. Midpoint 1 is also 4, so hi becomes 1. Midpoint 0 has value 2, so lo becomes 1. The interval is empty at lo = hi =1. A final equality test returns index 1. This “lower bound” version does not stop as soon as it sees a matching middle. It keeps searching left because a duplicate could be earlier. For target 5 on the same list, the boundary becomes 4, and a[4] =9 fails the final test. An empty list yields boundary 0, and the final test must guard against reading position 0. Invariant and cost Claim. On a sorted finite list, this procedure returns the first target occurrence if one exists. The invariant is: every position below lo has value less than the target, and every position at or above hi has value at least the target. Initially these outside regions are empty. If the midpoint value is smaller, sortedness makes every position through mid smaller, so increasing lo preserves the invariant. Otherwise the midpoint and all later positions have value at least the target, so lowering hi preserves it. When the interval is empty, lo = hi is the first position whose value could be at least the target. The guarded equality test distinguishes presence from a larger successor. Each nonempty round removes at least half of the candidate interval, rounding as needed. If its current length is m , the next length is at most floor( m /2). After k rounds its length is at most floor( n /2 k ). Hence for n >0, at most floor(log 2 n )+1 midpoint comparisons make it empty; one final equality comparison may be needed. This bound counts comparisons, not all machine operations. The interval length strictly decreases, proving termination separately from correctness. Sortedness is essential. On [9,2,4] searching for 9, midpoint 1 holds 2, so the algorithm discards index 0 and reports absence. The code still terminates, but its invariant justification is false. Nor does binary search help when you must inspect an unsorted list from scratch merely to establish order. T ( n ) ≤ ⌊ log 2 n ⌋ + 1 Worked example: a target beyond every entry Search [2,4,4,9] for 12. Initially [ lo , hi ) is [0,4). Midpoint 2 holds 4, smaller than 12, so lo becomes 3. The remaining interval [3,4) has midpoint 3 with value 9, also smaller, so lo becomes 4. We finish at the boundary 4, equal to the list length. The equality check must first ask whether the boundary is below n . Here it is not, so the target is absent without reading a nonexistent entry. The invariant tells us every valid position lies below this boundary and has a value smaller than 12. A boundary position is allowed to be just beyond the list; it names an insertion place, not necessarily an existing element. That distinction also explains the empty-list case. Test the boundary 1. Trace the intervals when searching [1,3,5,7,9] for 6, and state the returned answer. Hint for question 1 Use half-open intervals and choose midpoint 2 first. Full solution to question 1 Start [0,5). At midpoint 2, value 5 is smaller than 6, so move to [3,5). Midpoint 4 has value 9, so move to [3,4). Midpoint 3 has value 7, so move to [3,3). The boundary is 3, but entry 3 is 7, so the target is absent. 2. Why does stopping at the first equal midpoint fail to satisfy the first-occurrence specification? Use a concrete list. Hint for question 2 Put several equal values around the initial midpoint. Full solution to question 2 On [1,4,4,4,8], target 4, the first midpoint is 2 and equals 4, yet the first occurrence is index 1. Returning 2 satisfies a presence specification but violates the requested first-position contract. Continuing with hi =2 leads to boundary 1. The useful promise Binary search converts order into a proof of safe elimination. The interval invariant identifies what cannot be discarded; repeated halving supplies a logarithmic comparison bound. The failure on unsorted input shows why an algorithmic guarantee must carry its preconditions. For a formal language of growth bounds, continue to Big O ; for algorithms that reuse answers rather than discard candidates, see remembering subproblems .

title: When input size changes the story
summary: A fast laptop cannot rescue an exploding search space forever. Compare linear, quadratic, and exponential operation counts.
text: How much does doubling cost? A program can be quick on ten items and hopeless on a hundred. To reason about scaling, count a specified basic operation as a function of input size n . This is a mathematical model: its units might be comparisons, additions, or candidate checks. Calling every counted operation “one unit” does not assert that real hardware executes them in equal time. Background capsule. The expression n 2 means n multiplied by itself; 2 n means multiplying 2 by itself n times. A function maps an input size to a count. We compare positive integer sizes and exact counts before using asymptotic notation. A finite table records examples, not behavior at every possible size. Three exact bills Worked example. Imagine three procedures. Procedure L inspects each of n entries once and performs exactly n inspections. Procedure Q checks every ordered pair of entries, including self-pairs, and makes exactly n 2 checks. Procedure E considers every subset of an n -element set and makes exactly 2 n checks. These are deliberately simple models with counts you can derive from their descriptions. Exact model counts n L: n Q: n² E: 2ⁿ 4 4 16 16 8 8 64 256 16 16 256 65,536 Doubling n doubles L's count, multiplies Q's count by four, and squares E's count: 2 2n =(2 n ) 2 . The table makes the differences visible, but the formulas supply the exact claims. Why the formulas have those shapes Claim. For a set with n distinct labelled elements, the number of subsets is exactly 2 n . Every element has two independent choices, included or omitted. Encode a subset by an n -bit string, putting 1 exactly where an element is included. This gives a one-to-one correspondence: every subset yields one string and every string yields one subset. There are two choices for each of n bit positions, so the product is 2 n . The argument is a complete count, not an extrapolation from the table. The quadratic count likewise follows from n choices for the first ordered position and n for the second. If the procedure excludes self-pairs, its exact count becomes n ( n −1), still close in scale but no longer n 2 . Be precise about the operation being counted. A faster machine with 1,000 times the throughput gives a factor of 1,000 on a fixed count model; it does not change an exponential count into a quadratic count. Do the three formulas alone establish a theorem that 2 n eventually exceeds every polynomial? That broader claim needs a proof about arbitrary fixed polynomial degree; the table cannot supply it. Here is a narrower, proved comparison: for n ≥5, 2 n > n 2 . The base case is 32>25. If 2 n > n 2 and n ≥5, then 2 n+1 >2 n 2 >( n +1) 2 , since n 2 −2 n −1>0. Induction proves the stated range. A failure case for a casual slogan is n =2: 2 2 =2 2 , so “exponential always beats quadratic” is false. A large constant can also make a nominally linear procedure slower on practical sizes. Growth comparisons answer eventual questions only after constants and thresholds are specified. n , n 2 , 2 n Worked example: a constant changes the early ranking Suppose two exact operation counts are A ( n ) = 100 n and B ( n ) = n ², for positive integer sizes. Dividing the inequality 100 n < n ² by positive n gives 100 < n . Therefore A has the smaller count exactly for sizes above 100; at 100 they tie, and below 100 B is smaller. For instance at size 20, the counts are 2000 and 400; at size 200 they are 20000 and 40000. Neither observation alone locates every later comparison. The algebra supplies the threshold and its complete range. Calling A linear and B quadratic describes their growth mechanism, while the multiplier 100 still matters to a finite choice between these two operation-count models. Actual running times require further assumptions about what each counted operation costs. Count what is actually done 1. A routine inspects every unordered pair of distinct people among six people exactly once. How many inspections? Explain why n 2 is the wrong exact count. Hint for question 1 Count ordered choices first and divide by the two possible orders. Full solution to question 1 There are 6·5=30 ordered distinct pairs. Each unordered pair appears twice, so the routine makes 30/2=15 inspections. The count n 2 =36 includes self-pairs and double counts each distinct pair. 2. Compare 2 n and n 2 at n =3 and n =8. Does either check prove the inequality for every larger n ? Hint for question 2 Calculate both columns; distinguish a checked input from an induction step. Full solution to question 2 At 3 the values are 8 and 9, so the exponential count is smaller. At 8 they are 256 and 64, so it is larger. Neither isolated check proves a universal later claim. The induction argument above supplies that proof for all integers n ≥5. Model the right operation Linear, quadratic and exponential counts describe different scaling mechanisms. Exact combinatorial arguments justify these model counts, while measured wall time needs additional hardware and implementation assumptions. The article has proved a particular eventual inequality, not a universal runtime ranking among programs. Big O makes eventual upper bounds precise, including the constants that a growth slogan usually hides.

title: Big O is an eventual bound
summary: A tiny program can lose to a bigger one at large scale. Use constants and thresholds to justify an asymptotic upper bound.
text: What “eventually no faster” means Suppose one routine costs 3 n +5 operations and another costs 100 n . Which grows faster? The first has fewer operations at n =1, but its expression is still linear. Big O records an eventual upper bound after allowing a fixed multiplier. It is a statement about functions over arbitrarily large inputs, not a stopwatch verdict on one size. Background capsule. We consider nonnegative functions f and g on positive integers, with g(n) >0 from some point onward. “For all n ≥ n 0 ” includes every larger integer. A constant C must be chosen once, independently of n . These quantifier details are the whole meaning of the notation. Find witnesses, not just a trend Worked example. For f(n) =3 n +5 and g(n) = n , choose C =8 and n 0 =1. For every n ≥1, 5≤5 n , so 3 n +5≤8 n . That pair of numbers is a certificate for the Big O claim. A tighter option is C =4, n 0 =5. Neither is uniquely correct. By contrast, the first few values of n 2 and 100 n can mislead: at n =10, they are 100 and 1,000, but at n =1,000 they are 1,000,000 and 100,000. A crossing point is interesting; a table of crossings alone cannot prove a statement extending to all later inputs. Here algebra does: n 2 ≤100 n exactly when n ≤100 for positive n . The quantified upper bound Definition. f(n) =O( g(n) ) means that there exist constants C >0 and n 0 such that, for every integer n ≥ n 0 , 0≤ f(n) ≤ Cg(n) . The displayed formula states the same claim. This is an upper bound, not necessarily a tight description. For example, n =O( n 2 ) by taking C =1, n 0 =1, but the reverse fails. Proof of failure in the reverse direction. If n 2 =O( n ), then some fixed C would make n 2 ≤ Cn for all sufficiently large positive n . Dividing by n gives n ≤ C . Choose any integer larger than both C and the alleged threshold. This contradicts the bound. The ability to choose n after C is fixed matters. Big O does not mean “worst case” by itself. First decide which cost function is under study: worst-case comparisons, average expected comparisons under a named distribution, or something else. Then apply the same mathematical bound to that function. A finite benchmark can reveal a coding error or practical crossing point, but cannot establish the quantified claim. Also, a bound like O( n 2 ) may be true for a linear algorithm; for a precise order of growth one would need matching upper and lower bounds. f ( n ) = O ( g ( n ) ) ⇔ ∃ C , n 0 ∀ n ≥ n 0 : f ( n ) ≤ Cg ( n ) Worked example: trading a multiplier for a threshold Consider f ( n ) = 2 n + 100. To prove f ( n ) = O( n ), one possible certificate is C = 102 and n ₀ = 1, because 100 ≤ 100 n whenever n ≥ 1. A smaller multiplier is possible if we wait longer: choose C = 3 and n ₀ = 100. For every later input, 100 ≤ n , so 2 n + 100 ≤ 3 n . Could we take C = 2 with some still larger threshold? No. The inequality 2 n + 100 ≤ 2 n is false for every input. Raising the threshold cannot fix it. In contrast, C = 2.5 works from n = 200 onward, since 100 ≤ 0.5 n . The definition requires a positive real multiplier, not necessarily an integer, and it requires one fixed choice for the entire remaining range. These certificates prove an upper-bound claim. None states that exactly three operations occur per input item, and a failed choice of constants does not refute Big O when another valid pair exists. To refute the claim itself, one must defeat every possible fixed pair, as the quadratic-versus-linear argument does. Supply or defeat a certificate 1. Prove 7 n 2 +2 n +9=O( n 2 ) for positive integers. Hint for question 1 For n ≥1, compare n and 1 with n 2 . Full solution to question 1 For n ≥1, 2 n ≤2 n 2 and 9≤9 n 2 . Therefore 7 n 2 +2 n +9≤18 n 2 . Choose C =18 and n 0 =1. 2. A friend claims 100 n =O(1) because it runs quickly for n ≤20. Refute the mathematical claim. Hint for question 2 Suppose a fixed bound C exists and choose a larger input. Full solution to question 2 O(1) would require 100 n ≤ C for every integer beyond some threshold. Choose n larger than that threshold and C /100. Then 100 n > C . Finite fast timings say nothing about this infinite quantifier. Read the constants in the claim A Big O proof provides a multiplier and a point after which the inequality always holds. It permits loose bounds and says nothing alone about actual seconds. The linear example and quadratic counterexample were proved by inequalities; no finite timing chart can replace them. With that language in hand, recurrence costs show how a divide-and-conquer algorithm can have a logarithmic number of levels but still perform n work per level.

title: A machine with finite memory
summary: A turnstile remembers locked or unlocked with one bit. Run a deterministic finite automaton and define acceptance.
text: A tiny memory can recognize a pattern A turnstile that alternates locked and unlocked after each coin needs only two memory states. For a mathematical machine, we can ignore the motor and ask what a finite memory can recognize from a stream of symbols. Our example reads bits and accepts exactly those strings containing an odd number of 1s. The machine never needs to store the entire string. Background capsule. An alphabet is a finite set of symbols; here Σ={0,1}. A string is a finite sequence of those symbols, including the empty string ε. A state is a name for the machine's current memory. A transition function assigns exactly one next state to each state-symbol pair. “Accept” means the state after the entire string has been read belongs to a designated accepting set. Walk through the bits Worked example. Use states E and O for even and odd parity, start at E, and accept at O. Reading 0 leaves the state unchanged; reading 1 switches it. The transition table makes the whole machine explicit. Parity DFA transitions Current state On 0 On 1 E E O O O E Trace 1011: E→O after 1, O→O after 0, O→E after the next 1, and E→O after the last 1. Since O is accepting, 1011 is accepted. The empty string leaves the machine at E and is rejected. So is 11, because two toggles restore E. These traces let us test the table; they do not by themselves justify the result for every string. State the general machine and prove its meaning A deterministic finite automaton is a tuple M =( Q ,Σ,δ, q 0 , F ). Here Q is a finite state set, Σ a finite alphabet, δ: Q ×Σ→ Q a total transition function, q 0 a start state q 0 ∈ Q , and F ⊆ Q a set of accepting states. For the parity example, Q ={E,O}, q 0 =E, and F ={O}. “Total” matters: every possible state and input symbol has an instruction. A missing transition is an incomplete specification unless an explicit rejecting sink is supplied. Claim. After reading any finite prefix, the machine is in E exactly when that prefix has an even number of 1s. Prove this by induction on prefix length. For length zero, the count is zero and state E is correct. Suppose the claim holds for a prefix. Appending 0 does not change the count and the table holds the state. Appending 1 changes parity and the table toggles the state. Thus the invariant holds for the extended prefix. At the end, acceptance at O is equivalent to an odd count. This is a complete proof for every finite binary string, not just the traced examples. The machine reads one symbol per transition, so a string of length n uses exactly n transitions and then a final state check. This finite-state model has no unbounded counter. It can remember parity because only two categories matter, but the proof here says nothing about which languages no finite automaton can recognize. That requires a separate impossibility tool. M = ( Q , Σ , δ , q 0 , F ) Worked example: changing the accepting set Keep exactly the parity transition table, but make E the sole accepting state. On input 101, the run is E → O → O → E. It now accepts, because the final count of 1s is two. On input 1, the run ends at O and rejects. The empty string stays at E and accepts without taking a transition. The earlier state invariant is unchanged: E still means an even number of 1s and O an odd number. Only the final decision rule changed. Consequently the new machine recognizes strings with an even number of 1s. A DFA consists of its accepting set as well as its transition table and start state. Reusing a correct transition proof does not mean that every different accepting set recognizes the same language. Try altered strings and machines 1. Trace 00101 through the parity machine and decide acceptance. Hint for question 1 Only the 1 symbols change the state; record the state after each symbol. Full solution to question 1 Starting E, the states after 0,0,1,0,1 are E,E,O,O,E. There are two 1s, so the final state E is rejecting. Both the trace and the parity invariant agree. 2. Someone erases the transition from O on input 0 and says the result is still a DFA for odd parity. What fails? Repair it. Hint for question 2 Check the formal domain of δ and try string 10. Full solution to question 2 δ must assign an output to (O,0), but the modified table does not. The run on 10 reaches O after 1 and then has no defined next state. Restore δ(O,0)=O, because adding zero does not change the number of 1s or its parity. Remember only what matters A finite automaton trades a full input history for a finite state that preserves exactly the information needed for its acceptance question. The parity invariant proves the chosen two states are sufficient for this language. An individual accepted trace is evidence for one word, while the induction covers all words. Patterns and machines uses a different state meaning: the suffix relevant to whether a word ends in 01.

title: Patterns and machines
summary: A text pattern can be a small machine in disguise. Build an automaton for binary strings ending in 01.
text: What must a pattern reader remember? Suppose a message is accepted only when its last two bits are 01. A human can glance at the end, but a machine reading left to right needs to carry just enough information from its prefix to decide at the finish. A regular expression for this language is (0|1)*01: any finite binary prefix followed by 0 then 1. We will build a deterministic machine directly and prove what its states mean. Background capsule. A binary string is a finite word over {0,1}; ε is the empty word. A suffix is a sequence at the end of a word. The notation * in this theoretical regular expression means zero or more repetitions; | means choice. This is formal-language notation, not a promise about the extra features of a particular programming language's regex engine. A DFA has a finite set of states, one transition per state and symbol, a start state, and accepting states. Three memories Worked example. Use states A, B, C. A means the word has no useful trailing 0 and does not end in 01. B means it ends in 0. C means it ends in 01. Start at A and accept only C. For input 0, every state moves to B because the new word ends in 0. For input 1, B moves to C because appending 1 to a trailing 0 creates 01. A and C move to A on 1: their new ending is 1, but not 01. Machine for strings ending in 01 State On 0 On 1 A B A B B C C B A Trace 1101: A→A→A→B→C, so accept. Trace 010: A→B→C→B, so reject. The latter contains 01 as an internal substring, but does not end in it. That difference is the reason the machine cannot stop as soon as it reaches C. Prove the state labels Claim. After reading any binary prefix w , the machine is in B exactly when w ends in 0, in C exactly when it ends in 01, and in A otherwise. The three descriptions are disjoint and exhaustive. For ε, neither ending condition holds, so A is correct. Assume the descriptions are correct for a prefix. Appending 0 always yields a word ending in 0, and every table entry on 0 leads to B. Appending 1 yields an ending 01 exactly when the former word ended in 0, which is exactly state B; hence B→C and both other states go to A. Induction proves the claim for all finite words. Since C is the only accepting state, the machine accepts exactly the language described by (0|1)*01. The proof gives one explicit correspondence between this expression and a DFA. It does not prove the full theorem that every theoretical regular expression has an equivalent finite automaton and vice versa. That theorem needs a general construction for union, concatenation and star, plus the reverse state-elimination construction. Those are outside this short lesson. Here we only need the concrete machine and its suffix invariant. One tempting two-state design remembers whether the most recent bit is 0. That tells you what to do when a 1 arrives, but it cannot distinguish a word that has just ended in 01 from an arbitrary word ending in 1 at the final check. In the three-state machine, C records this accepting condition, while B records the precursor that could make it true after one more bit. L = { w ∈ { 0 , 1 } * : w ends in 01 } Read beyond the first match 1. Trace 00101 and 00100. Which ends are accepted? Hint for question 1 Use the table symbol by symbol, especially after the first visit to C. Full solution to question 1 For 00101, states are A→B→B→C→B→C, so it is accepted. For 00100, the final two states after 0,0 are B,B, so it is rejected. The first word ends in 01; the second ends in 00. 2. A proposed machine accepts as soon as it ever visits C. Give a string it would accept incorrectly and explain the actual final state. Hint for question 2 Begin with 01 and add another symbol. Full solution to question 2 String 010 visits C after its first two symbols, but its final 0 moves C→B. It ends in 10, not 01, and must be rejected. Acceptance is decided after all input is read, not on an earlier visit to an accepting state. A pattern with a proof attached The expression (0|1)*01 and the three-state machine define the same particular set of finite strings. The table supplies a runnable object; the suffix invariant supplies a proof of its behavior. The example does not cover all regex syntax used in software or the full equivalence theorem. To revisit the basic DFA tuple and transition discipline, see finite automata .

title: A recursive algorithm's bill
summary: Splitting a task in half creates many smaller bills. Derive and solve a simple recurrence for merge-style division.
text: Many small bills add up A divide-and-conquer procedure splits a task into two equal subtasks, solves each, then performs a linear amount of combining work. It is tempting to say “the pieces get smaller, so the whole algorithm must be linear.” That ignores how many pieces there are. A recurrence records both the number of subproblems and the work performed at the current call. Background capsule. Let input size n be a positive power of two, so every split is exact until size one. Set T(1) =1 operation. For n ≥2, suppose a call makes two size- n /2 recursive calls and does exactly n additional operations. A recurrence is an equation linking T(n) to costs at smaller inputs. Log 2 n is the integer k such that n =2 k in this restricted setting. Open the recursion tree Worked example. For n =8, the root spends 8 combining operations. Its two children each handle size 4, spending 4+4=8. The four grandchildren each handle size 2, spending 2+2+2+2=8. Finally eight size-one leaves spend 1 each, another 8. Total cost is 32. Directly applying the recurrence agrees: T(2) =2·1+2=4, T(4) =2·4+4=12, and T(8) =2·12+8=32. There are log 2 n internal splitting levels and one leaf level. At each level, the number of calls doubles while the size at each call halves, so the total cost remains n . Thus the tree suggests n (log 2 n +1). A tree picture is useful, but we can prove the formula without assuming it from a few examples. Solve the recurrence on its domain Claim. If T(1) =1 and T(n) =2 T(n/2) + n for powers of two n ≥2, then T(n) = n (log 2 n +1). Prove by induction on k where n =2 k . At k =0, n =1 and the proposed value is 1·(0+1)=1. Assume it holds for n /2=2 k−1 . Then T(n) =2·[( n /2)(log 2 ( n /2)+1)]+ n = n (log 2 n −1+1)+ n = n (log 2 n +1). Every step uses a smaller size and the specified base case, so the derivation is complete for powers of two. This exact formula implies an O( n log n ) upper bound for n ≥2: log 2 n ≥1, so log 2 n +1≤2 log 2 n . Choose constant 2 and threshold 2. More strongly, the exact count is at least n log 2 n , so the order is tight on the stated domain. We have not analyzed arbitrary n with uneven splits; floor and ceiling terms require their own treatment. The base cost matters. If T(1) =0 while internal combine work remains n , the answer becomes n log 2 n . And if the procedure makes only one recursive call, the recurrence changes to T(n) = T(n/2) + n ; borrowing the two-branch answer would be wrong. A recurrence must describe the actual algorithm. T ( n ) = 2 T ( n / 2 ) + n Worked example: separating leaf work from combining work For size 16, the internal levels contain respectively 1, 2, 4, and 8 calls. Their individual sizes are 16, 8, 4, and 2. Multiplying within each level gives total combining costs 16, 16, 16, and 16, so internal work totals 64. The final level has sixteen size-one calls, each costing one, adding 16. Thus the complete total is 80. This accounts for the two terms in n log₂ n + n : internal work and leaf work. There are 31 calls altogether, but multiplying that count by 16 would charge every call the root's combining cost. Conversely, charging only one call per depth would omit most calls. The right ledger records both how many calls exist at a level and what each costs. These sizes are all powers of two, so no rounding convention is needed. Pay for each level 1. Compute T(16) from the formula and verify it using T(8) =32. Hint for question 1 Log 2 16=4, and the recurrence doubles the size-eight cost before adding 16. Full solution to question 1 The formula gives 16(4+1)=80. The recurrence gives 2·32+16=80. The agreement checks the calculation for this input; the induction establishes all powers of two. 2. With S(1) =1 and S(n) =S( n /2)+ n for powers of two, find S(8) and explain why the previous formula fails. Hint for question 2 Follow one chain of sizes 8,4,2,1. Full solution to question 2 S(8) =8+4+2+1=15. The previous formula would give 8(3+1)=32 because it counts two child calls at each split. This recurrence has only one child; its costs form a geometric sum along one path. Keep the model attached The recurrence expresses a precise accounting model: two equal recursive calls, linear combining work, and unit leaves. Its solution is exact for powers of two and supports a tight asymptotic claim there. Changing any of those assumptions changes the bill. Dynamic programming addresses a different source of waste: repeatedly recomputing the same subproblem.

title: Remembering subproblems
summary: A route puzzle repeats the same small question many times. Turn Fibonacci recurrence into memoized and bottom-up algorithms.
text: The same question keeps returning Computing a Fibonacci number by directly following its recurrence creates repeated calls. To find F 6 , both the F 5 and F 4 branches ask for F 4 or smaller values again. Dynamic programming replaces this repeated tree of work with a table of distinct subproblems. The method needs a valid recurrence and an order that makes dependencies available. Background capsule. Define F 0 =0, F 1 =1, and F n = F n−1 + F n−2 for n ≥2. An array is a finite indexed store. Memoization stores answers after a recursive calculation; bottom-up tabulation fills answers in dependency order. Both reuse results, but their control flow differs. We count additions in an ideal arithmetic model, not bit-level time for very large integers. Fill a small table once Worked example. To compute F 6 , write entries for indices 0 through 6. Begin [0,1]. The next entries are 1,2,3,5,8, each the sum of the previous two. The complete row is [0,1,1,2,3,5,8]. Exactly five additions were made, one for each index from 2 to 6. You can also retain only the last two values if the final answer is all you need. A memoized recursive version begins with the same base cases, checks whether an answer is already stored, and otherwise computes and saves it. On this input it may visit indices in a different order, but each distinct F i is calculated at most once. The dependency structure is a directed acyclic graph: arrows from F i to F i−1 and F i−2 point to smaller indices, so cycles cannot arise. Correctness and cost Claim. The bottom-up table computes the defined F n for each integer n ≥0 using max(0, n −1) additions. For n =0 or 1, return the stated base value with no addition. For larger n , initialize the first two cells correctly. Assume cells 0 through i −1 match the recurrence values. The assignment table[ i ]=table[ i −1]+table[ i −2] uses previously correct cells, so cell i is correct. Induction covers every filled cell, and the loop runs exactly once for each index 2,…, n . There are n −1 such indices, proving the addition count. The same reasoning shows termination: the loop index increases until it passes n , and the input is finite. Storing the whole table uses n +1 cells, while a rolling pair uses constant many cells. Neither “linear time” statement counts the increasing number of bits in large Fibonacci values. If additions of large integers are charged according to bit length, the bit-operation cost is greater; the unit-addition model should be named when quoting O( n ). Memoization is useful only when subproblems recur. If every recursive call has unique inputs, a cache adds bookkeeping without avoiding duplicate calculation.
