It can also be wrong to cache by too small a key. For a recurrence whose answer depends on both position and remaining budget, caching only by position can merge different questions and return incorrect results. The key must include every part of a subproblem's state that affects its answer. F n = F n − 1 + F n − 2 Worked example: updating a rolling pair safely After computing F₅, a rolling store may hold the pair (F₄,F₅) = (3,5). To advance, first calculate the sum 3 + 5 = 8, then replace the pair by (5,8). The invariant is that the stored pair consists of two consecutive Fibonacci values. The recurrence proves its preservation because the new second entry is the sum of the old two, while the new first is the old second. If we overwrite the first entry with 5 and then sum the two stored entries, we obtain 5 + 5 = 10, losing the old 3. An intermediate sum or a simultaneous assignment prevents that mistake. Constant storage is therefore a concrete implementation of the recurrence with a carefully stated state meaning. It saves cells when only the final value is wanted; it does not retain every earlier value for later lookup. Check the table and its key 1. Compute F 7 bottom-up and state the number of additions. Hint for question 1 Extend the row for F 6 by one sum. Full solution to question 1 The row becomes [0,1,1,2,3,5,8,13]. The new entry is 8+5=13. Indices 2 through 7 each needed one addition, so the total is six, equal to 7−1. 2. A route problem asks whether a destination can be reached from position i with b remaining fuel units. Why might memoizing only by i be wrong? Hint for question 2 Imagine arriving at the same position with zero fuel and with two units. Full solution to question 2 The two arrivals can have different future possibilities: from the same position a next edge costing one unit is impossible with b =0 and possible with b =2. A cache entry keyed only by i would reuse one answer for both states. Use the pair ( i , b ) as the subproblem key. Reuse with a precise state Dynamic programming works here because the recurrence reduces every question to smaller indexed questions, and each indexed answer is reused. The table proof covers correctness and the unit-addition count. It does not make every recursive problem cheap: some have exponentially many distinct states, and others need a richer key. The recurrence analysis in a recursive algorithm's bill shows how to count a split where the subproblems are distinct.

title: The program no checker can always judge
summary: Could one program always tell whether another will stop? Follow diagonal contradiction for the halting problem.
text: Could a checker foresee every stop? A program reviewer might wish for a perfect tool: provide any program and input, and it answers whether that run eventually stops. We can test a particular program for a long time, but “not stopped yet” never settles what happens later. The halting problem asks whether a single algorithm could always settle every case. The answer is no, under a standard model of programs that can encode and run other programs. Background capsule. A program is a finite description interpreted by a fixed universal computational model. It can receive a finite input, halt with an output, or continue forever. Its description can itself be encoded as input data. A decider is an algorithm that halts on every valid input and returns the correct yes/no answer. We will reason by contradiction: assume such a decider exists, build a program from it, and derive incompatible answers on one input. This argument concerns all encoded programs in the model, not whether a particular everyday script has an obvious stopping condition. Make the hypothetical checker precise Worked example. Suppose H(P,x) always halts and returns YES exactly when program P eventually halts on input x . Its answers are required to be correct even when P receives its own code. Define a new program D(y) : ask H(y,y) ; if the answer is YES, loop forever; if the answer is NO, halt immediately. The definition is a finite procedure if H exists. Its only potential endless behavior is the deliberately chosen loop. What D does with an alleged answer about self-run H(y,y) says D(y) does YES Loops forever NO Halts immediately This table describes D's code; it does not simulate an infinite run to completion. The critical input is D's own finite description. The ability to encode and pass program descriptions makes that substitution legal. The diagonal contradiction Theorem, scoped to the stated universal-program model. No total algorithm H correctly decides, for every encoded program P and input x, whether P halts on x. Assume H exists. Run D on its own description. If H(D,D)=YES, the definition of D makes D(D) loop forever, contradicting H's YES. If H(D,D)=NO, D(D) halts immediately, contradicting H's NO. H must return one of the two answers because it is total, and both lead to contradiction. Therefore the assumed H cannot exist. This is a complete contradiction argument given the machine-model assumptions that programs have finite encodings, can inspect encoded programs as data, and can implement the simple branch and loop used by D. A formal text can encode these operations in a Turing machine or equivalent universal language. We have not proved universality of a particular programming language here. The Church–Turing thesis is a separate claim connecting informal effective computation with a formal model; the diagonal theorem is a mathematical result within the chosen model. The theorem is about one algorithm that works for every program-input pair. It does not prevent useful analyzers from deciding special families. A loop that decrements a nonnegative counter until zero can be proved to terminate; a program that immediately prints and exits plainly halts. A checker may also answer “unknown” on hard cases, but then it is not the promised total yes/no decider. This distinction prevents the impossibility result from being mistaken for a claim that no termination proof is ever possible. For a concrete failed shortcut, suppose we run P for a million steps and label it nonhalting if it has not stopped. A program that waits a million and one steps before halting refutes that rule. Increasing the timeout merely moves the counterexample. This finite observation cannot certify nontermination for arbitrary code. H ( D , D ) = YES ⇒ D ( D ) loops Check both branches 1. Suppose an alleged H answers YES to H(D,D). State the exact contradiction without appealing to a simulation. Hint for question 1 Read the YES branch of D's definition and compare it with what YES is supposed to mean. Full solution to question 1 YES asserts that D eventually halts on input D. But D is defined to enter an endless loop whenever H answers YES on that self-input. Thus D(D) does not halt, so H's YES is incorrect. The contradiction comes from the definition, not from waiting for the loop to finish. 2. A program checker always halts and returns HALTS, LOOPS, or UNKNOWN. Does the theorem prohibit it? Explain with the scope of the theorem. Hint for question 2 Compare its possible outputs with a total correct yes/no decider. Full solution to question 2 No. The theorem rules out a checker that gives a correct HALTS or LOOPS answer for every pair. A checker that sometimes says UNKNOWN does not meet that promise. It may be useful if every definite answer is sound, but the diagonal proof forces an all-case yes/no promise to fail. A limit with a boundary The self-application construction defeats a universal halting decider because its output is designed to disagree with the checker on the diagonal input. It says nothing against proofs for specific programs or conservative tools with an unknown result. This is a logical impossibility theorem about computability, separate from the question of how quickly solvable problems can be handled. P versus NP asks one such efficiency question and remains open.

title: Checking and finding are different questions
summary: A completed crossword can be checked faster than it may be found. Define P and NP through decision problems and certificates; explain open status of P vs NP.
text: Checking a proposed answer Imagine a puzzle asking whether a set of stops admits a route under a distance limit. A proposed route may be easy to check, while finding one seems harder. That intuition motivates a formal question, but intuition alone cannot prove a gap. Complexity theory makes “easy” mean polynomial time in the length of a finite input, and “check” mean a deterministic algorithm verifies a short certificate. P versus NP asks whether every such efficiently checkable decision problem is also efficiently solvable. Background capsule. A decision problem has a YES or NO answer for each encoded input string x . Input size is the bit length | x |, not a hidden numeric parameter that might require many bits to write. A polynomial bound is at most C | x | k for fixed constants C , k at sufficiently large sizes. A certificate c is a finite string supplied with a YES instance. The verifier must check it in polynomial time and certificates must have polynomially bounded length. A concrete certificate Worked example. For a finite undirected graph and two specified vertices, the decision question “is there a path with at most three edges?” has a short certificate: a list of up to four vertices from start to finish. A verifier checks that the listed endpoints are correct, each consecutive pair is an edge, and at most three edges are used. This shows how a witness can be checked. It does not show that the problem is hard to solve; in fact breadth-first search can decide this particular question efficiently without being handed a path. The route example illustrates the difference between a witness and a solver without proving those tasks require different complexity. For a YES instance, a valid witness must exist. For a NO instance, the verifier must reject every alleged witness within the allowed length. A verifier that accepts a false route is not correct, even if most sample routes are checked accurately. Definitions, inclusion, and an open boundary Definitions. P is the class of decision problems solvable by a deterministic algorithm in polynomial time. NP is the class of decision problems for which a deterministic polynomial-time verifier V(x,c) and a polynomial bound on | c | exist such that x is a YES instance exactly when some certificate c makes V accept. Equivalent nondeterministic-machine language is common, but the certificate definition is enough here. NP does not mean “not polynomial.” Theorem. P⊆NP. If a problem has a deterministic polynomial-time solver A, define V(x,c) to ignore c and run A(x). Choose the empty string as the certificate for every YES instance. For a NO instance, A rejects, so no certificate can make V accept. The verifier's runtime is A's polynomial runtime plus negligible certificate handling, and the empty certificate has length zero. This proves the inclusion from the definitions. The proof does not require finding a nontrivial witness. Whether P=NP is open. The inclusion just proved does not tell us if it is strict. Many important problems are known to be NP-complete: if any one of them has a polynomial-time algorithm, every problem in NP does. Establishing that statement for a named problem requires explicit reductions and completeness proofs; none is supplied here, so no hardness conclusion is drawn from the route example. Also, a worst-case polynomial bound does not promise that a practical implementation is fast, and an exponential worst case does not say every input is difficult. A common invalid argument is “I cannot see a fast way to solve this puzzle, therefore it is outside P.” Failure to find an algorithm is not a lower-bound proof. Another is “I verified one candidate quickly, therefore the problem is in NP.” Membership requires one polynomial verifier and polynomial certificate bound that work for every encoded input, with correctness in both YES and NO cases. The proof of P⊆NP meets that standard by construction. P ⊆ NP ; P = ? NP Use the definitions exactly 1. Suppose A decides a problem in at most 5| x | 3 +2 steps. Construct the certificate verifier used in the inclusion proof and state its bound. Hint for question 1 The verifier need not use a certificate if it can already decide the answer. Full solution to question 1 Let V(x,c) run A(x) and return its YES or NO answer, ignoring c. Use ε as the certificate for each YES input. Its length is zero. Apart from fixed overhead, V takes at most 5| x | 3 +2 steps, a polynomial bound. For NO inputs A rejects for every c, as required. 2. Someone says NP means “not polynomial,” so P and NP cannot overlap. Identify the error and use one explicit decision problem to refute it. Hint for question 2 Recall the empty-certificate construction; choose an easy input property. Full solution to question 2 NP means nondeterministic polynomial time or, equivalently here, polynomially verifiable YES certificates. The problem “does a binary string contain a 1?” is in P by a left-to-right scan of at most | x | bits. By the inclusion proof it is also in NP, using the empty certificate and the scan as verifier. Thus P and NP overlap; indeed P⊆NP. What remains unsettled Formal definitions make the easy inclusion P⊆NP provable. They do not settle whether the two classes coincide. A quickly checked example is not a proof that finding is intrinsically slower, and a timeout experiment cannot prove a lower bound. The scope here is decision problems over finite encodings with polynomial resource bounds; richer questions such as approximation, randomized algorithms, and reductions need their own lessons. The mathematical open question remains P=?NP.

title: Bayes with two bags of marbles
summary: Count red draws from two bags to update a hidden bag choice, including the impossible-evidence case.
text: A red marble is a clue. Which bag was used? Imagine a craft table with two bags. Bag A contains mostly red marbles; bag B contains mostly blue ones. A friend chooses one bag out of sight, draws one marble, and shows you red. You want to know the chance that the hidden bag was A. The tempting answer is “the fraction of red marbles in A.” That answers a different question: how likely red would be if A had already been chosen. Background capsule. A probability is a number from 0 to 1. The notation P(A) means the chance of event A before a new clue. P(R | A), read “probability of red given A,” means that we consider only draws made from A. A conditional probability changes the denominator. Multiplying P(A) by P(R | A) gives the chance of both A and red. We need only fractions and this rule. Suppose A is chosen 30% of the time and B 70%. Within A, 80% of marbles are red; within B, 20% are red. The bag frequencies are stipulated parts of this toy experiment, not guesses about an unknown real-world process. After seeing red, should A become more likely than B? Count a hundred possible plays Worked example. Picture 100 repetitions of the same rule. We expect 30 choices of A and 70 of B. Of the 30 A plays, 80%—or 24—show red. Of the 70 B plays, 20%—or 14—show red. These are natural frequencies : small whole-number groups that make the changing denominator visible. A hundred gives whole counts here, but the argument works for any probabilities. Expected counts in 100 plays of the stipulated bag experiment Hidden bag All plays Red shown Not red A 30 24 6 B 70 14 56 Total 100 38 62 Once red is shown, all 62 non-red plays are irrelevant to this question. Among the 38 red plays, 24 came from A. Thus P(A | R) = 24/38 = 12/19, about 63.2%. The clue has raised A from 30% to about 63%, because red is four times as likely under A as under B. Yet red does not make A certain: 14 of the red plays still came from B. The optional lab changes A’s prior from 1% to 99% and each red chance from 0% to 100%. At 30%, 80%, and 20%, its proportions match the table; its 10,000-case counts are 100 times as large. The table suffices. Why the fraction works Let R mean “the shown marble is red.” The bags are mutually exclusive and exhaustive: exactly one of A and B was chosen. The red outcomes therefore split into two groups, red from A and red from B. This gives an exact identity under the stated probability model: P ( A | R ) = P ( R | A ) P ( A ) P ( R | A ) P ( A ) + P ( R | B ) P ( B ) In our example the numerator is 0.8 × 0.3 = 0.24 and the denominator is 0.24 + 0.2 × 0.7 = 0.38. Dividing yields 0.24/0.38 = 12/19. The numerator represents red and A; the denominator represents every route to red. This follows from P(A | R) = P(A and R)/P(R). Hypothesis and boundary. The formula needs P(R) > 0. If both bags have a 0% chance of red, red cannot occur under this model and P(A | R) is undefined: it is a zero denominator, not 0% or 50%. If only A has 0% red and B can show red, seeing red rules out A, provided B had a positive prior chance. The lab should say “undefined under these settings” for an impossible red observation. These are expected proportions. Finite simulated draws fluctuate; the algebraic identity remains exact under its assumptions. Try the update yourself 1. Calculation. A is chosen on 20 of 100 plays and B on 80. Red occurs on half of A plays and one quarter of B plays. After red, what fraction of plays came from A? Hint for question 1 Count red plays separately for A and B before forming the new denominator. Full solution to question 1 A contributes 20 × 1/2 = 10 red plays. B contributes 80 × 1/4 = 20. Of 30 red plays, 10 came from A, so P(A | R) = 10/30 = 1/3. The answer is greater than the 1/5 prior but less than one half because B was chosen much more often. 2. Explanation and edge case. Both bags contain no red marbles. A friend nevertheless reports a red draw. What does the formula return? Is it legitimate to replace the answer with 50%? Hint for question 2 Find the chance of red by adding the red contributions of both bags. Full solution to question 2 Both contributions are zero, so P(R) = 0 and the formula has denominator zero. P(A | R) is undefined under the model. Assigning 50% would silently introduce a new rule, such as an unreliable report or another bag. To analyse that new situation, specify it first. Stop with the new denominator Bayes’ rule asks, “Of all ways this clue could appear, what share came from the hypothesis of interest?” For our bags, the answer is 24 out of 38 red plays. The prior bag choice matters as much as the color composition: even a strong clue can have a modest effect when its favored bag was rare to begin with. The word odds is another convenient form—posterior odds equal prior odds multiplied by a likelihood ratio—but the count table already contains the full reasoning. For a next idea, change the prior while keeping the bags fixed and ask when a red clue fails to make A more likely than B. For reference, Penn State’s open lessons on conditional probability and Bayes’ theorem give the general definitions. This original bag example remains a finite, stipulated model; it does not establish how to choose probabilities in a real investigation.

title: When every subgroup wins but the total loses
summary: Change a fictional puzzle club’s board allocations, prove the exact reversal threshold, and separate a common-mix comparison from a causal claim.
text: How can the better route finish worse overall? A puzzle club records whether members finish a practice board within ten minutes. Members can use Route A or Route B, two ways of approaching a puzzle. The club also labels boards easy or hard. In the fictional record below, A has a higher finish rate than B among easy boards and among hard boards. Yet B has a much higher finish rate when all boards are pooled. Which comparison has changed? Background capsule. A rate is a count divided by its relevant total. “9 of 10” is 90%; “72 of 90” is 80%. A weighted average combines subgroup rates according to how much of the total each subgroup contributes. Here each route has its own mix of easy and hard boards. We need only fractions and ordinary averages, but we must keep each denominator beside its numerator. These invented data reveal a mathematical effect. Read four groups before the totals Worked example. Route A was used on 10 easy boards and 90 hard ones. Route B was used on 90 easy boards and 10 hard ones. Each route was therefore tried 100 times, but on very different collections of boards. Fictional puzzle finishes; each rate is finished divided by attempted in that cell Board difficulty Route A finished/attempted Route A rate Route B finished/attempted Route B rate Easy 9/10 90% 72/90 80% Hard 36/90 40% 3/10 30% Both pooled 45/100 45% 75/100 75% Check each total independently: A has 9 + 36 = 45 finishes in 10 + 90 = 100 attempts. B has 72 + 3 = 75 finishes in 90 + 10 = 100 attempts. Within each difficulty, A exceeds B by ten percentage points. The pooled comparison goes the other way by thirty percentage points. The pooled row has not “corrected” the two difficulty rows; it asks a different descriptive question about two different mixtures. Try reading the table without the difficulty labels. You might say B did better, 75% versus 45%, and that statement accurately describes these 200 attempts. But it hides that B received far more easy boards. The difficulty labels reveal why that total cannot, on its own, compare how the routes perform on equally difficult boards. Move only the mixture weights Before using the controls, predict how much extra easy-board work B needs to cancel A’s within-group advantage. Would any unequal mix suffice? Would a twenty-percentage-point difference suffice? Keep the four subgroup rates fixed while testing your prediction. The activity is a separate hypothetical model with 1,000 attempts per route, so every permitted setting has integer finish counts. Its initial setting scales the original table by ten. These are constructed counts, with no sampling noise or new evidence about actual puzzle solvers. The weights turn the comparison around For a route with easy-board share w , its pooled finish rate is an exact weighted average of its easy and hard rates: r pooled = w easy r easy + w hard r hard , w easy + w hard = 1 Route A’s weights are 10/100 = 0.10 easy and 90/100 = 0.90 hard. Its rate is 0.10 × 0.90 + 0.90 × 0.40 = 0.09 + 0.36 = 0.45. Route B’s weights are 0.90 easy and 0.10 hard. Its rate is 0.90 × 0.80 + 0.10 × 0.30 = 0.72 + 0.03 = 0.75. The formulas reproduce the counts exactly. Each route’s overall number is pulled toward the difficulty category it encountered most often. For a descriptive like-for-like comparison, suppose we used the same hypothetical mix for both routes: half easy and half hard. A’s standardized rate would be 0.5 × 90% + 0.5 × 40% = 65%; B’s would be 0.5 × 80% + 0.5 × 30% = 55%. This is an arithmetic reweighting, not an observed result for a new set of boards. It makes clear which comparison the rates answer. This reversal is called Simpson’s paradox. The “paradox” is a warning about aggregation, not a contradiction in arithmetic. Its exact mechanism here is unequal mixture weights. If both routes had the same difficulty weights, A’s ten-point advantage in each difficulty would remain a ten-point advantage in their weighted averages. Whether Route A causes better performance is another question: participants may have chosen routes based on experience, and “easy” versus “hard” may omit other differences. The table cannot settle those issues. Find the exact boundary, beyond the slider Write u for A’s easy-board fraction and v for B’s; both lie in [0,1]. The pooled rates are A(u) = 0.9u + 0.4(1−u) = 0.4 + 0.5u and B(v) = 0.8v + 0.3(1−v) = 0.3 + 0.5v. Subtracting gives A(u)−B(v) = 0.1 − 0.5(v−u). Thus B leads precisely when v−u > 0.2. At v−u = 0.2 they tie; for a smaller difference A leads. Unequal weights alone do not guarantee reversal. For example, with u = 0.1, v = 0.29 gives A = 45% and B = 44.5%; v = 0.30 gives a 45% tie; v = 0.31 gives A = 45% and B = 45.5%. The strict inequality decides the boundary without numerical rounding. The derivation covers every real u and v in [0,1], including fractions unavailable on the integer-percent controls. Why a common mix preserves an advantage. Let q be any common easy-board fraction. The standardized difference is q(0.9−0.8) + (1−q)(0.4−0.3) = 0.1. More generally, for any finite set of groups, common weights w g ≥ 0 summing to 1 give difference ∑ g w g (a g −b g ). If every subgroup difference is nonnegative, the sum is nonnegative. It is strictly positive if at least one strictly positive difference receives positive weight. This is a proof from nonnegative terms; checking many slider settings would not establish the general statement. Optional deeper investigation: the same table can hide opposite causal effects (about 15–25 minutes) State a different question before answering it Return to the original 200 attempts , rather than the 2,000-attempt slider model. For this investigation, stipulate that these were 200 different people, each facing one fixed board. Route A and Route B are well-defined instructions; one person’s route does not change another’s outcome. Let Y i (A) be 1 if person i would finish their fixed board using A, otherwise 0. Define Y i (B) similarly. Their recorded outcome equals the potential outcome for the route actually used. This is a hypothetical two-outcome model, not a claim that the original record measured both outcomes. The causal quantity we want is the average of Y i (A)−Y i (B) over these same 200 people : the finish fraction if everyone used A minus the finish fraction if everyone used B. This compares two assignments to one cohort. The observed 45% minus 75% instead compares two different groups of 100 people. For the 100 A users we know 45 values Y(A)=1 and 55 values Y(A)=0, but none of their Y(B) values. For the 100 B users we know 75 values Y(B)=1 and 25 values Y(B)=0, but none of their Y(A) values. Difficulty labels retain exactly their original values. Ask whether those missing outcomes can be filled in two ways that preserve every observed cell but change the causal answer’s sign. Construct two compatible completions Fill only the outcome under the unused route; the original observations stay fixed Completion Missing outcomes for A users Missing outcomes for B users A favorable Set every Y(B) to 0 Set every Y(A) to 1 A unfavorable Set every Y(B) to 1 Set every Y(A) to 0 In the first completion, assigning everyone A gives 45 + 100 = 145 finishes, while assigning everyone B gives 0 + 75 = 75. The average causal effect is (145−75)/200 = 7/20 = +0.35 . In the second, the corresponding totals are 45 + 0 = 45 and 100 + 75 = 175, giving (45−175)/200 = −13/20 = −0.65 . Neither construction changes which people actually used which route, their difficulty labels, or their observed successes. This proves the original table, even with its difficulty rows, does not determine the causal effect’s sign under this setup. The two completions are logical possibilities, not equally plausible explanations or estimated probabilities. The standardized descriptive difference of +0.10 is still correct in both; it uses the same observed conditional rates and common weights. Say exactly what the missing information permits Let x count the missing A outcomes equal to 1 among B users, and z the missing B outcomes equal to 1 among A users. Each is an integer from 0 to 100. Then the causal effect is (45+x−75−z)/200 = (x−z−30)/200. It lies between −0.65 and +0.35, and both endpoints are attained by the completions above. All 201 values in steps of 1/200 between those endpoints can occur. These are exact bounds for this fixed fictional cohort with unrestricted missing binary outcomes; they are not confidence limits or a result about a larger sampled population. To estimate a causal effect from future observations, the club needs a justified design and assumptions. Randomly assigning routes within difficulty before play would make a future experiment informative about effects; finite randomization still has uncertainty. An observational adjustment would require comparable potential outcomes within the chosen groups, positive chance of each route, and the consistency setup above. A two-way table alone cannot certify those assumptions. Nor should one automatically adjust for every recorded variable: a variable changed by the route can answer a different question. This lesson establishes the arithmetic and its identification boundary; it does not develop a full causal-inference method. The potential-outcome definition follows Larry Wasserman’s causal-inference notes, sections 2–2.1 . The general bounded-outcome argument is treated in Richardson, Hudgens, Gilbert and Fine, section 2.1 . Their population/sampling setting differs from our finite-cohort construction; the counts and proof here are derived for this fictional table. Work with the denominators 1. Calculation. Using the same four subgroup rates, imagine a common mix of 20% easy and 80% hard boards for both routes. Calculate each standardized rate. Which route is higher? Hint for question 1 Multiply each easy rate by 0.2 and each hard rate by 0.8, then add within a route. Full solution to question 1 A: 0.2 × 0.90 + 0.8 × 0.40 = 0.18 + 0.32 = 0.50, or 50%. B: 0.2 × 0.80 + 0.8 × 0.30 = 0.16 + 0.24 = 0.40, or 40%. A is higher by ten percentage points. These are standardized calculations, not new observed counts. 2. Explanation and counterexample. A friend says, “If A is better in every difficulty group, B cannot possibly have the better overall rate.” Which numbers in the table disprove the claim, and what differs between the routes? Hint for question 2 Compare both within-group rows, then count the easy-board attempts for A and B. Full solution to question 2 A leads 90% to 80% on easy boards and 40% to 30% on hard boards, but B leads 75% to 45% overall. A had only 10 easy attempts and 90 hard attempts; B had 90 easy and 10 hard. The different weights allow the pooled reversal. The numbers describe these attempts and do not establish which route caused more finishes. 3. A changed problem, before using the hint. New preset rates are A: 85% easy, 50% hard; B: 75% easy, 30% hard. A’s easy fraction is u = 1/5. Find the exact range of B’s easy fraction v giving a pooled reversal. Test v = 7/10. Does the earlier “twenty extra percentage points” rule still apply? Finally, show whether a common easy fraction q can reverse these new within-group comparisons. Hint for question 3 Start again from the two weighted averages. This time the easy-to-hard rate gaps differ between routes; do not reuse the old difference formula. Full solution to question 3 A(u) = 1/2 + 7u/20 and B(v) = 3/10 + 9v/20. Hence B > A exactly when 9v−7u > 4. At u = 1/5, this is v > 3/5. For v = 7/10, A = 57/100 and B = 123/200, so B leads by 9/200 = 4.5 percentage points. The threshold depends on the rates: here B needs more than forty extra easy-board percentage points when A has 20% easy. A common mix gives A(q)−B(q) = 1/5−q/10, between 1/10 and 1/5 for 0 ≤ q ≤ 1, always positive. 4. Find a missing hypothesis. Another table has A rates 80% easy and 30% hard, B rates 70% easy and 40% hard. With a common mix q easy, find when A leads, ties or loses. Why does this not contradict the common-weight proof? Hint for question 4 Compare 0.1q with 0.1(1−q). Second hint for question 4 Write the common-weight difference as q times the easy-group rate difference plus (1−q) times the hard-group rate difference. Then check the sign and the hypothesis about both within-group differences. Full solution to question 4 The difference is q(0.8−0.7)+(1−q)(0.3−0.4)=0.2q−0.1. A leads for q > 1/2, ties at q = 1/2 and loses for q < 1/2. The proof required nonnegative differences in every group; A loses on hard boards here, so that hypothesis fails. 5. Optional causal transfer. In a new fixed cohort of 80 people, 40 used A with 28 finishes, and 40 used B with 16 finishes. Use binary potential outcomes as above. Find the smallest and largest possible causal effects if the unused-route outcomes are unrestricted. The observed difference is positive; can the causal effect be negative? Hint for question 5 Let x be missing A finishes among B users and z be missing B finishes among A users; each lies between 0 and 40. Keep the denominator 80. Full solution to question 5 The effect is (28+x−16−z)/80 = (12+x−z)/80. It is smallest at x=0,z=40: −28/80 = −0.35, and largest at x=40,z=0: 52/80 = +0.65. Both preserve all observed data. Thus even the observed +0.30 comparison does not fix the sign of the same-cohort causal effect. These are fixed-cohort logical bounds, with possible values in steps of 1/80; they do not quantify sampling uncertainty. Keep the question attached to the rate A pooled rate describes the mix that actually occurred. A subgroup rate describes a restricted set. Before comparing routes, ask which mix matters and whether the groups are comparable. Equalizing the weights can expose the source of a reversal, but it cannot remove every source of bias. You can stop here with a complete explanation: the numerator counts finishes, the denominator counts attempts, and unequal difficulty weights produce the reversal. For another view, Penn State’s open lessons on categorical relationships and Simpson’s paradox in tables explain the general phenomenon. Their examples are separate from this invented puzzle-club record. A next exploration would ask how to assign routes fairly if the club wanted a causal comparison; this descriptive table alone does not answer it.
